title: The Guardian climate pledge 2026  | Environment | The Guardian
description: Each year, the Guardian reaffirms its commitment to the environment – both in our reporting and how we operate as a business. From critical tipping points to war in Iran, this is how the last 12 months have looked
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Each year, the Guardian reaffirms its commitment to the environment – both in our reporting and how we operate as a business. From critical tipping points to war in Iran, this is how the last 12 months have looked
Content: Composite: The GuardianView image in fullscreenComposite: The GuardianInside the GuardianEnvironmentThe Guardian climate pledge 2026Each year, the Guardian reaffirms its commitment to the environment – both in our reporting and how we operate as a business. From critical tipping points to war in Iran, this is how the last 12 months have lookedSupport the Guardian’s environment coverageThe Guardian climate forum 2026Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTShareToday marks the end of the Guardian’s annual climate support campaign. Each year, during the campaign, we remind our audience about the Guardian’s role in covering the threats to our planet and the importance of independent journalism in telling that story. Our climate pledge is a reminder of the environmental values we place at the heart of our reporting and our organisation.Since our2025 climate pledge, the world has experienced extreme levels of heat as well as extreme forms of denial and abdication in the face of the climate crisis. But, across the world, there have also been inspiring efforts to tackle it.This update reflects how the Guardian has remained steadfast in exposing those who have tried to block or reverse the transition to a clean energy world, as well as highlighting the efforts of those who have been bravely confronting the greatest challenge of our time.In the past three weeks, more than 30,000 Guardian readers have supported our backed our annual climate support campaign. If you believe in the power of independent journalism, please considerjoining them today.1. We will continue our longstanding record of powerful, independent environmental reportingThe Guardian’s commitment to agenda-setting climate journalism has become even more crucial this year asother news outlets have scaled backtheir own climate coverage. While the news cycle continues to be dominated by conflict, division and the abuses of autocrats, we have worked tirelessly to keep the health of the planet firmly on the public agenda.We have highlighted how the climate emergency has pitted theinterests of billionairesagainst the wellbeing of billions of ordinary people. For example, our journalists have been reporting extensively on theenvironmental impact of the AI revolution, revealing how the race to build giant datacentres has been driving upbig tech’s carbon emissions– as well as how US tech giants lobbied the EU tohide the environmental tollof their datacentres.The Guardian has also examined how the oil crisis triggered by the war on Iran has helped a coalition of business interests, rightwing populists and media outlets toramp up their attacks on net zero goals. We revealed that major oil companiesmade £93bn in profitsin three months following the start of the conflict.As the climate emergency has increasingly become part of theculture wars, we have countered dangerous andwidespread disinformation– from myths about thecost of clean energyto itsimpact on jobsandthe economy. We have also highlighted how the transition to green energy canmake countries more resilient.The Guardian’s independence from corporate interests means we have been able to speak truthfully and plainly while the statements from climate scepticshave become ever more contorted. While the northern hemisphere has been scorched this summer by themost severe and widespread heatwaveon record, some of those who have long denied the crisis have suggested we nowembrace the devastation. Guardian journalists have reported on how the world’s most powerful climate denier, Donald Trump, has continued reneging on the US’s international climate commitments andundermining federal climate regulations. We have examined how the US president has been pouring taxpayer money into hiscrusade against clean energyand also into boosting coal.If it feels as if tackling the climate crisis has been eclipsed by climate culture wars, disinformation and toxic discourse, our journalists have continued to shine a light on the remarkable progress being made in some places and the possibility for positive change. For instance, we have looked at countries, such as Spain, that have embraced renewables and arebenefiting from lower utility prices. We have reported on how Australia haspioneered a revolution in home renewablesand battery use, providing inspiration for the rest of the world. And we captured people’s imaginations about what is possible by covering how Paris is building agigantic cooling machine using river waterfrom the Seine. As some countries forge ahead with the transition to a clean energy world while those in hock to fossil fuels try to turn back the clock, we have also examined the implications for the shiftinggeopolitical balance of power.2. We will report on how climate breakdown is already affectingthe natural world, people and other species, as well as what to do about itOur daily reporting on climate impacts and extreme weather events has drawn on the Guardian’s network of correspondents around the world and our genuinely global outlook.We have reported on the toll the warming climate is having ongig workers in India, as well as how the closure of schools across the country meansworking mothers have been bearing the bruntof the climate crisis, either forced to stay at home or switch jobs.With Europe heating uptwice as fast as other continents, Guardianreporters spoke to localsand tourists about their experiences of this year’s heatwaves. We also reported on the experiences of those on the frontline tackling the effects of extreme heat,speaking to firefightersabout how the scale of this year’s wildfires has forced them to make incredibly difficult choices. Our reporters also highlighted the impact on other people providing essential services in dangerous levels of heat, such asnurses, teachers and bus drivers.As wildfires raged across Europe and North America, another impact of climate breakdown has been the unprecedented rains in other parts of the world. We reported on the extreme flooding and typhoons across Asia,from Taiwan to Afghanistan. We reported on how floods in Nigeria have been inducing“climate anxiety” that can trap people in a sense of anticipation and dread, and we explained how thefloods across west Africahave been supercharged by global heating, displacing thousands of people.We have continued to remind our audience how the poorest suffer most from the climate catastrophe – while rightwing populists continue to claim that action on climate is merely an elite concern.Guardian journalists have also highlighted the consequences for the natural environment, for example travelling 100 miles along the Danube to witness howdrought has devastated the EU’s longest river.Our coverage of the natural world and precious wildlife has highlighted howother specieswe share this planet with have also experienced the catastrophic consequences of the year’s extreme weather.Given such far-reaching impacts of the climate emergency, Guardian journalists have written about how amore just and equitable world is possible, for instance by amplifying a new report by Thomas Piketty and others at the World Inequality Lab, as well as the work of influential economists and social thinkers such asMariana Mazzucato.Meanwhile, our ongoingThe Alternativesseries has highlighted the practical work being undertaken by local communities and political parties coming up with low-carbon ways of living.And we looked at how communities are developing ways to prepare for the effects of climate change, such as aColombian neighbourhoodthat has been adopting tree nurseries and rainwater harvesting.By encompassing these practical initiatives and everyday human stories alongside the macro perspectives and analysis of geopolitical shifts, our climate coverage has sought to inspire people by showing what is possible at both a global and local level.3. We will publish up-to-date global indicators that point to the urgency of the situationAs climate records continue to be broken, we reported on new data that illustrates how planetary conditions are changing rapidly.This year we have closely monitored the scale and impact of the devastatingback-to-back summer heatwavesin the northern hemisphere – including in Europe, where such extreme weather would have beenimpossible without the climate crisis, and in the US, which saw itshottest-ever monthin July.We are closely tracking and explaining the impact of the fast-developingEl Niño eventtoo,, forecast to be the biggest in a century and which is already intensifyinga spike in ocean temperatures. Our reporting has also highlighted critical changes linked to climate breakdown, includingocean currents,Arctic ice levels,Antarctic temperaturesandthe Earth’s energy balance, alongside other important tipping points such as the loss of permafrost.4. The Guardian will eliminate two-thirds of its emissions by 2030 and reduce our impact on natureSince 2020, our company’s greenhouse gas emissionshave reduced by 48%, meaning we remain well positioned to achieve our target of a 67% reduction by 2030. Our emissions decreased by 9% during the 2024/2025 reporting period, and we are continuing to make headway in reducing the footprint of our print operations, which still represent the largest share of our overall emissions (64%).Lowering our emissions remains a key priority, and our progress over the last year will be included in our sustainability report published in the autumn.5. We will seek to decouple our business and finances from fossilfuel-extractive companiesThe Guardian has refused advertising from all fossil fuel-extractive companies since January 2020.The Guardian is supported by the Scott Trust and the returns from its endowment fund. The fund’s environmental strategy is focused on contributing to a reduction of emissions in the real world and to protecting nature and biodiversity. The fund has made significant investments supporting the transition to a net zero economy and environmental solutions, with around £150m invested in areas ranging from renewable energy to decreasing emissions in manufacturing and industrial processes. Additionally, the fund has made a commitment to invest at least 3% of its value in natural capital and biodiversity solutions.6. We will be transparent with our progressWe believe transparency is the key to tackling the climate crisis. By sharing our data, our successes and our challenges, we can be part of the global movement to make businesses accountable for their climate and nature impacts. As part of this commitment, we continue to hold ourselves accountable to B Corporation standards, which recognises companies who meet the highest levels of environmental and social performance and public transparency.We will be publishing our annual company emissions data in the autumn, explaining what drives our emissions and where they have risen and fallen.We have started the process of estimating our emissions from generative AI usage. We hope to report on this next year.We have undertaken our B Corp recertification in line with the new standards introduced by B Lab in 2026. We will find out our result later this year.We have participated in advertising industry working groups that published a methodological framework that aims to capture the emissions impact of digital and print advertising.We open ourselves up to scrutiny by independent third parties, such as theScience Based Targets initiative(SBTi) and B Corp, so they can assess the robustness of our targets and our internal policies.On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carringtonand our panel of experts – includingProfAndy Haines,Katie White MP,Asad Rehman,Shruti Suresh,Gareth ThomasandAmy Fairman– for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. Book ticketshereor atguardian.live

title: The Rainmaker review – please don’t hurt your eyes trying to find anything good in this legal drama | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: From dialogue so hokey it could be printed on a tea towel to mind-numbing storylines – how can a glossy take on John Grisham’s novel about a fiery law graduate be so tedious?
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: From dialogue so hokey it could be printed on a tea towel to mind-numbing storylines – how can a glossy take on John Grisham’s novel about a fiery law graduate be so tedious?
Content: ‘Ah just wanna be a lawyer’ … Lana Parrilla and Milo Callaghan in The Rainmaker.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Ah just wanna be a lawyer’ … Lana Parrilla and Milo Callaghan in The Rainmaker.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewThe Rainmaker review – please don’t hurt your eyes trying to find anything good in this legal dramaFrom dialogue so hokey it could be printed on a tea towel to mind-numbing storylines – how can a glossy take on John Grisham’s novel about a fiery law graduate be so tedious?Sarah DempsterFri 28 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Rainmaker was once merely an average film about lawyers starring Matt Damon. Now, thanks to the magic of television, it’s a below-average series about lawyers starring a man who looks like Matt Damon. This is one Milo Callaghan, whose jawline suggests a certain mettle, but whose acting suggests much woe. Or at least a fitful unease with the role in which he finds himself. Accordingly, he drifts around this 10-partJohn Grishamadaptation with the air of a man who has forgotten what he came into the courtroom for, certain only that whatever it was, it was not a drama that compels him to say things like: “Ah just wanna be a lawyer.”Callaghan plays Rudy Baylor, an ambitious South Carolina law graduate with a social conscience and a thirst for justice. Rudy wants to make a difference but dammit if his fiery temper don’t keep conspirin’ to screw up his plans. The huffing greenhorn is even late for his first day at prestigious law firm Tinley Britt, having spent the morning hurling his mom’s lunkish boyfriend around the garden (“You think ah’m gonna let you keep leechin’ off ma mother?Gnyaaarrr!”).Insouciant new boss Leo F Drummond (Mad Men’s John Slattery) promptly fires the sod. “I am the punishment of God,” he drawls, gliding around the boardroom like a shaved eagle on castors. “If you had not committed great sins, God would not have sent a punishment like me upon you.” A smirk. “Genghis Khan. Warrior. Would’ve made a great litigator.”View image in fullscreenThe Genghis Khan of South Carolina … John Slattery with Madison Iseman in The Rainmaker.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyAlas, this is the sort of programme that equates tea-towel quotations with gravitas, and we must endure several more such guffstorms as the series progresses. (Or rather, as the series goes on. “Progresses” feels too optimistic a term for a drama that features the line, “This kid’s got balls.”)Unlike the 1995 novel from which it takes (some of) its characters and (fewer of) its themes, The Rainmaker is a startlingly uncomplicated affair. This is not the type of legal drama in which characters harbour tortuous secrets and plots contort themselves into unexpected shapes. This is not The Good Fight, or Suits, or Damages, or even Boston Legal, the sporadically magnificent mid-00s comedy-drama in which an empurpled William Shatner puffed and rumbled like the world’s cheeriest internal organ. Instead, it’s a straightforwardly soapy affair, a glossy show-and-tell in which linear storytelling is soundtracked by incessant MOR country-rock and characters are introduced with lines such as: “You’re Wilfred Keeley, CEO of Great Benefit Hospital Systems, one of Tinley Britt’s most important clients!”The plot? If we must. Having been booted out of Tinley Britt, Baylor washes up at a one-horse personal injury firm operating out of an abandoned taco joint. Here he finds sassy maverick Joceyln “Bruiser” Stone (Lana Parrilla), who does her bit for feminism by hoisting her bosom nostrilwards and refusing to pay Baylor a living wage. His first case? An unlawful death suit that will offer the hothead a chance to subject The Man to the full force of his pleated chinos. Unfortunately, it will also pit him against both his former boss and his lawyer girlfriend (“What happens when Leo finds out my boyfriend is suing his prize client?!”) – but them’s the judicial breaks, kid. And so forth.It’s peculiar, in this day and age, to find a series so wilfully devoid of depth, authenticity and nuance. So much so that you may find yourself initially denying The Rainmaker’s pounding simplicity, assuming that if you squint for long enough, interesting things will start to appear, emerging as if from a magic eye picture composed solely of gavels and shouting. But no. It’s tedious. Baylor’s boohoo backstory is revealed in the first few minutes (his brother died before he could fulfil his dream of bein’ a lawyer) and everything from motivation to the identity of the baddies is spelled out in 800pt HOPE YOU’RE GETTING ALL THIS AT THE BACK typeface.Will Baylor stop punchin’ and start litigatin’? And thus, in turn, start livin’? The answer is yawnin’ in the wind.The Rainmaker is available on ITVX in the UK, Peacock in the US and Stan in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewJohn GrishamThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: An $18bn settlement – and Zuckerberg barely blinked. The tech titans must be stripped of their power, and soon | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: Those who said Meta harms children struck a blow, but the ability of big tech to gouge profits and cause harm is barely diminished. That’s the battle to come, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: Those who said Meta harms children struck a blow, but the ability of big tech to gouge profits and cause harm is barely diminished. That’s the battle to come, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg leaves Los Angeles superior court after testifying, 18 February 2026.Photograph: Wally Skalij/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMeta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg leaves Los Angeles superior court after testifying, 18 February 2026.Photograph: Wally Skalij/Getty ImagesOpinionMetaAn $18bn settlement – and Zuckerberg barely blinked. The tech titans must be stripped of their power, and soonJonathan FreedlandThose who said Meta harms children struck a blow, but the ability of big tech to gouge profits and cause harm is barely diminished. That’s the battle to comeFri 28 Aug 2026 12.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTShareFollow the money. If you want to know how the tech giant Meta really feels about the $18bn it agreed to fork out to end a landmark lawsuit against it – an outcome widely hailed as a victory for campaigners – justlook at its share price. It didn’t go down when word came on Wednesday that Meta had settled with the 29 US states that had argued that the company’s Facebook and Instagram platforms harmed children. On the contrary, Meta stock went up, initially surging by 5%, before levelling out at a gain of just over 1.25%. There could be no clearer proof that the money men reckon Meta dodged a bullet.To be sure, there was plenty to hearten those who have long believed that social media damages teenagers especially, whether by exposing them to content they shouldn’t see or by sapping their self-esteem, offering them filters that show how much prettier they would look if they had cosmetic surgery or giving them a metric of their popularity – and unpopularity – in the form of a running tally of “likes” and views.For one thing, $18bn is a lot of money. For another, Meta has agreed toa series of changes in the way young people use their platforms. There’ll be a two-hour daily cap on use; restricted access during the night and the school day; likes will not be shown automatically and assorted safety and parental supervision measures will no longer be opt-in extras but the default standard. You can see why Lori Schott of Colorado, who believes the content her daughter encountered on Instagram played a part in her suicide aged 18, declared Wednesday to be“a good day”.But look closer and you see that, for Meta, $18bn is not exactly a bank-breaking sum. It amounts toless than a month’s revenue. And it has 10 years to pay it out: the monthly payments could come out of petty cash. What’s more, nearly a third of that sum is contingent on Meta’s rivals YouTube and TikTok agreeing to the same restrictions. All told, the financial penalty is less than a tenth ofthe $200bn the 29 states were seeking, and a tiny fraction of the$1.4tn the company told the court it feared it would have to cough up. No wonder Meta’s shareholders were doing fist bumps on Wednesday.Beyond the money, Meta will be thankful it has escaped a court ruling against it, a legal verdict on the behaviour detailed so compellingly in the California courtroom in the first week of the trial before it was abruptly halted. Jurors heard from the former Meta safety engineer Arturo Béjar, who spoke of his own teenage daughter’s experience on Instagram – how she received unwanted sexual advances, crude misogynistic insults and photos of male genitalia on the platform – and of a survey he had conducted that found 51% of teen users had had bad or harmful experiences on Instagram within the previous seven days, and that content was taken down only 0.02% of the time. Béjar reported his findings toMark Zuckerbergdirectly, but got no reply. As Béjar told me when we spoke on Thursday: “They knew that harm to kids was happening, but they were telling the world it wasn’t.” Under Wednesday’s settlement, Meta hasn’t even made an admission of liability.View image in fullscreenOlivia Konar holds a banner with names of young people who advocates say died as a result of social media outside the Ronald V Dellums federal building and US courthouse in Oakland, California, 18 August 2026.Photograph: Noah Berger/APAs for the new restrictions, anyone who has seen a teenager on a computer or phone will have little confidence that they won’t find a way around them. If they do, then, according to this week’s deal,Metawill not be accountable. And crucially, says Béjar, it is Meta itself that still gets to define what constitutes harm.No less frustrating, these new terms apply inside the US only, even though Meta’s reach, and its capacity to do damage, is global. As the gagged former Facebook employee Sarah Wynn-Williams described in her riveting bookCareless People, the company was assiduous in hunting for new users in those overseas territories with few legal safeguards. There’s a parallel here with the tobacco industry: long after the US and Europe had cracked down on cigarettes, big tobacco was energetically selling into developing countries that had not yet put up their defences.Above all, this week’s settlement addresses only the safety of children, despite the copious evidence of danger to adults, whether in the form of addiction or exposure to toxic misinformation. The danger lies not in this or that specific feature, but rather in the fundamental business model of social media: namely, tracking and surveilling individuals online, using the data gathered to construct a profile, which is then sold to advertisers eager to target potential consumers with extraordinary precision.It’s this model that keeps users hooked, scrolling for hour after hour, as they are served content aimed directly at their interests and anxieties. As Ravi Naik, the lawyer who acts for Wynn-Williams and others, told me: “The algorithm preys on you.” The trouble with this latest settlement, he explains, is that “it reaches the features of Meta’s platforms but not the engine that drives them. The recommendation algorithm is untouched.”What, then, can be done? For Béjar, the answer is to approach social media as a public health crisis, akin to the road traffic accidents that led to mandatory safety belts in cars (and not only for children). Governments need to say that any company involved in this crisis has to be involved in tackling it. And no one should fall for the line that the nature of the internet is such that it cannot be subject to meaningful regulation. When the music industry objected to copyright infringements online, incentives were swiftly arranged to fix the problem. As Béjar so damningly puts it: “A song has more protection than a kid.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are ample other precedents that can serve as guides to action, though none of them will please the titans of big tech. For decades, they have avoided being viewed as publishers, liable for what appears on their platforms. Nor do they want to be treated like carmakers, responsible for product safety. And they don’t like being likened to cigarette firms, selling a product they know is dangerous. Perhaps policymakers need to make a new comparison.More than a century ago, when Standard Oil’s de facto monopoly was deemed harmful to consumers, it was broken up by order of the US supreme court into 34 smaller companies. Meta operates like a monopoly, with users feeling they can’t move, because all their friends and contacts are on the same few platforms. “Meta knowingly exploit this and refuse to make changes to their platforms that they know would deliver safer user experiences,” Damian Collins, a former chair of the UK parliamentary committee that oversees the digital realm, told me. If users could move their data and contacts over to new services, giving them more options, “break-up would work”.This week’s settlement has been a disappointment to those longing to see the tech giants finally brought to heel, found guilty by courts and made to pay for it with costs too big to ignore. For now, Meta has swerved judgment day. But that day must surely come.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
