title: King Harald V of Norway obituary | Norway | The Guardian
description: Monarch who opened up the Norwegian royal family and its palaces to the public, and married a commoner despite his father’s opposition
Author: Stephen Bates
Headline: Monarch who opened up the Norwegian royal family and its palaces to the public, and married a commoner despite his father’s opposition
Content: King Harald V of Norway at the Notre-Dame Cathedral in Luxembourg, after attending at the funeral of the Grand Duke Jean of Luxembourg, May 2019.Photograph: Francisco Seco/APView image in fullscreenKing Harald V of Norway at the Notre-Dame Cathedral in Luxembourg, after attending at the funeral of the Grand Duke Jean of Luxembourg, May 2019.Photograph: Francisco Seco/APNorwayObituaryKing Harald V of Norway obituaryMonarch who opened up the Norwegian royal family and its palaces to the public, and married a commoner despite his father’s oppositionStephen BatesFri 28 Aug 2026 10.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKing Harald V of Norway, who has died aged 89, Europe’s oldest serving monarch, was the country’s third king since it regained independence in 1905 following the dissolution of its union with Sweden. Although he ceased to be head of the Lutheran state church in 2012 and subsequently lost his constitutional status as “holy” six years later, he did exhibit the Scandinavian moderation, stoicism and genial approachability that led a newspaper to name him Norway’s person of the year in 2017.The first Norwegian king to be born in the country since 1370, Harald was also related to both the Swedish and the British royal families. His parents were Crown Prince Olav, who was king as Olav V between 1957 and 1991, and his wife, Princess Märtha, a member of the Swedish royal dynasty. His grandparents were King Haakon VII, the first king of the independent country, who reigned for 52 years from 1905, and his wife, Queen Maud, daughter of Britain’s Edward VII. The family roots are Danish – from the Glücksburg dynasty – as were those of theDuke of Edinburghand the former Greek royal family. The mixed heritage made him sympathetic to refugees: “It is not easy to say where we come from. Home is where the heart is,” he said.View image in fullscreenKing Harald V greets Queen Elizabeth II at the Royal Palace, Oslo, during a state visit, May 2001.Photograph: Fiona Hanson/PAHe was Queen Elizabeth II’s second cousin and a knight of the garter. At the time of his birth, Harald was 16th in line to the British throne, though he had fallen in the rankings to around 80th in more recent years. Confusingly, he was not the fifth Harald to rule his country, but the sixth – the 10th-century Harald Bluetooth generally not being assigned a number in the list of Norwegian kings. The king never attracted a picturesque title as did some of his Viking predecessors – such as Bluetooth, Harald Fairhair and Harald Hardrada, who tried to seize the English throne a few weeks before the Norman invasion in 1066 and was killed at the battle of Stamford Bridge.Harald himself was only three at the time of the Nazi invasion ofNorwayin 1940, and he and his mother and two older sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, initially fled to Sweden, which, trying to maintain its neutrality while accommodating the Germans’ attack on their neighbour, was reluctant to let them in. It is alleged that the royal party was initially turned back at the border, and allowed to proceed only when the driver of their car threatened to ram it through the border post. Within three months, Harald, his sisters and mother had escaped to the US. They spent the war years in Washington DC and Harald thereafter spoke English with a slight American accent.Meanwhile, Harald’s grandfather and father escaped to England, where they led a government in exile. Famously Haakon, turning up at the BBC to make a broadcast to his people, was asked by a receptionist: “Where did you say you were king of, dear?”Following the liberation of Norway at the end of the war, the family was reunited and Harald was enrolled first at a state primary and then at Oslo cathedral school. From there he studied at Oslo University and the Norwegian military academy, before following in his father’s footsteps to read history, economics and politics at Balliol College, Oxford, where he also rowed for the college. A keen competitive yachtsman, he and his crews represented Norway at successive Olympics in Tokyo in 1964, Mexico City in 1968 and Munich in 1972, and won world championship medals through the 1980s and a European championship gold medal in 2005.If this was a conventional career, much less so was his determination to marry a commoner, Sonja Haraldsen, a shop assistant who was the daughter of an Oslo textile manufacturer, whom he had met at a sailing party in 1959. The friendship was kept secret for several years, partly because of Olav’s reluctance to have the heir to the throne marry someone who was not royal. In the end, Harald forced the issue by declaring to his father that if he was not allowed to marry her he would not marry anyone, thus bringing an end to the dynasty. The couple married in 1968.View image in fullscreenKing Harald V aboard the Fram XI vessel, as part of the One Ton Cup international sailing contest, Copenhagen, July 1992.Photograph: Lise Åserud/ReutersHarald was sworn in as king automatically following Olav’s death in January 1991. Although lacking his father’s easy bonhomie, the king attempted successfully – and popularly – to open up the institution and its palace and estates more freely to the public. The Norwegian monarch’s duties are similar to those in Britain, with non-exercised executive power, and all official acts having to be endorsed by the governing council of state, equivalent to a British cabinet. The Norwegian parliament constitutionally debates whether to continue the monarchy every four years, and earlier this year, despite controversies concerning the royal family, voted in favour of its continuation by 141 to 26.The greatest crisis in the country’s modern history occurred on 22 July 2011 when the domestic terrorist Anders Behring Breivik murdered 77 people, mainly at a young socialists’ holiday camp on Utøya island. The king attracted public praise in the wake of the tragedy, when he met bereaved relatives and called for national solidarity and mutual support. He was seen to weep at the memorial service for the victims.Harald was treated for bladder cancer in 2003, contracted Covid, had a pacemaker fitted in 2024 and was being treated for the blood disorder haemolytic anaemia.He is survived by Sonja and their children, Princess Märtha Louise and Prince Haakon, whose wife, Mette-Marit (nee Tjessem-Høiby), was obliged to apologise in February this year for email exchanges with the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, in which her name was mentioned nearly 1,000 times. The king said that she had not broken any law. Mette-Marit’s son by a previous relationship, Marius, was jailed for four years in June following convictions for two rapes and drug offences.Haakon succeeds Harald as King Haakon VIII and will adopt the monarchy’s traditional motto: “All for Norway”.Harald V, king of Norway, born 21 February 1937; died 28 August 2026Explore more on these topicsNorwayEuropeobituariesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t care if I look good’: French heartthrob Louis Garrel on fashion, fatherhood and his radically dorky new role | Movies | The Guardian
description: The star has long been French cinema’s favourite tousle-haired Adonis, which makes his latest performance – as a schlubby, stay-at-home dad – all the more surprising. ‘I appreciate people laughing at me,’ he says
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: The star has long been French cinema’s favourite tousle-haired Adonis, which makes his latest performance – as a schlubby, stay-at-home dad – all the more surprising. ‘I appreciate people laughing at me,’ he says
Content: Tall, dork and handsome … Louis Garrel.Photograph: WWD/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTall, dork and handsome … Louis Garrel.Photograph: WWD/Getty ImagesMoviesInterview‘I don’t care if I look good’: French heartthrob Louis Garrel on fashion, fatherhood and his radically dorky new rolePhilip OltermannThe star has long been French cinema’s favourite tousle-haired Adonis, which makes his latest performance – as a schlubby, stay-at-home dad – all the more surprising. ‘I appreciate people laughing at me,’ he saysFri 28 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Even though I’ve been working in film for over 20 years, I still have this desire to look beautiful on screen,” says Louis Garrel, on a video call from his bed inside a boat off the coast of Corsica. The French film star is lying on his stomach, occasionally kicking up his bare legs, ruffling his curls and running the nail of his thumb over his moustache. Ithinkthe person he sees on the laptop screen in front of him is me, but I am pretty certain he is flirting with his own reflection.The attraction between the Paris-born 43-year-old and the camera tends to be reciprocal. Long of limb, tousled of hair and chiselled of nose, Garrel has spent a career on screen as French cinema’s favourite Adonis – the man film-makers turn to when they need an erotic wrecking ball to smash up bourgeois twosomes and turn them into quivering menages a trois.His breakout role in 2003 was as a priapic student revolutionary who inserts himself in the sexual bond between his twin sister (Eva Green) and a visiting American student (Michael Pitt) in Bernardo Bertolucci’sThe Dreamers. Since then, he’s been reliably effective as smouldering sexpots whose intense stare cuts across dancefloors – bewitching two friends in Canadian director Xavier Dolan’s 2010 filmHeartbeats, enticing Angelina Jolie into a fling in high-fashion drama Couture, or hawkishly pouncing on the poor Yves Saint Laurent in the 2014 biopic Saint Laurent, where he played Karl Lagerfeld’s dandy companion Jacques de Bascher. “I fight against it because I know that good actors don’t care about looking good,” he excuses himself. “But I’m not such a good actor.”View image in fullscreenUptown hunk … Garrel in Just an Illusion.Photograph: Manuel MoutierThat is false modesty of the highest order. He hails from a dynasty of actor-film-makers that includes his mother Brigitte Sy, father (and ex-lover of Velvet Underground singer Nico) Philippe Garrel and grandfather Maurice Garrel, on whose advice he applied to and graduated from Paris’s prestigious Conservatoire drama school. On screen, he has not just impersonated dreamboats but also Alfred Dreyfus, King Louis XIII, Robespierre and Jean-Luc Godard. And in his latest film, Garrel does something that only good actors can do: to play magnificently against type.In the comedy Just an Illusion, he is Yves, a former executive at a kitchen appliance firm who has recently lost his job but can’t bring himself to tell his family. Befitting the film’s 80s suburban Paris setting, Garrel’s hair here is bouffy rather than tousled, the moustache more Ron Burgundy than The Leopard-era Alain Delon. He wears a billowing beige trenchcoat that makes him look as befuddled as Monsieur Hulot, the comical everyman in the films of Jacques Tati.In one scene, Yves is flicking through a magazine on the living room sofa while their apartment block’s caretaker Monsieur Berger (Pierre Lottin) shows Yves’ wife Sandrine (Camille Cottin, of Call My Agent fame) how to use her new desktop computer. As the mulleted Berger places his tattooed paw over Sandrine’s hand to guide the cursor, she giggles in delight. “If you go like this, Sandrine, it jerks.” “It jerks off all over the place,” she coos back. Yves, startled by echoes of the frisson that has long vanished from his marriage, rushes to put out the sparks and shows Berger the door. If reducing France’s go-to libertine to an anxiety-ridden gooseberry isn’t a feat of acting, what is?“When I was very young, a director told me that on screen you have to be like a gorilla,” Garrel says. “You have to be intense and fascinating to watch, but have absolutely no idea of yourself. When I’m playing a character like this one, I can do less, you know, modelling. I don’t care if I look good, and most of the time you are better on screen when you don’t care.”View image in fullscreenUpon reflection … Garrel with Eva Green in The Dreamers.Photograph: Severine Brigeot/Hachette Premiere/Kushner-Locke Co/Kobal/Rex/ShutterstockA hit upon its French release this spring, Just an Illusion is directed by film-making duo Éric Toledano and Olivier Nakache, who have been a major guarantee of box office success sinceUntouchable, about the relationship between a wealthy quadriplegic and his home helper. Like that predecessor, their new film’s comedy is of the non-inflammatory kind, its emotional timbre unashamedly sentimental. But along the way, it processes some surprisingly big political themes, including Franco-German reconciliation, the 1870 Crémieux Decree that granted French citizenship to Algerian Jews, the rise of the Front National and the anti-racism concerts that were organised in response. There is also the question of how a frustrated stay-at-home husband copes with a spouse embarking on a career. When Sandrine passes her computing exam and gets an executive-level job, Yves sheds tears of joy with her.“What strikes me when I watch modern movies these days is that everybody gets divorced or separated and couples never live together from the beginning to the end,” says Garrel, who separated last year from his wife of eight years, the actor and model Laetitia Casta. “This movie portrays one man and one woman who stay together without separating, which would have been bourgeois in the 1970s but now feels very punk.”The protagonist of Just an Illusion is not Yves but his younger son, 12-year-old Vincent (Simon Boublil), who has fallen hopelessly in love with a girl in his class. Vincent has caring parents, but the film’s central message is that at some point every generation has to tell the previous one to eff off, as well-meaning as they may be. I wonder how that message resonated with Garrel, given his profession is in keeping with family traditions? Has he ever told his parents to eff off? He answers in a way only someone whose family tree is mapped out on IMDb can. “Of course I love Pasolini, of course I love Godard, of course I love Truffaut. But I want to get inspired by films that don’t show at the Cinémathèque Française. Like Lethal Weapon. That is one of my favourite movies, I don’t care.” OK, but has he ever told his parents to do one? “It’s a small rebellion, I know, but that’s maybe my way to say fuck off.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJust an Illusion is the 62nd film Garrel has acted in and his first role that really interrogates fatherhood. In real life, he has a five-year-old son from his relationship to Casta, and an 18-year-old adopted daughter, Oumy Bruni Garrel, from a previous relationship with Valeria Bruni Tedeschi, sister of the former first lady of France, Carla Bruni. Oumy has starred in some films, but Garrel seems sanguine about the fact that the acting dynasty that shares his name may come to an end with his children. “She [Oumy] is a very talented actor, she has a gift. But I recently asked her, do you really want to become an actress? And she told me no, no, no, I don’t want that. So next year she’s going to study anthropology, sociology and philosophy. I’m very proud of that.” Did he discourage her? “She doesn’t need discouraging, because she’s seen the kind of life that we have.”‘It became like a real memory’: Louis Garrel on making a film aged five in which he found a man in bed with his motherRead moreSeeing yourself through the eyes of your own children might make it harder to still be in love with yourself the way you were as a young man. But for an actor, it also makes it easier to not care, and act like a gorilla. Garrel seems to be developing a taste for it. Later this year, he will play the lead in It Will Happen Tonight, the new work by Nanni Moretti, one of Europe’s great comic film-makers.“I’m 43 years old, and the moments that I appreciate the most as an actor now are when I’m in a screening room and I hear people laughing at me,” Garrel says. “It’s terrible. But this is what I’m waiting for.”Just an Illusion is out in UK and Irish cinemas on11 September.Explore more on these topicsFilminterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This place might look bad but it’s not’: fear and hope in Middlesbrough community after week of violence | Middlesbrough | The Guardian
description: Nine people have died in events police had linked to organised crime in an area shaped by deprivation and fading opportunities, but there is light, say residents
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Nine people have died in events police had linked to organised crime in an area shaped by deprivation and fading opportunities, but there is light, say residents
Content: Events of the past week have left the community reeling.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEvents of the past week have left the community reeling.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianMiddlesbrough‘This place might look bad but it’s not’: fear and hope in Middlesbrough community after week of violenceNine people have died in events police had linked to organised crime in an area shaped by deprivation and fading opportunities, but there is light, say residentsMark BrownNorth of England correspondentFri 28 Aug 2026 11.57 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 07.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“This place might look bad but it’s not, the people are good people,” said one woman before turning to her young daughter and asking: “Is this place bad?” The girl shakes her head vigorously.It’s a difficult thing to say given the week’s events in Grangetown and South Bank on Teesside.Around the corner is the burned-out shell of a house that was deliberatelyset on fire on Wednesday, killing Natalie McDonald, 34, and her seven-year-old niece Valentina Foster. Metres away is the A66 where, less than a mile away on Saturday, ahead-on crashkilled seven people, including two police officers.Cleveland police had linked the crash to organised crime and initially said they could not rule out it also being connected to the house fire, but on Friday said there was no link.The news will be of no surprise to neighbours and well-wishers who this week gathered sombrely opposite the house in Birchington Avenue, Grangetown. They had already said there was no link.“It’s smackheads. That’s the problem round here,” said one neighbour.View image in fullscreenThe house in Grangetown where Valentina Foster, seven, and her aunt, Natalie McDonald, died after it was was deliberately set on fire.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianJohn Kirton, the brother of McDonald, told reporters: “My sister was not involved with anything to do with gangs, or the [crash on the] A66.“That’s what makes this so senseless. People think they can do whatever they like. There’s some terrible people in the world and now my sister and Valentina have gone.”People, all reluctant to give their names, said the community was a tight-knit one. “Everyone looks out for each other,” said one woman.But they also agreed that there was a big problem with gangs of boys and young men involved in drug dealing and other crimes.View image in fullscreenTributes left to Natalie McDonald, 34, who died alongside her niece in a house fire.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianPeople felt trapped in their own homes, afraid to go to the shops, said theMiddlesbroughand Thornaby East MP, Andy McDonald. He called it a form of “terrorism”.Jonathan Brash, the MP for Hartlepool, said communities felt organised crime was “embedded”.There have been nine deaths and other possibly gang-related local crimes including a knife attack and the ramming of an empty house. On Thursday evening, video was shared on social media showing cars being torched at a vigil for one of the men who died in the A66 crash. It was in Haswell, County Durham, 20 miles north of the crash site.The events of the last week have clearly left a community shellshocked and in need of help, fearful of what might happen next.Alec Brown, the leader of Redcar and Cleveland council, said authorities were working “tirelessly” to ensure people feel safe. About 200 extra police from other forceshave been drafted inand some could be seen arriving at Cleveland’s police headquarters on Friday morning.The extra police are coming from the Northumbria, Durham, Humberside and North, South and West Yorkshire forces as well as the National Crime Agency. The hope is that a show of strength can dampen tensions and reassure the area.Anna Turley, the MP for Redcar, said on Friday that not every incident police attended was connected to the investigation into organised crime.“I think it’s really important to get across the fact that these incidents are not all linked,” she said. “It could feel that way at the moment because of the national spotlight on us, but unfortunately, we know we’ve had a high level of crime, and in this area for a long time now, these are incidents, sadly, that we see all the time.”View image in fullscreenTerry Chapman with his dog Charlie. The vast majority of people in the area were ‘absolutely fantastic’, he said.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianTerry Chapman is not from Grangetown, but was “born and raised” on a different Middlesbrough council estate.He didn’t quite know why he had come to the site of the house blaze, but felt he had to. “I know these areas, they are like where I’m from,” he said. “We have problems but when things happen like this … it’s just hard to believe. It’s really horrendous and scary.”Chapman said criminal gangsters were the minority. “The vast majority of people, including in places like Grangetown, are absolutely fantastic people.“They may not have a lot. Some do. Some are managing and some are barely managing. But fundamentally, the majority of people are decent and they’re law-abiding. The trouble is that the small minority seem to have a bigger influence in places like this and it’s gone unchecked for years.”View image in fullscreenThere is no obvious centre to Grangetown, with many shops shut.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianGrangetown and South Bank are clearly deprived, rundown areas. There are small terraces of shops, many shut, and no obvious centre.It’s also striking how few pubs there are. One former pub, the Magnet – which hosted early gigs for the Grangetown-born comedian Roy Chubby Brown – is now a branch of Heron Foods.Saturday’s collision took place on the A66 between Church Lane and Normanby Road. Police had been pursuing a VW Passat with five young men in it for seven minutes before it turned on to the dual carriageway, against the flow of traffic. The pursuit was aborted. Ten seconds later the Passat crashed into a police car. Everyone died at the scene, including the police officers Matthew Blades and Tom Clough.On the corner of Church Lane and the A66 a retired steelworker is looking desperately at the bouquets left for the PCs.He’s called Joe. “I better not give you my surname, because of the lunatics …”View image in fullscreenFloral tributes at the junction of the A66 and Church Lane in Grangetown.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianThe former steelworks, where most people in the area worked, was literally on the other side of the road, Joe said. “I could be out of work and back home in 10 minutes.”He is close to tears at what has happened in his community this week. “The problem is the police don’t have the resources. There used to be a station in South Bank, there used to be a station in Eston. Now there’s no police here and they [the criminal gangs] are doing whatever they like with drugs passing from one to another. They’ve got away with it for years.”It’s also true that the problems in this part of Teesside are not isolated. Countless other places everywhere, not just the UK, have major problems with gangs and organised crime. You can watch versions of the problem on TV whenever you want, whether it’s Naples, Baltimore or Liverpool.It’s easy to see places like Grangetown and South Bank as postcards for forgottenEngland, places tabloids sometimes say are controlled by feral gangs. But scratch the surface and there is light.In South Bank on Normanby Road, near the A66 junction, is a community gallery set up by the Iraqi artist and Teesside University graduate Azad Karim Mohammed.TheSaabat Galleryis a great place, currently showing and selling the work of the local artists Rita Readman and David Watson.View image in fullscreen‘Everyone is warm and welcoming around here,’ said Nathaniel McGovern at the Saabat Gallery.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianThe gallery’s coordinator, Nathaniel McGovern, has been there five years. “Everyone is warm and welcoming round here,” he said. “People are happy to help and it’s a close community.“It has been a mad week for everyone round here but you get nice people and bad people everywhere, don’t you? I’d say this area’s got more nice people than bad.”Explore more on these topicsMiddlesbroughNorth of EnglandCommunitiesPovertyEnglandSocial exclusionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Army helicopters ferry survivors from inaccessible areas to a camp at a barracks in Bidur
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Army helicopters ferry survivors from inaccessible areas to a camp at a barracks in Bidur
Content: A woman in Bidur covers her face with a cloth amid the flood devastation.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA woman in Bidur covers her face with a cloth amid the flood devastation.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianNepal-Tibet flood disaster‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in NepalArmy helicopters ferry survivors from inaccessible areas to a camp at a barracks in BidurHannah Ellis-PetersenandGaurav Pokharelin Bidur. Photographs and video byAhmer KhanFri 28 Aug 2026 14.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.00 EDTShareThe three women sat together in the army tent and wept. They cried out for their sons, their husbands, their homes. As flash floods coursed through the Himalayan mountains on Wednesday morning, a monstrous black wave took everything from them.View image in fullscreenMore than 1,900 people are missing and at least 579 are dead after part ⁠of a glacier crashed on to the valley floor in the Langtang national park.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWater, mud, rock and ice thundered down rivers and valleys, obliterating villages and destroying power stations, roads and bridges.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeople at the army camp in Bidur on Friday.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianAs a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas between Tibet andNepalsplintered and crashed into the valley below, it set off a deadly cascade of water, mud and debris down the Bhote Koshi River. The impact of the glacier collapse was so strong that experts initially reported it as an earthquake. The Nepali village homes that lined the riverbank and clung to the mountainside stood little chance.View image in fullscreenThe glacier impact set off a deadly cascade along the Bhote Khoshi River.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHomes near the riverbank and mountainside stood little chance.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSome of the affected areas can only be reached by helicopter.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEmergency workers search through the mud in Bidur.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianSangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”Flood victims evacuate to Nepal army camp - loopTwo days after the disaster, at least 579 people have been confirmed dead and more than 1,900 are still missing, the numbers rising by the day. Many in Nepal fear that the true scale of the disaster has yet to emerge, as the worst-hit areas in districts such as Rusawa are only accessible by helicopter. The situation remains even more opaque in Tibet, which is under tight Chinese media control. Though it was at the centre of the disaster, Chinese authorities insist only five people there have died.In the army barracks in the town of Bidur, where Nepal’s rescue efforts were being coordinated, helicopters carrying those rescued from flooded areas continued to arrive every few minutes, while others carrying vital supplies of food and clean water flew out and high up into the mountains.On Friday morning, ground rescue efforts were halted over fears that the river levels were rising once again. But the Nepali army spokesperson, Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet, said the helicopter rescues would continue for as long as people were missing. He accepted that the death toll was hard to calculate. “Right now, our focus is mostly on finding the living,” he said.Among those recently brought to safety was 60-year-old Murali Maiya Tamang, who had been in Rusawa and was found hanging in a tree. As the flash floods came down the valley, she had watched as her house was washed clean away. She convulsed with tears as she waited desperately for news of her son, who was in their village when the floods struck and has been missing since.View image in fullscreenRescuers found Murali Maiya Tamang, 60, hanging in a tree after her house was washed away.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSangke Dolma Tamang (in red), 61, had been cooking snacks in her village of Mailung when the floods came without warning.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTwo young survivors at the army camp.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHelicopters carrying people rescued from flooded areas continued to arrive at the barracks in Bidur every few minutes.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSurvivors fill the army camp and wait for news of missing relatives.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian“My husband had already died in Nepal’s 2015 earthquake,” she said. “Now this flood has taken away the only son I had left. I am all alone now. What is the point of living now?”Many in the barracks waited of news of their fathers, brothers and husbands who had been working on vast hydroelectric projects along the Bhote Koshi River, many of which were washed away and the tunnels filled with mud. On Friday, footage showed rescuers pulling some workers to safety from within the tunnels.A few miles from the army barracks stood the remains of the town of Bidur, on the banks of the Trishuli River. It was one of the last towns to be hit by the flash floods, but it took just a few minutes for it to be reduced to mangled debris. The ruins of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth stood still half submerged in mud. Rescuers said there were bodies buried inside, but it was still too dangerous and the terrain too unstable to collect them.Workers dig through debris after deadly flash flooding - loopOn Friday afternoon, Nepal’s newly elected home minister, Sudan Gurung, surveyed the damage. “It is so sad to see such a heavy loss of human lives,” he told the Guardian. “Our priority right now is rescuing people. We are searching for everyone who is still missing, assuming that they are all alive. We are searching for everyone, whether they are Nepali citizens or international nationals.”View image in fullscreenAshok Chaurasia (right) said he had heard the roar of the approaching flood moments before it appeared.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianDozens of local people made attempts to return to the site of their homes, in a bid to collect any remnant of their lives. Most just found a deep abyss of mud. Picking through the deep mud and devastation of the town, Ashok Chaurasia, a shopkeeper, said he had heard the terrifying roar of the water before he saw it. The dark muddy waters already snapped at his heels as they ran uphill for safety, a bridge over the river collapsing behind them. He survived by just 20 seconds, clinging on to the wall of a monastery for dear life. His nephew and his sister-in-law were not so lucky.Yet even as he blessed his survival, he wept at his losses. “We had a three-storey house here, and now there isn’t even a single brick left,” he said. “Nothing can be seen. We have nothing to eat or wear. The flood took everything I have.”

title: Police arrest seven more men in aftermath of deadly A66 crash | UK news | The Guardian
description: Cleveland police say a total of 24 people arrested in investigation after crash that killed two officers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cleveland police say a total of 24 people arrested in investigation after crash that killed two officers
Content: Floral tributes left after the A66 crash in Grangetown.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFloral tributes left after the A66 crash in Grangetown.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianUK newsPolice arrest seven more men in aftermath of deadly A66 crashCleveland police say a total of 24 people arrested in investigation after crash that killed two officersPress AssociationFri 28 Aug 2026 18.00 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 15.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven more men have been arrested as part of an operation tackling alleged organised crime after the head-on crash on the A66 that resulted in seven deaths, Cleveland police have said.Officers said four men, aged 21, 25, 35 and 40, were being held on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life after a vehicle crashed into a house in Steele Crescent, Middlesbrough.They were also being questioned over alleged arson after a caravan was set alight in Atlee Road on Wednesday morning, and over a drug offence.The force said the men were in a vehicle when they were stopped by police in Kingsley Road in Grangetown on Thursday night.Class A drugs were seized, officers confirmed.The three other men arrested were a 23-year-old man, on suspicion of threats to kill, a 42-year-old on suspicion of threats to kill and possession of criminal property, and a 30-year-old on suspicion of possession of criminal property.All three have been released on conditional bail.It brings the total number of people arrested since the crash to 24.Earlier on Friday, detectives confirmed they were not linking a house fire that killed a seven-year-old girl and her aunt to the A66 crash, which left two police officers and five young men dead.Hundreds of extra police officers have been drafted in to support officers after a series of incidents in the Middlesbrough and County Durham area.Inquests have been formally opened into the deaths of the seven people in the crash in the early hours of 22 August. The two police officers who died were PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38.The Teesside area coroner, Paul Appleton, said that there was a collision at South Bank between a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat.He said the provisional cause of death for Blades was head and neck injuries and for Clough it was neck injuries.Later, inquests were opened and adjourned into the deaths of the Passat occupants, named as Cole Worthy and Theo Rae, both 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jakub Matusiak.Police initially arrested 17 people after the crash, which followed a police pursuit, as part of an investigation into alleged organised crime.Cleveland police assistant chief constable Wayne Fox said of the latest arrests: “This latest disruptive activity now brings the total number of arrests to 24 since the investigation commenced.“Several suspects arrested throughout the course of this week have been charged with serious offences and a number of offenders have been recalled to prison.”On Friday, Cleveland police said Kai Inico, who was arrested on Monday on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, had been charged with possession with intent to supply a class B drug.The force said four other people arrested on Monday had been bailed – a 16-year-old boy and 18-year-old man arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, a 55-year-old man arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender, and a 23-year-old man arrested on suspicion of threats to kill.Earlier this week, two other people were charged with offences and appeared in court.Meanwhile, two men have been arrested on suspicion of murder in connection with the fire which killed Natalie McDonald, 34, and seven-year-old Valentina Foster, as well as injuring four others, in Grangetown.Matt Storey, the police and crime commissioner for Cleveland, said on Friday: “After what has been the most tragic week in its history, I want to extend my heartfelt thanks to local residents for the outpouring of love and support they have shown to Cleveland police.“My thoughts remain with the family, friends and colleagues of PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough. They will be remembered as selfless, professional and courageous police officers, dedicated to serving their communities.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia ‘losing 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit’ | Russia | The Guardian
description: Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day but western officials say it cannot keep up with casualty level
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day but western officials say it cannot keep up with casualty level
Content: Rehearsal for a military parade in Moscow in 2025. Putin is thought to have limited options for more recruitment.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRehearsal for a military parade in Moscow in 2025. Putin is thought to have limited options for more recruitment.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesRussiaRussia ‘losing 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit’Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day but western officials say it cannot keep up with casualty levelPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentFri 28 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia is losing about 6,000 more troops inUkraineeach month than it can recruit, western officials have said.WhileRussiais still acquiring new battlefield recruits at speed, with an estimated rate of 1,000 a day, in the last two months even this has not been sufficient to replace those killed or injured.“We estimate that the gap between the number of people Russia is losing to casualties and the number they’re being able to recruit is around 6,000 a month at the moment,” one western official said.“Putin’s response to this has been to escalate himself and to target civilian infrastructure and civilians in Ukraine, firing over 360 missiles since early July and exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of defence against ballistic missiles. It’s clear that Moscow intends to try and break Ukrainian morale by destroying its energy infrastructure this winter.”Such tactics are in part because Putin has limited options for overcoming the huge losses on the battlefield with more recruitment.Western officials believe further mobilisation would be a big risk both politically and economically, saying the last such event,in autumn 2022, saw about a million – often highly skilled – Russians leave the country, with less than half returning.It is also unclear whether the Russian military could absorb the several hundred thousand new recruits which would result, given a lack of equipment and officers.Ukraine has repeatedly attacked Russian targets connected to oil, creating fuel shortages, but has appealed repeatedly for more help from allies, both with offensive missiles and defence systems.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK will share information about Storm Shadow missile components with Kyiv.Photograph: Ukrainian presidency/Sipa/ShutterstockAndy Burnhamvisited Kyivon his first overseas trip as prime minister this week. He told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK wouldgive Ukraine previously classified informationon the British-manufactured components for long-range cruise missiles.Burnham has also urged the international community to do more to protect Ukraine against Russian attacks, particularly with more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles. He isexpected to make this argumentat next month’s UN general assembly in New York.In response, Russia hasmade repeated threatsof retaliation, including talk of attacks on UK military targets both inside and outside Ukraine.The western officials said that while the threat from Russia remained very real, the situation had not changed, and the assessment was that “Putin absolutely wants to avoid a direct confrontation with Nato”.One official said: “We are seeing a continuation of hostile rhetoric and various accusations against the UK. This is absolutely consistent with longstanding Russian military doctrine, which is to use rhetoric to both exploit fears in adversaries and to influence decision-making. So this is not a new phenomenon.”Ukraine war briefing: Missiles shot down during long Russian attack waveRead moreOfficials say Russia still has the capability to target the UK, with cyberattacks or physical attacks on civilian targets by proxies, for example on factories or warehouses. Last year, six men were jailed for their involvement in an attack ordered by Russia against a warehouse in east London housing aid to Ukraine.But officials said their assessment was that Putin would limit any such action to avoid more direct conflict with Nato.Putin’s overall aim in Ukraine, western officials believe, is to maintain a campaign of attrition, hoping that support from Ukraine’s allies will ebb away, particularly if governments are spooked by public alarm over Russian threats.Such threats should be seen, one official said, as attempts to create a “fractured and more vulnerable Europe”.Another said: “It’s important to keep in mind that this is not new. Russia has invoked the threat of the possible use of nuclear weapons numerous times in recent years to try to scare us into ending support for Ukraine.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineForeign policyEuropeVladimir PutinNatonewsShareReuse this content

title: Man, 41, dies after large sign falls at Christian festival in West Sussex | West Sussex | The Guardian
description: Six more people hospitalised after incident at Big Church festival near Steyning
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Six more people hospitalised after incident at Big Church festival near Steyning
Content: The Big Church festival on the Wiston Estate was cancelled after the incident on Friday afternoon.Photograph: bigchurchfestivalView image in fullscreenThe Big Church festival on the Wiston Estate was cancelled after the incident on Friday afternoon.Photograph: bigchurchfestivalWest SussexMan, 41, dies after large sign falls at Christian festival in West SussexSix more people hospitalised after incident at Big Church festival near SteyningNadeem BadshahFri 28 Aug 2026 19.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 41-year-old man has died and at least six other people have been injured after a large sign fell at a Christian festival inWest Sussex, police said.The man, from Eastbourne, East Sussex, was pronounced dead at the scene after the incident at the Big Church festival near Steyning on Friday afternoon.His next of kin have been told and are being supported by specialist officers, Sussex police said.The force added that at least six other people have been taken to hospital for treatment.DCS Richard McDonagh said: “This is a tragic incident and our thoughts go out to the man’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”Anyone with any information or relevant video footage has been asked to contact police.In a post on Instagram shortly after 5.30pm, organisers told attenders the show had been cancelled and all day visitors “must leave the site now”.Organisers later said they had decided to cancel the rest of the festival, which had been scheduled to run until Sunday.“We are devastated by the serious incident that took place at Big Church festival 2026 today, in which a sign fell, injuring at least seven people, one of whom tragically lost their life,” the festival said in an online statement.“First and foremost, all of our thoughts are with those who have been affected, their families and friends, and everyone who witnessed what happened.“Following today’s incident, we have made the decision to bring Big Church festival 2026 to a close.”Officers remained at the scene on Friday night, and people were advised to avoid the area.The incident has been reported to the Health and Safety Executive and local authority, Sussex police said.McDonagh added: “I recognise the immense distress this will have caused people at the festival, and we are working with a number of partners as we seek to establish exactly what happened.“We know there were thousands of people at the festival and we’re urging anyone with any information, or any relevant video footage, to please come forward.”Explore more on these topicsWest SussexnewsShareReuse this content

title: Salmonella cases in UK likely to rise until source of outbreak is found | Eggs | The Guardian
description: Experts say imported eggs served in cafes and restaurants may be behind infections linked to one death
Author: Tobi Thomas
Headline: Experts say imported eggs served in cafes and restaurants may be behind infections linked to one death
Content: About 1.6bn eggs are imported into the UK each year, according to the British Egg Industry Council.Photograph: Ezra Bailey/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAbout 1.6bn eggs are imported into the UK each year, according to the British Egg Industry Council.Photograph: Ezra Bailey/Getty ImagesEggsSalmonella cases in UK likely to rise until source of outbreak is foundExperts say imported eggs served in cafes and restaurants may be behind hundreds of infections and one deathTobi ThomasHealth and inequalities correspondentFri 28 Aug 2026 12.42 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSalmonella cases in the UK are expected to rise until the common source is identified, something that is notoriously difficult to establish, experts have warned.There have been 474 confirmed cases and one death linked to the current outbreak, according to the UKHealthSecurity Agency (UKHSA), with the latest investigations suggesting it is associated with eating imported eggs in cafes and restaurants.About 1.6bn eggs are imported to the UK every year, according to the British Egg Industry Council, with the number having risen 60% since 2021.The link to eggs consumed outside of the home is consistent with imported eggs commonly being used in catering, according to Paul Wigley, a professor of animal microbial ecosystems at the University of Bristol.Wigley said: “Bought in bulk these eggs are cheaper than UK lion mark eggs and so can end up being used in schools and nursing homes along with cafes, restaurants and takeaways. The eggs may be mixed batches from different batches, but the clustering of cases suggests there may be a single source.”He added: “As far as controls and the future, it’s difficult to judge, though identification of the source would help in being able to put specific controls on a producer or country in place. Avoiding runny eggs outside the home, unless lion mark eggs, is perhaps the only step an individual can make.”Although previous salmonella outbreaks in the UK have been linked to eggs imported from European countries such as Poland, the current source of this outbreak has yet to be identified. For some experts, this makes the current surge in cases particularly worrying.Prof Chris Elliott of the school of biological sciences at Queen’s University Belfast, said: “All we have been told is that the likelihood is that it’s been imported.“There is a huge amount of difficulty in tracing the origins of something like this, particularly when it’s food service. Within the UK’s retail industry, they really know their supply chains extremely well. But with food service, less so.”View image in fullscreenBritish lion-stamped eggs are from UK hens vaccinated against salmonella.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/ShutterstockHe added that the number of cases would keep rising until the source was identified, which could take “not days, but weeks”.Elliott added: “My expectation is those numbers will continue to rise until they can not only track the source, but right back to the country of production. It is fiendishly difficult to track the source of a food and ingredient, so I certainly wouldn’t be critical of the agencies. They’re under immense pressure, and the worst thing that can happen is that they feel pressurised to say that it came from Poland or it came from Romania when they’re not 100% sure about that.”Prof Brad Spiller, the head of medical microbiology at Cardiff University, said the fact that this particular outbreak was linked to a common source was “probably the most concerning aspect” of the cases.He said: “It is only once we have a better idea of which countries are involved, we can begin to track back the source.“This is how they identified that both of the previous outbreaks seen in recent years that were happening simultaneously, and were both linked back to Poland as the source of that. I think until they identify the source, the source won’t naturally stop.”Prof Mark Stevens, the chair of microbial pathogenesis at the University of Edinburgh, added that the outbreak was also unusual because cases were occurring at the same time, whereas salmonella cases across the UK were usually more spread out.He said: “This is obviously a real challenge for the health protection agencies because they have to now identify that source and try to restrict its entry into the food system.“It is of concern to have an outbreak of this size. There are thousands of salmonella cases each year, but rarely are they on this scale where hundreds of people are being infected by a common strain.”Stevens added: “I think until we really understand the source of these infections, it’s possible that we’ll continue to see more of them.”Explore more on these topicsEggsHealthFood safetyFoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump announces new US oil agreement with Venezuela | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves
Content: A Venezuelan flag in front of an oil tanker in Maracaibo, Venezuela, on 27 July.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Venezuelan flag in front of an oil tanker in Maracaibo, Venezuela, on 27 July.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump announces new US oil agreement with VenezuelaUS president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reservesGuardian staff and agenciesFri 28 Aug 2026 19.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves.The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with ⁠private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth.The administration,Trump wrote, has “secured majority U.S. control of more ​than 65 BILLION ‌BARRELS of proven Oil ‌Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the ‌American Taxpayer”.Trump said the agreement would more than double American oil reserves.“This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people,” Rubiowroteon social media.Trump’s announcement provided few details on the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved, or how the US would exercise majority control over the ⁠reserves.Venezuela has an estimated 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves, the world’s largest.Since the US captured and removed former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro from power in January, Washington has been trying ‌to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude oil for US refineries while promoting American investment ​into the Opec country’s deteriorated energy industry, which produces 1.25m barrels per day of crude.Trump is under pressure before November’s midterm elections over rising gasoline prices, ​which could ​be eased through ​cheaper oil supplies and expanded output.The US ​also has ‌been looking ​for solutions ​to replenish its strategic petroleum reserve, the oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers.Earlier this week,the Wall Street Journal reportedthat the Trump administration was “in advanced talks withVenezuelafor the U.S. to take a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields that house nearly one-third of the country’s massive energy reserves”. Axios also reported on the negotiations, quoting a US official who claimed the deal would be “massive”.The discussion was reportedly over a US stake in Venezuela’s most promising oil-and-gasfields, with some 90bn barrels of proven reserves.The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,”saidone well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticizing the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States.”The announcement comes as Chevron and other US energy companies are expected to sign a deal next week investing billions in Venezuela’s oil fields,according to the Journal.Tom Phillips and Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpVenezuelaOilTrump administrationUS politicsAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Large fire near Wembley Stadium disrupts tube and rail services | London | The Guardian
description: About 125 firefighters tackle blaze at Neasden waste facility as nearby Amazon warehouse is evacuated
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: About 125 firefighters tackle blaze at Neasden waste facility as nearby Amazon warehouse is evacuated
Content: Huge fire breaks out on industrial estate near Wembley stadiumLondonLarge fire near Wembley Stadium disrupts tube and rail servicesAbout 125 firefighters tackle blaze at Neasden waste facility as nearby Amazon warehouse is evacuatedNadeem Badshahand agenciesFri 28 Aug 2026 17.47 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA large fire broke out at a waste facility close toWembley Stadiumin north-west London, disrupting tube and train lines in the area.Twenty fire engines and about 125 firefighters were sent to tackle the blaze at a mixed-waste facility on an industrial estate in Neasden, less than a mile from the venue.There was no service on the entire Metropolitan line, which runs close to the blaze, and no service between Wembley Park and West Hampstead on the Jubilee line, with severe delays on the rest of the line, Transport forLondonsaid.Rail services into London Marylebone were also disrupted.View image in fullscreenAbout 125 firefighters and 20 fire engines were sent to tackle the blaze.Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesA nearby Amazon warehouse, separate from the industrial unit involved, was evacuated, according to PA Media.A London fire brigade assistant commissioner, Andy Pennick, said: “The brigade was called at 11.36[am] to reports of a fire on Hannah Close, Neasden. Upon arrival, firefighters were met by a well-developed fire involving a waste transfer facility.“Recognising the scale of the fire, the initial officer in attendance immediately requested 20 fire engines be mobilised to the scene.“An industrial unit, approximately 100 metres by 150 metres, was alight. At the height of the fire, around 125 firefighters were in attendance.”Pennick added: “This is a protracted incident that will see crews on scene for the remainder of the day as they work to fully extinguish the fire.”The LFB earlier said that the blaze was under control by about 5pm. Its cause was not yet known and was under investigation, the LFB added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is the third major fire at a recycling centre in London this summer.Earlier this month, about 100 firefighters responded toa blaze at a facility in Deptford, which involved about 50 tonnes of stored household waste.Fires at recycling centres caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries, such as those found in vapes, are occurring at the rate of more than 10 a week, according to figures from the Environmental Services Association.Battery fires at waste facilities are estimated to cost £1bn a yearand are causing growing frustration among fire chiefs.Explore more on these topicsLondonWembley StadiumEnglandWastenewsShareReuse this content

title: Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right political commentator, detained by ICE | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: A former editor of Breitbart News, Yiannopoulos has also served as an intern for Marjorie Taylor Greene
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A former editor of Breitbart News, Yiannopoulos has also served as an intern for Marjorie Taylor Greene
Content: Milo Yiannopoulos at a rally in Baltimore in November 2021.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APView image in fullscreenMilo Yiannopoulos at a rally in Baltimore in November 2021.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right political commentator, detained by ICEA former editor of Breitbart News, Yiannopoulos has also served as an intern for Marjorie Taylor GreeneGuardian staffFri 28 Aug 2026 17.13 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 16.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMilo Yiannopoulos, a far-right British political commentator, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Louisiana, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).In a statement on Friday, a DHS spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was arrested on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport (MSY). The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019, but that “he chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July, “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.“He will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the spokesperson added. “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”As of Friday afternoon, Yiannopoulosis listedin ICE’s online detainee database as being in “ICE Custody”. The database states that he was born in the United Kingdom, but it does not disclose any additional details, including where he is being held.The statement comes asmultipleoutletsreportedon Friday that Yiannopoulos had been detained in Louisiana.Fox Newsreported that Yiannopoulos is currently detained in Alexandria, Lousiana.Yiannopoulos, aformer editor of Breitbart News, previously servedas an internfor Marjorie Taylor Greene, a former US representative, in 2022, and alsoworked onthe 2024 White House campaign of Ye, formerly known as Kanye West. It is unclear why Yiannopoulos might have been in Louisiana, but Ye is scheduled toperform in New Orleanson Friday night.Last year, in posts on social media, Yiannopoulos had been supportive of immigration enforcement in the US.“California needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally,” hewrotein a social media post in June 2025.On social media on Friday, Laura Loomer, the far-right activist and ally of Donald Trump, claimed credit for Yiannopoulos’s detention andwrotethat she had previously reported him to ICE.Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Far right (US)Marjorie Taylor GreeneBreitbartnewsShareReuse this content

title: Artist defends Ronnie O’Sullivan mural in Sheffield saying it isn’t finished | Street art | The Guardian
description: Critics say painting looks more like a zombie but artist Chris Ashmore says ‘touch-ups’ are still to happen
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Critics say painting looks more like a zombie but artist Chris Ashmore says ‘touch-ups’ are still to happen
Content: The new mural of Ronnie O'Sullivan on the wall of the Spot On snooker club in Sheffield.Photograph: Charley Atkins/SWNSView image in fullscreenThe new mural of Ronnie O'Sullivan on the wall of the Spot On snooker club in Sheffield.Photograph: Charley Atkins/SWNSStreet artArtist defends Ronnie O’Sullivan mural in Sheffield saying it isn’t finishedCritics say painting looks more like a zombie but artist Chris Ashmore says ‘touch-ups’ are still to happenJamie GriersonFri 28 Aug 2026 11.34 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA street artist has defended his mural of the snooker player Ronnie O’Sullivan inSheffieldafter critics suggested the world champion looked like a zombie.Chris Ashmore was commissioned to produce the artwork featuring the former seven-time world champion for the back wall of the Spot On snooker club,the BBC reported.Many people have reportedly said they like the mural, while others suggested O’Sullivan was “zombie like” or “skeletal” and told the broadcaster the artwork was “shocking”.Ashmore said he had only completed two weeks of the five that have been assigned to the job and “touch-ups” were forthcoming. “I usually use a scissor lift, where you can stand back and see things as a whole, but I couldn’t use it as the land is too uneven,” he told the BBC.“When the scaffolding came down, I came away and boom – it’s gone viral.View image in fullscreenThe real Ronnie O’Sullivan in action.Photograph: Tai Chengzhe/VCG/Getty“I saw people saying it looks like Michael Jackson or a zombie. I’ve got thick skin, I’ll be OK, but it didn’t feel fair.”Gillian Jones, who lives near the mural told the broadcaster she liked it and it “brightened her day”.But Frank Short said: “The artwork is OK, but the eyes are all wrong. It looks like he’s taken something.”Shaun Spalding said the mural was “shocking”. “His eyes are all wrong, his teeth are wrong, it just don’t look like Ronnie. It looks like somebody who’s got a skeletal face.”View image in fullscreenRonnie O’Sullivan in action against China’s Zhao Xintong in 2025.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersDan Kirkland, the manager of Spot On, defended Ashmore’s work. “Yes, we’ve seen what you’ve seen. There are parts of the face that need tweaking, particularly around the eyes and mouth.“Some relatively small changes will make a huge difference, so we’ll arrange whatever access Chris needs. What has upset us is seeing some of the reactions becoming personal towards Chris,” said Kirkland.“People are absolutely entitled to like or dislike a mural. But having an opinion about a piece of artwork is one thing. Slagging off the person who created it is another.”Explore more on these topicsStreet artRonnie O'SullivanSheffieldSnookerArtnewsShareReuse this content
