title: Dads and dudes: the two style clans that dominate menswear | Fashion | The Guardian
description: The ‘dad’ look favours straight lines and muted colours, while ‘dudes’ prefer baggier clothes with adornments
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: The ‘dad’ look favours straight lines and muted colours, while ‘dudes’ prefer baggier clothes with adornments
Content: Jackie and ‘dude’ Adam Sandler at the Don’t Say Good Luck premiere on 10 August.Photograph: Noam Galai/Getty Images for NetflixView image in fullscreenJackie and ‘dude’ Adam Sandler at the Don’t Say Good Luck premiere on 10 August.Photograph: Noam Galai/Getty Images for NetflixFashionDads and dudes: the two style clans that dominate menswearThe ‘dad’ look favours straight lines and muted colours, while ‘dudes’ prefer baggier clothes with adornmentsEllie Violet BramleyFri 28 Aug 2026 14.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a competition going on at the US Open this week and it’s not the one involving rackets and balls. Instead, leading men who are not entered into this year’s draw are serving looks rather than aces.Tennis legend Roger Federer took to the court on Tuesday in navy blue polo shirt and shorts, navy blue sweatbands and navy blue socks. The cuts were trim and the top was tucked in. The young Spanish player Carlos Alcaraz wore a Nike vest, untucked and the colour of Ribena, maroon shorts, and trainers that looked like a sweetshop counter.The players represent two style clans that are dominating current menswear: the dads and the dudes. If you’re not sure what side of the sartorial net they’re on, here’s a quick form guide. Novak Djokovic, Taylor Fritz and Félix Auger-Aliassime are all “dads”, while Arthur Fils and Andre Agassi are “dudes”.View image in fullscreenRoger Federer – a ‘dad’.Photograph: Guerin Charles/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz – a ‘dude’.Photograph: Guerin Charles/ABACA/ShutterstockAway from baselines and backhands, David Beckham in his slim, sometimes three-piece suits, actor Theo James, in real life as well as in Netflix series The Gentleman, the second series of which will land next week, Idris Elba and Andy Burnham are all prime examples of “dads”.Dudes, meanwhile, include Brad Pitt, who appears on the cover of September’s Esquire in a red shirt with hot-pink neckerchief, Adam Sandler inchaotic ensembles, and men across Britain.The “dad” look, which has nothing to do with paternal status, is summed up by straight, tight lines, on the whole more muted colours and embellishment for practicality’s sake – a carefully placed sweatband for a tennis player, a pair of neat little cufflinks on a suit. What it is not, says men’s fashion editorHikmat Mohammed, “is just your dad who wears normcore. It’s an elevated dad … they wear Ralph Lauren, they wear Brunello Cucinelli, they wear Loro Piana.” Or, if thousand-pound price tags aren’t in reach, they wear Cos and Arket.Mohammed cites Mark Zuckerberg in caramel-hued cashmere on the Prada front row earlier this year as “dad”. But it’s trickled down to the latest John Lewis menswear lookbook, which is full of sensible overcoats, cashmere cardigans and argyle knits. According to Jacqui Markham, fashion creative director, “a lot of what we’re calling ‘dad style’ is really just great menswear fundamentals rediscovered, after a few years of fashion having moved so fast in the other direction.” Searches for “elevated wardrobe staples” have increased significantly this season, she says – “polo shirts with proper collars, chinos that actually fit, the perfect cut blazer”. Plus “sales of tailoring are up 17% so far this year, making it one of our fastest-growing menswear categories right now.” In high fashion, one of the biggest recent menswear launches also offers up dad style in spades: the luxury label Toteme’s first foray into men’s clothes.View image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg – a ‘dad’ – at a Prada show in Milan earlier this year.Photograph: Alessandro Garofalo/ReutersDudes wear things baggier, have adornments for adornment’s sake – a backwards cap or a chunky chain. It’s an atmosphere that has seenthe late Bill Oddie hailed a style icon. But the patron saint of the style is the aforementioned Sandler, who in 2019 was declared a fashion icon for his unapologetic “grocery-run look” by Vogue writer Liana Satenstein.Influences on the “dude” look include Justin Bieber and his brand Skylrk,which launched last yearand sells baggy hoodies and baggy shorts. “It’s more street wear. It’s more relaxed, it’s more fun, it’s more colourful,” says Mohammed. “They have more camouflage. It’s, like, Chrome Hearts,” he says, referring to the LA brand beloved of Timothée Chalamet (in his current iteration: a “dude”). “The ‘dude’ maybe not stoner, but they’ll take a gummy here and there.”Therise of the so-called “schlub hub”– men who dress as slobs relative to their maximalist, often very on-social media partners – shows that neither does marital status (Bieber,who became a meme for his hoodie and Crocs, worn alongside his wife in a red evening dress, is the prime example). While it can be about age, it’s not about age: “dudes” Pitt and Bieber are 62 and 32 respectively. Luca Guadagnino-favoured actor Drew Starkey (a “dad”) is 32. According to Ben Hewitt, brand director at men’s tailoring brand Hawes & Curtis: “The real shift towards ‘dad style’ is no longer generational, it’s about intentional dressing, whether dressing for the working week or downtime.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt isn’t, of course, a binary: Harry Styles, whose 30-show run at Madison Square Garden began this week, wears “dad”-style togs but with a “dude” energy (see the cut of his suits, the billowing white shirts), plus “dude”-style togs with “dad” energy (see short-shorts with sensible loafers). JFK Jr, who recently re-dominated the zeitgeist thanks to Love Story, was both. For Hikmat Mohammed, who says he is more dude in summer, “dad” in winter: “JFK Jr out of hours was dude but when he was working that was ‘dad’.”View image in fullscreenHarry Styles – ‘dude’ togs with ‘dad’ energy.Photograph: Jason Howard/Bauer-Griffin/GC ImagesWhy are these style camps so prevalent now? The march of the dad has been happening for a while:in 2019 the New York Times Style Magazine heralded“The Unstoppable Rise of the Zaddy,” meaning an older man with impeccable style. Mohammed thinks it could be a recession indicator: “People just want a full look that’s clear and really sharp,” he says. It is also a case of the slower menswear cycle playing out: “I feel like finally the quiet luxury that womenswear had is finally catching up to men.”Plus, actual dads became a menswear inspiration.As the writer Jason Diamond wrote in The Cut this week: “Just a few years ago, there was the idea of a stereotypical dad look that usually included denim shorts, New Balance sneakers, wearing socks with sandals, and higher-rise, more-relaxed jeans. Then, in one of the oddest cases of cultural appropriation, style-conscious and young people started borrowing those looks and making them their own.”For dudes, it helps that menswear in recent years has become more interesting in general, and men, from Colman Domingo to your colleagues, have perhaps felt more comfortable to experiment. The perfect example is Daniel Craig, known as a sharp-suited, small-c conservative dresser (“dad”), he caused a stir with a run of chaotic styling in tandem with becoming the face of Loewe, then under JW Anderson, in 2024. He became fully dude.But who feels comfortable – and who is able – to dress like a dude is complicated. There’s a privilege to being able to present so baggily. Plus, “it’s more expensive to dress ‘dude’,” says Mohammed. Dude-style streetwear can take a lot of searching for, and can cost far more than a shirt and chinos, especially some of the rare, vintage stuff, which “[has] almost become memorabilia. It’s like having a blue chip painting in your house.” It’s not, says Mohammed, “like a grey suit [that] you can buy in Reiss or M&S.”Explore more on these topicsFashionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Infallible style: Pope Leo appears in Vanity Fair’s ranks of most fashionable  | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Pontiff, who has caught the eye in trainers and a baseball cap, praised for taking dress to ‘heavenly heights’
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Pontiff, who has caught the eye in trainers and a baseball cap, praised for taking dress to ‘heavenly heights’
Content: Pope Leo XIV wearing a Chicago White Sox baseball cap in St Peter's Square.Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPope Leo XIV wearing a Chicago White Sox baseball cap in St Peter's Square.Photograph: Sopa Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesFashionInfallible style: Pope Leo appears in Vanity Fair’s ranks of most fashionablePontiff, who has caught the eye in trainers and a baseball cap, praised for taking dress to ‘heavenly heights’Chloe Mac DonnellFri 28 Aug 2026 12.44 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the first time in a decade, Vanity Fair has released abest-dressed list. Featuring 70 names, the list ranks the most fashionable people in the world in 2026. The lineup includes the usual suspects spanning Hollywood actors and global pop stars but nestled among the Hollywood stars is an unexpected entrant. Pope Leo XIV.The 70-year-old head of the Catholic church has been praised by the magazine for taking papal style “to heavenly heights”. His most memorable look? A simple white cassock styled with a pair of Nike trainers.Vanity Fair’s style correspondent José Criales-Unzueta, who worked on compiling the list, said he and the team were impressed by the “innate Americanness” of the way the pope dressed.View image in fullscreenPope Leo in a pair of Nike trainers.Photograph: Vatican NewsThe Chicago-born pontiff has carved out a style niche and garnered a loyal fashion following with his enthusiasm for both bespoke vestments and vintage fashion accessories. Alongside trainers, he prefers simple black oxford shoes to the traditional red papal slippers.He wears a discontinued Swiss-made quartz watch, carries his own battered briefcase and in June 2025 popped a White Sox baseball cap over his papal cap for a general audience in St Peter’s Square. For more formal occasions, he turns to the Italian designer Filippo Sorcinelli, who also created liturgical vestments for the previous popes Benedict XVI and Francis.The Catholic church, with its long mastery of symbolism and optics, is experiencing an uptick driven by gen Z. For Leo, being featured in a publication that its global editorial director, Mark Guiducci, hasdescribedas a “magazine about personalities” and that feels “like the pantheon” works well with the papacy’s own aim to position itself as a modern power.“The world’s embrace of this pope has been stunning to me,” said Robert Orsi, a professor of religious studies at Northwestern University in Illinois. Orsi pointed to Leo’s criticism of AI and calls for peace as also speaking to gen Z.Carol Richardson, a professor of early modern art history at the University of Edinburgh, said the pope, who has his own Instagram account, would be aware of his inclusion on the list. “He and the people surrounding him are very savvy,” she said. “The majority will think it’s fun. They will like the fact it has been noticed how busy he is, that he has to wear trainers to run around in. That he is working.”From Christian Lacroix ecclesiastical riffing in the 80s and the Met’s Heavenly Bodies exhibition in 2018 to crucifixes anddepictions of Christon the most recent catwalks, the papacy has long fascinated fashion. Criales-Unzueta says its appeal lies in its vastness. “There is so much to take in and so much to find inspiration in.”View image in fullscreenA model in the Dolce & Gabbana fashion show at Milan fashion week in June.Photograph: WWD/GettyThe pontiff is listed in Vanity Fair’s “originals” division, a category of individuals commended by the magazine for being “the most outlandish and innovative dressers” with “a singular point of view”. Others on the list include the film-maker Spike Lee and the singers Björk and Rosalía.Criales-Unzueta described the list as “an opportunity to showcase the way fashion and style are deeply embedded in culture and society” and that “style, good style, is a practice that is not reserved for celebrities or their stylists”.View image in fullscreenAn AI-generated image of Pope Francis in a white puffer jacket.Illustration: RedditWhen Leo was first spotted last May wearing Nike trainers in a still from Leone a Roma, a Vatican-produced documentary that retraces his time in Rome before he became pope, the image instantly went viral. Many people mistook it as fake. It was compared to the AI-generated image of Pope Francis wearing an oversized Balenciaga puffer jacket, which has since been described as“the first real mass-level AI misinformation case”. Criales-Unzueta said that was the moment Leo became “a talking point in and outside of fashion”. Trainer fans were quick to identify Leo’s Nikes as a discontinued retro tennis-style shoe that was first sold in the 70s. “What a papal flex,” declaredEsquire, while some online users were quick to christen his style as “holy drip”.By the end of last year, Leo found himself featured alongside A$AP Rocky and Bad Bunny in Vogue’s best-dressed list, while the New York Times named him as one of its 67 Most Stylish People of 2025.Orsi said he had been thinking about what the trainers symbolised. “A sportiness? A familiarity with track and field, basketball courts, running?” he pondered. For him it was “a lightness on his feet, a readiness to move quickly to where he is needed the most”, he said. “They signal that he is approachable, like a good coach, and also humble.”Explore more on these topicsFashionPope Leo XIVThe papacyReligionCatholicismChristianitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Spencer Jones: Dogs review – barking comic sniffs out community through canines | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Behind this grab-bag of papier-mache heads and walkies banter lies a celebration of simply talking to one another
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Behind this grab-bag of papier-mache heads and walkies banter lies a celebration of simply talking to one another
Content: The innocent idealism of nonsense … Spencer Jones.View image in fullscreenThe innocent idealism of nonsense … Spencer Jones.Edinburgh festival 2026ReviewSpencer Jones: Dogs review – barking comic sniffs out community through caninesPleasance Dome, EdinburghBehind this grab-bag of papier-mache heads and walkies banter lies a celebration of simply talking to one anotherBrian LoganFri 28 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst cameRicky Gervais’s cynical cats; now here are Spencer Jones’s optimistic Dogs. One was tawdry, the other couldn’t be sweeter, as the prop-comic delivers this hymn to the canine-human relationship. Likemuch of Jones’s work, it’s a grab-bag, as he circles seemingly at random between character comedy in papier-mache heads, loop-pedal nonsense and dopey dog-walking business with an animatronic mutt. Not all of it is dog-related. And yet, it adds up to something winning, as Jones leads his four-legged friends towards a closing message about social cohesion in acrimonious times – and how our pets can help.It begins as a chat with the audience about their animals, with Jones poshing it up in character as a snobby dog-walker. One strand of the show, taking as its motto the question “Aren’t humans weird?”, functions as a gleeful anthropology of dog owners. They carry bags of poo by their sides. They lose control of their hounds, and in that panic reveal their true selves. Their armoury includes something resembling a ladle – cueing, apropos of nothing, a very funny sequence in which Jones, in horsey false teeth, samples soup supposedly cooked by his audience.Li Jin Hao: Falling from a Moon review – comedy’s Mr Nostalgia is now the man of the momentRead moreAnd crucially, they talk to one another – which might just save us, says Jones, in a homily bolted on to the end of his show. Coming from this performer, who radiates innocent idealism even at 50, you might even believe it. And if not, there’s still the pleasure of an hour spent celebrating the inner child, and spirit of play, in all of us. Highlights here, as Jones bounds way beyond the limits of his theme, include the tale of a brutal parental separation as seen through the eyes of an unwitting kid, and a chat between two blokes competing to suspend the most ash from the end of their ciggies.There are arguably too many instances when Jones displays then abandons an idea (“I haven’t got any material for that …”) rather than develops it. I accepted that, finally, as part of the bricolage appeal of this very charming hour, a scrapbook full of wonky images of dogs, their owners and much else besides.AtPleasance Dome, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Reading and Leeds have dropped BBC Introducing for a new ‘nepo baby stage’. Where does it leave DIY artists? | Reading and Leeds festival | The Guardian
description: As R&L replace the BBC’s unsigned artists stage with one filled with rock scions and a Simon Cowell boyband, many are decrying disappearing opportunities for grassroots acts
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: As R&L replace the BBC’s unsigned artists stage with one filled with rock scions and a Simon Cowell boyband, many are decrying disappearing opportunities for grassroots acts
Content: Gene Gallagher, son of Liam, performs with band Villanelle at All Points East, London, earlier this month.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGene Gallagher, son of Liam, performs with band Villanelle at All Points East, London, earlier this month.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesReading and Leeds festivalReading and Leeds have dropped BBC Introducing for a new ‘nepo baby stage’. Where does it leave DIY artists?As R&L replace the BBC’s unsigned artists stage with one filled with rock scions and a Simon Cowell boyband, many are decrying disappearing opportunities for grassroots actsDaniel Dylan WrayFri 28 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis year’sReading and Leeds festivallineups are a testament to the catholic tastes of a generation who have little regard for musical tribalism or the concept of genre: brash pop stars rub up against drum’n’bass acts, underground rappers, meat-and-potatoes indie bands and much more.What at least 70% of those acts have in common, however, is that early on in their careers they were supported by the BBC’s Introducing scheme, a combination of regional and national radio shows playing music submitted by unsigned artists and festival stages that platform them. For almost 20 years, a BBC Introducing stage has been a core part of Reading and Leeds – until it was scrapped last month.“It’s a loss,” says Juliette Jackson, of the Mercury-nominated indie band the Big Moon, who played the stage in 2015, a year after forming. “It was a really big deal to play that as a new band with no money. It’s huge when you’re starting out – it gives you an opportunity and puts you on a platform.”Over the years, major British artists including Ed Sheeran, Charli xcx, the 1975 and Sam Fender started their careers with support from the initiative, which has few of the barriers to entry of the traditional music industry. Regional DJs suggest local acts for festival slots, with final decisions made by a wider BBC team.View image in fullscreenCharli xcx at Reading festival in 2013.Photograph: Joseph Okpako/Redferns/Getty ImagesReading and Leeds organisers Festival Republic did not respond to detailed questions from the Guardian about why it had pulled the plug on an unsuspecting BBC, who were already planning their 2026 lineup. It has been replaced by the Canopy stage, billed as a “home for new and breaking acts”. In a public statement, Festival Republic claimed it offers greater opportunity: “Previously, only artists who had been selected by the BBC were qualified to play the Introducing Stage – now, we are able to open up this important platform to a much wider pool of emerging talent and book any new music artist for the stage.”But that so-called “wider pool” has come under scrutiny. Fans have been highlighting the connections behind many of the acts booked for the stage, such as Violet Grohl (daughter of Dave Grohl), Cruz Beckham (son of Victoria and David) and Villanelle frontman Gene Gallagher (son of Liam). The boyband December 10 are already signed to a label after they formed on Simon Cowell’s Netflix series The Next Act.It has led some to nickname the Canopy “the nepo baby stage”, and prompted coverage in Private Eye. In an Instagram post, music industry commentator the Secret DJ decried “nepotism and the rising use of famous names over new talent [that] is rapidly destroying the arts”.In a general statement provided to the Guardian, Festival Republic said their booking policy for the stage is “open to emerging artists from all backgrounds and at different stages of development. Artists may be independent or signed and may have come through a variety of routes into the industry.”BBC Introducing editor Kelly Betts told the Guardian: “We will miss being at Reading and Leeds for this year. Programming decisions for that stage are made by the festival organisers, so it’s not really for me to comment on how they choose to curate it.”View image in fullscreenEd Sheeran on Reading’s BBC Introducing Stage in 2011.Photograph: Andy Sheppard/RedfernsJason Carter, who founded BBC Introducing in 2007 and was responsible for forging the relationships with festivals to put on live events, said he was “disappointed to hear [the news] and sad to see it no longer there” but that he “can see both sides”, adding that the industry has changed and “there’s a lot more ways today to access new music that the festival probably wants the opportunity to feed off”.Ex-BBC Introducing presenter Tom Robinson said that while “the beauty of BBC introducing was that you needed no inside access”, it could still occasionally be an “arcane” process. It was also not immune from someone in the industry “having a whisper in the ear of somebody, and an act that a record company was supporting would mysteriously appear on the BBC Introducing stage. But on the whole, it worked, and it was great.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘The working class can’t afford it’: the shocking truth about the money bands make on tourRead moreBut with Glastonbury having a fallow year this year – and with it their BBC Introducing stage – it’s an extra blow for young artists. “Reading and Leeds is a big moment in our calendar,” says Jess Iszatt, who hosts BBC Radio 1’s Introducing show. “Because it’s got such a young audience, it’s a really important one, and it means there’s less opportunity for the artists that we share each week on the show. It’s really sad and it feels like the end of an era.”BBC Introducing is far from finished – it has just announced a full month of live events in 10 cities across the country in November, has recently expanded into the US, and continues to host stages at other festivals. But the sole grassroots pipeline to a major UK event has now been closed off. “When we talk about the successes of it, it [the decision] doesn’t make sense to me,” says Iszatt.View image in fullscreenViolet Grohl, daughter of Dave, who is lined up to play the Canopy stage.Photograph: Bella NewmanAs for accusations of the new model favouring already well-established artists, Robinson prefers to see this as an opportunity rather than a threat. “Let the nepo babies go and do their nepo baby thing. If they make shit music, it’ll still be shit music. If they make great music, they deserve to succeed, but let’s not worry about them.”Instead, he thinks it’s time to go back to celebrating the core purpose of Introducing. “At a time when we’re getting shat on from a great height by multinational streaming giants, I think the grassroots is the future,” he says. “And I’m hopeful that Introducing will carry on supporting gobsmacking talent and helping them find a wider audience.”“I don’t know how they’ve booked their stage,” Iszatt says of Reading and Leeds’ Canopy offering, “but I do know how we book ours. And that would have been committing to supporting artists regardless of their means and wanting to make sure that it would be diverse in every aspect. Because that’s fair.”Explore more on these topicsReading and Leeds festivalFestivalsMusic festivalsPop and rockIndiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Choking is sold to teens as a safe sexual practice. The research says it never is | Sexual consent | The Guardian
description: More and more young people are engaging in sexual strangulation. But experts say there’s no safe pressure – and we have to start talking to teenagers about it
Author: Alyx Gorman
Headline: More and more young people are engaging in sexual strangulation. But experts say there’s no safe pressure – and we have to start talking to teenagers about it
Content: Only a small percentage of adults in midlife and beyond reported being choked in a survey by Dr Debby Herbenick a decade ago; but for those aged 18-39, ‘more than a third of them had reported being choked during sex’.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOnly a small percentage of adults in midlife and beyond reported being choked in a survey by Dr Debby Herbenick a decade ago; but for those aged 18-39, ‘more than a third of them had reported being choked during sex’.Photograph: Getty ImagesSexual consentChoking is sold to teens as a safe sexual practice. The research says it never isMore and more young people are engaging in sexual strangulation. But experts say there’s no safe pressure – and we have to start talking to teenagers about itAlyx GormanFri 28 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen touching someone’s throat, it can only take the pressure of a handshake to cause serious injury, unconsciousness or death. These injuries, which include brain damage and stroke, are often internal and invisible, showing up days or even months after the initial incident occurred. Experts say many who participate in sexual choking are not aware of the risks.Choking or sexual strangulation is common among young people, says Prof Heather Douglas of the Melbourne Law School. In a 2024 survey of 4,702 Australians aged between 18 and 35, she and her research team found that 57% reported ever having experienced sexual strangulation; 51% reported ever having strangled a partner and 43.9% reported participating in both.A police investigation intothe death of a 16-year-old girl in Sydney, who is believed to have become unconscious as a result of asphyxiation during sexual intercourse, has brought the practice to national attention again this week.Douglas says their survey found gender differences in prevalence rates. Young women were more likely to report having been strangled (61%) and young men were more likely to report strangling a partner (59%). Among trans and gender-diverse young people the rates were even higher, with 78% reporting ever having been strangled and 74% reporting ever having strangled someone else. Many had positive perceptions of the act – believing it was safe and led to more enjoyable sex. “I don’t think that a lot of young people know how dangerous it is,” Douglas says.Families need to openly talk to children about misogyny, consent and sexual violence. Here’s how to start | Stephanie Wescott and Jane Gilmore for the ConversationRead moreThere have been similar findings globally. Dr Debby Herbenick is the world’s leading researcher on sexual choking.When Herbenick conducted her first nationally representative survey asking about sexual choking in the United States a decade ago, “the data came back and I was just floored,” she says. Only a small percentage of adults in midlife and beyond reported being choked, but for those aged 18-39, “more than a third of them had reported being choked during sex”.The issue “felt really urgent”, says Herbenick, who is director of Indiana University’s Center for Sexual Health Promotion. When she spoke to her students about it, “they were like, ‘Oh no, it’s OK. We’re all doing the same thing.’“I think what bothered me about it, and worried me, was I felt like they weren’t making informed choices. They were making choices, but they weren’t informed.”Choking, or strangulation?In Australia, when choking results in serious harm, the laws are straightforward. Every state and territory has specific assault laws around strangulation. “Injuries or a strangulation that causes death or really serious harm can’t be consented to,” Douglas says.But the fact that many young people believe choking is low-risk and enjoyable is a vexed public health issue.When Women’s Health New South Wales was funded to improve workforce capacity to respond to strangulation, they ran headlong into this problem. Jackie McMillan, a senior project officer, says: “When we started that work, we realised that we couldn’t do that without also talking about sexual choking.”Physically, strangulation and sexual choking carry the same risks, but “they’re slightly different conversations,” McMillan says.“If people are calling what they’re doing ‘sexual choking’, it’s because they’re making a distinction between what they see as a consensual sexual practice about freedom of sexual expression, and something that is violence. And if you start in with a language of violence, you often lose those people … They’re not interested in what you have to say. They turn off because they think that what you’re talking about is not what they’re doing.”View image in fullscreenObservations of women who frequently participate in choking and women who recently participated in choking both suggested it can cause brain injury.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesHerbenick agrees. “Our research here is very clear that we need to be using the word ‘choking’,” she says. “If people think about what they’re doing as choking, and you call it strangulation, they think, ‘oh, well, I’m not strangling or being strangled. I’m doing choking and choking is safe’.”When Herbenick has asked young people to describe how they choke in detail, overwhelmingly they describe applying pressure to the neck, and list symptoms like dizziness, seeing stars and shortness of breath. “And so certainly anyone in those buckets has some evidence of doing what we would call strangulation,” she says.Herbenick’s research includes a partnership with neuroscientists, testing for brain changes in women who have been choked. While there is a large body of evidence about the neurological effects of strangulation in domestic violence contexts, because the subjective experience of choking can be so different, “in some ways I felt like we had to start from scratch,” she says.For instance, in domestic violence contexts, there is strong evidence that repeat strangulation has more pronounced neurological effects. “But when you look at those multiple versus single strangulation studies, multiple is often like two or three or four times, right? But then if you look at sexual choking, people are often choked, in our studies, an average of 25 times – but sometimes 50 or 100 or 200 or 500 times, because it’s become such a common thing that people do.”Observations of women whofrequently participate in chokingandrecently participatedin choking both suggested it can cause brain injury.But data on effective public health messaging is still nascent.double quotation markWhen we ask college students how old they were when they first learned about choking, on average the age is 15Dr Debby HerbenickHerbenick’s team tried educational messages around the health implications of sexual choking, the importance of receiving specific consent for choking, and messages about the potential legal consequences if an injury occurs. While they found “all three message types were very well received by young adults”, for women, “only the health and consent messages were especially effective” in changing their intentions around choking.For men to change their intentions, “they needed to know about potential legal consequences in the event of injury or death,” Herbenick says. “It was tough to see, because of course we would like to think that knowing that something could be harmful for somebody’s health would be enough to make a lot of people change their behaviour.” That finding persisted regardless of whether men were choking or being choked.All the experts who spoke to the Guardian agreed that widespread and robust sexual education that engages specifically with choking is a vital first step in preventing catastrophic health outcomes.But school systems are not prepared to engage in this level of sexual education, and young people’s information environment, especially on social media, is flooded with misinformation.“There are some sex educators … who claim that there are safe ways to choke. And there’s just a lot of regular people out there making TikTok videos claiming there are safe ways to choke,” says Herbenick.“Pornography is one piece of it,” she adds. “Social media is one piece of it. Anyone whose kids are reading fan fiction or … dark romance novels is almost certainly coming across choking.”On social media, it is often referred to lightheartedly as a “hand necklace” or through memes like “Choke me daddy”.Non-judgmental sex educationThere are no circumstances under which exerting pressure on the soft tissue of someone’s neck is safe; and when drugs or alcohol are involved, the practice becomes even riskier. But this information is not easy to find. McMillan created a website,It Left No Marks, to help combat this void. “We had to build it because it wasn’t there,” she says.Wellington-based criminology academic Dr Samantha Keene says the tragic death ofUK woman Grace Millane in New Zealand in 2020“put conversations about rough sex and sexual choking or sexual strangulation on the public agenda”. But lately, she says, it has fallen off the radar.“We know that sexual choking and sexual strangulation is eroticised in a whole range of media … yet we aren’t addressing that in sexual and relationships education.”“What we know works is having an evidence-based approach,” she says. That means “meeting people where they are” in a non-judgmental way, by giving them access to information that outlines the range of risks associated with this form of sexual practice.A 16-year-old girl has died from suspected sexual choking. How do we come to terms with this? | Lucy ClarkRead moreMeeting young people where they are is not a comfortable conversation, Herbenick says. “A lot of parents are thinking, ‘How am I living in a world where I’m supposed to be talking about strangulation during sex, with my … 13-year-old, 15-year-old?’“I don’t know, but I can tell you that in our studies, when we ask college students how old they were when they first learned about choking, on average the age is 15. Which means that about half of them are learning about it younger than 15.”McMillan says it takes “endorsement” to deliver this kind of education.“That’s endorsement from parents. That’s endorsement from the school. That’s endorsement from the principals. We can’t leave teachers out there alone to discuss websites that they can’t even go to without there being a panic,” she says.“How can we get teachers to talk about pornography if they can’t even visit the sites that the kids are on? We’ve created an impossible situation.”International research has found that many of the young people who engaged in choking felt some degree of pressure from their partner, or their wider social environment, to do so. “So there’s questions around whether that is true consent, if we say it’s truly free and voluntary,” Douglas says.Beyond understanding the consequences physically and legally, “what we need to do is make sure that people are skilled up with the things they need to redirect sexual activities to something else they might find pleasurable,” McMillan says.“And also that particularly young women know sex is meant to be pleasurable. So if you’re not having fun, don’t do that bit.”Explore more on these topicsSexual consentYoung peopleSexualityAustralian educationAustralian police and policingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis | Sunil Acharya | The Guardian
description: Nepalis and Tibetans must not pay the price – with their lives, livelihoods and money meant for education and health – for global heating caused by wealthy states, says Kathmandu-based climate policy specialist Sunil Acharya
Author: Sunil Acharya
Headline: Nepalis and Tibetans must not pay the price – with their lives, livelihoods and money meant for education and health – for global heating caused by wealthy states, says Kathmandu-based climate policy specialist Sunil Acharya
Content: People look out over a damaged building after devastating floods hit Nepal,  28 August 2026.Photograph: Shankar Bhujel/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPeople look out over a damaged building after devastating floods hit Nepal,  28 August 2026.Photograph: Shankar Bhujel/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisisSunil AcharyaNepalis and Tibetans must not pay the price – with their lives, livelihoods and money meant for education and health – for global heating caused by wealthy statesSunil Acharya is an international climate policy and just transition specialist based in Kathmandu, NepalFri 28 Aug 2026 06.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTShareAs a Nepali citizen working on international climate policy for more than a decade, it is difficult to look at the harrowing images coming out of thecatastrophic flash floodthat thundered down valleys in Nepal, sweeping down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, and not feel angry.Not just because of the destruction, but because it comes after years of warnings from scientists and civil society that a rapidly warming planet would make disasters more frequent, more intense and harder to predict. This is what the cost of delaying global climate action looks like.On 26 August, a wall of ice, water, rock and mud tore through communities, destroying homes, markets, bridges, roads and hydropower infrastructure in Nepal and Tibet. Hundreds of people were killed and many more remain missing. The devastation came with terrifying speed. For people living along the rivers and the tourists trekking in the hills, there was little time between the hazard emerging high in the mountains and destruction reaching the valleys below.The immediate questions are rightly being asked about what happened and whether people could have been warned. Nepal needs stronger early warning systems, better monitoring of glaciers and unstable slopes, cross-border communication between Nepal andTibetand greater investment in preparedness.But Nepal’s flash floods expose something more fundamental: the problem is not the absence of a warning system – it is a climate crisis that is producing hazards that behave differently from those the systems were designed to detect.Murderous heat, an endangered food supply, decimated landscapes: embrace the Mediterranean life | George MonbiotRead moreThe warning system in the high-mountain Bhotekoshi valley illustrates the problem. The sudden,debris-laden flood destroyedupstream hydrological stations before they could register a rising water level and trigger an alert.The system was designed to detect a more gradual rise in water levels. This flood arrived as a massive surge of rock, mud and water, destroying the very instruments meant to detect it.Preliminary assessments indicate that a large glacial collapsetriggered an ice-rock avalanche and debris flow, temporarily blocking the river before a massive surge travelled downstream. The precise sequence is still being investigated. Whatever the final scientific explanation, the event shows how quickly hazards can cascade in a warming mountain environment.By the time authorities received information about the flood and warnings were sent downstream, communities closest to the source hadvirtually no time to respond. The monitoring infrastructure did not simply fail to communicate the warning. It was destroyed before it could see the flood coming. That distinction matters. An early warning system designed around yesterday’s floods can be dangerously inadequate for tomorrow’s extremes.This does not make early warning futile. It means we need to be honest about its limits. A warning is useful only if there is time to act. It cannot stop a mountain of ice and rock from collapsing. It cannot protect infrastructure in an increasingly hazardous corridor. And it cannot bring back a home, a hydropower station or a livelihood once it has disappeared.Adaptation has limits, too. For years, Nepal and other vulnerable countries have been ramping up efforts to adapt: by strengthening infrastructure, improving preparedness, and protecting livelihoods – but often without financial support from the countries that historically contributed most to the climate crisis through historical emissions.Nepal needs much greater international support for adaptation: early warning, mountain monitoring, climate science, anticipatory action, resilient infrastructure and disaster preparedness. Because Himalayan hazards originate beyond national borders, this must also include stronger cross-border cooperation and timely sharing of information.The Nepal Himalayais changing rapidly. Glaciers are retreating, while warming is altering the conditions in which glaciers, permafrost and mountain slopes remain stable. The climate in which these hazards occur is changing, and continued warming will make an already difficult risk landscape harder to manage. That is why the global response cannot stop at adaptation.The first task must be to stop making the crisis worse. The countries that benefited most from decades of fossil fuel-driven growth have a particular responsibility to cut emissions rapidly. They also have far greater resources to do so. A just transition away from coal, oil and gas towards renewable energy is therefore a matter of global justice.The fossil-fuel industry cannot be separated from this conversation. Companies have made enormous profits extracting and selling the fuels that have driven global heating, while communities on the climate frontline are being asked to prepare for increasingly destructive impacts with far fewer resources. Even rapid mitigation cannot undo the warming already baked into the climate system or immediately reverse changes already taking place in the Himalaya.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is also a lesson for Nepal. It should not copy the economic model that created the climate crisis and call it development. We have an opportunity to build something different: an economy that puts people, livelihoods and ecological resilience before extraction.The second task requires historical polluter states to pay for loss and damages. Nepal has contributedless than 0.1%of historical global greenhouse gas emissions. Its per-capita emissions remain among the lowest in the world. Yet we are increasingly paying for a crisis we did almost nothing to create. There is something profoundly unfair about this.The cost of such an event is not an abstract figure in a post-disaster risk assessment. It is the lives of people killed by the flood; a hydropower station that took years to build and disappeared in minutes; livelihoods; public money that must now be spent on recovery instead of health and education.Nepal and other vulnerable countries have repeatedly called on developed countries for compensation. The country should not be forced to borrow to recover from disasters to which it contributed so little. Nor should its scarce domestic resources repeatedly be diverted to repair damage caused by emissions of the global north.Loss and damage financemust therefore be additional to existing official development assistance, adaptation and mitigation finance. It needs to be accessible and predominantly grant-based. But it cannot substitute for mitigation. No amount of compensation will be enough if the world continues to burn fossil fuels at the scale it does today. No adaptation programme can keep pace indefinitely with a climate that becomes more dangerous every year.The people living along the Bhotekoshi river did not choose a warming Himalaya. They did not choose the fossil-fuel economy that drove most of the warming. However, with enough support, they can prepare better and build more resilient livelihoods. Sadly, they cannot adapt their way out of every disaster. This is why loss and damage finance is not charity – it is an obligation to people already paying the price.Sunil Acharya is an international climate policy and just transition specialist based in Kathmandu, NepalDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterOpinionClimate crisisNepalTibetSouth and central AsiaChinacommentShareReuse this content

title: The Home Office must not be allowed to bury the spycops inquiry | Imran Khan | The Guardian
description: Doreen Lawrence and other victims of police surveillance have waited decades for justice. Delays and expense due to Met intransigence are no excuse to deny them that, says solicitor Imran Khan
Author: Imran Khan
Headline: Doreen Lawrence and other victims of police surveillance have waited decades for justice. Delays and expense due to Met intransigence are no excuse to deny them that, says solicitor Imran Khan
Content: A protest outside the spycops inquiry hearings in London, 17 October 2025.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA protest outside the spycops inquiry hearings in London, 17 October 2025.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianOpinionUndercover police and policingThe Home Office must not be allowed to bury the spycops inquiryImran KhanDoreen Lawrence and other victims of police surveillance have waited decades for justice. Delays and expense due to Met intransigence are no excuse to deny them thatFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 08.14 EDTShareIn June 2013 Peter Francis, a former Metropolitan police officer, broke a 20-year silence about the role he had played in surveilling the family of Stephen Lawrence in a documentary jointly made bythe Guardian and Channel 4’s Dispatches programme. Two years later, thanks in part to the programme, the Home Office established anundercover policing inquiry, commonly known as the spycops public inquiry, to shed light on the scale of surveillance of activists and trade unionists. That inquiry is now under threat.Francis had served in the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), a Met unit founded in 1968 whose officers lived for years at a time inside political and campaigning organisations under false names.In the months afterStephen Lawrence’s murder in 1993 Francis had been deployed to pose as an anti-racist campaigner. His superiors pressed him to find “dirt” that could be used against the Lawrence family and their supporters. Stephen’s mother, Doreen,told the Guardian and Channel 4that nothing she had heard since her son died had topped the revelation that police had been spying on her while she grieved. She had always suspected the police were watching. She never had proof.The Lawrences were not an isolated case. Justice campaigns and trade unionists across the country were also monitored.At least 139 officers adopted fake names, pretending to be political activists, to spy on people between 1968 and at least 2010. Dozens of anti-racist campaigners, family members of victims of police violence and leftwing activists have been surveilled by police.Suresh Grover, whose Monitoring Group stood behind many of these victims of police surveillance, has told the inquiry that the suspicion directed at Black campaigners was rooted in racist stereotyping. Complaints from Black communities were treated as a public order threat in a way that identical complaints from others were not.The government has justified theconsultation they launched on 16 Julyinto the future of the inquiry on the grounds that it has gone on for more than 11 years and cost £137m. The figures are accurate but their explanation is missing.Applications for anonymity and restriction orders, the vast majority sought by police officers, have slowed down this inquiry. Litigation over cover names, and a persistent unwillingness among former officers and their commanders to say what they did has also hampered the process. The Met, which ran the SDS, made the inquiry slow and expensive. The same government department that funded and served the squad now cites the inquiry’s slowness and expense as reasons to cut it short.Despite a push to wind up the inquiry, it is still producing revelations about the conduct of England’s police forces. Just last year, it revealed that an undercover officer, James Thomson, who had deceived two women into intimate relationships, was suspected of fabricating an elaborate plot tolink an anti-foxhunting activist to a gunthat he told managers the activist intended to collect in France.Before the inquiry, Thomson’s managers admitted that in order to protect the SDS, nothing was done either about his intimate relationship with women he was surveilling or his possible fabrication of evidence. The unit, it seemed, trumped almost anything.The inquiry also exposed numerous instances in which managers appeared to have knowledge of undercover officers having had sexual relationships that continued long after undercover deployments ended, in one case evenafter the announcement of the inquiry.Another shocking discovery from the inquiry is that theMet spent £2.5m hiding an officer– John Dines – from his former lover, going as far as to relocate him from New Zealand to Australia for that purpose.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor the spycops scandal to be possible courts had to be misled. Officers were arrested alongside activists, appeared in court under false names and in some cases gave evidence under them without the court being told.Surveillance was not limited to political activists and victims of racist violence. The Met’s own investigation concluded that special branch and the security services fed material to construction companies that blacklisted more than3,000 workerssuspected of being members of trade unions.More instances of misconduct may come to light in the future, which is all the more reason to keep the inquiry running. The consultation is scheduled to end on 20 September, but there isstill time to write to the Home Officeto make sure that the government knows your views.An inquiry that was set up because the state spied on the parents of a murdered child should not be closed down because the state has heard enough about itself. Doreen Lawrence has been told for 33 years that the truth is coming if she will wait just a little longer. She – and other victims of spying – have waited long enough. The inquiry should finish the job it was given.Imran Khan KC is a practising solicitorDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
