title: Burnham electrified the Labour party by talking about electoral reform – now he needs to act on it | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: The prime minister has lifted the spirits of the public and party members, and must use that goodwill to push through change, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: The prime minister has lifted the spirits of the public and party members, and must use that goodwill to push through change, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Andy Burnham in Kyiv, Ukraine, 24 August.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham in Kyiv, Ukraine, 24 August.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersOpinionElectoral reformBurnham electrified the Labour party by talking about electoral reform – now he needs to act on itPolly ToynbeeThe prime minister has lifted the spirits of the public and party members, and must use that goodwill to push through changeFri 28 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 11.51 EDTShareHe bounded into the packed rally, a spring-heeled intruder whose very presence announced a coup at last year’s Labour conference. And so it was.Andy Burnhamspoke with ebullient self-confidence, yet without aggression or a barrage of insults. They tried to stop him with a bogus constitutional fix barring him from standing in Gorton and Denton. But those Labour hierarchs lost it without him. His subsequent Makerfield victory proved their mistake and opened the door right into No 10 without dispute.At that standing-room-only rally on proportional representation he made a pitch-perfect noteless speech of personal passion about the failure of politics to connect, the decline of Westminster, the public’s distrust and the risk of this lost public belief in democracy. His hands were clean, he never benefited from the monster majority that first past the post had delivered so unfairly toLabourMPs: he wasn’t there at the last two elections. He quit out of despair, returning to repair.Now here we are with an amendment to the representation of the people bill next week that calls for a national commission on the electoral system. A new YouGov poll finds thatmost Labour MPs support it, by 55% to 29%. Many new MPs sitting on wafer-thin majorities, who don’t know which system helps them personally, are voting purely on principle.If, as expected, Burnham gives a clear signal that he intends to put electoral reform into the next manifesto to get public consent, if he confirms it needs a national commission ahead of the election, the amendment may be withdrawn with no needless division.Meanwhile, the Labour conference next month is likely to vote strongly for a motion put up by Labour for a New Democracy, backed by many constituencies,calling for a national commission. In the face of all this groundswell, it would plainly be good for Burnham to get ahead of the mood and own the initiative.This surge in support for proportional representation has been electrified in the past two years by the rise of Nigel Farage. The threat to democracy became brutally real when his party soared 10 points ahead, though thanks to Burnham he nowroughly level pegs with Labour. What was once a constitutional nice-to-have reform, not a priority for Labour people, has become an essential safeguard in the face of real danger to democracy. The prospect of Farage winning a landslide on even less than Labour’s 34% that won 63% of the seats is unconscionable. In May’s council elections, some candidateswon seats on little more than 20% of the vote. Imagine the rebellion if Farage became prime minister despite being by farthe most disliked political leader. That would feel like the complete breakdown of democracy, where the “losers” would no longer peacefully consent to be ruled by “winners” who had been rejected by about three-quarters of voters.Burnham’s magnetic performance at that rally set him on the path to leadership in a party now strongly supporting PR,with 66% of members backing it, and similarpublic approval. Tony Blair knew reform was necessary whenhe commissioned Roy Jenkinsto draw up a system that compromised between absolute proportionality and keeping the constituency link. But he backed off when confronted with the bared teeth of old-time opponents, the unions plus John Prescott and Jack Straw. Keir Starmer plainly supported reform, but then backed off – goodness knows why – as in so many of his self-inflicted errors. It’s Burnham’s time.More puzzling isBurnham’s retreat on capping party donations. The bill will do away with the worst aspect, banning donations of more than £100,000 from foreign donors. But the unions have balked at having UK donations limited, and with it their sometimes threatening influence. Large political donations are a prime cause of corrosive public cynicism about Westminster politics for sale. Burnham’s authenticity is worth many more votes for Labour than can be bought with political advertising. Think again.These have been precious days since Burnham walked through that black front door on 20 July, when you meet people everywhere expressing a rare optimism. Often those who are not natural Labour supporters will confess to unaccustomed hope. Burnham has lifted national spirits through small gestures that address people’s feelings of gloom. Keep that flame alight, don’t drop thatMing vase. Perversely that requires not caution, but boldness.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsElectoral reformOpinionProportional representationFirst past the postAndy BurnhamLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Dear culture-war motorists, look to the future. We’ll all be driving at 20mph soon | Christian Wolmar | The Guardian
description: There are howls of protest from the right about plans for Birmingham to be a 20mph city. But it will be a good thing, and others will follow, says transport writer and podcaster Christian Wolmar
Author: Christian Wolmar
Headline: There are howls of protest from the right about plans for Birmingham to be a 20mph city. But it will be a good thing, and others will follow, says transport writer and podcaster Christian Wolmar
Content: The ‘Spaghetti Junction’ motorway interchange near Birmingham.Photograph: Karl Hendon/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe ‘Spaghetti Junction’ motorway interchange near Birmingham.Photograph: Karl Hendon/Getty ImagesOpinionBirminghamDear culture-war motorists, look to the future. We’ll all be driving at 20mph soonChristian WolmarThere are howls of protest from the right about plans for Birmingham to be a 20mph city. But it will be a good thing, and others will followFri 28 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 06.56 EDTShareIf it can happen in Birmingham, it can happen anywhere. Moves by Birmingham city councilto impose a 20mph speed limit on all roads, apart from a few major thoroughfares, marks a turning point in transport policy that could and should attract imitators.Remember that in the 60sBirminghamwas the city that had a racetrack ​style networks of roads at its heart, ​and a tangle of elevated ro​utes and roundabouts that pushed pedestrians underground and ensured no one would be mad enough to try to cycle. Moreover, it was the headquarters of the UK’s car industry, and its roads were designed more as a test track for new models than a way for people to get to the shops. The emphasis on roads above all else was a deliberate strategy by a city that saw its future inextricably bound up with motoring manufacturers.This ode to the motorcar has gradually been dismantled over the past couple of decades, with the removal of roads turning the city centre into a far more pedestrian-friendly environment. The tram system is being expanded and soon – well actually, not that soon, thanks to endless delays – there will be a new station to accommodate high-speed rail services. Birmingham has been changing, but this latest move will accelerate the process. The imposition of a 20mph zone throughout the city seals the deal. No longer will the needs of cars dominate. Instead, walking, cycling and public transport will be the modes of choice, as car travel becomes slower and more of a hassle.View image in fullscreenDouble-decker buses and tram tracks on Broad Street near the Five Ways entertainment complex in Birmingham.Photograph: Aleksey Zotov/AlamyThe opposition, Conservatives and Reform alike, are already on the warpath, emphasising that this is part of a “war on the motorist” – the cliche brought out whenever any politician attempts to redress the balance between speed and livability in the urban environment. Gradually, far too slowly, they are losing the war, even if they occasionally win the battles: in Toronto, the Ontario premier, Doug Ford, isplanning to rip out 19km of cycle lanes.Diehards such as Ford are on the losing side of history. Birmingham’s shift of emphasis in the urban realm is part of a global phenomenon that is manifested in numerous ways: a pedestrianised main streetin Vancouver, a congestion chargein New York City, 500km of new cycle pathsin Bogotáand so on. Sadiq Khan has got in on the act with the imminentpedestrianisation of Oxford Street(a measure I advocated in a 1998 Evening Standard op-ed).Wales has led the way with “20’s plenty”, the brilliant campaignfounded by Rod Kingtwo decades ago that has influenced policymakers across the country. All Welsh local urban roads were restricted to 20mph in September 2023. Though a few busy streets have reverted to 30mph, by and large the concept has been accepted – and research has shownreductions in road deaths and injuries.View image in fullscreenA ‘20’s plenty’ sign in the village of St Bride’s Major, Wales, where the concept was trialled.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesIn the global race to sustainability and livability, the leader is probably Copenhagen, where ambitions of havinga 50% modal share of cyclingfor commuters may already have been achieved and there are ambitions to go further. Paris, however, is quickly catching up – and demonstrates that change can be rapid once momentum picks up. Since the election of Anne Hidalgo as mayor in 2014, the transformation has been astonishing. It has involved a raft of measures, building on the creation of Paris’s largebike hire schemein 2007 andthe pedestrianisation of the left bank of the Seinein 2013. There has been a comprehensive refocusing of the city’s roads in favour of cyclists and pedestrians, with more than 1,000km of cycle lanes, the removal of thousands of parking spaces, the closure of dozens of school streets and the creation of low-traffic neighbourhoods.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow Paris swapped cars for bikes – and transformed its streetsRead moreAnd here’s the rub: ultimately, the opponents are right. This is an attempt to make life more difficult for motorists, in order to improve the situation for people not travelling in large metal boxes. That does and should involve a raft of measures. Parking spaces need to be removed, access to town centres limited to deliveries, congestion charges imposed. This will give rise to noisy opposition, such as the fanatics in Londonwho broke camerasmonitoring compliance with the ultra-low emission zone (Ulez).We need politicians to explain – and to keep explaining – why the unrestricted use of cars in urban centres is damaging to the local economy as well as to the environment, to people’s health and to the overall feel of a place. It’s no good dodging the fact that the policies that prevailed until the late 1960s, and which still seem to be favoured by backward-looking opponents, were a mistake. Brave politicians need to take on opponents without compromise. Khan did this with the Ulez, standing firm against critics even though some were inside his own party, and the success is for all to see. Not only does research show thatchildren’s lungs are becoming biggerbecause the air is cleaner, but just go to Parliament Hill in Hampstead Heath and look over London: there is no longer a foul yellow miasma permanently overhanging that famous view.Khan could push through his Ulez because he has some mayoral powers, though less than those of his counterparts abroad. Hidalgo and her successor,Emmanuel Grégoire, have powers that British mayors can only dream of. However, opportunity is at hand. Andy Burnham’s emphasis on devolution may offer the opportunity for brave new mayors to follow the examples of Paris, Bogotá and Copenhagen – and Birmingham. Twenty is plenty: get used to it.Christian Wolmar is the presenter of the Calling All Stations podcast and writes a weekly Substack entitled Transport NewsThis article was amended on 28 August 2026. Doug Ford is the premier of Ontario, not the governor as an earlier version saidExplore more on these topicsBirminghamOpinionAutomotive industryRoad safetyRoad transportCyclingEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Dolly Parton was the polar opposite of our bullying president | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: Terrified of being seen as a loser, Donald Trump is nonsensically lashing out – even against our old friend Canada
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: Terrified of being seen as a loser, Donald Trump is nonsensically lashing out – even against our old friend Canada
Content: ‘Her death leaves a hole in the firmament.’Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Her death leaves a hole in the firmament.’Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpDolly Parton was the polar opposite of our bullying presidentRobert ReichTerrified of being seen as a loser, Donald Trump is nonsensically lashing out – even against our old friend CanadaFri 28 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 18.39 EDTShareI’m still grievingDolly Parton. I never met her and always wanted to. She was almost exactly my age and my height and had values I deeply admired. Her death leaves a hole in the firmament.Which brings me to the person whose values are as far from Dolly Parton’s as any human could possibly be and still claim to be human. I’m referring, of course, to the current occupant of the Oval Office.“I knew her a little bit,” Trumpboastedabout Parton on Glenn Beck’s radio show. “She really liked me, I will tell you!” at which Beck laughed out loud.Trump has become mad as a hatter. Loonier than looney tunes. Totally nuts. An enraged, engorged child who’s frightened to death of being seen as a loser.With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael BehrRead moreHe’s losing his war in Iran – the war he decided to startwithout consulting Congress, without eventelling the American peoplehis goal or exit strategy.Now he’s trapped there – with a stronger and more extreme groupin control of Iranthan before his attack, probablymore intenton making a nuclear bomb, blocking the strait of Hormuz (it was open before Trump attacked), causing oil prices to rise again.His current attempt to stop other countries from dealing with Iran is a bad joke. Iran is becoming the dominant power in the Gulf, having demonstrated its ability to damage the oil and gas infrastructure of its neighbors.Besides, China can supply almost everything Iran needs and has a strong incentive to do so.So – now clearly revealed as a loser – what does Trump do? Like any bully, he lashes out.If the courts won’t allow him to put his name on the Kennedy Center, he’lldemolish it. If they say hedoesn’t have authorityto build his ballroom, he’ll fight tobuild it anyway.If his blue paint on the reflecting pool is peeling and the green algae are back and his US attorneywon’t prosecute “vandals”for causing the problem, he’ll stick to his story andblame vandals anyway.It’s all going so badly for Trump that his lizard brain is compelled to show he can bullysomeone. So who does Trump choose? Our old neighbor and friendCanada, who has always gone along with whatever the American colossus ever wanted.Trumpimposed 50% tariffson all cars, trucks, auto parts and steel coming from Canada.Why? Because, hesays: “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years. On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!”In other words, we’re in a trade war with Canada because, well, Trump wants one. A trade war with Canada probably seemed easier to win than a hot war with Iran. And he had to save facesomehow, right?Even though the supreme court found his attempt to use emergency powers for his last round of tariffsto be unconstitutional, he’s nowusing the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930– which, not incidentally, worsened the Great Depression.But maybe a trade war with Canadawon’tbe all that easy to win. Canada has now retaliated withits own tariffsof up to 50% againstabout 700 American products.As the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney,noted on Saturday: “Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us so they can own us, and I promised that will never, ever happen. We are keeping that promise.”Carney is now a hero in Canada with approval ratings in the 60s, while Trump’s have sunkto the low 30s.Humiliation upon humiliation for the man who can’t stand to be humiliated.It gets worse by the day.Netanyahu hasrejected Trump’s planfor Gaza. Congressional Republicans areblasting himfor increasing imports of ground beef.Universities arerejectinghis latest directives. ABC hassued his regimefor threatening its broadcast licenses.Even the bond market won’t be cowed. It’s in open revolt against his bonkers fiscal policies.How Mark Carney’s speeches have become political earthquakes | Ted WidmerRead moreThank goodness for him that Darline Grahamwon South Carolina’s special electionRepublican runoff to replace her brother. Trump had made her race all about himself – of course –telling supportersthat her opponents were “only fighting Darline because they want me to lose”.I’m sure that’s what he’s telling himself about his many losses and humiliations – that they’re all due to his opponents plotting and scheming against him.(Hopefully, he’s about to lose Congress, too.)That’s an easier story for Trump to accept than the truth: that his carefully cultivated aura of invincibility has just about disappeared.The would-be emperor has no clothes. Almost everybody now sees the thin-skinned, peevish, petty, incompetent, corrupt, naked infant who’s been parading around in presidential garb.And they’re not going to obey him any more.Dolly Parton was a huge winner, bless her soul. Trump is the biggest loser on the planet.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionDolly PartonUS politicsCanadaUS-Israel war on IranRepublicansMark CarneycommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: Is there anything sadder than the end of summer? | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: Plus, views from the Cotswolds of Harry and Meghan’s return, and the embarrassing anachronism that is Ali G
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Plus, views from the Cotswolds of Harry and Meghan’s return, and the embarrassing anachronism that is Ali G
Content: ‘Distraction comes in the form of the back-to-school shop, which, stupidly, I think will be nice to do the old-fashioned way, in an actual shopping centre.’ People on an escalator in Liverpool.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreen‘Distraction comes in the form of the back-to-school shop, which, stupidly, I think will be nice to do the old-fashioned way, in an actual shopping centre.’ People on an escalator in Liverpool.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPADigested weekSchoolsDigested week: Is there anything sadder than the end of summer?Emma BrockesPlus, views from the Cotswolds of Harry and Meghan’s return, and the embarrassing anachronism that is Ali GFri 28 Aug 2026 06.11 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 06.37 EDTShareMondayIs there anything sadder than the end of summer? As schools go back next week and parents rely on the boosting effect of a return to routine, we look around for other ways to soften the blow. A few things this year that might make it easier: the need for rain ensures that the advent of autumn is slightly less depressing than usual; people with attic conversions in which you could bake a muffin over the summer will be able to use them again; and if you happen to be a woman of 50 or thereabouts, the fresher weather is ... a relief.Still, looking down the barrel of dark nights and the slow descent towards Christmas clenches the spirit and I find myself pining for the very recent past. I think of this as micro-nostalgia, a form of self-indulgence that, in this case, involves looping back in my mind to the first days of summer when it was all still ahead of us. There should be a word for this particular and intense kind of yearning, which might be described as: a wistfulness for past anticipation based on the certainty of future nostalgia. Even the Germans might struggle to find a compound to cover it.Distraction comes in the form of the back-to-school shop, which, stupidly, I think will be nice to do the old-fashioned way. And so we take our actual bodies to an actual shopping centre, walk around for five hours, visit 700 shops, buy two lip glosses and some stick-on nails, then come home and order the entire back-to-school haul online. So much for nostalgia.TuesdayAt the National Theatre in London for a production ofthe musical Pride, which has been making people weep since it first opened in Cardiff in March, and London in June, and will, presumably, continue to do so when it transfers to the Bridge Theatre in Southwark this winter. I was ready with tissues but managed to hold on – just – despite the show’s absolute best efforts to take me down.If you know the story, which chronicles the solidarity between striking Welsh miners and gay activists in the mid-1980s, you’ll understand the show’s potential for poignancy. The stage production is, if anything, even more moving than the 2014 film. Part of this is because it leans slightly more heavily than the film into the Aids story. Towards the end of the show, Pride uses a trope popularised in recent times by Madonna, who, during her Celebration tour in 2023, sang Live to Tell while images flashed up on screens of all her old cohorts from the 80s who had died of Aids, and everyone in the audience lost it. The recently shuttered Broadway show, Cats: Jellicle Ball, which celebrates the 80s drag queens of Harlem, did a similar thing to stunning effect.And it’s not spoiling anything to say that Pride uses a similar method to flay the audience into a final state of sniffing, gulping and hiccuping disintegration as fallen heroes come up on screens in black and white – captured in a youth made more glorious by its horrifically truncated end.WednesdayHarry and Meghanfly back into Britainafter six years in the US, and the world’s media is treated to the opinion of British people stopped on the street for their thoughts. It always strikes me how much better prepared the average American is when called on by a passing TV hack to offer a spontaneous view. This was particularly in evidence this week as passers-by in Nashville were asked about Dolly Parton and were, by and large, effortlessly fluent, while those in the Cotswolds, where the not-quite-royal couple are reported to be moving, were required to say something sensible about them. (There was a lot of shifty body language, sliding eye contact and “made their bed and lie in it” sort of commentary, all of which made me feel very fond of my people.)Meanwhile, the Daily Mail dug up the term “praetorian guard”, and raised, with relish, the prospect of the two brothers running rival courts, while the New York Timesspeculatedon William’s “silence” since his brother’s return. Which raised the question: feud or otherwise, what did anyone actually expect the Prince of Wales to say?ThursdayPushback against the forthcoming Ali G movie, Ali G: Who Iz I?, gathers force in the form of apetition– 35,000 signatures and counting – to keep the film out of cinemas on the basis that, under not very subtle cover of satire, it reinforces racist stereotypes. On the other hand, it may be the case that no petitions are necessary if Sacha Baron Cohen’s 20-year-old vehicle strikes modern audiences as an embarrassing anachronism that is as bafflingly bad as it is crashingly unfunny.Early indications aren’t good. You might have seen Baron Cohen in character earlier this year, towing a camera crew to Centre Court at Wimbledon and contriving to get himself thrown out. Dressed in a white tracksuit with a marijuana leaf insignia that turned on a joke about the All England club’s “grass”, he did a piece to camera in which he joked that tennis was a “crap version of ping pong” and made some gags about drug dealing. It’s a short video I defy you to get through without hiding your face in mortification.The other Baron Cohen characters haven’t aged well, either. Does anyone want to see the comedian as Bruno, a straight guy playing a screaming gay that plays on a tonne of homophobic tropes, ostensibly to flush out the bigotry of its targets but which invites the audience to recoil alongside them? Borat was the best of the bunch, somehow managing to retain an endearing core that gave the character more humanity than the others and lacked what feels like the speciousness of Ali G.Why is he doing this? (One can make a good guess.) Baron Cohen has also directed the movie and surely, nobody wants it. If Ali G had novelty value back in the day, he has long been replaced by characters such as Diana Morgan’s Philomena Cunk, who manage to send up dumb TV culture without humiliating people or trading in caricatures that get a charge off the very thing they purport to be spoofing.FridayA good end to the week in the form of an outdoor screening at London’s Barbican of the 90s film Beautiful Thing, an adaptation of Jonathan Harvey’s classic coming-of-age play and a movie I must have watched 100 times back in the day. The film, directed by Hettie Macdonald and starring Tameka Empson as Leah and Linda Henry as Sandra, Jamie’s mum, killed me then. This is partly down to the soundtrack from the Mamas and the Papas, and also to all those 90s references – peppermint foot lotion from the Body Shop, anyone? – that feel so far removed they might be signifiers of a lost world in a JG Ballard novel. Of all the film’s lines, it’s strange what sticks and the line I keep thinking of ahead of the screening is: “The whole of bloody Thamesmead can hear you!” More tissues!Digested week in picturesView image in fullscreen‘I could’ve been big, but politics needed me more …’ Andy Burnham in Kyiv in the mobile recording studio of the Ukrainian military and artistic unit, which performs on the frontlines, in hospitals and at rehabilitation centres.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘If that’s heavy rainfall I hear, please remember to enjoy the flooding as nature’s very own water park!’ Reform UK’s Richard Tice (left) at a press conference with Lee Anderson in London.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe British army road tests new ‘scare-them-to-death’ uniform. The armed forces minister, Louise Sandher-Jones, meeting British troops in Estonia, where they are deployed as part of Operation Cabrit.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAExplore more on these topicsSchoolsDigested weekMusicalsSacha Baron CohenPrince HarryMeghan, the Duchess of SussexTheatrecommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s midterm campaign theme is unrequited love | Sidney Blumenthal | The Guardian
description: The president senses a crisis in his cult of personality. He believes the path to victory is through unwavering devotion
Author: Sidney Blumenthal
Headline: The president senses a crisis in his cult of personality. He believes the path to victory is through unwavering devotion
Content: ‘He is running against Isaac Newton, and Newton always prevails.’Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘He is running against Isaac Newton, and Newton always prevails.’Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpTrump’s midterm campaign theme is unrequited loveSidney BlumenthalThe president senses a crisis in his cult of personality. He believes the path to victory is through unwavering devotionFri 28 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 06.15 EDTShareDonald Trump has framed his theme for the midterm elections. It has come to him as naturally and inevitably as staring into the mirror, beyond any logic or argument, his definitive answer to no specific issue, providing no understanding of any particular problem, but transcending all of them. His political theme is more primal than programmatic, more instinctive than analytical, a heartfelt expression to protect his greatest romantic attachment, his obsessive fixation, his idealized object: himself.Trump’s campaign theme is unrequited love. Unlike the pollsters, media consultants and pundits, he alone has grasped the magnitude and the source of the existential crisis threatening his politics. He has identified the problem for theRepublicansas the faltering measure of complete devotion to him. His demand has nothing to do with mutual affection. It is a ploy to reassert his slipping control, a manipulative test to prove loyalty to him, or else. There can be no absolute rule without an absolute ruler; no absolute ruler without absolute submission; no absolute submission without the expression of absolute love. His sadness at its fading gives way to anger, paranoia and greater acts of retribution. He equates the fear he instills as a form of love. Trump accepts subservience, from whatever motive, as affection or its closest equivalent. He cares nothing about sincerity, so it’s all in the show. The less love displayed, the more fear required. Yet there is no rebound, but only deeper rejection.With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael BehrRead moreTrump isheading towardthe floor for presidential unpopularity –Nixon during Watergateon the eve of his resignation, Trumanlate in his second termat the depth of the Korean war, and George W Bushat the 2008 financial crash. But Trump’s breakdown differs uniquely from theirs. His decline has come earlier in his term, been more sustained, and his disintegration has not stabilized but is accelerating. He is being crushed by the accumulation of catastrophic events of his own making to which his impulsive response is to double down in each and every area. Stalemated in his reckless Iran war, he has nowlauncheda heedless trade war against Canada that will devastate Republican candidates in the northern tier of states. His latest vanity project is gestural retribution torenameLake Ontario as “Lake America”, a watery ballroom. Admission of error for Trump would be the denial of self-love.Trump began his campaign on his unrequited love theme on 16 August during a Fox News interview in which he discussed his press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, leaving her job after just having a baby. He had held her up as meeting his highest criterion inremarkslast December: “Isn’t she great? Is Karoline great? … She gets up there with that beautiful face and those lips that don’t stop,ba ba balike a little machine gun.” Now,he triedto make a joke of her departure that expressed resentment at abandonment. “In fact, she likes her children more than she likes Trump. I’m very concerned about that,” he said. Then herepeatedhis unfunny “joke” at a campaign rally in South Carolina on 21 August: “I just learned she loves the baby more than she loves Donald Trump, and I’m very angry …” Trump’s lame attempt at humor was a rare instance of his truth-telling and self-revelation, a contemporary illustration of Freud’s Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious.Trump was in South Carolina to campaign for his chosen candidate in the Republican primary, Darline Graham, who hehad insistedbe appointed to the Senate seat of her brother Lindsey Graham afterhe diedon 11 July. Darline Graham confessed to cluelessness when asked in a debate about her position on Taiwan. “National security is not my thing,”she answered. “I’m not … that informed on national security.” But she was fully informed on the necessity of obedience to Trump. “You saved our country, and I want to thank you for that,” shesaidat the rally. Trump praised his worshipper: “She’s got a good gene pool.” She was born to love him. She stood in stark contrast to the immigrants he had described as “poisoning the blood of our country”.Then Trumpcalled on the crowdto embrace his new theme. “So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot … So just say that I’m on the ballot one more time. You got to say it.” He wishes every candidate to sound like Darline Graham in proclaiming him the national savior. He insists he is beloved, and if those who revere him turn out the Republicans must win. In fact, though he is not on the ballot in the midterm elections, Trump is the central issue. Voters do not have to “pretend, please”.Trump intuitively comprehends that the midterm elections are about him in a way that makes this midterm unlike any other. In the marrow of his bones, he senses it is a crisis of his cult of personality.double quotation markWhen charisma fails, the movement implodes. If the leader is not worshipped, his uber-principle – the leader principle – collapses: no fuhrerprinzip, no FührerTrump’s Maga was never a new party structure, but constructed on his wreckage of the old Republican party. In its place, every particle of the replacement is connected to the leader to advance his supremacy and self-enrichment. Everything flows upward, all heads tilted, all knees bent. Maga has always been Maga Inc of, by and for one man. The movement is the man.When charisma fails, the movement implodes. If the leader is not worshipped, his uber-principle – the leader principle – collapses: nofuhrerprinzip, no Führer.Trump’s plea for their unconditional love – “pretend, please” – defies gravity. He is running against Isaac Newton, and Newton always prevails. Intensity is gauged by “strongly approve” and “strongly disapprove” poll numbers. More than the general statistics of approval or disapproval, these provide insight into the motivation of voters that determine the contour of elections. Trump now stands at 13% “strongly approve” in the most recentReuters-Ipsos Poll. His “strongly disapprove” rating is at 49%. His total approval is at 33%, while disapproval is at 65%. Those in the “somewhat approve” category include low propensity soft voters especially inclined to skip midterm elections. And this poll was taken before his declaration of trade war against Canada.All along, the Republicans have been Trump’s indispensable accomplices. Even if they were disposed to object, they could do nothing to draw him back from his “pretend, please” campaign. His anxiety to rescue his invincible image from the reality he’s created makes him more inescapable than ever. Any effort to restrict him will provoke his rage. He will not diminish himself for the sake of the party or even his own future. He plans tospend millionsfrom his Maga Inc political action committee to tell the voters that they have never had it so good – “the greatest economy we’ve ever had, by far”, hesays. He has mocked the suggestion that “affordability” might be a problem for many – it’s “a word they”, the media, “devised”, hehas said. Trump intends to stage amini conventionin Dallas on 9 September, featuring Donald Trump to “celebrate … our achievements”. Republicans are locked almost uniformly into blind support, with the Maine senator Susan Collinsventuring hollow criticismof the Canadian tariffs that makes her seem powerless and infuriates the remaining Maga base. Just as Trump has trapped himself, he has trapped the Republicans. The expenditure of tens of millions to depict his dire consequences as paradise on earth will have the unintended effect of supercharging the already motivated “strongly disapprove” voters and disillusion those who cannot help but be aware of the actual conditions of their own lives.Jon Ossoff went low on Natalie Harp. The plan worked | Moira DoneganRead moreThe sudden surfacing of Natalie Harp as a meme at this particular moment propitiously coincides with the wobbling of Trump’s cult. The 35-year-old is his model of the perfect staffer, perfect companion and perfect American citizen. If unrequited love is the problem, she is the solution. In Trump’s hierarchy of need, his pyramid of status, love and self-actualization, she is at the apex.Harp is his “binky”, asMaggie Habermanof the New York Times has called her, his comfort blanket, his plush bunny rabbit. The “human printer” who trails after him, pressing the button to churn out an endless stream of adulatory articles, conspiracy theories and “alternative facts”, has become an extension of his nervous system. The former anchor at the fringe far-right One America News Network serves as Trump’s personal anchor. Harp broadcasts around the clock to an audience of one. She is the connector to the neurons of the far right, serving as aconduitto dodgy characters such as Laura Loomer with herlists of national security officialswho were supposedly disloyal. Harp is Trump’s neurotransmitter who distributes a steady supply of dopamine and delusion.Harp’s self-abasing devotion to Trump, expressed in herlettersto him, serves as a kind of inadvertent political manifesto for the cult, a template for followers. Harp tellingly muddles a line from Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice – Mr Bennet blessing his strong-willed daughter Elizabeth in her engagement to Darcy – to demean herself andoffer subservienceto Trump: “To modify a classic, ‘I could not have parted with you, to anyone less worthy’ – And, I will add, it is I who is unworthy.” In another letter, after self-disparaging apologies, Harp writes: “You are all that matters to me. I don’t want to ever let you down. Thank you for being my Guardian and Protector in this Life … With all my Heart.”As public opinion curdles on Trump, no longer able to “pretend, please”, Harp has not come to the wisdom of Conway Twitty in his 1959rockabilly hit:My only prayer will beSomeday you’ll care for meBut it’s only make believeSidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln:A Self-Made Man,Wrestling With His AngelandAll the Powers of Earth. title: The Guardian view on political donations: Labour should curb the power of big money | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham favoured a £500,000 donations cap. In office, he’s backing away. That is a mistake
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham favoured a £500,000 donations cap. In office, he’s backing away. That is a mistake
Content: ‘Mr Burnham was right in May. He is wrong now.’Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Mr Burnham was right in May. He is wrong now.’Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersOpinionPoliticsThe Guardian view on political donations: Labour should curb the power of big moneyEditorialBefore becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham favoured a £500,000 donations cap. In office, he’s backing away. That is a mistakeFri 28 Aug 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTShareOn the campaign trail in Makerfield, Andy Burnham told a democracy activist that he favoured a political donations cap of around£500,000and wanted it reduced over time. His government is now resisting amendments that would move in precisely that direction. Mr Burnham was right inMay. He is wrong now. It is difficult to argue that restricting a single person to giving half a million pounds a year to a political party would damage democracy. Such a cap would only affect themega-rich. Reducing the cap would force parties to wean themselves off the present regime that allows the rich too much say.There are two contra arguments swilling aroundLabour. The first is that there should be room for wealthy, progressive donors – whose cash helps rebut claims that Labour is in the pocket of the trade unions. The second is the warning from unions that a cap could undermine their ability to contribute to the Labour party.Neither of these arguments holds much water. Whatever benefit Labour might derive from rich friends is dwarfed by the wider damage caused by parties being bankrolled by a few rich individuals. Mr Burnham has registered £345,000 of donations over the past year, including £164,000 frombillionaireLord Sainsbury. In comparison, Thai-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne gave Reform UK a single£9mdonation in August 2025 – a sum which exceeds the£8min trade union donations that Labour will get this year.The timing makes Labour’s retreat baffling. This newspaper’s revelation of Nigel Farage’sundisclosed£5m gift from Mr Harborne in 2024 has turned big money in politics from an abstract concern into a live issue. Reform’s support has fallen markedly in recent months.View image in fullscreenStella Creasy.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianMr Burnham could recover the situation by backing amendments from two Labour MPs. Stella Creasy’schanges, which have cross-party support, start with a £500,000 cap – Mr Burnham’s own figure – before reducing it, while allowing parliament to alter the level. She proposes to exclude trade union political funds, recognising that money aggregated from thousands of members differs fundamentally from a donation controlled by a single billionaire or company. The former represents many individual contributions; the latter concentrated economic power. Unions warn that a cap might restrict their political activity. But Ms Creasy explicitly protects their member-funded campaigning cash. Opponents should explain why that safeguard is inadequate.Anneliese Dodds, a former Labour cabinet minister,asksthe right question: if ministers believe the growth of big money in politics is a risk, why retain the Conservatives’ sharply increased election spending limits? A donations cap limits how much concentrated private wealth can enter party politics; lower expenditure limits reduce how much money parties need to raise in the first place.Instead of backing these measures, tabled as amendments to therepresentation of the people billat next week’s report stage vote, ministers are pressing ahead with elaborate rules governing where political money comes from and how it reaches parties. Yet this year’s Rycroftreview, which ministers are responding to, urged parliament, “if it wishes to restore confidence in the political process and to keep big money out of UK politics”, to consider spending limits. Given the scandals of recent years, it is astonishing that Labour is declining to regulate how much political influence any single wealthy donor can purchase.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the loan of the Bayeux tapestry: a manifestation of soft power | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The British Museum’s landmark cultural exchange is a symbol of post-Brexit rapprochement between Britain and France
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The British Museum’s landmark cultural exchange is a symbol of post-Brexit rapprochement between Britain and France
Content: A scene from the Bayeux tapestry. ‘In these fractured times, the enduring appeal of this 11th-century artefact speaks of a need for a national story.’Photograph: Ardee Napolitano/ReutersView image in fullscreenA scene from the Bayeux tapestry. ‘In these fractured times, the enduring appeal of this 11th-century artefact speaks of a need for a national story.’Photograph: Ardee Napolitano/ReutersOpinionBayeux tapestryThe Guardian view on the loan of the Bayeux tapestry: a manifestation of soft powerEditorialThe British Museum’s landmark cultural exchange is a symbol of post-Brexit rapprochement between Britain and FranceFri 28 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTShare“Harold Rex interfectus est”: King Harold is killed. As every British schoolchild knows, the Bayeux tapestry depicts a turning point in the history of these islands: defeat at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, which would lead to the ascent of William the Conqueror to the English throne. Itsreturn to the UKfor the first time in nearly 1,000 years is being hailed as a hugely historic moment in its own right. The loan of the tapestry (technically an embroidery of wool on linen) to the British Museum inexchangefor UK treasures from Sutton Hoo is the ultimate manifestation of soft power – a 70-metre symbol of post-Brexit Anglo-French rapprochement in comic-strip form.Ticket sales for the exhibition, which opens on 10 September, werethe biggest in a single day in the museum’s history, with online queues of 80,000. Radio 4 is devotinga day of special broadcaststo mark the arrival of the tapestry, including a new drama with verse from the poet laureate Simon Armitage. Themuseum’s videosexplaining this tale of ambition, friendship, betrayal and revenge are fittingly narrated by Traitors presenter Claudia Winkleman. Norman-mania is here.“It probably took more years to deliver this project than all the Brexit talks,”Emmanuel Macron jokedin a speech to the British parliament last year. To the list of 623 men, 190 horses, 35 dogs and only three womendepictedon the tapestry, one might add a 21st-century British king, a French president, and three British prime ministers who have helped to bring it here – not to mention the millions of pounds it has cost.Two previous attempts – one for Queen Elizabeth’s coronation in 1953 and another in 1966 – failed. It would not have succeeded this time if the tapestry had not needed to be moved for renovations to the Bayeux Museum in Normandy. Many curators and restorers still believed the risks of bringing it to London were too great. The late David Hockney called the transferral“madness”. One of his final works, the 90-metre iPad friezeA Year in Normandie, on display this summer at the Serpentine gallery in London, was testament to his lifelong fascination with the tapestry. Anonline petitionagainst the move attracted nearly 80,000 signatures. However, political will won.From poetry to parody – from Tennyson’s 1876 epic verse drama Harold to anepisodeof The Simpsons – the tapestry has enjoyed a rich cultural afterlife. But its message has always been political. Napoleon and the Nazis recognised its potential as a propaganda tool. In 2014 Nigel Farage, then leader of Ukip, sported a Bayeux tapestry silk tie during the Rochester byelection, as a reminder of“the last time we were invaded and taken over”. The tie sold out in 24 hours.In these fractured times, the enduring appeal of this 11th-century artefact speaks of a need for a national story. The Bayeux tapestry is a devastatingly human saga. With war raging in Europe, this medieval masterpiece is a reminder of conflict’s brutality, human suffering and the importance of collaboration between countries. The tapestry will return to France for the 1,000th anniversary of William the Conqueror’s birth next year. According to Philippe Bélaval, Mr Macron’s former culture adviser:“Such a loan will only happen once and never again.”This is truly a once-in-a millennium event. Hopefully, its success will pave the way for equally ambitious cultural exchanges in the future.Vive l’entente cordiale!Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Russ Abbot: a class act, on stage and off | TV comedy | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Simon Hattenstone’s interview with the retired actor and comedian
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Simon Hattenstone’s interview with the retired actor and comedian
Content: Russ Abbot in a sketch from the BBC television series The Russ Abbot Show on 1 April 1989.Photograph: Radio Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRuss Abbot in a sketch from the BBC television series The Russ Abbot Show on 1 April 1989.Photograph: Radio Times/Getty ImagesTV comedyLettersRuss Abbot: a class act, on stage and offReaders respond to Simon Hattenstone’s interview with the retired actor and comedianFri 28 Aug 2026 11.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTShareSimon Hattenstone’s wonderful interview with Russ Abbot (‘In 1984, I worked 363 days’: how Russ Abbot soared to success – then walked away, 24 August) brought back a treasured story that leaves my family eternally grateful to him.During the summer of 2010, we travelled from Scotland on holiday, staying in Windsor, and attended Oliver! at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. When the show ended late at night, I had to set off on a 30-minute walk just to retrieve our car.With my wife in a broken-down electric wheelchair and our two daughters, aged just eight and six, beside her, they faced a long, vulnerable wait on the pavement. Making matters worse, I then got caught in a central London driving nightmare, desperately trying to navigate back to them with a broken satnav, no map, and no knowledge of the city streets.When Russ walked out of the stage door, he didn’t just pass by. Seeing my stranded family and my young daughters deeply distressed, he stayed and went to work comforting them, running through multiple Fagin monologues right there on the street. The girls were so completely sidetracked that they forgot anything was amiss. They were absolutely buzzing to meet “Fagin”, and it became an overriding memory they talked about all night. He turned a stressful situation into pure magic.Our evening was saved not only by Russ’s incredible warmth, but also by the extraordinary humanity of two Polish doormen from a nightclub across the street. They rushed over to assist, letting my children stay warm in the back of one of their family cars until I finally found my way back.To my family, the man who stepped out of the Drury Lane stage door that night was a true class act, both on and off the stage.Philip ShowellHamilton, South LanarkshireSimon Hattenstone’s interview with Russ Abbot took me straight back to our living room in the early 1980s – Saturday evening, dinner over, and all of us settling into that post-dinner golden hour of family television.Russ always seemed such a happy chap, and his humour was wonderfully infectious. I can still hear my dear mother’s uncontrollable laughter one evening in particular as he launched into a gloriously over-the-top Bruce Forsyth, complete with cries of “higher! Higher!”More than 40 years on, the memory still makes me smile. Thank you, Simon, for taking me back to that very happy time and place. And to Russ and his wife, Trish, after 60 years together, may the laughter continue.Noel HineyDublin, IrelandReading the Russ Abbot interview reminded me of a time when Saturday afternoon telly into the early evening would be a gathering force for our family.Wrestling and Big Daddy and the latest American show like The A-Team or Airwolf, followed by gameshows hosted by the big comedian of the time and then the sketch comedy series. It didn’t matter if it was a repeat such as The Two Ronnies or Russ Abbot’s Madhouse.Strict timings were adhered to and tea worked around a Radio Times-driven schedule – that, or you mastered the recording settings on your VCR.Something’s been lost in an era where each of us has an individual screen and streaming services, meaning we can watch as and when we like. My father had the remote, and dictated the narrative on the box, but at least we were all in the same room at the same time, laughing simultaneously.It’s never as good as you remember – but I do miss it. Lovely article.David HowesHebden Bridge, West YorkshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: There can be huge comfort in end-of-life preparation | Death and dying | The Guardian
description: Letter: Gill Empson says her husband wanted to make sure that the family would not have a mess to sort out after his death from a terminal illness
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Gill Empson says her husband wanted to make sure that the family would not have a mess to sort out after his death from a terminal illness
Content: ‘He passed on his watch to our grandson and his rings to our sons. To do this himself gave him tremendous pleasure.’Photograph: Nicolas McComber/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘He passed on his watch to our grandson and his rings to our sons. To do this himself gave him tremendous pleasure.’Photograph: Nicolas McComber/Getty ImagesDeath and dyingLettersThere can be huge comfort in end-of-life preparationGill Empsonsays her husband wanted to make sure that the family would not have a mess to sort out after his death from a terminal illnessFri 28 Aug 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTShareSarah Phillips’ article struck such a chord (What end-of-life experts know about living well: love your wrinkles, celebrate birthdays and don’t obsess over work, 13 August). My husband, Dick, died last month with pulmonary fibrosis. His last few months were physically very difficult, but he gained an enormous amount of comfort from sorting out his affairs; he said it was so that the family wouldn’t have a mess to sort out when he had gone.He changed everything into my name and prepared lists of passwords for our three sons. He passed on his watch to our grandson and his rings to our sons. To do this himself gave him tremendous pleasure.Dick regarded himself as very lucky to have had 80 years largely free of illness, and he spent his last three years, when he had a terminal diagnosis, making sure that those left behind would be able to manage without him.Gill EmpsonAston-on-Trent, DerbyshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Protect fossils from hammer-wielding tourists | Fossils | The Guardian
description: Letter: Jill White responds to an editorial calling for fossils to be given legally protected national-treasure status
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Jill White responds to an editorial calling for fossils to be given legally protected national-treasure status
Content: An ammonite at the fossil graveyard at Lyme Regis in Dorset.Photograph: Loop Images/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn ammonite at the fossil graveyard at Lyme Regis in Dorset.Photograph: Loop Images/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesFossilsLettersProtect fossils from hammer-wielding touristsJill Whiteresponds to an editorial calling for fossils to be given legally protected national-treasure statusFri 28 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTShareI write this while sitting on Charmouth beach in Dorset with my required reading of the Saturday Guardian, as I do regularly. Your editorial (The Guardian view on the export of fossils: they deserve national treasure status, 21 August) produced a hollow laugh as – this being the centre of fossil hunting on the Jurassic Coast – I am surrounded by armies of hammer-wielding tourists busy smashing the daylights out of any rock available around them. The vast majority have no idea which stone types are likely to bear fossils and don’t report any finds even if they are lucky. Others take carrier bags full of stones back to their cars.Thus, we have no idea what fossils are being lost to the record every single day here, and so I completely support the suggestion of giving them legal protection. Of course, amateur collecting has a valuable place in unearthing important fossil finds, but only if they are shared and documented. The Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre valiantly tries to educate and inform visitors, but sadly these will inevitably be the minority.Charmouth is a key part of the designated Jurassic Coast world heritage site, but I can’t think of any others where visitors are allowed, or even encouraged, to bring or rent hammers to wreck the protected features and/or remove them from the site unrecorded. If we want to protect our fossil heritage for future generations to study, we could make a start by regulating this geological vandalism.Jill WhiteMusbury, DevonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Abbey Road | Putin is no Marxist | Nort a homophone | 35mm film canisters
Content: On the Abbey Road LP cover, Paul McCartney was not only barefooted but was actually leading with his right foot.Photograph: Hugh Williamson/AlamyView image in fullscreenOn the Abbey Road LP cover, Paul McCartney was not only barefooted but was actually leading with his right foot.Photograph: Hugh Williamson/AlamyBrief lettersPaul McCartneyLettersFocus on Paul McCartney’s feet down below his kneeAbbey Road | Putin is no Marxist | Nort a homophone | 35mm film canistersFri 28 Aug 2026 11.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTShareJonathan Jones writes that, on the Abbey Road LP cover shot, the Beatles were “in perfect step” (Four blokes and a zebra crossing: the banality and beauty of the Beatles’ Abbey Road cover, 22 August). As was much commented on at the time, three of them were as described, all leading with their left leg, but Paul McCartney was not only barefoot (as indeed Jones noted), but was actually leading with his right. Imagery- and symbolism-wise, we may make of that what we will.David BarlowWorcesterIn an otherwise interesting and thought-provoking read, Miriam Margolyes laments that she hasn’t “the courage to be a Marxist now” because Vladimir Putin “puts me right off” (‘The country of my birth has lost its heart’: Miriam Margolyes on how to fix broken Britain, 23 August). Putin is a rightwing nationalist and conservative who leads a state-capitalist economic system. Although he was a KGB officer during the Soviet era, his actual governance and ideology stand in direct opposition to Marxism.Rose WoolstencroftBlackpool, LancashireThe cryptic crossword (25 August) has “court” as a homophone for “caught”. It is not, neither is it nort.Peter McIlhennyFortrose, HighlandOf course people owned cameras in the 1970s (Letters, 26 August). title: Cherki and Haaland double up in Manchester City cruise at Crystal Palace | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Rayan Cherki and Erling Haaland both scored twice in Manchester City’s 4-1 win at Crystal Palace
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Rayan Cherki and Erling Haaland both scored twice in Manchester City’s 4-1 win at Crystal Palace
Content: Rayan Cherki shows his delight after scoring City’s second goal.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRayan Cherki shows his delight after scoring City’s second goal.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesPremier LeagueCherki and Haaland double up in Manchester City cruise at Crystal PalaceJacob Steinbergat Selhurst ParkFri 28 Aug 2026 16.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll who attend the Rayan Cherki show know the ticket comes with a guarantee of entertainment. Enzo Maresca, a manager famed for his obsessive positional control, does not need to put limits on theManchester Citywizard. Cherki has to feel free and he was at his creative best against Crystal Palace, who were in this game before City’s creative heartbeat took it away from them in the second half.It has been a fine start to the former Lyon player’s second year in England. Cherki was inspired against Bournemouth last week, coming off the bench to spark City’s fightback from 1-0 down with two assists, and this was better. The Frenchman scored twice and the first, a little prod with the outside of his left foot after a mazy run, left you wondering if you have seen something like it before.Crystal Palace 1-4 Manchester City: Premier League – live reactionRead morePalace, stuck on zero points despite fleeting signs of encouragement in Pierre Sage’s first two outings, had no answer to Cherki’s magic. He is an irrepressible talent and a deep thinker. Listening to the post-match plaudits, Cherki smiled, shrugged and said his performance in the first half was “so shit”. Maresca, though, had a different view.“His performance for me was very good, not because of the two goals, but the way he worked off the ball,” City’s manager said. “He has to press. His game was complete. He loves football. We know how good he is. We know the quality he has.”Cherki was not alone in starring for City. Phil Foden impressed and Erling Haaland, who is up and running for the season, grabbed an emphatic double in a performance strong enough to make Maresca think his post-Pep team have moved on from their Community Shield debacle. “We struggled the first five, 10 minutes, because we were pressing in the wrong way,” the Italian said. “After that we were in control.”A challenge for Maresca is working with an incomplete midfield after the exits of Rodri and Bernardo Silva. Ayyoub Bouaddi has arrived from Lille, £86m an eye-catching fee for an 18-year-old after his exploits for Morocco at the World Cup, but there is room for one more. Enzo Fernández, desperate to leave Chelsea, is the top target before Tuesday’s deadline.Not that anyone is going to argue that City are short on midfield options. Maresca, ever the tinkerer, shuffled the pack again. The experiment with Marc Guéhi in the engine room was discontinued, allowing him to slot into central defence against his old side. The £116m Elliot Anderson was the sole pivot, Nico O’Reilly pushed high in a 4-1-4-1 system and Josko Gvardiol inverted from left-back, much like Marc Cucurella in Maresca’s Chelsea side.There are subtle tweaks to the Guardiola template, though some things never change. City led through a familiar source in the 17th minute, Antoine Semenyo crossing from the left and Haaland finding space to loop a clever header over Dean Henderson.View image in fullscreenErling Haaland wraps up victory with the fourth goal.Photograph: Richard Heathcote/Getty ImagesThe defending was poor from Palace, who have had an uncertain summer. They were arranged in familiar fashion, Sage sticking with Oliver Glasner’s 3-4-2-1, but some key faces have gone and others were missing.Jørgen Strand Larsen led the line in the absence of the unsettled Jean-Philippe Mateta, who may be out for four weeks. Ismaïla Sarr, keen to join Galatasaray, was unavailable and Daniel Muñoz was on the bench amid suggestions of interest from Nottingham Forest. Frailties were inevitable. The defence has lost Maxence Lacroix, sold to Chelsea. Anderson, Semenyo and Foden had chances before half-time. “You saw how we want to play until the 65th minute,” Sage said. “We trust in our process.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSage likes to play on the front foot. Adam Wharton, subject of a failed enquiry from City recently, swept a ball through for Eddie Nketiah to test Gianluigi Donnarumma in the second minute. Daichi Kamada went close and Tyrick Mitchell fluffed a header after more enterprising play from Wharton.Palace lacked incision, Nketiah missing again early in the second half. City pressed, O’Reilly and Foden hustling Kamada. Foden advanced and Cherki took over. The Frenchman danced in from the left, danger rising as he wriggled into the area. A host of Palace defenders were thrown off balance, unable to live with Cherki’s footwork and close control. Expect the unexpected. Cherki floated past Jaydee Canvot and held off Chris Richards. For a moment the ball seemed stuck under his feet but he used Takehiro Tomiyasu as a shield and unveiled a finish that was less poke and more dab, Henderson rooted to the spot as the ball rolled tantalisingly over the line.Palace quickly grabbed a lifeline, Yéremy Pino’s free-kick hitting the woodwork and bouncing in off Donarumma for an own goal, but Cherki was in his element. He scored again in the 59th minute, a fierce shot from 20 yards deceiving Henderson after flicking off Richards.City sent Bouaddi on for his debut, Anderson withdrawn. They wanted more. Foden, catching the eye in front of Thomas Tuchel, released Haaland. The Norwegian, who has scored in all six of his league games against Palace, was never going to miss.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueCrystal PalaceManchester Citymatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Archer illuminates fading summer as Pakistan’s marzipan men melt away | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: The tourists offered little but Jofra again invited us to marvel at what he is and mourn what could have been
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: The tourists offered little but Jofra again invited us to marvel at what he is and mourn what could have been
Content: Jofra Archer lit up Lord’s on a day in which his elite quality stood out.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreenJofra Archer lit up Lord’s on a day in which his elite quality stood out.Photograph: The GuardianEngland cricket teamArcher illuminates fading summer as Pakistan’s marzipan men melt awayThe tourists offered little but Jofra again invited us to marvel at what he is and mourn what could have beenBarney Ronayat Lord'sFri 28 Aug 2026 16.26 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt almost exactly 4.19pm on the second day of the second Test something almost happened. The sun, only ever grudgingly present, appeared just enough overhead to offer a lime green sheen to the late-season outfield, as weathered as an antique heirloom carpet.Pakistan had gradually slumped under the table between lunch and tea at Lord’s. They were lolling at 110 for nine, product of 37 overs of almost entirely anonymous batting. This is an unusual Pakistan, if only in their absolute and unyielding ordinariness. The classic Pakistan Test team are an uneasy balance of stars, perhaps a little overwhelmed by their own weapons: speed, seam, spin, luminous top-order batting, all mixed in with the ballast of some unspectacular other guys.Azan Awais offers Pakistan ray of hope amid their second Test gloomRead moreThis Pakistan are something else. This is like watching an entire team of other guys, an Other Guys XI. No actual guys. Just those guys.At 4.20pm the sun was still just about there as Mohammad Abbas, Pakistan’s 36-year-old tailender, braced his knees and faced up toJofra Archer, gliding in horribly from the Pavilion End. The ball from Archer was 90mph, back of a length and on Abbas’s hip, propelled from that oddly chilling run and gather, the arm that seems to hold itself very slightly in place before whipping down in a controlled arc, all grace and high physical craft.Abbas rocked back and defended, left arm jerking down like a man surprised by a hornet at a picnic. The ball struck somewhere near the shoulder of his bat and travelled in a slow arc towards mid-off, where Josh Tongue dived and fell just short with Archer, bent double, watching this tableau play out.The next ball was full, eluding the guesswork of Abbas’s airy drive, the kind of shot you might play with a loofah in the bathroom mirror. The stumps were splayed with a lovely thick clunking sound. Abbas was already walking off as he finished his swing, the innings closed.Archer was utterly high grade here, charged with menace and easy power, and producing not only his fastest Test-match opening spell but a kind of one-man elite sport event that felt entirely separate to the cricket match taking place whenever he wasn’t bowling.He clearly loves running in from that Pavilion End, likes the slope in his legs, the low gauze sight screen behind him, the shifting throng of men in salmon trousers. But there was also something oddly brittle about this spectacle, almost exactly seven years on from his debut on this ground.The dismissal of Abbas left him with three for 26 from 11.2 overs, on a day when he could have had five, seven, eight, whatever. And through all that he looked like a rare bird, out there reeling off its remaining rare bird moments on a stage that feels like it is itself sagging under the weight of time and change.This was a strange day of Test cricket, and a strange version of Lord’s in August. For the most part the vibe was a kind of nothingness. The vibe was: no vibe. Not exactly garbage cricket, not exactly that. But at times, maybe that.Even on the concourses by the Nursery End there was a dog days feel. Traditional British Fudge, the sign by the stairs announced, among the usual fried crispy crumb stuff, the desultory Pimm’s, a flute of throat-clagging white wine, and in between the strollers and stragglers, odd weaving figures in shorts, ties and crumpled linen. Saturday is already promising a Chornobyl of rain.View image in fullscreenJofra Archer dismantles Mohammad Abbas’s stumps on day two of the second Test.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianOn the field Pakistan have looked not so much underprepared or underdone, as just not very good. The entire setup is damaged structurally by its exclusion from an India-centred universe, and harpooned from within by its own room-temperature team selection.Even here the Test team feels like it has been shunted to the wings of the summer. But then this is how we treat that shamefaced old red-ball game, like an awkward maiden aunt with a legacy still to give. Days like this are what happens when Test cricket is asked to give a little bit of itself away too many times in return for the promise of money later. Once again, a classic British fudge.Here we had Archer to illuminate the day, touching 94mph, peppering the thigh pad, the hip, the point of the shoulder. At times there was the strange sight of Pakistan’s Test-match batters doing things club players do when the gangly 15-year-old is cranking it up, swatting down with the bottom hand, ducking when you don’t really need to duck, you just haven’t seen it, trying to keep this thing off you.The odd catch was dropped. Lbws were narrowly reprieved. Azan Awais was beaten 14 times outside his off stump.Meanwhile at the other end, Ollie Robinson rumbled in like a combine harvester trundling across the horizon, doing skilful things with the seam and the angles. It might be tempting to look at this as a partnership, to eulogise a perfectly balanced attack. But Pakistan also collapsed like a soggy marzipan castle. And also, well, you kind of expect Robinson to hoover up four for 11 in these conditions. This was excellence in its least surprising form.Whereas Archer was the one element of fire here, a note of excellence that felt like it was holding the whole day together at times.It has been a strange career. Seven years ago, there was talk of gamechanging menace, of a Jonah Lomu effect, a cricketer for whom, in the words of Ben Stokes, the sky was the limit.It took England six months to break him for the first time. In November Archer bowled 42 overs in a single innings in Mount Maunganui. In December he trudged his way through a full-bore eight-over fitness Test under the eyes of Chris Silverwood, already with a stress fracture in his elbow.That Test career has been brief, interrupted, and somehow never quite facing forward at the right time. By the end of the day the outline numbers stood at 77 wickets at 28 (could have been so much more; might still have been so much less). And with the sense now of a career that will be remembered for these scattered moments of light.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamJofra ArcherEngland v Pakistan 2026CricketPakistan cricket teamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Shaky Sabalenka and wide-open men’s draw set stage for US Open drama | Aryna Sabalenka | The Guardian
description: The defending women’s champion arrives in poor form, while Jannik Sinner’s absence and Carlos Alcaraz’s rustiness make Alexander Zverev men’s favourite
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: The defending women’s champion arrives in poor form, while Jannik Sinner’s absence and Carlos Alcaraz’s rustiness make Alexander Zverev men’s favourite
Content: Aryna Sabalenka must win the US Open to stand a chance of retaining her No 1 ranking.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka must win the US Open to stand a chance of retaining her No 1 ranking.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesAryna SabalenkaShaky Sabalenka and wide-open men’s draw set stage for US Open dramaDefending champion arrives at Flushing Meadows in poor form and with a host of challengers looking to usurp herTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsFri 28 Aug 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 16.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnder any normal circumstancesAryna Sabalenkawould not have lost her third-round match at the Cincinnati Open last week. For all of her unforced errors, indecisiveness and the obvious tension surrounding her tennis, the world No 1 had led the unheralded Sára Bejlek 5-1 in the first set tie-break and then 4-1 in set two. She gave herself more than enough chances to close out a comfortable win.Instead Sabalenka returns to New York trying to find apath through her greatest crisissince she first reached No 1 in the rankings more than three years ago. That straight-sets loss in Cincinnati extended a mediocre 17-7 record dating back to the beginning of April during which she has not reached a final. She has just one more chance to turn her fortunes around as she tries to claim her first grand slam title of the year at the US Open, the tournament she has won on the last two occasions.US Open: Carlos Alcaraz to face Safiullin on return as Sabalenka gets tricky drawRead moreSuch is the competition at the top of women’s tennis, her rivals are congregating at her front door. Elena Rybakina begins this tournament sitting at No 1 in the live standings and in control of her own destiny. Sabalenka must win the title to have any hope of retaining the top ranking, but Rybakina will become the new No 1 regardless of all other results if she reaches the semi-finals. Should either Coco Gauff or Jessica Pegula win the title and Rybakina fails to make the semi-finals, they would take top spot. This additional pressure could further add to Sabalenka’s woes, but perhaps, after 97 consecutive weeks as the undisputed best player in the world, this is exactly what she needs.There are other unanswered questions. Rybakina’s physical condition is uncertain after she was forced to retire from her quarter-final against Iga Swiatek last week due to a leg injury. A year after she spent this lead-in week to the US Open changing her service action, and parts of her matches in tears, Gauff has rebuilt confidence in her serve and the 2023 champion produced some of her best tennis during herCincinnati Open title run. Fresh from her own success in Toronto, the 2022 US Open champion Swiatek looks similarly rejuvenated after struggling badly with anxiety and nerves in many matches this year. Pegula, a finalist in Cincinnati having defeated Swiatek, remains as consistent as ever and will put pressure on her rivals.The strength at the top of women’s game is reflected in the fact that every player inside the top 11 currently holds a WTA 1000 title or above. They have each shown that they are capable of winning the biggest tournaments in the world.View image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz looked rusty on his return from a four-month injury layoff in the mixed doubles competition.Photograph: Marcin Cholewinski/Zuma Press /ShutterstockThings could hardly be more different in the men’s draw. As was the case when he exited the French Open in round two,Jannik Sinner’s withdrawal from the US Openwith a knee injury has cracked this tournament wide open. Carlos Alcaraz is clearly capable of greatness whenever he enters the court, but the prospect of him launching a serious challenge in hisfirst event back after a four-month layoffdue to a right wrist injury and only a few weeks of training seems fanciful. Although he has never been the strongest doubles player, Alcaraz’s rustiness and the caution with which he hit his serve in themixed doubles competition alongside Serena Williamsonly reinforced this sentiment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hollowing out of Tennis.com is a warning for American sports journalismRead moreIt was Alexander Zverev who took advantage of the void in Paris towin his first grand slam titleand, as the top seed, he is high on the list of contenders again. The two biggest winners in the weeks leading up to the US Open, Montreal and Cincinnati champions Ben Shelton and Arthur Fils, are young players who have long viewed themselves as worthy of competing for major titles. Such is the cruelty of the draw, the close friends have been drawn to face each other in the fourth round.Otherwise, just about everyone is in with a shot. The French Open finalist Flavio Cobolli continues to play some of the best tennis of his career, reaching the semi-final in Cincinnati. The rise of 19-year-old Rafael Jódar, who was ranked No 369 this time last year, continues unabated. A group of US players, including Taylor Fritz, Frances Tiafoe, Learner Tien and Brandon Nakashima have found their best form at the right time. Félix Auger-Aliassime, the third seed, will try to replicate the immense level he demonstrated on these courts last year on his run to the semi-final.Perhaps the most interesting question of all is where Novak Djokovic will land over the next few weeks. Had any of the grand slam tournaments been this wide open in 2025, he would have been heavily favoured to become the oldest champion in history. But a year is an eternity at Djokovic’s advanced age. He has continued to put himself in contention at the grand slams, reaching the Australian Open final and Wimbledon semi-final, but he also has to manage a constant stream of physical problems that only worsen over the course of a fortnight. However, these are not normal circumstances, and he is far from a normal tennis player, so the pursuit of grand slam No 25 is still alive in New York.Explore more on these topicsAryna SabalenkaUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: All Blacks brace for Bok-lash as Erasmus adds late fly-half plot twist | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu’s inclusion may be a classic piece of misdirection from South Africa in their must-win match against New Zealand
Author: Gerard Meagher
