Headline: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu’s inclusion may be a classic piece of misdirection from South Africa in their must-win match against New Zealand
Content: Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu struggled in the 33-16 first Test defeat, but will replace Handré Pollard at fly-half for the second Test against New Zealand.Photograph: Themba Hadebe/APView image in fullscreenSacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu struggled in the 33-16 first Test defeat, but will replace Handré Pollard at fly-half for the second Test against New Zealand.Photograph: Themba Hadebe/APRugby unionAll Blacks brace for Bok-lash as Erasmus adds late fly-half plot twistSacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu’s inclusion may be a classic piece of misdirection from South Africa in their must-win match against New ZealandGerard MeagherFri 28 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the face of it, South Africa have been beset by disruption before their most significant match since the successful defence of their World Cup title. Rassie Erasmus had sought to lean further on the Springboks’ set-piece strengths by selecting Handré Pollard at fly-half for the second Test against New Zealand in Cape Town, suggesting a narrow gameplan. A return to the tried and tested. A reliance on what he knows best. Then came news of the “niggle”.Out goes Pollard, who, according to the Friday morning bulletin, suffered said niggle in training on Wednesday and failed a fitness test 24 hours before the match, and back comes the far more adventurous Sacha Feinberg‑Mngomezulu into the No 10 jersey. Feinberg‑Mngomezulu struggled in last week’s33-16 defeat at Ellis Park, as he did on his comeback from injury against Argentina earlier this month, but the 24-year-old has a skill set that has marked him out as a future global star.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJordan double stuns South Africa as New Zealand clinch statement victoryRead moreThe upshot is that South Africa head to the Mother City for their must-win match against the All Blacks with a completely different type of fly-half. Pollard is experienced, reliable from the tee and, as Erasmus said this week, has delivered “under extreme pressure” time and again for the Springboks. His nerveless goal-kicking guided them to the2023 World Cup titleand, in what are forecast to be wet conditions, South Africa’s initial approach seemed clear. As Erasmus had said when reflecting on his side’s game management in the first Test, “we made a lot of stupid calls. Three points is two less than five [for a try]. Handré is a guy that has always done it for us”.In turn, it is a fair conclusion to reach that the approach changes somewhat with the introduction of Feinberg-Mngomezulu, while the return of Cheslin Kolbe, who has replaced Kurt-Lee Arendse in the starting XV as of Friday, is significant because he will assume goal‑kicking duties.It does not take much looking on social media, however, to find the conspiracy theorists spouting what, truth be told, most of us are wondering – was this a classic piece of misdirection from Erasmus? Was it the plan all along? The fact that Erasmus has previous further fuels that particular fire, as does the convenience of recalling Kolbe to kick at goal, but Pollard’s selection did make a degree of sense.View image in fullscreenCheslin Kolbe will assume goal‑kicking duties during the second Test.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersIn the 2023World Cup semi-final against England, Erasmus hooked Manie Libbok after half an hour, sending on Pollard to steer the Boks home. When the chips are down, Pollard is the Springboks’ go-to move. As the 1995 World Cup-winning captain, Joel Stransky, says: “Handré brings maturity and stability, and an ability to close the game off. I think there’s a bit of a message in that saying we might just go back to what we used to do best and maybe not the running game.”New Zealand have clearly been preparing to face Pollard, and the type of gameplan he would carry out, and as a result will have to adapt on the hoof. But to what extent can the same be said for the Springboks? Injuries, of course, happen and South Africa are not the first side to possess a variety of options at fly-half. But the significance here is that his particular selection speaks to the identity of the Springboks just a year out from their tilt at a third straight World Cup title.Do they intend to try to defend it with the set-piece-heavy gameplan that has served them so well or, with Feinberg-Mngomezulu running the show, to do so with more creativity and imagination? It is to South Africa’s credit that hitherto in the World Cup cycle, they have looked a side perfectly equipped to do both. But when the “extreme pressure” comes on, which way will they turn? Erasmus has been forced to change tack at the 11th hour. On the face of it.The All Blacks, for their part, will try to shut out the noise. They are walking tall after ending South Africa’s run of 12 straight victories and the penny has dropped that, whoever is playing at fly-half for the Springboks, the scrum contest will be pivotal in Cape Town. Such was South Africa’s profligacy in the New Zealand 22 last week, the All Blacks ran out comfortable winners despite conceding six scrum penalties in a barrage by the Boks. That they were able to turn the tide, winning a crucial scrum penalty of their own near their own line, and achieve relative parity thereafter was key to their victory; Dave Rennie wasted little time in flagging concerns this week over South African tactics.“Scrum-wise, we’ve spoken with World Rugby around a couple of issues from our point of view, and so we think – scrum-wise – we’ll be a lot better,” Rennie said. “That was massive for them last week. We think if they’re forced to scrum square and not allowed to step sidewards and walk around us, then we’ll be able to stay in front and we’ll be able to get the footie going off that.”As pre-match comments go, they are about as predictable as a late Springboks team change but, with rain expected, the close-quarters battle will be the most significant aspect of the match on Saturday. Having lost 43-10 in Wellington last year, a week after edging home in Auckland, the All Blacks know the Bok-lash is coming.Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSouth Africa rugby teamNew Zealand rugby union teamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Andoni Iraola tells Liverpool’s forwards to ‘exhaust themselves’ | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Andoni Iraola has said it is more important for Liverpool’s forwards to exhaust themselves than perform for 90 minutes as he prepares for an ‘emotional’ Premier League bow at Anfield
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Andoni Iraola has said it is more important for Liverpool’s forwards to exhaust themselves than perform for 90 minutes as he prepares for an ‘emotional’ Premier League bow at Anfield
Content: Andoni Iraola brought Victor Muñoz and Alexis Mac Allister off the bench at Newcastle.Photograph: Molly Darlington/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndoni Iraola brought Victor Muñoz and Alexis Mac Allister off the bench at Newcastle.Photograph: Molly Darlington/Getty ImagesLiverpoolAndoni Iraola tells Liverpool’s forwards to ‘exhaust themselves’‘I tell them they don’t need to give us 90 minutes’Head coach takes charge of first home game on SaturdayAndy HunterFri 28 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndoni Iraola has said it is more important for Liverpool’s forwards to exhaust themselves than perform for 90 minutes as he prepares to make an “emotional” Premier League bow at Anfield.The Liverpool head coach hopes his attacking options will be improved by thearrival of Bradley Barcola from Paris Saint-Germainand another winger before Tuesday’s deadline, with only Victor Muñoz added to his front line so far. The Basque coach has outlined the demands he will put on his forwards as they adapt to a new era at Liverpool.Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendRead moreIraola said: “For me, wingers, forwards, I always tell them that they don’t need to give us 90 minutes. I tell them it is good news when they are exhausted because then we have taken everything from you and someone else will come in.“We have the situation now with Jérémy [Jacquet], who hasn’t had a proper pre-season but he is close to getting there. But normally defenders can last 90 minutes easier. For offensive players, it’s not mandatory that you play the whole game. Once you are done, we can change you. I think it’s the best way, and they all have to understand it like this.”Iraola said Muñoz was “ready to start games” having missed the opening weeks of pre-season as he recuperated from Spain’s victorious World Cup campaign. The 23-year-old impressed from the benchat Newcastle last weekendand was signed for £34.5m from Osasuna on Iraola’s recommendation.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“I had never coached against Victor because he made his debut in La Liga when I was already here in the Premier League but I had very good references of him,” Iraola said. “The club put his name [to me] and we started to analyse his game. We all liked what he gives us. It’s early for him in terms of him not being able to speak the language, and he needs to get a better relationship with teammates, but I like his attitude. He works very hard. He is ready to play right side, left side, and he impacted the game the other day. The subs all played very well.”Iraola’s wife and two young children will be at Anfield on Saturday – as will the club’s new vice-chair, Amit Bhatia – to witness his first competitive home game, against Nottingham Forest.“My wife never normally comes to my games,” he said. “But now she is starting to go because my kids want to go. The kids are starting to understand football a little bit and they will sometimes go. Not all the time, but they will be there for the first game because the timing is very good.“I think there will be an emotional part that is going to be probably only for me. I know it’s my first game but I will not be trying to think too much about those things. Probably when the game finishes, and if it finishes well, then I will be more thinking of myself.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolanewsShareReuse this content

title: St Helens playoff hopes hang by a thread after thrashing by Leeds | Super League | The Guardian
description: St Helens’ hopes of reaching the playoffs were dealt a major blow by a 34-6 defeat at home by Leeds
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: St Helens’ hopes of reaching the playoffs were dealt a major blow by a 34-6 defeat at home by Leeds
Content: Ryan Hall touches down Leeds’ fourth try in their convincing victory against St Helens.Photograph: Paul Currie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRyan Hall touches down Leeds’ fourth try in their convincing victory against St Helens.Photograph: Paul Currie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueSt Helens playoff hopes hang by a thread after thrashing by LeedsSt Helens 6-34 LeedsRhinos return to top of table after running in six triesAaron Bowerat BrewDog StadiumFri 28 Aug 2026 17.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you needed any further proof that Super League’s two most successful sides are travelling in different directions in 2026, this was about as conclusive as you can get.There are two very different fates awaitingLeeds Rhinosand St Helens in three weeks or so. The Rhinos will now almost certainly be resting up for a Super League playoff semi-final, having earned a bye through the opening week of the playoffs by virtue of a top-two finish. They are still favourites to end the regular season on top after this latest impressive victory.Wigan rise to occasion against Hull KR as town unites to remember Sir Billy BostonRead moreBut the Saints, barring a late miraculous run of results involving themselves and the teams around them, will be resting up and preparing for 2027, with their 60-year record of making the end-of-season playoffs ending. After back-to-back wins in the last fortnight, you wondered if this was the night thatSt Helenscould really make people sit up and take notice.Win here, and they would not only dent Leeds’ chances of the League Leaders’ Shield, but they would put themselves right back in the mix for the top six. Instead, what we saw was an 80 minutes very much played out to the form of 2026 on the whole. The Rhinos were impressive, Jake Connor was sensational yet again and the Saints ultimately disappointed.With two rounds to go, Leeds can now look ahead to what is in effect a decider for top spot next Saturday against Wigan. It is a playoff game before the playoffs start, and is a truly unmissable meeting of Super League’s two standout sides in 2026. “Next week decides the league leaders, and what a great position to be in,” Brad Arthur, the Leeds coach, said.His side were very good again when it mattered. With Connor the influential figure throughout, he helped guide the Rhinos into an 18-0 half-time lead. Saints began brightly but couldn’t turn any pressure into points, and when Leeds forged attacking opportunities, they offered their great rivals a lesson in how to be ruthless, with Connor at the heart of it.Tries for Chris Hankinson, Harry Newman and Cameron Smith before one for Ryan Hall shortly after the restart made it 22-0 in Leeds’ favour, and ended it as a contest with half an hour remaining. It all means that for St Helens, their destiny is now out of their own hands – and the chances of the top six look slim at best.View image in fullscreenHarry Newman shows his delight at full timePhotograph: Paul Currie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockIn all probability, they now have to win their last two games and win them well to stand any chance of making the playoffs. Their opponents are fifth-placed Leigh and sixth-placed Hull KR; and while both those sides lost themselves this weekend, this season has presented enough evidence to suggest Saints simply do not have the quality to drag it back from here.“I’m really disappointed,” their interim coach, Eamon O’Carroll, said. “Not in the players, but for them. The start was what we wanted, it was attritional and we went after it but we lost some big moments after that, and Leeds showed their class.”Australia’s coach, Kevin Walters, will take charge of the Saints in 2027 and were he watching this game, he would have seen first hand the size of the task that awaits. Jack Welsby’s magnificent solo try at least ensured Saints got on the scoresheet, but they ended with their worst post-war defeat to Leeds at home after Connor helped Leeds respond with a sumptuous kick for Ash Handley to touch down and put them back in control.Connor’s boot then caused mayhem amongst the St Helens defence again to allow his half-back partner, Brodie Croft, to score his 28th try of the season. That made it 34-6 but by then the home support had already begun to filter away. Their season is ebbing away and is almost over: but in truth, Leeds’ may just be beginning.St HelensSailor; Douglas, Macdonald, Welsby, Cross; Robertson, Lomax; Suluka-Fifita, Shorrocks, Klemmer, Davies, Wright, Host.InterchangeWalmsley, Humphreys, Keeley, Evans.TryWelsby.GoalSailor.LeedsMiller; Hall, Bird, Handley, Newman; Croft, Connor; Oledzki, O’Connor, Jenkins, Watkins, Hankinson, Cassell.InterchangeSmith, Holroyd, Levi, Holroyd.TriesHankinson, Smith, Newman, Hall, Handley, Croft.GoalsConnor 5.RefereeMarcus Griffiths.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueSt HelensLeeds RhinosRugby leaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Special for Norway’: Leknessund breaks clear to win stage seven of Vuelta | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Norway’s Andreas Leknessund launched a solo attack on ⁠the final climb to win stage ⁠seven of the ⁠Vuelta ​a España as his country mourned King Harald
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Norway’s Andreas Leknessund launched a solo attack on ⁠the final climb to win stage ⁠seven of the ⁠Vuelta ​a España as his country mourned King Harald
Content: Andreas Leknessund celebrates as he crosses the finish line to win the Vuelta’s seventh stage.Photograph: José Jordan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndreas Leknessund celebrates as he crosses the finish line to win the Vuelta’s seventh stage.Photograph: José Jordan/AFP/Getty ImagesVuelta a España‘Special for Norway’: Leknessund breaks clear to win stage seven of VueltaNorway in mourning after death of King Harald‘It’s only a small thing in the bigger picture’ReutersFri 28 Aug 2026 12.23 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Norwegian Andreas Leknessund launched a successful solo attack on ⁠the final climb to the summit finish of Aramón Valdelinares to win stage ⁠seven of the ⁠Vuelta ​a España, ahead of his Uno-X Mobility teammate and compatriot Tobias Johannessen on a day ⁠when theircountry mourned the death of King Harald.Leknessund made his move from ⁠a five-rider breakaway 7.5km from the finish at ​the end of the ‌149.8km ride from ‌Vall d’Alba, and pulled away to win his first ‌Grand Tour stage on his Vuelta debut.“It’s been a special day for the team and also for the whole of Norway,” Leknessund said. “Obviously it’s only a small thing in the bigger picture but still, it ‌makes the day more special.” A minute’s silence was held for King Harald before the stage began in Vall d’Alba, and the Uno-X Mobility team wore black armbands as a mark of respect.“I didn’t expect it to be this emotional, but for sure there’s so much feelings around this,” Leknessund added. “I’ve ​been fighting really hard, and it means a ‌lot.”Johannessen came in 34sec behind, having left the Belgian Wout van ​Aert in his wake close to the finish, with the Visma-Lease a Bike rider having to settle for third after he had made the initial attack from the ⁠off and spent most of the day out in ​front with ​Leknessund.Tadej Pogacar, winner of ​three stages already, was happy to sit ​back in ‌the peloton before ​pulling away ​from his general classification rivals approaching the summit to gain more seconds. The Slovene now leads Spaniard Enric Mas by 3min 50sec.Van Aert and Leknessund got away early and were joined by ‌another three riders, Johannessen, Eddie Dunbar (Pinarello Q36.5) and Alexey Lutsenko (NSN) coming to the top of the first of five climbs.View image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar gained 16sec on Enric Mas of Movistar, his closest rival in the general classification. The Slovenian leads by 3min 50sec.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/GettyThe leaders worked together, building a substantial gap and at the foot of the ​final climb the five were one minute ahead of a chasing group of 13 riders with the peloton out of the running with less than 10km to the finish.Leknessund was the first to try to get away, and when nobody followed he was able to claim his stage win at last, having finished runner-up three times at this year’s Giro d’Italia.“I said ⁠to Andreas that he should try to go early and then we check if the ​other guys are willing to work together,” ​Johannessen said. “That’s what you always dream about ​when you try to be two guys in the breakaway and you can play it ​like this. I think we ‌played it perfectly.“A special ​day with what is ​happening back home in Norway so we are super proud.”Felix Gall, fifth overall, tried to get away from Pogacar, but the Slovene responded and in the end gained 16sec on his closest rival Mas, with Pogacar’s compatriot Primoz Roglic a further minute behind in third.Stage eight on Saturday is a flat 176.4km route from Pucol to Xeraco.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaCyclingTadej PogacarnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I want to be seen as a bloody good trainer’: Gihan Arnolda’s journey from sleeping rough to beating Britain’s top stables | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: Gihan Arnolda tells Greg Wood about his remarkable journey from sleeping rough to delivering five winners in his first three months as a trainer
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Gihan Arnolda tells Greg Wood about his remarkable journey from sleeping rough to delivering five winners in his first three months as a trainer
Content: Gihan Arnolda retrained as a chef after a broken pelvis ended his riding career but is back flourishing in the sport as a trainer.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGihan Arnolda retrained as a chef after a broken pelvis ended his riding career but is back flourishing in the sport as a trainer.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTalking HorsesHorse racingInterview‘I want to be seen as a bloody good trainer’: Gihan Arnolda’s journey from sleeping rough to beating Britain’s top stablesGreg WoodFormer jockey reflects on remarkable story from overcoming hardship to breaking barriers as the first trainer of black or Asian heritage at Flat racing’s HQFri 28 Aug 2026 08.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 14.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It’s just unbelievable, isn’t it?” Gihan Arnolda says as he reflects on his first three months as a trainer: five winners from 33 runners, £50,000 prize money banked and a string that is, according to the much-respected Timeformoperation’s “run to form” statistic, outperforming every other Flat yard in Britain.But it could equally apply to the story of Arnolda’s journey from the east end of London to Cadland Cottage Stables at the bottom of Warren Hill in Newmarket. He was the first trainer of black or Asian heritage in Flat racing’s HQ when he received his licence earlier this year, and that is just one among a host of unlikely firsts and Sliding-Doors moments along the way.It is safe to assume that he is also the first trainer to have slept rough on the streets of east London as a teenager.“My mum and dad are Sri Lankan and Portuguese background,” Arnolda explains. “My mother passed away of leukaemia when I was very young. My dad was off the rails, really. [From 12 years of age] I used to run away and I was just living on the streets for weeks at a time.Quick GuideGreg Wood's racing tips for SaturdayShowGoodwood1.25 Rhythm Of My Heart 2.00 Ghost Mode 2.35 High Degree 3.10 Zavateri 3.45 Evening Call 4.20 Arcturus Flame 4.55 Toca MaderaSandown1.40 Thi Qar 2.15 Alcarath 2.50 Calendar Girl 3.30 Breacher 4.05 Desert Shadow 4.35 Victory Gold 5.10 RosarioBeverley1.45 Cinque Verde 2.20 L’Eagle Aid 2.55 Rapide Vega 3.35 Necromancer 4.10 Mudamer 4.45 Glen NevisCartmel2.05 Alvesta 2.40 Gambino 3.15 Secret Secret 3.53 Drombeg Lad 4.25 Passing Diamond 5.05 Judicial ReviewWindsor4.30 Goldtrader 5.00 Space Bear 5.30 Angel Gabriel 6.00 Sovereign Dawn 6.30 Sea Scout 7.00 Maximising 7.30 Regulus BlackChepstow4.40 Minster Man 5.15 Dowman 5.45 Flight Tracker 6.15 Sovereign Beach 6.45 Emery Down 7.15 Wonderful Wendy 7.45 KnightmareWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“I was stealing from shops to live, not that I was that person but I had no other way of living. I remember living in people’s gardens and I couldn’t see any way out, and then you’re on the verge of the gang stuff. I could easily have gone down a very, very different path, because people I knew at that stage have gone down very different paths.”The starting point for Arnolda’s escape from the downward spiral was unexpectedly close to home after a confrontation with his father.“I went next door to a neighbour and they said whatever happens, we’re going to back you and try to foster you.“I didn’t believe it really, and obviously the police came and I got taken back into care, but literally a year later that English family fostered me. I went from a rough school in east London to going to Wimbledon College. It was amazing. I got all my GCSEs, six As, four Bs, and went on to a law course at college.”View image in fullscreenGihan Arnolda already has five winners this season with the target of 10 by the end of the year within sight.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianBy this point, though, an alternative plan had already started to form in Arnolda’s mind thanks to his Saturday routine of watching racing on TV with his foster dad.At 18, he applied for the foundation course at the British Racing School in Newmarket, and sat on a racehorse for the first time on day one. Less than nine months later, in July 1998, his fifth ride in public, Knave’s Ash, squeezed home by a short head in an apprentice handicap at Thirsk.Arnolda had more than 200 rides and rode five more winners over the next decade, but he struggled to shake off the lingering effects of his tough early years.“I went on to be a jockey but I really struggled mentally when I went into the big, wide world, and I couldn’t really focus on being a jockey. It’s really tough [to leave the care system], you’re kind of let go. You’re 18, but you’re not a normal 18-year-old that has had that guided upbringing.”A broken pelvis in 2009 ended his riding career, by which point he had become “disillusioned” with racing. JETS – the retraining scheme for ex-jockeys – helped him to enrol to retrain as a chef. After a spell with the Michelin-starred Andrew Pern in Yorkshire, he moved to Gordon Ramsay’s Maze in London.Five years on from his injury, though, racing was back on his mind. “I just felt like I had missed something in racing,” he says. “In 2014, I got offered a job at Godolphin with Charlie Appleby, then moved to Chris Wall and then Roger Varian, and I learned so much off them. They were my biggest mentors, and then I moved from assistant at Roger’s to [the Derby-winning trainer] Peter Chapple-Hyam, and he was a massive help too.”View image in fullscreenGihan Arnolda was the first trainer of black or Asian heritage in Flat racing’s HQ when he received his licence earlier this year.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianEven with a dozen years of experience behind him, however, training in his own right still felt like a step too far from his East End roots.“People were saying to me: ‘You’ve got so much knowledge, you’re such a horseman,’ and I’d say: ‘Yeah, well, there’s no chance of training,’ because I didn’t see anyone else like myself training. It’s normally handed down, or people have a massive connection in racing. I thought, I’ll just rattle around as an assistant.”But an opening appeared when an owner with Denis Quinn, the previous licence holder at Cadland Cottage Stables, offered to support him, and Arnolda seized his chance.“I’ve got that will to win, and the drive and the work ethic as well,” he says. “I’ve started with my partner [Charlotte] and we have two small children, so it’s a family thing and we’ve got friends that work with us as well, and it’s just slowly growing.“I’ve got orders for six or seven yearlings at the [autumn] sales and I feel like having two-year-olds will add another string to the bow. Our aim was 10 winners by the end of the year, so we’re halfway there already, fingers crossed.”Damascus Steel was Arnolda’s first winner, at the 11th attempt, in a handicap at Goodwood in mid-June. The six-year-old grey gelding followed up in a race at Epsom a month later and will attempt to take his trainer a step closer to his target on Monday in the Amateurs’ Derby, one of the feature events of the bank holiday programme.Arnolda’s blossoming future as a Newmarket trainer is the focus now. “I love the heritage thing, don’t get me wrong,” Arnolda says. “But I want to be seen as just a bloody good trainer, and put it out there that you can have a really horrible start in life, but if you work twice as hard, you can actually get somewhere.”Breacher bred to relish SandownRecent winners of the Solario Stakes have a mixed record in the top three-year-old events a year later, as three – including Masar, the 2018 Derby winner – went on to record Group One wins, but for several more this Group Three prize was as good as it got. Today’s latest renewal, though, looks unusually strong on paper, with three unbeaten colts at the top of the market.Charlie Appleby’s Rock Montreal, a 1m gns (£1.05m) yearling, was highly impressive on debut at Yarmouth this month, while Sonic Angel is two-from-two in all‑weather novice events. The pick of the field, though, could be William Muir & Chris Grassick’sBreacher (3.30), a comfortable winner on debut at Salisbury in June from a stable whose juveniles find plenty for a run. He is bred to relish middle-distances next year so Sandown’s stiff seven furlongs looks sure to suit.Goodwood 1.25 Rhythm Of My Heartwill appreciate this step up to a mile after a promising run into a three-length second on debut at Kempton this month.Sandown 1.40Charlie Appleby’s Flower Show is a definite “lurker” on debut for a stable with a four-in-10 strike rate with its two‑year-olds this year, but John and Thady Gosden’sThi Qar, second amid greenness first time up, is the one to beat on what little form there is.Goodwood 2.00Ghost Mode’s waywardness in the closing stages when successful over course and distance last time is a concern, but he has been nudged up only 4lb for that success and has also drawn well in stall six given his prominent running style.Sandown 2.15Alan King’sAlcarathis lightly raced for a four-year-old and looks overpriced at around 8-1 on his close second over track and trip last time.Goodwood 2.35Cheekpieces coaxed a first win of the season fromHigh Degreeearlier this month and he has decent prospects of a follow-up off 4lb higher.Sandown 2.50A highly competitive Group Three for fillies and mares where Owen Burrows’sCalendar Girlcould add another Pattern-race win to her record after a convincing victory at Listed level first time up this season.Goodwood 3.10A strong field for the Celebration Mile includes three of the beaten runners behind Bow Echo in last month’s Sussex Stakes, and the ease in grade could see a first win of the year forZavateri, a Group One-winning juvenile last season.Goodwood 3.45William Haggas’sEvening Callwas last of three on debut at Newmarket a fortnight ago but was not beaten far and could find sufficient improvement to get off the mark.Greg Wood is away on his sabbatical for the next four weeks but his daily tips will be updated on this page so please check back in for them.Explore more on these topicsHorse racingTalking HorsesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bournemouth and Sunderland land Milan in Europa League, Crystal Palace get Lyon | Europa League | The Guardian
description: Bournemouth face a home game against Milan, the European champions in 2007 when the Cherries finished 19th in League One
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Bournemouth face a home game against Milan, the European champions in 2007 when the Cherries finished 19th in League One
Content: The Europa League and Conference League trophies on display in Monte Carlo at the draw.Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Europa League and Conference League trophies on display in Monte Carlo at the draw.Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty ImagesEuropa LeagueBournemouth and Sunderland land Milan in Europa League, Crystal Palace get LyonCeltic will host Marseille and travel to BenficaBrighton and Hearts play Monaco in Conference LeagueNick Amesin Monte CarloFri 28 Aug 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBournemouth and Sunderland will play mouthwatering ties against Milan in their Europa League campaigns, while theCrystal Palacehead coach, Pierre Sage, faces a return to his previous employers Lyon.The Cherries’ first season in Europe will bring Milan, the seven-times continental champions, to Dean Court in a match-up that once seemed unthinkable. In 2006-07, when Milan won their most recent Champions League title,Bournemouthfinished 19th in League One. Sunderland will make the trip to San Siro to face Ruben Amorim’s side during their first season in Europe since 1973-74.The rest of Bournemouth’s home league phase assignments will bring Viktoria Plzen, Sturm Graz and the Israeli side Hapoel Be’er Sheva to the south coast. Hapoel’s visit will be the first to England by a team from Israel since Aston Villa played Maccabi Tel Aviv last November. Marco Rose will take his side to Real Sociedad, Sparta Prague, Celta Vigo and Lillestrøm.Sunderland will also visit Anderlecht, Lech Poznan and the Portuguese second-tier side Torreense, while welcoming AZ, Dinamo Zagreb, Poland’s Jagiellonia Bialystok and Levski Sofia to the Stadium of Light.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Palace, who qualified by winning last season’sConference League, visit in Lyon a club coached by Sage between 2023 and 2025. The clubs have other common history in the form of ownership, John Textor having been a part-owner at Palace and the president of Lyon. Selhurst Park will host Real Sociedad, Lech Poznan, Sparta Prague and Hoffenheim, while Palace’s remaining trips abroad will be to Red Bull Salzburg, Jagiellonia and Besiktas.Celtic, still licking their wounds from theirChampions League playoff capitulationagainst Lask, will host Marseille, Ferencvaros, Celta and Besiktas. They will travel to Benfica, Omonia, Union Saint-Gilloise and Torreense.Brighton, having comfortably disposed of Tromsø in their playoff, can savour a first Conference League campaign. They were handed an attractive home meeting with Monaco, with Romania’s Universitatea Craiova and the Lithuanian club Kauno Zalgiris also travelling to Sussex. Their away ties will take place against Panathinaikos, Getafe and the Czech side Jablonec, who disposed of Rangers on Thursday.Hearts will visit Mohamed Salah’s Trabzonspor in their third Conference League proper campaign. Trips to Pafos and Thun also lie in store, while Tynecastle can await ties with Monaco, Borac Banja Luka and Nordsjælland.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe schedule and dates for the matches will be announced this weekend.Explore more on these topicsEuropa LeagueConference LeagueSunderlandBrighton & Hove AlbionBournemouthCrystal PalaceCelticnewsShareReuse this content

title: New heart attack definition promises better care for women | Heart attack | The Guardian
description: Leading cardiovascular health groups reclassify overlooked causes and introduce sex-specific diagnostic thresholds
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Leading cardiovascular health groups reclassify overlooked causes and introduce sex-specific diagnostic thresholds
Content: There has been ‘unintended systematic bias against women’ in the previous guidance, the doctors say.Photograph: David Sillitoe/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThere has been ‘unintended systematic bias against women’ in the previous guidance, the doctors say.Photograph: David Sillitoe/The GuardianHeart attackNew heart attack definition promises better care for womenLeading cardiovascular health groups reclassify overlooked causes and introduce sex-specific diagnostic thresholdsAndrew GregoryHealth editor in MunichFri 28 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoctors have agreed the world’s first universal definition of a heart attack, paving the way for millions of women to finally receive better treatment after decades of being “deprioritised”.In one of the biggest procedural shake-ups in a generation, the world’s four leading cardiovascular health groups have signed off on new guidance for healthcare professionals when seeing suspected heart attack patients.Historically, some less common forms of heart attack, which evidence shows typically affect women far more than men, have been coded as less important, with treatment and care often worse as a result.Until now, experts said, women had been getting less effective treatments, which did not always target the specific cause of their heart attack and could even make them more unwell.Now the world’s top cardiologists have promised a “revolution” in care after agreeing the biggest overhaul of how heart attacks are defined and diagnosed in decades, in part to reduce the often deadly delays afflicting women.The landmark agreement was announced in Munich on the opening day of the annual congress of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), the world’s largest heart conference.The new guidance will upgrade three types of attack that are up to 10 times more common in women and often caused by childbirth, exercise and emotional stress.Why gender is at the heart of the matter for cardiac illnessRead moreThe most serious cases, previously known as “type 1” and now classed as “primary” heart attacks, had previously prioritised those caused by a clot blocking blood flow to the heart.However, the types of attacks more common in women involve reduced blood flow for other reasons, such as a tear or tightening of arteries, and are more likely to be missed or not treated as urgently, with delays to care.The new guidelines will also reduce the threshold for any type of heart attack to be diagnosed in women based upon the levels of a protein called troponin in their blood.Until now, women had been expected to reach the same threshold as men for troponin – which is released when the heart is injured and damaged – to get a diagnosis.Speaking to reporters in Munich, Prof Bryan Williams, the chief scientific and medical officer of the British Heart Foundation, Britain’s biggest heart charity, said: “This is a landmark moment, a radical shift in how we define and diagnose heart attacks worldwide which will transform people’s care.“For decades, women have missed out on accurate diagnoses and treatment. This focus on finding less common causes of heart attacks, which predominantly affect women, should help to change that. It could be life-changing for huge numbers of women in the UK and worldwide.”Crucially, the new streamlined heart attack categories will also help patients to fully understand the cause of their heart attack and what comes next, Williams said.The three types of heart attacks that have been upgraded – and which mostly affect women – are coronary artery spasm, coronary embolism, and spontaneous coronary artery dissection (Scad).The first involves the tightening of the artery, which can deprive the heart muscle of blood and oxygen and cause a heart attack, and can be caused by emotional stress, exercise or extreme cold.The second is where a blood clot or fatty deposit travels to a coronary artery and causes a blockage.And the third is caused by a tear in the coronary artery, which occurs in women at least 80% of the time and often happens during or soon after pregnancy.I work in a hospital – and didn’t know I was having a heart attack. Here’s what more women should knowRead moreProf Nicholas Mills, a cardiologist at the University of Edinburgh who led the international taskforce of doctors that agreed the new guidelines, said it was “the first time that we’ve had a truly global approach to aligning how we diagnose what is probably the most important diagnosis there is”.“It kills so many people, and we’ve never got everyone together around the world to agree how we’re going to describe it, classify it, explain it to our patients,” he said.“Our job now is to implement this as widely as possible. It’s just as relevant for the UK as it is for any other country around the world. It is a revolution. It’s going to make care better for patients.”Mills said there had been “unintended systematic bias against women”, including by using the key blood test for diagnosing heart attacks at an average level, which picks up all men but misses some women.“This is used for all types of heart attack in every emergency department in the world, and we want to make sure that it’s used correctly,” he said.The new guidelines, published in the European Heart Journal, were drawn up by the world’s four leading cardiovascular health groups: the ESC, the American College of Cardiology, the American Heart Association and the World Heart Federation.Explore more on these topicsHeart attackWomen's healthHealthGermanynewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham says he will not vote on assisted dying bill to avoid swaying debate | Assisted dying | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: PM also warns his ministers against trying to influence vote when bill returns to Commons next month
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Exclusive: PM also warns his ministers against trying to influence vote when bill returns to Commons next month
Content: ‘There is no single right position and I have deep respect for MPs on all sides, and the expertise they bring to this debate,’ Burnham said.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/WPA Pool/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘There is no single right position and I have deep respect for MPs on all sides, and the expertise they bring to this debate,’ Burnham said.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/WPA Pool/Getty ImagesAssisted dyingAndy Burnham says he will not vote on assisted dying bill to avoid swaying debateExclusive: PM also warns his ministers against trying to influence vote when bill returns to Commons next monthPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentFri 28 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has told Labour MPs that he will not cast a vote when the assisted dying bill returns to the Commons next month, to avoid influencing the debate.While supporters of the measure welcomed his move, No 10 officials said the prime minister had no wish to affect the process in either direction, and was just doing what he thought was best to allow MPs to reach their own collective view.In a separate letter to his ministers on Friday, Burnham warned them against trying to influence the process. When an earlier version of the bill was before parliament, Wes Streeting, the then health secretary who now holds the defence brief,voiced worriesabout its impact on the NHS.An original version of the private member’s bill to permit assisted dying in limited circumstances in England and Wales, led by the Labour MP Kim Leadbeater,ran out of timein the last parliament after peers tabled 1,200 amendments.Another Labour MP, Lauren Edwards, who came second in May’s new ballot for private members’ bills,has tableda near-identical version to allow adults with less than six months to live to apply for an assisted death, subject to the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.It has its second reading in the Commons – the first opportunity MPs get to vote on a bill – on 11 September.View image in fullscreenThe original version of the bill, led by Kim Leadbeater, the MP for Spen Valley, ran out of time in the last parliament.Photograph: House of Commons/PAKeir Starmer voted for Leadbeater’s bill as prime minister on its second and third readings, while otherwise remaining neutral on an issue seen as a matter of conscience, and where parties gave their MPs a free vote. In his letter to MPs, Burnham said he was taking a different approach.“The government remains neutral on the question of assisted dying and on the passage of the bill,” he said, stating it was “vital that every view is respected”.Burnham wrote: “There is no single right position and I have deep respect for MPs on all sides, and the expertise they bring to this debate.”Saying he had his “own personal views on the issue”, Burnham went on: “However, I am also clear that this is a matter for parliament to decide and my role, as the prime minister, will be to lead a government that implements the will of parliament in this area – whether that is to change the law or not.“I also do not want to unduly influence the debate as prime minister and for every colleague to know it is a genuinely free vote. For these reasons, I have taken the decision that it is most appropriate for me not to vote at second reading.”As the Greater Manchester mayor, Burnham previously said he supported the idea in principle. But in July,he said it would be“very challenging” to introduce the change before palliative care and social care were improved.Supporters of the bill argue that, with a proposed implementation period of up to four years, there is time for this to happen.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLauren Edwards, the MP for Rochester and Strood, has tabled a near-identical version of the assisted dying bill.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianIn his letter to ministers, Burnham confirmed that, as is the convention for issues involving conscience, collective responsibility would be again set aside, with frontbenchers free to vote or abstain as they wanted.MPs should be “able to reach those conclusions without feeling that the government is seeking to influence the debate”, he wrote, adding: “At the dispatch box, I ask that ministers reiterate that this is a question for parliament, on which the official government position is to remain neutral, with the same approach taken outside parliament when dealing with all forms of media, including social media.“Of course, ministers do not need to resile from their previously stated views when directly asked about them and can correspond with constituents about their previous position, but they should avoid being part of the public debate, and should not express views about the implications of the bill for their department’s responsibilities.”When he was health secretary under Starmer, Streeting used a message to constituents to express doubts about whether the NHS could afford to establish an assisted dying service given other budgetary pressures.Edwards said: “Andy Burnham is absolutely right to say that people’s personal experiences around terminal illness lie at the heart of the debate and I welcome his view that everyone’s views should be treated with dignity and respect. That is certainly the approach I will be taking and I look forward to what will be a very important debate in two weeks’ time.”Sarah Wootton, the chief executive of the campaign group Dignity in Dying, said: “We welcome the prime minister reaffirming the government’s neutrality and requesting that ministers do not attempt to influence the debate.“More and more countries are introducing choice at the end of life. France hasjust legalised assisted dying. This week Australia completed the set; every single state and territory offers dying people this choice. The will of the public is settled. The will of the Commons is clear, and parts of the British Isles have already moved. On 11 September, MPs must finish what they started.”Explore more on these topicsAssisted dyingAndy BurnhamLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Drumcree ruling raises fears of sectarian confrontation in Northern Ireland | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: High court quashes latest restriction on Orange Order march, reigniting political row over Garvaghy Road
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: High court quashes latest restriction on Orange Order march, reigniting political row over Garvaghy Road
Content: The high court ruling has divided politicians over what it could mean for next summer’s marching season.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAView image in fullscreenThe high court ruling has divided politicians over what it could mean for next summer’s marching season.Photograph: Niall Carson/PANorthern IrelandDrumcree ruling raises fears of sectarian confrontation in Northern IrelandHigh court quashes latest restriction on Orange Order march, reigniting political row over Garvaghy RoadRory CarrollIreland correspondentFri 28 Aug 2026 13.11 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boiling cauldron known as Drumcree that used to scald and tormentNorthern Irelandeach summer gradually cooled two decades ago, leaving it as a name for the history books.Instead of pitched battles between Orangemen and police around the parish church near Portadown in County Armagh, and the murderous sectarian violence they triggered across the region, gave way to a de facto truce.The Orange Order still wished to march down Garvaghy Road in the run-up to 12 July celebrations – a route opposed by the mainly Catholic residents – but its members no longer tried to storm lines of police who dug trenches and erected barbed wire to stop them.Fury dwindled after 1998, when the mayhem threatened the nascent Good Friday agreement, and the Orangemen settled for annualpeaceful, ritualised protests.However, a court ruling this week ignited a political row over Drumcree and raised the spectre of renewed confrontation next July.On Tuesday, the high court in Belfast quashed the latest in a series of determinations that have prevented the march from proceeding down Garvaghy Road since 1998. The commission accepted that its decision-making process had been flawed. Billy Gamble, one of six commissioners, resigned.Unionist parties hailed the ruling as an overdue comeuppance for a statutory body that adjudicates on contentious marches. Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party leader, said: “The outcome of the legal challenge is a totemic victory, which has laid bare why confidence in the Parades Commission has collapsed within the unionist community.”Nationalist politicians, in contrast, expressed foreboding.Michelle O’Neill, theSinn Féinfirst minister, visited Garvaghy Road and said residents feared a return to the violence of the 1990s. “Does anybody really want to see those days? This community certainly doesn’t. I certainly do not want to see those days visited upon us and I think the question here is: for the leaders of unionism, why do they want us to revisit those dark days?”The dispute centres on the legitimacy and workings of the Parades Commission. It adjudicates on thousands of marches each year and is credited with a dramatic reduction in parade-related disorder, but unionists have long alleged bias.The Orange Order accused the commission of a “copy and paste” response in refusing applications and of overlooking the order’s willingness to engage with communities that oppose certain marches.Last month, a Portadown Orangeman launched a legal challenge over the most recent decision on Drumcree, which led to Mr Justice McAlinden ruling that the commission had not followed procedure.He said: “Public administration must have the confidence of the public and that means that when errors are made, when shortcuts are taken, when sloppy procedures are manifest, those issues come to the public knowledge and appropriate corrections are made within that administrative body to ensure that such behaviour does not occur again.”Unionist leaders want all the commissioners to resign, but the chair, Evelyn Collins, vowed to stay and fix the problems. “We will work hard to regain the trust of all sections of the community,” she said.Chris Bryant, the secretary of state for Northern Ireland, said the commission “simply can’t function” without respect from all communities. On a visit to Belfast, Andy Burnham, the prime minister, declined to say whether commissioners should quit and called for “a calm and a measured” response.The Orange Order signalled it would return to court if the commission rejected an application to march down Garvaghy Road next year. Analysts said Northern Ireland assembly elections next year might tempt some nationalist and unionist parties to exploit the issue.Residents told reporters they dreaded any return to the chaos of the 1990s.The Portadown branch, known as the Vatican of Orangeism, said it was ready to engage in mediation. Breandán Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition said marches through the mainly Catholic neighbourhood “finished” in 1998 and “will not be repeated”.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandSinn FéinDemocratic Unionist party (DUP)Northern Irish politicsShareReuse this content

title: Is the environmental impact of datacentres finally cutting through? | Environment | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: Anti-datacentre sentiment is growing across the political spectrum in the US – and the public is only just finding out about the potential effects on their energy bills
Author: Dharna Noor
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: Anti-datacentre sentiment is growing across the political spectrum in the US – and the public is only just finding out about the potential effects on their energy bills
Content: The Meta El Paso datacentre, August 2026.Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Meta El Paso datacentre, August 2026.Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty ImagesDown to Earth newsletterEnvironmentIs the environmental impact of datacentres finally cutting through?In this week’s newsletter: Anti-datacentre sentiment is growing across the political spectrum in the US – and the public is only just finding out about the potential effects on their energy billsDon’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereDharna NoorFri 28 Aug 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnti-datacentre sentiment is growing from across the political spectrum in the US.More than a dozen states have considered moratoria on datacentres. New York became the first US state to enact atemporary banlast month. Progressive stalwarts Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez haveproposed a national moratorium. And even Greg Abbott, the far-right governor of Texas, called for a ban on datacentre development in rural swaths of his state.Fuelling alarm about datacentres are environmental concerns over water usage and toxic contamination, as well as worries about the kind of society that the artificial-intelligence technologies powered by the new datacentres are creating.Another of the most politically potent objections strikes closer to the wallet: data centres require enormous amounts of electricity, and that increase in demand can drive up utility bills.More on datacentres’ impact on electricity costs after this week’s most important reads …Essential reads‘Our new normal’: how marine heatwaves affect life in British seasIraq’s ghost villages: Islamic State drove people away – now a new enemy is preventing their returnDestroyed crops, riverbed cyclists and a ‘Rock of Starvation’: how drought has devastated the DanubeIn focusView image in fullscreenDemonstrators participate in a nationwide protest against data centres in Virginia, July 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/Larbert residents groupA stunning seven out of 10 Americans are opposed to the construction of datacentres for artificial intelligence in their area, amajor poll foundin May, with 48% saying they are strongly opposed. About one-fifth of participants specifically pointed to possible negative financial consequences associated with datacentres as a reason for their opposition, including the potential for higher utility bills.The backlash has created a bind for the Trump administration, which wants the US to become the world leader in artificial intelligence, but has also promised to bring down electricity bills. The US president’s answer so far has been the “Ratepayer Protection Pledge”, a voluntary agreement that he claims will keep families from footing the bill for the AI boom. Nearly 200 companies, utilities, datacentre developers and states signed on to the agreement, the administrationannouncedlast month.The pledge asks datacentre developers and artificial intelligence firms to agree to cover the costs of the electricity they use and the new infrastructure needed to connect their facilities to the grid. The problem, critics say, is that the pledge has no teeth. It is not legally binding, and there are no clear consequences for companies that fail to follow through.Green groups have beenparticularly unimpressed: Patrick Drupp, climate policy director at the Sierra Club, last month called it a “paper-thin commitment” for families struggling with their bills, and Lena Moffitt, executive director of nonprofit Evergreen Action, described the announcement as a mere “photo op with big tech”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolicymakers and developers have put forth other ideas for how to ensure ratepayers don’t bear the brunt of the artificial intelligence boom with their utility bills, fromenacting tariffsfor datacentres to simply banning the construction of the facilities until further regulations – including on energy usage – can be put in place.In June, US utility prices were up 4% from a year earlier, federal data shows, outpacing inflation. The concern has shown no signs of dissipating.Read more:Bipartisan bill fails to protect US consumers from datacentres’ true costs, critics warnA huge AI datacentre is planned near Mar-a-Lago. The Everglades could pay the price‘This is very real redlining’: outrage in Little Rock as two datacentres loomTo read the complete version of this newsletter –subscribe to receive Down to Earthin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentDown to Earth newsletterAI (artificial intelligence)Climate crisisWaterDatacenters – USDatacentres - UKnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: The chefs turning down the heat by switching from gas to electric | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: As well as being quieter, cheaper to run and easier to clean, induction cookers can cut kitchen temperatures by up to 10C
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: As well as being quieter, cheaper to run and easier to clean, induction cookers can cut kitchen temperatures by up to 10C
Content: Tens of thousands of kitchen staff are thought to have carried on working this summer in ‘furnace-like’ conditions.Photograph: PhotoTalk/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTens of thousands of kitchen staff are thought to have carried on working this summer in ‘furnace-like’ conditions.Photograph: PhotoTalk/Getty ImagesExtreme heatThe chefs turning down the heat by switching from gas to electricAs well as being quieter, cheaper to run and easier to clean, induction cookers can cut kitchen temperatures by up to 10CFiona HarveyEnvironment editorFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeaping flames, searing heat, copious sweat and scorchingly inventive swearing – restaurant kitchens are never a place for the faint-hearted, but this summer they have been sweltering in successive heatwaves to a dangerous degree.Some restaurants, cafes and bakeries in the UK grew so hot that they wereforced to close, orreduce their hours, for the safety of their staff. There is still no maximum working temperature,despite calls from the TUC, and tens of thousands of kitchen staff are thought to havecarried on working in “furnace-like” conditions.Now a number of chefs are calling for one route to cooling kitchens that may be deeply unpopular with some of their colleagues. Swappinggas hobs for electric induction cookingcan reduce temperatures by as much as 10C, asinduction cookers only heat the food in the pans. They are more efficient, can reduce costs, are safer as they avoid the harmful pollutants emitted by gas cookers, and make it easier for air conditioning to work in crowded kitchen environments. But up to now many chefs have been reluctant to make the change.View image in fullscreenJeremy Pang: ‘We have found that we can get just as high temperatures, and just as good cooking, with electric.’Photograph: Pål Hansen/The Observer“There is that sense of theatre with fire and flames,” says Jeremy Pang, a third-generation Chinese chef in London and founder of the School of Wok. “It feels quite traditional and exciting. But we have found that we can get just as high temperatures, and just as good cooking, with electric.”The secret to traditional Chinese cookery lies in the “wok hei” – literally, the breath of the wok, meaning the smoke and heat that the chef must master, to give all ingredients the right degree of scorching and flavour. Pang was worried that this would be harder to achieve with electric, but soon found that he could reach temperatures of 350-400C, and in an easily controllable fashion.“We use carbon steel with oil, and you can still get that actual smoke and flavour that you would with gas,” he said. “Gas cookers are incredibly good equipment, but you get so much heat off them, it’s a huge problem.”Areport from the Global Cooksafe Coalitionfound that restaurants could save thousands of pounds on their energy bills alone from making the switch. One gastropub was able to cut its energy use by almost two-thirds, saving £9,000 on bills. The cost of the retrofit would be repaid within three years, and the pub was likely to save £65,000 over 10 years, the report found.Ellen Chew, founder of the Rasa Sayang restaurant in London’s Chinatown, found an unexpected benefit: chefs no longer had to shout. Turbo gas burners raise a racket, but induction hobs are silent. “The whole atmosphere and environment is different now, it’s super quiet,” she told the Guardian. “Some chefs are difficult to convince to move away from gas, but when you show them the difference, it’s a gamechanger.”Switching can also benefit the climate: the pub’s carbon emissions also fell by about two-thirds.For Chantelle Nicholson, who stipulated electric hobs in place of gas when opening her Apricity restaurant in Mayfair in 2022, cleaning and safety are also key. Induction hobs are quicker and easier to clean, which is popular with staff. “I used to have burn marks all up my arms from scrubbing gas hobs,” Nicholson told the Guardian. “And when anything goes wrong with the gas, it’s a total nightmare to get it fixed. Induction is controllable and really reliable.”View image in fullscreenChantelle Nicholson, at Apricity in London: ‘To me, electric is clearly the way forward.’Photograph: Beca B Jones/The GuardianShe was also concerned aboutstudiesshowing thatgas cookers emit harmful pollutantsand have beenlinked to asthma. “To me, electric is clearly the way forward,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDiners at the chef’s table in her restaurant have also noticed. “They compliment us on how calm the kitchen is,” she said. Apricity won a coveted Michelin Green Star for its efforts.Lowering the temperature of the kitchen also means fridges have to work less hard, and there is less need for air conditioning and ventilation. Chet Sharma, chef-patron at London’s Bibi restaurant, said: “A hot kitchen doesn’t really exist with induction, since there is no heat loss. Induction is super-efficient. It keeps our bills down and keeps the staff happier, not sweating away at the stoves all day.”View image in fullscreenInduction cookers are more efficient, can reduce costs, are safer and make it easier for air conditioning to work in crowded kitchen environments.Photograph: Getty ImagesLuke Burgess, owner of Scholé in Australia, quoted in the GCC report, found that cleaning time was reduced from 24 minutes for a gas cooktop to 21 seconds for an induction cooktop, which he calculated saved over AU$30,000 (£15,700) over a year in wages alone.Camilla Born, the chief executive of Electrify Britain, a body funded by energy companies that campaigns for a switch to electrification throughout the UK economy, called for Andy Burnham to make electricity cheaper, to encourage businesses to switch and help consumers move off gas. “The prime minister has made some welcome moves on business rates, but his government can go further,” she said. “He should look to make electricity cheaper – by removing levies and policy costs from existing bills – and quicken the rollout of the heating and cooking systems that run on it.”Explore more on these topicsExtreme heatFood & drink industryHospitality industryPollutionEnergy billsEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: How Britain’s railways are struggling in the heat – and can they be fixed?  | Rail industry | The Guardian
description: Problems including derailments have hit network during one of the hottest and driest summers on record
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Problems including derailments have hit network during one of the hottest and driest summers on record
Content: The derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, earlier this month.Photograph: RAIB/PAView image in fullscreenThe derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, earlier this month.Photograph: RAIB/PARail industryExplainerHow Britain’s railways are struggling in the heat – and can they be fixed?Problems including derailments have hit network during one of the hottest and driest summers on recordNatalie Wint andAlex DanielFri 28 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s railways have faced a string of heat-related problems this summer, including a derailmentnear Lewesin East Sussex two weeks ago that injured 30 people, and another the next day when the rear carriages of a Greater Anglia train derailed “in an upright position” atWickford railway station in Essex, with no reported injuries.The problems came during one of the hottest and driest summers on record, with a series of heatwaves, anddrought declaredacross large parts of England and Wales. Britain’s railways, built for a cooler, wetter climate, have been put under pressure. Network Rail said the summer had “presented exceptional challenges to the railway”.Here’s what we know about how heat affects the rail network and what can be done to tackle it.What happens to railways in the heat?Steel expands when it gets hot, and the long, welded steel sections that make up modern railway tracks are no exception. “The classic concern for railways with hot weather is that the track might buckle,” said William Powrie, a professor of geotechnical engineering at the University of Southampton.As temperatures rise, the rails expand, but their continuous design means there is little room for movement. “If they haven’t got anywhere to go, they end up generating compressive stresses,” Powrie said. “The problem with any sort of structure which has got a compression in it is that it can fail by buckling.”The consequences can be serious. Just two days of record heat in 2022 led to almost 7,700cancelled trains and an estimated £30m in costs, according to ataskforceset up by Network Rail after that heatwave.On a hot day, the rail can reach much higher temperatures than the air. Network Rail says most of the network can operate when track temperatures reachup to 46C, roughly equivalent to an air temperature of 30C. But rails have been recorded at temperatures as high as 51C.The sleepers and ballast that rails sit on can help stop them from buckling, keeping the track in place – but long periods of heat and drought can dry the soil beneath them. That soil can shrink when it dries, a problem given it “is essentially the foundation for anything on top of it”, said Manu Sasidharan, an assistant professor of infrastructure asset management at University College London.The weight of passing trains makes the problem worse, putting pressure on the weakened soil and causing it to settle unevenly. Whatever sits on top, including the track, “will follow suit”, Sasidharan said.While tracks and stations have been continually updated over the decades, some embankments, tunnels and other structuresdate to the 1800s, when much of the network was first laid.How do hotter countries cope?To stop rails from buckling, engineers lay them slightly stretched, a process called pre-stressing. It means the rail has some give in it before it starts expanding in the heat.In the UK, rails are stretched so that they do not undergo compression until the air temperature passes 27C. That figure sits between the UK’s highest and lowest seasonal rail temperatures, protecting against buckling in the summer and breaking under tension in the winter.Other countries set that figure differently. In parts of Australia and the US, the so-called stress-free air temperature can exceed 35C. In southern Europe too, where winters rarely get as cold as in the UK, rails are designed for more heat, since there’s less risk of the rail snapping in the cold.“If you’re looking at Italy, where you don’t really get very low winter temperatures, then you can afford to increase the stress-free temperature,” Powrie said. “The problem is the range of temperatures that we have [in the UK] … in the winter, they go into tension and that can cause the rails to break.”One option, in theory, could be to re-stress rails between seasons, loosening and retensioning them so the stress-free temperature is set higher for summer and lower for winter, rather than fixed year-round.Network Rail says: “In Britain, the variations in short-term weather and long-term climate mean that it is neither practical nor cost-effective to implement these measures permanently.”Another option is to lay track on solid concrete slabs, as in some countries, rather than the more common bed of sleepers and ballast. However, slab track costs about four times as much to install as standard ballasted track, which is why it remains rare across most of the UK network.What can be done?One idea under discussion is raising the temperature British rails are built to withstand. The post-2022 taskforce said that on modern, well-supported track the stress-free temperature could rise from 27C to 30C.“You might say we should actually have a different stress-free temperature in the south of England compared to, say, the north of Scotland,” Powrie said. However, higher stress-free temperature also leaves rails more vulnerable in a cold snap.Simpler measures are already in use. Some sections of track arepainted whiteto reduce how much heat they absorb. Network Rail says a rail painted white is typically 5-10C cooler.Both tactics may be necessary as summers get hotter – somethingthat will be increasingly normalamid the climate crisis. All five of the UK’s warmest summers on record have happened since 2000, according to the Met Office.Monitoring for faults remains difficult, though. The Network Rail taskforce found that fewer than half of the track buckles recorded in 2022 had been identified before they happened.Part of the issue is the sheer amount of data modern trains generate. Many now carry sensors that pick up rough riding or unusual vibrations, but sifting through it all is a challenge that needs to be automated, experts say.Much, therefore, still relies on judgment rather than data – for example, a train driver detecting rough riding on one part of the line and reporting it.As a temporary measure, speed restrictions were imposed on trains in southern Essex in the aftermath of theWickford derailment.Did the Lewes derailment happen because of the heat?It’s impossible to say for sure. An interim report by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) found that a“track geometry irregularity”existed before the derailment, and said investigators had since received reports of rough riding from passengers on that stretch of line.Sasidharan said early evidence pointed to the track itself. “The initial indication of the derailment … is that it’s a track infrastructure fault, most likely,” he said.At the site of the derailment, the embankment is built on clay, which shrinks more than other types of soils as it dries out. The RAIB said the clay was “sensitive to variations in water content”, and there was evidence it had shifted before the derailment, though not enough to amount to a significant slip.Powrie said the location had several things working against it at once, making it a case of what safety experts call the“Swiss cheese” theoryof accidents, where one only happens when several small failures line up together.The derailment happened on a bend – where more force is exerted on the track – and close to where the track leaves a bridge and moves on to the embankment.Powrie said these transition points were a natural weak spot because the track had to cope with a sudden change from something rigid to ground that could shift, especially when it was dried out. “It wouldn’t surprise me if the defect turned out to be related to the dryness,” he said, “but I don’t really want to speculate.”Network Rail has said it is “fully committed to supporting the continuing investigation and acting on any lessons that emerge from its findings”.It said: “Safety is and will always remain our highest priority. While Britain’s railway is one of the safest in the world, when incidents like this occur it is essential that we understand exactly what happened and identify any lessons that can be learned.“Given the complexity of the issues being examined, it is important that the independent investigation is allowed to reach its conclusions. We will continue to cooperate fully with the RAIB throughout this process.”Explore more on these topicsRail industryNetwork RailRail transportTransportExtreme heatClimate crisisexplainersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Nature thrives when given a chance’: restored Cheshire wetland now a haven for rare grebe | Birds | The Guardian
description: Woolston Eyes in Warrington, a dumping ground for canal dredgings, has become best place in UK for black-necked grebe
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Woolston Eyes in Warrington, a dumping ground for canal dredgings, has become best place in UK for black-necked grebe
Content: The rare birds have distinctive tufts of gold feathers and bright red eyes.Photograph: Ben Andrew / RSPBView image in fullscreenThe rare birds have distinctive tufts of gold feathers and bright red eyes.Photograph: Ben Andrew / RSPBBirds‘Nature thrives when given a chance’: restored Cheshire wetland now a haven for rare grebeWoolston Eyes in Warrington, a dumping ground for canal dredgings, has become best place in UK for black-necked grebePatrick BarkhamFri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 06.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA dumping ground for dredgings from the Manchester Ship Canal has become the best place in Britain for the rare and beautiful black-necked grebe, hosting 64% of Britain’s breeding population.Since 2021,Woolston Eyesin Cheshire has been restored, extended and turned into a mosaic of freshwater pools, reedbeds, willow scrub and rough grassland, managed by the RSPB and Woolston Eyes Conservation Group.Wetland areas on a dried-out and overgrown settlement lagoon were revived and nesting islands created, with the aim of attracting black-headed gulls, which black-necked grebes nest beside for protection from predators. The wetlands also provided a new wealth of invertebrate food for the glossy black and chestnut-coloured birds, which sport tufts of gold feathers behind ruby-red eyes.Rewilded land remains green amid drought-stricken English countryside, images showRead moreIn 2023, four pairs of black-necked grebes bred on the newly restored area, successfully raising 15 young. By 2025, 35 pairs of black-necked grebes were recorded, 29 of which nested on the newly restored wetland area. The total represents 64% of the average number of breeding pairs recorded annually across the UK.View image in fullscreenA pair of black-necked grebes.Photograph: Ben Andrew / RSPB“It is fantastic to see black-necked grebe numbers increasing at Woolston Eyes thanks to the hard work of staff, volunteers and partners to create prime habitat for this rare and attractive species,” said Gavin Thomas, anRSPBecologist. “The rapid growth in numbers shows how effective targeted conservation action can be and is a great example of nature thriving when it is given a chance.”The site of special scientific interest (SSSI) in Warrington is also a stronghold for other rare and unusual species including willow tit, pochard and grasshopper warbler.While Woolston Eyes relies entirely on rainfall to remain wet, water can be moved between areas so they can be dried out, refreshed and reflooded – a crucial rotation for the black-necked grebe, which will abandon wetlands that become too “mature”.Thomas added: “Black-necked grebes are just a handful of the millions of breeding, wintering and migratory birds that rely on the UK’s internationally important wetlands. Seeing the number of black-necked grebes continuing to increase at Woolston Eyes makes all the hard work worthwhile.“It demonstrates that restoring and managing wetlands is vital for species recovery, but we absolutely need to scale this up and deliver far more sites like Woolston throughout the UK.”Explore more on these topicsBirdsCheshireWildlifeConservationWetlandsRSPBnewsShareReuse this content

title: England braces for flooding as thunderstorms forecast in parts of UK | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Festivalgoers brave rain and strong winds as ‘unsettled’ conditions expected to last over bank holiday weekend
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Festivalgoers brave rain and strong winds as ‘unsettled’ conditions expected to last over bank holiday weekend
Content: Festivalgoers at Leeds seem unfazed by the damp conditions.Photograph: Matthew Baker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFestivalgoers at Leeds seem unfazed by the damp conditions.Photograph: Matthew Baker/Getty ImagesUK weatherEngland braces for flooding as thunderstorms forecast in parts of UKFestivalgoers brave rain and strong winds as ‘unsettled’ conditions expected to last over bank holiday weekendKevin Rawlinsonand agencyFri 28 Aug 2026 11.47 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHeavy rain is expected over the weekend, forecasters have said, with people heading to major music festivals warned of unseasonably strong winds.That came after large parts ofEnglandbraced for flooding on Friday. The Environment Agency (EA) issued flood alerts across the Midlands and into South Yorkshire, having earlier sent out a more-serious flood warning in the town of Nelson, Lancashire.Met Office forecasters said parts of the country would see thunderstorms. They issued a yellow warning on Friday, saying heavy showers and thunderstorms could cause travel disruption. The forecasters predicted “unsettled” weather throughout the weekend and into the start of next week, with “heavy, thundery showers in many areas on Sunday”. But, as of Friday afternoon, the conditions were not expected to be severe enough to warrant renewed weather warnings.“It’s a rather unsettled bank holiday weekend. Saturday will start for many with a band of rain spreading north-east. That will be replaced by heavy showers with the potential for more thunderstorms, it will also be a windy day, particularly in the south and south-west of England,” theMet Officesaid.“Sunday, a mix of sunshine and showers, winds will be generally lighter for most places than Saturday.
