Monday will continue to be changeable, sunny spells and scattered showers, there will be some dry weather around, and breezy conditions.”Temperatures are likely to reach 20-22C on Saturday, and 20C on Sunday and Monday.View image in fullscreenThe heavy rain follows weeks of exceptionally dry weather in England. Pictured: a woman in Liverpool.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAMuch of England andWaleswas covered by the warnings issued for Friday. They suggested flooding of a small number of homes and businesses in England was likely, trains could be delayed and car journeys could take longer.The thunderstorm warning covered all inland areas in Wales, from the Severn to the Wash in England, including all of the Midlands, up as far north-east as Teesside and across to Lancashire.There were 16 flood alerts, meaning floods are possible, in England as of Friday afternoon. The flood warning in Lancashire, which indicated flooding was “expected”, was issued in Nelson, on Walverden Water. But it was removed later in the day.The Met Office saidflooding could cause damage to buildingsor structures, and that the same could be caused by lightning strikes. They said brief power cuts could occur and disruption to road and rail travel was likely.The forecaster said thunderstorms would probably bring 10-20mm of rain in a short period in a few places, with the potential for 30-40mm where there are repeated downpours.Festivalgoers heading toReading and Leeds, Creamfields and other live music events were warned about windy conditions.Trains were disrupted at Knebworth towards London because of flood water making the railway potentially unsafe on Friday, National Rail said.Throughout the summer, continued hot weather across the UK coincided with extremely dry conditions. The Met Office has previously said the UK is on course for its hottest summer on record after five heatwaves, with temperatures of up to 38.1C recorded in London, as the effects of the climate crisis become ever more apparent.The EA said that after a National Drought Group meeting on Thursday morning, 71.3% of England remained in drought. It said August so far had received only 34% of the expected rainfall.Filey in North Yorkshire had the most rainfall with 55mm between 8pm on Thursday and 7am on Friday, the Met Office said.Explore more on these topicsUK weatherEnglandReading and Leeds festivalWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Four men admit destroying Jewish community ambulances in Golders Green  | UK news | The Guardian
description: Prosecutors allege men were deliberately targeting Jewish community when four vehicles were set ablaze in March
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Prosecutors allege men were deliberately targeting Jewish community when four vehicles were set ablaze in March
Content: The burnt-out remains of Hatzola ambulances in Golders Green, north London, in March.Photograph: Jamie Lashmar/PAView image in fullscreenThe burnt-out remains of Hatzola ambulances in Golders Green, north London, in March.Photograph: Jamie Lashmar/PAUK newsFour men admit destroying Jewish community ambulances in Golders GreenProsecutors allege men were deliberately targeting Jewish community when four vehicles were set ablaze in MarchEmine Sinmazand agenciesFri 28 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 16.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack causing about £1m of damage.Hamza ⁠Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, and Judex Atshatshi and Saif Ali, both 18, admitted to a charge of destroying or damaging property being reckless whether life would be endangered.Atshatshi, Khan and Iqbal entered their pleas by video link from Wandsworth and Pentonville jails, with Ali in the dock of the Old Bailey on Friday.Four ambulances belonging to the Jewish volunteer emergency service Hatzola were set on fire on the morning of 23 March while they were parked near a synagogue in Golders Green, an area of north London that has a large Jewish community. Prosecutors said the attack caused about £1m of damage.The prosecutor, Leo Seelig, suggested the incident had a “terrorist connection” although no mention was made in court of potential proxies working for Iran.Previously, counter-terror police had looked into the possible involvement of Iranian proxies in the Jewish ambulance arson, as well as other attacks on Jewish sites in London. Most have been claimed online by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamia, the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right.However, in April, Iran’s embassy in the UK said it “categorically rejects” allegations of involvement in “violent activities or incidents in the United Kingdom”.Three of the defendants were said to have set fire to the fully stocked vehicles while a fourth waited in a blue Toyota Avensis. The resulting blaze caused gas canisters inside the ambulances to explode and nearby flats and a synagogue were also damaged by the fire.View image in fullscreenNearby flats and a synagogue were also damaged by the fire.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesThe four men were arrested after an investigation by counter-terrorism police.On his arrest on 1 April, Ali threw his mobile phone out of the window, the court was previously told. The defendant, then aged 17, had been in contact with someone in February with a view to buying a blue Toyota Avensis and had researched online the cost of ambulances.The prosecution had alleged Ali went on to source the Toyota that was used in the attack, with WhatsApp messages between him and a co-defendant relating to the purchase.Prosecutors have said they believe the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community.Hatzola is a Jewish charity established in 1979 and run by volunteers, providing free medical transportation and emergency response to Jewish and non-Jewish people in north London.As well as the ambulances, said to have cost between £240,000 and £250,000 each, four electrical charging stations and cables costing about £5,000 each were also damaged.Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb ordered pre-sentence reports for Iqbal and Khan, from Leyton, east London, Atshatshi, from Dagenham, east London, and Ali, of dual British-Pakistani nationality, from Walthamstow.Remanding them in custody, the senior judge said their sentencing would take place in the spring of 2027 at the conclusion of a separate trial.At the same hearing, a fifth defendant, Subhan Ahmed, 18, from Walthamstow, pleaded not guilty to a charge of assisting an offender.Ahmed, who is alleged to have helped to get rid of the car used in the attack, will go on trial at the Old Bailey on 27 January next year.Explore more on these topicsUK newsLondonShareReuse this content

title: London Science Museum cuts links with BP after decades of partnership | Museums | The Guardian
description: Campaigners say ‘seismic shift’ follows years of pressure to sever ties with oil and gas firm
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Campaigners say ‘seismic shift’ follows years of pressure to sever ties with oil and gas firm
Content: Climate protesters outside the London Science Museum in 2021.Photograph: Anna VickerstaffView image in fullscreenClimate protesters outside the London Science Museum in 2021.Photograph: Anna VickerstaffMuseumsLondon Science Museum cuts links with BP after decades of partnershipCampaigners say ‘seismic shift’ follows years of pressure to sever ties with oil and gas firmPippa NeillEnvironment reporterFri 28 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheLondonScience Museum has ended its decades-long partnership with the oil and gas company BP in what has been described as a “seismic shift” for the museum.The Science Museum Group academy, which was established in 2018 to provide training and resources, announced on Friday that it would be ending its partnership withBP. In a statement, the director and chief executive of the Science Museum Group, Sir Ian Blatchford, said the partnership had “drawn to a close at the end of the current contract term”.Blatchford said BP’s “generous contributions helped us to inspire more than 11,000 education, museum and science professionals through research-informed science engagement training, supporting vital work to spark curiosity and bring science to life for more than 1 million young people across the country”.BP’s relationship with the Science Museum, which goes back decades, has come under previous scrutiny, with the company accused by campaigners of havingan “insidious influence” over the teaching of science, technology, engineering and maths(Stem) in the UK through its relationship with the museum.A spokesperson for BP said: “BP and the Science Museum Group Academy’s partnership will draw to a close on Monday 31 August at the end of its agreed term.”View image in fullscreenScientist Rebellion activists demonstrate in the Science Museum’s energy hall against the museum’s sponsorship by Adani, BP and Equinor.Photograph: Andrea Domeniconi/AlamyIn 2024, the museumcut tieswith the oil company Equinor over its failure to lower carbon emissions sufficiently to ensure it was aligned with theParis climate agreementgoal of limiting global heating to 1.5C.Chris Garrard of the campaign group Culture Unstained said this “seismic shift” came after years of campaigning and growing pressure from educators and schools, some of which have pledged to boycott trips to the museum over its partnership with BP.“BP’s commitment to climate action was never worth the paper it was written on but the Science Museum’s director passionately championed his partnership with the major polluter year after year. Now, with the world facing droughts and wildfires and BP recklessly ramping up its production of dirty fossil fuels, the museum has finally come to its senses and followed the rest of the culture sector in cutting ties to BP,” he said.However, Garrard said this decision represented only a “partial victory”. The museum still takes money from Adani GreenEnergyLtd, a subsidiary of the Adani Group, one of the world’s largest private coal mining and energy conglomerates.The academy provides training and resources to teachers, museum practitioners and the Stem industry nationally and internationally.Explore more on these topicsMuseumsCorporate sponsorshipBPFossil fuelsFossil fuel divestmentOil and gas companiesEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: TalkTV under fire for not disclosing reporter’s ties to Reform UK in Channel crossing film | TalkTV | The Guardian
description: Christian Drogan’s Invading Britain shows former builder turned journalist trying to travel from France to England in small boat
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Christian Drogan’s Invading Britain shows former builder turned journalist trying to travel from France to England in small boat
Content: Christian Drogan (right in mask) with other passengers on the dinghy.Photograph: TalkTVView image in fullscreenChristian Drogan (right in mask) with other passengers on the dinghy.Photograph: TalkTVTalkTVTalkTV under fire for not disclosing reporter’s ties to Reform UK in Channel crossing filmChristian Drogan’s Invading Britain shows former builder turned journalist trying to travel from France to England in small boatMichael SavageMedia editorFri 28 Aug 2026 08.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 08.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRupert Murdoch’s online channel TalkTV is facing criticism after it did not disclose that a journalist who travelled to Britain in a small boat for a documentary was a Reform party member and activist.The channel revealed the “world exclusive” this week, stating that the treacherous journey had made the former builder turned journalist Christian Drogan the first British man “to invade his own country”.The documentary, Invading Britain: The Undercover Migrant Returns, was released on TalkTV’sYouTubechannel. It showed a year-long effort to board a small boat and cross the Channel from France into England.Small boat crossings are the most prominent campaigning topic for Nigel Farage’sReform UK. Drogan’s story was picked up by other outlets including the Times, the Telegraph and the Sun.However,TalkTVdid not mention that Drogan had previously been clear that he is a Reform member who harbours ambitions of running for office for the party.Appearing onReform’s in-house podcast in June, Drogan said: “I’m a Reform party member. I attend my branch meetings. I would like to stand at some level … that’s my official tie with Reform.”Mic Wright, the media critic whoraised concerns about Drogan’s political background, said audiences should be given the full picture about the reporter’s affiliations, given he was pursuing issues that chimed with Reform’s agenda.Wright said: “It is fair enough to go and do this activity, but he’s not being represented as what he is – which is a Reform activist. He is not being presented in his totality.“If someone who was a member of the Labour party was on a podcast saying they were a Labour member … and then they went out and made a piece of media and an investigation that was machine-tooled to fit with the campaigning lines of the Labour party, Reform would say: ‘Well, this is ridiculous – this is Labour propaganda.’“It is deceptive to the viewers, readers and listeners of these titles and broadcasters.”The criticism was strongly rejected by Isabel Oakeshott, TalkTV’s international editor, who is married toRichard Tice, Reform’s deputy leader, and worked with Drogan on the documentary.“This is a truly desperate attempt to find something negative to say about an exposé that is very uncomfortable for all those who keep making excuses about Channel migrant crossings,” she said. “There is nothing deceptive about repeatedly risking your life to establish the truth about the ongoing invasion of our country.“It is, in any case, abundantly clear, in both the documentary itself and accompanying TalkTV coverage, that this groundbreaking investigation was led by me. My political links could hardly be more public. The extraordinary footage obtained by my colleague Christian Drogan speaks for itself. How he chooses to vote is his own business.”Drogan said he had been motivated by “getting to the heart of the biggest issues facing our country”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I’m a working-class lad from the north of England, watching my country change before my eyes,” he said in a statement. “The camera doesn’t lie. Video footage and audio recordings used to evidence an investigation are about as pure as you can get when it comes to trying to find and document issues that others would prefer to hide and deny.”Murdoch’s company News UK, which owns TalkTV, did not respond to requests for comment.Drogan is part of a “citizen journalism” website called Watchman. He also posts material on social media and has previously appeared on TalkTV asa reporter who was on the ground during a riot in Belfastearlier this year.In the wider coverage of Drogan’s channel crossing, only the Times appears to have mentioned that he was “a journalist who has campaigned for Reform UK”.Appearing on TalkTV, Farage said Drogan’s claim that the crossings were “a national security emergency” was the “exact phrase” he had been using.“These are aggressive, dangerous young males,” Farage said. “There are some who say: ‘Could some of them turn into a force within this country, perhaps even an army within this country’? I don’t think we’re there yet, but the risk remains.”Explore more on these topicsTalkTVReform UKImmigration and asylumRupert MurdochDocumentaryYouTubeFactual TVnewsShareReuse this content

title: White House construction played part in Trump helicopter incident, safety officials say | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Helipad relocation led in part to incident where Marine One, carrying the president, had close call with passenger jet
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Helipad relocation led in part to incident where Marine One, carrying the president, had close call with passenger jet
Content: Marine One lifts off from the White House Ellipse on Thursday.Photograph: Andrew Leyden/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMarine One lifts off from the White House Ellipse on Thursday.Photograph: Andrew Leyden/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockDonald TrumpWhite House construction played part in Trump helicopter incident, safety officials sayHelipad relocation led in part to incident where Marine One, carrying the president, had close call with passenger jetRichard Luscombeand agencyFri 28 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSafety officials say the relocation of a helipad amid Donald Trump’s multi-project White House reconstruction led in part to an incident earlier this month in which a military helicopter carrying the president cametoo close to a passenger jet.A preliminary report published on Thursday by the National Transportation ⁠Safety Board (NTSB) blamed “communication issues” for the failure of the crew of Marine One, the presidential helicopter, to give the required three minutes’ notice to air traffic controllers that they were about to take off from the White House.Consequently, commercial flights from nearby Ronald Reagan Washington national airport were not halted as they normally would be, and there was a “loss of separation” between the helicopter and an Embraer E170 jet operated by an American Airlines subsidiary taking off for Florida.In May, helicopter flights were moved from the White House South Lawn to the nearby Ellipse, a small park immediately south of the White House, because of construction work. Projects under way include Trump’scontroversial new ballroomplanned to replace the East Wing of the White House and a new helipad for Marine One to use. During the 4 August incident, the NTSB found, the Marine One crew attempted at least twice to radio controllers to give the required notice, but were unable to do so.Bryan Bedford, head of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), said the agency relocated an antenna and changed procedure following the incident, and the NTSB said checks made after the relocation showed no subsequent communication issues.However, the Associated Press reported on Friday that air traffic controllers again lost contact with Marine One briefly on Thursday as Trump was heading for an event in Texas, adding that communication was quickly restored and there was no safety issue.According to the NTSB report of the earlier incident, air traffic controllers met with Marine One staff on 30 July, seeking “to discuss concern with recent reports of their not receiving the required ‘three minute to liftoff’ call”.The Marine One crew responded that communications “had been spotty”, the report said, and they agreed to use other means of communicating with the tower in situations where they were unable to reach them.But the back-up failed on 4 August when Marine One was also unable to contact controllers via a helicopter facility at Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling in south-west Washington DC and the helicopter took off with Reagan traffic still departing.Marine One took off at 2.33pm, and the passenger jet one minute later. The Embraer was rerouted “out of caution”, the NTSB said. At the time of the incident, an FAA statement said “it didn’t appear to be a dangerous close call and the aircraft weren’t apparently converging”.FAA rules require aircraft to remain separated by at least 1.5 miles (2.4km) horizontally ⁠and 500ft (152 metres) vertically around airports. The NTSB said Marine One and ​the plane were at one ​point separated by 0.82 nautical mile (0.94 ​mile or 1.5km) laterally and 700ft vertically.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe episode followed a tightening of proximity rules in the wake of aJanuary 2025 collisionbetween a commercial airliner and an army Black Hawk helicopter over the nation’s capital that killed 67 people.Meanwhile, a helipad under construction on the South Lawn to accommodate a new supersized Marine One helicopter is undergoing changes because Trump is unhappy with its appearance and an apparent slope, it wasreportedthis month.Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Volunteers rescue man stuck on 10,000ft-high ledge in Sierra Nevada | US news | The Guardian
description: Climber, stuck on 6in ridge, had veered off treacherous path and ‘any fall would almost certainly be fatal’
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Climber, stuck on 6in ridge, had veered off treacherous path and ‘any fall would almost certainly be fatal’
Content: Rescue team on the way to secure man stuck in Sierra Nevada.Photograph: Mono County Sheriff Search and Rescue TeamView image in fullscreenRescue team on the way to secure man stuck in Sierra Nevada.Photograph: Mono County Sheriff Search and Rescue TeamUS newsVolunteers rescue man stuck on 10,000ft-high ledge in Sierra NevadaClimber, stuck on 6in ridge, had veered off treacherous path and ‘any fall would almost certainly be fatal’Uwa Ede-OsifoFri 28 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn ill-fated move left a man stranded on a 6in ledge over 10,000ft off the ground for hours in California’s Sierra Nevada mountain range, before a volunteer rescue team came to his aid.The climber, who has not been publicly identified, had been scaling the Mendenhall couloir, a gully on the face of Laurel mountain, with a friend on Saturday.The route is steep with portions of potentially destabilizing loose rock. The section the man, reportedly an experienced climber, had been traversing had no route markers,accordingto the San Francisco Chronicle.Veering off path, which the man did by accident, can be deadly, according to the Mono county search and rescue team.Trump administration pushing to hand parcel of Yosemite land to private developer – reportRead more“Traveling off-route quickly leads to increasingly vertical, un-protectable 5th-class terrain with no viable means of continuing either up or down. With thousands of feet of vertical exposure below, any fall would almost certainly be fatal,” the volunteerswrotein a Facebook post last weekend.The rescuers were in a race against time.After thesheriff’s office alerted themto the stranded climber, they searched for two hours without coming across the man, the New York Times reported, until at last a voice in the distance became audible.The climber alternated his weight between each foot, which indicated to rescuers his legs could be cramping. “It was determined that, without intervention, a fatal fall was increasingly possible if the subject remained in place overnight,” reads the Facebook post.A hoist operation, when a helicopter crew lifts someone to rescue, was not viable due to powerful winds.The team opted to go by foot, operating at night using their headlamps for light.“It was incredibly dangerous and a little scary moving around in the dead of night – everyone’s operating on pure trust,” Mitchell Quiring, a rescuer, told the Chronicle. “It’s navigable terrain during the day but it becomes unnavigable at night.”Still, it was not an acceptable option to leave the man there overnight, once the team saw his situation, Quiring told the paper.A rescuer reached the climber from overhead, attaching him to a secure rope system, to prevent a fall, according to the team’s post.The operation wrapped in the early hours of Sunday morning.“He did not give up, and that is really one of the biggest takeaways from this,” Quiringsaidto the New York Times. “This could have been a very different story if he didn’t push through the adversity.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsCaliforniaWest CoastMountainsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Norway’s King Harald dies aged 89  | Norway | The Guardian
description: Norwegians gather to remember monarch whose death comes amid scandal over links between crown princess and Jeffrey Epstein
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Norwegians gather to remember monarch whose death comes amid scandal over links between crown princess and Jeffrey Epstein
Content: 1:15Norwegians pay tribute to 'grandfather figure' King Harald V – videoNorwayNorway’s King Harald dies aged 89Norwegians gather to remember monarch whose death comes amid scandal over links between crown princess and Jeffrey EpsteinJon HenleyEurope correspondentFri 28 Aug 2026 11.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 02.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNorwegians have gathered in their thousands to pay their respects to King Harald V, Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, who has died, aged 89, in Oslo. He was succeeded immediately by his son, King Haakon VIII.The new king thanked “the government and Norwegian people for their support and sympathy for the royal family at this time”. A period of national mourning was announced as crowds left wreaths and messages outside the royal palace in Oslo.Flags around the country were lowered to half mast and church bells rang out at midday. “An era has ended. A new one begins. The king is dead. Long live the king,” the prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said after meeting Haakon.The new king, whose wife, Mette-Marit, has recently come under scrutiny over scandals including amuch-criticised associationwith the late US child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, formally notified the government of his father’s death on Friday morning.View image in fullscreenPeople gather outside the royal palace in Oslo after the death of King Harald.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersHaakon, 53, told the cabinet at an extraordinary council of state that he would take the name Haakon VIII, as expected. He also chose as his personal motto: “Everything forNorway.”The new king will swear an oath of accession in parliament within the next few days. Coronation ceremonies were abolished in Norway more than a century ago, but Haakon could choose to have his reign blessed at a consecration ceremony.The palace had said on Thursday that Harald’s health had deteriorated and that the king, who was seen as a unifying figure and a force for stability amid a string of recent family scandals, was in an “extremely serious” condition.View image in fullscreenKing Harald during a welcoming ceremony for the Danish king and queen in Oslo in May 2024.Photograph: Per Ole Hagen/Getty ImagesStøre said earlier that he had received the news “with deep sadness”, adding: “A whole nation is in mourning, and ⁠the people of Norway are left with a ​deep sense of ‌gratitude for a ‌long life in the service of Norway.”Royalty around Europe sent their condolences, with Spain’s royal family hailing Harald’s “responsibility, dignity, humility and tireless dedication”, and Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary saying he was “loved like few others”.King Carl XVI Gustaf, of Sweden, said: “Throughout the years, King Harald has been a good friend to me, my family, and to Sweden … I ​wish ​my dear godson Haakon, ​who now succeeds his father as head ​of state, ‌success and ​good ​fortune.”Belgium’s royal family recalled Harald’s “humour, humanity and sincerity”, while Britain’s King Charles mourned the loss of his “dear cousin”, paying tribute to a “towering figure” who guided his country with “warmth and humility”.View image in fullscreenPeople gather at Palace Square in Oslo to pay their respects to King Harald.Photograph: Rune Hellestad/GettyGermany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said Norway had “lost a great figure who stood for prudence and unity”, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, expressed “deep sadness”.Norway’s ceremonial head of state since 1991, Harald was being treated in Oslo’s University hospital for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of the body’s red blood cells.He had had numerous health problems – an operation for bladder cancer in 2003 and a pacemaker fitted in 2024 – but always ruled out abdicating, saying he had taken a lifelong oath before the Norwegian parliament.His death comes amid aturbulent periodfor Norway’s royal family. Documents published in the US in January showed thatMette-Marit corresponded with Epsteinbetween 2011 and 2014, long after he was convicted.View image in fullscreenHaakon had taken on additional royal duties while his father was ill.Photograph: Per Ole Hagen/GettyThe files appeared to contain almost 1,000 mentions of Mette-Marit, including intimate exchanges. They drew fierce public criticism, with Støre accusing her in unprecedented comments of “poor judgment”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMette-Marit subsequently released a statement via the royal household expressing her “deepest regret for my friendship with Jeffrey Epstein” and apologising for “the situation that I have put the royal family in, especially the king and queen”.View image in fullscreenMette-Marit had a successful lung transplant in July.Photograph: Lise Åserud/NTB Scanpix/APMarius Borg Høiby, 29, Mette-Marit’s son from a previous relationship, has also been in the spotlight after beingsentenced in June to four years in prisonfor two rapes and 32 other charges, including violence against a former partner. He has appealed against the decision.The scandals have affected public support for Norway’s monarchy, with a poll in February finding support down to 54% from 72% in 2024. Several polls found nearly half of the population felt Mette-Marit could not become queen.View image in fullscreenThe royal family pictured in 2022. Front, left to right: King Harald, Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Queen Sonja. Back, left to right: Marit Tjessem, the mother of Crown Princess Mette-Marit, Crown Prince Haakon, Prince Sverre Magnus and Marius Borg Høiby.Photograph: Lise Åserud/NTB/AFP/Getty ImagesHarald was seen as the Norwegian monarchy’s great moderniser, revamping the crown estates and changing the way the court is run. He married Sonja, a commoner, in 1968 and welcomed two others, Mette-Marit and Ari Behn, as the spouses of his children.A great-great-grandchild ‌of Britain’s Queen Victoria, he succeeded his father, Olav V, at the age of 54 after studying at Oxford and representing his country in sailing events at the Tokyo, Mexico City and Munich Olympics. He was widely appreciated in Norway for his unassuming lifestyle and commitment to national unity.In an emotional speech in 2011 after the far-right extremistAnders Behring Breivikkilled 77 in two terror attacks, he told his subjects that “freedom is stronger than fear” and as “a father, grandfather and spouse, I can only begin to sense some of the pain you feel. As king of the nation, I feel for every one of you.”In a widely praised 2016 speech, he laudeddiversity, tolerance and LGBTQ+ rights, saying Norwegians came from Afghanistan and Pakistan, believed “in God, in Allah and in nothing”, and included “girls who love girls, boys who love boys and girls and boys who love each other”.View image in fullscreenKing Harald and Queen Sonja at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan, Italy.Photograph: Heiko Junge/ReutersMette-Marit, 53, who has a serious lung disease and had a transplant in July, was a single mother to Høiby, who was four years old when her engagement to Norway’s crown prince was announced in late 2000.The marriage, which marked the first time in modern European history that a direct heir to a throne had brought a stepson into a royal family, caused huge controversy in Norway but was strongly backed by King Harald and Queen Sonja.Mette-Marit acknowledged having what she described as a rebellious youth and prior drug use, holding an emotional press conference a week before the wedding in which she expressed regret for her choices and strongly condemned drug use.Explore more on these topicsNorwayEuropeJeffrey EpsteinnewsShareReuse this content

title: Venezuelan opposition up in arms over reports US wants big stake in oil and gas | Venezuela | The Guardian
description: Critics call move to gain long-term access to country’s massive energy reserves ‘predatory’ and ‘unconstitutional’
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Critics call move to gain long-term access to country’s massive energy reserves ‘predatory’ and ‘unconstitutional’
Content: An oil pumpjack on Lake Maracaibo in Cabimas, Zulia state, Venezuela.Photograph: Gaby Oraa/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn oil pumpjack on Lake Maracaibo in Cabimas, Zulia state, Venezuela.Photograph: Gaby Oraa/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesVenezuelaVenezuelan opposition up in arms over reports US wants big stake in oil and gasCritics call move to gain long-term access to country’s massive energy reserves  ‘predatory’ and ‘unconstitutional’Tom PhillipsLatin America correspondentFri 28 Aug 2026 13.41 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s massive energy reserves have sparked an outcry, with critics describing the move as “predatory” and a “rapacious” land grab.Several media outlets this week reported that theTrump administration– which abducted Venezuela’s authoritarian president, Nicolás Maduro, in January and has steered the South American country ever since – hopes to secure long-term access to its oil and gasfields.Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn.On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal saidTrump officials were in “advanced talks”with Venezuelan officials to take “a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields” containing 90bn barrels, nearly a third of Venezuela’s energy reserves.“This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the US and Venezuelan governments,” a source told Reuters, which said the fields being negotiated were in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions.Axios claimed the dealwould be “a legacy-defining moment for President Trump”, with one unnamed official telling the US outlet: “Calling this deal huge would be an understatement … It is massive.”Bloomberg, citing sources familiar with the negotiations, said one deal under discussion was a 100-year lease on several oilfields.The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’sfailure to bring about genuine political changeafter capturing Maduro.“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticising the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States,” they added.Since January’s special forces raid on Caracas, Venezuela has been led by an interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president and minister of petroleum. Other key members of Maduro’s regime have also retained positions of power, including the interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, who has been collaborating with Trump officials –despite having a $25m (£18m) US bounty on his headfor alleged drug trafficking. Meanwhile, the exiled opposition leader, María Corina Machado, whose movement is believed to have won the 2024 presidential elections, has been sidelined.Ricardo Hausmann, an exiled former minister and opposition supporter, wrote on X: “An illegitimate interim government with an illegitimate hydrocarbons law has no legitimacy to strike this unconstitutional deal. It will be a fiasco for all involved.”The economist Francisco Rodríguezurged Venezuela’s national assemblyto reject what he called a “predatory deal”. “Handing over Venezuela’s oil wealth to the US contravenes the constitution and is not in the interest of the Venezuelan people – much more when it is done at gunpoint,” Rodríguez said.Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent journalist and government critic,sarcastically calledthe “surrender” of Venezuela’s natural riches “the deal of the century”.Gregory Brew, an energy historian and Eurasia Group analyst, anticipated “quite a lot of suspicion and rejection of any deal that would hand the United States government effective control over Venezuelan resources”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBrew said the reported deal reminded him of how BP, then the Anglo-PersianOilCompany, controlled the oil resources of Iraq and Iran at the start of the last century.“Anglo-Persian was given a concession by the shah of Iran in 1901 … in exchange for what was essentially a bribe to the Persian government, and it gave the company sweeping rights. The company was essentially in total control of any oil it found and would be able to retain virtually all the profits of any other oil it found and exploited and exported,” Brew said.“From Trump’s point of view, the control over oil is something of an end in and of itself,. But if you do try to rationalise it, I think US dominance over Venezuelan oil reserves allows the US to regard Venezuelan reserves as its own reserves: a source of oil from which the United States can draw and that nobody else has access to. I think that’s how the administration is conceiving of this – excluding China, excluding Russia, but I think also excluding other potential customers for Venezuelan oil,” he said. “It sounds colonial, because it is.”Venezuela’s post-Maduro conversion into what many call a US protectorate is the most dramatic play in Trump’s push to reassert Washington’s influence over Latin America as part of the so-called “Donroe Doctrine”.That policy is a 21st-century adaptation of the 19th-century Monroe doctrine by which President James Monroe sought to keep European powers out of theAmericas. Trump’s version is about countering China’s growing footprint in the region and imposing US will through economic and military pressure.Maduro’s downfall has brought some change to Venezuela, with hundreds of political prisoners freed under Rodríguez and talks about reforming the regime-controlled supreme court taking place.But no date has been set for a fresh presidential election and Machado has been unable to return from exile. “Delcy’s been doing a fantastic job,” Trump told reporters last month, claiming Venezuela was “not really ready” for a vote.Explore more on these topicsVenezuelaAmericasOilGasCommoditiesTrump administrationUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: UK petrol prices hit highest level in almost four years as bank holiday getaway looms | Petrol prices | The Guardian
description: Average cost of petrol reaches 161.6p a litre, while diesel costs average of 183.4p, according to the AA
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Average cost of petrol reaches 161.6p a litre, while diesel costs average of 183.4p, according to the AA
Content: Millions of people are preparing to make car journeys over the bank holiday weekend in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenMillions of people are preparing to make car journeys over the bank holiday weekend in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAPetrol pricesUK petrol prices hit highest level in almost four years as bank holiday getaway loomsAverage cost of petrol reaches 161.6p a litre, while diesel costs average of 183.4p, according to the AALauren AlmeidaFri 28 Aug 2026 07.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK petrol prices have hit their highest level since 2022, piling more financial pressure on motorists before the bank holiday weekend.The average cost of petrol has reached 161.6p a litre, while diesel costs an average of 183.4p a litre, according to the AA breakdown company.The last time the petrol price was so high was in November 2022, when it soared in the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.It comes as millions of people prepare to make car journeys over the bank holiday weekend, which will be marked in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. The RAC estimates that the UK’s motorways and major roads could have the most traffic since its records began in 2015.The services company has predicted Friday is likely to be the worst day for heavy traffic, with more than 4.1m cars expected on the roads.Luke Bosdet of the AA said the rise in petrol prices showed that “UK pump pricing is back to its worst”. It is “too often overpriced and uncompetitive, with too many communities denied road fuel at a reasonable price”, he said.View image in fullscreenThe Competition and Markets Authority found this summer that many petrol stations were too slow to pass on cuts in wholesale prices to their customers.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAThe UK’s competition regulator told fuel retailers this year that it would step up its monitoring of pump prices amid concern over profiteering as the US war with Iran drives up wholesale costs.Before the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – traded at about $72 a barrel. It hit a peak of $126 a barrel in April, before dipping to $71 at the start of July on hopes of a peace deal. It now trades at $89.63.The Competition and Markets Authority found this summer that many petrol stations weretoo slowto pass on falls in wholesale energy prices to their customers.A government scheme called Fuel Finder allows drivers to compare the cost of fuel offered by petrol stations across the UK. The AA found that in some areas, petrol was sold at about 10p below the national average cost for a litre on Thursday night, at stations in areas such as Aylesbury, Wembley and Gloucester.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBosdet said just one competitively priced forecourt “can often pull down the price of fuel locally, including at nearby supermarkets”.He said: “Drivers just need to find them and go to them.”Earlier this month the CMA said it hadsent out more than 1,000 warning lettersto retailers who had failed to share their prices with the Fuel Finder service.Explore more on these topicsPetrol pricesMotoringTravel & leisureTransportOilUS-Israel war on IranRoad transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fed chair says delivering ‘stable prices’ is central bank’s job as inflation persists | Federal Reserve | The Guardian
description: However, Kevin Warsh didn’t say if interest rates would change in coming months, as inflation remains stubborn
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: However, Kevin Warsh didn’t say if interest rates would change in coming months, as inflation remains stubborn
Content: Kevin Warsh at the Jackson Hole economic symposium on Thursday in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.Photograph: Natalie Behring/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKevin Warsh at the Jackson Hole economic symposium on Thursday in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.Photograph: Natalie Behring/Getty ImagesFederal ReserveFed chair says delivering ‘stable prices’ is central bank’s job as inflation persistsHowever, Kevin Warsh didn’t say if interest rates would change in coming months, as inflation remains stubbornGaya GuptaFri 28 Aug 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS Federal Reserveis not done fighting high inflation, its chair, Kevin Warsh, said in his first major speech in the role on Friday, emphasizing that it was “the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices”.Warsh did not indicate where the Fed will take interest rates in the coming months, despite US inflation remaining stubbornly above the central bank’s 2% target amid the war in Iran. But his speech was taken by markets as a signal that rates may rise in the coming months, a move that may put him at odds withDonald Trump, who has aggressively called for rates to be cut.The Fed chair painted a rosy view of the economy that contrasts with recent data. He said the economy “appears to have strengthened” given how it has held up to shocks.Is the Trump Treasury panicking over the level of US debt?Read more“On that score, both Main Street and Wall Street have been resilient,” Warsh said at the Fed’s annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, on Friday.The Jackson Hole symposium has typically served as a platform for Fed chairs to offer clarity on the central bank’s general direction. For example, former Fed chair Jerome Powell foreshadowedrate cuts at his keynote addresslast year.But Warsh on Friday insisted the days of such “forward guidance” were over, saying that the practice was adopted by the Fed during the 2008 financial crisis. “As with other legacies of crises past, I believe that the practice has overstayed its welcome,” he said.Markets are still expected to carefully gauge Warsh’s speech for signs of the Fed’s next move. At the central bank’s last board meeting in July, three out of 12 voting members wanted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point – the first time in a decade so many board members shared dissent over a policy position. But a majority of the members voted to hold rates, which currently sit at a range of 3.5% to 3.75%, steady.Since he was appointed in May, Warsh has had to strike a delicate balance between managing an economy that has been shaken by higher oil prices brought on by the war in Iran without provoking the ire of the White House. Trump has continued to insist the Fed should lower interest rates, despite economists who warn that that would further exacerbate inflation. After hitting a three-year high of 4.2% in May, US inflationcooledto 3.4% in July – still 1% higher than figures seen last year.Warsh said progress on inflation over the past several years has been “modest”, and though price readings from over the summer came in better than expected, they did not indicate that “underlying trends have meaningfully improved”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe US bond market has been particularly sensitive to higher inflation, with the yield on 10-year notes hitting its highest level since 2007 in recent weeks. Yields briefly went down after the US treasury announced a bigdebt buy-back scheme, though the relief proved to be temporary. Rising rates in the US have driven yields higher abroad – bond rates in the UK, Germany, France and Japan have all hit their highest levels in decades. Meanwhile, the US grossnational debttopped $40tn for the first time in history last week.In reaction to Warsh’s opening remarks, the two-year and 10-year US treasury yields increased slightly, while the 30-year treasury remained largely the same. The S&P 500 remained leveled while the Dow Jones ticked down slightly.Explore more on these topicsFederal ReserveInflationUS interest ratesBondsEconomic policyEconomicsUS economynewsShareReuse this content

title: Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes city | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races
Author: Tom Perkins
Headline: Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races
Content: View of the Gordie Howe international bridge during the opening ceremony in Windsor, Ontario, on 24 July 2026.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenView of the Gordie Howe international bridge during the opening ceremony in Windsor, Ontario, on 24 July 2026.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsDetroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes cityUnpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan racesTom Perkinsin DetroitFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery day$1bnworth of goods crosses the river dividing Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry.News this week of Donald Trump’sescalating trade spatwith Canada has everyone worried. Political and economic leaders and observers labeled the move an act of “hubris” , blamed Trump’s “ego”, and called the escalation “insanity”.“We don’t needCanada, they need us,” Trump declared.But many are hoping that Trump’s imposition of50% tariffson Canadian goods this week will not last long, with the upcoming midterm elections as a pivotal reason the plan may be scrapped.Control of the US Congress hangs in the balance and will almost certainly be decided by several close Michigan races. It also comes just two months after polling highlighted Michiganders’ fatigue with and opposition to the president’s unprecedented tariff program.By a 63%-31% margin, residents here oppose tariffs on Canadian goods, according to a June Epic-MRA poll, including 35% of Republicans. Meanwhile, nearly 75% of Michiganders said the tariffs are fueling high prices.Trump doubling down on an unpopular policy deep into election season is viewed by many observers as a gift to Democrats, and there is a real possibility that it contributes to a midterm loss for the Republicans. Meanwhile, there seems to be little upside for Trump.“I don’t understand what Trump is thinking,” the Epic-MRA pollster Bernie Porn said.Regardless, Michiganders have already suffered disproportionately as theypay on averageover $3,200 annually for tariffs, or about 142% more than the rest of the country, because of the state’s shared border with Canada.The Canadian economy would also take a major hit if the tariffs are imposed, said Patrick Anderson, a Michigan-based economist with the Anderson Economic Group.View image in fullscreenThe Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters at Renaissance high school in Detroit, Michigan, on 7 August.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images“Both will suffer – there are no two ways about it,” Anderson added.This critical upper midwest swing state has picked the presidential winner in five consecutive elections, going from Barack Obama to Trump to Joe Biden and back to Trump. Democrats’ chances to retake the Senate rest heavily on the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed beating Trump ally Mike Rogers in the 3 November general election race. Rogers has supported the tariffs, but so far has been silent on the latest escalation.The tariffs and theunpopular Iran war’scontribution to inflation represent a “double hit” for Republicans, Porn said, and Trump is handing ammo to a particularly adept candidate in El-Sayed. He has energized people with his anti-establishment, populist political vision, and a no-holds-barred delivery.“El-Sayed has proven to be very, very articulate on a number of issues,” Porn added. “I think that he is going to try and just throw bombs at Rogers [in an upcoming debate] because Rogers supports these tariffs and trade war. Trump’s low popularity is an anchor around Rogers’ neck.”In a statement, El-Sayed hammered Trump and Rogers, saying that the president “cares more about his ego and saber-rattling than addressing the affordability crisis.“Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he’s asking Michigan families to pay the price,” El-Sayed said. “Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long, and Mike Rogers won’t do anything but rubber-stamp them.”El-Sayed said he would push for “real, fair trade deals that create good-paying jobs”. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment.The United Auto Workers (UAW), which has 350,000 members in Michigan and is often a political kingmaker here, has supported some of Trump’s targeted tariffs, but said in a statement it “rejects” the latest escalation.“If we’re going to increase tariffs anywhere, it should be on countries where automakers continue to offshore jobs because they can pay workers $3 an hour, force them to work in unsafe conditions, and crack down on independent unions,” the UAW president, Shawn Fain, said. Canada has strong unions, and the UAW supports those.“Tariffs work, but only if they are deployed intentionally to protect workers and grow our manufacturing communities, and it’s time to permanently end offshoring and the race to the bottom,” Fain added.Mexico and Canada currently face 25% US tariffs on autos, though partial exemptions in the nations’ free trade agreement make the effective rate much lower, overall. Andersonestimatedtariffs cost US auto companies about $12.5bn in 2025.The Canadian government has announced it will impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of goods starting 8 September. The actions leading to the latest blow-up have been “rife with miscalculations, overreactions, and hubris”, Anderson said. He read through the list of goods on which tariffs would be imposed – feathers, sweaters, girls’ dresses, lobster.“This is not a trade war. This is an annoyance list. Chest pounding,” Anderson said.The North American auto industry over the last 60 years has integrated across the continent, and auto parts cross a border an average of six times before they land in a final product. That means there would be shared pain, Anderson said, and it would reverberate across the upper midwest, where bigger manufacturing cities are typically powered by industries that are often reliant on international trade.But the Canadian economy is smaller, and Ontario’s economy is so concentrated that it would hit harder north of the border, Anderson added. Ultimately, the real threat is that “these two countries go pell-mell into it” and impose tariffs on oil, energy and commodities that hit harder than lobster.The dialogue has devolved into the usual petty antagonism that is a hallmark of Trump’s beefs. Trumpsigned an executive orderto rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, and Vice-President JD Vance referred to Canada as the 51st state.“Let me say with great understatement that this is not helpful,” Anderson added.View image in fullscreenThe American and Canadian flags fly at the midway point on the Gordie Howe International Bridge, that connects Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, Michigan.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockIndeed, the Windsor mayor, Drew Dilkens, took exception to that particular comment. In an interview, he expressed deep frustration over Trump’s moves, and labeled justifications Trump has used for issuing tariffs, including framing them as a response to illegal immigration on the northern border, “nonsense”.The latest escalation “is an aggressive move, one that could not be ignored by our country”, added Dilkens, who leads the city of 230,000 people. “It’s just offensive that he launches these attacks at Canada, who is your largest trading partner, your closest ally, and your neighbor.”The chaos has cooled investment in Windsor, and prices remain high on both sides of the border. He pointed out how much more US consumers are paying not just for automobiles, but for beef, which in part stems from tariffs on Canadian beef.“What is really crazy is that he is willing to throw his own citizens under the bus to pursue his tariff agenda,” Dilkens said. “They have Donald Trump to thank.”Highlighting the tension among the president and some in his base, the Michigan chamber of commerce, a trade organization that lobbies on behalf of the state’s largest corporations, normally vocally supports the president on economic issues. It has not made a public statement, and did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.However, the typically pro-TrumpDetroitchamber of commerce did not mince words.“Escalating tensions and tariffs will only cause economic pain on both sides of the border, especially in Michigan and the binational Detroit-Windsor region,” the chamber said in a press statement, adding that global competitors like China benefited most.“Our economies are intertwined, interconnected, and stronger together; the sooner normalcy is restored the better.”This article was amended on 28 August 2026. An earlier version gave incorrect commencement dates for the US and Canadian tariffs.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsDetroitUS politicsCanadaUS economyEconomicsAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Asda returns to growth after more than two years | Asda | The Guardian
description: Chair Allan Leighton says lower prices and an improved online service are attracting more shoppers
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Chair Allan Leighton says lower prices and an improved online service are attracting more shoppers
Content: An Asda supermarket in Leeds. The company’s chair, Allan Leighton, said fresh produce was the ‘pinch point’.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn Asda supermarket in Leeds. The company’s chair, Allan Leighton, said fresh produce was the ‘pinch point’.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAsdaAsda returns to growth after more than two yearsChair Allan Leighton says lower prices and an improved online service are attracting more shoppersSarah ButlerFri 28 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsda has heralded its first trading growth in more than two years as the supermarket’s boss said it was attracting more shoppers with lower prices and an improved online service.Allan Leighton, the executive chair of the UK’s third-largest grocer, said a 0.2% rise in sales at established stores, excluding fuel, in the seven weeks to 18 August was “a huge milestone” that was “psychologically important for the business”. In the preceding three months, sales had fallen 2.3%.“Our price position is strong, we are now getting more customers in the business and we have got some momentum online and that’s been the biggest drag,” Leighton said. The last time Asda’s sales rose was in the first three months of 2024.He said Asda’s performance had been aided by more stability in its IT systems after a traumatic and expensive shift from the technology of its former owner Walmart. In 2020 the billionaire Issa brothers and the private equity firm TDR Capital bought Asda in a£6.8bn takeover. TDR now controls the business.Since the buyout, Asda has been struggling with falling sales and profits as well as a huge debt pile, while paying out close to £1bn to revamp its IT systems. Leighton returned to helpturn around the businessfor the second time in his career in November 2024 after a 20-year absence.View image in fullscreenAllan Leighton embraces World Cup fever. He said growth had been led by food, sales of which were up 0.7% at established stores during a seven-week period.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianDespite inflation on groceries in the UK, Asda’s sales had been falling as the problems with its technology meant it struggled to keep shelves stocked, while it also faced heavy competition from the cut-price chains Aldi and Lidl as well as from bigger rivals Tesco and Sainsbury’s.Aldi is less than one percentage point behind Asda in terms of market share and continues to grow at a faster pace, threatening to steal its rival’s spot as the UK’s third-largest chain.Leighton has said it isnot inevitablethat Aldi will leapfrog Asda, as the bigger chain is fighting back with measures including a deal with the online specialist Ocado toprovide technology to improve its websiteand delivery systems from next year.“There is some momentum in the business and it is upwards and that is important,” Leighton told the Guardian. He had “never felt not confident” and Asda could be revamped as “the business is too good not to be turned around”.He said growth had been led by food, sales of which were up 0.7% at established stores during the seven-week period. Sales of clothing and other non-food products fell as, Leighton said, the wider market was tough, and the late August bank holiday had delayed shoppers’ spending on back to school items.Inflation on food is appearing in some areas of produce, such as tomatoes and cucumbers, as the hot dry summer hit crops, but Leighton said Asda was managing stocks and pricing of petrol well despitehigh fuel priceslinked to the war in Iran. “Produce is the pinch point,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLeighton said it was not clear if shoppers’ sentiment had improved since Andy Burnham became prime minister, and there was a sense households were waiting to see how things panned out in the autumn and with the October budget announcement.“People are waiting to see,” he said. “I think John Healey is a good choice as chancellor; he is very sensible and objective.”But “clarity on the budget and economic plan” would be key to consumer and business confidence, he said. “The key economic policy of the [Labour] government so far has been to inhibit growth.” He wanted to see a minimum policy that “doesn’t inhibit growth and [ideally] enhances growth”.Leighton added: “That has got to be by not pulling more cost into business.” He called on the government to consider excluding retailers from the additional business rates for larger buildings.Explore more on these topicsAsdaSupermarketsRetail industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Bigmouth strums again: was Andy Burnham’s Smiths jam in Kyiv the perfect soundtrack to a Britain in freefall? | The Smiths | The Guardian
description: The UK prime minister clearly still adores the band. Perhaps he’s attracted to songs about sham justice and murderous meat factories, shot through with nihilism and exquisite despair
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The UK prime minister clearly still adores the band. Perhaps he’s attracted to songs about sham justice and murderous meat factories, shot through with nihilism and exquisite despair
Content: Plangently nostalgic … Burnham jamming Rusholme Ruffians in a mobile recording studio near the front line in Kyiv this week.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/POOL AFP/APView image in fullscreenPlangently nostalgic … Burnham jamming Rusholme Ruffians in a mobile recording studio near the front line in Kyiv this week.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/POOL AFP/APThe SmithsBigmouth strums again: was Andy Burnham’s Smiths jam in Kyiv the perfect soundtrack to a Britain in freefall?The UK prime minister clearly still adores the band. Perhaps he’s attracted to songs about sham justice and murderous meat factories, shot through with nihilism and exquisite despairZoe WilliamsFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs an origin story, Andy Burnham: Smiths Fan has a lot going for it. It’s plainly authentic: he can name the time he saw them live (Salford University, Queen Is Dead tour, 1986). A cynical young man in a hurry might fake that now, but not back when he first said it, in 2013. Asked by Labour Uncut for his desert island tracks during his 2010 leadership bid, three of the eight were sung by Morrissey (two Smiths singles and one off Viva Hate), which is superfan territory.That’s a softball exercise to endear yourself to Labour members; you have eight chances to hit every base, and to blow three lives on an artist who had already, by then, been dabbling in nationalism for 18 years (we’ll come back to this) was dicey and brave. You’ll recall that Burnham did not win that election. If you were an enemy state, amassing this hinterland for an asset, you’d have basically done a really good job.View image in fullscreen‘Put me on the train for London Town’ … Burnham outside the Salford Lads Club, made famous by the Smiths’ Queen Is Dead album, after launching his mayoral re-election campaign in 2024.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesIn the business of projecting a human being, through a miasma of talking points and half-answers, it’s more important that the passion be genuine than that it hit the right cultural and social touch points, but in the late 90s and early 00s, the Smiths hit those too. Bear in mind that they’d already been split for a full decade by the time Tony Blair came into power and Burnham first appeared in parliament, so they already signalled a bygone youth, rather than: “I am a cool dude who still goes clubbing to this day.”But the Smiths’ body of work has a worldview and it’s explicitly political: the lyrics describe a nation in permanent decline, its justice a sham, its education a meat factory, its meat factories (obviously) murder, its subjects shot through with nihilism and exquisite despair. People who called the Smiths miserablist were wilfully ignoring what they actually sounded like, which was the opposite of despair, a kind of penetrating vivacity that obliterated the greyness its words described.It was funny, ironic, complicated and even its counterculturalism was knowingly passé, declinist. There was so much in there about the queen – and who really cared about the royals by the mid-80s? It had a defiant intellectualism and prefigured the 90s spirit in which everything was infinitely interpretable, and to be contradictory was a sign you were alive.In that sense, Burnham’s fandom encapsulated the long 90s pretty well. You didn’t have to beliterallyleft behind to be alienated by modernity. You could justvibeleft-behindness. WhenBurnham jammed Rusholme Ruffians on guitar in Kyiv on Monday, there was something plangently nostalgic about it – not for 1985, when the song was released, but for the turn of this century, when we could all be lonely yet not alone, where death wishes were routinely expressed but also a metaphor for whatever you liked, where fairgrounds were empty but also full. It was the era when history was over, when ideological differences had collapsed; and while that turned out not to be true, it did allow in a spirit of openness and intellectual experiment that was extremely rich.It was the kind of attitude that would now be derided as “metropolitan elitist” and Burnham noticed that pretty early, caveating in an interview in 2015, during his second leadership bid, that he went off the Smiths in his mid-20s when hedecidedthat they were “for people who almost want to make themselves slightly superior: ‘I’m into the Smiths and I look down on people who listen to Level 42’”. That, too, was a little risky, since this was the musical love of his life, and he was suddenly prepared to throw them under the bus just to gate off the possibility that Level 42 fans might vote for Liz Kendall. You’ll remember that he did not win that leadership election either, and nobody voted for Kendall, except, conceivably, Level 42 fans (she got 4.5%).Two things complicated the picture further. First, Morrissey’s own politics. By 1992, he was lyrically and performatively flirting with a nativism that is now, unavoidably, Islamophobia (in 2017, he expressed support for Anne Marie Waters, a name now lost to public life, thena Tommy Robinson ally and proponent of Great Replacement theory). Burnham has addressed, in pretty weak terms, the fact that he and Morrissey no longer see eye to eye, but that probably does it.View image in fullscreen‘He’ll die a Smiths fan. He may as well enjoy it’ … Burnham going up to 11.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesMorrissey’s politics were ugly from the start of his solo career – the lyrics of Bengali in Platforms are honestly stomach-churning – but the Smiths were never just him (as a judge famously determined in 1996, ruling in favour of Mike Joyce on the matter of royalty-sharing, callingMorrissey“devious”). It seems unlikely to me that even Johnny Marr, (the late) Andy Rourke and Joyce could tell what Morrissey would later become, when they were making that work in the 80s, let alone any of the fans.Second, in 2006, David Cameron just marched in and vandalised everything, choosing This Charming Man on Desert Island Discs, describing listening to the Smiths at Eton. It tested the proposition – we can all be as alienated as each other – to destruction, and with the most insulting imaginable song: “Why pamper life’s complexity / When the leather runs smooth on the passenger seat?” can function as so much, but it cannot work as karaoke for the guyin the seat.Marr and Morrissey both publicly forbade him from liking the Smiths, which I guess may have mollified true fans such as Burnham but did nothing to head off Cameron’s callow, low-affect, “I’d like to capture all the wealth but also join in your economic alienation, it looks meaningless and kinda fun” politics, and their ruinous effect on the nation.At the age Burnham is now – 56 – there’s no going back. He’ll die a Smiths fan. He may as well enjoy it. Judging by his Kyiv jam and his July “I left the north again / I travelled south again” video on socials, quoting Is It Really So Strange?, it looks like he is.Explore more on these topicsThe SmithsAndy BurnhamMorrisseyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A kids TV star to Jimmy Carr: who will host the new Top Gear? | Top Gear | The Guardian
description: A new series has finally been confirmed, with Carr rumoured to be the next Clarkson. But there are others ready to steer the wheel, including a Cbeebies host, a Celebrity Traitors favourite and a motor-head model
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: A new series has finally been confirmed, with Carr rumoured to be the next Clarkson. But there are others ready to steer the wheel, including a Cbeebies host, a Celebrity Traitors favourite and a motor-head model
Content: Taking the wheel … Jimmy Carr.Photograph: Matt FrostView image in fullscreenTaking the wheel … Jimmy Carr.Photograph: Matt FrostTop GearA kids TV star to Jimmy Carr: who will host the new Top Gear?A new series has finally been confirmed, with Carr rumoured to be the next Clarkson. But there are others ready to take the wheel, including a Cbeebies host, a Celebrity Traitors favourite and a motor-head modelStuart HeritageFri 28 Aug 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTop Gear is the show that cannot die. Nothing can kill it; not the dryness of the original, the violence that ended the Clarkson era, orthe horrifying crash that brought its most recent incarnation to a halt. And so, inevitably, yesterday theBBC confirmed that Top Gear was being resurrected once again. The corporation’s director of entertainment, Ed Havard, told the Edinburgh TV festival: “There has been a lot of speculation about this, and we can confirm that Top Gear is coming back. I’m not going to talk about talent today.”Which is fair enough – but I can. Casting a show likeTop Gearis a dangerously tricky proposition. Whoever the BBC picks to host needs to be funny, charismatic, good at driving and knowledgable about cars. Lots of people are good at one of these things, but few are good at more than that and almost none are good at everything.View image in fullscreenRallying call … Michael Fassbender at Le Mans in Barcelona in 2021.Photograph: TF-Images/DeFodi Images/Getty ImagesClearly, the smartest thing to do is take a leaf out of Prime Video’s newly revived The Grand Tour, cast three relative unknowns and let them find their feet over a couple of years. That is, after all, what happened with the original Top Gear cast of 2002.But that won’t happen. Top Gear is now too established to be a grower, and the BBC will want it to land with immediate impact. Plus, all the rumours and press speculation suggest thatJimmy Carris going to host it anyway, so they’re clearly aiming high. So with that in mind, let’s idly speculate about who could be signed up.Jimmy CarrWe’ll start with the obvious one. Carr fits the Clarkson bill incredibly well: he’s sharp and knowledgable about cars, and he got rich by making lazy jokes about minority groups. Also – like former hosts Matt LeBlanc and Chris Evans – he has a proven record as aStar in a Reasonably Priced Car. Plus, his name is literally Carr, so there’s also that. One downside is that, if you’ve heard Carr on a podcast lately, he seems to have swapped comedy for making the sort of faux-profound philosophical statements you tend to hear from the most boring man in the pub, which might turn some viewers off.Suitability: 8/10Jodie KiddStrangely, Kidd might be the best like-for-like Clarkson replacement around. A part of Top Gear since 2003, when she recorded a blazingly fast lap time, Kidd has since gained an international racing licence, presented Channel 5’s The Classic Car Show and ITV4’s Isle of Man TT coverage, hosted a motoring podcast and launched a car-based YouTube channel. She was even shortlisted to present the revived Top Gear a decade ago, but turned it down. The BBC would be foolish not to try its luck again.Suitability: 9/10Joe MarlerMarler is another name linked to the job, although that seems to be less down to his extensive trackside experience and more because he was quite good on Celebrity Traitors a year ago. Nevertheless, you can see him fitting in here. Not necessarily as the lead host, but as the colour co-presenter; a full-bore enthusiast who (unlike Kidd or Carr) would probably be OK with being shoved down a ski jump ramp in a Reliant Robin.Suitability: 6/10Catie MunningsView image in fullscreenShiny ... rally driver Catie Munnings.Photograph: Nigel Jones/Purple TangerineAn outside bet, but one worth making. If you have young children, Munnings is best known for being the host of the CBeebies show Catie’s Amazing Machines, in which she bombed around tracks in a variety of vehicles and was very shiny and enthusiastic about everything. But she’s also a professional rally driver and (handily) has been a Top Gear magazine columnist.Suitability: 7/10Michael FassbenderLet me stop you right there. Again, Fassbender knows his cars – the man has spent most of this decade as a professional race car driver – and he posted a competitive Star in a Reasonably Priced Car lap back in the day. However, I need to invoke the Matt LeBlanc clause. At some point, a person becomes too famous to submit to the rigours of a weekly magazine show. Once you’re already rich and successful, all those wet Tuesdays spent power-sliding a Vauxhall around Dunsfold will quickly start to feel like a chore. Soon you’ll leave and Top Gear will be left desperately trying to reboot itself for the billionth time.Suitability: 2/10OgmiosListen, a boy can dream. Ogmios’ YouTube videos, and his 2022 BBC Three series, Zen Motoring, would be a necessary tone corrective for something as boisterous as Top Gear. His stock in trade is long, slow drives through north London, softly making calm remarks about the various behaviours of his fellow road users. Ogmios is the logical endpoint of the James May type, and I would watch the hell out of him. Others might disagree, and Top Gear would almost certainly rob him of everything that’s good about him. But that won’t stop me stumping for Ogmios here.Suitability: 1/10Explore more on these topicsTop GearTelevisionJimmy CarrMichael FassbenderfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The 50 best TV shows to watch this autumn | Television | The Guardian
description: Nigella on Bake Off! Attenborough in Blue Planet III! Blade Runner 2099! Plus Adrian Mole, Harry Potter and a certain Celebrity Traitors … here are all the must-see shows of the season
Author: Kate Abbott
Headline: Nigella on Bake Off! Attenborough in Blue Planet III! Blade Runner 2099! Plus Adrian Mole, Harry Potter and a certain Celebrity Traitors … here are all the must-see shows of the season
Content: Coming up … David Tennant in Time and Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer in Bladerunner 2099.Composite: Guardian Design/BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyView image in fullscreenComing up … David Tennant in Time and Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer in Bladerunner 2099.Composite: Guardian Design/BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyAutumn arts preview 2026TelevisionThe 50 best TV shows to watch this autumnNigella on Bake Off! Attenborough in Blue Planet III! Blade Runner 2099! Plus Adrian Mole, Harry Potter and a certain Celebrity Traitors … here are all the must-see shows of the seasonRising star Lara Ricote on the real heartache behind her new breakup comedyKate AbbottandStuart HeritageFri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTShareThe Lycett ArmsWayward and chaotic, in the grand tradition of The Word and TFI Friday,Late Night Lycettproved that Joe Lycett had fully inherited Friday nights on Channel 4. Its follow-up sounds even more TFI-esque. The Lycett Arms is a real east London pub, open for just one hour a week, which required Lycett to train to be accredited with a level 2 award for personal licence holders. The show promises “top-drawer comedy entertainment from Joe and a pub full of celebrity guests”. What could possibly go wrong?Channel 4, 4 SeptemberLast SeenColin from Accounts’Patrick Brammallis totally changing tack with this intense drama about a one-time cop whose three-year-old daughter Mags disappeared more than a decade ago. When the remains of a young girl are found nearby, Ian Ridley (Brammall) is first on the scene – and his former colleagues in the police force know there’s nothing they can do to stop him from doing some digging. But the truth about the victim is far murkier. A twisty six-parter that will keep you guessing.Apple TV, 9 SeptemberSlow HorsesView image in fullscreenBeing picked off one by one … Jack Lowden and Gary Oldman in Slow Horses.Photograph: Jack English/AppleJackson’s Joes are being picked off one by one – and everyone who has ever worked at Slough House has been wiped from the system at MI5 HQ the Park, so no one will even know they’re goners. The sixth season of thesmash-hit dramaabout supposedly second-rate spies kicks off with a horrifying fire in a shipping container and a very violent funeral, and only ramps up from there. The usual suspects, from Gary Oldman and Kristin Scott Thomas to Jack Lowden, are still at it. Plus, the brilliant Lenny Rush joins the cast – and turns out to be a dab hand at spycraft.Apple TV, 16 SeptemberYouthView image in fullscreenScabrous and hilarious … Sharon Horgan in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBO“Has any man ever said: ‘Have you met my girlfriend? She’s sexy, she’s fun, she’s 60.’ I need to meet someonenow. I think I’ve got 10 years left as a sexual person, tops.”Sharon Horgan’s new comedy is as scabrous and hilarious as always. Things aren’t going great for Alex (played by Horgan herself): her body is failing her, her son Ruari is veering off the rails (mooning at his school graduation) and her ex is moving abroad, leaving her even more of a single parent.
