Let’s hope she’s able to spice things up with some “new dick energy”.HBO Max, 20 SeptemberBrothersView image in fullscreenThe bizarre new Curb Your Enthusiasm … Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey in Brothers.Photograph: Ryan Green/AppleFirst Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey starred inTrue Detective. Then McConaughey revealed that he recently discovered hemight have the same father as Harrelson. And now, bizarrely, they are basically Curb Your Enthusiasming this new dynamic. In Brothers, the pair play fictionalised versions of themselves who learn that … well, you can see where this is going. You have to applaud the effort, since making an entire television series about some family gossip seems like so much more hard work than simply getting a DNA test.Apple TV, 23 SeptemberStrictly Come DancingView image in fullscreenWill any other scandals befall the show? … The new Strictly hosts Johannes Radebe, Josh Widdicombe and Emma Willis.Photograph: BBC/Ray BurmistonAll eyes on the Elstree and Borehamwood ballroom for the first series of the sparkly dance staple without Claudia Winkleman and Tess Daly. How on earth will the trio of new hosts – former pro dancer and all-round icon Johannes Radebe, Emma “safe pair of hands” Willis and comedian and former penguin suit-wearing Christmas contestant Josh Widdicombe – fare? And will any other scandals befall the show as it attempts this reset? The contestants include Shaun Wright-Phillips, Jaime Winstone, Dani Dyer, Delta Goodrem and, er, celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton.BBC One, SeptemberThe Great British Bake OffView image in fullscreenThe queen of spoon-licking TV joins … The Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Channel 4/Love Productions/PAStale no more! Bake Off has been in serious need of a revamp for a while now – and who better tozhuzh it upthan the queen of sass herself, Nigella Lawson. The grande dame of spoon-licking cookery TV, and all-time winner of best pronunciation of the word microwavay, joins as the new judge. Expect to be whisked away by her charm, withering putdowns and (fingers crossed) fantastic repartee with Paul Hollywood.Channel 4, SeptemberKill JackieView image in fullscreenBonkers … Catherine Zeta-Jones in Kill Jackie.Photograph: Unai Mateo/PrimeWell, this one looks bonkers.Catherine Zeta-Jonesplays a former international cocaine dealer who has spent 20 years hiding in plain sight as an ostentatiously wealthy art dealer. But her cover is blown when she discovers that a group of elite assassins called the Seven Demons has been hired to kill her. Needless to say, she tries to kill them first. Co-starring Daniel Ings, Julian Barratt and Julian Rhind-Tutt, this has the potential to be the most entertaining thing in forever.Prime Video, 2 OctoberWarView image in fullscreenJuicy, bitchy and very starry … Dominic West and Sienna Miller in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesIt’s juicy, it’s bitchy and it’s very starry indeed: George Kay’s tentpole divorce drama looks at the bitter end of a relationship from both sides, meeting the lawyers making cases for all parties. Here, the movie star and tech billionaire going through proceedings are played bySienna MillerandDominic West. The cast is absolutely stacked, from reunited Celebrity Traitors matesNick MohammedandCelia Imrie(who could forget when he dug up her grave?) to Aran Murphy (son of Cillian – and set to be everywhere on our screens) as the feuding couple’s son.Sky/Now, 2 OctoberLast One Laughing Halloween specialLast One Laughingis such an ingenious money-maker – a whole series spun out from putting some comedians in a room for less than a day! – that we were always going to get more of it. While we await the third series (which stars Harry Hill!) this Halloween special features Jack Dee, Phil Wang, Reece Shearsmith, Harriet Dyer and Tom Allen, alongside the returning Lou Sanders and Daisy May Cooper, and there’s an intriguing new rule: competitors will be punished not just for laughing, but also for screaming.Prime Video, 23 OctoberNocturneRowan Joffé has long been a writer worth paying attention to, most recently for Edward Berger’s filmBallad of a Small Player. Nocturne sounds like it might cement his reputation once and for all. A drama about a homicide cop who relocates to Pennsylvania and finds himself having to deal with a serial killer, it stars Liev Schreiber and Zazie Beetz. Best of all,Stephen Grahamplays the serial killer. Entertaining grisliness should ensue.Apple TV, 30 OctoberThe AltruistsTelevision loves to adapt real-life things that have only just happened, and that’s the case with The Altruists, which deals with the rise (and subsequent implosion) of cryptocurrency exchange FTX. This is the one where Sam Bankman-Fried came out of nowhere to become the 41st richest man in the US, only to get sentenced to 25 years in jail for fraud, conspiracy and money laundering. When this genre gets it right, it makes for gripping TV. When it gets it wrong, it leaves you wondering why you didn’t just read the Wikipedia page. Fingers crossed for the former.Netflix, 19 NovemberBlade Runner 2099View image in fullscreenBack to the future … Michelle Yeoh in Blade Runner 2099.Photograph: PrimeAfter two dazzling big-screen outings (neither of which were commercially successful at the time) comes the inevitable TV adaptation. Set 80 years after the original, and 50 since the sequel, Blade Runner 2099 revolves round the aftermath of a Replicant uprising. Michelle Yeoh plays a dying Replicant Blade Runner. Hunter Schafer plays a human pretending to be a replicant. The amount of money thrown at this thing must be staggering, not least because the production design looks absolutely gorgeous. A must-see.Prime Video, 25 NovemberRivalsView image in fullscreenSex, more sex and a funeral … David Tennant in Rivals.Photograph: Ana Blumenkron/Disney+Where can TV’s mostrollicking bonkfestpossibly go after part one of thissecond seriesended harrowingly in the 1987 hurricane – and denied us the queer epiphany we’d all been waiting for? As we return to Rutshire, will Lizzie actually leave her abominable husband? Will Declan find out his wife Maud slept with his sworn enemy? Will Taggie ever move on from Rupert Campbell-Black? Expect sex, more sex, some gleefully evil regional TV wars and at least one funeral.Disney+, NovemberHarry PotterView image in fullscreenThe wizarding classic reborn … Dominic McLaughlin in Harry Potter.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/HBO MaxBoth anticipation and trepidation are high for thesmall-screen version of JK Rowling’s wizarding classic. Security has had to be ramped up on set because of intense heat on stars such as Paapa Essiedu (who plays Severus Snape) and John Lithgow (Albus Dumbledore), and there have been calls for actors to quit the project. But the first teaser looks truly epic – and child actors have upped their game since the movies.HBO Max, Christmas DayA Bitter Pill: The Sodium Valproate ScandalSodium valproate is an effective epilepsy treatment. However, if it is taken during pregnancy, one in nine babies will have a physical birth defect. It is estimated that 20,000 children in the UK were affected. A Bitter Pill (made by the co-producers ofMr Bates vs the Post Office) follows the story of two mothers – Janet Williams and Emma Murphy – who spent decades battling doctors and drug companies to first find answers and then compensation. It is an incredible story of bloody-minded tenacity, and hopefully this documentary will help it reach a wider audience.BBC, TBCApocalypseA reality show/social experiment in which 16 participants/foolish guinea pigs are dropped in an actual ghost town in the US to see if they could survive the end of days. There will be no electricity or water or any mod cons, and they will be stuck there for a month. Think The Road for the influencer age. Sure to be utterly bananas.Channel 4, TBCBig SwissJen Beagin’s 2023 novel has all the hallmarks of a television adaptation – it’s full of rich people with good taste, almost all of whom have endured some form of terrible trauma – and so it has come to pass.Jodie Comerwill star as Flavia, a woman in a sexually unfulfilling marriage who embarks on an affair with a woman she meets at the dog park. However (possible spoiler, although probably not), the woman is secretly employed as her sex therapist’s transcriber. It is a dynamic that cannot possibly hold.HBO Max, TBCBlack DovesThe Ben Whishaw-Keira Knightleyspy epicreturns for more killer espionage fun with incredible new cast members Ambika Mod, Sam Riley and the Scream queen herself, Neve Campbell. Better still: Sarah Lancashire will have a far more prominent role in season two! Always a reason to celebrate.Netflix, TBCBlue LightsView image in fullscreenStunning … Martin McCann and Siân Brooke in Blue Lights.Photograph: BBC/Two Cities TelevisionTheBafta-winning showabout the “peelers” of Blackthorn police station in Belfast always sets out its stall with a stunning set piece in the opener. Season four is no exception, as police are called to a gathering at a migrant centre where multiple far-right groups are converging and ready to attack. Somehow it gets even more gripping and politically on point every time.BBC One, TBCBlue Planet IIIView image in fullscreenUnmissable … Blue Planet III.Photograph: BBC Studios/ Photographer copyright Anoushka FreedmanIt was announced onDavid Attenborough’s 100th birthdaythat he would be back to narrate the final part of this world-changing trilogy – and we got a sneak peek of him in his home studio intoning about the mating rituals of a whale. Given that this follows his spectacular feature-length film on the urgency of protecting our oceans to ensure human survival, and that it might well be the last time we hear his honeyed tones adorn something new, this will be totally unmissable. What a way to cap off his centenary year.BBC One, TBCThe Boys from BrazilIra Levin’s bracing Nazi thriller has already been adapted into one masterpiece – the1978 filmstarring Gregory Peck and Laurence Olivier – and now it is heading for the small screen. Peter Morgan has adapted the story into a five-part limited series starring Jeremy Strong, Gillian Anderson, Daniel Brühl and Lizzy Caplan. A film about a resurgence of nazism feels painfully relevant, although it remains to be seen how straight the show will play some of the story’s battier sci-fi elements.Netflix, TBCBreak ClauseView image in fullscreenCharming … Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4Many of us may have experienced the peculiar anguish of being trapped in a tenancy agreement with someone you’ve just broken up with, and this premise forms the spine of the new Channel 4 comedy Break Clause. Lara Ricote and Samuel Bottomley play the couple, working from a script by Jess Bray from the brilliantWe Might Regret This. The series originated as a 16-minute Comedy Blap that you can – and should – watch on Channel 4. If the series maintains the charm of the original, this should be something very special.Channel 4, TBCCarrieMike Flanagan is very much The Stephen King Guy at this stage, having written and directed the 2017 adaptation ofGerald’s Game, the 2019 adaptation ofDoctor Sleepand 2024’sThe Life of Chuck. And now (while he apparently readies adaptations of The Dark Tower and The Mist) he has adapted Carrie for television. You know the story already – a telekinetic teen with a horrible mother has to navigate school bullies – but this will apparently be an update, complete with modern technology and a sorority of telekinetic girls.Prime Video, TBCThe Celebrity TraitorsView image in fullscreenFull house … Top row, left to right: Amol Rajan, Bella Ramsey, James Acaster, James Blunt, Jerry Hall, Joanne McNally, and Joe Lycett. Middle row, left to right: Julie Hesmondhalgh, King Kenny, Leigh-Anne Pinnock, Maya Jama, Michael Sheen, Miranda Hart, and Myha’la. Bottom row, left to right: Prof Hannah Fry, Richard E Grant, Rob Beckett, Romesh Ranganathan, Ross Kemp, Sebastian Croft, and Sharon Rooney in The Celebrity Traitors’s new series.Photograph: PAWe didn’t think it was possible to trump the first lineup of celebrities entering the castle with Claudia – but this year’s casting may just have done it. With superstar luvvies such as Jerry Hall, Richard E Grant and Michael Sheen, double act Rob and Romesh pitted against each other and some tantalising curveballs – what will Ross Kemp, Myha’la and Bella Ramsey possibly chat about? – it’s sure to be another winner. This can’t come soon enough.BBC One, TBCColin from AccountsView image in fullscreenA beautiful thing … Harriet Dyer, Patrick Brammall and Colin the dog in Colin from Accounts.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 CBS Studios Inc, Easy Tiger Productions Pty Ltd, Foxtel Management Pty Ltd, Create NSW/Lisa TomasettiWhat a beautiful thingColin from Accountsis. A relationship dramedy written by its stars,the husband and wife teamof Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer, it is a funny and tender exploration of romantic compatibility in the modern age. In season one, Ashley and Gordon met and fell in love. In season two they tried to work out if they should stay together. In its third and final season, we learn that they didn’t. But might they again?BBC, TBCDamilola Taylor: The Last 24 HoursThe murder of 10-year-old Damilola Taylor in a Peckham stairwell 26 years ago has lost none of its horrors with age. One of the last people to see Taylor alive was actor John Boyega, then eight, who was friends with the family. In this documentary, Boyega explores Taylor’s final day, along with other close friends and family members, discussing both the events that led to his death and the impact his murder had on their lives.BBC, TBCDeadpointBetweenBaby Reindeer,Somewhere Boyand Misfits, Clerkenwell Films has developed an incredible pedigree when it comes to television. Deadpoint looks primed to continue this. A five-part action thriller set in Wales, it is the story of a man forced back to Snowdonia after the disappearance of his sister, only to discover that a far-right faction is planning to carry out a violent attack there. So it’s a survival thriller, a missing persons mystery and a domestic terrorism drama all in one. What could be better?Channel 4,TBCEast of EdenYou don’t adapt Steinbeck unless you’re willing to go all in on it, and happily this seems to be the case with Netflix’s new show. This epic tale of family, inheritance and jealousy spans decades, and judging by the trailer its writer, Zoe Kazan, has committed entirely.Florence Pughplays Cathy Ames, the beautiful monster at the story’s heart, with Christopher Abbott, Tracy Letts and Martha Plimpton rounding out the cast. This looks as sumptuous and panoramic as television will allow. On first impressions, it could be an award winner.Netflix, TBCI Am HelenView image in fullscreenShould be essential viewing … Nicola Coughlan in I Am Helen.Photograph: Joss Barratt/Channel 4Dominic Savage’s semi-improvised I Am … series has drawn some of the best female performers to its flame since it began, including Vicky McClure, Samantha Morton, Lesley Manville and Kate Winslet. Now it is the turn of Nicola Coughlan who (in a break from tradition) is starring in a two-part story. I Am Helen will explore themes of control and toxic masculinity in the setting of a modern relationship. Early reports suggest that it will deal heavily in the manosphere. If it manages to broach this as well asAdolescencedid, it might be essential viewing.Channel 4, TBCIt Gets WorseA fresh comedy from Leo Reich, whose debut Edinburgh fringe show Literally Who Cares?! was such a barnstorming success that it immediately got picked up by HBO Max. It Gets Worse is a look at three young mates in London who are on the verge of getting evicted. But what’s really staggering here is the sheer number of A-listers who have signed on – from Andrew “hot priest” Scott to Lena Dunham. This should be special.Channel 4, TBCLegacy of SpiesIf you can see a theme emerging in this list, it might be the Big Legacy Television Adaptation. Not being ones to miss out, the BBC has adapted this series from John le Carré’s The Spy Who Came in from the Cold, also drawing on material from his2017 novel A Legacy of Spies. If nothing else, it has been exquisitely cast, with Matthew Macfadyen playing George Smiley, Charlie Hunnam as Alec Leamas, Hugh Laurie as Control and supporting roles played by Daniel Brühl, Joe Alwyn and Agnes O’Casey.BBC, TBCMayaView image in fullscreenDark and very funny … Daisy Haggard and Bella Ramsey in Maya.Photograph: Channel 4Daisy Haggard’s writing is always dark and very funny, and her new witness protection thriller Maya is no exception. Anna (Haggard) and her daughter Maya (Bella Ramsey, as wonderful and unrestrained as ever) are forced to leave their home with no notice and move to the back of beyond in Scotland to escape her abusive ex (played by a chilling Tobias Menzies). It’s a moving look at survival and hope, with cliffhangers galore and gags about Frazzles crisps. What’s not to love?Channel 4, TBCNumber 10View image in fullscreenLudicrously anticipated … Jenna Coleman as Katie Flynn in Number 10.Photograph: Rob Youngson/Channel 4Steven Moffat’s ludicrously anticipated comedy-drama is finally almost here. A workplace show set in Downing Street – starring Rafe Spall as the prime minister, with Jenna Coleman as his deputy chief of staff – it could well be the British West Wing. And given Moffat’s flair for witty dialogue (and his form writing Press Gang), this has the potential to be one of the year’s best. But let’s hope it doesn’t run and run, because at this stage a British prime minister lasting more than a couple of years is nothing short of fantasy.Channel 4, TBCPierreView image in fullscreenThe starring vehicle he deserves … David Harewood in Pierre.Photograph: Channel 4Finally, David Harewood gets the starring vehicle he deserves. In Pierre, he plays a London duty solicitor described as “charming and funny, a glamorous character in an unglamorous profession”. However, he is forced to step up when he realises that the death of one of his clients might have been the result of a vast institutional cover-up. Pierre sounds like old-school television at its best; a show with something to say, and the smarts to wrap it in an irresistible character.Channel 4, TBCPride and PrejudiceView image in fullscreenDownright hilarious … Olivia Colman with Emma Corrin, Rhea Norwood, Hollie Avery, Hopey Parish and Freya Mavor in Pride and Prejudice.Photograph: Ludovic Robert/Netflix“Miss Elizabeth Bennet? I’m all astonishment!”​ There’s long-awaited, and then there’s Dolly Alderton’s update of Pride and Prejudice, which comes with sky-high expectations. Thankfully, Olivia Colman is downright hilarious as ​the busybody Mrs Bennet, determined to marry off ​o​ne of her five daughters to the swanky neighbour who just moved in next door. Emma Corrin stars as Elizabeth andJack Lowdenis heralding himself as the first “ginger” Mr Darcy. We’re promised even more ​s​park than the Colin Firth ​classic from the 90s – though there will be no lake scene.Netflix, TBCThe Rachel IncidentBased on Caroline O’Donoghue’s 2023 novel, beloved of countless millennial women, this is a new Channel 4 show about a young student’s attempt to seduce her married professor. The cast, including Máiréad Tyers, Ellis Howard, Daniel Ings and Ardal O’Hanlon, is worth getting excited about. But the real draw is the fact that O’Donoghue collaborated on the script with Jen Statsky, fresh from conquering the world with Hacks. If she can bring even a hint of the same sparkle to this, we will be in for a treat.Channel 4, TBCThe Reluctant VampireView image in fullscreenHouse of fun … Sian Clifford, Lenny Rush, Gabriel Nagy and Tom Davis in The Reluctant Vampire.Photograph: James Pardon/BBC/Buffola Pictures“You don’t pick up being a vampire … it’s not conversational French!” Valentine hates drinking blood, ​has no truck with violence and –​ horror of horrors –​ he has a reflection. But his vampire family still don’t know he’s actually a human and they want him to pass his initiation ceremony in front of the whole community of Katchem-By-the-Throat. This BBC comedy from the Gibbons brothers (renowned for keeping Alan Partridge alive), based on a book by Eric Morecambe, has an incredibly high gag rate and a cracking cast​. It ​includes​ Lenny Rush as the titular non-vamp, ​Sian Clifford and Tom Davis as his parents, Asim Chaudhry as Igon the family assistant and Bill Bailey and Ross ​Noble as ​a hilarious pair of gargoyles​.BBC One, TBCReputationWell this one sounds like fun. Written by Anya Reiss and starring Naomie Harris and Christina Hendricks, Reputation is a glossy drama about a celebrity lawsuit that spirals out of control. A pop star writes a song accusing her husband of infidelity. He fires accusations back. Social media goes wild, and a phalanx of dirty PR tricks comes into play. The enjoyment won’t just come from seeing the inner workings of the lawsuits we only hear about in the news, but presumably also trying to guess which precise celebrity lawsuits the show is based on.BBC One, TBCThe Secret Diary of Adrian Mole Aged 13¾View image in fullscreenThere aren’t many characters more loved … Oliver Savell as Adrian Mole.Photograph: BBCThere aren’t many characters in literature more beloved than Sue Townsend’s self-importantly earnest adolescent, whose diaries enthralled a nation across four decades and eight books. After 1985’s classic ITV adaptation, David Nicholls has come on board to bring him back to life as a period piece. Writers for this new version include Caitlin and Caroline Moran, Dillon Mapletoft, Oliver Taylor and Jack Rooke, while Oliver Savell from Changing Ends will play the lead. Can lightning strike twice?BBC, TBC70 UpOne of the most seminal documentaries ever made finally concludes. Since 1964, the Up series has followed the lives of several perfectly normal people across the social spectrum at increments of seven years. Through the decades, the participants have fallen in love and endured hardships, and now they are almost at the end of the road. The final chapter –directed by the Oscar-winning Asif Kapadiaafter the death of Michael Apted – is bound to be poignant, but the series as a whole will remain an important document about life in Britain in the 20th and 21st centuries for ever.ITV1, TBCSherwoodFresh from his job consulting onSNL UK, of all things, James Graham gets back to his masterwork. In its two series so far, Sherwood has been an almost unbearably dark investigation of a community left to hold itself together with threads. Six months have passed since the climax of season two, in which evil matriarch Ann Branson drowned, yet more human remains have been found. Who in the town has a dark secret this time?BBC, TBCThe Slightest TouchView image in fullscreenUplifting … Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell in The Slightest Touch.Photograph: HBOA documentary in whichColin Farrellmeets up with his friend and discusses running a marathon. The catch is that his friend is Emma Fogarty, a survivor of epidermolysis bullosa, a rare and painful genetic condition that renders the skin fragile enough to blister and tear at the slightest touch. Fogarty has already confounded medical science once before – she was never expected to reach the age of 40 – so why not go the whole hog and run the Dublin marathon? Powerfully emotional and uplifting in equal measure.HBO Max, TBCThe Split UpView image in fullscreenHanding over the reins … Aysha Kala and Ritu Arya in The Split Up.Photograph: BBC/SisterOver its three series (and Christmas special), Abi Morgan’s divorce dramaThe Splitbecame one of the highlights of the annual schedule. Rather than ending, it has now morphed into The Split Up. This is a new, Manchester-set series about a powerful family struggling to decide who should inherit its prestigious divorce firm. Morgan is just executive producing this one, handing the reins to Ursula Rani Sarma. Ritu Arya, Sanjeev Bhaskar, Aysha Kala and Arian Nik star.BBC One, TBCThis City Is OursThefirst seasonof this swaggering Liverpool gangland thriller didn’t quite get the dues it deserved (that rooftop scene in the finale was gasp-inducing), but it did establishJames Nelson-Joyce– who got his big break after chatting to his idol Stephen Graham at Nando’s – as a swiftly rising star. He returns for more explosive drama, as well as Endeavour star Shaun Evans, who joins the cast.BBC One,TBCTimeView image in fullscreenAbsolutely gripping … Siobhan Finneran, Chukwubuikem Molokwu and David Tennant in Time.Photograph: Peter Marley/BBC StudiosJimmy McGovern’sprison anthologyhas so far been absolutely gripping. And now, following runs led by Sean Bean andJodie Whittaker, David Tennant gets a turn at the wheel. This story is set at a young offenders institution, and Tennant plays a custodial manager concealing knowledge about a serious incident. As connective tissue, Siobhan Finneran returns as prison chaplain Marie-Louise O’Dell, now undergoing a crisis of faith, who clashes with Tennant over it.BBC One, TBCThe Unlikely Cook With AwkwafinaView image in fullscreenExtremely unskilled in the kitchen … The Unlikely Cook With Awkwafina.Photograph: Christina Belle/Courtesy of AppleOnce a mainstay of the television schedules, the food show has lost no end of ground to YouTube in recent years. Perhaps this series is the thing to regain it. In The Unlikely Cook With Awkwafina, the titular star will travel across the US exploring modern Asian-American cuisine. Why isAwkwafinaan unlikely cook? Because she is apparently extremely unskilled in the kitchen and will have to rely on a host of people more talented (but less famous) than she is to show her the way.Apple TV, TBCThe WargamePicture this: Michael Gove is the prime minister. Nicola Sturgeon is his deputy. His cabinet comprises Penny Mordaunt, Baroness Harman, Baroness Warsi and Kim Darroch, while Anthony Scaramucci plays the US secretary of state. If that doesn’t sound awful enough, Russia has just invaded the UK. Welcome to The Wargame, a series where these figures enter a Cobra-style briefing room and attempt to deal with the minute-by-minute developments of such a crisis. This could be gripping or it could be the television equivalent of banging yourself on the head with a tin tray. Either way, it will probably be worth watching.Sky, TBCThe Witch FarmView image in fullscreenFlat-out terrifying … Gabrielle Creevy, Sian Gibson and Michael Socha in The Witch Farm.Photograph: BBCFew things have been as flat-out terrifying as Danny Robbins’spodcast The Witch Farm, about the supposedly true haunting of an isolated Welsh farmhouse 30 years ago. Now the podcast has been made into a TV show. If it can cram as many unsettling incidents as the podcast – think apparitions, dead animals and unusually high utility bills – while maintaining its tone of sceptical unease, this will hands down be the scariest thing on television in several years.BBC, TBCYagaView image in fullscreenRaunchy and ritualistic … Hudson Williams in Yaga.Photograph: Bell Media/SkyAKA whatHeated Rivalry’sHudson Williams did next. He stars alongside Carrie-Anne Moss and Noah Reid in a raunchy and ritualistic take on the terrifying folklore tale of Baba Yaga. It should fall somewhere between Jodie Foster’sTrue Detective: Night Countryand a wildly freewheeling fairytale.Sky, TBC

title: ‘I’m not even an actor – I was just grieving!’ Rising star Lara Ricote on the heartache behind her new breakup comedy | Television | The Guardian
description: The Mexican-American comedian had just split from her boyfriend when she filmed Break Clause, about an ex-couple living together in London. She talks trading telenovelas for Edinburgh and embracing your feelings
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: The Mexican-American comedian had just split from her boyfriend when she filmed Break Clause, about an ex-couple living together in London. She talks trading telenovelas for Edinburgh and embracing your feelings
Content: ‘It was kind of a gift to be able to go to work and cry every day’ … Lara Ricote.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It was kind of a gift to be able to go to work and cry every day’ … Lara Ricote.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianAutumn arts preview 2026Television‘I’m not even an actor – I was just grieving!’ Rising star Lara Ricote on the heartache behind her new breakup comedyThe Mexican-American comedian had just split from her boyfriend when she filmed Break Clause, about an ex-couple living together in London. She talks trading telenovelas for Edinburgh and embracing your feelingsThe 50 best TV shows of autumn 2026Rachel AroestiFri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Break Clause, recent graduates Lil and Ben move from Leeds to London after the former lands a job at an architecture firm. Yet as soon as the couple start settling into their new flat, everything goes horribly wrong. Ben (Samuel Bottomley) reveals he slept with someone else at their leaving drinks the night before, so Lil (Lara Ricote) immediately ends the relationship – but quickly discovers their rental contract is far harder to get out of. Cue an agonising six months of cohabitation and a novel will-they-won’t-they (get back together) setup for a winningly bittersweet new sitcom.You may recognise Ricote from recent appearances in two other Channel 4 comedies:Mitchell and Webb Are Not Helpingand Sam Campbell’s crackersMake That Movie(although probably not from the “funny and crazy” telenovela she briefly worked on as a teen). But Break Clause is the Mexican-American comedian’s first leading role. It also happened to be the “best case scenario” for Ricote’s debut: let’s just say getting into character wasn’t a problem.Shortly before filming began, the 29-year-old broke up with her own long-term boyfriend. Then she moved to London for the first time. She originally played Lil in Break Clause’s 2024 pilot, meaning creator Jess Bray had already shaped the character around Ricote when writing the full series – like Ricote, the character is Latin American and hard of hearing. But now the pair were in eerily similar emotional states, too. Bursting into tears at the drop of a hat was easy. “I’m not even an actor – I was just grieving!” says Ricote. The job ultimately allowed her to “process things. It was kind of a gift to be able to go to work and cry every day.”View image in fullscreenBest case scenario? … Samuel Bottomley and Lara Ricote in Break Clause.Photograph: Kerry Spicer/Channel 4Mercifully, however, her real-life living situation was less stressful: she currently houseshares with actor and comedian Charly Clive, who offered her a room after they met on the set of Mitchell and Webb Are Not Helping (and who also happens to play Lil and Ben’s neighbour in Break Clause).Ricote isn’t at home when we speak via video call; it’s early August and she’s in Edinburgh, sitting on the bed she’s sharing for the month with her sister Maya, a clown, in a flat belonging to a woman who answered her Instagram plea for a room to rent at the fringe. She’s at the festival to perform her latest standup show,Inkling, which will go on to receive universal praise for its zany braininess, as well as a nomination for the main Edinburgh comedy award (the winner will be announced on 29 August).Inkling is partly themed around the aforementioned breakup – itself precipitated by an argument with a man in a museum who refused to speak more clearly even after she told him she was hard of hearing.double quotation markYour feelings are messages from you to you, and you should be checking those out!Despite the disconcerting subject matter, Ricote’s natural buoyancy means it’s hard to imagine Inkling being anything other than life-affirming: she begins our conversation by expressing her astonishment at the lyrical genius ofDavid Byrne, whose oeuvre she only recently discovered. I presume her personality also provided the inspiration for Lil’s sometimes ludicrous exuberance (in one scene she impulsively joins in with a troupe of baffled street dancers), but she says that’s closer to Bray’s vibe. Ricote’s style is slightly more cerebral; her comedy is often powered by a goofy yet genuine sense of awe at the human condition. Inkling centres on her epiphany that “your feelings are messages from you to you, and you should be checking those out!” she says with evangelistic urgency.Lara Ricote: Inkling review – this fizzy standup’s smart new set is her best yetRead moreYet much of her wonder is reserved for the strange path her life has taken. The daughter of a telenovela actor (hence that early role as “Maria” who “just loved her dad, loved to go to church and was brokenhearted by her mom’s alcoholism”), she grew up in Miami, before moving to the Netherlands to study politics. There, she started performing comedy and soon found acclaim in the UK, winning the Funny Women stage award in 2021 and the Edinburgh newcomer prize the following year. Nowadays, she is a core part of the alternative – and increasingly, thanks to her primetime TV appearances, mainstream – British comedy scene, something she finds utterly bizarre. “There are so many elements that have nothing to do with what I thought was my life 10 years ago. I’m grateful but very confused.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s a hopeful thing to bring into such a rigid world’ … Lara Ricote.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianFilming Break Clause in Manchester opposite 25-year-old Yorkshireman Bottomley (“I had a real sense of: I don’t know anybody like you”) was also “surreal”. That said, Ricote has managed to find a way to rationalise her standup success. The UK has a comedy scene that embraces difference; Ricote can “operate in that space because I’m from random places for you guys – I’m Mexican, but I’m also American, but I’m also Venezuelan, and Latin America isn’t really a continent that [Britons] are relating to that often”. The fact that her other qualities are also quite “random” (“the way I talk is kind of weird,” she says – she has previously described her voice as “Bart Simpson with a lisp”) means she has avoided being pigeonholed, often an advantage for a comedian.Another upside is that she rarely gets starstruck. Break Clause’s supporting cast is full of great up-and-coming comedy talent – Cat Cohen, SNL UK alumni Jack Shep and Hammed Animashaun – plus a bona fide legend in The Fast Show’s John Thomson. Ricote’s co-stars were “freaking out” at his presence; she was nonplussed. “I was like, that’s so special that I get to meet him … but also not …”What is very special, thinks Ricote, is Break Clause itself. As a viewer, it’s incredibly difficult to decide whether Lil and Ben should get back together – something Ricote has a typically deep take on. She views the show’s ambiguity in this area as an antidote to kneejerk judgments and an allegory for the unpredictability of life. “The premise, basically, is that people are continuous – people aren’t one action. And that’s such a hopeful thing to bring into such a rigid world. You want so badly to just decide: bad guy. And you can’t in the series. You gotta wait. You have to see it out,” she says. “You never know what things are gonna mean for you.”Break Clause is onChannel 4this autumnExplore more on these topicsTelevisionAutumn arts preview 2026TV comedyComedyEdinburgh festival 2026Channel 4featuresShareReuse this content

title: The Whisper Man review – Robert De Niro sleepwalks through silly Netflix potboiler | Robert De Niro | The Guardian
description: A father and son must team up to find a serial killer in a cheaply made and increasingly uninteresting thriller
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: A father and son must team up to find a serial killer in a cheaply made and increasingly uninteresting thriller
Content: Robert De Niro, Adam Scott and Michelle Monaghan in The Whisper Man.Photograph: David Lee/Netflix ©2026View image in fullscreenRobert De Niro, Adam Scott and Michelle Monaghan in The Whisper Man.Photograph: David Lee/Netflix ©2026Robert De NiroReviewThe Whisper Man review – Robert De Niro sleepwalks through silly Netflix potboilerA father and son must team up to find a serial killer in a cheaply made and increasingly uninteresting thrillerBenjamin LeeFri 28 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 03.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not as ifRobert De Niro’s choices have improved all that much since the nadir of the mid-2000s (last year did see him crop up in aScott Eastwood-led actionerandThe Alto Knights) but there’s something specifically rubbishy about his latest that transports us back to that particularly cursed time. The Whisper Man, a film as openly stupid as its title would suggest, could have been released in between the evil clone horrorGodsendand imaginary friend thrillerHide and Seek, the kind of bottom-tier project that offers the actor a nice big cheque and the audience a nice little nap.It’s a familiar pile of B-movie schlock – serial killers, missing children, bumps in the night, more imaginary friends – and there issomeinitial junky fun to be had as we wonder just where it all might be headed. I was hoping for a destination a little more deranged or vaguely surprising, the film making a silent promise that we’re hurtling toward somewhere wildly unexpected before dumping us in a ditch instead.The Dog Stars review – Ridley Scott’s lethargic postapocalyptic drama is a misfireRead moreIt’s based on the British author Alex North’snovelthat enough people tore through back in 2019 before it got picked up byNetflix. It’s at least been mercifully adapted into a film rather than a baggy limited series, as is too often the way with plot-heavy airport novels these days, but even stretching thin characters like this across a runtime just under two hours proves to be a struggle. Central is Tom Kennedy (Adam Scott), a crime fiction-writing widower moving back to his home town with young son Jake (which leads to ungainly lines including “you know your mom always wanted us to move back to the town we grew up in”). But he returns just as a child-stealing murderer is on the loose (whoops!), hunted by ambitious, stony-faced detective Amanda (Michelle Monaghan). His methods recall those employed by an infamous, and now imprisoned, serial killer called Frank (Michael Keaton) who was captured by the now-retired detective Pete (De Niro) who also happens to be Tom’s estranged father (“a shitty father but a good fucking detective!”). When Jake goes missing, the three are forced to combine efforts.I have a nostalgic fondness for the grimy post-Sevenattempts to bring infinitely hokier serial killer stories to the big screen, from Kiss the Girls to The Bone Collector, before theSawfranchise replaced mystery and suspense with gristle and innards. But while The Whisper Man overloads on hoariness – a killer who taunts the cops, a spookily underlit house, a gothic nursery rhyme repeated on a loop, a father taking matters into his own hands, a snarling criminal offering clues behind bars, a too-obvious suspect who might as well be called Mr Red Herring – it’s all taken far more seriously than it deserves to be. Any real, transporting throwback appeal is also spoiled by the dreadedNetflix look,flatter and greyerthan ever here, that juicy studio gloss of the films it’s trying to recall relegated to the past. It’s a bland director-for-hire gig for the New Zealand director James Ashcroft, a shame after his last film, the reasonably jolting care home-set thrillerThe Rule of Jenny Pen, a nasty slice of male hagsploitation with two ferocious lead performances.Marketing meltdown: why has Andrew Garfield’s new film suddenly added Robin Hood?Read moreLike Ashcroft, De Niro is on full checked-out autopilot mode, quietly mumbling perfunctory dialogue while seemingly focused on what he’ll be having for dinner, and Scott feels uncomfortably miscast, hisother hard-drinking, fiction-writing genre turn of the yearproving to be considerably more effective. An actor traditionally associated with comedy, he often falls into the Steve Carell trap of confusing sitcom histrionics with dramatic hysteria and so his pain and anger at the disappearance of his son never really registers (it would also require some miraculous heavy lifting to sell some of his character’s bafflingly dumb decisions).The final act is unfortunately short on both surprise and suspense, a reveal only painted as such because of a stupidly unexplored line of investigation earlier in the film. The inevitable overwrought jostling for weapons while characters tumble down stairs and into the basement is too shoddily choreographed to excite while a sudden last scene twist is so inelegantly abrupt that I had to rewind to check I was right. It’s a choice that shovels on some sugar seemingly stolen from the set of an entirely different film, a left turn that’s too sentimental to be the fun kind of silly (I prayed for a twist ending as charmingly dumb-as-rocks as the one inHide and Seek, De Niro’s other imaginary child B-movie). After adumpier August than usual, I could have done with some of that fun kind of silly, the kind we used to have that much more of, back when a film like The Whisper Man might have been worth shouting about.The Whisper Man is now available on NetflixExplore more on these topicsRobert De NiroNetflixMichael KeatonAdam ScottThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s the story of what happens when the music stops’: bringing tormented jazz legend Bill Evans to life | Movies | The Guardian
description: Having directed documentaries about David Bowie, Radiohead and Joy Division, Grant Gee takes on a biopic of the turbulent and tragic American pianist
Author: John Lewis
Headline: Having directed documentaries about David Bowie, Radiohead and Joy Division, Grant Gee takes on a biopic of the turbulent and tragic American pianist
Content: Heavyweight Hollywood support … Laurie Metcalf with Anders Danielsen Lie in Everybody Digs Bill Evans.Photograph: 2026 Cowtown Pictures/Hot PropertyView image in fullscreenHeavyweight Hollywood support … Laurie Metcalf with Anders Danielsen Lie in Everybody Digs Bill Evans.Photograph: 2026 Cowtown Pictures/Hot PropertyMoviesInterview‘It’s the story of what happens when the music stops’: bringing tormented jazz legend Bill Evans to lifeJohn LewisHaving directed documentaries about David Bowie, Radiohead and Joy Division, Grant Gee takes on a biopic of the turbulent and tragic American pianistFri 28 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 05.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1997, Grant Gee directed the video forRadiohead’s single No Surprises, a four-minute film that featured Thom Yorke miming the song inside a water-filled diver’s helmet, apparently almost drowning in the process. In the three decades since that promo, Gee has made a host of diverse feature-length films about artists: Radiohead, David Bowie, Joy Division, the Turkish Nobel laureateOrhan Pamuk, the émigré German novelistWG Sebald. They are often impressionistic, dreamlike explorations of art, memory, place and the strange pressures put upon artistic lives.“It’s a narrative form I’ve used again and again,” says Gee. “A character begins in one condition; a crisis slowly develops; the viewer watches that crisis in a forensic yet empathetic way; the crisis passes; the person returns to something like the original state, but transformed. Someone comes very close to drowning, but doesn’t drown. What does that do to them?”Gee’s new film,Everybody Digs Bill Evans, is also a study of an artist, only this time it is not a documentary but a narrative feature. Yet it feels like a fictional extension of his longstanding preoccupations. The subject is Bill Evans, the jazz musician whose lyrical introspection helped reshape the piano; he was a crucial voice on Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue and the man who introduced Debussy-ish romanticism to jazz. But the film does not attempt the usual biopic sweep. It concentrates instead on a few months in 1961, a time when Evans was numbed with grief after the death of his double bassist Scott LaFaro.Watch the trailer for Everybody Digs Bill Evans.“All my films start from a fan’s perspective,” says Gee. “It’s like falling in love. An initial interest turns into an obsession that turns into wanting to find out everything you can about the subject.In the WG Sebald film, the novelist Rick Moody uses the phrase ‘textual compulsion’, which I like. It describes the way a work of art can compel you to keep going, a love for something non-human.Innocence of Memoriesstarted with me falling in love with Istanbul and wanting to immerse myself in the museum that Orhan Pamuk had created.”Gee’s love affair with Evans started with a photograph. “It’s in an old book of photos bythe great Lee Friedlander, from late 1961 or early 1962. It shows Bill hunched over the piano, with his new bassist and drummer smiling behind him, thrilled to be there. Evans is plumb centre, this super-cool, Ivy-League-looking guy, but he looks haunted, shocked, concentrated. I hadn’t even heard of Bill Evans at that point, but I felt that I had to know everything I could about him and why he looked so spooked.”View image in fullscreen‘You’ve got to show people what the fuss is all about’ … Grant Gee.Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The GuardianThe answer came inIntermission, Owen Martell’s novel about Evans. Inspired by real events, it lingers on the few months when a grief-stricken Evans was unable even to sit at a piano. It follows Evans as he is babysat by his brother in New York, then looked after by his retired blue-collar parents in Florida, before returning to his heroin-fuelled life in Manhattan with his girlfriend Ellaine.In adapting Martell’s novel, Gee says he relished the shift from nonfiction to drama. “With documentaries, you get used to working with whatever situation you’re presented with. You don’t have a script; you just have to react to what your interviewees say. In contrast, every shot in a narrative movie is blocked off and beautifully lit and choreographed. I was surrounded by so many brilliant actors and photographers and designers that I had little to worry about.”The novel also offered a way out of one particular biopic cliche. “The moment where I quite often lose interest is when they start showing the actor playing the music,” he says. “In a way, this is the story of what happens when the music stops. I liked how Martell’s novel suggested the possibility of a music biopic that didn’t have any performance in it at all. In the end, I didn’t quite have the guts, or the madness, to follow that through – you’ve got to show people what the fuss is all about.”View image in fullscreenA scene from Innocence of Memories, Evans’ 2015 film about Orhan Pamuk.It is a quiet, emotionally turbulent film, but it does contain a few short recreations of Evans’s music (including his best-known tune,Waltz for Debby, written for his beloved niece). Most are performed by Anders Danielsen Lie, the Norwegian actor who seems to have been born to play the role. “Anders has the same physique and bone structure as Bill, he has the same quiet intensity, and when he gets in movie mode he looks frighteningly like Bill,” says Gee. “And, as well as being a qualified doctor who was working as a GP in Oslo until very recently, Anders is also a great musician. When I approached him to play the role, he told me that he had been listening to Bill Evans’s music since he was a child and transcribing his solos for piano since he was a teenager.”The film’s celebratory title, borrowed from a1959 LP of the same name, has a darker inflection, says Gee. “Everybody digs Bill because everybody’s eyes are on him; everybody is trying to care for him and he can’t handle that.” It recalls the ironic title of Gee’s 1998 Radiohead filmMeeting People Is Easy, a queasily beautiful montage of gruelling, disorienting interviews and promotional appearances, filmed backstage by Gee over the course of a world tour, that shows the biggest band in the world spiralling into mental exhaustion. “Musicians are often only themselves when they’re playing music, which is why they do it so intensely. But I guess what the Bill Evans and Radiohead films have in common is that they’re about artists forced to live on some other trajectory, one they’re much more uncomfortable in.”A delicate subject was the portrayal of Evans’s catastrophic heroin habit. Gee was keen not to impose modern therapeutic language about addiction on to the story. “I’m just about old enough to remember 1960s attitudes, when addicts were seen as criminals. It was like having a burglar in the family, rather than someone with an illness. It also had a slightly romanticised, underworld glamour.”View image in fullscreenPiano man … Anders Danielsen Lie as Evans.Photograph: Cowtown Pictures/Hot PropertyHe cites interviews with Evans in the late 1970s, when he was reluctant to talk about the music that he made in the 1950s and 1960s, but instead recounted the high jinks of scoring drugs and fixing up. “He was really proud that he had a fake police ID, which he’d flash at dealers if they were giving him trouble.”Although largely set in 1961 and shot in a crisp monochrome, the film shifts into garish colour for a few flash-forwards into the 1970s, where we learn how Evans’s last decade was haunted by two suicides: first Ellaine, in 1973, and then Harry, the hitherto ultra-reliable brother who had tried to hold him together, in 1979. After Evans’s death at 51 in 1980, from a combination of cirrhosis, pneumonia, peptic ulcer and untreated hepatitis, the critic Gene Lees declared that Evans’s protracted struggle with drugs was “the longest suicide in history”, a phrase that recurs in almost every article and biography of the pianist.Gee, whose 2007 film Joy Division covered the death of Ian Curtis, who killed himself in 1980, rejects this diagnosis. “Me and Anders talked a lot about this while making the film,” he says. “And we both agree that Evans was far too disciplined in his art to contemplate suicide.”View image in fullscreenThe singer Ian Curtis in Gee’s 2007 rockumentary Joy Division.However, for the last few years of his life, Evans would regularly perform an instrumental version of Suicide Is Painless, the theme from his favourite TV show, M*A*S*H. The song developed a horrific poignancy. “Apparently, the versions he played in the days after Harry’s death didn’t sound anything likeBill Evans,” says Gee. “So, for the recreation of that 1979 performance, we got [the Welsh pianist] Joe Webb to create this heavy, noisy, furious, virtuosic freakout that’s quite unlike Bill’s usual performances.”The film is an Anglo-Irish production, partly funded by Screen Ireland, but manages to convincingly recreate Manhattan apartments, upstate New York and sun-drenched Florida on location in County Cork with a largely Irish cast (although heavyweight Hollywood support comes from Bill Pullman and Laurie Metcalf, who play Evans’s parents). But its real territory is interior: the place an artist goes when the thing that makes him himself suddenly becomes unreachable.It ends with Evans playing a version ofLucky to Be Me, a song fromLeonard Bernstein’s On the Town. The title sounds almost cruel after everything the film has shown us. “I liked the irony,” says Gee. “I thought it interesting and sweet. It seemed important to have some kind of minor lift after everything we’ve been through.”Everybody Digs Bill Evans is in UK and Irish cinemas from 11 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmBill EvansBiopicsJazzMiles DavisDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m an ever-changing vessel’: Erykah Badu on defying definition, life as a birth and death doula and her first album in 11 years | Soul | The Guardian
description: Why do the Texan innovator’s records take so long to make? ‘It’s important to gather the data,’ she says: the death, dating and dopamine behind her exquisite comeback alongside the Alchemist
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Why do the Texan innovator’s records take so long to make? ‘It’s important to gather the data,’ she says: the death, dating and dopamine behind her exquisite comeback alongside the Alchemist
Content: ‘I denounced my throne’ … Erykah Badu.Photograph: Adraint BerealView image in fullscreen‘I denounced my throne’ … Erykah Badu.Photograph: Adraint BerealSoulInterview‘I’m an ever-changing vessel’: Erykah Badu on defying definition, life as a birth and death doula and her first album in 11 yearsShaad D'SouzaWhy do the Texan innovator’s records take so long to make? ‘It’s important to gather the data,’ she says: the death, dating and dopamine behind her exquisite comeback alongside the AlchemistFri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 06.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleErykah Badu needs the lights downlow. The singer, producer, actor and registered doula shuffles into a private room at London’s Soho hotel and quietly asks for some changes to the atmosphere: lights dimmed, soft seat. A green juice would be great.As it turns out, Badu was out last night with Dave Chappelle, sitting with the comedian at a grand piano and playing songs into the wee hours. She looks mischievous when she thinks about the impromptu party, but declines to go into detail about what, exactly, went on. Instead, the 55-year-old smiles at me, eyes wide, her gold teeth glinting in the low light: “Oh yes,” she says slowly and quietly, like some kind of mysterious warlock. “Itwasa late one …”Meeting Badu, in other words, is everything you want it to be and more. She and I are here to talk about Before the World Blows: The Abi and Alan Experiment, a collaborative record with famed underground producer the Alchemist. It’s Badu’s first full-length project since the release of 2015’s But You Caint Use My Phone mixtape, and its dense, layered sound feels like an internet-fried take on her era-defining New Amerykah albums, from 2008 and 2010.It’s surprising, I suggest, that she has taken so long between records, given how much she analyses the world around her. She says that’s the point. “Procrastinating and living, learning and stuff – that gives you stuff to write about,” she says. “It’s important to gather the data, upload as much as I can. I don’t have a choice. But when the thing gets kind of full, I download it through writing music.”Erykah Badu and the Alchemist: Witch Doctor – videoBadu has been a star since 1997, when the release of her debut album, Baduizm, announced her as one of the leading lights of what music industry executive Kedar Massenburg called “neo soul”, a new wave of alternative soul and R&B. In the years since, a handful of wild, boundary-pushing records have made Badu one of the most revered artists in the world. The Alchemist – LA producer Alan Maman – was one of those early fans. In 1997, he was a roadie for Cypress Hill, who were co-headlining the Smokin’ Grooves tour alongside Badu. “I was such a fan – I used to go out in the crowd and watch her show every night,” he says on the phone later. “I never would have thought in a million years that one day I would be making music with her.”Since then, Maman has produced a number of hits, including Mobb Deep’s 1999 track The Realest, and enjoyed a recent career renaissance in collaborations with underground rappers such as the duos Armand Hammer and Mike & Wiki. A few years ago, while DJing a party, he ran into an old friend named Cold Cris who happened to work for Badu, and told him that working with her was on his bucket list. Two years after that, he got the call that Badu was interested in playing around with his beats. She came to his studio in LA, and the pair, he says, “instantly became friends, and realised how much shit we had in common, in the way we create, the way we think”.View image in fullscreen‘His compositions are like classical music to me’ ... Badu and the Alchemist.Photograph: Adraint Bereal“His compositions are like classical music to me – how he layers chimes and voices and strings and horns,” says Badu. “Our process is the same. The way we build is the same. I don’t know what it is exactly, but it’s a burning, beautiful fire. I get chills when I hear his music.”Badu was born in Dallas, Texas. Her mother was an actor; her uncle, an avid record collector; Badu’s grandmother bought her her first piano. She still remembers the first artwork she ever made, in a primary school art class: a sculpture of a spaceship made out of a rubber glove, which she called Lady Luna 2. Attending a performing arts high school in Dallas, she was “the first person at school and the last person to leave”, and would spend hours dancing while facing a mirror.“In the beginning, there was no audience – there was just me and the things I loved – music, painting, dancing,” she says. “I grew up listening to Earth, Wind & Fire, the Emotions, Deniece Williams, Eric Clapton of course, Joni Mitchell, Phoebe Snow, Parliament Funkadelic … they were creating from a place that nothing else came from.”Badu started making music in earnest when she was a theatre major at Grambling State University in Louisiana after her cousin Robert “Free” Bradford mailed her a cassette tape with beats on it. Their collaboration ended up becoming Baduizm. It was an instant hit – No 2 in the US – and, thanks to Massenburg’s clever marketing, announced Badu as “the queen of neo soul”, a term she quickly rejected. “I was the first one who denied it – I denounced my throne” she says. “I’m an ever-changing vessel, and I just didn’t want to be pigeonholed. When I hear the algorithm today, when I type in Erykah Badu somewhere, I don’t like everything that’s with it, because it limits what I feel.”View image in fullscreen‘Joni Mitchell touches my spirit’ ... Badu in 1997.Photograph: Paul Natkin/WireImageBadu says she had her whole life to write Baduizm; for its follow-up, 2000’s Mama’s Gun, she only had three years, but everything in her life had changed. In 1997, she had a son, Seven, with André 3000; the pair split a year later. “I had a kid. I had a heartbreak. I had a new house. I had money. I could do things for my family members. The expectations were enormous, that I had for myself, but I didn’t feel like I had enough time,” she says. “I had to learn, from Baduizm and Mama’s Gun, to ignore the negative things and the positive things – people who are lifting you up, because you can feel so high that you don’t want to learn anything any more.”double quotation markThey’re not giving out enough ass-whoopings no more!Eventually, Badu was able to re-centre herself by thinking about those artists who had been so formative for her – artists such as Joni Mitchell, who she returns to a couple of times throughout our conversation. “She touches my spirit – the simplicity of scaled-back voice and music, because her voice is a true instrument, with perfect pitch,” she says. “Her emotions are an instrument as well. I can hear the tears and laughter in the music, and because it’s scaled down so beautifully. It’s just a feeling that I have when I listen to her, or sing about her. Think about her. Talk about her.”Badu became a doula “by accident”. Four years after having Seven, she promised to be with a friend during her birth. “I didn’t know her labour was going to be 52 hours – she soldiered through this thing, and after the 52nd hour, I realised I had not been to sleep. I felt fine. I was the support system, I was the restaurant, and I didn’t have any fear,” she recalls. “That’s when I realised, I am the welcoming committee – my contract was with that baby.”View image in fullscreen‘How do you stay friends with exes? Suck hard!’ ... Badu and André 3000.Photograph: Mike Vitelli/BFA.com/ShutterstockBadu began studying and received her doula certification in 2006. From 2001 to 2023, she supported two mothers a year – because she tours eight months of the year, she was reluctant to take on any more – and coached them through their pregnancies, ensuring they had access to what she calls “the five doctors”: sun, earth, nutrients, exercise and spirit. She has doula’d for celebrity friends including, she tells me, Teyana Taylor and Summer Walker. And she is also an end-of-life doula, sitting “at the bedsides of people who are passing, going the other way – I want to provide the exact same peace.”I ask if being an end-of-life doula can be distressing, but she says the fact that it’s not for her is why she does it. “It’s another art for me,” she says. “I feel the same way when I’m servicing people on stage, singing. That’s doula work, too. I have the same thing in mind – I want the room to become one living, breathing organism.”If there is a common thread that runs though many of the songs on Before the World Blows, it’s gender politics: the ways in which men and women interact, screw each other over and take central roles in each other’s lives. Badu has always been interested in this theme, but it feels different this time, as if she is an omniscient narrator, spreading wisdom to the world. “Some of these songs are autobiographical, and some of them are messages I want to give to my daughters” – she has two, Puma (born 2004) and Mars (2009) – “or the daughters of the world, to the people of the world who have to go through these initiations, too.”View image in fullscreen‘Phones have become our pseudo-husband and wife’ ... Badu performing in 2026.Photograph: Astrida Valigorsky/Getty ImagesI ask if she sees right now as a particularly fractious moment for heterosexual dating, and she looks at me quizzically. “Your mama had trouble dating, and your grandma, and your great-grandma. You say more fractured – I think more transparent, maybe.” Legs outstretched, bare toes occasionally tickling my thigh by accident, Badu puts forward her theory. “I think we’re so hyper-aware that we notice things that maybe the people before us didn’t notice. The vocabulary we’re using, the definitions that we can put on our inconsistencies and weirdness, narcissism, and the ADHD. The definitions are becoming bigger than who we are.”That scrutiny means we’re stealing from ourselves, she says. “It doesn’t give us room to create or laugh or be free. It’s hard to find somebody that is accepting you completely because we don’t accept ourselves completely any more. When I was young, you didn’t get the grace of being defined as something. You just got an ass-whooping! And when all you need is an ass-whooping, everybody can straighten up. They’re not giving out enough ass-whoopings no more. We’re pardoning behaviour by defining it, I think.”Black Box, the album’s final track, is a wild odyssey about phone addiction, and a worthy addition to her canon of phone songs she started with But You Caint Use My Phone. Social media is a constant bugbear for Badu – she loves using it, and is prolific on Instagram, but hates how tied she is to her phone. “It’s the first thing we reach for in the morning – it has become our pseudo-husband and wife – and one thing I do know is that the first thing we do in the morning that gives us dopamine is what we will reach for all day long,” she says. “If we’re able to bypass the phone and go outside and get air and nutrients and all that, that’s what we’re going to keep running back to all day. But we pick this up first. I wanted to speak to that.”View image in fullscreenWith daughters Mars (left) and Puma (right) in 2017.Photograph: Leon Bennett/Getty Images for BETBadu’s children are 17, 22 and 28 – and she sees how they don’t have the same freedom she did, growing up without social media. Everyone is “vibrating at a higher rate” now, she says. “I noticed that it was different when I tried to show my daughters Fred Flintstone – that cartoon is hilarious to me, and they couldn’t resonate with it because it just doesn’t vibrate at the same rate they do.” Even so, she and her daughters, Mars and Puma, still have things in common. “Mars put me on to Faye Webster and Beabadoobee. Mars went backwards and got me listening to Abba! Puma loves musical theatre and Broadway, so she has me listening to Chicago or operas. We share an aux cord in the house, so I don’t have a choice.”‘I used to do acid on a Wednesday. I don’t have time for that now’: alt-pop star Steve Lacy on his struggles after huge hit Bad HabitRead moreThey all love Steve Lacy, too: Badu took her daughters to see him perform in Dallas a few years ago, and this year, they make reciprocal guest appearances on each other’s albums. “We had stuff in common, and mostly sent memes to each other starting out. That’s how you know if you rock with somebody – you have a similar sense of humour,” she says. “You kind of don’t have the same music taste, either, if you don’t have the same sense of humour.”Before the World Blows includes an interlude by Jay Electronica, the elusive rapper she dated for many years, and the father of Mars. Badu has tended to remain close with her exes – André 3000 contributed a rare, memorable guest verse to But You Caint Use My Phone – so I ask if she has any advice for maintaining ties with former lovers. “You just gotta suck hard. That’s it,” she says, bursting into laughter, her voice rising above a whisper for the first time in our conversation. “They were my friends first, and I think that’s what makes a difference. Watch that be the headline – Erykah remains friends with her exes because she sucks hard!”Our time is up; Badu gently swings her legs off the couch and stands up. She shuffles over to me and leans in, peering deeply into my eyes. I’m a little scared that she might drop some kind of bombshell – the time and place of my death, for example, or that I was a terrible interviewer – but instead, she just mutters: “You pretty as fuck!” Before I can even respond, she’s gone.Before the World Blows is out now on Control Freaq/YoungExplore more on these topicsSoulErykah BadufeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the spectral, fathoms-deep folksong of June McDoom and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Rich harmonies mix with synth, harp and aquatic grace on the intriguing first single from the New York songwriter’s debut album
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: Rich harmonies mix with synth, harp and aquatic grace on the intriguing first single from the New York songwriter’s debut album
Content: Spectral folk … June McDoom.Photograph: Ryley PaskalView image in fullscreenSpectral folk … June McDoom.Photograph: Ryley PaskalAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the spectral, fathoms-deep folksong of June McDoom and the week’s best new tracksRich harmonies mix with synth, harp and aquatic grace on the intriguing first single from the New York songwriter’s debut albumJasper Willems andLaura SnapesFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 08.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromNew York, USARecommended if you likeJessica Pratt, Minnie Riperton, Cocteau TwinsUp nextDebut LPFollow the Light released via Jagjaguwar on 16 OctoberIn Robert Silverberg’s 1973 sci-fi anthology New Dimensions 3, there’s a story by author Terry Carr called They Live on Levels. The simplest outline of this tale is that thanks to a technological breakthrough, humans are able to exist and communicate through different planes of existence. Through musical styles and generational layers, the spectral folk of New York-based songwriter June McDoom expresses this very notion in stunning fashion.Learning her craft through jazz standards, McDoom found her bread and butter within the time-honoured harmonies of folk music (she covered the Appalachian ballad Black is the Color of My True Love’s Hair on her 2023 EP With Strings). There’s a vast confluence of musical movements spooking beneath that foundation, anchored deeply within McDoom’s own family lineage. Growing up in a Jamaican household in south Florida, her father would build his own sound systems around the house. A generation before that, McDoom’s grandfather Colin Smith was a performer and preservationist of mento, the Jamaican strain of folk that would spawn reggae and dub.On Without You, the first single from her forthcoming debut album Follow the Light, McDoom reflects on a momentary spell of distance from a lover. As the song progresses, the lush instrumentation – acoustic guitars, synths, harps and piano – float with almost aquatic grace, naturally as if rising towards the glow beyond the surface. It’s emblematic of McDoom’s output leading up to now: intimate and warm, yet somehow disembodied and mysterious as well. Her songs, indeed, live on many levels.Jasper WillemsThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenBetty Hammerschlag.Photograph: Awaiting credit infoBetty Hammerschlag – Damn BirdAn invitation to a private world: choppy lo-fi guitar with a little Chicago post-rock in its harmonics underpins the enigmatic songwriter’s mysterious incantations about a cursed bird.Sylvan Esso – On and OnFlickering like a stomach full of anxiety, the intricacy of the instrumentation here is remarkable, the North Carolina duo joined by Wilco’s Glenn Kotche and Flock of Dimes’ Jenn Wasner. [Listenon Bandcamp]Underscores – Unlimited LoveA second serving of a year-best pop album: a puckish hyperpop take on the acoustic guitar-addled pop of the early millennium, with a cataclysmic, Vegas-ready outro for good measure.Sofii – GodEvery sound in God is made by the human voice, spliced as if across church organ pipes, providing the backing for the French-American artist’s crushing hymnal about trying to forget a lover.Sarah Meth – Don’t Touch Me You’re My HeroFor fans of Sophia Stel and Lana Del Rey’s casual self-abasement, the Londoner’s songs are lo-fi, droll and make blunt truths slip down easy: “Does it make you feel bigger to make a bitch wait?”Jeshi – Linea Rossa (ft Cameo Blush)The east Londoner’s new mixtape celebrates his youthful clubbing exploits. “Shoulda stayed home but I said that last night,” he raps over a beat that zips by like street lights seen from a speeding car.Boy Harsher – Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call)The warped-mirror bass of Tough Luck is a time machine back to the best of gothy post-punk – nakedly Cure, transparently New Order – but decades on, it still hits the spot when done this well.Laura SnapesSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistFolk musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dahi: Black Boy (Alternative) review – Kendrick producer takes the spotlight for all-star guitar celebration | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: The Grammy winner unites former clients including Lamar and Ravyn Lenae for a playful, dazzling voyage through the guitar’s diversity, from alt-rock to Afrobeat
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: The Grammy winner unites former clients including Lamar and Ravyn Lenae for a playful, dazzling voyage through the guitar’s diversity, from alt-rock to Afrobeat
Content: Into the spotlight … Dahi.Photograph: Marissa BlairView image in fullscreenInto the spotlight … Dahi.Photograph: Marissa BlairPop and rockReviewDahi: Black Boy (Alternative) review – Kendrick producer takes the spotlight for all-star guitar celebration(ALTER)The Grammy winner unites former clients including Lamar and Ravyn Lenae for a playful, dazzling voyage through the guitar’s diversity, from alt-rock to AfrobeatKatie HawthorneFri 28 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn this long-awaited debut, Grammy-winning hip-hop producer Dahi steps out from the booth and into the spotlight. He’s best known for transforming a dreamy Beach House sample into Kendrick Lamar’s hit Money Trees, alongside chameleonic production work for SZA, Madonna, Drake and many more. Now that Dahi’s got the mic, what does he want to say?View image in fullscreenDahi: Black Boy (Alternative) album cover.Blending the brittle 90s British rock he loved as a California teen with the west African grooves his father played in the house, Black Boy (Alternative) celebrates the guitar as a transcendent tool that spans genres and continents. No other album this year will boast such starry guest features – Dahi calls up former clients Lamar, Childish Gambino, Vince Staples and Ravyn Lenae alongside experimentalists such as Moses Sumney, Baby Rose and Fousheé – but it’s testament to the strength of his vision that these distinct voices come together like a bedded-in, playful house band. All trust, no ego.Twisty, tactile tracks reference Radiohead and Fela Kuti, toy with time signatures and chord changes, and are just as likely to deploy open-hearted sax solos as gnarly vocoder – all in the service of showing off the guitar’s versatility. And through it all, Dahi asks questions about artistic ambition and integrity: They Don’t Know Me, with rapper Mez, loops one lyric – “they said that I couldn’t fly, but I end up in the sky” – while subtle shifts in production turn its tone from defiant to awestruck, fearful then victorious. Black Boy (Alternative) is grounded in Dahi’s musical history, but it’s the sound of his future.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Klara Lewis: Opening review – enigmatic, ecstatic sound sculptures from a Swedish slowburn master | Music | The Guardian
description: Lewis mines beauty and intimacy from her minimalist blend of samples and rich instrumentation, sounding as profound whether they last 11 minutes or 38 seconds
Author: Safi Bugel
Headline: Lewis mines beauty and intimacy from her minimalist blend of samples and rich instrumentation, sounding as profound whether they last 11 minutes or 38 seconds
Content: ‘Sound sculptor’ … Klara Lewis.Photograph: Hampus HögbergView image in fullscreen‘Sound sculptor’ … Klara Lewis.Photograph: Hampus HögbergExperimental album of the monthMusicReviewKlara Lewis: Opening review – enigmatic, ecstatic sound sculptures from a Swedish slowburn master(Editions Mego)Lewis mines beauty and intimacy from her minimalist blend of samples and rich instrumentation, sounding as profound whether they last 11 minutes or 38 secondsSafi BugelFri 28 Aug 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first thing you hear on Opening, the new record from Swedish musician Klara Lewis, is a grainy fog of ambient noise: the sound of waves, a roadside or perhaps just the creaks and echoes of the room she’s recording in. The whining reversed strings that soon emerge from the murk create a wistful atmosphere, but then things take a turn: the loop clips and distorts with strobe-like intensity; after several minutes, it cuts off mid-bar, as though it’s been unplugged.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Opening.This deconstructed, shape-shifting approach is typical of the self-styled “sound sculptor”, who has been composing uncanny instrumentals from a combination of acoustic instruments and processed samples since 2014. As always, she imbues the harsh experimentalism with real feeling throughout this gorgeous collection of tracks. On City, the lo-fi guitar loop and faint traces of chatter lend a sense of warmth and intimacy to the whooshing field recordings and churning electronics. On standout Vaknar, Lewis builds something soaring and beautiful, where the reverse tape effect creates a dreamlike wooziness and the high-pitched bursts of noise feel increasingly ecstatic, in the spirit of Joshua Chuquimia Crampton or early Arca.Usually, however, she resists such extremes: most of these tracks are stripped-back and unshowy, with only subtle left-field touches. Despite its name, Hardcore is a slow, waltzing affair with flickering layers of looped instrumentation and twinkling effects that evoke birdsong. The 11-minute Tide remains horizontal, indulging in a textural slow burn in lieu of a climax. Other understated highlights include Bud and Small Harp, both of which sit under the two-minute mark (the shortest track on the album lasts 38 seconds). Even at their most simple and ephemeral, Lewis’s vignettes build something rich and moving.Also out this monthHorizont, the new record from Ukrainian musicianRegina Collage, is a meditation on her motherland and her new life in Bristol (Do You Have Peace?). These 13 tracks are suitably introspective and intimate, as she mumbles languidly over home-spun, candle-lit loops that nod to dream pop and cold wave.Curbside Lambsearare a new London duo connected to groups such as Caroline and the Umlauts (violinist Magdalena McLean also tours with Astrid Sonne). Their debut album Put Rings on All My Fingers to Weigh Down My Hands (Scenic Route) wades through grubby post-rock and experimental noise, with disaffected singsong-style vocals and a lovely viola section on the closer. Doom dubstep, deconstructed hyperpop and free-jazz solos: these are just a few of the elements Tokyo musicianHakushi Hasegawafuses into one cacophonous jumble on their new record Honest Feeling Album (Brainfeeder). It’s a disorientating, genre- and tempo-hopping affair, featuring a handful of comparatively sweet and subtle moments.Explore more on these topicsMusicExperimental album of the monthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Children’s books roundup – the best new picture books and novels | Children and teenagers | The Guardian
description: Poetry with wonder and wit; a heartwarming tale for horse lovers; a portal to the future; a brilliant YA wartime romance and more
Author: Imogen Russell Williams
Headline: Poetry with wonder and wit; a heartwarming tale for horse lovers; a portal to the future; a brilliant YA wartime romance and more
Content: Small Monster, Big Monster by Allan Sanders.Photograph: Allan SandersView image in fullscreenSmall Monster, Big Monster by Allan Sanders.Photograph: Allan SandersChildren's book roundupChildren and teenagersReviewChildren’s books roundup – the best new picture books and novelsPoetry with wonder and wit; a heartwarming tale for horse lovers; a portal to the future; a brilliant YA wartime romance and moreImogen Russell WilliamsFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSmall Monster, Big Monsterby Allan Sanders, Phaidon, £7.95Refrigerator is EMPTY. Monster is FULL (of pizza!). An eye-wateringly bright board book, featuring splendidly zany, toddler-pleasing pairs of opposites.View image in fullscreenThe Flying Machine of Dreamsby Kate Wakeling, illustrated by Viviane Schwarz, Otter-Barry, £12.99A delectable picture-book collaboration that perfectly distils the wonder of the everyday, from the textures of a leaf to a squishy-cushioned den. Wakeling’s irresistible poetry is richly heightened by Schwarz’s sweet, strange illustrations.The Weather Shopby Thomas Lee, translated by Deborah Smith, Do Re Mi, £12.99Translated from Korean, this intricate, inviting, Scarryesque picture book features a shop full of rain balloons, cloud pillows and snow sprays (and a sunshine scarf to warm everyone after the blizzard).Bison Rule, OK!by Sarah Ziman, illustrated by Nia Havilliard, Otter-Barry, £8.99What annoyed Big Sister this week? What’s the cure for everything in the school medical room? And what’s so good about having a bison as your friend?
