Witty, satisfying, resonant and fun, this enticing poetry collection will tempt a range of 6+ readers.African Queensby Onyinye Iwu, Walker, £12.99From Hatshepsut, the pharaoh her successors tried to erase, to Amanirenas, the Sudanese queen who fought the Romans and won, these strikingly illustrated stories of bold and fearless African rulers will grip 7+ history buffs.View image in fullscreenThe Palace of Factsby Kate Olesin, illustrated by Andy Smith, What on Earth Books, £22This gigantic, spectacularly colourful nonfiction treasury is crammed with 400 facts, displayed in the Hall of Mirrors, the Fossil Hall, the Aquarium, the Maze (“The world’s largest maze, in Yancheng, China, is designed in the shape of an elk”) and many more. A rainy-day delight for trivia mavens of 7 or 8+.Stableheart: Helping Heroby Nicci Johnson, S&S, £7.99Sad to leave her foster parents and the pony she loved to ride, Pres isn’t yet ready to trust her Aunty Janelle, or form a new bond with the rescue pony at the city stables. But what if he really needs her? This heartwarming, layered, readable story will please 8+ horse lovers and Jacqueline Wilson fans.View image in fullscreenHow to Steal the Futureby Christopher Edge, Macmillan, £7.99At the heart of a dangerous, ever-changing maze hides the Avenir, a mystery with the power to unlock the future. Drew is looking for his sister Evie, who disappeared during her own attempt to reach the centre. As the traps and puzzles get deadlier, can Drew find Evie and save his own future before time runs out? A high-concept, brain-twisting 9+ thrill ride from the author ofEscape Room.Wilomina: The Land of Dreams and Nightmaresby John Chalmers and Sandra Marrs, Scholastic, £9.99On her way to visit Mum in hospital, a weird train ride strands Wilomina in a parallel world of dreams, where she befriends a talking cat, seeks out a mysterious library, and begins metamorphosing into a ferocious werepire. Fabulously odd, with a colour scheme of visceral purples and lurid greens, this surreal, gripping graphic novel will appeal to 9+ Ghibli fans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy Name Is Zaynby Fidan Meikle, Floris, £7.99After a long, dangerous journey fleeing the Taliban, Zayn is wrenched away from his best friend Samim when their dinghy sinks in the English Channel. Sent to a hotel housing other asylum seekers, Zayn’s attempts to start a new life are disrupted when his roommate disappears … A standalone companion to the award-winningMy Name Is Samim, this moving, compelling 10+ story of courage and adaptability shines a searchlight on the asylum system and gangs who prey on vulnerable children.Traitors’ Nestby Frances Hardinge, Macmillan, £16.99In the kingdom of Thaletal, castles move as a Great Game is played, disrupting the lives of ordinary people. When teenage Burr’s village is threatened by an ominous new castle, a coup attempt backfires and Burr finds himself spirited away to an unknown corner of Thaletal. Can Burr and his sisters – and the strange heiress Burr has unwillingly kidnapped – learn to beat the players at their own Game? Humane, complex and inimitably inventive, this magnificent 12+ fantasy is yet another barnstormer from the Costa-winning Hardinge.View image in fullscreenCut Him Outin Little Starsby Lucy Strange, Chicken House, £8.99When her fighter pilot fiance is shot down, heartbroken Juliet is sent to stay by the sea with her sister. But the discovery of a local girl’s body plunges her into mysteries past and present, and meeting handsome, scarred flight lieutenant Bertie Campbell complicates everything even more. Can Juliet overcome trauma and terror to risk falling in love again? This enchanting, atmospheric, poignant second world war romance is the brilliant Strange’s first foray into writing for teenagers.Encoreby Miles Toriko Burks, Farshore,£12.99Kindergarten besties Clayton Noguchi and Aron Santos fell out in middle school; now they’ve unwillingly reunited in senior theatre class. As they navigate improv, drama games and conversations in and out of school, will they end up as friends – or something more? Based on a popular Webtoon, this funny, touching, addictive queer YA graphic novel should delight Heartstopper fans.Hell to Payby Lora Beth Johnson, Hot Key, £8.99Accomplished thief Elle Fields steals secrets from the Dead, just like her brother used to, until a botched attempt cost him his soul. When charismatic stranger Rook offers her a commission promising a chance at resurrection, she can’t resist assembling her former crew for one last Afterlife heist. But there are things Elle doesn’t know about her brother’s death, or the job she’s accepted … Original and fast-paced, boasting taut characterisation and impressive emotional heft, this supernatural YA thriller will electrify Leigh Bardugo devotees.Explore more on these topicsChildren and teenagersChildren's book roundupChildren's books: 7 and underChildren's books: 8-12 yearsTeen booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sophie, Standing There by Meg Mason review – a tale of literary obsession, with cameos from real-life authors | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A heartbroken woman becomes fixated on a famous writer in this witty, touching follow-up to Sorrow and Bliss
Author: Sam Leith
Headline: A heartbroken woman becomes fixated on a famous writer in this witty, touching follow-up to Sorrow and Bliss
Content: Nothing if not knowing … Meg Mason.Photograph: Anne PeetersView image in fullscreenNothing if not knowing … Meg Mason.Photograph: Anne PeetersBook of the dayFictionReviewSophie, Standing There by Meg Mason review – a tale of literary obsession, with cameos from real-life authorsA heartbroken woman becomes fixated on a famous writer in this witty, touching follow-up to Sorrow and BlissSam LeithFri 28 Aug 2026 05.23 EDTFirst published on Mon 27 Jul 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe protagonist of Meg Mason’s new book, the follow-up to the2020 tragicomedy Sorrow and Bliss, is an invisible woman. She might well be standing there but you won’t notice her. She’s a techie at literary festivals – the person who shuffles up to a famous writer a few minutes before their event and apologetically slides a microphone cable down their shirt while they’re making small talk with the chair or accepting a bottle of room-temperature mineral water from an anxious publicist.No man is a hero to his valet, and no writer is a hero to the technical staff lurking in the wings of a venue. Mason’s opening pages present a teasing but not quite libellous series of cameos from real writers: George Saunders deciding at an inconsiderately late stage to insist on swapping his headset for a lapel mic; Ann Patchett being frosty with a fan; Mick Herron accidentally stepping on someone’s foot and not apologising.double quotation markMason is brilliant at describing the small but intense joys of everyday lifeSophie lurks in the wings of her own life, too. She likes her job but she has much to be sad about. Not long ago, her husband brought their relationship to an end with oafish callousness (she was in the shower; he didn’t bother to take his earbuds out while he delivered the news), and with it her hope of becoming a mother. Now her beloved books are in storage in the garage of her old house and she’s living alone in a dingy rental flat owned by her husband: “The water in Sophie’s glass tasted like pipes. She felt very tired … The coffee table was actually a cable spool with ‘12 AWG’ spray-painted on the drum.”Mason’s prose is wan and witty, handling the admixture of pathos and bathos well; and her sinuous sentences capture the wavering movements of thought with less fuss and more laughs than, say, Virginia Woolf. As a bookish person, and one inhabiting a lightly metafictional narrative, Sophie is glumly aware of her literary analogues. There’s “a lot of sad girl fiction” on her Kindle. “Eleanor Oliphant,” she reflects. “That was the worst. Even though it was extremely well written and Sophie had recommended it to about 10 people when it first came out, in this moment, she wished she’d never heard of it and couldn’t recall the cheese scones and those cappuccinos Eleanor always ordered, the saddest of all the coffees.”Mason is brilliant, too, at describing the small but intense joys of everyday life – getting your scalp massaged at the hairdresser, for instance, or owning one really nicely designed pair of trousers. She’s likewise good at life’s routine humiliations and inanities, such as bumping into your ex with a leaky bottle of coconut water in your handbag, or asking a favour from someone whose text messages you have been ignoring, or realising how much it’s going to cost to take an Uber back from Ikea.The engine of the plot is a parasocial relationship but an old-fashioned one: Sophie becomes obsessed with a famous writer. (The writer is just “the author” for the first part of the book but then, perhaps finding the conceit unwieldy, Mason gives her a name, Lilac Dunne.) Sophie rereads her books, talks to an imaginary version of Lilac, and spends hours scrolling images of her and listening to her on podcasts. Then fantasy and reality collide when, to Sophie’s terror, Lilac is booked to appear after Elizabeth Strout drops out of an event.An infatuation with the idea of Lilac, with her public persona and her authorial voice, is complicated by a first glancing and then apparently deepening encounter with the real thing. Lilac takes Sophie up, a little, and Sophie is flattered and flustered. She thinks of herself as a nobody but Lilac seems not to. And then … well, no spoilers.If there’s a fault to be identified in this continuously witty and touching narrative, it’s in the person of Lilac. As a writer she appears to be unstuffy, poised, wise and at ease in the world; Sophie isn’t the only one to fall for her. When we encounter Lilac in person, she’s harder and more ruthless than her public persona but no less impenetrable, with none of the psychological complexity or vulnerability displayed elsewhere. She’s moredeus ex machinain Sophie’s story than fully realised character.But perhaps that’s by design. In this Bridget-Jones-meets-Pirandello caper, Mason is nothing if not knowing. As she writes in one of the closing chapters, opening a little postmodernmise en abyme: “If someone wrote a novel about Sophie, which they wouldn’t, but if they did, it could end there.” It doesn’t.Sophie, Standing There by Meg Mason is published by Bloomsbury (£20). title: The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past – Geralt of Rivia returns after a decade in the sun | Games | The Guardian
description: Before The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Before The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’
Content: ‘We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years’ … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedView image in fullscreen‘We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years’ … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedSummer games previewsGamesThe Witcher 3: Songs of the Past – Geralt of Rivia returns after a decade in the sunBefore The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’Elliot GardnerFri 28 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 09.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe game that graced us withBathtub Geralt, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, arrived more than a decade ago. So it was a touch surprising this summer when developers CD Projekt Red announced a new expansion to the venerable adventure, titled Songs of the Past, for next year. It will release alongside a full remaster of the original game, which will be free for anyone who bought it back in 2015. (The studio is also working on a sequel, The Witcher 4, but that’s not due until 2028.)As it turns out, this is all possible thanks to a partnership with Fool’s Theory, a studio founded by CD Projekt Red veterans, which took on the brunt of the development work. “We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years,” explains Marcin Blacha, VP story director at CD Projekt Red. “Of course, we moved on to Cyberpunk 2077 and now The Witcher 4, as well as our other projects. But because we knew The Witcher 4 would take time, we saw a gap in our release calendar where Songs of the Past could go. Thankfully, we were able to find the right partner to help execute it.”View image in fullscreenSeemingly idyllic … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedThe elephant in the room, though, is that The Witcher 3’s 2016 expansion Blood and Wine felt like a natural conclusion to Geralt’s tale. After decades covered in entrails, the legendary monster slayer hangs up his dual swords for a well-earned life of luxury on his recently acquired vineyard estate. What can he possibly have left to do?“That is certainly something we thought through,” says Blacha. “Geralt retired in Toussaint – but then his best friend comes calling. I don’t think many of us would turn down that request.”So, foppish fan favourite Dandelion the bard pulls the witcher back into action, asking Geralt to come to his aid in his homeland of Letten. It’s a seemingly idyllic land of bountiful harvests and rowdy festivals that hides some sinister secrets.View image in fullscreenSinister secrets … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedIt’s been exciting, and nostalgic. We spent so long with Geralt, but have also learned a lot in the 10-plus years we’ve been away from him,” says Blacha. “With Songs of the Past, we really wanted to return to The Witcher’s roots. That meant drawing on old beliefs and folklore, revisiting landscapes inspired by Poland’s history and countryside, and staying true to the series’ tradition of difficult dilemmas. Going back to all of this has been a pleasure.”The team has also put to bed rumours that this expansion will be a prequel to The Witcher 4. Songs of the Past is focused on the gruff, grey witcher we’ve already come to love, not Ciri, the younger protagonist of the forthcoming title. Rather, the expansion has all the trappings that seasoned Witcher fans should recognise, with a morally murky narrative brought to life by returning voice actors Doug Cockle and John Schwab, who reprise their roles as Geralt and Dandelion.There are a few new features to play around with, though: CD Projekt has enhanced Geralt’s combat and skill trees, and he now wields a chain weapon alongside his steel and silver swords. There are also new DNA-modifying mutagens to play around with, tweaking Geralt’s biology and, therefore, his supernatural skills.The Witcher 3 is a modern classic that has already come to a gratifying end: bringing Geralt out of retirement is a risky move. But when his medallion starts humming, the White Wolf is still ready to answer the call.The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past is in development for PC, Switch 2, PS5, andXboxSeries X/S, and is due for release in 2027.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsRole playing gamesPlayStation 5PCXboxfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tom Towelling Teaches You to Knit review – quirky yarns and a pop quiz in maths | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Hopping from a PowerPoint on hairlines to songs about favourite motorways, Towelling’s set is fun but drops a stitch or two
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Hopping from a PowerPoint on hairlines to songs about favourite motorways, Towelling’s set is fun but drops a stitch or two
Content: Gently cocooning … Tom TowellingView image in fullscreenGently cocooning … Tom TowellingEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewTom Towelling Teaches You to Knit review – quirky yarns and a pop quiz in mathsPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghHopping from a PowerPoint on hairlines to songs about favourite motorways, Towelling’s set is fun but drops a stitch or twoBrian LoganFri 28 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe route fromthe classroom to the comedy stageis well travelled, and ex-maths teacher Tom Towelling makes it the thread of his show here, conducting his audience like so many recalcitrant pupils under his charge. In case that sounds triggering, never fear: this debut show is unlike any other schoolroom you’ve been in. Towelling is one of several oddball comics elevated to the best newcomer shortlist forthis year’s Edinburgh comedy awards, and his show is a noodly, mellow collage of sketch, song and educational back-and-forth with the crowd.Let’s get the title – Tom Towelling Teaches You to Knit – out of the way early. When audience members play ball with this or that bit of interaction, the Birmingham man rewards them by binding them together loosely with wool. As the show progresses, a cat’s cradle unspools, towards – well, nothing in particular. The idea goes undeveloped. That’s not the only instance here when you feel you’re on the receiving end of quirkiness for quirkiness’s sake – see his song about favourite motorways, or a fairly cheap closing routine revealing his supposed life ambition.Marty Gleeson: Dog Ear review – hangdog standup with an unexpected request for SantaRead moreAt the performance I saw, that latter skit was memorably interrupted by an invader from the courtyard outside, demanding to see his 12-inch penis. Hilarity ensued – and Towelling can take some credit for the chaos, having set that process in motion when he expelled an audience member for requesting to hear his supposed “forbidden joke”, one that would ruin the show. Harness that level of unpredictability to his act and he really could be in business.In the meantime, he’s got a gently cocooning hour of low-level eccentricity,Rob Auton-like in its dreaminess, which features an amusing PowerPoint on the parabolic hairlines of his various uncles, an act-out of the pep talk he’d love to give to the England football team, and an impromptu maths test with his crowd. Awinner last year of Channel 4’s Sean Lock awardfor comic invention, Towelling showcases that quality here, even if inventive parts are yet to knit together into a satisfying whole.At Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalComedy (Culture)FestivalsSchoolsKnittingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Li Jin Hao: Falling from a Moon review – comedy’s Mr Nostalgia is now the man of the moment | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: In his award-nominated show, the standup ruminates on myth and memory with some lovely observations
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: In his award-nominated show, the standup ruminates on myth and memory with some lovely observations
Content: Ravishing insights … Li Jin Hao.Photograph: Rebecca Need MenearView image in fullscreenRavishing insights … Li Jin Hao.Photograph: Rebecca Need MenearEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewLi Jin Hao: Falling from a Moon review – comedy’s Mr Nostalgia is now the man of the momentPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghIn his award-nominated show, the standup ruminates on myth and memory with some lovely observationsBrian LoganFri 28 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘There’s a moment whenthatends,” muses Li Jin Hao, “andthisbegins …” As well as being jam-packed with swoonsome one-liners like that, Li’s show traces the tension between this and that; the draw the past exerts on this self-proclaimed Mr Nostalgia, versus the necessity of living in the present. Beginning with a yearning sun-and-moon myth learned at his granny’s knee, Li’s show –nominated for the Edinburgh comedy award– toggles between a day in his current London life and memories of his upbringing in east Asia, and a long-gone romance he can’t quite shake off.What makes the show distinctive, though, is the ruminative angle at which Li addresses his experiences, and the quality and consistency of its joke-writing – so many ravishing little insights revealing the world to us in shapes askew. It’s a leap forward fromhis 2024 debut, which signalled the talent but was sheepish in its delivery. The only thing sheepish here is the twisty livestock gag that opens Li’s show, with a swagger that marks a performer now in his element onstage.Marty Gleeson: Dog Ear review – hangdog standup with an unexpected request for SantaRead moreSo if his present is in such good nick, what’s with the nostalgia? That question won’t initially trouble you, as we follow our host from his London flat with a sloping floor, on to public transport (on pressing the stop button: “I’m tickling the bus!”), then to the cinema. The trip detours via countless sumptuous routines and notions: on how differently letters and numbers behave; on rhyme versus reason; on “how come when two people give each other their virginities, they’re left with none?” Then we flash back to a Chinese childhood and Singaporean youth, flooding Li with memories of a life lived in more vivid colour.But looking back, as myths from Lot to Orpheus remind us, can be a dangerous business. Li’s show, finally, is about the need to put that past behind him – a theme it over-articulates in its closing moments. There’s no need: we can glean plenty from what goes before, while glorying in the linguistic and observational invention at play in image after joke after slantedaperçu.Thatwas the show I saw; this is Li’s moment.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsComedy (Culture)Comedy (Stage)Awards and prizesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Clown Show review – after 250 years, the American dream explodes over one anarchic night | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The pranks and pratfalls in Geoff Sobelle’s show mark the US’s 250th anniversary with nihilistic excess
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: The pranks and pratfalls in Geoff Sobelle’s show mark the US’s 250th anniversary with nihilistic excess
Content: Weather-beaten glitz … Clown Show.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWeather-beaten glitz … Clown Show.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewClown Show review – after 250 years, the American dream explodes over one anarchic nightKing’s theatre, EdinburghThe pranks and pratfalls in Geoff Sobelle’s show mark the US’s 250th anniversary with nihilistic excessMark FisherFri 28 Aug 2026 09.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 09.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey are a forlorn lot, this bunch who shuffle glumly to the front of the stalls. In white face, funeral veils, mismatched jodhpurs and tailcoats, they gaze across the auditorium to the timeless strum of a folk song. They cheer up after the curtain rises and – to audience applause – their big top reveals itself in all its weatherbeaten glitz.This is where these motley figures belong and for much ofGeoff Sobelle’s characteristically uncategorisable show, they play it exactly as you would expect clowns to play it – albeit with some scenes more entertaining than others. There are musical skits, sight gags with false hands and spare legs, upturned boxes of bees and bags of popcorn thrown from the stage with lawless abandon.There is an innocence about these clowns. Like children, they are clumsy and needy. They seek our approval and, having got it, are unsure what to do with it.View image in fullscreenApproval-seeking … Clown Show.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAre they merely here to make us laugh or could they be symbols of something else – pioneers muddling by in the early days of a new nation, perhaps? Amid the silent comedy, there is a Yankee Doodle energy and the trappings of Americana. The turning point comes in a wild west routine that begins with knockabout humour – three cowboys entering a saloon on horseback – and turns darker as a banana-toting gunman starts firing. The bullets go everywhere and an American bald eagle drops from the sky.Sami Abu Wardeh Hates You review – a clown strides into the mainstream with styleRead moreThe rampant individualism of the American dream finds form in a human cannonball – the hubris of go-getting accomplishment combined with platitudes about everyone working together.Commissioned by the Edinburgh international festival as part of its commemoration of the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, Clown Show goes from the joy of discovery to a planet in peril, a Spanish song of liberty and a phalanx of ICE agents. Anarchic exuberance becomes nihilistic excess.AtKing’s theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)ClownsComedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalCircusreviewsShareReuse this content

title: BBCSSO/Runnicles review – resplendent recounting of Mahler’s fratricidal fairytale | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Colliding complex and contrasting moods, Mahler’s Das Klagende Lied was rendered with clarity and conviction
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Colliding complex and contrasting moods, Mahler’s Das Klagende Lied was rendered with clarity and conviction
Content: Achieved delicate pianissimos … Donald Runnicles.Photograph: Bettina StoessView image in fullscreenAchieved delicate pianissimos … Donald Runnicles.Photograph: Bettina StoessClassical musicReviewBBCSSO/Runnicles review – resplendent recounting of Mahler’s fratricidal fairytaleUsher Hall, EdinburghColliding complex and contrasting moods, Mahler’s Das Klagende Lied was rendered with clarity and convictionMichael DownesFri 28 Aug 2026 05.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 06.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenSigmund Freud met Gustav Mahlerin 1910, he suggested that, following a childhood trauma, “the conjunction of high tragedy and light amusement was inextricably fixed in Mahler’s mind”. Freud was famously uninterested in music, but had he knownDas Klagende Lied, he would have found ample supporting evidence for his diagnosis. Composed in Mahler’s late teens and fusing opera, symphony, oratorio, lieder, part-song and even church music, the cantata collides comedy and tragedy at every turn – most remarkably towards the end, when the offstage wind band continues cheerfully as a wedding goes disastrously wrong with the revelation that the bridegroom won his bride by murdering his younger brother.Mahler withdrew the first movement, Waldmärchen, and its manuscript remained unavailable until 1969. Performing all three movements but incorporating Mahler’s later revisions, the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra under former chief conductorDonald Runniclesmade a strong case for the original tripartite structure.Emulating Wagner, Mahler wrote his own libretto, adapting a fairytale famously recounted by the Grimms, among others. Kathleen O’Mara,Catriona Morison, John Findon and Nicholas Brownlee made an eloquent quartet of storytellers, the last’s rich bass-baritone projecting particularly well. The choral sections are initially fragmented, and the Edinburgh Festival Chorus’s first entries were tentative, but they came into their own in extended passages. The girls of theNational Youth Choir of Scotland, singing from memory, were outstanding in appearances as the murdered brother’s ghostly voice.If the cantata’s vocal writing is sometimes disjointed, the instrumental music’s ambition and accomplishment is astonishing for a teenage composer with little practical orchestral experience. The BBCSSO rendered Mahler’s complex textures with clarity and conviction; horns, led by Chris Gough and gifted the finest music, were resplendent.Schubert, like Mahler, often abruptly juxtaposes contrasting moods, and the first-half performance of the“Unfinished” Symphonysensitively balanced classical and romantic aspects. Dispensing with baton and with strings reduced to chamber-orchestra proportions, Runnicles achieved delicate pianissimos and highlighted both movements’ dance-like character. But marked broadening of tempi at junctions and tightly stretched skeins of string sound were reminders that Wagner’sLohengrinlay barely 20 years in the future.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicGustav MahlerEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivallive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: How Katseye became the world’s biggest girl group – while falling apart | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Their raucous pop music has made Katseye the biggest girl band in two decades. Can they weather toxic fandom, critical pans and a dwindling member count?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Their raucous pop music has made Katseye the biggest girl band in two decades. Can they weather toxic fandom, critical pans and a dwindling member count?
Content: Katseye on the Today show in New York on 14 August 2026.Photograph: Eric Acquaye/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKatseye on the Today show in New York on 14 August 2026.Photograph: Eric Acquaye/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockPop and rockHow Katseye became the world’s biggest girl group – while falling apartTheir raucous pop music has made Katseye the biggest girl band in two decades. Can they weather toxic fandom, critical pans and a dwindling member count?Erica RussellFri 28 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore screenings of their new documentary, the members of Katseye appear in a video message to thank fans for their support. Their followers, Eyekons, have played a critical role in their rise to stardom, so it makes sense thatKatseye: Wild Hearts, released in global theaters this month, takes a beat to shout out to them. Perhaps more than many other big music groups today, the group’s rise has depended on their relationship with their devotees who ensure that few corners of the world are safe from Katseye mania.Katseye’s multinational members – Daniela, Lara, Manon, Megan, Sophia and Yoonchae – were selected through a combination of fan votes and judge scores on the 2023 YouTube reality competition The Debut: Dream Academy. The joint project between the American record label Geffen Records and Korean entertainment company Hybe aimed to create a global girl group, with hopefuls participating in a rigorous bootcamp to test their singing and dancing skills. The following year, Netflix’s docu-seriesPop Star Academy: Katseye– which documented the group’s nascent era, behind-the-scenes drama and all – catapulted them to a new level of visibility.‘We’re at a crisis point’: Chappell Roan, Shirley Manson and Eli on playing Olivia Rodrigo’s women-led festivalRead moreKatseye blend western pop’s individualism with the intense training and choreography of the well-oiledK-popmachine. Though they identify as a “global girl group”, much of Katseye’s domination can be credited to their K-pop DNA. “Katseye started with that core K-pop training [and high standards], which ensured they were firing on all cylinders from the start,” said K-pop columnist Jeff Benjamin. “Often in pop, there is a rewarding payoff in seeing an artist finally get backed by a big-label budget for a certain song, music video, or project, but K-pop ensures everything is supported from the start.”As a $5bn company with offices in Seoul, LA, Mexico City, Tokyo, Miami and Mumbai, Hybe’s resources have certainly contributed to the group’s success, but Katseye don’t adhere to all of K-pop’s structural norms. “There’s no hiding that many top-down decisions are made for them,” said Benjamin. “But Katseye divert by openly speaking about decisions they don’t agree with – the members seem not to like Pop Star Academy and the competition format they were created from – and addressing things mostK-popacts don’t speak about, including their personal lives and sexualities.”In 2026, Katseye are experiencing a surge of popularity that’s impossible to ignore, including a sold-out tour, nearly 40m monthly Spotify listeners and two Grammy nominations. Katseye: Wild Hearts, which features behind-the-scenes footage, interviews and fan-submitted videos, pulled in nearly $4m its opening weekend. The band have vacuumed up majormarketing deals: they’ve worked with State Farm, Pandora, Target and the bougie LA grocery story Erewhon, where they have their own $22 smoothie. Their GapBetter in Denim campaignsparked a wildly viral TikTok trend and saw an upswing inrevenue growthfor the brand.Fans in their 20s, teens and younger are eating up what Katseye are serving far beyond retail shelves thanks to their hybrid western pop/K-pop mythos, high-energy performances and inclusive cultural and LGBTQ+ representation. (Two members identify as queer.) There’s also their digital posturing: Katseye is quick toleverage a viral memeto promote their product as well as build relatability with their fans. They reference zoomerDisney Channel nostalgia, collaborate with other chronically online stars such asTroye Sivanand rally fan participation with popular TikTok dances.“Katseye emerged in a landscape where social media isn’t just a promotional tool, but part of how pop culture is made and circulated,” said Dr Lucy Bennett, senior lecturer in Popular Music and Fandom at Cardiff University. “Fans can take a song, performance or interaction and repackage it for their own social media, promoting the group further.”In short, the Eyekons are better than any marketing team. “This is particularly significant for a new group because fandom can help create a sense that something is happening around the group, such as a feeling of momentum and cultural relevance.”View image in fullscreenWhen there were six: Katseye at the 2026 Grammy awards.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersKatseye’s core gen Z and Alpha fanbase isn’t by accident. Their easy-to-replicate dance trends, collaborations with toy brands such as Monster High and Gui Gui slime, and “brain rot” lyrics are targeted to young audiences. “Boba tea (gnarly) / Tesla (gnarly) / Fried chicken (gnarly),” they sing on Gnarly, while their latest single features lines such as: “Carry my matcha / Mount Valley water / I like my mochi drenched in chocolata.”The group’s fast-tracked success has not come without friction. Katseye say they have faced “heavy” racist and sexist harassment, dealt with extreme toxic fandom and received death threats. Lara, a Connecticut-raised US citizen of Tamil Indian background, told theBBCshe was falsely reported to ICE, while Sophia, who is Filipina-American, revealed their family members had received hateful comments. Manon, who is of Swiss-Ghanaian heritage, called the experience “terrorizing on the mind”.Miley Cyrus, Taylor Swift and more pay tribute to Dolly Parton: ‘Her legacy will be everlasting’Read moreLike the Pussycat Dolls, Fifth Harmony and other girl groups before them, Katseye have faced an onslaught of rumors of tensions within the group. Shadily edited clips of the girls have been presented on social media as proof of enmity between members. Some have outright pitted the girls against each other. “People see us as women to rank. They’ll grade us based on how pretty we are, our singing skill, dancing skill, and then add it up and give us a percentage. That’s so dystopian,” Lara said.The all-too-familiar parasocial expectations fans have of artists weigh heavily over Katseye, but that’s nothing new in pop. “The more intimate the digital relationship becomes, the more complicated it can be to maintain boundaries,” said Bennett. “Because fans can invest so much time and emotional energy in an artist, this can create expectations around access and responsiveness.”Other public scrutiny surrounding the band has been murkier. In February, the group announced Manon was taking a temporary step back to “focus on her health and wellbeing”, leaving the band to perform at Coachella as a five-piece. Soon after, she removed references to Katseye from her Instagram bio.View image in fullscreenKatseye greeting fans gathered for their Today show performance.Photograph: Lev Radin/ShutterstockIn August, just months after Manon stepped back, Hybe announced Sophia was similarlygoing on hiatusfor her “mental health and wellness”, casting another shadow of uncertainty over the group’s seemingly dwindling roster. It’s unclear if she will return in time to join her bandmates on their global Wildworld Tour this September. Meanwhile, the active members havevoiced their supportfor both bandmates during recent promotional activities and appearances.Bennett said “the participatory nature of Katseye’s formation” makes their relationship with fans complex. “If fans have voted, promoted, defended and helped shape the formation of the group, they may feel they have a genuine stake in what happens to it. That can be a really positive thing, creating a strong sense of loyalty and investment in the group. At the same time, fans may feel that their investment gives them a particular interest in questioning or discussing decisions about [the band].”‘I feel like I’m at war’: are we losing the battle against machine-made music?Read moreKatseye’s trajectory has so far triumphed over hiatuses, controversies and sneery rumors. Released on 14 August, Wild is a mega-success. The EPdebuted at No 1on the Billboard 200, setting a remarkable new record for the biggest week by a girl group in the streaming era. Wild also marks the biggest US debut for a girl group since Danity Kane’s 2008 album Welcome to the Dollhouse, and is the fourth No 1 album by a girl group this decade following K-pop releases such as Blackpink’s Born Pink, NewJeans’ second EP Get Up, and Twice’s With You-th.Despite record-breaking sales, critics are less enthused about the band’s recent output.Vulturecalled Wild a “war between bittersweet pop … and deliberately juvenile singles”, whilePitchforkshrugged at its “hollow” songs. Perhaps a testament to their rebellious gen Z pop swag, Katseye refuse to be chained to any one rhythm in particular – for better or worse.When the EP bangs, it bangs:Pinky Up, the spiritual successor to the initially polarizing Gnarly, is an intoxicating blast of thumping techno-pop. Co-penned byEd Sheeran, Animal is a slice of radio-primed, early-2010s throwback pop. Tragically, one of the EP’s best songs, Unloveu, is a Target physical CD exclusive. Written by Lara, the ballad highlights the individual members’ voices as they harmonize about recovering from a toxic relationship. It hints at what could be if Katseye’s artistic input and vocals were emphasized above viral choreography and brand endorsements.Wild’s sonic incohesiveness and genre-hopping make for an uneven listening experience. It’s also woefully devoid of standout solo moments, the girls’ voices often blending into a sleek but frustratingly symmetrical monovocal. Bel Air, an unreleased 13-year-oldCharli xcxsong, is so languid it sounds more like a raw demo than the original. Then there’s Hootie Frutti. The Brazilian funk-flavored single is the EP’s most divisive, with some celebrating its chaotic, campy silliness and others criticizing its sexually charged, comedically product placement-heavy music video. (Manon and Sophia might be on hiatus. Orange-flavored Tic Tacs are decidedly not.)Amid a whiplash-inducing string of brand deals and promotions, fans are worried Katseye are being overworked. Maybe so. Representatives for the band did not respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment for this article. K-pop has long been under scrutiny for its infamously intense work schedules, while the western pop industry is no better for the many pressures facing female artists in particular. Coupled with various health-related hiatuses and public controversies, a cloudy patina of skepticism lies over the group’s nonstop schedules. In the past two weeks alone they have performed at the Disney Legends awards, appeared on the Today Show and Tonight Show, performed a Spotify event called Klub Katseye, signed CDs at Hot Topic and Barnes & Noble and headlined a music festival.Katseye’s potential for mainstream pop staying power is undeniable. Astheglobal pop group of today, they are heralded by fans for their confidence, vibrant and distinct personalities – they embody an attitude emblematic of modern sisterhood in all its messy, magical glory – and celebration of diversity and digital culture. But something feels unsustainable. While one demand of the pop industry seems to be maintaining momentum at all costs, Katseye’s grueling commitments coupled with unrelenting public scrutiny could be harmful in the long run. Nonstop activity could also be holding the group back from more intentionally developing their core image and artistic perspective – both paramount to solidifying a musical legacy outside of flash-in-the-pan trends.Time will tell if the band’s current hyper-saturation is a natural outcome of the well-earned hype surrounding them, or a consequence of a larger, more insidious system that views pop stars as products. Perhaps after the Wild promotion is done, the band would benefit from a collective recalibration to figure out what artistic goals exist for Katseye beyond going viral. These talented performers deserve as much.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockK-popfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Memo to Ridley Scott: no one needs more Alien: Covenant movies – get the franchise back to stalk’n’slash | Movies | The Guardian
description: News that Scott is working on a follow-up to his maligned 2017 film leaves me worried the franchise has run out of shocks
Author: Ben Child
Headline: News that Scott is working on a follow-up to his maligned 2017 film leaves me worried the franchise has run out of shocks
Content: Michael Fassbender in Alien: CovenantPhotograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenMichael Fassbender in Alien: CovenantPhotograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyWeek in geekMoviesMemo to Ridley Scott: no one needs more Alien: Covenant movies – get the franchise back to stalk’n’slashBen ChildNews that Scott is working on a follow-up to his maligned 2017 film leaves me worried the franchise has run out of shocksFri 28 Aug 2026 07.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 11.25 EDTShareIf any science-fiction saga looked beyond recovery, it was the Alien franchise. For the 38 years that followed James Cameron’s Aliens, film-makers contrived to find every imaginable way ofnotmaking a good Alien film. They tried killing everyone the audience cared about before the opening credits,marooning Sigourney Weaver on a planet populated entirely by bald British character actors,cloning Ripley,pitting xenomorphs against Predators, and sending scientists across the universe to ask an enormous, hairless space bodybuilderwhy he made them. They even ponied up the thick end of $100m for a film in whichMichael Fassbender teaches himself to play the flute.And then in 2024, we gotFede Álvarez’s Alien: Romulus, in which actual xenomorphs chase actual human beings down actual corridors for the clearly defined purposes of either killing them or putting smaller xenomorphs inside them. Better still, a year later we gotNoah Hawley’s Alien: Earth, which reminded us that giant, murderous space insects are in fact less awful than tech trillionaires.Life was good, but as long-term fans of the franchise, we ought to have known it wouldn’t last. This week, Ridley Scott – who kicked off the entire saga with 1979’s seminal Alien but has yet to make a good sequel or prequel to it – revealed that he is developing a follow-up to his much-maligned2017 film Alien: Covenant. It would see the return of Fassbender’s David, the murderous android who may or may not have started the ball rolling towards the horrors that eventually became the xenomorphs with his genetic tinkering, and who was last seen steering a colony ship packed with sleeping settlers and human embryos into the great cosmic beyond.According to the 88-year-old film-maker, the new film will detail how David creates, in Scott’s own words, “a brave new world for himself”. Further plot details remain undisclosed, but the British director did helpfully observe that AIs “can go off” and, when they do, are “like a bomb”.View image in fullscreenRidley Scott on the set of Alien: CovenantPhotograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyIt’s not the first time Scott has talked up sequels to Covenant. During the publicity run for the film, he said a follow-up was already being written andthat he would start shooting within 14 months. He also suggested he could make as many assix more Alienprequels, with the series eventually leading up to the original Alien. Eight years and no prequels later,Scott announced that he had “done enough”with the franchise and merely hoped it would continue without him. Now he appears to have reverted to an earlier mode.Part of the issue is that, alongside season two of Alien: Earth, a sequel to Romulus is already in development. Álvarez and his co-writer Rodo Sayagues have finished the script for the film, which Álvarez will produce (alongside Scott), while another director takes over. That leavesAlienpursuing three different futures at once: Hawley’s corporate small-screen nightmare, the stripped-back survival horror of Romulus, and Scott’s portentous, quasi-theological android opera. Of these three approaches, only one has already been tried twice, to diminishing enthusiasm. Yet Scott apparently remains determined to finish answering questions the franchise is now thriving without.To be fair, Fassbender’s David is one of Alien’s most intriguing antagonists, but he has been the principal attraction in two films that made little case for a third. If we really need to see him again, a high-end television offshoot would surely offer enough room to complete his story. Eight hours ought to be enough for even David to finish explaining himself, and most Alien fans would watch to the end. But another movie in which David quotes poetry and perfects his egg collection while yet another crew of unwitting space colonists inspect it at suicidally close range? That is somewhat more doubtful. There are only so many times you can explain a nightmare before abject terror turns to outright tedium. Give David his limited series, then let the xenomorphs return to the honest work of killing supporting actors in ventilation shafts. In space, nobody needs to hear your origin story.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekAlienRidley ScottScience fiction and fantasy filmsHorror filmsTelevisionMichael FassbendercommentShareReuse this content

title: A gallery glow up, spooky sculpture and a magical modern – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: A grand survey of light art illuminates Durham, St Ives gets macabre and London goes big on land art – all in your weekly dispatch
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: A grand survey of light art illuminates Durham, St Ives gets macabre and London goes big on land art – all in your weekly dispatch
Content: Our Spectral Vision, 2016, by Liz West at Victory Over the Sun, The Light, Durham.Photograph: The Light/Liz WestView image in fullscreenOur Spectral Vision, 2016, by Liz West at Victory Over the Sun, The Light, Durham.Photograph: The Light/Liz WestArt Weekly newsletterArt and designA gallery glow up, spooky sculpture and a magical modern – the week in artA grand survey of light art illuminates Durham, St Ives gets macabre and London goes big on land art –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 28 Aug 2026 09.47 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekVictory Over the SunA Russian futurist spectacle from 1913 gives this grand survey of light art its title. Luminous works by Olafur Eliasson, Ceal Floyer and many more mark the opening of Durham’s new art gallery.The Light, Durham, until 17 JanuaryAlso showingAna MendietaDon’t on any account miss this magical journey through the imagination of a great modern artist.Tate Modern, London, until 17 JanuarySgàire WoodHeraldry, fashion and sectarian politics are among the themes this Irish artist brings to a wooded sculpture park near Edinburgh.Jupiter Artland, Edinburgh, until 18 OctoberClaire CurneenSpooky sculptures that brood on death, if your day by the sea needs a macabre salting.Anima Mundi, St Ives, until 4 SeptemberEyes in the SoilArt that engages with the earth, featuring Neal Jones, Vivian Lynn and more.Phillida Reid, London, 1 September to 1 OctoberImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sonja Blom/AlamyOne of the most prolific and beloved artists of our age, Yayoi Kusama died this week at 97. The Japanese artist became a global superstar many times over in different eras for her sculptural works, her political artistic “happenings” and the spotty style and selfie-inducing infinity mirror rooms that came to be synonymous with her name. Kusama’s work was often centred on ideas of the infinite and “self-obliteration”, a concept inspired by the hallucinations that would engulf her. Despite her superstar success she identified herself as an outsider artist until her death. The image above shows her in June, painting a work from her My Eternal Soul series.Read more hereWhat we learnedBetye Saar, whose found object assemblages explored racism and religion, died aged 99Freddie Mercury’s ‘splendid things’ – eight iconic costumes – are to go on displayA plan for a waterfront site in Rotterdam looks ‘like something Shrek would throw up’Gao Zhen, known for sculptures of Mao, was jailed for slandering ‘heroes and martyrs’The Wulz sisters defied fascist Italy by shooting modern women – and their catPhotographer William Yang looked back on 60 years of capturing LGBTQ+ lifeThe Nazis hounded out the Bauhaus; now the far right is turning on them againskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKorean painter Ha Chong-Hyun, 91, believes abstraction is a form of rebellionA priceless collection of bronze age gold artefacts were stolen in a Spanish heistMasterpiece of the weekA Herdsman with Five Cows by a River by Cuyp Aelbert, 1650-55There’s not much happening here, but that’s what is so revolutionary. Cuyp is centuries ahead of his time in simply showing a moment in the countryside without feeling he has to make it more significant by adding a story from Greek mythology or the Bible. Artists including Constable and Turner would be imitating his accepting natural eye almost 200 years later. They would also be thrilled by the subtle but omnipotent sunlight that Cuyp sees pervading everything here, from the gold-fringed clouds to the luminous river. Light was being understood in new ways in the 1600s by Galileo, Newton and other early scientists. Cuyp uses the very quietness of his rustic scene to let our minds focus on the ethereal magic of reflective water, set off by the brown, black and bronze masses of the cows. It is a lesson in weightless light and weighty flesh, a painting in which nothing happens and everything does.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Vidimages/AlamyNational Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in TouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

Sign up hereJane HoskynFri 28 Aug 2026 10.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAugust bank holiday is summer’s Boxing Day: the fun’s over, you’ve got no money left, and it’s probably raining. (As someone whose birthday falls at the fuzzy end of August, I can confirm that it always,alwaysrains.) And, just as on Boxing Day, the shops erupt in discount fever.Retailers aren’t cutting prices to soothe our post-holiday blues. They’ve got a whole season’s stock to shift, and need to free up space for autumn/winter pieces and (sorry) Christmas. There’s also a solid chance that they need to encourage online spending, because when the sky turns grey the high-street looks as inviting as wet socks.Here we round up the best bank holiday reductions on products our testers love, including autumn essentials such as dehumidifiers, duvets and women’s walking boots. But it really works, and it doesn’t take up much storage space because you use it with your existing clothes horse. Load your clothes horse with washing, cover it (cover included, or use a sheet), and use the Minky pod to blast hot air into it for speedy drying results. A fine choice if you're after a no-frills dryer that won't blow a hole in your bank account.BaBylissHydro-Fusionfrom£40£40 at Lookfantastic£40 at AmazonThe best value LED face maskSilk’nLED face mask 100from£88.73£99 at Lookfantastic£88.73 at AmazonView image in fullscreenSilk’n LED face mask 100, £99 (was £160)£99 at Lookfantastic£88.73 at AmazonYour favourite of all the products tested by Sarah Matthews for her guide to thebest LED face masks, this comfortable silicone mask lacks the premium features of its more expensive counterparts (no timer or near-infrared, for instance), but is a good choice for “light-touch anti-ageing, and for soothing, acne-busting blue light treatments.” Lookfantastic’s deal undercuts other retailers (including Amazon) by £46 or more at the time of writing, but others may follow, so we’ll keep you posted.Silk’nLED face mask 100from£88.73£99 at Lookfantastic£88.73 at AmazonThe cult Korean SPFBeauty of JoseonRelief sun rice + probiotics SPF50+, 100mlfrom£11.59£11.63 at Lookfantastic£11.59 at AmazonView image in fullscreenBeauty of Joseon relief sun rice + probiotics SPF50+, 100ml, £11.63 (was £15.50)£11.63 at Lookfantastic£11.59 at AmazonI bought this light, silky cream after reading Sarah Matthews’best face moisturisers, and it feels so gorgeous that I can’t get my head around it being SPF50+ – but SPF50+ it is. Just a shame I forked out just before its price dropped for the bank holiday sale. “It’s too lightweight to work as a stand-alone moisturiser for dry skin,” said Sarah, but “it can be layered over other moisturisers to provide lightweight protection”.Beauty of JoseonRelief sun rice + probiotics SPF50+, 100mlfrom£11.59£11.63 at Lookfantastic£11.59 at AmazonThe best body moisturiser for mature skinCharlotte TilburyMagic body cream£39.20£39.20 at Cult BeautyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianCharlotte Tilbury Magic body cream, £39.20 (was £49)£39.20 at Cult BeautyWith peptides that calm inflammation, support hydration and promote skin barrier health, this “gorgeous, lightweight formula” was a hit in Sarah Matthews'best body moisturisersroundup. People like me who have crepey, post-menopausal skin may find it particularly beneficial, thanks to the humectants and oils that add a smoothing emollient layer, but it’s a great all-rounder for soothing dryness after being outdoors.Charlotte TilburyMagic body cream£39.20£39.20 at Cult BeautyThe LED mask to cool tired eyesSharkCryoGlowfrom£254.99£254.99 at John Lewis£269.99 at SharkNinjaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianShark CryoGlow, £254.99 (was £299)£254.99 at John Lewis£269.99 at SharkNinjaShark’s venture into beauty products is a hit with our beauty writer Sarah Matthews. This is the only one of Sarah’s 12best LED face masksto offer built-in undereye cooling alongside targeted light therapy for anti-ageing and acne repair. “The blemish mode did a brilliant job of calming spots and redness with sustained use,” she wrote, while noting that because it’s made of plastic it’s “noticeably heavier than its silicone competitors”.SharkCryoGlowfrom£254.99£254.99 at John Lewis£269.99 at SharkNinjaThe best oscillating toothbrushOral-BiO3£65£65 at BootsView image in fullscreenOral-B iO3 toothbrush, £65 (avg £94)£65 at BootsThe best circular-motion brush in Alan Martin’s roundup of thebest electric toothbrushes, the Oral-B iO3 has an RRP of £160 and an average Amazon price of £93.95, so this is a genuinely decent deal from Boots. “While it has fewer modes than the higher-numbered iOs, it delivers the same dentist-fresh-feeling performance,” wrote Alan, whose only criticism was the priciness of the brand’s ownreplacement heads(£15 for two).Oral-BiO3£65£65 at BootsThe lash-lengthening Armani mascaraGiorgio ArmaniVertigo Lift mascara, 10mlfrom£21.75£21.75 at Lookfantastic£23.20 at John LewisView image in fullscreenGiorgio Armani Vertigo Lift mascara, 10ml, £21.75 (was £29)£21.75 at Lookfantastic£23.20 at John Lewis“Perks up the look of my tired eyes every time I use it,” wrote Sabine Wiesel in her guide to thebest mascaras, naming it “best mascara for length” and hailing its budge- and smudge-free formula that never left her with panda eyes. You have to work the formula quickly before it dries, she said, but the results are “eye-awakening”.Giorgio ArmaniVertigo Lift mascara, 10mlfrom£21.75£21.75 at Lookfantastic£23.20 at John LewisThe best hair dryer we’ve testedHershesonsThe Great hair dryerfrom£235£235 at Hershesons£235 at AmazonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianHershesons the Great hair dryer, £235 (was £295)£235 at Hershesons£235 at AmazonIt takes some confidence to call your hair dryer “the Great”, but Sarah Matthews reckons it’s justified, saying it “perfects the basics and irons out any common niggles”. A tenner off makes this purchase even more pleasurable.Je JoueHera Flex£89.10£89.10 at Je JoueView image in fullscreenDon’t buy anything until you’ve read the Filter, the Guardian’s home for truly independent product reviews and recommendations.
