title: From skipping ropes to Swiss balls: personal trainers on the best home gym kit | Fitness | The Guardian
description: Exercise mats that don’t slip, easy-grip kettlebells and floor sliders … fitness experts share their best buys for staying active at home
Author: Charlie Allenby
Headline: Exercise mats that don’t slip, easy-grip kettlebells and floor sliders … fitness experts share their best buys for staying active at home
Content: Home stretch: with the right equipment you can exercise effectively without always hitting the gym.Photograph: mixetto/GettyView image in fullscreenHome stretch: with the right equipment you can exercise effectively without always hitting the gym.Photograph: mixetto/GettyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterFitnessFrom skipping ropes to Swiss balls: personal trainers on the best home gym kitExercise mats that don’t slip, easy-grip kettlebells and floor sliders … fitness experts share their best buys for staying active at homeThe best massage guns – testedCharlie AllenbyFri 28 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou don’t have to spend a fortune on gym membership, or need loads of space, to get into shape. From the best basics to larger equipment for more complex workouts, here’s the home workout kit loved by fitness professionals, along with equipment I’ve personally put through its paces.The best home gym equipmentAffordable basicsView image in fullscreenFitBeast resistance bands, set of five£19.99 at AmazonThese are versatile, enabling you to do a lot of exercises for just £20. The lighter resistance bands (yellows and reds) don’t tend to last as long – the thinner the band, the more likely it is to break – but the purples and greens last for ages. They’re also easy to pack and keep things ticking over while you’re on holiday.Andy Griffiths,personal trainerView image in fullscreenLululemon 5mm exercise matFrom £88 at LululemonIt’s better to invest in one good mat than buy loads of poorly made cheap ones. The things to look out for are non-slip qualities and a good grip with the skin. I have a lot of experience with Lululemon’s 5mm mat: it has a nice thickness, good grip and rolls up neatly.Maiken S Wrighton,coach, Equinox KensingtonView image in fullscreenFreyja Fit dumbbells,4kgpair£18 at FreyjaDumbbells are great to have at home as they’re versatile – you can do entire workout plans with just one pair, and they’re not too big to store under the sofa. It’s hard to pick the right weight if you haven’t used weights before, but you should aim for 8-10 repetitions – like a biceps curl – with correct form. I would recommend that a beginner starts with a pair of 3kg or 4kg ones. The Freyja Fit dumbbells aren’t too expensive but are good quality.Charlie Launder, founder,Bumps& BurpeesView image in fullscreenGravityFitnessgym rings£37.95 at Gravity Fitness£37.95 at AmazonUnlike a fixed bar or machine, gym rings move independently, meaning your shoulders, scapulae, and core must stabilise through every rep, which dramatically improves control and resilience. They can be hung from a range of sturdy overhead anchor points, including pull-up bars if already in place, ceiling beams or joists.Or you can use them outdoors in the summer and just hang off a tree.Simon King,founderand performance coach,Cre8 FitnessView image in fullscreenWolverson Fitness kettlebellFrom £61.83 at Wolverson FitnessKettlebells are mostly used for swinging and dynamic movements, but you can get a lot of other exercises out of them. Also they take up little space. The Wolverson kettlebells are easy to grip, made of cast iron and will last a long time.Maiken S WrightonView image in fullscreenDecathlon door-mount pull-up bar, 70cm£19.99 at DecathlonPull-ups are an excellent, high-intensity exercise for building grip strength, which is a key, science-backed indicator of longevity, metabolic health and lower mortality risk. This one from Decathlon can be mounted on a door frame, takes up almost no room and is easy to set up.Simon KingView image in fullscreenEverlast skipping rope£4 at Studio£4 at Sports DirectSkipping improves cardiovascular fitness, coordination and foot stiffness, as well as strengthening the skeleton, with minimal space required. For a beginner who hasn’t skipped before, it’s best to start gradually, as the calves and achilles tendons usually fatigue quickly. Try two sessions a week, keeping the sessions at about 5–10 minutes in total. Begin with simple intervals, such as 30 seconds of skipping followed by 30–45 seconds of rest, for 8–10 rounds. Focus on relaxed wrists, small jumps, and staying light on the balls of the feet. As coordination and tolerance improve, you can gradually increase the duration of each round, and reduce rest periods.Simon KingView image in fullscreenPure2Improve Swiss ball£27.99 at Mountain WarehouseFrom £24.95 at AmazonA Swiss ball, or just an exercise ball, can serve a good purpose if you know how to use it. The unstable surface forces your body to work a bit extra. I sometimes use it for plank movements for an extra challenge – and it can add a level of difficulty to body weight movements, making the muscles work harder without the use of additional weights. Plus it doesn’t cost much, is easy to inflate, and when not in use can be deflated and packed away.Maiken S WrightonView image in fullscreenMirafit Core workout slidersskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£7.95 at MirafitFloor sliders are deceptively powerful. They’re brilliant for hamstring curls, moving planks, mountain climbers and sliding lunges, all of which demand strong core engagement and hip control. They’re also cheap, portable and versatile, and are an excellent way to challenge and stimulate the muscles using just your body weight.Simon KingMore advanced equipment to splash out onView image in fullscreenYoleo adjustable bench£79.99 at AmazonWhen you combine an adjustable bench with a set of dumbbells, you gain a wider variety of exercises, as well as more options that offer better control and a greater range of motion. For example, there aren’t many dumbbell-specific exercises that can target your chest, but add a bench and you can perform a classic chest press to achieve the optimal range of motion (with your elbows able to dip below the torso and stretch your chest, unlike when lying flat on the floor). The inexpensive Yoleo bench is great because you can fold it up and store underneath a bed.Andy GriffithsView image in fullscreenBlk Box squatstand£251.99 at Blk BoxDuring Covid, the first thing I bought myself was a squat stand. It’s great if you’re focusing primarily on strength and it gives you the versatility to do heavy compound movements without having to worry about lifting a bar on to your shoulders first. The two stands can be tucked away somewhere when not in use.Arby Keheli,performance coachView image in fullscreenMirafit 2in barbellFrom £69.95 for 4ft bar at MirafitView image in fullscreenMirafit bumper plates, set of twoFrom £49.95 at MirafitThe barbell is the most iconic tool in strength training for a reason. Every major compound lift involves one, and it can be loaded up with eye-watering amounts of weight. The plates determine how quietly, safely and precisely you can train. Bumper plates protect floors and joints and I would always recommend them for their versatility.Arby KeheliView image in fullscreenWahoo Kickr Core 2 turbo trainer£449.99 at Sigma Sports£499.99 at DecathlonA turbo trainer transforms your outdoor bicycle into a stationary one, letting you spin and slog away from the comfort of your own home. This model from Wahoo is easy to set up if you know your way around an Allen key. Installing it on your bike is as simple as removing the back wheel and slotting the remainder of your bike on to the trainer (if this sounds daunting, there’sa step-by-step tutorial online).I’ve used it for pretty much everything from two-hour rides to short, sharp Hiit sessions, and it’s a great way to do specific workouts that can be hard to emulate in real-life conditions. Compatible with most road, hybrid or mountain bikes, it also takes up less space when not in use than a traditional spin bike.Charlie AllenbyRead our guide to thebest exercise bikes for home workoutsView image in fullscreenMirafit Concept2 Rowerg rower£990 at Argos£990 at AmazonRowers allow precise intensity control and integration into circuits – where you use the rower in between strength exercises like push-ups or squats. It can also be used in some Hiit workouts, or you could do a lower-intensity aerobic workout with it. Also, the sliding seat means it can be used like a reformer too, so I’ll do hamstring curls on it and plank variations, using it like an abs wheel.Arby KeheliView image in fullscreenTherabody Theragun Mini 3.0 massage gun£169 at Therabody£169 at HealfAlthough a luxury item for a home gym setup, amassage guncan become an essential tool in your workout and recovery armoury if you’re regularly hitting the weights or cranking up the cardio. This travel-size option from Therabody might be the cheapest model in its range, but it still packs a vibrating punch, and is great for easing soreness and even activating muscles ahead of a session.Charlie AllenbyFor more fitness inspiration from the Filter:The best treadmills for your home – testedThe best fitness tech and gadgets, according to expertsThe fitness gear that made you fitterExplore more on these topicsFitnessThe FilterHealth & wellbeingTraining programmesHobbiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Legare’s mini bay leaf martini – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: Make a batch of this vodka- and vermouth-infused tipple to keep fresh in the fridge and sip over the weeks ahead
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Make a batch of this vodka- and vermouth-infused tipple to keep fresh in the fridge and sip over the weeks ahead
Content: Legare’s bay leaf martini.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenLegare’s bay leaf martini.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Legare’s mini bay leaf martini – recipeMake a batch of this vodka- and vermouth-infused tipple to keep fresh in the fridge and sip over the weeks aheadAlex Mammone and Matt BeardmoreFri 28 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe came up with this when we were looking to create some fun, bespoke but easy-to-serve cocktails that we could pre-batch for busy services but that still had an edge. Vodka is an especially good base for infusions because it’s so neutral, while martinis are having a real moment right now, so this ended up ticking all our boxes, being something that’s recognisable but fun, and also noticeably our own.Bay leaf martiniFor the infusion20g fresh bay leaves750ml vodkaFor the batch serve (to serve 12-13)400ml bay-infused vodka100ml dry white vermouth– we useMartini Bianco150ml chilled filtered waterUnpitted green olives, to garnishFirst make the infusion by steeping the bay leaves in the vodka for 10-plus days. Fine-strain, ideally through muslin, into a clean bottle, seal and store in the fridge for up to a month (or almost indefinitely in the freezer).To make the batch serve, pour the bay-infused vodka into a clean large jug, then add the dry vermouth and filtered water.To serve, pour 50ml of the mix into chilled mini-martini glasses and garnish each one with an olive.Alex Mammone, general manager, and Matt Beardmore, executive chef,LegareandLuna, London SE1Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for rum punch ice lollies | Food | The Guardian
description: These sweet and fruity frozen refreshers will get you in the carnival spirit.
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: These sweet and fruity frozen refreshers will get you in the carnival spirit.
Content: Totally tropical: Benjamina Ebuehi’s rum punch ice lollies.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenTotally tropical: Benjamina Ebuehi’s rum punch ice lollies.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotFoodBenjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for rum punch ice lolliesThese sweet and fruity frozen refreshers will get you in the carnival spiritBenjamina EbuehiFri 28 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s only right that on the weekend of the Notting Hill carnival, rum punch is your drink of choice. Whether or not you’re heading to west London to celebrate, these ice lollies will get you in the party mood. They’re fruity, sweet and balanced with plenty of fresh lime, and I always like to make sure there’s enough leftover rum mixture to pour over ice to drink while the lollies are setting.Rum punch ice lolliesThis is more a guide than a strict recipe; all punches have differing ratios, so adjust the lime or sweetness to taste. Just don’t be tempted to add more rum or they won’t freeze and you’ll end up with slush – although that’s not entirely a bad thing.Prep5 minCook10 minFreeze6 hr+Makes8-10500ml pineapple juice250ml orange juice100ml grenadine syrup100ml fresh lime juice70ml dark rum70ml coconut rum1 dashAngostura bitters(optional)Put the pineapple juice, orange juice and grenadine in a large jug or bowl. Stir in the lime juice followed by both rums and a dash of bitters, if using.Give it a taste and add a little more lime juice, if you’d like it sharper, or a splash more grenadine for something sweeter.Fill eight to 10 ice-lolly moulds with the punchmix,add sticks and freeze for at least six hours, and ideally overnight. (Keep any excess punch in the fridge and serve over ice.) Release the lollies and enjoy straight away.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotDessertFruitSpiritsCaribbean food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Lapped by the turquoise, crystal seas’: readers’ favourite unsung European islands | Europe holidays | The Guardian
description: From secluded coves in Ireland to an evening passeggiata on Italy’s Aeolian islands, readers share their discoveries
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From secluded coves in Ireland to an evening passeggiata on Italy’s Aeolian islands, readers share their discoveries
Content: Cres is the least populated of the four main islands of the Kvarner Gulf in Croatia.Photograph: ah_fotobox/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenCres is the least populated of the four main islands of the Kvarner Gulf in Croatia.Photograph: ah_fotobox/Getty Images/iStockphotoReaders' travel tipsEurope holidays‘Lapped by the turquoise, crystal seas’: readers’ favourite unsung European islandsFrom secluded coves in Ireland to an evening passeggiata on Italy’s Aeolian islands, readers share their discoveriesTell us about your most memorable food and drink discoveries in EuropeGuardian readersFri 28 Aug 2026 05.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWinning tip: a bird’s-eye view of wild CroatiaGiantgriffon vulturesglided parallel with my bus as it reached the highest point ofCres, the least populated of the four main islands in the Kvarner Gulf at the very north of the Croatian Adriatic. Covered in scrubby heath, olive groves and lavender, with small towns and villages on its coastline, its wildness is its appeal. Some, like Cres town, are unobtrusively set up for holidaymakers; in others local people just quietly get on with the life they’ve lived since the Venetians ruled here. All are lapped by the turquoise, crystal seas Croatia is known for.RhiannonProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Swimming off the Kerry coastView image in fullscreenThe view across Valentia island and beyond.Photograph: David Lyons/AlamyEarlier this summer, my sister and I took a road trip along the south-west coast of Ireland. Our favourite place wasValentia island, a small land mass slightly off the more touristy Ring of Kerry, accessed via a bridge to the south and a ferry to the north. Head for Glanleam beach, an idyllic secluded cove surrounded by rich vegetation, which looks out on to the mountains of the Dingle peninsula, and take a dip in the Atlantic. Like us, you’ll probably want to return the next day and do it again.EllieGoing back in time in GreeceView image in fullscreenApella beach on Karpathos is one of Europe’s finest.Photograph: Straga/Getty ImagesBetween Rhodes and Crete,Karpathosslips under the radar: no package crowds, just goats, wildflowers and twisting mountain roads that cling to the cliffs. The remote village of Olympos feels frozen in time, its older women still in traditional dress, drying pasta-likemakarounesin the open air. Apella and Achata rank among Europe’s finest beaches, with turquoise water backed by unspoilt pine-covered mountainsides.Hotel Lefkoramaprovides a spectacular valley-to-sea view and a breakfast feast of fruit, jams, yoghurt and freshly baked bread. End the day at a family-run taverna, sipping local wine as the sun drops into the Aegean.Stephen and LucaA car-free outpost off BrittanyView image in fullscreenThe waterfront of the car-free Île de Sein.Photograph: Crystite RF/AlamyAfter an exciting 60-minuteferry crossingfrom Audierne, which includes the Pointe du Raz where currents off the Breton coast create weird wave formations that carry bemused seabirds in opposite directions even when they are only feet apart, you arrive on theÎle de Sein, an island mostly only 1.5 metres above sea level. There are no cars and you can walk the entire island in a couple of hours. We loved the cowrie shell-rich beaches and plants forming carpets over pebbles. There is plenty of history here, an impressive lighthouse and a handful of stylish cafes (we had crepes inChez Bruno). We felt very jealous of those people who had bags to stay the night.MilesCastles and cocktails in ItalyView image in fullscreenLipari is one of the volcanic Aeolian islands.Photograph: AP Photo/AlamyJauntily perched off the north-east coast of Sicily,Liparihas an energy to it that perhaps comes from its volcanic origins. It is the largest of the Aeolian islands and great fun to visit. Lipari town hugs the water and is dominated, Game of Thrones-style, by a brooding castle. The cathedral and thearchaeological museum, with its ancient statues and artefacts, are worth checking out. My family and I enjoyed taking part in the evening passeggiata, sipping island-themed cocktails – the worryingly named Volcano, for example – or eating delicious gelatos. The Corso Vittorio Emanuele II is lined with restaurants down to the picturesque port of Marina Corta. We swam on the nearby beaches of Papesca and Porticello – the rocky white seabed and clear waters create a magical shimmering sea that enticed us in hour after hour.AprilLanzarote’s quiet, tiny neighbourView image in fullscreenLa Graciosa pictured from Mirador del Rio on Lanzarote.Photograph: Rusm/Getty ImagesMost visitors toLa Graciosaarrive from Lanzarote for the day, but if you stay overnight it becomes wonderfully peaceful. This tiny volcanic island feels different from the rest of the Canaries, with sandy, largely traffic-free streets in Caleta de Sebo. Swim or snorkel in the clear turquoise water, walk or cycle among the volcanic peaks and enjoy fresh fish in the village. You can take a boat around the coast or simply find a quiet stretch of sand. By evening, the island feels a world away from the busy resorts of Lanzarote – exactly what an island escape should be.Susannaskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPuffin-watching in PembrokeshireView image in fullscreenPuffins off the coast of Skomer.Photograph: WL Davies/Getty ImagesMy absolute favourite island trip isseeing the puffinsoff the coast ofSkomerin Pembrokeshire. Arriving at an unassuming pier (and getting on a somewhat unassuming boat), we were slightly unsure about whether the planned family outing would succeed or flop. But, in fact, Dr Samuel Johnson’s quote should be amended: a man who is tired of watching puffins is tired of life. A few hours spent on the Welsh coastline watching potentially the world’s most joyful bird can cure many an ill.RosieMedieval city walls and fossils in the BalticView image in fullscreenVisby is a preserved medieval town on the island of Gotland.Photograph: Makasana Photo/AlamyGotlandis a magical island in the Baltic. Get there via a three-hour ferry from Nynäshamn, south of Stockholm. The main town, Visby, is a perfectly preserved medieval dream complete with wraparound city walls, cobbled streets and few cars. Take the bus and ferry to theisland of Fårö, hire bikes and cycle to the famous rauks – massive limestone columns by the sea. It’s also a fantastic place for fossil hunting as the whole island was once a coral reef.GaynorWalk around meteorite craters in EstoniaView image in fullscreenA crater lake in Kaali.Photograph: Tomasz Wozniak/AlamyOn the Estonian island ofSaaremaa, you can walk around meteorite craters. The nine Kaali craters were formed when meteorites crashed into the island about 3,500 years ago. The area later became a cult site, with archaeological finds suggesting animal offerings, and has been linked to old Finnic tales of the sun falling from the sky. The tiny Meteoritics Museum costs just €2 (£1.70). Cosmic drama on a very Estonian budget.ElinaView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsEurope holidaysReaders' travel tipsBeach holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I brought a bear back to life  | Life and style | The Guardian
description: I was in India, performing dentistry on my first animal patient, and it was supposed to be a straightforward operation
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I was in India, performing dentistry on my first animal patient, and it was supposed to be a straightforward operation
Content: ’When he woke up, I felt triumphant’: Paul Cassar, photographed in Chichester.Photograph: Julian Anderson/The GuardianView image in fullscreen’When he woke up, I felt triumphant’: Paul Cassar, photographed in Chichester.Photograph: Julian Anderson/The GuardianExperienceLife and styleExperience: I brought a bear back to lifeI was in India, performing dentistry on my first animal patient, and it was supposed to be a straightforward operationPaul CassarFri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been a dentist for 40 years. I spend most of my time treating patients at my surgery in Chichester, West Sussex. When I studied to become a dentist in the 1980s, I didn’t think I’d be getting my hands anywhere near the teeth of any exotic animals.Twenty years later, in 2000, that changed. A patient of mine, Alan Knight, the CEO of International Animal Rescue (IAR), showed me photographs of the inside of a bear’s mouth. The bear was called Jojo and his teeth had been broken off by poachers. Some of the teeth were too rotten to be saved – if left untreated, Jojo would become more prone to infection and abscesses.Alan told me Jojo wasn’t the only bear in need of dental care. Poachers would kill mother bears and grab their cubs. When the cubs got older, the poachers would break their teeth using a hammer to make them look more docile. I knew I had to help.That was how I ended up in India ready to perform dentistry on my first animal patient – a 14-year-old sloth bear named Anthony. He had a massive benign tumour on his gum that was preventing him from eating. He was 180kg, which is especially big for an Indian sloth bear, and already anaesthetised when I first saw him.It was supposed to be a relatively straightforward operation – remove the tumour and any bad teeth. I was working alongside a veterinary dentist, Lisa Milella. We’d prepared for over a year – I felt ready.I started by removing the grapefruit-sized tumour from Anthony’s gum, then the tooth that had been underneath the lump. More than three hours into surgery, I was feeling more at ease – perhaps treating a bear wouldn’t be so different from treating a human.double quotation markI’ve operated on 200 bears, half a dozen tigers, a couple of lions, hyenas and gorillasView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Julian Anderson/The GuardianI was about to take out some of Anthony’s other broken teeth when his pulse rate plummeted. Within minutes, the local vets monitoring him could no longer detect a pulse. His breathing stopped and he was pronounced dead.The anaesthesia had killed him. In those days, the local anaesthetists only had experience injecting anaesthesia, and had used darts to put Anthony to sleep. We did not know how long it would last, so it had to keep being topped up. If an animal is unwell, administering too much anaesthetic can be lethal.The local vets walked out of the operating room, saying: “You’ve killed our bear.” I couldn’t process what had happened. I’m a dentist – I had never dealt with a patient dying mid-surgery before.Lisa brought me back to reality. She said: “We’re going to get him back. Get the emergency drug box! Get the crash kit!”I started performing CPR on Anthony. We gave him adrenaline, and I pounded his chest. It was an excruciatingly long three minutes before he was able to breathe by himself again. He was still under anaesthetic. We knew he was alive, but not if he was well. We waited. When he woke up, I felt triumphant. He went on to live for another 10 years.Since then, I’ve continued working with the IAR, performing dentistry on 200 bears, half a dozen tigers, a couple of lions, a few hyenas, and a handful of gorillas and orangutans. I’ve even been nicknamed “Bear Drills”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExperience: a bear moved into my houseRead moreOperating on animals presents a unique set of challenges. For one, their teeth are much larger than a human’s – and with big teeth come big tools. A file used for root‑canal treatments on people is about a quarter of the size of those used on tigers.Over the years, I’ve seen all sorts – a 300kg tiger with multiple facial abscesses, a bear we fitted with a gold crown and nicknamed Bling Bear, and a lion having a ketamine-induced fit during an extraction. I very nearly had to do some crowns on beluga whales that were used for submarine warfare by the Soviet Union, but they escaped from their holding pen before I flew out.Anthony’s resuscitation was a memorable introduction to animal dentistry. I travel to IAR sanctuaries to treat rescued animals every year. It’s more stressful than my day job, but it’s incredibly fulfilling. The local teams at every sanctuary monitor the animals after I leave, and always report positive changes in their behaviour. They have suffered so much, and I feel privileged to play a part in bringing them relief.As told to Emmy RaynorDo you have an experience to share? title: How have my plants fared this summer? Some better than others | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: It’ll soon be autumn, but the record-breaking weather has taken its toll on my vegetables
Author: Claire Ratinon
Headline: It’ll soon be autumn, but the record-breaking weather has taken its toll on my vegetables
Content: Grapes were one of the crops that thrived in the heat.Photograph: RA Kearton/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGrapes were one of the crops that thrived in the heat.Photograph: RA Kearton/Getty ImagesGardening adviceHow have my plants fared this summer? Some better than othersIt’ll soon be autumn, but the record-breaking weather has taken its toll on my vegetablesClaire RatinonFri 28 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 06.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve grown plants in heatwaves before, but this year has been different. Back-to-back heatwaves feel far more intense than the shorter ones I’m used to. Records for heat and dryness were broken in August, and my veg patch has dealt with it in myriad ways.You might think more sun equals more growth, but that isn’t necessarily the case. When under heat stress, plants close their stomata – the pores on the underside of their leaves – hindering the movement of water and exchange of gases needed for photosynthesis. This can result in a check on growth that I’ve seen in several of my plants, some of which dropped their flowers before they could start bearing fruit.Stressed-out plants can be vulnerable to pest attacks, which might explain why so many leaf miners have found my chard this year. Even some established perennials have struggled in the heat. The golden raspberries, which are in their second season, had canes that were growing well then suddenly turned brown and died.double quotation markSpecial mention goes to the cucumbers in the greenhouse and the grapevine by my back doorI also became reacquainted with the importance of gauging a plant’s wilting point when I planted out some lettuces that were desperate for more space on a 32C day – silly me! I did it when the patch was shaded by a willow tree, but when I checked on them at the end of the day, they had flopped over and started to wither. Regular glugs of targeted watering miraculously saved them from the brink – otherwise known as the “permanent wilting point” – and they’re doing well enough. But if another bout of hot weather comes, I expect they’ll bolt like the last round of lettuces did.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFancy fresh cabbages next spring? Then it’s time to get sowingRead morePlants can suffer from damage and discoloration when exposed to high levels of UV. The golden marjoram, self-seeded nasturtiums and newly planted-out beans all had leaves with signs of sun scald, despite being warmth-loving plants. Scalding can affect a plant’s growth, but if the damage is confined to a few leaves, which are removed, the plant can recover and grow normally.I’ve long struggled with compaction in my very clay-heavy soil, and despite mulching regularly, the heat caused the ground to dry out more than usual, becoming less penetrable by my crop’s roots. I’m blaming the stunted growth of my courgettes on this sorry situation as the bed they’re in seems unusually solid. Now my water butts are empty, I’m working on accepting that some of my crops won’t be offering much of a harvest this year.Yet some of my plants are actually doing really well. Special mention goes to the cucumbers in the greenhouse and the grapevine that grows by my back door. Most years, it gets mould or mildew before the grapes swell but I’m hopeful this year will see its first real harvest.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm? | Meta | The Guardian
description: Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands
Content: Mark Zuckerberg was not forced to testify in the US lawsuit, which Meta settled on Wednesday.Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg was not forced to testify in the US lawsuit, which Meta settled on Wednesday.Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty ImagesMetaWhat could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the NetherlandsAisha DownFri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supportingMeareg’s lawsuit against the companyin Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly askedFacebookto remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media companyagreed to pay $18bnand to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement,Metahas said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the stateshad sought– $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.View image in fullscreenMeta’s headquarters in Menlo Park, California.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesFor the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.It sees teenage girls watch diet content andshows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content andshows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to haveamplified contentthat promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. Itcontributedto the election victory of Donald Trump.Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in eastAfricadid almost nothing to prevent this.In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make somechangesto this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily havepersonalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.Arturo Béjar, anex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenProtests in Malaysia in 2012 against the persecution of Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar. Meta was alleged in a lawsuit to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya.Photograph: Mohd Rasfan/AFP via Getty ImagesIn Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands foralleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”The European Commission released a charge sheet against Metathis summersaying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.Earlier this year itmanagedtododgea class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed backforcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, ithas saidit employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”Explore more on these topicsMetaFacebookSocial mediaEthiopiaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: How the Iran war unfolded: every attack and oil price change – visualised | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: From the first US and Israeli strikes six months ago to the battle for Hormuz, this timeline plots how Trump’s war on Iran quickly became a regional conflict with global economic consequences
Author: Ana Lucía González Paz
Headline: From the first US and Israeli strikes six months ago to the battle for Hormuz, this timeline plots how Trump’s war on Iran quickly became a regional conflict with global economic consequences
Content: US-Israel war on IranHow the Iran war unfolded: every attack and oil price change – visualisedFrom the first US and Israeli strikes six months ago to the battle for Hormuz, this timeline plots how Trump’s war on Iran quickly became a regional conflict with global economic consequencesAna Lucía González Paz,Garry Blight,Prina ShahandAshley KirkFri 28 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTShareOn 28 February 2026, the US andIsraelbegan large-scale strikes on Iran. Tehran responded by attacking Israeli and US allies across the Gulf.Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, was killed on the first day of strikes, and the strait of Hormuz – a crucial waterway for transporting oil – was effectively closed soon after. The conflict quickly became a regional war with global economic consequences.Since then, bursts of fighting have repeatedly given way to ceasefires and negotiations. Each diplomatic opening has been followed by fresh threats, disputed agreements and renewed attacks.The strait of Hormuz remains at the centre of the conflict. In normal times, more than 100 vessels passed through the narrow waterway each day, carrying about a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil trade. Any closure or attack on shipping can disrupt global supplies and send prices higher.This timeline traces six months of strikes, public threats and failed diplomacy - and shows how the war has disrupted shipping and driven swings in the oil price.MethodologyThe Guardian looked at about 4,000 Truth Social posts, 7,700 IRGC Telegram messages and a selection of X posts from 28 February 2026. Some social media posts have been edited for conciseness. All times included in the piece are GMT.Oil price data is sourced fromLSEG. Data on the amount of shipping traffic through the strait of Hormuz is sourced fromLloyd’s List Intelligence, and only includes traceable transits of cargo-carrying vessels over 10,000 deadweight tonnage. Dark transits included in figures after 28 Feb.Airstrikes data is sourced fromAcled, and includes data on explosions or remote violence events, including air/drone strikes and shelling, artillery and missile attacks, by the Iranian, US and Israel military forces. It excludes interceptions.Image credits:Donald Trump: EPA/Trump Vance transition teamUS CENTCOM: APAbbas Araghchi: APEsmail Baqaei: Getty/AnadoluMasoud Pezeshkian: APMohammad Bagher Ghalibaf: Getty/NurPhotoIran flag: Alamy

title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid | Art theft | The Guardian
description: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours
Content: The 200-carat platinum and diamond-encrusted necklace.Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenThe 200-carat platinum and diamond-encrusted necklace.Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/GettyArt theftEgyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raidPolice hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hoursDeborah Colein BerlinFri 28 Aug 2026 10.46 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.Authorities in the capital releasedpictures of the suspectscaptured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.View image in fullscreenA visitor takes a picture of the platinum and diamond necklace, which dates from 1939 and belonged to Queen Nazli of Egypt, at the Pierres Précieuses exhibition in Paris.Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/GettyIn an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince,Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold bySotheby’s in New Yorkin 2015 for $4.3m.View image in fullscreenQueen Nazli of Egypt, right, wearing the necklace at Princess Fawzia’s wedding in Cairo, 1939. Also pictured, from left, are: Queen Farida, King Farouk, Fawzia and Crown Prince Mohammad.Photograph: Bettmann ArchiveThe MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thievesbroke into the Louvre museum in Parisduring the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 200-carat platinum necklace.In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided theTreasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance masterAntonello da Messinawere stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.Two days earlier, Italian police said they hadrecovered three paintingsby the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.Areport by Europolthis month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.Explore more on these topicsArt theftExhibitionsMuseumsArtEgyptAustriaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands foralleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”The European Commission released a charge sheet against Metathis summersaying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.Earlier this year itmanagedtododgea class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed backforcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, ithas saidit employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”Explore more on these topicsMetaFacebookSocial mediaEthiopiaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump announces new US oil agreement with Venezuela | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves
Content: A Venezuelan flag in front of an oil tanker in Maracaibo, Venezuela, on 27 July.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Venezuelan flag in front of an oil tanker in Maracaibo, Venezuela, on 27 July.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump announces new US oil agreement with VenezuelaUS president says US will have ‘majority’ control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reservesGuardian staff and agenciesFri 28 Aug 2026 19.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump announced Friday a new US oil agreement with Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez, saying the US will have “majority” control of 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves.The terms of the agreement remain to be seen, but the US president said on his social-media platform that it had been brokered “through a partnership with ⁠private business” by his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, and defense secretary, Pete Hegseth.The administration,Trump wrote, has “secured majority U.S. control of more ​than 65 BILLION ‌BARRELS of proven Oil ‌Reserves in Venezuela, at no cost to the ‌American Taxpayer”.Trump said the agreement would more than double American oil reserves.“This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people,” Rubiowroteon social media.Trump’s announcement provided few details on the structure of the agreement, the fields or companies involved, or how the US would exercise majority control over the ⁠reserves.Venezuela has an estimated 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves, the world’s largest.Since the US captured and removed former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro from power in January, Washington has been trying ‌to secure a stable flow of Venezuelan crude oil for US refineries while promoting American investment ​into the Opec country’s deteriorated energy industry, which produces 1.25m barrels per day of crude.Trump is under pressure before November’s midterm elections over rising gasoline prices, ​which could ​be eased through ​cheaper oil supplies and expanded output.The US ​also has ‌been looking ​for solutions ​to replenish its strategic petroleum reserve, the oil stockpile, including the possibility of crude swaps with US producers.Earlier this week,the Wall Street Journal reportedthat the Trump administration was “in advanced talks withVenezuelafor the U.S. to take a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields that house nearly one-third of the country’s massive energy reserves”. Axios also reported on the negotiations, quoting a US official who claimed the deal would be “massive”.The discussion was reportedly over a US stake in Venezuela’s most promising oil-and-gasfields, with some 90bn barrels of proven reserves.The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,”saidone well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticizing the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States.”The announcement comes as Chevron and other US energy companies are expected to sign a deal next week investing billions in Venezuela’s oil fields,according to the Journal.Tom Phillips and Reuters contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpVenezuelaOilTrump administrationUS politicsAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Venezuelan opposition up in arms over reports US wants big stake in oil and gas | Venezuela | The Guardian
description: Critics call move to gain long-term access to country’s massive energy reserves ‘predatory’ and ‘unconstitutional’
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Critics call move to gain long-term access to country’s massive energy reserves ‘predatory’ and ‘unconstitutional’
Content: An oil pumpjack on Lake Maracaibo in Cabimas, Zulia state, Venezuela.Photograph: Gaby Oraa/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn oil pumpjack on Lake Maracaibo in Cabimas, Zulia state, Venezuela.Photograph: Gaby Oraa/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesVenezuelaVenezuelan opposition up in arms over reports US wants big stake in oil and gasCritics call move to gain long-term access to country’s massive energy reserves  ‘predatory’ and ‘unconstitutional’Tom PhillipsLatin America correspondentFri 28 Aug 2026 13.41 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s massive energy reserves have sparked an outcry, with critics describing the move as “predatory” and a “rapacious” land grab.Several media outlets this week reported that theTrump administration– which abducted Venezuela’s authoritarian president, Nicolás Maduro, in January and has steered the South American country ever since – hopes to secure long-term access to its oil and gasfields.Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn.On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal saidTrump officials were in “advanced talks”with Venezuelan officials to take “a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields” containing 90bn barrels, nearly a third of Venezuela’s energy reserves.“This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the US and Venezuelan governments,” a source told Reuters, which said the fields being negotiated were in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions.Axios claimed the dealwould be “a legacy-defining moment for President Trump”, with one unnamed official telling the US outlet: “Calling this deal huge would be an understatement … It is massive.”Bloomberg, citing sources familiar with the negotiations, said one deal under discussion was a 100-year lease on several oilfields.The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’sfailure to bring about genuine political changeafter capturing Maduro.“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticising the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States,” they added.Since January’s special forces raid on Caracas, Venezuela has been led by an interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president and minister of petroleum. Other key members of Maduro’s regime have also retained positions of power, including the interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, who has been collaborating with Trump officials –despite having a $25m (£18m) US bounty on his headfor alleged drug trafficking. Meanwhile, the exiled opposition leader, María Corina Machado, whose movement is believed to have won the 2024 presidential elections, has been sidelined.Ricardo Hausmann, an exiled former minister and opposition supporter, wrote on X: “An illegitimate interim government with an illegitimate hydrocarbons law has no legitimacy to strike this unconstitutional deal. It will be a fiasco for all involved.”The economist Francisco Rodríguezurged Venezuela’s national assemblyto reject what he called a “predatory deal”. “Handing over Venezuela’s oil wealth to the US contravenes the constitution and is not in the interest of the Venezuelan people – much more when it is done at gunpoint,” Rodríguez said.Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent journalist and government critic,sarcastically calledthe “surrender” of Venezuela’s natural riches “the deal of the century”.Gregory Brew, an energy historian and Eurasia Group analyst, anticipated “quite a lot of suspicion and rejection of any deal that would hand the United States government effective control over Venezuelan resources”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBrew said the reported deal reminded him of how BP, then the Anglo-PersianOilCompany, controlled the oil resources of Iraq and Iran at the start of the last century.“Anglo-Persian was given a concession by the shah of Iran in 1901 … in exchange for what was essentially a bribe to the Persian government, and it gave the company sweeping rights. The company was essentially in total control of any oil it found and would be able to retain virtually all the profits of any other oil it found and exploited and exported,” Brew said.“From Trump’s point of view, the control over oil is something of an end in and of itself,. But if you do try to rationalise it, I think US dominance over Venezuelan oil reserves allows the US to regard Venezuelan reserves as its own reserves: a source of oil from which the United States can draw and that nobody else has access to. I think that’s how the administration is conceiving of this – excluding China, excluding Russia, but I think also excluding other potential customers for Venezuelan oil,” he said. “It sounds colonial, because it is.”Venezuela’s post-Maduro conversion into what many call a US protectorate is the most dramatic play in Trump’s push to reassert Washington’s influence over Latin America as part of the so-called “Donroe Doctrine”.That policy is a 21st-century adaptation of the 19th-century Monroe doctrine by which President James Monroe sought to keep European powers out of theAmericas. Trump’s version is about countering China’s growing footprint in the region and imposing US will through economic and military pressure.Maduro’s downfall has brought some change to Venezuela, with hundreds of political prisoners freed under Rodríguez and talks about reforming the regime-controlled supreme court taking place.But no date has been set for a fresh presidential election and Machado has been unable to return from exile. “Delcy’s been doing a fantastic job,” Trump told reporters last month, claiming Venezuela was “not really ready” for a vote.Explore more on these topicsVenezuelaAmericasOilGasCommoditiesTrump administrationUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Tropical Storm Dolly downgraded to ‘open tropical wave’ as it heads to Caribbean | Caribbean | The Guardian
description: Remnants from tropical storm could cause heavy rainfall on Leeward Islands and affect Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and Hispaniola
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Remnants from tropical storm could cause heavy rainfall on Leeward Islands and affect Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and Hispaniola
Content: Tropical Storm Dolly over the Atlantic Ocean on Thursday.Photograph: Noaa/APView image in fullscreenTropical Storm Dolly over the Atlantic Ocean on Thursday.Photograph: Noaa/APCaribbeanTropical Storm Dolly downgraded to ‘open tropical wave’ as it heads to CaribbeanRemnants from tropical storm could cause heavy rainfall on Leeward Islands and affect Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and HispaniolaAnna BettsFri 28 Aug 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRemnants of Tropical Storm Dolly, which has been downgraded to an “open tropical wave”, were moving still across the Atlantic Ocean toward the Leeward Islands, and could bring heavy rainfall to parts of the Caribbean this weekend, the US National Hurricane Center (NHC)saidon Friday..Dolly, which formed on Thursday, had maximum sustained winds of near 40mph (65km/h) with higher gusts on Friday morning. Later on Friday, forecasterssaidthat Dolly was no longer a Tropical Storm, and had “become an open tropical wave”.In an update on Friday headlined “Remnants of Dolly”, the NHC warned that “heavy rains from the remnants of Dolly could affect the Leeward Islands late on Saturday into Sunday with possible impacts in theVirgin Islands, Puerto Rico, and Hispaniola Sunday and Monday.”“This heavy rain may produce flash flooding within areas of higher terrain of the Leeward Islands,” it added.No coastal watches or warnings are currently in effect. The Leeward Islands stretch from the Virgin Islands to Guadeloupe, with the Caribbean Sea on their west side and the Atlantic to the east, while Hispaniola is the island where Haiti and theDominican Republicare located, east of Puerto Rico.The storm’s name has drawn unusual attention online, with observers noting that it formed just days afterthe deathof the country music starDolly Partonin the US earlier this week and wondering whether it was named in her honor. However, the name is a coincidence and has no connection to Parton’s death. Tropical storms are assigned names from predetermined alphabetical lists managed by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).For the names of storms in the Atlantic,there is a list of male and female nameswhich are used on a six-year rotation. Dolly is the fourth name on the 2026 list, making it thefourth namedstorm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.Earlier this summer,Tropical Storm Arthurbrought heavy rainfall to the US Gulf coast, whileTropical Storm Berthamade landfall in Louisiana, bringing rain and strong winds. Earlier this month, another storm, Tropical Storm Cristobal, formed butquickly dissipated.The Atlantic hurricane seasonrunsfrom 1 June to 30 November. So far, the season has been quieter than usual,with experts pointing toseveral factors.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Tropical storm activity in the Atlantic basin is expected to be tempered byEl Niñoconditions, which first emerged in the equatorial Pacific in June,” according to forecasters with theNational Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. “El Niño increases wind shear, which tends to prevent tropical storms from forming or from getting stronger once formed.”Explore more on these topicsCaribbeanExtreme weatherPuerto RicoVirgin IslandsDominican Republic (Weather)Dominican Republic (World news)HaitinewsShareReuse this content

title: Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes city | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races
Author: Tom Perkins
Headline: Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races
Content: View of the Gordie Howe international bridge during the opening ceremony in Windsor, Ontario, on 24 July 2026.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenView of the Gordie Howe international bridge during the opening ceremony in Windsor, Ontario, on 24 July 2026.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsDetroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes cityUnpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan racesTom Perkinsin DetroitFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery day$1bnworth of goods crosses the river dividing Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry.News this week of Donald Trump’sescalating trade spatwith Canada has everyone worried. Political and economic leaders and observers labeled the move an act of “hubris” , blamed Trump’s “ego”, and called the escalation “insanity”.“We don’t needCanada, they need us,” Trump declared.But many are hoping that Trump’s imposition of50% tariffson Canadian goods this week will not last long, with the upcoming midterm elections as a pivotal reason the plan may be scrapped.Control of the US Congress hangs in the balance and will almost certainly be decided by several close Michigan races. It also comes just two months after polling highlighted Michiganders’ fatigue with and opposition to the president’s unprecedented tariff program.By a 63%-31% margin, residents here oppose tariffs on Canadian goods, according to a June Epic-MRA poll, including 35% of Republicans. Meanwhile, nearly 75% of Michiganders said the tariffs are fueling high prices.Trump doubling down on an unpopular policy deep into election season is viewed by many observers as a gift to Democrats, and there is a real possibility that it contributes to a midterm loss for the Republicans. Meanwhile, there seems to be little upside for Trump.“I don’t understand what Trump is thinking,” the Epic-MRA pollster Bernie Porn said.Regardless, Michiganders have already suffered disproportionately as theypay on averageover $3,200 annually for tariffs, or about 142% more than the rest of the country, because of the state’s shared border with Canada.The Canadian economy would also take a major hit if the tariffs are imposed, said Patrick Anderson, a Michigan-based economist with the Anderson Economic Group.View image in fullscreenThe Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters at Renaissance high school in Detroit, Michigan, on 7 August.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images“Both will suffer – there are no two ways about it,” Anderson added.This critical upper midwest swing state has picked the presidential winner in five consecutive elections, going from Barack Obama to Trump to Joe Biden and back to Trump. Democrats’ chances to retake the Senate rest heavily on the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed beating Trump ally Mike Rogers in the 3 November general election race. Rogers has supported the tariffs, but so far has been silent on the latest escalation.The tariffs and theunpopular Iran war’scontribution to inflation represent a “double hit” for Republicans, Porn said, and Trump is handing ammo to a particularly adept candidate in El-Sayed. He has energized people with his anti-establishment, populist political vision, and a no-holds-barred delivery.“El-Sayed has proven to be very, very articulate on a number of issues,” Porn added. “I think that he is going to try and just throw bombs at Rogers [in an upcoming debate] because Rogers supports these tariffs and trade war. Trump’s low popularity is an anchor around Rogers’ neck.”In a statement, El-Sayed hammered Trump and Rogers, saying that the president “cares more about his ego and saber-rattling than addressing the affordability crisis.“Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he’s asking Michigan families to pay the price,” El-Sayed said. “Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long, and Mike Rogers won’t do anything but rubber-stamp them.”El-Sayed said he would push for “real, fair trade deals that create good-paying jobs”. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment.The United Auto Workers (UAW), which has 350,000 members in Michigan and is often a political kingmaker here, has supported some of Trump’s targeted tariffs, but said in a statement it “rejects” the latest escalation.“If we’re going to increase tariffs anywhere, it should be on countries where automakers continue to offshore jobs because they can pay workers $3 an hour, force them to work in unsafe conditions, and crack down on independent unions,” the UAW president, Shawn Fain, said. Canada has strong unions, and the UAW supports those.“Tariffs work, but only if they are deployed intentionally to protect workers and grow our manufacturing communities, and it’s time to permanently end offshoring and the race to the bottom,” Fain added.Mexico and Canada currently face 25% US tariffs on autos, though partial exemptions in the nations’ free trade agreement make the effective rate much lower, overall. Andersonestimatedtariffs cost US auto companies about $12.5bn in 2025.The Canadian government has announced it will impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of goods starting 8 September. The actions leading to the latest blow-up have been “rife with miscalculations, overreactions, and hubris”, Anderson said. He read through the list of goods on which tariffs would be imposed – feathers, sweaters, girls’ dresses, lobster.“This is not a trade war. This is an annoyance list. Chest pounding,” Anderson said.The North American auto industry over the last 60 years has integrated across the continent, and auto parts cross a border an average of six times before they land in a final product. That means there would be shared pain, Anderson said, and it would reverberate across the upper midwest, where bigger manufacturing cities are typically powered by industries that are often reliant on international trade.But the Canadian economy is smaller, and Ontario’s economy is so concentrated that it would hit harder north of the border, Anderson added. Ultimately, the real threat is that “these two countries go pell-mell into it” and impose tariffs on oil, energy and commodities that hit harder than lobster.The dialogue has devolved into the usual petty antagonism that is a hallmark of Trump’s beefs. Trumpsigned an executive orderto rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, and Vice-President JD Vance referred to Canada as the 51st state.“Let me say with great understatement that this is not helpful,” Anderson added.View image in fullscreenThe American and Canadian flags fly at the midway point on the Gordie Howe International Bridge, that connects Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, Michigan.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockIndeed, the Windsor mayor, Drew Dilkens, took exception to that particular comment. In an interview, he expressed deep frustration over Trump’s moves, and labeled justifications Trump has used for issuing tariffs, including framing them as a response to illegal immigration on the northern border, “nonsense”.The latest escalation “is an aggressive move, one that could not be ignored by our country”, added Dilkens, who leads the city of 230,000 people. “It’s just offensive that he launches these attacks at Canada, who is your largest trading partner, your closest ally, and your neighbor.”The chaos has cooled investment in Windsor, and prices remain high on both sides of the border. He pointed out how much more US consumers are paying not just for automobiles, but for beef, which in part stems from tariffs on Canadian beef.“What is really crazy is that he is willing to throw his own citizens under the bus to pursue his tariff agenda,” Dilkens said. “They have Donald Trump to thank.”Highlighting the tension among the president and some in his base, the Michigan chamber of commerce, a trade organization that lobbies on behalf of the state’s largest corporations, normally vocally supports the president on economic issues. It has not made a public statement, and did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.However, the typically pro-TrumpDetroitchamber of commerce did not mince words.“Escalating tensions and tariffs will only cause economic pain on both sides of the border, especially in Michigan and the binational Detroit-Windsor region,” the chamber said in a press statement, adding that global competitors like China benefited most.“Our economies are intertwined, interconnected, and stronger together; the sooner normalcy is restored the better.”This article was amended on 28 August 2026. An earlier version gave incorrect commencement dates for the US and Canadian tariffs.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsDetroitUS politicsCanadaUS economyEconomicsAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red Cross | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Federation says it fears death toll of nearly 600 will continue to rise as rescuers reach cut-off areas
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Federation says it fears death toll of nearly 600 will continue to rise as rescuers reach cut-off areas
Content: Soldiers help a family disembark from a helicopter after they are rescued from an area affected by flash flooding in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/APView image in fullscreenSoldiers help a family disembark from a helicopter after they are rescued from an area affected by flash flooding in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/APNepal-Tibet flood disasterAt least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red CrossFederation says it fears death toll of nearly 600 will continue to rise as rescuers reach cut-off areasNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesVisual guide: how the deadly flooding unfoldedTell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?Hannah Ellis-Petersenin Bidur,Sam Jonesand agenciesFri 28 Aug 2026 11.55 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, which have killed nearly 600 people, left another 1,900 missing, and triggered a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.“The trauma of this event is enormous,” David Fisher, the IFRC head of delegation forNepal, said on Friday.“Thousands of homes have been destroyed or suffered significant damage. We believe that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are in great need. The death toll is very high and unfortunately likely to continue to rise.”The deadly floods occurred on Wednesday morning after an enormous section ⁠of a glacier in the Himalayas broke loose and crashed on to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, unleashing a massive surge of water, mud, rock and ice that thundered down rivers and valleys. The resulting floods obliterated villages and destroyed power stations, roads and bridges.Map of key locations affected by the flash floodsNepal’s steep slopes and the lush valleys below are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events, such as intense monsoons, andmelting glaciers have become more commonbecause of warming due to human-caused climate change.“The damage is just incredible,” Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN resident coordinator for Nepal, said on Friday, adding that more than 40 bridges had been destroyed or badly damaged and “over 40km of road completely destroyed”.By Friday afternoon, the death toll stood at 584 people: 579 in Nepal and five across the border in Tibet, China. Authorities in Nepal said 1,942 people were still missing,includinghundreds of foreign nationalswho were in the area to work, trek with guides or make a pilgrimage.On the ground in Nepal after deadly flash floods - videoRescue teams have reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Indian border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.Rescuers were forced to suspend operations on Friday morning after a dam of debris overflowed on Friday, increasing the risk of further flooding.
