Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses.View image in fullscreenRelatives display photos of missing people outside a hospital in Kathmandu, where they have travelled from Rasuwa to seek information about family members.Photograph: Subaas Shrestha/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the border overflowed.Rescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.View image in fullscreenPeople surveying the aftermath of the flooding in Bidur.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianThe mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.Nearby, people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.View image in fullscreenA woman among the ruins of Bidur.Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The GuardianMost areas battered by the flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, from where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned in a matter of minutes.The international community isscrambling to get aid to flood-stricken partsof Nepal and Tibet.10:11‘Erased before their eyes’: desperate rescue efforts continue after Nepal-Tibet floods - The LatestNepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search and rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of bridges and roads across the mountainous region – continues.“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”TheKathmandu Postreported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search and rescue teams to assist in the operation.3D map of area affected by floodingDinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ⁠ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to ​accept foreign assistance may ​be linked to sensitivities over ​Rasuwa district and its border with Tibet.“They may have thought about ​the locational sensitivity ‌of the region and ​decided not to ​accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities.Scant information has emerged from Chinese authoritiesabout the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only five deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.View image in fullscreenExcavators clear debris to restore a road damaged by the flash floods on the Tibet side of the border.Photograph: China News Service/GettyWith Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalChinaTibetNatural disastersAsia PacificSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Families of 33 missing Britons rush to Nepal as fears grow of more floods | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Desperate relatives trying to reach loved ones last seen in area where entire villages have been swept away
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Desperate relatives trying to reach loved ones last seen in area where entire villages have been swept away
Content: (From left) Missing Britons Sumitra Sapkota, Neetu Goyal Tiwari and Sarada Simkhada.Composite: FacebookView image in fullscreen(From left) Missing Britons Sumitra Sapkota, Neetu Goyal Tiwari and Sarada Simkhada.Composite: FacebookNepal-Tibet flood disasterFamilies of 33 missing Britons rush to Nepal as fears grow of more floodsDesperate relatives trying to reach loved ones last seen in area where entire villages have been swept awayNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesVisual guide: how the deadly flooding unfoldedTell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?Rachel HallandNadeem BadshahFri 28 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 09.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFamilies are rushing toNepalto search for the 33 British nationals who are still missing, as fears mount over the risk of a second wave of flooding in the region.The catastrophic flash floods that hit Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and sweeping away entire villages, have killed at least 538 people, while more than 1,500 remain missing.Among them are hundreds of foreign tourists who were visiting the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims for its natural beauty and religious significance.Relatives of missing Britons have shared their devastation as they desperately try to reach their loved ones who were last seen in the Rasuwa district, where power and communication lines are down. Many are scrambling to book flights to Kathmandu, the Nepalese capital.On Friday, authorities in Nepal andChinaissued warnings about the risk of a second wave of flooding. Chinese authorities said an artificial lake had formed after a mudslide hit the Tibet-Nepal border, posing a risk of “sending flood waters downstream”, according to state media. Nepal’s disaster authority said a lake that had formed after debris blocked a river at the site was also rising and ‌at risk of bursting.Barrier lake forms at base of mountains near Nepal borderRescuers were forced to suspend their search for survivors, while residents who had returned to Rasuwa were told to evacuate their homes. Many were seen fleeing up the hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river.In a video on YouTube, Jaggi Vasudev, known as Sadhguru, a spiritual leader who founded the nonprofit Isha Foundation, told followers at the foundation’s camp at Saga inTibet, China, that 80 members of an Isha group returning from Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists, were missing, including nine British people.Among them was Neetu Goyal Tiwari, 51. Her brother Naresh Goyal told the BBC that completing the pilgrimage was “her dream”.Neetu’s nephew, Anmol Goyal, said she had been travelling with a friend, and that her last known location was at the immigration centre on the Tibet-Nepal border. He said she had been added to the Nepalese government’s official list of missing persons.The family have been desperately phoning contacts in Nepal in an attempt to find her, though they increasingly believe her to still be in China. As many of them are based in India, it is difficult for them to obtain visas to search for her. Goyal said her husband and daughter remained in the UK for now.“We’re not sure what the next second holds and what we should do from our end, because we’re trying to reach everyone we can,” he said. “She was a very fun-loving woman [and] really had a great heart. I really hope she comes back soon.”The Telegraph reported that an NHS psychiatrist, Pravin Atmakur, 54, was leading a group of 77 pilgrims on Isha Foundation’s journey to Mount Kailash. The group’s last-known location was an immigration centre in Timure, in the mudslide’s direct path.His wife, Manjula Atmakur, who arrived in Kathmandu to search for him on Friday, told the newspaper she was disappointed by the British government’s response to the disaster.Fishtail Tours and Travels confirmed Leena Bector, 53, from Slough, was among 27 travellers in its group who were unaccounted for.View image in fullscreenFamily members of missing flood victims look at the list of missing people at the emergency ward of the Maharajgunj medical campus in Kathmandu.Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/GettyHer husband, Bhupesh Bector, told the Times he was booking the next flight to Kathmandu after the Home Office had failed to confirm whether Leena was on its missing persons list. “Even if they find her today or tomorrow, I need to be there,” he said. “She must be in trauma.”Also missing are an A-level student from Surrey, Spandan Sahu, 18, and his father, Santosh Sahu, 46, the chief executive of the UK pharmaceutical technology company Charac; Spandan’s mother, Surabhi Manmath Padhy, 44; and sister Syna Kumari Sahu, 13.Mahadev Semwal, a friend of Sahu’s for about 15 years, said: “I had WhatsApp communication with him on Monday: they were going to Nepal then Manasarovar in Tibet.“When I heard on Wednesday about the flooding, I lost contact with him – when I am trying to message him it is getting delivered but not read.“Our heart says they are safe somewhere. It’s possible because the communication is jammed.“But when you see the videos, it is unbelievable. It feels so bad.”Also confirmed missing was Sarada Simkhada, a senior nurse from Dartford, Kent, who left for Nepal last Saturday on a religious journey.Deepesh Patel told the Press Association that his parents, Bipin Patel, 66, and Mala Patel, 60, from Coventry, were missing after flying to Nepal on 22 August for a pilgrimage. His brother Anant Patel told Sky News he was “shocked” at the lack of information on their whereabouts.10:11‘Erased before their eyes’: on the ground in decimated Nepal flood zone - The LatestVikram Kolagatla, from London, told the BBC he had not heard from his wife, Geetha Reddy. Reddy, who has two daughters aged 12 and 14, had been in Hotel Kailash in Rasuwagadh when the flooding hit.“We’re not sure what to do. I have two little girls, and their schools are starting next week,” Kolagatla added.Tatjana Phillips, from Folkestone in Kent, told the BBC she had not been able to contact her sister, Julija Jakovicka, who was attending a yoga and meditation retreat near the Nepal-Tibet border when flash flooding hit.Tanay Ranjan told the BBC he had not heard from his older brother Ankit Ranjan, 39, or sister-in-law, Ankita Chandra, 35, who had gone on a pilgrimage.Ranjan added: “We don’t know if they crossed the border … We don’t have a clue where they are. We are very much devastated.”The tour operator Alpine Eco Trek said it had been unable to make contact with a party of 12 Britons aged 13 to 65 who had booked a tour to Mount Kailash in Tibet, and were in the vicinity when the flash floods hit.View image in fullscreenFirefighters conduct search and rescue operations at a damaged area in Gyirong county, Tibet.Photograph: cnsphoto/ReutersSunil Amin, from Croydon in south London, shared with the Daily Mail the “horrible, horrible feeling” of repeatedly trying to phone his wife, Hema Amin, 63, who was on a pilgrimage with Alpine Eco Trek from Nepal to Tibet with her sister. “I’m devastated,” he said.The Trekkers’ Society, which organises tours across Nepal, Tibet and Bhutan, said nine UK nationals on a pilgrimage had gone missing. The organisation confirmed that four men and boys aged between 14 and 50 and five women aged 40 to 53 were unaccounted for.Himalayan Glacier US said it had lost contact with a group of 47 guests and staff, including two Britons, who were also on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, regarded as the spiritual home of the Hindu god Shiva.Location mapThe tour operator Kailash Journeys confirmed it had not been able to account for seven UK nationals – five women and two men aged between 18 and 55 – who were travelling with it.Leaf Holidays, which runs Himalayan treks and expeditions from Kathmandu, wrote in a Facebook post that its group of 55 travellers remained missing, including four British citizens, Tara and Babar Gurung and Thaneswar and Tejkumari Gurung, who have not been heard from since Tuesday.Twelve of the missing British citizens were on a tour to Mount Kailash led by Nabhi Nandan Das, a 64-year-old Hindu priest who works at the Sanatan Mandir and community centre in Surrey, the Telegraph reported. He is understood to have been leading 11 Britons on a tour that was due to visit Kailash and Lake Mansarovar, two Hindu holy sites in Tibet.View image in fullscreenPeople wait for information about their missing relatives outside a military camp in the Trishuli area of Nepal’s Nuwakot district.Photograph: Manan Vatsyayana/AFP/GettyPramod Poudel, who runs a Nepalese street food company in Sussex, told the Daily Mail his wife, Sumitra, mother, Tulisa, brother Pradip and uncle Madav were all missing. His father, Purusottam, has been found alive.The Non-Resident Nepali Association in the UK launched anemergency fundraising appealon Thursday and more than £12,000 has been raised.Rajendra Pudasaini, a nurse in Essex who is president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association UK, said Nepal was witnessing an “irreplaceable loss” and Nepal was “paying the price for global warming”.Pudasaini told BBC Radio 4 Today’s programme that many of his family members were missing. “My godson, we found the body yesterday morning, you know, he (was) just buried under the mud at his house, and yes, lots of other dead bodies being found.”He added: “It’s a very difficult situation to describe, actually.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetSouth and central AsiaChinaAsia PacificFloodingnewsShareReuse this content

title: USS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at sea | US military | The Guardian
description: Thai navy says ‘routine’ visit’ will allow personnel to rest and recuperate amid reports of poor conditions onboard
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Thai navy says ‘routine’ visit’ will allow personnel to rest and recuperate amid reports of poor conditions onboard
Content: In a photo supplied by the US navy, the USS Abraham Lincoln is seen in the Indian Ocean on 22 August.Photograph: Zoe Simpson/US Navy/Handout Via ReutersView image in fullscreenIn a photo supplied by the US navy, the USS Abraham Lincoln is seen in the Indian Ocean on 22 August.Photograph: Zoe Simpson/US Navy/Handout Via ReutersUS militaryUSS Abraham Lincoln to visit port in Thailand after more than 250 days at seaThai navy says ‘routine’ visit’ will allow personnel to rest and recuperate amid reports of poor conditions onboardAnna BettsFri 28 Aug 2026 09.15 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier is set to make a temporary stop inThailandnext week as it heads back to the United States, Thai navy officials said, after spendingmore than 250consecutive days at sea supportingUS operationsagainstIranamid recentreportsof poor living conditions and low morale onboard the vessel.The Lincoln left the Middle East several days ago after being relieved by theUSS George Washington, and is now headinghometo San Diego. A Thai navy official toldReutersthis week that the carrier was expected to make a brief port visit in Thailand next week for the crew to rest and recuperate before continuing their journey home.“The stop is ‌a ⁠routine port visit intended to allow personnel to rest and recuperate … as well as to receive logistical support,” the spokesperson for the Thai navy said.Earlier this week, the Thai navysaidthat three ships from a US navy carrier strike group would be making a brief port call in eastern Thailand to allow personnel to rest. No military exercises would take place during the visit, the statement added. The Thai navy did not identify ​the vessels or provide a date.Families of US sailors denounce Trump and Hegseth for ‘dismissing their experiences and calling them liars’Read moreThe planned stop comes as the Lincoln’s deployment has faced scrutiny in recent weeksamid reportsof poor living conditions onboard among its crew. Family members of sailors have described shortages of supplies and water, plumbing problems, low morale, andworsening mental healthamong the roughly5,000 personnelon the carrier. TheNavy Timesalso reported that there had been several attempts by sailors to jump overboard.On Wednesday, the wife of a sailor who jumped overboard toldMS Nowthat her husband, who she said had since returned to the US, was now facing disciplinary action from the navy.Charging documents viewed by MS Now reportedly accuse the sailor of violating Article 83 for “malingering”, which isdefined assomeone who, “with the intent to avoid work, duty, or service”, fakes “illness, physical disablement, mental lapse, or mental derangement” or “intentionally inflicts self-injury”.The document also reportedly accuses the sailor of violating Article 86 for “absence without leave” whichis whenthe service member, without authority, “fails to go to his appointed place of duty at the time prescribed”, “goes from that place” or “absents himself or remains absent from his unit, organization, or place of duty at which he is required to be at the time prescribed”.The couple, both 19, have a three-year-old son and welcomed a daughter in February while he was deployed. His wife told the outlet that he had requested paternity leave but was denied.The sailor is now reportedly facing non-judicial punishment, which MS Now notes is typically used by commanding officers to address minor rule-breaking without a court martial.In a statement to the Guardian on Friday, a navy official said “our first responsibility following this incident was the Sailor’s safety and well-being”.“He was safely recovered, medically evacuated from the ship and evaluated by medical professionals,” they said. “He continues to have access to appropriate care and support.”They added that “medical care and administrative or disciplinary processes are separate, and one does not preclude the other”, and “the command has the discretion to address misconduct based on the totality of the circumstances”.“Because this involves an individual Sailor’s protected medical information and an ongoing personnel matter, we cannot discuss the specific evidence, medical care or ongoing proceedings,” the navy added.The Lincoln left San Diego on 21 Novemberbound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East. It has since spent more than250 consecutivedays without a significant port visit.Reports about the conditions onboard havepromptedseveral Democratic lawmakersto demandanswers from the Pentagon.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryThailandAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nepal-Tibet flood rescue efforts resume after being halted by overflowing lake | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Risk of fresh flooding had forced rescue teams to withdraw as residents rushed up hills to escape possible river surge
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Risk of fresh flooding had forced rescue teams to withdraw as residents rushed up hills to escape possible river surge
Content: 2:02Timeline of how deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – explainerNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepal-Tibet flood rescue efforts resume after being halted by overflowing lakeRisk of fresh flooding had forced rescue teams to withdraw as residents rushed up hills to escape possible river surgeNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesVisual guide: how the deadly flooding unfoldedTell us: have you been affected by the flash floods?Hannah Ellis-Petersenin Bidur,Sam Jonesand agenciesFri 28 Aug 2026 06.17 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 01.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRescuers searching for survivors of deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have resumed their efforts after suspending operations when a debris dam burst its bank on Friday, increasing the risk of fresh flooding.Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides ⁠on Friday to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses. Fears of another flood came as authorities in Nepal andChinasaid that at least 543 people had been killed in the disaster.Barrier lake forms at base of mountains near Nepal borderMore than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing inNepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said, including 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.Climate crisis could be destabilising mountain areas like Nepal, experts warnRead moreThe flood on Wednesday had destroyed power stations, roads and bridges along a route that links Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet and is ⁠popular with trekkers and pilgrims.The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the China border burst its banks.10:11‘Erased before their eyes’: on the ground in decimated Nepal flood zone - The LatestRescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when a tide of mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were still bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.Nearby, local people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.Most areas battered by flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said that in a matter of minutes, the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned.The international community isscrambling to get aid to flood-stricken partsof Nepal and Tibet.View image in fullscreenSludge inundates homes after flash floods in Nuwakot district.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesNepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search-and-rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and miles of roads across the mountainous region – continues.“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”TheKathmandu Postreported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search-and-rescue teams to assist in the operation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ⁠ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to ​accept foreign assistance may ​be linked to sensitivities over ​Rasuwa district and its border with China’s Tibet region.“They may have thought about ​the locational sensitivity ‌of the region and ​decided not to ​accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities involving China.Scant information has emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.In Nepal earlier on Friday, army helicopter rescue teams were working to free about 100 people trapped in a tunnel at a flooded hydropower project.Map showing location of the disaster“Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” said the Nepal army spokesperson, Raja Ram Basnet.“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.”The prime minister’s office said the army was working in challenging conditions and had rescued 350 workers and local people who were trapped in the tunnel.Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.CCTV said 499 Chinese nationals and 555 foreigners had been transported out of the disaster zone as of Friday.With Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalSouth and central AsiaTibetChinaFloodingLandslidesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Controversial plans for a Daniel Andrews sculpture officially scrapped by Victorian government  | Victoria | The Guardian
description: The $134,000 cost of the statue of the former Victorian premier has been heavily criticised by the Liberal opposition
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: The $134,000 cost of the statue of the former Victorian premier has been heavily criticised by the Liberal opposition
Content: Work began in May on the statue commemorating Daniel Andrews’ (left) tenure – but Victorian premier Ben Carroll (right) announced the statue will not go ahead.Composite: Joel Carrett/Dean Lewins/AAPView image in fullscreenWork began in May on the statue commemorating Daniel Andrews’ (left) tenure – but Victorian premier Ben Carroll (right) announced the statue will not go ahead.Composite: Joel Carrett/Dean Lewins/AAPVictoriaControversial plans for a Daniel Andrews sculpture officially scrapped by Victorian governmentThe $134,000 cost of the statue of the former Victorian premier has been heavily criticised by the Liberal oppositionGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPetra StockFri 28 Aug 2026 19.47 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 21.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Carroll government in Victoria has cancelled controversial plans for a statue of former Labor premierDaniel Andrews.Work began in May on the statue commemorating the former premier’s more than 3,000 days in office, as part of a 1999 policy recognising long-serving Victorian premiers.But the premier,Ben Carroll, announced an end to the Kennett government policy on Saturday, appointing an independent panel to review how Victoria commemorates officials with statues and state services.He directed work on the Andrews statue to cease.Daniel Andrews defends actions as opposition labels Labor ‘a gangster government’ after Ibac report releasedRead more“We are grateful to former premiers for their service. But gratitude does not require a taxpayer-funded statue,” Carroll said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“I respect your money. That means being careful and deliberate about how government spends it.”The policy automatically recognising long-serving Victorian premiers with a statue on Treasury Place was introduced ahead of the 1999 state election by then-premier Jeff Kennett. Kennett himself fell short of the milestone.The “independent and bipartisan” panel will make recommendations about the future state funerals and memorial services. Thestatuecontract will not be cancelled, instead the panel will select an alternative subject and location for the commissioned work.The $134,000 cost of the planned statue of Andrews has been heavily criticised by the Liberal opposition.View image in fullscreenA statue of former Labor premier John Cain stands outside Treasury Place in Melbourne.Photograph: James Ross/AAP“If we come to government we will not allow that statue to proceed,” the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, said on 30 July.“Victorians are fed up with Labor’s waste – that’s why it’s time for a Government that treats your money with respect,” she wrote in a social media post.Andrews was premier of Victoria from 4 December 2014 to 27 September 2023. While the former premier was yet to comment on the decision to axe his effigy, in 2023he claimedthere was “no magic” to the 3,000 day milestone.“People who spend a lot of time talking about legacy usually spend not enough time actually building one,” he said at the time.In May, the state government confirmed Meridian Sculpture, the company that created the statues of the other four Victorian premiers who reached the milestone, was selected after a standard procurement process.At the time, a Victorian government spokesperson said: “Daniel Andrews led Victoria through some of its toughest moments and never stopped fighting for working people. Under a policy introduced by the Kennett government, Victorian premiers who serve more than 3,000 days in office are recognised with a statue along Treasury Place in honour of their service to the state.”Four former Victorian premiers have been commemorated in bronze at Treasury Gardens, they include Sir Albert Dunstan, Sir Henry Bolte, Sir Rupert Hamer and John Cain junior. Sir James McCulloch, who served more than 3000 days over non-consecutive terms has not been recognised with a statue.Explore more on these topicsVictoriaDaniel AndrewsBen CarrollVictorian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Number of Australians missing in Nepal’s deadly floods rises again, as Albanese deploys more personnel | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: There are now 41 Australians missing, and four rapid response team members are expected to arrive in Kathmandu
Author: Cait Kelly
Headline: There are now 41 Australians missing, and four rapid response team members are expected to arrive in Kathmandu
Content: Four Dfat crisis response teams officers are expected to arrive in Kathmandu later Saturday to support consular efforts on the ground.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFour Dfat crisis response teams officers are expected to arrive in Kathmandu later Saturday to support consular efforts on the ground.Photograph: Matt Jelonek/Getty ImagesNepal-Tibet flood disasterNumber of Australians missing in Nepal’s deadly floods rises again, as Albanese deploys more personnelThere are now 41 Australians missing, and four rapid response team members are expected to arrive in KathmanduAt least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floodsHow the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guideGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastStephanie ConveryandCait Kellyin KathmanduFri 28 Aug 2026 18.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 20.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe number of Australians who were reported missing in the catastrophicNepalflooding disaster has risen to 41, as one family celebrates after an unaccounted-for woman made contact with them yesterday.It means three additional Australians were confirmed missing overnight – up from 38 who remained unaccounted for on Friday evening.The Australian government’s Department of Foreign Affairs has been urgently working with local authorities to contact Australian woman Cara Severino, 25, who became the first Australian reported missing who has been confirmed safe.‘So desperately loved’: ADF member among dozens of Australians missing in Nepal floods as families pray for safe returnRead moreSeverino contacted her parents, Debbie and Frank Severino, on Friday morning, informing them she was hiking away from the disaster zone to Kathmandu with a group of Nepali hikers – a trek of more than 110km.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe Red Cross has said about 600 people are dead and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, with a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.Dfat has received more than 450 calls in relation to the disaster.View image in fullscreenSome of Australia’s missing in Nepal as of Friday, 28 August. Clockwise from left: Karan Bhardwaj, Chitra Venkatraman, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, Sumi Adhikari and family: Shylaja Muralitharan, Aarush Muralitharan, Ashwin Muralitharan & Chandrasekaran Muralitharan.Composite: Supplied by the familiesNepal’s disaster management agency says there are 1,924 people unaccounted for – 517 of those people are foreign tourists.About 7:30pm on Friday evening, the authority said 121 foreigners had been rescued – none of them were Australians.View from Kathmandu hospitalOutside the hospital in Kathmandu yesterday, there were scenes of anxiety as families put up posters of loved ones, and authorities hung pictures of the dead that need to be identified.One woman said her cousin was on his way back from Australia because his brother had gone missing.Like many others, she was putting pictures of him up, in case he was brought back to the hospital.At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red CrossRead moreAustralian charities are starting to pump in aid, with the Emergency Action Alliance – a peak body representing major Australian charities – raising funds to build emergency shelters, get food and safe drinking water, hygiene supplies and medical care to communities.But conditions on the ground are difficult and unpredictable owing to the scale of the damage and the heavy monsoon. Rescue operations in Nepal and China resumed as of Saturday morning after being suspended due to the risk of further flooding.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view shows the aftermath of massive flooding along the Bhotekoshi River, which affected low-lying areas and settlements near the riverbanks in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe flooding caused widespread damage to homes, roads, bridge, hydropower station and other infrastructure in the area.Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockFour Dfat crisis response team officers are expected to arrive in Kathmandu later on Saturday to support consular efforts on the ground.Four rapid response team members are also expected to arrive in Kathmandu – humanitarian response specialists with expertise in communications, logistics and planning.These extra deployments add to about 20 personnel Australian already has on the ground with the Australian embassy in Kathmandu.On Friday night, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, spoke with the Nepali foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, to affirm that Australia would provide further humanitarian assistance, including to aid rescue and recovery efforts, where required.Australia has pledged $5m in aid and support for the disaster, with $2m going to the World Food Programme to provide emergency food and water provisions, and the remaining to the Emergency Action Alliance.Australia’s assistant minister for foreign affairs and trade, Matt Thistlethwaite, said on Saturday morning that the aid was being provided on request of the Nepalese authorities. Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Thistlethwaite said Australian officials in Beijing were also working with the Chinese Government, but that China had not so far requested support.“We’re doing our best to support both the Nepalese and Tibetan diasporas here in Australia,” Thistlethwaite said.“Yesterday I held two online forums, one with the Nepalese community one with the Tibetan community to outline the latest situation, to advise of the support that Australia is providing, the $5m in humanitarian aid, and the best way for us to keep in contact with them. We’re providing them with the latest information through our officials.“I also attended a vigil last night with the Nepalese community in Strathfield and obviously there was quite a bit of despair and anxiety in that community, but we’re doing our best to support the Tibetan and Nepalese communities here in Australia.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalAnthony AlbanesenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘So desperately loved’: ADF member among dozens of Australians missing in Nepal floods as families pray for safe return | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Relatives ‘really worried, but hopeful’ as they wait anxiously for news in the aftermath of the flash flooding disaster
Author: Henry Belot
Headline: Relatives ‘really worried, but hopeful’ as they wait anxiously for news in the aftermath of the flash flooding disaster
Content: Australian's missing in Nepal - Clockwise from left - Karan Bhardwaj, Chitra Venkatraman, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, Sumi Adhikari and Family: Shylaja Muralitharan, Aarush Muralitharan, Ashwin Muralitharan & Chandrasekaran Muralitharan; Suhasini Kandimalla; Narayan PanthiComposite: Supplied by the familiesView image in fullscreenAustralian's missing in Nepal - Clockwise from left - Karan Bhardwaj, Chitra Venkatraman, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, Sumi Adhikari and Family: Shylaja Muralitharan, Aarush Muralitharan, Ashwin Muralitharan & Chandrasekaran Muralitharan; Suhasini Kandimalla; Narayan PanthiComposite: Supplied by the familiesNepal-Tibet flood disaster‘So desperately loved’: ADF member among dozens of Australians missing in Nepal floods as families pray for safe returnRelatives ‘really worried, but hopeful’ as they wait anxiously for news in the aftermath of the flash flooding disasterFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastHenry Belot,Nino BucciandKat WongFri 28 Aug 2026 14.32 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 22.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe families of an Australian defence force member and two Sydney boys who went missing with their parentsin Nepalremain hopeful they will be found safe.Dozens of Australians are missing afterdevastating floodingon the Nepal-Tibet border. Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday that the total number of people missing had risen sharply to more than 1,900 swelled by 933 workers on hydropower projects on the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers where a wall of water powered down on Wednesday morning. The number of people killed is at least 584.One Australian womancontacted her familyon Friday morning to tell them that she had survived the flood, the first of those reported missing to be confirmed safe.Among the missing Australians is Karan Bhardwaj, a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian air force who was travelling in Nepal with Kailash Journeys.“Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law,” said his family member Jen, who did not want her surname published.Race to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burstRead more“He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.”Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, her husband, Chandrasekaran Muralitharan, 47, and their two sons Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11, were taking part in a pilgrimage when the flood hit on Wednesday.Shylaja’s younger sister, Vaishnavi, said that she had lost contact with the family shortly after breakfast on the morning of the flood.2:02Timeline of how deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – explainerThe family of four planned to head towards an immigration checkpoint on the Tibet-Nepal border soon after, as part of the group of 15 Australians trekking with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour.“Just like everyone else that’s part of that group, we’re really worried, but hopeful,” Vaishnavi said.“Hopeful that they’re safe and just waiting to be rescued.“It’s a very difficult time for our whole family … I just want to make people aware that they’re there, and we’re waiting, and we just want them to return.”Vaishnavi, who asked that her surname not be published, confirmed the family were close with other members of the group who had also travelled from Sydney for the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe family had been training together for the long walk, she said.“They had been planning for some time, and preparing, because it’s quite a trek.“They were all working very hard together to make sure they could successfully complete it.“We just didn’t expect anything like this.”A map of the flood affected areasVaishnavi said it was difficult to get clear information about what was being done to find those missing. She has spoken with Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials.“We do want to know what efforts are being made … we’re not aware of what is actually happening there.”Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was at an immigration office at the Gyirong Post crossing when the flood waters hit. She was travelling with an Isha Foundation pilgrimage to the region.Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal and is desperately seeking information about her whereabouts.“She was in the same area when the flood happened,” said a flyer produced by Adhikari’s family, and published with their permission. “If anyone has seen her or has any information about her, please contact the family immediately.”View image in fullscreenSumi Adhikari was travelling as part of an Isha Foundation pilgrimage.Illustration: suppliedBharat Mangwani, 42, was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning.He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu and then Delhi, his close friend Kushagra Tiwari said.Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has gone on to Kathmandu to look for any information.“All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” Tiwari said.Suhasini Kandimalla, a mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, has also been reported missing.Her sister, Supreethini Kandimalla, said that she was doing the hike with another Springfield local.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSuhasini Kandimalla from Queensland who has been reported missing in Nepal.Photograph: SuppliedWhile she was a New Zealand citizen, Suhasini had been approved for Australian citizenship, her sister said. She had planned to attend a citizenship ceremony for it to be granted soon after she returned.“I don’t know if it was a religious calling for her to do it,” Supreethini told the Guardian.“But she certainly loved the treks in New Zealand too, and would go on lots of long hikes.”A Brisbane man, Narayan Panthi, is also missing in the region. According to Nepal police, he was travelling with Kathmandu Holiday but he has also been conducting charity work in the capital with an education fund, the NeNas Foundation.View image in fullscreenNarayan Panthi from Brisbane is missing in Nepal.Photograph: SuppliedPanthi’s cousin, Amrit Bhusal, said his family was devastated but “holding on to hope and praying for positive news”.“We are still hoping,” Bhusal said. “We are still searching. We are still praying for Narayan to come home safely.”Bhusal said Panthi was “helping disadvantaged children in Nepal reach their full potential through education”.New South Wales couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and his wife, Chitra Venkatraman, 46, were also among the 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash.So too were Sreedharan and Lakshmi Iyer, and their adult sons Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20.The brothers played cricket for West Pennant Hills Cherrybrook Cricket Club in Sydney’s north-west.“WPHCCC is aware of the reports that two of our players, Rishab and Rudhra Iyer, along with their family members and other Australians, are unaccounted for in the ongoing floods in Nepal,” the club said in a statement.What caused the catastrophic flood in Nepal and Tibet – and how does a glacier collapse?Read more“We continue to live in hope, and our thoughts are currently with them, their loved ones and all affected by this tragedy in Nepal.”The University of Newcastle’s vice-chancellor, Alex Zelinsky, said Rishab and Rudhra were both medical students the at the university.“We are thinking of them, their families, their fellow students and teaching staff, as well as the many people who have been impacted by this devastating event and we hope that both students can be located soon,” Zelinsky said in a statement.Separate groups of Australians – 11 travelling with Trekkers Society and six with Kailash Journeys – are also unaccounted for. Both tour companies have been contacted for comment.Several other Australians were travelling with other tour groups. It is understood the majority of missing Australians are from New South Wales, but there are also some from Victoria and Queensland.The founder and chief executive of Himalayan Glacier Adventures, Sagar Pandey, said he had lost all contact with his tour group of 47 people, which included the 15 Australians.Pandey told the Guardian on Thursday he had flown by helicopter over the Rasuwa area, where the tour was staying, since the flood and had little hope they survived.“To be honest … you would think there was no human civilisation there at all.“The flash flood swept away everything, everything. You couldn’t see any human creations.“Still, I have a hope.”The Isha Foundation confirmed that 11 Australians were among a group of 80 missing pilgrims who had been in an immigration building when the flood hit.The foreign minister, Penny Wong, spoke to her Nepali counterpart, Shisir Khanal, on Friday evening to convey Australia’s deepest condolences following the devastating floods.She outlined Australia’shumanitarian assistance packagein which Australia was “rapidly mobilising consular and humanitarian support in response” to the flooding.Wong said the government would send an initial team of three humanitarian response specialists “within the next 48 hours’” to help Australian staff already on the ground.“The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery.”Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasternewsShareReuse this content

title: How Nepali diaspora is responding to flood disaster and how Australians can help in relief effort | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Nepali and Tibetan communities plan vigils and work to raise funds for recovery in ‘devastating’ time
Author: Adeshola Ore
Headline: Nepali and Tibetan communities plan vigils and work to raise funds for recovery in ‘devastating’ time
Content: Mourners light candles for the victims of the Nepal flood disaster during prayers in Sydney’s Rockdale on Thursday night.Photograph: George Chan/AAPView image in fullscreenMourners light candles for the victims of the Nepal flood disaster during prayers in Sydney’s Rockdale on Thursday night.Photograph: George Chan/AAPNepal-Tibet flood disasterHow Nepali diaspora is responding to flood disaster and how Australians can help in relief effortNepali and Tibetan communities plan vigils and work to raise funds for recovery in ‘devastating’ timeGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAdeshola OreCommunity affairs reporterFri 28 Aug 2026 11.50 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s Nepali community plan to host vigils to remember the victims of theNepal-Tibet flood disasterto coincide with a day of mourning, as the number of people killed continues to rise.As Australia’s Nepali diaspora wait for the full scale of the disaster to become clear, community members are desperately waiting to hear from missing relatives and friends.Nepali authorities said on Friday that the death toll had risen to 579, with the number missing rising sharply to more than 1,900, after massive flash floods and landslides tore through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river basins on Wednesday.‘We just want them to return’: relatives of Australians missing in Nepal floods wait anxiously for news of loved onesRead moreThe foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, on Friday morning confirmed the number of Australians missing in the floods hadincreased to 39as she unveiled a $5m support package.Wong told the ABC that Australians who wished to donate could do so via theEmergency Action Alliance website– run by a group of Australian charities and humanitarian organisations.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailNepali Australians gathered for candlelight prayers on Thursday night and held a minute’s silence for those lost to the floods.Dr Tilak Pokhrel, president of the Australian Nepalese Multicultural Centre (ANMC), said community organisations in Victoria would host a vigil when the Nepali government announced an upcoming national day of mourning.“Community members just want to say we are with you for those who are affected,” he said.“We want to have an event where we all can gather and show our solidarity to support them.“Let’s work together, let’s pray together, and let’s go through this pain together.”View image in fullscreenCandles arranged in the shape of the Nepali flag at prayers in Rockdale, Sydney.Photograph: George Chan/AAPPokhrel said the centre would extend its opening hours for the next few days so faith leaders could provide support.“People are waiting for the news. They are checking the news every hour,” he said.Chudamani Sapkota, the general secretary of Non-Resident Nepali Association, said its New South Wales branch would host a candlelight vigil on Saturday evening inSydney.“This is devastating news for all the Nepalese diaspora,” he said.Sapkota said the organisation was trying to support Nepali Australians seeking to locate their missing relatives.“There’s no network, nothing at the moment,” he said. “This is a very tough time.”Melbourne student Rakshya Pandey’s family home and two grocery shops in the Nuwakot district, hit by the flash flooding, have been destroyed. Her father, who was injured after being struck by an object in the flooding, is receiving treatment in a Kathmandu hospital.“Whenever I see the detail of the people missing or the flood or everything, it’s just so scary, and I’m scared … I can’t do anything. I feel so helpless,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPandey fears there will be future flooding in Nepal.Ashok Bahadur Dhungel, who lives in Canberra, has been trying to reach his nephew who works for the Upper Trishuli hydropower plant, which sat on one of the Nepali rivers that flooded. He said his nephew has not been online for two days.“We hope he is still alive,” he said.View image in fullscreenMelbourne student Rakshya Pandey (far right) with her family. The family’s home was destroyed by the floods that hit Nepal’s Nuwakot district.Photograph: suppliedDhungel heard through friends that his mother, who lives in the Nuwakot district, had survived. But he has been unable to speak to her due to power outages.“She is everything to me,” he said.Tenzin Khangsar, co-chair of the Australia Tibet Council, said the Tibetan community was “shocked and devastated” about the flooding. He said prayer events would be planned to commemorate the victims.Diaspora community organisations are also crowdfunding for the Nepali government’s disaster relief fund.Climate crisis could be destabilising mountain areas like Nepal, experts warnRead moreChiran Tiwari, president of the Nepalese Welfare Society based in Sydney, said the organisation had created a GoFundMe page to raise money for the Nepali prime minister’s natural disaster relief fund.Tiwari said one of the welfare society’s executive member’s relatives was missing in Nepal, with the community rallying around to provide support to them.“The situation is very sad for the community,” he said. “Everyone’s eyes is tearing so the situation is very difficult.”On Thursday night, the ANMC hosted a candlelight multi-faith prayer night in Melbourne for people grieving the disaster.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalSydneyMelbourneNatural disastersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Charles Perrottet becomes Icac’s main character amid claims of hidden payments and political hit jobs | Independent Commission Against Corruption | The Guardian
description: The brother of former premier questioned over what, if anything, was done in return for $2m from developer turned fugitive Jean Nassif
Author: Anne Davies
Headline: The brother of former premier questioned over what, if anything, was done in return for $2m from developer turned fugitive Jean Nassif
Content: Charles Perrottet giving evidence at Icac in Sydney.Photograph: IcacView image in fullscreenCharles Perrottet giving evidence at Icac in Sydney.Photograph: IcacIndependent Commission Against CorruptionCharles Perrottet becomes Icac’s main character amid claims of hidden payments and political hit jobsThe brother of former premier questioned over what, if anything, was done in return for $2m from developer turned fugitive Jean NassifGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAnne DaviesFri 28 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinally, we are hearing from one of the central characters, Charles Perrottet, in a saga that has occupied the Independent Commission against Corruption (Icac) for nearly four years.It began with the dismissal of the Hills Shire council and a late night 2022 speech in NSW parliament alleging secret payments from a developer. It pirouetted to a pressure campaign allegedly to remove the then NSW building commissioner, and ended with real world impacts: defective high-rise buildings and thousands of unhappy homebuyers, with the developer nowhere to be seen.Charles Perrottet, brother of the former NSW premier, Dominic Perrottet, finallybegan giving evidencelate Friday.He told the commission that he had met the Toplace developer, Jean Nassif, now a fugitive in Lebanon, in December 2019 and had, over several years, provided him with advice on how to progress his developments.Charles and Nassif bonded over their “frustrations” with David Elliott, the former member for Baulkham Hills, and a key figure in the rival centre-right faction of the Liberals, Charles told Icac.‘We execute the prick’: Charles Perrottet sent text plotting downfall of NSW Liberal minister, Icac hearsRead more“He was frustrated with a number of things. I would listen to him, I would appease him, because I wanted information from him,” Charles said.Elliott had opposed some of Nassif’s developments in the Hills Shire area, earning the developer’s ire. Charles, for his part, was angry about Elliott’s attempts to unseat his brother Dominic and was looking for information on him.Despite having a full-time job at BP as head of strategy, Charles was remunerated for his advice, though not directly.“Jeremy [Greenwood, one of the Reformers] wanted to know if I wanted to share in their success,” Charles Perrottet said.“I said, I have a full-time job. I didn’t want to be paid. I said, you can continue to pay Anita [Perrottet’s wife] and look after her.”View image in fullscreenSydney property developer Jean Nassif, who is now a fugitive in Lebanon.Photograph: NSW police/AAPIcac is investigating whether Nassif paid $2m in an undeclared political donation to a group of Liberal-aligned conservative men known as the Reformers,including Greenwood and Christian Ellis, in the pursuit of certain political outcomes.In the first weeks of its investigation it focused on how these allegedly illegal donations were allegedly used to fund this group and stack branches with highly conservative members, and ultimately shift theLiberal partyto the right.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsBut this week the inquiry has focused on a potentially far more serious issue from a public policy perspective: what, if anything, was done, primarily by Charles Perrottet, for the $2m from Nassif?People like Charles Perrottet are not registered lobbyists. They do not appear in ministerial diaries because meetings on “political matters” with ministers do not have to be disclosed.They can engage casually with key ministerial staff because meetings with staff don’t need to be disclosed anywhere. Many of those working for ministers have their own ambitions within the party and would be flattered by the attention.First the good news: Icac works, but slowlyThe inquiry might have taken four years to get off the ground but now we are seeing why.Icac is painstakingly testing allegations of hidden payments made to Liberal operatives allegedly for consulting, and outcomes that were either delivered or sought from the Perrottet government.Icac has gone through phone records, text messages, WhatsApp messages, mobile phone tower information, bank records, computers, tax returns and flight records, to track the movements of the key players and the money flow.They even obtained CCTV footage of the main persons of interest meeting up in a hotel.More challenging is establishing whether there is any nexus between payments and political outcomes.View image in fullscreenDavid Chandler speaks to the media at a building site in Sydney in 2023.Photograph: Jenny Evans/AAPFormer builder commissioner David Chandler gave evidence this week of a whisper campaign, which he believed was aimed at ministers and the media, to have him removed.Chandler, a 40-year veteran of the construction industry, is not under investigation by Icac.A former minister, Eleni Petinos, gave evidence that she believed she was “used” in that campaign. She also said she believed she was sacked precipitously by the premier and that she thought there was something else at play. Petinos is not under investigation by Icac.We’ve also heard about Hills Shire Liberal councillors being disendorsed and replaced by a committee of the state executive of the Liberal party.Charles Perrottet and other Reformers occupied key positions on the committee.The old Hills council had been opposing a Toplace development at Cherrybrook.And of course Elliott lost his seat in parliament.Conflicts of interestsThe Reformers and others involved, like Anita Perrottet, deny that these payments were nefarious and argue instead that they actually did real consulting or lobbying work.Charles Perrottet’s wife, Anita Perrottet, was paid $313,500 from lobbying company Beckington for 18 months in 2021 and 2022 for Greyhounds NSW work and $347,000 in 2022 in “project consulting fees” in the space of three months, “for being a sounding board” for Greenwood and JPG Advisory on Catholic Cemeteries Trust.“That’s $660,999, that’s an enormous amount of money?” said counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC.“I believe that is what I was worth. Jeremy believed I was a huge value-add,” Anita replied.View image in fullscreenAnita Perrottet gives evidence at an Icac hearing on Friday.Photograph: Icac/AAPAnita Perrottet nominated three clients: Greyhounds NSW, while engaged by Beckington, and Catholic Cemeteries Trust and a vaping company, whose name she could not recall, for JPG Advisory,“A sounding board on what?” Dwyer asked.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnita said her advice was entirely oral and delivered during face-to-face meetings with Greenwood or using her husband’s phone.But she “could not recall” a single detail of her advice. By the end of her two days in the witness box she had said the phrase more than 500 times.Icac has been unable to uncover a single document relating to these clients other than invoices issued by Anita’s company, Macquarie Consulting. No research, emails, marketing strategies or even a text were uncovered.This was 2022, the same time as the NSW premier Dominic Perrottet and his cabinet were debating whether to merge the Catholic-owned cemeteries with the state-owned cemeteries.The Catholic Cemeteries Trust was vigorously resisting the merger.The Catholic Cemeteries Trust was very successful. Despite the issue coming before cabinet several times during 2021 and 2022 and an independent report describing the situation as urgent, the Perrottet government declined to act.Dominic Perrottet did not respond to requests for comment regarding disclosures of family ties to cabinet.Do you know Jean Nassif?At first Anita Perrottet denied that she knew Jean Nassif or that Toplace was a client.But in true Icac style, the bomb was about to drop.She was shown texts about a lunch at Nassif’s house. She said she didn’t remember her husband attending the lunch, but was shown photographs of her children playing at Nassif’s house and texts showing she suggested her husband pick up a bottle of wine to take.Anita was shown a detailed email she allegedly sent to Antony Anisse at another Liberal-aligned lobbying firm, Premier National, regarding a Toplace development in Epsom Road, Rosebery,Dominic Perrottet’s brother allegedly shared ‘dirt’ including secret phone recording of minister, Icac hearsRead moreThe development was facing delays in getting its final occupancy certificate and the email purported to outline an eight-point plan to overcome the difficulties. Anita was unable to say even what some of the acronyms she had allegedly used meant.Dwyer put to Anita that she was being put in “an impossible position” and that she was attempting to cover for her husband, who in fact, was working for Nassif.Anita denied she was lying.“It was a transparent attempt to create a cover for a sham arrangement that had been established by Charles,” Dwyer said. “No,” said Anita.‘You understand that there is an offence committed if you lie to Icac,”Dwyer said. “Yes,” Anita said.What did the premier know about his brotherWhen he appeared at Icac, former cabinet minister David Elliott described Dominic and Charles Perrottet’s relationship as “joined at the hip”.Dominic Perrotet is not a person of interest.Chandler gave evidence that Dominic Perrottet had begged him to stay on as commissioner, which was exactly the opposite of what Nassif wanted.“I went up and had a cup of tea with the premier and he said: “David, you’ve heard the sentiment of the members and myself and we would like you to reconsider,” he told Icac this week.View image in fullscreenDominic Perrottet speaks to the media in Parramatta in 2023.Photograph: Louise Kennerley/AAPOn the other hand we saw texts that indicate Charles was intimately involved in securing the NSW premiership for his brother.In October 2021, Dominic Perrottet became premier after the surprise resignation of Gladys Berejiklian.In theIndependent Commission Against Corruptionon Friday we got a rare glimpse into the frantic manoeuvreing to secure him the leadership and the key people involved in the number wrangling.One was Charles Perrottet, the NSW Liberal party right-faction power broker and younger of Dominic, Icac heard.In text messages he and his wife, Anita, discussed his role: “Well, it’s definitely true that he couldn’t have done it without you!!” Anita texted.“But hopefully, you can work together now and going forward to both achieve your goals. Does he feel bad about Kean?”Charles replied: “Yep, I told him what he needs to do there.”Matt Kean had had an agreement with Dominic to become his deputy leader, in return for delivering moderate votes, but ultimately appointed Stuart Ayres.They also discussed pushing council matters with the premier,and also getting rid of David Elliott.“That’s a call for tomorrow. I told him to turn his phone off and savour the moment with Helen, as tomorrow and Tuesday is going to be crucial in showing unity, we execute the prick as soon as party room is over.”Explore more on these topicsIndependent Commission Against CorruptionNew South Wales politicsLiberal partyNew South WalesAustralian politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Russia ‘losing 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit’ | Russia | The Guardian
description: Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day but western officials say it cannot keep up with casualty level
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day but western officials say it cannot keep up with casualty level
Content: Rehearsal for a military parade in Moscow in 2025. Putin is thought to have limited options for more recruitment.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRehearsal for a military parade in Moscow in 2025. Putin is thought to have limited options for more recruitment.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesRussiaRussia ‘losing 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit’Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day but western officials say it cannot keep up with casualty levelPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentFri 28 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia is losing about 6,000 more troops inUkraineeach month than it can recruit, western officials have said.WhileRussiais still acquiring new battlefield recruits at speed, with an estimated rate of 1,000 a day, in the last two months even this has not been sufficient to replace those killed or injured.“We estimate that the gap between the number of people Russia is losing to casualties and the number they’re being able to recruit is around 6,000 a month at the moment,” one western official said.“Putin’s response to this has been to escalate himself and to target civilian infrastructure and civilians in Ukraine, firing over 360 missiles since early July and exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of defence against ballistic missiles. It’s clear that Moscow intends to try and break Ukrainian morale by destroying its energy infrastructure this winter.”Such tactics are in part because Putin has limited options for overcoming the huge losses on the battlefield with more recruitment.Western officials believe further mobilisation would be a big risk both politically and economically, saying the last such event,in autumn 2022, saw about a million – often highly skilled – Russians leave the country, with less than half returning.It is also unclear whether the Russian military could absorb the several hundred thousand new recruits which would result, given a lack of equipment and officers.Ukraine has repeatedly attacked Russian targets connected to oil, creating fuel shortages, but has appealed repeatedly for more help from allies, both with offensive missiles and defence systems.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK will share information about Storm Shadow missile components with Kyiv.Photograph: Ukrainian presidency/Sipa/ShutterstockAndy Burnhamvisited Kyivon his first overseas trip as prime minister this week. He told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK wouldgive Ukraine previously classified informationon the British-manufactured components for long-range cruise missiles.Burnham has also urged the international community to do more to protect Ukraine against Russian attacks, particularly with more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles. He isexpected to make this argumentat next month’s UN general assembly in New York.In response, Russia hasmade repeated threatsof retaliation, including talk of attacks on UK military targets both inside and outside Ukraine.The western officials said that while the threat from Russia remained very real, the situation had not changed, and the assessment was that “Putin absolutely wants to avoid a direct confrontation with Nato”.One official said: “We are seeing a continuation of hostile rhetoric and various accusations against the UK. This is absolutely consistent with longstanding Russian military doctrine, which is to use rhetoric to both exploit fears in adversaries and to influence decision-making. So this is not a new phenomenon.”Ukraine war briefing: Missiles shot down during long Russian attack waveRead moreOfficials say Russia still has the capability to target the UK, with cyberattacks or physical attacks on civilian targets by proxies, for example on factories or warehouses. Last year, six men were jailed for their involvement in an attack ordered by Russia against a warehouse in east London housing aid to Ukraine.But officials said their assessment was that Putin would limit any such action to avoid more direct conflict with Nato.Putin’s overall aim in Ukraine, western officials believe, is to maintain a campaign of attrition, hoping that support from Ukraine’s allies will ebb away, particularly if governments are spooked by public alarm over Russian threats.Such threats should be seen, one official said, as attempts to create a “fractured and more vulnerable Europe”.Another said: “It’s important to keep in mind that this is not new. Russia has invoked the threat of the possible use of nuclear weapons numerous times in recent years to try to scare us into ending support for Ukraine.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineForeign policyEuropeVladimir PutinNatonewsShareReuse this content

title: Norway’s King Harald dies aged 89  | Norway | The Guardian
description: Norwegians gather to remember monarch whose death comes amid scandal over links between crown princess and Jeffrey Epstein
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Norwegians gather to remember monarch whose death comes amid scandal over links between crown princess and Jeffrey Epstein
Content: 1:15Norwegians pay tribute to 'grandfather figure' King Harald V – videoNorwayNorway’s King Harald dies aged 89Norwegians gather to remember monarch whose death comes amid scandal over links between crown princess and Jeffrey EpsteinJon HenleyEurope correspondentFri 28 Aug 2026 11.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 02.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNorwegians have gathered in their thousands to pay their respects to King Harald V, Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, who has died, aged 89, in Oslo. He was succeeded immediately by his son, King Haakon VIII.The new king thanked “the government and Norwegian people for their support and sympathy for the royal family at this time”. A period of national mourning was announced as crowds left wreaths and messages outside the royal palace in Oslo.Flags around the country were lowered to half mast and church bells rang out at midday. “An era has ended. A new one begins. The king is dead. Long live the king,” the prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said after meeting Haakon.The new king, whose wife, Mette-Marit, has recently come under scrutiny over scandals including amuch-criticised associationwith the late US child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, formally notified the government of his father’s death on Friday morning.View image in fullscreenPeople gather outside the royal palace in Oslo after the death of King Harald.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersHaakon, 53, told the cabinet at an extraordinary council of state that he would take the name Haakon VIII, as expected. He also chose as his personal motto: “Everything forNorway.”The new king will swear an oath of accession in parliament within the next few days. Coronation ceremonies were abolished in Norway more than a century ago, but Haakon could choose to have his reign blessed at a consecration ceremony.The palace had said on Thursday that Harald’s health had deteriorated and that the king, who was seen as a unifying figure and a force for stability amid a string of recent family scandals, was in an “extremely serious” condition.View image in fullscreenKing Harald during a welcoming ceremony for the Danish king and queen in Oslo in May 2024.Photograph: Per Ole Hagen/Getty ImagesStøre said earlier that he had received the news “with deep sadness”, adding: “A whole nation is in mourning, and ⁠the people of Norway are left with a ​deep sense of ‌gratitude for a ‌long life in the service of Norway.”Royalty around Europe sent their condolences, with Spain’s royal family hailing Harald’s “responsibility, dignity, humility and tireless dedication”, and Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary saying he was “loved like few others”.King Carl XVI Gustaf, of Sweden, said: “Throughout the years, King Harald has been a good friend to me, my family, and to Sweden … I ​wish ​my dear godson Haakon, ​who now succeeds his father as head ​of state, ‌success and ​good ​fortune.”Belgium’s royal family recalled Harald’s “humour, humanity and sincerity”, while Britain’s King Charles mourned the loss of his “dear cousin”, paying tribute to a “towering figure” who guided his country with “warmth and humility”.View image in fullscreenPeople gather at Palace Square in Oslo to pay their respects to King Harald.Photograph: Rune Hellestad/GettyGermany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said Norway had “lost a great figure who stood for prudence and unity”, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, expressed “deep sadness”.Norway’s ceremonial head of state since 1991, Harald was being treated in Oslo’s University hospital for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of the body’s red blood cells.He had had numerous health problems – an operation for bladder cancer in 2003 and a pacemaker fitted in 2024 – but always ruled out abdicating, saying he had taken a lifelong oath before the Norwegian parliament.His death comes amid aturbulent periodfor Norway’s royal family. Documents published in the US in January showed thatMette-Marit corresponded with Epsteinbetween 2011 and 2014, long after he was convicted.View image in fullscreenHaakon had taken on additional royal duties while his father was ill.Photograph: Per Ole Hagen/GettyThe files appeared to contain almost 1,000 mentions of Mette-Marit, including intimate exchanges. They drew fierce public criticism, with Støre accusing her in unprecedented comments of “poor judgment”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMette-Marit subsequently released a statement via the royal household expressing her “deepest regret for my friendship with Jeffrey Epstein” and apologising for “the situation that I have put the royal family in, especially the king and queen”.View image in fullscreenMette-Marit had a successful lung transplant in July.Photograph: Lise Åserud/NTB Scanpix/APMarius Borg Høiby, 29, Mette-Marit’s son from a previous relationship, has also been in the spotlight after beingsentenced in June to four years in prisonfor two rapes and 32 other charges, including violence against a former partner. He has appealed against the decision.The scandals have affected public support for Norway’s monarchy, with a poll in February finding support down to 54% from 72% in 2024. Several polls found nearly half of the population felt Mette-Marit could not become queen.View image in fullscreenThe royal family pictured in 2022. Front, left to right: King Harald, Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Queen Sonja. Back, left to right: Marit Tjessem, the mother of Crown Princess Mette-Marit, Crown Prince Haakon, Prince Sverre Magnus and Marius Borg Høiby.Photograph: Lise Åserud/NTB/AFP/Getty ImagesHarald was seen as the Norwegian monarchy’s great moderniser, revamping the crown estates and changing the way the court is run. He married Sonja, a commoner, in 1968 and welcomed two others, Mette-Marit and Ari Behn, as the spouses of his children.A great-great-grandchild ‌of Britain’s Queen Victoria, he succeeded his father, Olav V, at the age of 54 after studying at Oxford and representing his country in sailing events at the Tokyo, Mexico City and Munich Olympics. He was widely appreciated in Norway for his unassuming lifestyle and commitment to national unity.In an emotional speech in 2011 after the far-right extremistAnders Behring Breivikkilled 77 in two terror attacks, he told his subjects that “freedom is stronger than fear” and as “a father, grandfather and spouse, I can only begin to sense some of the pain you feel. As king of the nation, I feel for every one of you.”In a widely praised 2016 speech, he laudeddiversity, tolerance and LGBTQ+ rights, saying Norwegians came from Afghanistan and Pakistan, believed “in God, in Allah and in nothing”, and included “girls who love girls, boys who love boys and girls and boys who love each other”.View image in fullscreenKing Harald and Queen Sonja at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan, Italy.Photograph: Heiko Junge/ReutersMette-Marit, 53, who has a serious lung disease and had a transplant in July, was a single mother to Høiby, who was four years old when her engagement to Norway’s crown prince was announced in late 2000.The marriage, which marked the first time in modern European history that a direct heir to a throne had brought a stepson into a royal family, caused huge controversy in Norway but was strongly backed by King Harald and Queen Sonja.Mette-Marit acknowledged having what she described as a rebellious youth and prior drug use, holding an emotional press conference a week before the wedding in which she expressed regret for her choices and strongly condemned drug use.Explore more on these topicsNorwayEuropeJeffrey EpsteinnewsShareReuse this content

title: French far-right leader Jordan Bardella to address Reform UK party conference  | Marine Le Pen | The Guardian
description: Speech part of effort to strengthen National Rally party’s international ties before Marine Le Pen’s presidential bid
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Speech part of effort to strengthen National Rally party’s international ties before Marine Le Pen’s presidential bid
