Content: Marine Le Pen launched her campaign for the French presidency this summer, pitching a joint ticket with Jordan Bardella as candidate for prime minister.Photograph: Chesnot/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarine Le Pen launched her campaign for the French presidency this summer, pitching a joint ticket with Jordan Bardella as candidate for prime minister.Photograph: Chesnot/Getty ImagesMarine Le PenFrench far-right leader Jordan Bardella to address Reform UK party conferenceSpeech part of effort to strengthen National Rally party’s international ties before Marine Le Pen’s presidential bidAngelique Chrisafisin ParisFri 28 Aug 2026 09.57 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French far-right leaderJordan Bardellais to give a speech at Reform UK’s party conference in Birmingham next week as he attempts to boost international ties beforeMarine Le Pen’s bid for the French presidency next spring.Le Pen’s far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN) is high in the polls and she is predicted to reach the final round of the French presidential race in May.Populism unites Le Pen and Farage. But she is a step closer to powerRead moreLe Pen launched her presidential campaign this summer despite a Paris appeal courtupholding her convictionfor being at the centre of theembezzlementof more than €2.8m (£2.4m) in European parliament funds and funnelling the money into her party between 2004 and 2016. She has appealed against the ruling to France’s highest court.Le Pen, the RN’s parliamentary leader in the National Assembly and the party leader from 2011 to 2021, has said she will run for president on a joint ticket with Bardella as prime minister. Under the French political system, the president, who is head of state and has authority on foreign policy and national security, directly appoints a prime minister as head of government to run domestic affairs.Bardella’s team confirmed that he would travel to Birmingham to address theReform UK conferencenext Friday and hold a joint press conference with the Reform leader, Nigel Farage.View image in fullscreenMarine Le Pen has said she will run for president on a joint ticket with Jordan Bardella as prime minister.Photograph: Yoan Valat/EPABardella, 30, and Farage, 62, held a private lunch in London at the end of last year, where they discussed anti-immigration policy.“Nigel Farage is a great patriot, he has fought all his life to defend his country’s independence, freedom and sovereignty,” Bardella said after his talks with Farage. He said he hoped the Reform leader would be Britain’s next prime minister.Bardella said: “We could perhaps tomorrow be at the head of our respective governments, in a situation where he would be leading a British government and me at the head of a French government. So we’re preparing our future cooperation.“I think that we share a joint determination to stop immigration – to protect our countries from a wave of immigration toEuropethat is just beginning. We’re conscious that our people want to protect their identity, and I think we can find extremely pragmatic and extremely firm solutions to control immigration together.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBardella, who is a member of the European parliament and president of RN, has supported tighter police cooperation between London and Paris on people crossing the Channel on small boats but wanted migrants returned to their countries of origin, not toFrance.View image in fullscreenMarine Le Pen and Nigel Farage have clashed in the past, Farage rejecting a suggestion from Le Pen that Ukip could join a European parliament coalition with the Front National.Photograph: Global Radio/PALe Pen has had a thorny relationship with Farage. In 2014, when he was the Ukip leader and her party was still called Front National (FN), they were competing to be seen as the EU’s leading Eurosceptics in European parliament elections. That year, Faragerejected a suggestionfrom Le Pen that Ukip could join a European parliament coalition with the FN, saying there was “prejudice and antisemitism” in Le Pen’s party. She rejected his comments, saying Farage had made “defamatory” and “extremely disagreeable declarations” in an attempt to boost his popularity.TheReform UKleader was recentlyre-electedin a byelection in Clacton. However, parliament’s standards commissioner immediately reopened an investigation into whether he should have declared a series of gifts provided to him shortly before the last general election. These include a£5m personal gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, and further financial support from his friend and convicted fraudster George Cottrell.Explore more on these topicsMarine Le PenFranceReform UKThe far rightEuropeNigel FarageBirminghamnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Confluence of errors’ led to Belgian tourist Celine Cremer’s death in Tasmanian wilderness, coroner finds | Tasmania | The Guardian
description: Coroner finds 31-year-old deviated from a walking track as dusk fell, four days before the winter solstice
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Coroner finds 31-year-old deviated from a walking track as dusk fell, four days before the winter solstice
Content: Overnight temperatures were close to freezing and Belgian backpacker Celine Cremer, 31, had insufficient clothing, including nothing waterproof, the coroner found.Photograph: Supplied by Tasmania police/AAPView image in fullscreenOvernight temperatures were close to freezing and Belgian backpacker Celine Cremer, 31, had insufficient clothing, including nothing waterproof, the coroner found.Photograph: Supplied by Tasmania police/AAPTasmania‘Confluence of errors’ led to Belgian tourist Celine Cremer’s death in Tasmanian wilderness, coroner findsCoroner finds 31-year-old deviated from a walking track as dusk fell, four days before the winter solsticeFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressFri 28 Aug 2026 00.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 04.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOverlapping errors, including a lack of preparation in near-freezing winter weather, contributed to the death of a Belgian tourist on a wilderness track.Celine Cremer set off on a walk at Philosopher Falls in Tasmania’s remote north-west on 17 June 2023 and was reported missing almost 10 days later.Extensive initial police efforts found no trace of the 31-year-old before private searches organised by her friends and family discovered her remains near a river in January 2026.In findings published on Friday, the coroner, Madeleine Wilson, ruled Cremer died between 17 and 21 June, 2023 as a result of an accident.MapHer death followed a “confluence of errors” that began when she took a walking track towards Magnet Dam after visiting the Philosopher Falls lookout.“The track to Magnet Dam was not well defined and she wandered off track and became lost,” Wilson said.“The deviation from the track occurred late in the day, four days before the winter solstice, at which time the afternoon light was starting to fade.”View image in fullscreenSearchers scoured wilderness in 2023 near the Philosopher Falls track in Tasmania in the hunt for Cremer. Her remains were found earlier this year.Photograph: Tasmania policeOvernight temperatures in the area at the time were close to freezing and Cremer had insufficient clothing, including nothing waterproof, Wilson said.Phone reception was intermittent and she lost her mobile, which was her only form of communication, late in the afternoon on the day she set out.Her phone was found by a search party of volunteers in December 2025.Recovered data showed she took several photos and videos between 2.21pm and 2.42pm and used Google maps several times afterwards with the last input recorded at 4.18pm.It is likely Cremer got lost around 3.49pm and subsequently became disorientated without her phone and mistakenly changed direction, the coroner said.“It is not possible to determine the route taken once Cremer lost her mobile phone, to her final resting place in the Arthur River,” Wilson said.It was possible Cremer slipped and fell, or tried unsuccessfully to cross the river.Cremer had travelled to Australia in 2022 on a working holiday and was planning to return to the mainland four days after the Philosopher Falls walk.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWilson praised the efforts of a private search company and volunteers which ultimately led to the first discovery of Cremer’s remains.The police response to the missing person report was appropriate and their search efforts were guided by “accepted methodologies”.Police efforts were somewhat limited by weather, Wilson said, noting water levels in the Arthur River were significantly higher in 2023 than when her remains were found.View image in fullscreenThe car of then-missing Belgian tourist Celine Cremer in northwest Tasmania in 2023.Photograph: Tasmania police/AFP/Getty ImagesTasmania Police has committed to a review into the use of private search groups in missing persons investigations, including consideration of formal protocols.Cremer failed to follow standard safety precautions, such as taking appropriate equipment and telling people where you are going, Wilson said.“Walkers should familiarise themselves with these standard safety messages before embarking on short walks, day walks or multi-day hikes,” she said.“Walkers should also be aware that mobile coverage is often intermittent or unavailable in remote areas of the Tasmanian wilderness and should plan accordingly.”Wilson recommended the local council put up signs at the entrance to the Philosopher Falls track, explaining it is not managed for recreational use and the surface is degraded, uneven and may be hazardous.Explore more on these topicsTasmaniaBelgiumEuropenewsShareReuse title: Bondi library returns book How to Sell a Genocide to shelves after State Library ‘outlines the law’ | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Book was removed for review earlier this month following complaint but reinstated after petition and State Library letter to Waverley council
Author: Jordyn Beazley
Headline: Book was removed for review earlier this month following complaint but reinstated after petition and State Library letter to Waverley council
Content: How to Sell A Genocide is back on the shelves at Waverley library in Bondi Junction after previously being removed for review.Photograph: Ellen Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHow to Sell A Genocide is back on the shelves at Waverley library in Bondi Junction after previously being removed for review.Photograph: Ellen Smith/The GuardianAustralia newsBondi library returns book How to Sell a Genocide to shelves after State Library ‘outlines the law’Book was removed for review earlier this month following complaint but reinstated after petition and State Library letter to Waverley councilFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJordyn BeazleyFri 28 Aug 2026 00.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Sydney library has returned to its borrowing shelves a book critical ofIsraelcalled How to Sell a Genocide following a public campaign and an intervention from the State Library of New South Wales.Waverley libraryremoved the book “for review” earlier this month after the Jewish news outletJWire reportedit had approached the council.JWire said a survivor of December’santisemitic attack at Bondi, during which 15 people were killed, saw How to Sell a Genocide on the “new release / hot item” shelf and wrote on Facebook that the display was distressing for survivors and bereaved families.Guardian Australia was unable to locate the Facebook post. Waverley library at Bondi Junction is in the same council area as Bondi beach.Bondi library removes book How to Sell a Genocide from shelves after complaintRead moreA staff member at the council-operated library on Friday confirmed the book was back on its shelves. Waverley council was contacted for comment.The State Library had written to the council reminding it of its obligations under guidelines issued by the Library Council of NSW and the Library Act “which was amended in 2026 to reinforce their independence to develop and maintain collections”.“The State Library of NSW supports free and equitable access to information,” a spokesperson said.“The library acknowledges that some books and materials may not align with everyone’s personal views, experiences or beliefs, but supports the right of individuals to make their own choices about what they read, view and access.“The library has outlined to Waverley council the law and policy relevant to this situation.”Ramia Abdo Sultan, a lawyer, helped organise a change.org petition calling for the book to be returned to the shelves. She said in a social media post on Thursday that Waverley library’s manager had notified staff that was happening.“There are 21 people so far queued up in a waiting list for that book,” Abdo Sultan, a board member of the AustraliaPalestineAdvocacy Network, said.The petition to restore the book was signed by almost 2,500 people.“We acknowledge and respect the grief and trauma experienced by victims of violence and antisemitism,” it stated.“However, individual distress, offence or political disagreement should not determine what the broader public is permitted to access through a public library. Readers should be afforded the opportunity to access books freely and form their own opinions on the contents of the book.”The book, published by Pluto Press and written by Adam Johnson, critiques what it claims is the US media’s “complicity in the destruction of Gaza”.Johnson welcomed the decision to reinstate his book but criticised the council for “thus far refusing to answer what complaint prompted the book’s removal”. Johnson said he hoped to find out “through legal channels”.“It’s obviously a good development the council decided to end their ban of the book amid pressure from free speech and Palestine activists, whose support I am grateful for,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But it was never about one library or one book, but about the increased suppression of pro-Palestine speech in Australia, which has radically escalated over the past seven months. Attempts to blame Palestine solidarity and sympathies for the Bondi attack, as the book ban advocates repeatedly did, is the real story. This false and sleazy conflation must stop.”Guardian Australia approached the Executive Council of Australian Jewry (Ecaj) and the NSW Jewish Board of Deputies for comment.Alex Ryvchin, the co-chief executive officer of Ecaj, previously welcomed the book’s removal.“A book of this sort has no place on the shelves of a library, especially one within minutes of where Australians were slaughtered [at Bondi],” Ryvchin told the Sydney Morning Herald.“I commend the individual who spotted the book, herself a survivor of the massacre, and acted to have it removed.”Bart Shteinman, an executive member of the progressive Jewish Council of Australia, said the book should “never have been removed in the first place”.“This debacle should be a lesson for other councils that stifling literary freedom only confuses and undermines the critical struggle against antisemitism and all forms of racism,” he said on Thursday.“Banning books is not something any council should be doing.”The president of the Australia Palestine Advocacy Network, Nasser Mashni, said: “That a single complaint was enough to trigger the removal of a book about the genocide in Palestine should concern every Australian who values free inquiry and open debate. These efforts must be resisted.”Multiple human rights groups have said Israel’s actions in Gaza amount to genocide, which Israel denies. In June, an ⁠independent UN inquiry foundIsrael continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.At the time the book was removed, a Waverley council spokesperson said: “The book has been removed from library shelves for review, and council will further consider processes to ensure closer oversight of book selection.”Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsGazaMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chinese control of information hampers assessment of Tibet flood damage | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Scale of devastation emerges in Nepal as reporters reach disaster area, but Chinese state media focus more on rescue efforts
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Scale of devastation emerges in Nepal as reporters reach disaster area, but Chinese state media focus more on rescue efforts
Content: Search and rescue operations in Shigatse, Tibet, on Friday.Photograph: China News Service/GettyView image in fullscreenSearch and rescue operations in Shigatse, Tibet, on Friday.Photograph: China News Service/GettyNepal-Tibet flood disasterChinese control of information hampers assessment of Tibet flood damageScale of devastation emerges in Nepal as reporters reach disaster area, but Chinese state media focus more on rescue effortsNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesAmy HawkinsSenior China correspondentFri 28 Aug 2026 10.25 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the days since an enormous glacier in the Himalayas snapped away from a mountaintop and cascaded into the valley below, the true scale of the devastation caused by theflash floods in Nepal and Tibetis still unfolding.But the picture is emerging far more quickly inNepalthan in China, where strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.The floodsdevastated villagesalong the Himalayan border region that straddles Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet. On Friday, the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, while in China it was just five, despite the fact that the villages around the Gyirong border crossing are home to several thousand people.1:17Survivors pulled from mud in Nepal after deadly flash floods – videoIn Nepal, journalists rushed to get as close to the disaster zone as possible to interview survivors and rescue workers. Villagers provided minute-by-minute accounts of what happened when the floods, the exact cause of which is still being studied by scientists, tore through their homes.In China, state media carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalistdid not speak toany of the people sitting behind him.Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country. Sporadic protests, including self-immolations, by Tibetans calling for more autonomy and religious freedom have been cracked down on by the authorities. International journalists cannot visitTibetapart from on tightly choreographed government tours. Many Tibetans are not allowed passports and have very limited contact with the outside world. Tibetans can be punished for speaking to journalists. Human rights groups have for years criticised Beijing’s policies on Tibetan language and culture, which activists say are under attack.Map of affected areasThat makes independent assessments of how the flash floods have affected the Tibetan side of the border difficult.“Everything about Tibet is seen through the national security prism. And therefore nobody is going to say anything or report anything that has not been cleared from the very top,” said Steve Tsang, the director of theChinaInstitute at Soas University of London.For anyone on the ground, “you can’t report a higher figure of deaths, even if you have seen more bodies yourself, until the official statement says that the figure has gone up”.What caused the catastrophic flood in Nepal and Tibet – and how does a glacier collapse?Read moreChina’s tight controls on information are limiting international coverage of its relief efforts. That may mean China is missing an opportunity to tell its own good news story.10:11‘Erased before their eyes’: on the ground in decimated Nepal flood zone - The LatestChinese emergency services, including the People’s Liberation Army, are vastly better resourced than their Nepalese counterparts. Navigating the difficult, mountainous terrain where conditions are still unsafe requires specialised expertise. China has dispatched hundreds of emergency service personnel but there is scant detail on what they are doing. “The Chinese have missed a trick,” Tsang said. But “they don’t have that confidence. Their instinct is control.”Still, China has been keen to stress that the disaster is a national priority. China’s leader, Xi Jinping, chaired a meeting on Friday to direct rescue work, according to state media. Xi called on the authorities to “make every effort to search for missing people from China and abroad”. He also dispatched his number two, premier Li Qiang, to visit the affected area. According to the state-run Xinhua news agency, Li “emphasised that General Secretary Xi Jinping is deeply concerned about the people in the disaster-stricken areas”.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterTibetChinaFloodingNepalSouth and central AsiaCensorshipnewsShareReuse this content

title: Race to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burst | Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | The Guardian
description: Flash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Flash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept away
Content: The aftermath of the floods in Nuwakot, Nepal. More than 1,300 people are missing.Photograph: Skanda Gautam/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the floods in Nuwakot, Nepal. More than 1,300 people are missing.Photograph: Skanda Gautam/SOPA Images/ShutterstockNepal-Tibet flood disasterRace to get aid into Nepal and Tibet amid warnings flood lake could burstFlash floods have killed at least 469 people while homes and infrastructure have been swept awayNepal-Tibet flash flood – latest updatesWhat caused the flash flood in Nepal and Tibet?Hannah Ellis-PetersenandGaurav Pokharelin Kathmandu,Sam JonesandAmy HawkinsFri 28 Aug 2026 00.48 EDTFirst published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe international community was scrambling to get aid into flood-stricken parts of Nepal andTibeton Thursday as authorities warned that a lake ⁠formed at the ⁠site ⁠where the ​deadly torrents occurred ⁠was rising and ⁠at risk ​of ‌bursting.The catastrophic flash floods that hitNepaland Tibet on Wednesday, thundering down valleys and obliterating entire villages, killed at least 469 people and left more than 1,300 missing.Efforts to locate those unaccounted for – including hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada – have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 25 miles (40km) of roads in the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.Satellite images showing before and after collapseNepali army helicopter rescue teams were working on Friday to rescue about 100 people trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by the devastating flood.“Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” said Nepal army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet.“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.”The prime minister’s office said the army was working in tough conditions and had already rescued 350 workers and local people who were trapped in the tunnel amid the risky conditions.Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the border with India. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.Videos from Wednesday showed amassive wall of water crashing down on the borderas people tried to flee. The power, volume and speed of the floods gave little time for escape.Trucks were overturned and houses, roads ⁠and power plants were swept away in Nepal, while ​officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties” after a mudslide hit a border crossing.How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guideRead moreTom Fletcher, the UN’s humanitarian chief, described the flood as “horrifying”. He said emergency teams had been mobilised and an initial $2m (£1.5m) of disaster funds allocated to cover emergency medical care, shelter and water.9:21‘Tsunami from the sky:’ floods leave trail of devastation in Nepal and Tibet - The LatestNepal’s disaster authority warned of continuing danger on Thursday, appealing to residents and rescuers to stay away from a swelling lake that had formed at the flood site. Chinese authorities said a barrier lake at the confluence of the Tsogyal and Purupqiangzangbu rivers was overflowing and could burst.Girilal Budhathoki, 36, who lives in the Rasuwa district of Nepal’s Bagmati province, said the flood waters swept away his wife and four children while he was away from the family home.“A huge surge of water came,” he said. “Everything turned completely black, and I couldn’t understand what was happening. Suddenly, something heavy crushed me and I fell down.”Budhathoki realised what had happened only when he returned to the place where his house had stood. “I searched desperately for my wife and children but I couldn’t find them,” he said. “They didn’t make it out. My wife was swept away too. I am all alone now.”Map showing location of the disasterKamal Kharel, who works at a hydropower plant in Chilime, also in Rasuwa district, was in the office when the floods hit. “The whole place shook as if there had been a huge earthquake,” he said. “But when I went outside, I saw everything a storm and raging water.”Kharel and some of his colleagues managed to climb a hill, where they stayed until they were rescued by the army on Thursday morning. “I had never seen waves crashing that high. You only see waves like that in the sea.”People from the hard-hit districts of Nuwakot and Dhading, in Bagmati province, were seen gathering outside an army training centre – the base for helicopter rescue operations – seeking information about missing family members.Police were recording the names of the missing outside the barracks gate. Mobile phone torches were their only source of light as the area remained without electricity because of damaged hydroelectric infrastructure.View image in fullscreenFlooding has caused widespread damage to homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure in Nuwakot, Nepal.Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/Zuma Press/ShutterstockThe village of Soley, in Nuwakot, which had about 25 homes, was almost wiped out, according to Nirajan Paudyal, a Kathmandu-based journalist whose parents and other relatives lived there. Desperate for information, he had travelled to the area on Thursday for news of his family. “There is no update till now,” he said. “I fear there won’t be any update.”More than 500 foreigners were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.Many of the victims were on a pilgrimage to Kailash Mansarovar, a high-altitude site in ‌Tibet revered by Hindus and Buddhists among others.Early reports from Nepali ​officials suggested an earthquake could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger ‌the floods. But the US Geological Survey later said what was initially reported ‌as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was a seismic shock generated by glacial rock and ice collapsing, causing the flood of debris. “No earthquake had occurred,” it said.A graphic showing how the situation unfolded.Srijana Gurung, the acting Nepal director for the international NGO Plan International, said communities across the Himalayan country were facing “climate shock after shock” with hardly any time to recover.“Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense,” she said. “The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need.”Gurung said children and families who had lost their homes and livelihoods would be in urgent need of medical help, food, shelter and hygiene kits. “There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged,” she said.View image in fullscreenPeople look at the devastation left by flash flooding in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/APScant information emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction. Tibet is the most tightly controlled part ofChinaeven under normal circumstances. Foreign journalists cannot visit the region unless they are part of a government-controlled tour and the authorities have cracked down harshly on calls for greater autonomy from the Tibetan people. Tibetans have almost no contact with the international media because of fears of retribution.Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.Locator map for the wider regionMaya Wang, the deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch, wrote on X: “The floods raise questions about whether Chinese authorities could’ve done more to reduce disaster risks, given longstanding concerns from Tibetan diaspora groups and experts about rapid, state-led development in areas where Tibetans have little say.”She called on Beijing to “allow Tibetans access to information and international researchers and journalists unfettered access to the region, and conduct a rigorous investigation into the disaster”.This article was amended on 28 August 2026. The Nepalese district of Chitwan borders India, not Tibet as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepalTibetChinaSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Man, 41, dies after large sign falls at Christian festival in West Sussex | West Sussex | The Guardian
description: Six more people hospitalised after incident at Big Church festival near Steyning
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Six more people hospitalised after incident at Big Church festival near Steyning
Content: The Big Church festival on the Wiston Estate was cancelled after the incident on Friday afternoon.Photograph: bigchurchfestivalView image in fullscreenThe Big Church festival on the Wiston Estate was cancelled after the incident on Friday afternoon.Photograph: bigchurchfestivalWest SussexMan, 41, dies after large sign falls at Christian festival in West SussexSix more people hospitalised after incident at Big Church festival near SteyningNadeem BadshahFri 28 Aug 2026 19.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 41-year-old man has died and at least six other people have been injured after a large sign fell at a Christian festival inWest Sussex, police said.The man, from Eastbourne, East Sussex, was pronounced dead at the scene after the incident at the Big Church festival near Steyning on Friday afternoon.His next of kin have been told and are being supported by specialist officers, Sussex police said.The force added that at least six other people have been taken to hospital for treatment.DCS Richard McDonagh said: “This is a tragic incident and our thoughts go out to the man’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”Anyone with any information or relevant video footage has been asked to contact police.In a post on Instagram shortly after 5.30pm, organisers told attenders the show had been cancelled and all day visitors “must leave the site now”.Organisers later said they had decided to cancel the rest of the festival, which had been scheduled to run until Sunday.“We are devastated by the serious incident that took place at Big Church festival 2026 today, in which a sign fell, injuring at least seven people, one of whom tragically lost their life,” the festival said in an online statement.“First and foremost, all of our thoughts are with those who have been affected, their families and friends, and everyone who witnessed what happened.“Following today’s incident, we have made the decision to bring Big Church festival 2026 to a close.”Officers remained at the scene on Friday night, and people were advised to avoid the area.The incident has been reported to the Health and Safety Executive and local authority, Sussex police said.McDonagh added: “I recognise the immense distress this will have caused people at the festival, and we are working with a number of partners as we seek to establish exactly what happened.“We know there were thousands of people at the festival and we’re urging anyone with any information, or any relevant video footage, to please come forward.”Explore more on these topicsWest SussexnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police arrest seven more men in aftermath of deadly A66 crash | UK news | The Guardian
description: Cleveland police say a total of 24 people arrested in investigation after crash that killed two officers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cleveland police say a total of 24 people arrested in investigation after crash that killed two officers
Content: Floral tributes left after the A66 crash in Grangetown.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFloral tributes left after the A66 crash in Grangetown.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianUK newsPolice arrest seven more men in aftermath of deadly A66 crashCleveland police say a total of 24 people arrested in investigation after crash that killed two officersPress AssociationFri 28 Aug 2026 18.00 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 15.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeven more men have been arrested as part of an operation tackling alleged organised crime after the head-on crash on the A66 that resulted in seven deaths, Cleveland police have said.Officers said four men, aged 21, 25, 35 and 40, were being held on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life after a vehicle crashed into a house in Steele Crescent, Middlesbrough.They were also being questioned over alleged arson after a caravan was set alight in Atlee Road on Wednesday morning, and over a drug offence.The force said the men were in a vehicle when they were stopped by police in Kingsley Road in Grangetown on Thursday night.Class A drugs were seized, officers confirmed.The three other men arrested were a 23-year-old man, on suspicion of threats to kill, a 42-year-old on suspicion of threats to kill and possession of criminal property, and a 30-year-old on suspicion of possession of criminal property.All three have been released on conditional bail.It brings the total number of people arrested since the crash to 24.Earlier on Friday, detectives confirmed they were not linking a house fire that killed a seven-year-old girl and her aunt to the A66 crash, which left two police officers and five young men dead.Hundreds of extra police officers have been drafted in to support officers after a series of incidents in the Middlesbrough and County Durham area.Inquests have been formally opened into the deaths of the seven people in the crash in the early hours of 22 August. The two police officers who died were PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38.The Teesside area coroner, Paul Appleton, said that there was a collision at South Bank between a police vehicle and a Volkswagen Passat.He said the provisional cause of death for Blades was head and neck injuries and for Clough it was neck injuries.Later, inquests were opened and adjourned into the deaths of the Passat occupants, named as Cole Worthy and Theo Rae, both 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jakub Matusiak.Police initially arrested 17 people after the crash, which followed a police pursuit, as part of an investigation into alleged organised crime.Cleveland police assistant chief constable Wayne Fox said of the latest arrests: “This latest disruptive activity now brings the total number of arrests to 24 since the investigation commenced.“Several suspects arrested throughout the course of this week have been charged with serious offences and a number of offenders have been recalled to prison.”On Friday, Cleveland police said Kai Inico, who was arrested on Monday on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, had been charged with possession with intent to supply a class B drug.The force said four other people arrested on Monday had been bailed – a 16-year-old boy and 18-year-old man arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, a 55-year-old man arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender, and a 23-year-old man arrested on suspicion of threats to kill.Earlier this week, two other people were charged with offences and appeared in court.Meanwhile, two men have been arrested on suspicion of murder in connection with the fire which killed Natalie McDonald, 34, and seven-year-old Valentina Foster, as well as injuring four others, in Grangetown.Matt Storey, the police and crime commissioner for Cleveland, said on Friday: “After what has been the most tragic week in its history, I want to extend my heartfelt thanks to local residents for the outpouring of love and support they have shown to Cleveland police.“My thoughts remain with the family, friends and colleagues of PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough. They will be remembered as selfless, professional and courageous police officers, dedicated to serving their communities.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Large fire near Wembley Stadium disrupts tube and rail services | London | The Guardian
description: About 125 firefighters tackle blaze at Neasden waste facility as nearby Amazon warehouse is evacuated
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: About 125 firefighters tackle blaze at Neasden waste facility as nearby Amazon warehouse is evacuated
Content: Huge fire breaks out on industrial estate near Wembley stadiumLondonLarge fire near Wembley Stadium disrupts tube and rail servicesAbout 125 firefighters tackle blaze at Neasden waste facility as nearby Amazon warehouse is evacuatedNadeem Badshahand agenciesFri 28 Aug 2026 17.47 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA large fire broke out at a waste facility close toWembley Stadiumin north-west London, disrupting tube and train lines in the area.Twenty fire engines and about 125 firefighters were sent to tackle the blaze at a mixed-waste facility on an industrial estate in Neasden, less than a mile from the venue.There was no service on the entire Metropolitan line, which runs close to the blaze, and no service between Wembley Park and West Hampstead on the Jubilee line, with severe delays on the rest of the line, Transport forLondonsaid.Rail services into London Marylebone were also disrupted.View image in fullscreenAbout 125 firefighters and 20 fire engines were sent to tackle the blaze.Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesA nearby Amazon warehouse, separate from the industrial unit involved, was evacuated, according to PA Media.A London fire brigade assistant commissioner, Andy Pennick, said: “The brigade was called at 11.36[am] to reports of a fire on Hannah Close, Neasden. Upon arrival, firefighters were met by a well-developed fire involving a waste transfer facility.“Recognising the scale of the fire, the initial officer in attendance immediately requested 20 fire engines be mobilised to the scene.“An industrial unit, approximately 100 metres by 150 metres, was alight. At the height of the fire, around 125 firefighters were in attendance.”Pennick added: “This is a protracted incident that will see crews on scene for the remainder of the day as they work to fully extinguish the fire.”The LFB earlier said that the blaze was under control by about 5pm. Its cause was not yet known and was under investigation, the LFB added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is the third major fire at a recycling centre in London this summer.Earlier this month, about 100 firefighters responded toa blaze at a facility in Deptford, which involved about 50 tonnes of stored household waste.Fires at recycling centres caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries, such as those found in vapes, are occurring at the rate of more than 10 a week, according to figures from the Environmental Services Association.Battery fires at waste facilities are estimated to cost £1bn a yearand are causing growing frustration among fire chiefs.Explore more on these topicsLondonWembley StadiumEnglandWastenewsShareReuse this content

title: New heart attack definition promises better care for women | Heart attack | The Guardian
description: Leading cardiovascular health groups reclassify overlooked causes and introduce sex-specific diagnostic thresholds
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Leading cardiovascular health groups reclassify overlooked causes and introduce sex-specific diagnostic thresholds
Content: There has been ‘unintended systematic bias against women’ in the previous guidance, the doctors say.Photograph: David Sillitoe/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThere has been ‘unintended systematic bias against women’ in the previous guidance, the doctors say.Photograph: David Sillitoe/The GuardianHeart attackNew heart attack definition promises better care for womenLeading cardiovascular health groups reclassify overlooked causes and introduce sex-specific diagnostic thresholdsAndrew GregoryHealth editor in MunichFri 28 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoctors have agreed the world’s first universal definition of a heart attack, paving the way for millions of women to finally receive better treatment after decades of being “deprioritised”.In one of the biggest procedural shake-ups in a generation, the world’s four leading cardiovascular health groups have signed off on new guidance for healthcare professionals when seeing suspected heart attack patients.Historically, some less common forms of heart attack, which evidence shows typically affect women far more than men, have been coded as less important, with treatment and care often worse as a result.Until now, experts said, women had been getting less effective treatments, which did not always target the specific cause of their heart attack and could even make them more unwell.Now the world’s top cardiologists have promised a “revolution” in care after agreeing the biggest overhaul of how heart attacks are defined and diagnosed in decades, in part to reduce the often deadly delays afflicting women.The landmark agreement was announced in Munich on the opening day of the annual congress of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC), the world’s largest heart conference.The new guidance will upgrade three types of attack that are up to 10 times more common in women and often caused by childbirth, exercise and emotional stress.Why gender is at the heart of the matter for cardiac illnessRead moreThe most serious cases, previously known as “type 1” and now classed as “primary” heart attacks, had previously prioritised those caused by a clot blocking blood flow to the heart.However, the types of attacks more common in women involve reduced blood flow for other reasons, such as a tear or tightening of arteries, and are more likely to be missed or not treated as urgently, with delays to care.The new guidelines will also reduce the threshold for any type of heart attack to be diagnosed in women based upon the levels of a protein called troponin in their blood.Until now, women had been expected to reach the same threshold as men for troponin – which is released when the heart is injured and damaged – to get a diagnosis.Speaking to reporters in Munich, Prof Bryan Williams, the chief scientific and medical officer of the British Heart Foundation, Britain’s biggest heart charity, said: “This is a landmark moment, a radical shift in how we define and diagnose heart attacks worldwide which will transform people’s care.“For decades, women have missed out on accurate diagnoses and treatment. This focus on finding less common causes of heart attacks, which predominantly affect women, should help to change that. It could be life-changing for huge numbers of women in the UK and worldwide.”Crucially, the new streamlined heart attack categories will also help patients to fully understand the cause of their heart attack and what comes next, Williams said.The three types of heart attacks that have been upgraded – and which mostly affect women – are coronary artery spasm, coronary embolism, and spontaneous coronary artery dissection (Scad).The first involves the tightening of the artery, which can deprive the heart muscle of blood and oxygen and cause a heart attack, and can be caused by emotional stress, exercise or extreme cold.The second is where a blood clot or fatty deposit travels to a coronary artery and causes a blockage.And the third is caused by a tear in the coronary artery, which occurs in women at least 80% of the time and often happens during or soon after pregnancy.I work in a hospital – and didn’t know I was having a heart attack. Here’s what more women should knowRead moreProf Nicholas Mills, a cardiologist at the University of Edinburgh who led the international taskforce of doctors that agreed the new guidelines, said it was “the first time that we’ve had a truly global approach to aligning how we diagnose what is probably the most important diagnosis there is”.“It kills so many people, and we’ve never got everyone together around the world to agree how we’re going to describe it, classify it, explain it to our patients,” he said.“Our job now is to implement this as widely as possible. It’s just as relevant for the UK as it is for any other country around the world. It is a revolution. It’s going to make care better for patients.”Mills said there had been “unintended systematic bias against women”, including by using the key blood test for diagnosing heart attacks at an average level, which picks up all men but misses some women.“This is used for all types of heart attack in every emergency department in the world, and we want to make sure that it’s used correctly,” he said.The new guidelines, published in the European Heart Journal, were drawn up by the world’s four leading cardiovascular health groups: the ESC, the American College of Cardiology, the American Heart Association and the World Heart Federation.Explore more on these topicsHeart attackWomen's healthHealthGermanynewsShareReuse this content

title: London Science Museum cuts links with BP after decades of partnership | Museums | The Guardian
description: Campaigners say ‘seismic shift’ follows years of pressure to sever ties with oil and gas firm
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Campaigners say ‘seismic shift’ follows years of pressure to sever ties with oil and gas firm
Content: Climate protesters outside the London Science Museum in 2021.Photograph: Anna VickerstaffView image in fullscreenClimate protesters outside the London Science Museum in 2021.Photograph: Anna VickerstaffMuseumsLondon Science Museum cuts links with BP after decades of partnershipCampaigners say ‘seismic shift’ follows years of pressure to sever ties with oil and gas firmPippa NeillEnvironment reporterFri 28 Aug 2026 12.57 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheLondonScience Museum has ended its decades-long partnership with the oil and gas company BP in what has been described as a “seismic shift” for the museum.The Science Museum Group academy, which was established in 2018 to provide training and resources, announced on Friday that it would be ending its partnership withBP. In a statement, the director and chief executive of the Science Museum Group, Sir Ian Blatchford, said the partnership had “drawn to a close at the end of the current contract term”.Blatchford said BP’s “generous contributions helped us to inspire more than 11,000 education, museum and science professionals through research-informed science engagement training, supporting vital work to spark curiosity and bring science to life for more than 1 million young people across the country”.BP’s relationship with the Science Museum, which goes back decades, has come under previous scrutiny, with the company accused by campaigners of havingan “insidious influence” over the teaching of science, technology, engineering and maths(Stem) in the UK through its relationship with the museum.A spokesperson for BP said: “BP and the Science Museum Group Academy’s partnership will draw to a close on Monday 31 August at the end of its agreed term.”View image in fullscreenScientist Rebellion activists demonstrate in the Science Museum’s energy hall against the museum’s sponsorship by Adani, BP and Equinor.Photograph: Andrea Domeniconi/AlamyIn 2024, the museumcut tieswith the oil company Equinor over its failure to lower carbon emissions sufficiently to ensure it was aligned with theParis climate agreementgoal of limiting global heating to 1.5C.Chris Garrard of the campaign group Culture Unstained said this “seismic shift” came after years of campaigning and growing pressure from educators and schools, some of which have pledged to boycott trips to the museum over its partnership with BP.“BP’s commitment to climate action was never worth the paper it was written on but the Science Museum’s director passionately championed his partnership with the major polluter year after year. Now, with the world facing droughts and wildfires and BP recklessly ramping up its production of dirty fossil fuels, the museum has finally come to its senses and followed the rest of the culture sector in cutting ties to BP,” he said.However, Garrard said this decision represented only a “partial victory”. The museum still takes money from Adani GreenEnergyLtd, a subsidiary of the Adani Group, one of the world’s largest private coal mining and energy conglomerates.The academy provides training and resources to teachers, museum practitioners and the Stem industry nationally and internationally.Explore more on these topicsMuseumsCorporate sponsorshipBPFossil fuelsFossil fuel divestmentOil and gas companiesEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: Los Angeles fire survivors face record wait for federal disaster aid under Trump | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: Nearly 600 days after the devastating 2025 fires, thousands of Los Angeles residents are still waiting for more than $15bn in federal funds to rebuild their communities
Author: Gabrielle Canon
Headline: Nearly 600 days after the devastating 2025 fires, thousands of Los Angeles residents are still waiting for more than $15bn in federal funds to rebuild their communities
Content: Donald Trump has rejected disaster aid for Democratic-run states far more often than his predecessors, approving only 23% of their requests compared to 89% of requests from states largely represented by Republicans.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump has rejected disaster aid for Democratic-run states far more often than his predecessors, approving only 23% of their requests compared to 89% of requests from states largely represented by Republicans.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersLos AngelesLos Angeles fire survivors face record wait for federal disaster aid under TrumpNearly 600 days after the devastating 2025 fires, thousands of Los Angeles residents are still waiting for more than $15bn in federal funds to rebuild their communitiesGabrielle CanonFri 28 Aug 2026 18.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 18.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs thousands of residents in Spokane, Washington, begin to grapple with a long recovery after a destructive set of blazes that consumed hundreds of homes in the state’s second most populated city this month, victims of the Los Angeles firestormbroke a grim record– they have faced the longest delay in modern history for federal aid.Nearly 600 days since a historic firestorm roared into communities across Los Angeles, reducing more than 16,000 structures to ash and toxic debris, the Trump administration has failed to appropriate more than $15bn in long-term recovery funds that are crucial to rebuilding. The delay in supplying the badly needed funds is months longer than the last record set when victims of the Maui fires had to wait 500 days to receive the support,LAist notedthis week.Recoveries from large-scale disasters like these have long stretched across years. But there are concerns that lags or lapses in support from the federal role will add new challenges to already complex rebuilding efforts in devastated areas across the US.Donald Trumphas repeatedly been accused of politicizing disasters, to the detriment of communities left in limbo.“Spokane has joined a rapidly growing list of our communities that have been devastated by these climate-exaggerated fires,” Jay Inslee, the formerWashington stategovernor said, adding that he had recently visited Altadena, one of the areas of Los Angeles decimated by the fires. It has just been absolutely ripped open and has not been able to recover yet,” he said. “Donald Trump has strangled these communities by refusing to give emergency assistance.”View image in fullscreenThe Palisades Fire ravages a neighborhood amid high winds in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles on 7 January 2025.Photograph: Ethan Swope/APAlong with withholding funds,the president has also imposed “unlawful” conditions on states requesting federal grantsfor disaster response and preparedness, according to attorneys general from 25 Democratic-led states that sued the administration in July.The group, which was led by California’s Rob Bonta, claimed the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) have used a “campaign of coercion”, leveraging the needed disaster support in an attempt to force states to implement voting and immigration policies pushed by the president.Trump has rejected disaster aid for Democratic-run states far more often than his predecessors, approvingonly 23% of their requests compared with 89% of requests from states largely represented by Republicans, Politico reported in March. The president alsoinitially threatened to attach political conditionsto federal aid he said would go to Los Angeles fire victims.Meanwhile, recovery there has been painful and slow.The fires, which erupted in the parched southern California hillsides andcascaded into the surrounding suburbs with shocking ferocityin January 2025, left behind unprecedented levels of destruction in the city and county of Los Angeles. Thirty-one people were killed directly by the disaster. Homes, businesses, churches and schools were leveled in the aftermath, with thousands more structures left uninhabitable or damaged from smoke and surrounding toxic debris.View image in fullscreenAerial view of the Pacific Palisades community undergoing reconstruction after the Eaton fire on 17 July in Los Angeles.Photograph: Qian Weizhong/VCG/Getty Images“Eighteen months after the Eaton and Palisades fires, the challenges facing impacted communities continue to grow more urgent,” the Department of Angels, a non-profit founded to support recovery efforts in the immediate aftermath of the fire,wrote in its latest report, which noted that LA had experienced the longest wait for major disaster funding from the federal government in modern history.With the second anniversary of the fires just months away, scores ofAngelenos remain in limbo.Roughlytwo-thirds of survivors were still displaced as of late July, according to a report from the Department of Angels. In their sixth survey done with more than 2,000 fire victims, the group found that all forms of financial assistance had decreased in recent months, while homeowners typically face a roughly $500,000 gap in trying to rebuild.Close to half of those affected had to take on debt to stay afloat and 20% have had to delay rebuilding or repairs due to financial constraints. “Recovery has stalled while families wait for the federal resources that have long helped communities rebuild after disasters,” they wrote.While it can take years for federal funds to be allocated in the aftermath of a complex disaster, the Trump administration has yet to begin the long process. State officials have accused the president of politicizing the disaster, which affected acounty that largely votes Democratic.“Donald Trump’s desire to punish Los Angeles and the state of California for not voting for him, means once again that thousands of Angelenos are left watching this administration fight for anything but them, their businesses, and their communities,” the California Democratic senators, Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff said in a joint statement issued in June, after the president’s$87.6bn budget request focused on military funding for the war in Iran omitted funds for disasters.California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, hasreportedly made several additional requests to Trump over the last 18 months,urging immediate action to support victims of the fire. These requests had yet to be approved as of early August, according to the governor.In March,the state issued an updated accounting of what’s neededfrom the federal government, which includes roughly $10.5bn in Community Development Block Grants to help with rebuilding both housing and infrastructure, $179m in economic development administration business grants and $3bn for public assistance projects meant to replace damaged or destroyed schools, senior centers, libraries and parks. The governor has also requested support to restore damaged water systems and improve affected streets and sidewalks.Newsom called on Trump to make good on his pledge to provide the support while the president was visiting LA earlier this month. The trip, however, has come and gone.Advocates and officials in Washington are also urging Trump to take urgent action to support the fire recovery just beginning there.“There is a major effort to put pressure on this president to do his job, which is to help these families and communities – and he hasn’t done that,” Inslee said.In 2020, while Inslee was governor, Trump neglected to issue a disaster declaration that would help victims in the rural town of Malden, Washington, after a fire destroyed roughly 80% of the homes there,due to a political feud between the two politicians.The order came a year later, after Biden took office.“We’re hoping that that does not happen again in the Spokane fires,” Inslee said. “We’re hoping that he will have an epiphany to understand what his job is, which is to help all Americans, no matter who they voted for.”Explore more on these topicsLos AngelesCaliforniaWildfiresDonald TrumpTrump administrationWest CoastGavin NewsomnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump arch will alter sightlines of many Washington DC landmarks, report says | Washington DC | The Guardian
description: National Park Service, which backs the 250ft arch, says it is likely to disrupt historical significance of dozens of sites
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: National Park Service, which backs the 250ft arch, says it is likely to disrupt historical significance of dozens of sites
Content: Donald Trump holds models for his proposed ‘Independence Arch’ in the East Room of the White House on 15 October 2025.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump holds models for his proposed ‘Independence Arch’ in the East Room of the White House on 15 October 2025.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty ImagesWashington DCTrump arch will alter sightlines of many Washington DC landmarks, report saysNational Park Service, which backs the 250ft arch, says it is likely to disrupt historical significance of dozens of sitesAssociated PressFri 28 Aug 2026 17.36 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new National Park Service report backsDonald Trump’s proposed arch, despite what it says are adverse effects to the sightlines of a host of landmarks in Washington, including the Washington Monument and the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials.The report released on Friday says the 250ft-tall (76-meter) memorial arch is likely to disrupt the historical significance of dozens of sites near its planned location adjacent to the Arlington Memorial Bridge.Many of Washington’s monuments, buildings and sites have been carefully planned over decades to reflect significant moments in the nation’s history and to evoke symbolism through sightlines that connect them to other sites. The arch will disturb the sightline between more Washington landmarks than anticipated, the report said.But the Park Service report says “the same characteristics that make Memorial Circle sensitive from a preservation perspective are also the characteristics that make it the historically appropriate location for the undertaking”.The project’s effects cannot be “fully avoided without either relocating the Arch away from the historically identified site or eliminating the principal commemorative feature, both of which would fail to meet the undertaking’s purpose and need”, the report said.“For this reason, alternative locations outside Memorial Circle are not reasonable avoidance alternatives,” the report said.The 133-page report by the park service supports Trump’s plans for the arch and could play an important role in bolstering the administration’s case in its fight against a legal challenge filed by three veterans and a group of historians.The proposed towering gilded arch, which last month received initial approval from a key federal commission, would affect the “integrity” of dozens of historic properties because it would change “character-defining visual and spatial relationships” among them.One of the most obvious elements the report cited is that the arch would break alignment among the Lincoln Memorial, Memorial Bridge and Arlington House, which was the Confederate general Robert E Lee’s home. That alignment was “intended to physically and symbolically unite North and South through a coordinated monumental composition extending across the Potomac River”, the report said.The Lincoln Memorial-Arlington House connection was one of dozens listed as being affected directly by the proposed structure. It added that the National Mall, the US Capitol, the Washington Monument, the Jefferson Memorial, the Georgetown Historic District, the Old Naval Observatory, the Francis Scott Key Bridge, the National Cathedral and other sites also would be affected.Nicolas Sansone, an attorney with Public Citizen Litigation Group, which is representing the plaintiffs, said the report “confirms what we’ve been saying all along: the project will have an enormous impact and transform that National Mall”.The report underscores the legal challengers’ claim that a project of this size and importance “is a decision for Congress to make” and should not be rushed through by executive decree, Sansone said.Explore more on these topicsWashington DCDonald TrumpUS politicsNational parksnewsShareReuse this content

title: Volunteers rescue man stuck on 10,000ft-high ledge in Sierra Nevada | US news | The Guardian
description: Climber, stuck on 6in ridge, had veered off treacherous path and ‘any fall would almost certainly be fatal’
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Climber, stuck on 6in ridge, had veered off treacherous path and ‘any fall would almost certainly be fatal’
Content: Rescue team on the way to secure man stuck in Sierra Nevada.Photograph: Mono County Sheriff Search and Rescue TeamView image in fullscreenRescue team on the way to secure man stuck in Sierra Nevada.Photograph: Mono County Sheriff Search and Rescue TeamUS newsVolunteers rescue man stuck on 10,000ft-high ledge in Sierra NevadaClimber, stuck on 6in ridge, had veered off treacherous path and ‘any fall would almost certainly be fatal’Uwa Ede-OsifoFri 28 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn ill-fated move left a man stranded on a 6in ledge over 10,000ft off the ground for hours in California’s Sierra Nevada mountain range, before a volunteer rescue team came to his aid.The climber, who has not been publicly identified, had been scaling the Mendenhall couloir, a gully on the face of Laurel mountain, with a friend on Saturday.The route is steep with portions of potentially destabilizing loose rock. The section the man, reportedly an experienced climber, had been traversing had no route markers,accordingto the San Francisco Chronicle.Veering off path, which the man did by accident, can be deadly, according to the Mono county search and rescue team.Trump administration pushing to hand parcel of Yosemite land to private developer – reportRead more“Traveling off-route quickly leads to increasingly vertical, un-protectable 5th-class terrain with no viable means of continuing either up or down. With thousands of feet of vertical exposure below, any fall would almost certainly be fatal,” the volunteerswrotein a Facebook post last weekend.The rescuers were in a race against time.After thesheriff’s office alerted themto the stranded climber, they searched for two hours without coming across the man, the New York Times reported, until at last a voice in the distance became audible.The climber alternated his weight between each foot, which indicated to rescuers his legs could be cramping. “It was determined that, without intervention, a fatal fall was increasingly possible if the subject remained in place overnight,” reads the Facebook post.A hoist operation, when a helicopter crew lifts someone to rescue, was not viable due to powerful winds.The team opted to go by foot, operating at night using their headlamps for light.“It was incredibly dangerous and a little scary moving around in the dead of night – everyone’s operating on pure trust,” Mitchell Quiring, a rescuer, told the Chronicle. “It’s navigable terrain during the day but it becomes unnavigable at night.”Still, it was not an acceptable option to leave the man there overnight, once the team saw his situation, Quiring told the paper.A rescuer reached the climber from overhead, attaching him to a secure rope system, to prevent a fall, according to the team’s post.The operation wrapped in the early hours of Sunday morning.“He did not give up, and that is really one of the biggest takeaways from this,” Quiringsaidto the New York Times. “This could have been a very different story if he didn’t push through the adversity.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsCaliforniaWest CoastMountainsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right political commentator, detained by ICE | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: A former editor of Breitbart News, Yiannopoulos has also served as an intern for Marjorie Taylor Greene
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A former editor of Breitbart News, Yiannopoulos has also served as an intern for Marjorie Taylor Greene
Content: Milo Yiannopoulos at a rally in Baltimore in November 2021.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APView image in fullscreenMilo Yiannopoulos at a rally in Baltimore in November 2021.Photograph: Julio Cortez/APICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Milo Yiannopoulos, a far-right political commentator, detained by ICEA former editor of Breitbart News, Yiannopoulos has also served as an intern for Marjorie Taylor GreeneGuardian staffFri 28 Aug 2026 17.13 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 16.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMilo Yiannopoulos, a far-right British political commentator, was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Louisiana, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).In a statement on Friday, a DHS spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was arrested on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport (MSY). The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019, but that “he chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”.The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July, “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”.“He will remain in ICE custody pending removal,” the spokesperson added. “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”As of Friday afternoon, Yiannopoulosis listedin ICE’s online detainee database as being in “ICE Custody”. The database states that he was born in the United Kingdom, but it does not disclose any additional details, including where he is being held.The statement comes asmultipleoutletsreportedon Friday that Yiannopoulos had been detained in Louisiana.Fox Newsreported that Yiannopoulos is currently detained in Alexandria, Lousiana.Yiannopoulos, aformer editor of Breitbart News, previously servedas an internfor Marjorie Taylor Greene, a former US representative, in 2022, and alsoworked onthe 2024 White House campaign of Ye, formerly known as Kanye West. It is unclear why Yiannopoulos might have been in Louisiana, but Ye is scheduled toperform in New Orleanson Friday night.Last year, in posts on social media, Yiannopoulos had been supportive of immigration enforcement in the US.“California needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally,” hewrotein a social media post in June 2025.On social media on Friday, Laura Loomer, the far-right activist and ally of Donald Trump, claimed credit for Yiannopoulos’s detention andwrotethat she had previously reported him to ICE.Explore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Far right (US)Marjorie Taylor GreeneBreitbartnewsShareReuse this content

title: Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes city | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races
Author: Tom Perkins
Headline: Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races
Content: View of the Gordie Howe international bridge during the opening ceremony in Windsor, Ontario, on 24 July 2026.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenView of the Gordie Howe international bridge during the opening ceremony in Windsor, Ontario, on 24 July 2026.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump tariffsDetroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes cityUnpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan racesTom Perkinsin DetroitFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery day$1bnworth of goods crosses the river dividing Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry.News this week of Donald Trump’sescalating trade spatwith Canada has everyone worried. Political and economic leaders and observers labeled the move an act of “hubris” , blamed Trump’s “ego”, and called the escalation “insanity”.“We don’t needCanada, they need us,” Trump declared.But many are hoping that Trump’s imposition of50% tariffson Canadian goods this week will not last long, with the upcoming midterm elections as a pivotal reason the plan may be scrapped.Control of the US Congress hangs in the balance and will almost certainly be decided by several close Michigan races. It also comes just two months after polling highlighted Michiganders’ fatigue with and opposition to the president’s unprecedented tariff program.By a 63%-31% margin, residents here oppose tariffs on Canadian goods, according to a June Epic-MRA poll, including 35% of Republicans. Meanwhile, nearly 75% of Michiganders said the tariffs are fueling high prices.Trump doubling down on an unpopular policy deep into election season is viewed by many observers as a gift to Democrats, and there is a real possibility that it contributes to a midterm loss for the Republicans. Meanwhile, there seems to be little upside for Trump.“I don’t understand what Trump is thinking,” the Epic-MRA pollster Bernie Porn said.Regardless, Michiganders have already suffered disproportionately as theypay on averageover $3,200 annually for tariffs, or about 142% more than the rest of the country, because of the state’s shared border with Canada.The Canadian economy would also take a major hit if the tariffs are imposed, said Patrick Anderson, a Michigan-based economist with the Anderson Economic Group.View image in fullscreenThe Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters at Renaissance high school in Detroit, Michigan, on 7 August.Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images“Both will suffer – there are no two ways about it,” Anderson added.This critical upper midwest swing state has picked the presidential winner in five consecutive elections, going from Barack Obama to Trump to Joe Biden and back to Trump. Democrats’ chances to retake the Senate rest heavily on the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed beating Trump ally Mike Rogers in the 3 November general election race. Rogers has supported the tariffs, but so far has been silent on the latest escalation.The tariffs and theunpopular Iran war’scontribution to inflation represent a “double hit” for Republicans, Porn said, and Trump is handing ammo to a particularly adept candidate in El-Sayed. He has energized people with his anti-establishment, populist political vision, and a no-holds-barred delivery.“El-Sayed has proven to be very, very articulate on a number of issues,” Porn added. “I think that he is going to try and just throw bombs at Rogers [in an upcoming debate] because Rogers supports these tariffs and trade war. Trump’s low popularity is an anchor around Rogers’ neck.”In a statement, El-Sayed hammered Trump and Rogers, saying that the president “cares more about his ego and saber-rattling than addressing the affordability crisis.“Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he’s asking Michigan families to pay the price,” El-Sayed said. “Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long, and Mike Rogers won’t do anything but rubber-stamp them.”El-Sayed said he would push for “real, fair trade deals that create good-paying jobs”. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment.The United Auto Workers (UAW), which has 350,000 members in Michigan and is often a political kingmaker here, has supported some of Trump’s targeted tariffs, but said in a statement it “rejects” the latest escalation.“If we’re going to increase tariffs anywhere, it should be on countries where automakers continue to offshore jobs because they can pay workers $3 an hour, force them to work in unsafe conditions, and crack down on independent unions,” the UAW president, Shawn Fain, said. Canada has strong unions, and the UAW supports those.“Tariffs work, but only if they are deployed intentionally to protect workers and grow our manufacturing communities, and it’s time to permanently end offshoring and the race to the bottom,” Fain added.Mexico and Canada currently face 25% US tariffs on autos, though partial exemptions in the nations’ free trade agreement make the effective rate much lower, overall. Andersonestimatedtariffs cost US auto companies about $12.5bn in 2025.The Canadian government has announced it will impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of goods starting 8 September. The actions leading to the latest blow-up have been “rife with miscalculations, overreactions, and hubris”, Anderson said. He read through the list of goods on which tariffs would be imposed – feathers, sweaters, girls’ dresses, lobster.“This is not a trade war. This is an annoyance list. Chest pounding,” Anderson said.The North American auto industry over the last 60 years has integrated across the continent, and auto parts cross a border an average of six times before they land in a final product. That means there would be shared pain, Anderson said, and it would reverberate across the upper midwest, where bigger manufacturing cities are typically powered by industries that are often reliant on international trade.But the Canadian economy is smaller, and Ontario’s economy is so concentrated that it would hit harder north of the border, Anderson added. Ultimately, the real threat is that “these two countries go pell-mell into it” and impose tariffs on oil, energy and commodities that hit harder than lobster.The dialogue has devolved into the usual petty antagonism that is a hallmark of Trump’s beefs. Trumpsigned an executive orderto rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, and Vice-President JD Vance referred to Canada as the 51st state.“Let me say with great understatement that this is not helpful,” Anderson added.View image in fullscreenThe American and Canadian flags fly at the midway point on the Gordie Howe International Bridge, that connects Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, Michigan.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockIndeed, the Windsor mayor, Drew Dilkens, took exception to that particular comment.
