In an interview, he expressed deep frustration over Trump’s moves, and labeled justifications Trump has used for issuing tariffs, including framing them as a response to illegal immigration on the northern border, “nonsense”.The latest escalation “is an aggressive move, one that could not be ignored by our country”, added Dilkens, who leads the city of 230,000 people. “It’s just offensive that he launches these attacks at Canada, who is your largest trading partner, your closest ally, and your neighbor.”The chaos has cooled investment in Windsor, and prices remain high on both sides of the border. He pointed out how much more US consumers are paying not just for automobiles, but for beef, which in part stems from tariffs on Canadian beef.“What is really crazy is that he is willing to throw his own citizens under the bus to pursue his tariff agenda,” Dilkens said. “They have Donald Trump to thank.”Highlighting the tension among the president and some in his base, the Michigan chamber of commerce, a trade organization that lobbies on behalf of the state’s largest corporations, normally vocally supports the president on economic issues. It has not made a public statement, and did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.However, the typically pro-TrumpDetroitchamber of commerce did not mince words.“Escalating tensions and tariffs will only cause economic pain on both sides of the border, especially in Michigan and the binational Detroit-Windsor region,” the chamber said in a press statement, adding that global competitors like China benefited most.“Our economies are intertwined, interconnected, and stronger together; the sooner normalcy is restored the better.”This article was amended on 28 August 2026. An earlier version gave incorrect commencement dates for the US and Canadian tariffs.Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsDetroitUS politicsCanadaUS economyEconomicsAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fed chair says delivering ‘stable prices’ is central bank’s job as inflation persists | Federal Reserve | The Guardian
description: However, Kevin Warsh didn’t say if interest rates would change in coming months, as inflation remains stubborn
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: However, Kevin Warsh didn’t say if interest rates would change in coming months, as inflation remains stubborn
Content: Kevin Warsh at the Jackson Hole economic symposium on Thursday in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.Photograph: Natalie Behring/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKevin Warsh at the Jackson Hole economic symposium on Thursday in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.Photograph: Natalie Behring/Getty ImagesFederal ReserveFed chair says delivering ‘stable prices’ is central bank’s job as inflation persistsHowever, Kevin Warsh didn’t say if interest rates would change in coming months, as inflation remains stubbornGaya GuptaFri 28 Aug 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS Federal Reserveis not done fighting high inflation, its chair, Kevin Warsh, said in his first major speech in the role on Friday, emphasizing that it was “the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices”.Warsh did not indicate where the Fed will take interest rates in the coming months, despite US inflation remaining stubbornly above the central bank’s 2% target amid the war in Iran. But his speech was taken by markets as a signal that rates may rise in the coming months, a move that may put him at odds withDonald Trump, who has aggressively called for rates to be cut.The Fed chair painted a rosy view of the economy that contrasts with recent data. He said the economy “appears to have strengthened” given how it has held up to shocks.Is the Trump Treasury panicking over the level of US debt?Read more“On that score, both Main Street and Wall Street have been resilient,” Warsh said at the Fed’s annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, on Friday.The Jackson Hole symposium has typically served as a platform for Fed chairs to offer clarity on the central bank’s general direction. For example, former Fed chair Jerome Powell foreshadowedrate cuts at his keynote addresslast year.But Warsh on Friday insisted the days of such “forward guidance” were over, saying that the practice was adopted by the Fed during the 2008 financial crisis. “As with other legacies of crises past, I believe that the practice has overstayed its welcome,” he said.Markets are still expected to carefully gauge Warsh’s speech for signs of the Fed’s next move. At the central bank’s last board meeting in July, three out of 12 voting members wanted to raise rates by a quarter percentage point – the first time in a decade so many board members shared dissent over a policy position. But a majority of the members voted to hold rates, which currently sit at a range of 3.5% to 3.75%, steady.Since he was appointed in May, Warsh has had to strike a delicate balance between managing an economy that has been shaken by higher oil prices brought on by the war in Iran without provoking the ire of the White House. Trump has continued to insist the Fed should lower interest rates, despite economists who warn that that would further exacerbate inflation. After hitting a three-year high of 4.2% in May, US inflationcooledto 3.4% in July – still 1% higher than figures seen last year.Warsh said progress on inflation over the past several years has been “modest”, and though price readings from over the summer came in better than expected, they did not indicate that “underlying trends have meaningfully improved”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe US bond market has been particularly sensitive to higher inflation, with the yield on 10-year notes hitting its highest level since 2007 in recent weeks. Yields briefly went down after the US treasury announced a bigdebt buy-back scheme, though the relief proved to be temporary. Rising rates in the US have driven yields higher abroad – bond rates in the UK, Germany, France and Japan have all hit their highest levels in decades. Meanwhile, the US grossnational debttopped $40tn for the first time in history last week.In reaction to Warsh’s opening remarks, the two-year and 10-year US treasury yields increased slightly, while the 30-year treasury remained largely the same. The S&P 500 remained leveled while the Dow Jones ticked down slightly.Explore more on these topicsFederal ReserveInflationUS interest ratesBondsEconomic policyEconomicsUS economynewsShareReuse this content

title: How Britain’s railways are struggling in the heat – and can they be fixed?  | Rail industry | The Guardian
description: Problems including derailments have hit network during one of the hottest and driest summers on record
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Problems including derailments have hit network during one of the hottest and driest summers on record
Content: The derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, earlier this month.Photograph: RAIB/PAView image in fullscreenThe derailment near Lewes, East Sussex, earlier this month.Photograph: RAIB/PARail industryExplainerHow Britain’s railways are struggling in the heat – and can they be fixed?Problems including derailments have hit network during one of the hottest and driest summers on recordNatalie Wint andAlex DanielFri 28 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s railways have faced a string of heat-related problems this summer, including a derailmentnear Lewesin East Sussex two weeks ago that injured 30 people, and another the next day when the rear carriages of a Greater Anglia train derailed “in an upright position” atWickford railway station in Essex, with no reported injuries.The problems came during one of the hottest and driest summers on record, with a series of heatwaves, anddrought declaredacross large parts of England and Wales. Britain’s railways, built for a cooler, wetter climate, have been put under pressure. Network Rail said the summer had “presented exceptional challenges to the railway”.Here’s what we know about how heat affects the rail network and what can be done to tackle it.What happens to railways in the heat?Steel expands when it gets hot, and the long, welded steel sections that make up modern railway tracks are no exception. “The classic concern for railways with hot weather is that the track might buckle,” said William Powrie, a professor of geotechnical engineering at the University of Southampton.As temperatures rise, the rails expand, but their continuous design means there is little room for movement. “If they haven’t got anywhere to go, they end up generating compressive stresses,” Powrie said. “The problem with any sort of structure which has got a compression in it is that it can fail by buckling.”The consequences can be serious. Just two days of record heat in 2022 led to almost 7,700cancelled trains and an estimated £30m in costs, according to ataskforceset up by Network Rail after that heatwave.On a hot day, the rail can reach much higher temperatures than the air. Network Rail says most of the network can operate when track temperatures reachup to 46C, roughly equivalent to an air temperature of 30C. But rails have been recorded at temperatures as high as 51C.The sleepers and ballast that rails sit on can help stop them from buckling, keeping the track in place – but long periods of heat and drought can dry the soil beneath them. That soil can shrink when it dries, a problem given it “is essentially the foundation for anything on top of it”, said Manu Sasidharan, an assistant professor of infrastructure asset management at University College London.The weight of passing trains makes the problem worse, putting pressure on the weakened soil and causing it to settle unevenly. Whatever sits on top, including the track, “will follow suit”, Sasidharan said.While tracks and stations have been continually updated over the decades, some embankments, tunnels and other structuresdate to the 1800s, when much of the network was first laid.How do hotter countries cope?To stop rails from buckling, engineers lay them slightly stretched, a process called pre-stressing. It means the rail has some give in it before it starts expanding in the heat.In the UK, rails are stretched so that they do not undergo compression until the air temperature passes 27C. That figure sits between the UK’s highest and lowest seasonal rail temperatures, protecting against buckling in the summer and breaking under tension in the winter.Other countries set that figure differently. In parts of Australia and the US, the so-called stress-free air temperature can exceed 35C. In southern Europe too, where winters rarely get as cold as in the UK, rails are designed for more heat, since there’s less risk of the rail snapping in the cold.“If you’re looking at Italy, where you don’t really get very low winter temperatures, then you can afford to increase the stress-free temperature,” Powrie said. “The problem is the range of temperatures that we have [in the UK] … in the winter, they go into tension and that can cause the rails to break.”One option, in theory, could be to re-stress rails between seasons, loosening and retensioning them so the stress-free temperature is set higher for summer and lower for winter, rather than fixed year-round.Network Rail says: “In Britain, the variations in short-term weather and long-term climate mean that it is neither practical nor cost-effective to implement these measures permanently.”Another option is to lay track on solid concrete slabs, as in some countries, rather than the more common bed of sleepers and ballast. However, slab track costs about four times as much to install as standard ballasted track, which is why it remains rare across most of the UK network.What can be done?One idea under discussion is raising the temperature British rails are built to withstand. The post-2022 taskforce said that on modern, well-supported track the stress-free temperature could rise from 27C to 30C.“You might say we should actually have a different stress-free temperature in the south of England compared to, say, the north of Scotland,” Powrie said. However, higher stress-free temperature also leaves rails more vulnerable in a cold snap.Simpler measures are already in use. Some sections of track arepainted whiteto reduce how much heat they absorb. Network Rail says a rail painted white is typically 5-10C cooler.Both tactics may be necessary as summers get hotter – somethingthat will be increasingly normalamid the climate crisis. All five of the UK’s warmest summers on record have happened since 2000, according to the Met Office.Monitoring for faults remains difficult, though. The Network Rail taskforce found that fewer than half of the track buckles recorded in 2022 had been identified before they happened.Part of the issue is the sheer amount of data modern trains generate. Many now carry sensors that pick up rough riding or unusual vibrations, but sifting through it all is a challenge that needs to be automated, experts say.Much, therefore, still relies on judgment rather than data – for example, a train driver detecting rough riding on one part of the line and reporting it.As a temporary measure, speed restrictions were imposed on trains in southern Essex in the aftermath of theWickford derailment.Did the Lewes derailment happen because of the heat?It’s impossible to say for sure. An interim report by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) found that a“track geometry irregularity”existed before the derailment, and said investigators had since received reports of rough riding from passengers on that stretch of line.Sasidharan said early evidence pointed to the track itself. “The initial indication of the derailment … is that it’s a track infrastructure fault, most likely,” he said.At the site of the derailment, the embankment is built on clay, which shrinks more than other types of soils as it dries out. The RAIB said the clay was “sensitive to variations in water content”, and there was evidence it had shifted before the derailment, though not enough to amount to a significant slip.Powrie said the location had several things working against it at once, making it a case of what safety experts call the“Swiss cheese” theoryof accidents, where one only happens when several small failures line up together.The derailment happened on a bend – where more force is exerted on the track – and close to where the track leaves a bridge and moves on to the embankment.Powrie said these transition points were a natural weak spot because the track had to cope with a sudden change from something rigid to ground that could shift, especially when it was dried out. “It wouldn’t surprise me if the defect turned out to be related to the dryness,” he said, “but I don’t really want to speculate.”Network Rail has said it is “fully committed to supporting the continuing investigation and acting on any lessons that emerge from its findings”.It said: “Safety is and will always remain our highest priority. While Britain’s railway is one of the safest in the world, when incidents like this occur it is essential that we understand exactly what happened and identify any lessons that can be learned.“Given the complexity of the issues being examined, it is important that the independent investigation is allowed to reach its conclusions. We will continue to cooperate fully with the RAIB throughout this process.”Explore more on these topicsRail industryNetwork RailRail transportTransportExtreme heatClimate crisisexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Cherki and Haaland double up in Manchester City cruise at Crystal Palace | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Rayan Cherki and Erling Haaland both scored twice in Manchester City’s 4-1 win at Crystal Palace
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Rayan Cherki and Erling Haaland both scored twice in Manchester City’s 4-1 win at Crystal Palace
Content: Rayan Cherki shows his delight after scoring City’s second goal.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRayan Cherki shows his delight after scoring City’s second goal.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesPremier LeagueCherki and Haaland double up in Manchester City cruise at Crystal PalaceJacob Steinbergat Selhurst ParkFri 28 Aug 2026 16.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll who attend the Rayan Cherki show know the ticket comes with a guarantee of entertainment. Enzo Maresca, a manager famed for his obsessive positional control, does not need to put limits on theManchester Citywizard. Cherki has to feel free and he was at his creative best against Crystal Palace, who were in this game before City’s creative heartbeat took it away from them in the second half.It has been a fine start to the former Lyon player’s second year in England. Cherki was inspired against Bournemouth last week, coming off the bench to spark City’s fightback from 1-0 down with two assists, and this was better. The Frenchman scored twice and the first, a little prod with the outside of his left foot after a mazy run, left you wondering if you have seen something like it before.Crystal Palace 1-4 Manchester City: Premier League – live reactionRead morePalace, stuck on zero points despite fleeting signs of encouragement in Pierre Sage’s first two outings, had no answer to Cherki’s magic. He is an irrepressible talent and a deep thinker. Listening to the post-match plaudits, Cherki smiled, shrugged and said his performance in the first half was “so shit”. Maresca, though, had a different view.“His performance for me was very good, not because of the two goals, but the way he worked off the ball,” City’s manager said. “He has to press. His game was complete. He loves football. We know how good he is. We know the quality he has.”Cherki was not alone in starring for City. Phil Foden impressed and Erling Haaland, who is up and running for the season, grabbed an emphatic double in a performance strong enough to make Maresca think his post-Pep team have moved on from their Community Shield debacle. “We struggled the first five, 10 minutes, because we were pressing in the wrong way,” the Italian said. “After that we were in control.”A challenge for Maresca is working with an incomplete midfield after the exits of Rodri and Bernardo Silva. Ayyoub Bouaddi has arrived from Lille, £86m an eye-catching fee for an 18-year-old after his exploits for Morocco at the World Cup, but there is room for one more. Enzo Fernández, desperate to leave Chelsea, is the top target before Tuesday’s deadline.Not that anyone is going to argue that City are short on midfield options. Maresca, ever the tinkerer, shuffled the pack again. The experiment with Marc Guéhi in the engine room was discontinued, allowing him to slot into central defence against his old side. The £116m Elliot Anderson was the sole pivot, Nico O’Reilly pushed high in a 4-1-4-1 system and Josko Gvardiol inverted from left-back, much like Marc Cucurella in Maresca’s Chelsea side.There are subtle tweaks to the Guardiola template, though some things never change. City led through a familiar source in the 17th minute, Antoine Semenyo crossing from the left and Haaland finding space to loop a clever header over Dean Henderson.View image in fullscreenErling Haaland wraps up victory with the fourth goal.Photograph: Richard Heathcote/Getty ImagesThe defending was poor from Palace, who have had an uncertain summer. They were arranged in familiar fashion, Sage sticking with Oliver Glasner’s 3-4-2-1, but some key faces have gone and others were missing.Jørgen Strand Larsen led the line in the absence of the unsettled Jean-Philippe Mateta, who may be out for four weeks. Ismaïla Sarr, keen to join Galatasaray, was unavailable and Daniel Muñoz was on the bench amid suggestions of interest from Nottingham Forest. Frailties were inevitable. The defence has lost Maxence Lacroix, sold to Chelsea. Anderson, Semenyo and Foden had chances before half-time. “You saw how we want to play until the 65th minute,” Sage said. “We trust in our process.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSage likes to play on the front foot. Adam Wharton, subject of a failed enquiry from City recently, swept a ball through for Eddie Nketiah to test Gianluigi Donnarumma in the second minute. Daichi Kamada went close and Tyrick Mitchell fluffed a header after more enterprising play from Wharton.Palace lacked incision, Nketiah missing again early in the second half. City pressed, O’Reilly and Foden hustling Kamada. Foden advanced and Cherki took over. The Frenchman danced in from the left, danger rising as he wriggled into the area. A host of Palace defenders were thrown off balance, unable to live with Cherki’s footwork and close control. Expect the unexpected. Cherki floated past Jaydee Canvot and held off Chris Richards. For a moment the ball seemed stuck under his feet but he used Takehiro Tomiyasu as a shield and unveiled a finish that was less poke and more dab, Henderson rooted to the spot as the ball rolled tantalisingly over the line.Palace quickly grabbed a lifeline, Yéremy Pino’s free-kick hitting the woodwork and bouncing in off Donarumma for an own goal, but Cherki was in his element. He scored again in the 59th minute, a fierce shot from 20 yards deceiving Henderson after flicking off Richards.City sent Bouaddi on for his debut, Anderson withdrawn. They wanted more. Foden, catching the eye in front of Thomas Tuchel, released Haaland. The Norwegian, who has scored in all six of his league games against Palace, was never going to miss.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueCrystal PalaceManchester Citymatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: MLB suspends Dominican prospect after age-fraud plot involving fake grave | Cleveland Guardians | The Guardian
description: MLB has suspended a Dominican prospect after an investigation uncovered an extraordinary scheme involving falsified records and a staged gravesite
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: MLB has suspended a Dominican prospect after an investigation uncovered an extraordinary scheme involving falsified records and a staged gravesite
Content: The Cleveland Guardians had agreed to a $2.8m deal with Dominican prospect Daury David Severino Damaso, who was posing as a younger player named David Severino, before the agreement was canceled in May.Photograph: Michael Turner/MLB Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Cleveland Guardians had agreed to a $2.8m deal with Dominican prospect Daury David Severino Damaso, who was posing as a younger player named David Severino, before the agreement was canceled in May.Photograph: Michael Turner/MLB Photos/Getty ImagesCleveland GuardiansMLB suspends Dominican prospect after age-fraud plot involving fake graveReport: player posed as nearly two years youngerScheme allegedly included fake grave and records$2.8m agreement with Guardians was canceledReutersFri 28 Aug 2026 18.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 18.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA once-prized prospect from the Dominican Republic has been suspended by Major League Baseball after a league investigation revealed the player was part of an elaborate plot to portray him ⁠as nearly two years younger than he actually was, ESPNreportedFriday.The age-fraud plot included extreme efforts by the player’s handler such as falsifying school and medical records, faking birth and death certificates ⁠and even staging a gravesite, per ⁠the report.A switch-hitting infielder ​going by the name of David Severino agreed in December to a $2.8m pre-deal with theCleveland Guardians, who reportedly believed the player was 13 or 14 years old. The deal was ⁠set to be finalized in 2029, when Severino was expected to be 17 and eligible to officially sign.In reality, per ESPN’s sources, Severino is 16 years old and named Daury David Severino Damaso.In 2023, Francisco Nieves, Severino’s ⁠trainer at the time, allegedly created the false identity of David Severino Damaso, posed as Daury’s younger brother. Nieves reportedly created a false death ​certificate for Daury, claiming he died of a respiratory illness ‌two years after he was born, ‌and even built a fake tombstone that was planted at a gravesite in the Dominican Republic.John Pereyra is a trainer who has been ‌in the business for more than 30 years and currently runs an academy called Futuro Big Leaguers out of Santiago that he says has funneled more than 70 players toMLB.Pereyra said he was told when he first saw Severino work out that he was 11 years old, and he ultimately agreed to pay Nieves $20,000 for Severino’s rights.Pereyra trained Severino for two years leading up to the agreement with the Guardians but said he knew nothing about the age-fraud plot. He said he had some initial suspicions when ‌he learned Severino’s parents filed his birth certificate late, but this is not an uncommon practice in poor areas. When he learned Severino’s younger brother died young, “I did my own investigation,” he told ESPN, even visiting the ​brother’s supposed grave, which he said eased his concerns.He only learned of an issue when he received a message from Nieves in May that MLB was investigating Severino’s deal, which soon thereafter fell apart.Pereyra said he doesn’t place blame on Severino or his parents for going along with the plot, citing the desperation to escape poverty.“When you have a kid,” Pereyra said in Spanish, per ESPN, “and you tell him, ‘Look, your name ⁠is not Daury. If someone asks your name, you say, ‘David Severino Damaso” – [he will] do it.“Although poverty-stricken areas ​in the Dominican Republic and Venezuela have been ​ripe for age and identity fraud by ​players desperate for an advantage to make it to the majors, the extent of this scheme reportedly shocked ​team executives, trainers and scouts.“You have ‌to have [guts] to do ​something like this,” Pereyra said, ​per ESPN. “I’ve heard about false birth documents and stuff like that, but to put together what this guy did – that’s movie stuff. That’s the first time I’ve ever seen anything like that in the Dominican. In my life, I have never seen anything like that.“It is unclear what prompted MLB to investigate Severino, whose agreement with Cleveland was canceled back in May. The league, the Guardians and Nieves have not commented on the ‌matter.Explore more on these topicsCleveland GuardiansMLBBaseballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Judge grants hearing over bid to recant Jerry Sandusky sexual abuse allegations | Penn State sexual abuse scandal | The Guardian
description: Hearing set for 8 September after man who testified against former Penn State assistant football coach says his allegations were shaped by authorities
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hearing set for 8 September after man who testified against former Penn State assistant football coach says his allegations were shaped by authorities
Content: Jerry Sandusky arrives at the Centre County Courthouse in Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, in November 2019.Photograph: Gene J Puskar/APView image in fullscreenJerry Sandusky arrives at the Centre County Courthouse in Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, in November 2019.Photograph: Gene J Puskar/APPenn State sexual abuse scandalJudge grants hearing over bid to recant Jerry Sandusky sexual abuse allegationsMan claims he was coached extensively by authoritiesPennsylvania says recantation is ‘highly suspect’Sandusky serving sentence after 2012 convictionAgenciesFri 28 Aug 2026 15.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA judge has granted a hearing to explore claims that a man wants to recant allegations of sexual abuse years ago by Penn State assistant football coach Jerry Sandusky.Sandusky, 82, has been serving a decades-long prison sentence since he wasconvicted of 45 counts of sexual abusein 2012. Eight young men testified about what happened to them as boys. He has repeatedly lost efforts to get a new trial, but Sandusky’s lawyers are trying again.A man identified in court documents as RR said he was coached extensively by authorities.College football is booming, chaotic and more confusing than everRead more“I was told – both directly and indirectly – that trauma may have fragmented my memory, and that I could safely affirm details I did not fully recall. I was assured this was common and even expected,” RR said in an affidavit filed by Sandusky’s attorneys.A court hearing in Centre county has been scheduled for 8 September.RR’s allegations were “based on suggestive leading questioning, prosecutorial coercion and influence, confirmatory bias and memory manipulation, which permeated throughout each of the accusers as well”, Sandusky’s attorneys said in a court filing.The Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General said Friday that RR’s recantation is “highly suspect”.Sandusky coached the defense at one of the country’s top football programs under Hall of Fame head coach Joe Paterno. The scandal led to Paterno’s firing, and the university paid more than $100m to people who said they had been abused by Sandusky.Authorities said Sandusky found and groomed victims at The Second Mile, a charity that he started for at-risk youth. He has repeatedly declared his innocence.“I apologize that I’m unable to admit remorse for this because it’s something that I didn’t do,” Sandusky said during a 2019 court appearance.At trial, RR was 25 years old. He testified that he was 11 when Sandusky performed oral sex in the coach’s basement in 1998, a transcript shows.“He told me that if I told anybody that I would never see my family again,” said RR, who was in foster care at the time.Sandusky later apologized and said “he loved me,” RR testified.Explore more on these topicsPenn State sexual abuse scandalCollege footballCollege sportsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Shaky Sabalenka and wide-open men’s draw set stage for US Open drama | Aryna Sabalenka | The Guardian
description: The defending women’s champion arrives in poor form, while Jannik Sinner’s absence and Carlos Alcaraz’s rustiness make Alexander Zverev men’s favourite
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: The defending women’s champion arrives in poor form, while Jannik Sinner’s absence and Carlos Alcaraz’s rustiness make Alexander Zverev men’s favourite
Content: Aryna Sabalenka must win the US Open to stand a chance of retaining her No 1 ranking.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka must win the US Open to stand a chance of retaining her No 1 ranking.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesAryna SabalenkaShaky Sabalenka and wide-open men’s draw set stage for US Open dramaDefending champion arrives at Flushing Meadows in poor form and with a host of challengers looking to usurp herTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsFri 28 Aug 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 16.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnder any normal circumstancesAryna Sabalenkawould not have lost her third-round match at the Cincinnati Open last week. For all of her unforced errors, indecisiveness and the obvious tension surrounding her tennis, the world No 1 had led the unheralded Sára Bejlek 5-1 in the first set tie-break and then 4-1 in set two. She gave herself more than enough chances to close out a comfortable win.Instead Sabalenka returns to New York trying to find apath through her greatest crisissince she first reached No 1 in the rankings more than three years ago. That straight-sets loss in Cincinnati extended a mediocre 17-7 record dating back to the beginning of April during which she has not reached a final. She has just one more chance to turn her fortunes around as she tries to claim her first grand slam title of the year at the US Open, the tournament she has won on the last two occasions.US Open: Carlos Alcaraz to face Safiullin on return as Sabalenka gets tricky drawRead moreSuch is the competition at the top of women’s tennis, her rivals are congregating at her front door. Elena Rybakina begins this tournament sitting at No 1 in the live standings and in control of her own destiny. Sabalenka must win the title to have any hope of retaining the top ranking, but Rybakina will become the new No 1 regardless of all other results if she reaches the semi-finals. Should either Coco Gauff or Jessica Pegula win the title and Rybakina fails to make the semi-finals, they would take top spot. This additional pressure could further add to Sabalenka’s woes, but perhaps, after 97 consecutive weeks as the undisputed best player in the world, this is exactly what she needs.There are other unanswered questions. Rybakina’s physical condition is uncertain after she was forced to retire from her quarter-final against Iga Swiatek last week due to a leg injury. A year after she spent this lead-in week to the US Open changing her service action, and parts of her matches in tears, Gauff has rebuilt confidence in her serve and the 2023 champion produced some of her best tennis during herCincinnati Open title run. Fresh from her own success in Toronto, the 2022 US Open champion Swiatek looks similarly rejuvenated after struggling badly with anxiety and nerves in many matches this year. Pegula, a finalist in Cincinnati having defeated Swiatek, remains as consistent as ever and will put pressure on her rivals.The strength at the top of women’s game is reflected in the fact that every player inside the top 11 currently holds a WTA 1000 title or above. They have each shown that they are capable of winning the biggest tournaments in the world.View image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz looked rusty on his return from a four-month injury layoff in the mixed doubles competition.Photograph: Marcin Cholewinski/Zuma Press /ShutterstockThings could hardly be more different in the men’s draw. As was the case when he exited the French Open in round two,Jannik Sinner’s withdrawal from the US Openwith a knee injury has cracked this tournament wide open. Carlos Alcaraz is clearly capable of greatness whenever he enters the court, but the prospect of him launching a serious challenge in hisfirst event back after a four-month layoffdue to a right wrist injury and only a few weeks of training seems fanciful. Although he has never been the strongest doubles player, Alcaraz’s rustiness and the caution with which he hit his serve in themixed doubles competition alongside Serena Williamsonly reinforced this sentiment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hollowing out of Tennis.com is a warning for American sports journalismRead moreIt was Alexander Zverev who took advantage of the void in Paris towin his first grand slam titleand, as the top seed, he is high on the list of contenders again. The two biggest winners in the weeks leading up to the US Open, Montreal and Cincinnati champions Ben Shelton and Arthur Fils, are young players who have long viewed themselves as worthy of competing for major titles. Such is the cruelty of the draw, the close friends have been drawn to face each other in the fourth round.Otherwise, just about everyone is in with a shot. The French Open finalist Flavio Cobolli continues to play some of the best tennis of his career, reaching the semi-final in Cincinnati. The rise of 19-year-old Rafael Jódar, who was ranked No 369 this time last year, continues unabated. A group of US players, including Taylor Fritz, Frances Tiafoe, Learner Tien and Brandon Nakashima have found their best form at the right time. Félix Auger-Aliassime, the third seed, will try to replicate the immense level he demonstrated on these courts last year on his run to the semi-final.Perhaps the most interesting question of all is where Novak Djokovic will land over the next few weeks. Had any of the grand slam tournaments been this wide open in 2025, he would have been heavily favoured to become the oldest champion in history. But a year is an eternity at Djokovic’s advanced age. He has continued to put himself in contention at the grand slams, reaching the Australian Open final and Wimbledon semi-final, but he also has to manage a constant stream of physical problems that only worsen over the course of a fortnight. However, these are not normal circumstances, and he is far from a normal tennis player, so the pursuit of grand slam No 25 is still alive in New York.Explore more on these topicsAryna SabalenkaUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: College football is booming, chaotic and more confusing than ever | College football | The Guardian
description: America’s second most popular sport has never been richer or stranger, with old powers wobbling, new contenders rising and the rulebook under siege
Author: Alex Kirshner
Headline: America’s second most popular sport has never been richer or stranger, with old powers wobbling, new contenders rising and the rulebook under siege
Content: Texas offensive lineman Nick Brooks hoists the Lone Star Showdown trophy after the Longhorns beat rival Texas A&M in Austin last November.Photograph: Alex Slitz/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTexas offensive lineman Nick Brooks hoists the Lone Star Showdown trophy after the Longhorns beat rival Texas A&M in Austin last November.Photograph: Alex Slitz/Getty ImagesCollege footballCollege football is booming, chaotic and more confusing than everAmerica’s second biggest sporting obsession returns this weekend, which means marching bands, 100,000-seat stadiums, ancient rivalries and, increasingly, the operating model of a sport being invented in real timeAlex KirshnerFri 28 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 05.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs college football healthy? It’s a seductive question, one that now comes up every year around this time. Actually, it never recedes, so it’s just with the sport all the time. It’s also thewrongquestion, because whoever answers it is free to choose their own adventure. The television ratings are way up there in the galaxy. Money rains down on dozens of programs and thousands of players. Marching bands continue to march. Yet a lot of teams are stranded by realignment or an economic inability to keep up in a transfer arms race. Their fans – actuallyanyteam’s fans – may be exhausted by escalating asks for their dollars.If you have been checked out of the sport for a while ahead of this weekend’s first set of games, you may feel like your body has been frozen for a few decades. Indiana, (yes, really) are the defending national champs, fresh off a 16-0 season that puts them on the list of the handful of best teams ever. Texas Tech, once likened to Siberiaby a former coach who is now a US senator, are the fiercest program in the Big 12. Ole Miss are good for the first time since integration. At least Ohio State and Georgia are still powerhouses.View image in fullscreenUCLA defensive back Rodrick Pleasant breaks up a pass intended for Utah’s Devin Green during the teams’ meeting at the Rose Bowl in August 2025.Photograph: Sean M Haffey/Getty ImagesMeanwhile, college sports leaders are talking apocalyptically. “We’re on a runaway train and it’s not slowing down; it’s just getting worse,”West Virginia’s head coach says. We live in the “wild west”,Georgia’s president says, among many others. “The whole educational system is going to go out of business because of this,”claims Donald Trump, who may be unaware of how much money major college football programs generate for their universities. (Shocking that he’d be light on details, I know.) All of these groups are pushing fora now-stalled Senate billthat they think would calm the chaos.To be fair to the cynics, it’s not like everything’s fine. The NCAA has lost a handful of eligibility cases, or suffered temporary injunctions in them, that raise questions over whether the governing body can make its own rules. LSU are trying to play a tight endwho just got cut from his NFL team, as the SEC and other conferences race to outlaw such things. Texas Tech gave a real effort to starting a quarterback who bet on his own team’s games, and was set to succeed beforea misguided legal maneuver doomed them.View image in fullscreenOhio State players emerge from the tunnel before facing arch-rivals Michigan at the Big House in November 2025.Photograph: Luke Hales/Getty ImagesPlayers are paid but lack anything resembling a union or national standards over their pay and workplace conditions. Washington State and Oregon State are among the teams left out in the cold by conference realignment. They now make a fraction of the money they used to and can no longer compete with rivals Washington and Oregon, at least not consistently. The implicit message to their fans is, “You do not matter.”Then again, it’s not like “the sport” is in existential peril. At the top, things seem great. Michiganjust set an all-time college football ticket revenue recorddespite having a mediocre team. The TV ratings for theregular seasonandchampionship gamewere a bonanza. EA Sports’ popular video game is back on shelves and has spawned a big social media subculture. It’s not just the handful of best teams, either. At the power conference level, things have tightened. Once-dominant Alabama are struggling, while longtime outsiders are thriving. The two highest-rated quarterback recruits this season landed at Houston and Vanderbilt, two schools far away from blue-blood status. Fans at UCLA and Virginia Tech are dreaming of their schools being the next Indiana, and that’s no longer a ridiculous concept given how the past few years have gone.View image in fullscreenA general view of LaVell Edwards Stadium during BYU’s game against UCF in Provo in November 2025.Photograph: Andrew Wevers/Getty ImagesAnd, as herky-jerky as the current economic system is, you’d be strained to make a good argument that it isn’t an improvement. Roster-building has become precarious, and fans are understandably bummed that there are no longer guarantees or even high likelihoods of seeing a player develop across a four- or five-year career. The sport’s leaders can, should, and won’t get serious about recognizing players as employees and collectively bargaining with them in a fashion that would yield a more stable structure. But for now, playersdoget a piece of the enormous revenues they generate as a class, and that’s better than the organized theft of their wages that schools andNCAAleadership perpetrated for a century and a half.Thank the heavens, there will soon be actual football to discuss instead of the vaguely definable state of things. The season kicks off Saturday, appropriately enough several thousand miles from US soil, whenBill Belichick’s North Carolinaface Texas Christian University at Dublin’s Aviva Stadium. Alabama will try to rediscover their exceptionalism after two years of being just another SEC team. Lane Kiffin will try to justify the hype and the $40m roster that surround him after his move from Ole Miss to LSU. USC will try to make something, anything, of Lincoln Riley’s tenure before the school fires him or he leaves. Indiana and Texas Tech will adjust to life as the kind of team everyone wants to beat. The race for the playoff spot reserved for non-power teams should be electric, too, after most of last year’s contenders for that spot lost both their head coach and a lot of players to power schools.The sport will stay fun, the gains for players will be real, and the frustrations with all of it will be real and endless.Explore more on these topicsCollege footballNCAACollege sportsUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Esther González, Saudi Arabia and the questions around an unexpected transfer saga | Women's football | The Guardian
description: The striker’s surprise signing for Al Qadsiah after leaving Gotham sparked questions of professionalism and raised concerns of LGBTQ+ fans
Author: Abigail Segel
Headline: The striker’s surprise signing for Al Qadsiah after leaving Gotham sparked questions of professionalism and raised concerns of LGBTQ+ fans
Content: Esther González finished a four-year stint at the NWSL’s Gotham FC as the leading scorer in club history.Photograph: Chris Gardner/NWSL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEsther González finished a four-year stint at the NWSL’s Gotham FC as the leading scorer in club history.Photograph: Chris Gardner/NWSL/Getty ImagesWomen's footballEsther González, Saudi Arabia and the questions around an unexpected transfer sagaThe Gotham striker said she was stepping away from the sport, but then signed for Al Qadsiah. The move sparked questions over professionalism and raised concerns of LGBTQ+ fans who have disavowed the Saudi leagueAbigail SegelFri 28 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArecent World Cup winner joins a historically downtrodden club, immediately leads them to their first championship,praisesthe level of play in the league,speaksfondly of living in the club’s market, extends her contract with the club, leads the club to another championship, is named a league MVP finalist, and breaks the club’s all-time scoring record. That’s the fairytale of Esther González and Gotham FC – a story that ended abruptly, just nine days after that scoring record was set. On 27 July, Gothamannouncedthat they had mutually parted ways with the striker as she “temporarily steps away from soccer to attend to personal matters in Spain”. The announcement of her departure was full of gushing words going both directions, and was met withunderstanding and supportfrom the women’s soccer world.But less than a month after González left Gotham, Al Qadsiah, a club in the Saudi Women’s Premier League, announced her as their newest signing, on a one-season contract with an option to extend for a second. NWSL journalist Jenna Tonelli soonreported, “League sources tell me that Gotham did not expect Esther to sign with another club this soon.” Questions swirled: did she actually intend to take a break from soccer when she left Gotham? And why would a player who just had a child with her female partner choose to play in Saudi Arabia, a country where same-sex relations are criminalized?There’s a lot the public doesn’t know about the transfer saga, but the questions it raises, and the uncomfortable feelings that surround them, say a lot about the state of women’s soccer anyway.Stars, stakes and still some controversy: Gotham’s record-setting night sums up state of NWSLRead moreFor one, it raises questions about the base professionalism between players and clubs. If Gotham really didn’t expect González to sign with another club so soon, was that put into writing? Is it possible González misled Gotham to get out of a contract that ran through 2027? In either case, one result is that Gotham missed out on the chance to recoup a transfer fee that may well have been sizable – the Orlando Pride got $500,000 for transferring Adriana to Al Qadsiah in January 2025.The machinations around pay for NWSL players could also be a factor. Shortly before González departed Gotham, theysignedSam Kerr – another veteran elite striker with a history of success at the club. Outwardly, Gotham made no mention that one would replace the other. Yael Averbuch West, the club’s president of soccer operations, told reporters there were conversations with González about how the club would maximize her and Kerr’s talents, together. Still, perhaps González looked at Kerr and the club’s influx of summer signings and saw the writing on the wall: she wouldn’t be getting a raise anytime soon. Averbuch West is known for making the most of the NWSL’s roster rules, but she is limited by the league’s salary cap all the same. Athletes only have so many years to make the bulk of their income; González, being 33 years old, surely knows she’s closer to the end of her career than the beginning. Other players, from Portugal’s Jéssica Silva (as a free agent) to Nigerian star Asisat Oshoala (on a transfer fee) have moved from the US to Saudi Arabia in recent years. The SWPL is backed by the Saudi state and associated entities that have invested heavily in the country’s soccer leagues, national teams and infrastructure. It’s unclear how much money González will make at Al Qadsiah, but it’s likely to be more than she was making in the NWSL.If that is the case, then this is also a story about the financial precarity of female footballers, even in leagues that tout investment. TheNWSLis certainly one of the most well-paying destinations for a female athlete, but its salary cap prevents nearly every player from being paid what they deserve, let alone an amount that leaves them set for life. In other top leagues, different conditions lead to a similar reality: some players get paid well, but most don’t, and all should be paid more. Female soccer players are subjected to the same short and unpredictable careers as male players, but they do not have the same cushion of salaries that ensure comfort for well after their careers end. If González sees Al Qadsiah as a quick payday that could help secure her family’s future, that says as much about the NWSL as it does about its Saudi counterpart.There’s an element of González’s choice to sign in Saudi Arabia that raises questions unrelated to that country in particular. If she signed for a team in, say, Japan or Australia or Mexico, there would still be questions around the fact that she did not remain in or close to her home country of Spain, where she supposedly had to relocate to in order to attend to her personal life.View image in fullscreenThe Saudi women’s league has hailed Esther González as the first World Cup winner to sign with one of its clubs.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty Images,But there is, unavoidably, the Saudi Arabia of it all. The SWPL, which launched in 2022, is a key piece of Saudi Arabia’sVision 2030, the crown’s strategic plan to strengthen the country’s economy. The hope is that an elite women’s soccer league can become a sign to the outer world that the country is modernizing, and will inspire women in the country to get involved in sports and therefore be more active in society. The relative good the league may be doing for Saudi women aside, the league is undeniably part of the state’s sportswashing efforts; the country’shuman rights recordis marred with abuses – against women, the LGBTQ+ community, migrants, journalists and more.González missed Gotham’s bout in the Fifa Women’s Champions Cup in January while her partner, Estefanía Cruz, gave birth to their first child. Why would she turn around and sign with a team in a country thatcriminalizes same-sex relations? We don’t know what her personal life looks like now, or what it will look like in Khobar, and we don’t have the right to. However, given what she has shared about her family in the past, her signing is inevitably a jolt. Areportby El Mundo this week claimed she has deleted several Instagram posts featuring Cruz and their child. González’s personal life aside,any international playerjoining the SWPL is seen as an affront by LGBTQ+ soccer fans, who are fundamental to the sport around the world.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWomen’s soccer players have spoken out against the sport’s ties to the Saudi state. In 2024, 135 playerssigned a petitioncalling on Fifa to end its sponsorship deal with Aramco, a state-owned oil company, citing the country’s human rights abuses, particularly against women and LGBTQ+ people, as well as the company’s role in the climate crisis. Signatories include Maitane López and Sinead Farrelly, two of González’s former teammates at Gotham.The NWSL and other top leagues are far from perfect, with plenty of bad actors sponsoring clubs and working for them. But fans’ aversion to the Saudi league is understandable, since the country’s human rights abuses are especially abhorrent and antithetical to women’s soccer’s inclusive culture. González, whether she wants to or not, gives the league a huge dose of legitimacy – she is the first World Cup winner to join.González’s case is intriguing for all we don’t know. But what we do know is more than enough to say, without question: women’s soccer leagues across the globe must work toward an ecosystem where all players can have both security and their values.Explore more on these topicsWomen's footballNWSLUS sportsSaudi Arabia and sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Special for Norway’: Leknessund breaks clear to win stage seven of Vuelta | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Norway’s Andreas Leknessund launched a solo attack on ⁠the final climb to win stage ⁠seven of the ⁠Vuelta ​a España as his country mourned King Harald
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Norway’s Andreas Leknessund launched a solo attack on ⁠the final climb to win stage ⁠seven of the ⁠Vuelta ​a España as his country mourned King Harald
Content: Andreas Leknessund celebrates as he crosses the finish line to win the Vuelta’s seventh stage.Photograph: José Jordan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndreas Leknessund celebrates as he crosses the finish line to win the Vuelta’s seventh stage.Photograph: José Jordan/AFP/Getty ImagesVuelta a España‘Special for Norway’: Leknessund breaks clear to win stage seven of VueltaNorway in mourning after death of King Harald‘It’s only a small thing in the bigger picture’ReutersFri 28 Aug 2026 12.23 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Norwegian Andreas Leknessund launched a successful solo attack on ⁠the final climb to the summit finish of Aramón Valdelinares to win stage ⁠seven of the ⁠Vuelta ​a España, ahead of his Uno-X Mobility teammate and compatriot Tobias Johannessen on a day ⁠when theircountry mourned the death of King Harald.Leknessund made his move from ⁠a five-rider breakaway 7.5km from the finish at ​the end of the ‌149.8km ride from ‌Vall d’Alba, and pulled away to win his first ‌Grand Tour stage on his Vuelta debut.“It’s been a special day for the team and also for the whole of Norway,” Leknessund said. “Obviously it’s only a small thing in the bigger picture but still, it ‌makes the day more special.” A minute’s silence was held for King Harald before the stage began in Vall d’Alba, and the Uno-X Mobility team wore black armbands as a mark of respect.“I didn’t expect it to be this emotional, but for sure there’s so much feelings around this,” Leknessund added. “I’ve ​been fighting really hard, and it means a ‌lot.”Johannessen came in 34sec behind, having left the Belgian Wout van ​Aert in his wake close to the finish, with the Visma-Lease a Bike rider having to settle for third after he had made the initial attack from the ⁠off and spent most of the day out in ​front with ​Leknessund.Tadej Pogacar, winner of ​three stages already, was happy to sit ​back in ‌the peloton before ​pulling away ​from his general classification rivals approaching the summit to gain more seconds. The Slovene now leads Spaniard Enric Mas by 3min 50sec.Van Aert and Leknessund got away early and were joined by ‌another three riders, Johannessen, Eddie Dunbar (Pinarello Q36.5) and Alexey Lutsenko (NSN) coming to the top of the first of five climbs.View image in fullscreenTadej Pogacar gained 16sec on Enric Mas of Movistar, his closest rival in the general classification. The Slovenian leads by 3min 50sec.Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/GettyThe leaders worked together, building a substantial gap and at the foot of the ​final climb the five were one minute ahead of a chasing group of 13 riders with the peloton out of the running with less than 10km to the finish.Leknessund was the first to try to get away, and when nobody followed he was able to claim his stage win at last, having finished runner-up three times at this year’s Giro d’Italia.“I said ⁠to Andreas that he should try to go early and then we check if the ​other guys are willing to work together,” ​Johannessen said. “That’s what you always dream about ​when you try to be two guys in the breakaway and you can play it ​like this. I think we ‌played it perfectly.“A special ​day with what is ​happening back home in Norway so we are super proud.”Felix Gall, fifth overall, tried to get away from Pogacar, but the Slovene responded and in the end gained 16sec on his closest rival Mas, with Pogacar’s compatriot Primoz Roglic a further minute behind in third.Stage eight on Saturday is a flat 176.4km route from Pucol to Xeraco.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaCyclingTadej PogacarnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andoni Iraola tells Liverpool’s forwards to ‘exhaust themselves’ | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Andoni Iraola has said it is more important for Liverpool’s forwards to exhaust themselves than perform for 90 minutes as he prepares for an ‘emotional’ Premier League bow at Anfield
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Andoni Iraola has said it is more important for Liverpool’s forwards to exhaust themselves than perform for 90 minutes as he prepares for an ‘emotional’ Premier League bow at Anfield
Content: Andoni Iraola brought Victor Muñoz and Alexis Mac Allister off the bench at Newcastle.Photograph: Molly Darlington/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndoni Iraola brought Victor Muñoz and Alexis Mac Allister off the bench at Newcastle.Photograph: Molly Darlington/Getty ImagesLiverpoolAndoni Iraola tells Liverpool’s forwards to ‘exhaust themselves’‘I tell them they don’t need to give us 90 minutes’Head coach takes charge of first home game on SaturdayAndy HunterFri 28 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndoni Iraola has said it is more important for Liverpool’s forwards to exhaust themselves than perform for 90 minutes as he prepares to make an “emotional” Premier League bow at Anfield.The Liverpool head coach hopes his attacking options will be improved by thearrival of Bradley Barcola from Paris Saint-Germainand another winger before Tuesday’s deadline, with only Victor Muñoz added to his front line so far. The Basque coach has outlined the demands he will put on his forwards as they adapt to a new era at Liverpool.Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendRead moreIraola said: “For me, wingers, forwards, I always tell them that they don’t need to give us 90 minutes. I tell them it is good news when they are exhausted because then we have taken everything from you and someone else will come in.“We have the situation now with Jérémy [Jacquet], who hasn’t had a proper pre-season but he is close to getting there. But normally defenders can last 90 minutes easier. For offensive players, it’s not mandatory that you play the whole game. Once you are done, we can change you. I think it’s the best way, and they all have to understand it like this.”Iraola said Muñoz was “ready to start games” having missed the opening weeks of pre-season as he recuperated from Spain’s victorious World Cup campaign. The 23-year-old impressed from the benchat Newcastle last weekendand was signed for £34.5m from Osasuna on Iraola’s recommendation.Quick GuidePlay our football trivia game, On the ballShowThe Guardian'sdaily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues?Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“I had never coached against Victor because he made his debut in La Liga when I was already here in the Premier League but I had very good references of him,” Iraola said. “The club put his name [to me] and we started to analyse his game. We all liked what he gives us. It’s early for him in terms of him not being able to speak the language, and he needs to get a better relationship with teammates, but I like his attitude. He works very hard. He is ready to play right side, left side, and he impacted the game the other day. The subs all played very well.”Iraola’s wife and two young children will be at Anfield on Saturday – as will the club’s new vice-chair, Amit Bhatia – to witness his first competitive home game, against Nottingham Forest.“My wife never normally comes to my games,” he said. “But now she is starting to go because my kids want to go. The kids are starting to understand football a little bit and they will sometimes go. Not all the time, but they will be there for the first game because the timing is very good.“I think there will be an emotional part that is going to be probably only for me. I know it’s my first game but I will not be trying to think too much about those things. Probably when the game finishes, and if it finishes well, then I will be more thinking of myself.”Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolanewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League news: David Moyes unsettled by Manchester City’s interest in Iliman Ndiaye | Everton | The Guardian
description: Sunderland will visit San Siro in Europa League while Carlos Baleba must wait for his Manchester United debut
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Sunderland will visit San Siro in Europa League while Carlos Baleba must wait for his Manchester United debut
Content: Manchester City have yet to bid for Everton’s Iliman Ndiaye.Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManchester City have yet to bid for Everton’s Iliman Ndiaye.Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty ImagesThe talkEvertonPremier League news: David Moyes unsettled by Manchester City’s interest in Iliman NdiayeSunderland will visit San Siro in Europa League while Carlos Baleba must wait for his Manchester United debutGuardian sportand agenciesFri 28 Aug 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 18.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1.City’s Ndiaye bid unsettles MoyesDavid Moyes has responded to Manchester City’s interest in Iliman Ndiaye by insisting Everton do not have enough time to reinvest money raised through player sales before the transfer deadline. The Everton manager is determined to add to his squad before Tuesday’s deadline, not lose one of his better players such as Ndiaye, with the club still attempting to end their lengthy search for a new right-back.In contrast to the Everton chief executive, Angus Kinnear, who recently claimed the club were planning to challenge for Europe this season, Moyes insisted the squad needs “a lot of work” before it can achieve that target.City have yet to bid for Ndiaye, who has three years remaining on his Everton contract but declined several offers of an extension last season as they did not include a release clause for a Champions League club. “I think it would be very difficult to get it reinvested if anything came in, we are getting into a really late period now,” said Moyes, speaking of player sales in general.On Ndiaye, he added: “I’m certainly not encouraging a bid. I’m not encouraging that in a million years. I don’t know if it would be too tight for time. Deals and contracts are taking much longer now. There seems to be a lot more involved.”Everton remain interested in City’s Jack Grealish, who spent last season on loan at Hill Dickinson Stadium, but a right-back and centre-forward are more of a priority. Moyes added: “I’m saying there’s not much time but I’ll still try to see what we can do. I think we need to do much more if possible. We’re 100% trying to get a right-back and we will try and do that right up until the end of the window.”Everton’s positive start has been tainted by tensions created by Kinnear’s claims that The Friedkin Group, the club’s owners, viewed last season as “a failure” by missing out on European football and that Europe is achievable this term despite only modest investment in Moyes’s team.In response to the latter claim, Moyes said: “There would be a lot of work to do to put us in that category, but nobody put us in that category last year and for most of the season we ran close. You never know. We have started the season well and players have started the games good so that gives me hope that it could be a possibility.”Andy Hunter2.Milan fixture a riposte to Magpies, says Le BrisRégis Le Bris has said Sunderland’s forthcoming trip to Milan in the Europa League is “a symbol” of the club’s upward trajectory. For many years Newcastle fans have taunted their local rivals with chants of “You’ll never see a Mackem in Milan” and, after arriving from Brittany two years ago, Le Bris swiftly learned that St James’ Park regulars regarded themselves as distinctly superior to Sunderland supporters.Now, though, the tables have turned and Le Bris is enjoying the moment. Sunderland’s manager agreed that it seemed somehow appropriate that the first fixture involving his team to be drawn in Monaco on Friday featured a trip to San Siro.“To get back in Europe with this fixture, it’s a symbol,” said Le Bris, whose side finished seventh in the Premier League last season after beating Newcastle home and away. “It’s iconic. Milan is a massive club and it’s a massive story.“I’m aware of it [the Newcastle fans’ Milan jibes], but I want to speak more about us. We are proud to be in Sunderland and our fans deserve to be in this position. It’s [going to be] a huge experience and we are very proud to be part of it but we want to be efficient. We want to be competitive in the Europa League.”As Sunderland fans began ordering T-shirts and sweatshirts emblazoned with the message “Mackem in Milan” to wear in northern Italy, Le Bris seemed delighted that three players, goalkeeper Robin Roefs, winger Romaine Mundle and the forward Wilson Isidor have signed new long-term contracts at the Stadium of Light.Newcastle fans in Milan in 2023.  One of the banners shown says: ‘Have you ever seen a Mackem in Milan?’Photograph: PA Wire/PA“They see their future in Sunderland because they trust the club and like the environment and they trust the ambition of the club,” said a manager whose side will also face AZ, Dinamo Zagreb, Levski Sofia and Jagiellonia at the Stadium of Light and Anderlecht, Lech Poznan and Torreense away in the Europa League.Le Bris, whose team are at home to Fulham on Sunday, declined to comment on Sunderland’s attempt to sign Jack Grealish on loan from Manchester City but it is believed the former England winger is now most likely to rejoin Everton.Sunderland, meanwhile, remain in the hunt for a right winger and a striker this summer. “I trust the recruitment staff,” said Le Bris. “We are well aligned about the targets we need to make the team better and I still think that we will succeed in the transfer market.”Louise Taylor3.Gonzalez  ‘a smart player with huge potential’Matthias Jaissle is convinced new arrival Nico González will not take long to hit the ground running after his big-money arrival from Manchester City. The Spaniard could make his Newcastle debut on Saturday at Tottenham after a move from City that could rise to £52m this week, with the head coach excited by the 24-year-old’s ceiling.“He trained with us and he looks sharp,” Jaissle said. “It will take time [to adapt] and I can not tell you how long it takes but he’s a smart player, he has huge potential and already brings so much quality in the squad. He will adapt fast into our way of playing and then we can enjoy.”View image in fullscreenNico González is presented to the Newcastle fans at St James’ Park: ‘He will adapt fast into our way of playing,’ says Matthias Jaissle.Photograph: Serena Taylor/Newcastle United/Getty ImagesJaissle is hopeful that Gonzalez will not be the last player through the door at St James’ Park in this summer’s window, with the Belgium wideman Matias Fernandez-Pardo tipped to move to Tyneside from Lille. “It’s the first message of the morning – to push,” Jaissle said. “The management and Ross [Wilson], the sporting director, they’re doing an amazing job, trying everything. “We want to be smart, we don’t want to act in panic, so I’m really optimistic things will happen.”PA Media4.Glasner wants to bolster squad after Delap dealOliver Glasner expects more signings at Nottingham Forest after the arrival of the striker Liam Delap. The 23-year-old joined from Chelsea for a club-record £45m fee on Thursday, and Glasner plans to make further additions before Tuesday’s transfer deadline.Glasner would not comment on a reported £22m Forest offer for his former Crystal Palace wing-back Daniel Muñoz, but the Austrian did admit prospective deals were close to completion. “I think we will add two players,” Glasner said before Saturday’s trip to Liverpool and on the back of home league and Carabao Cup defeats by Leeds.“One we have added, that means we will have at least one more signing. Close deals, quite close to be done, but now from today our focus is on the Liverpool match. That is the most important thing in the next 30 hours and then we have three more days to get the deals over the line.”View image in fullscreenLiam Delap is looking to reignite his career at the City Ground after being frozen out at Chelsea.Photograph: Ritchie Sumpter/Nottingham Forest FC/Getty ImagesDelap left Chelsea after scoring only two goals in all competitions following his move from Ipswich last summer, and was made to train away from the first-team squad by new Blues manager Xabi Alonso. Glasner said: “It is clear you have to look for a club where you have better chances to get minutes and reignite your career, and that is why we think we are the right club for him.”PA Media5.O’Neil not finished in transfer marketGary O’Neil has insisted Ipswich are not finished in the transfer window after another busy week at the Premier League newcomers. Argentina international and World Cup winner Exequiel Palacios arrived at Portman Road on Thursday in the latest big-money move secured by the Suffolk club.Talks remain ongoing with the Aston Vila forward Tammy Abraham, who is yet to make a decision on whether to join on a season-long loan, it is understood, but O’Neil is hopeful more can occur in the coming days.Before Sunday’s trip to Manchester United, O’Neil told a press conference: “No, nothing to report on that [Abraham move]. We’re hopefully not finished. We’re still trying to do some business. As to who that is or what positions that will be in, there’s no update from me.“We’re still working hard to try and improve the group, but my focus now is firmly on the game at the weekend and making sure that we’re fully prepared for what is going to be an incredibly tough test.”Ipswich could have Florentino Luís involved at Old Trafford and Palacios is set to make his debut. Azor Matusiwa and Jack Taylor remain sidelined.PA Media6.United must wait for Baleba debutMichael Carrick has confirmed his “really exciting” addition Carlos Baleba will be unable to make his Manchester United debut for around three weeks due to an ankle injury.Following the summer arrivals of Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, United further bolstered their midfield by completing the £70m signing of the 22-year-old from Brighton on Tuesday. United’s director of football, Jason Wilcox, hailed Baleba as “an elite midfielder with immense potential to develop further” but fans will have to wait to see him play for the club.The Cameroon international arrived at Old Trafford with an ankle injury, which Carrick says will rule him out of Sunday’s Premier League home opener against promoted Ipswich and beyond. “He’s got a little ankle issue, so maybe a couple of weeks or so, maybe three weeks,” Carrick said. “We’ll see but we knew that before, so it’s no major issue but it’ll be great to have him back when we can.”View image in fullscreenCarlos Baleba  arrived at Old Trafford with an ankle injury, ruling him out of Sunday’s Premier League home opener against Ipswich and beyond.Photograph: Manchester United/Getty ImagesAsked if Baleba and Amad Diallo, another injured player, could return before the new three-week international break, the United manager said: “It’s obviously new, the break to deal with, but we’ll wait and see. We’re hopeful but I don’t want to put any deadlines on it just yet. Amad won’t be involved this week. He’ll be out for a little bit longer. Mase [Mason Mount] is back around the group, which was great. Trained this week, so that’s a big positive for us.”PA MediaExplore more on these topicsEvertonThe talkSunderlandNewcastle UnitedNottingham ForestIpswich TownManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Cole Palmer is a unicorn in this world inventing moments of pure footballing pleasure | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: Much like Central Cee, the Chelsea attacker is a distinct presence and right now is perhaps the only truly creative English player out there
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Much like Central Cee, the Chelsea attacker is a distinct presence and right now is perhaps the only truly creative English player out there
Content: Cole Palmer looks a little unusual in an era of hyper-athletes with a gangly, mischievous physicality.Illustration: David HumphriesView image in fullscreenCole Palmer looks a little unusual in an era of hyper-athletes with a gangly, mischievous physicality.Illustration: David HumphriesChelseaCole Palmer is a unicorn in this world inventing moments of pure footballing pleasureBarney RonayMuch like Central Cee, the Chelsea attacker is a distinct presence and right now is perhaps the only truly creative English player out thereFri 28 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.17 EDTShareThis weekCentral Ceelaunched his new Premier League song, called The Team. It owes its existence to a youth-centred, fist-bumping corporate tie-in with Coca-Cola, the press release for which appears to have involved a man in golf-casual clothing frowning at his computer screen for half an hour before typing “cool urban street words, what are?” into the AI search box, then nipping off for a quick brain-bowl strategy lunch with Roger from the Bluesky Synergy hub.The song is really good, because Central Cee is really good. He’s super-smart with words, funny and snappy, but also surprisingly tender and raw.And yes, this is an oh-no-dad’s-talking-about-rap moment. You can just scroll down if you like. The whole thing moves on to Cole Palmer very quickly, why he’s both the best English footballer and very easy to love currently, for various reasons.‘Armchair supporter’: do I still love going to football or just love the idea of it? | Max RushdenRead moreCentral Cee is a significant figure, perhaps the biggest British recording artist right now. He’s also oddly raw and fearless in the things he says, in a way that feels distinct from the standard, mannered modern person, and which has got him into trouble at least once.A few years back there was a furore when Central Cee decided to speak out against sexual prejudice. This sounds as if it should just be fine. Except, Central Cee’s call for tolerance was expressed via a lyric in the song Doja. And that lyric was: “How can I be homophobic? My bitch is gay.”Hmm. Problems there. What Central Cee is saying here, what Central Cee has done while appearing to express a progressive sensibility, is to introduce an entirely new tier of … Basically what he’s saying is: how can I be homophobic? I’m far too busy being sexist.This caused understandable offence. The b-word is demeaning and cheap, whatever your intentions. Don’t say it. Find better words. To his credit, Central Cee was very good at explaining and apologising, open to other views, while also seeming genuinely non-judgmental of other people regardless of difference or identity, with the exception, of course, of wastemen, mugs and snitches.He seems to have been forgiven now. More than that, he’s startlingly successful, the most streamed British rap artist of all time. Young people respond to him hungrily. He seems adaptive, fitted to the modern world. In the Coke video he looks blankly into the lens, gives you everything and nothing, risky but also weirdly fearless.What does this have to do with Cole Palmer, and the surge of heartfelt Palmer-love across all platforms this week after hisbrilliant performance against Fulhamon Monday?First, Palmer is good friends with Central Cee. He even turned up at the launch of the Coke song just before Chelsea’s Premier League opener. And Palmer really was sensational at Craven Cottage, twirling about between the defensive lines, all perfect touch and interesting angles.View image in fullscreenCole Palmer was sensational for Chelsea against Fulham at Craven Cottage.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe reaction was significant too. Everyone went wild for this. In particular passionate football men of a certain age went wild.This boy is gold, this boy gets people off their seats,the man in the TalkSport video chair growled, speaking from the gut and the spleen, coming off less like a piece of football analysis, more like a man offering a brave, husky funeral elegy for a very loyal family dog.This passion does have an edge to it. It is a mark of how hungry we are for something different, a counterpoint to the dominance of systems football, that despite being entirely academy-coded Palmer still seems to be a unicorn in this world.For the middle-aged proper football man he can look like a flicker of the pre-digital memory, football in the time of maverick authenticity, an age of mud, of landlines, of not wearing a seat belt, of smoking in pubs, of the casually discarded woodland porn mag, of Barry Davies shouting: “Oh, it’s magnificent and can’t they just taste it” while mods throw darts at each other in the background, because old fun is the best fun.This is, of course, both deluded and incorrect, because football encourages such feelings and because many middle-aged men are already both of these things. But Palmer is genuinely unusual in the modern game. He turns up in strange spaces, finds gullies and currents in between those static pegs.Right now he is perhaps the only truly creative English player out there, in the sense of inventing the game in front of him, dishing up in those moments the pure pleasure of a story being told in real time.He even looks a little unusual in an era of hyper‑athletes. Palmer is light and mobile. He can turn with balletic grace. But he also has that gangly, mischievous physicality, like a very clever cartoon alpaca has worked out how to put on a royal blue football kit and run around occasionally doing amusing celebrations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom here Palmer will benefit from having a very good club manager who gets his position. At Bayer Leverkusen Xabi Alonso designed an entire team around getting the best out of Florian Wirtz, the “free electron” in the structure.Beyond this, Palmer is clearly the player the national team should have been configured around after Euro 2024. It made some logical sensenot to pick himfor the World Cup, because merit and fitness are also important.
