But Thomas Tuchel simply has to play Palmer, Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane together now, even if you have to pack the team with cement sacks and tins of beans to make it work, because this is just incredibly hot, and there is literally no other point in playing these games.But it isn’t just the football. Palmer is also just weirdly likable. There is a temptation to cast him as a Lego-haired blank, some kind of urban idiot savant, a human being made entirely from white bread, energy drinks and discarded phone cases. But he’s clearly very smart, and also very modern in his own way.View image in fullscreenCole Palmer’s persona is unbothered, wry and oddly gentle.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesThis is another element of the Palmer persona. He looks unbothered, wry and oddly gentle. But the blankness is a thing, a way of being in the middle of all that glare. Palmer gives you nothing to bite on, no gaps in the armour. He even seems weirdly post-race, or just non-race, some kind of bowl-headed omni-man.It is both an attitude and a shield of sorts. There’s a thing young people do on the internet, known as Nonchalance. This is all about projecting indifference and impassive facial expressions, appearing comically unbothered while chaotic things happen around you. In the picture with Central Cee at the Coke thing they’re both doing it, staring blankly into the camera open but also closed.Palmer seems to do this naturally. He will sit with his legs crossed while a group of angry men have an on-pitch brawl nearby. He will have the sense of raw dramatic irony to look genuinely amused on the live TV feed as the refereestands right in the middle of the Chelsea huddle, one of the most comically weird sub-moments of the modern age.There is a theory nonchalance is a political attitude, a response by the post-Gen-Z demographic to the challenge of making the world you find less incoherent, less intrusive on your space, a blank against the constant wall of noise, dogma and ideological boilerplate hurled your way.Even the way Palmer plays has a kind of shrug about it, an existential creativity, making up your own patterns, making the world small, you-sized, following the lines in front of you.One of the best bits of Monday night’s game was his interview after. Sky’s reporter Emma Saunders asked Palmer: “How ready are you for this season?” His response was: “Did you not watch the game?” – which from some old‑school, spam-faced football man might have sounded a bit weird, a bit off on power dynamic, a bit man-woman.But it really wasn’t that at all. Palmer was already laughing. Saunders laughed back. And it was just a nice moment, banter-stuff, mate-chat, playing the game in front of you. English football has such an interesting figure here, not just a brilliant footballer, but a distinct presence, a way of existing in the middle of all that heat. Let’s try not to break him this time.Explore more on these topicsChelseaCentral CeecommentShareReuse this content

title: De Zerbi wants one more signing for Tottenham before transfer deadline | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: Roberto De Zerbi is keen to add one more signing to his Tottenham squad and departures are also possible before Tuesday night’s transfer deadline
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Roberto De Zerbi is keen to add one more signing to his Tottenham squad and departures are also possible before Tuesday night’s transfer deadline
Content: Roberto De Zerbi is still pushing to add another player to his squad despite a busy summer of signings at Spurs.Photograph: John Walton/PAView image in fullscreenRoberto De Zerbi is still pushing to add another player to his squad despite a busy summer of signings at Spurs.Photograph: John Walton/PATottenham HotspurDe Zerbi wants one more signing for Tottenham before transfer deadlineSpurs head coach pushing for ‘one specific position’Tottenham could offload players at end of hectic windowDavid HytnerFri 28 Aug 2026 10.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoberto De Zerbi is keen to add one more signing to his Tottenham squad and has said outgoing deals are also possible before Tuesday night’s transfer deadline.De Zerbi had dinner on Thursday night with Spurs’ owners and key executives and they discussed a final push to a window that has already exceeded his expectations. The manager welcomedOmar Marmoush to the clubon Thursday from Manchester City and is preparing to involve him in Saturday’s home game against Newcastle. Spurs have also been linked with a move for Liverpool’s Cody Gakpo.De Zerbi hopes Sávio’s fresh start will help Spurs’ much-needed rebrandRead more“I didn’t expect a market like we have done,” De Zerbi said. “I think we can do one player more and in one specific position. Yesterday we went for dinner with the owner, with Vinai [Venkatesham, the chief executive], with Johan [Lange, the sporting director] and with Enrico [Venturelli, De Zerbi’s assistant]. We spoke about this.“It can be possible out or in. The transfer market is crazy and we have to be able to find the new players. If some players go out, leave, or to make another player [come] in … I don’t know. We are very happy with the market we have done until now. It has been more than my expectation at the beginning.”De Zerbi is open to trimming his squad and mentioned midfielder Pape Sarr as one possible departure. “We have to see in the last day of the market what can happen with him,” he said. “I’ve been very clear with every player. If you speak clearly at the beginning you can’t expect a surprise. The players who want to leave, they left. Maybe we have some players who want to leave and they are waiting for the offer. We are waiting for the offer. To stay here, they have to feel proud and happy.“If you want to leave and you have not found the offer, it’s your problem, not my problem. I give respect, I kiss you, I hug you, but at the end [they] have to stay calm inside the dressing room. And not to speak too much because the rules have been clear.”De Zerbi said Mohammed Kudus, who has been out since January with a thigh injury, could return to the bench against Newcastle. He added that Micky van de Ven was “right to play” – in other words to start. He will make a decision on whether to start Pedro Porro and Sávio or use them as substitutes. “Marmoush is available to play, maybe also [at] the beginning of the game,” he said.De Zerbi considered his established, senior options for the front line, excluding No 10s – Kudus, Sávio, Marmoush, Dominic Solanke, Richarlison, Mathys Tel and Wilson Odobert.“Odobert is injured for a long time [after ACL surgery],” he said. “Before February, March, he is not available. And then maybe one of these players can leave before the end of the window. I think we are not too many players [in this department.]”De Zerbi made clear he wanted to include Dejan Kulusevski in the squad he submits to the Premier League after the closure of the transfer window. The attacking midfielder last played on 11 May 2025. Spurs are putting no timeframe on his return from a knee problem.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I hope and I will be very, very happy to see Kulusevski inside of the list and I want to put Kulusevski inside because he is working very well and he’s a different player,” De Zerbi said. “Also Xavi Simons … before March, April, he’s not ready [after ACL surgery]. Kulusevski feels good, he’s improving day by day. He deserves it because he suffered too much for his age. I’m not speaking of him as a player but as a human.”De Zerbi said he had paid for the meal with the club’s top brass at an Italian restaurant and he was effusive in his praise of how they have driven an expensive reboot of the squad. Spurs have spent £304.5m this summer – a figure that does include the £50m purchase obligation on Marmoush, which is due next summer. He has joined on an initial loan.“Really, it’s the first time [in my career] that I didn’t push to complete the squad,” De Zerbi said. “They pushed to build [with] the top players. Johan Lange was brilliant in terms of ideas to make solutions. Also, Vinai. I remember when we closed the Sandro Tonali deal, Vinai made a video call to me when I was on holiday and he had a big smile.”Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurRoberto De ZerbiTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Aston Villa close on Jackson and Mbaye as Emery clears air with departing Watkins | Aston Villa | The Guardian
description: Unai Emery is hopeful Nicolas Jackson will complete his £47.5m move from Chelsea in time to face Arsenal and should soon have PSG’s forward Ibrahim Mbaye in his squad
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Unai Emery is hopeful Nicolas Jackson will complete his £47.5m move from Chelsea in time to face Arsenal and should soon have PSG’s forward Ibrahim Mbaye in his squad
Content: Nicolas Jackson (left) and Ibrahim Mbaye, Senegal teammates, are poised to join Aston Villa from Chelsea and PSG respectively.Composite: Chelsea FC/Getty Images; Gongora/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNicolas Jackson (left) and Ibrahim Mbaye, Senegal teammates, are poised to join Aston Villa from Chelsea and PSG respectively.Composite: Chelsea FC/Getty Images; Gongora/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesAston VillaAston Villa close on Jackson and Mbaye as Emery clears air with departing WatkinsChelsea’s Jackson and PSG’s Mbaye poised to joinSaudi-bound Watkins says sorry for refusing to playBen FisherandJacob SteinbergFri 28 Aug 2026 12.09 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 09.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnai Emery said Aston Villa were embarking on a “new chapter” as he prepared to welcome Chelsea’s Nicolas Jackson and Paris Saint-Germain’s Ibrahim Mbaye in a near £100m remake of his forward line.Jackson, for whom Villa have paid an initial £47.5m, is in line to make his debut at home to Arsenal on Monday and the club are finalising a move for Mbaye, who will also cost about £47m. They needed to reshape up front after accepting a £50m bid from Al-Hilal for Ollie Watkins and are bringing in further funds by sellingEmiliano Martínez to Chelseafor £7.5m.Aston Villa’s squad is crumbling while Spurs splash out. Are the financial rules fair?Read moreJackson and Mbaye have been longstanding targets for the Villa manager. The 18-year-old winger Mbaye, a Senegal teammate of Jackson, was one of the preferred options to strengthen a key position. He played 24 Ligue 1 games for PSG last season, 10 from the start. In recent days, Villa pushed to sign Rafael Leão from Milan but the Portuguese winger is poised to join Galatasaray, whom Villa will visit in the Champions League.Jackson was Emery’s No 1 target to replace Watkins, who declined the offer of a new contract in favour of a £50m move to the Saudi Pro League club Al-Hilal. Both deals are yet to be formally confirmed. The one for Jackson could rise to a club-record £65m with add-ons.Emery said Watkins’s departure reduced him to tears and he revealed the England striker apologised to him and his teammates forrefusing to play in the 4-0 defeatat Brighton last weekend, leaving Villa without a recognised striker.“I can tell you his commitment and his behaviour was fantastic always,” Emery said. “He told us after the match he was sorry and he told us that he made a mistake, that he was wrong. We accepted it, the players as well, because he always had very good behaviour and commitment with the club, with us and with me.“For me, he is a fantastic guy, an even more fantastic a guy than a player. I told him bye with a huge hug and a small tear but now it’s a new chapter here with Nicolas Jackson. A new chapter, we replace him and of course all the best to Watkins in Saudi. With Nicolas Jackson replacing him, we are of course happy.”Emery dismissed the idea that the manner of Watkins’s departure could tarnish his standing among supporters. Watkins is Villa’s record goalscorer in the Premier League era, with 91 goals across 221 league appearances. “The four years working with him have been a high-level relationship with him as a professional,” Emery added. “Last week I was a little bit disappointed. I was disappointed, but we spoke about it, and now clear. One mistake is not closing all the good things he did here. For the supporters as well. He is class, and I think it’s a legacy here.”View image in fullscreenMaxim De Cuyper makes it 2-0 to Brighton on a bad day for Aston Villa.Photograph: James Marsh/ShutterstockEmery said the £50m fees generated for Watkins, who will be 31 in December, and Konsa, who turns 29 in October, were “crazy” given their ages. “We don’t want to be a club to sell players, but the responsibility is to accept it … because for the club it is a good deal. It does not change our objectives.”Emery acknowledged his side must perform much better against Arsenal than did against Brighton to avoid a second successive defeat. Leon Goretzka, who signed from Bayern Munich on Thursday, could make his debut against the champions, while Zion Suzuki could also feature for the first time afterhis £30m move from Parma, replacing Martínez.“Maybe we are not performing like we were performing but the objective is to get to the same way we did, the same performances we had,” said the Villa manager. “We will need time. Last year we showed we needed time. On Monday we will see, [whether] we will need more time or if some players are progressing quickly.”It promises to be a busy end to the window forChelseawho, as well as closing in on Martínez, have explored a move for the Monaco midfielder Lamine Camara while they wait for Manchester City to submit their first official offer for Enzo Fernández.City are yet to make contact with Chelsea over a deal for Fernández, who is desperate to leave before Tuesday night’s deadline. Chelsea are considering their next move and have Camara on a shortlist that also includes Bournemouth’s Alex Scott and Crystal Palace’s Adam Wharton. The Senegal international is not seen as a like-for-like replacement for Fernández but would strengthen Xabi Alonso’s midfield options if the Argentina international joins City.Chelsea are aware of Bournemouth’s determination not to sell Scott and have received similar messages from Palace regarding Wharton, while Arsenal are understood to have knocked back an inquiry for Martín Zubimendi.Although there have been suggestions that a deal for Fernández will be close to £106.7m, he will only be allowed to leave if Chelsea’s terms are met. Sources have warned City may have to pay more than the west London club’s initial £120m asking price for the 25-year-old.Explore more on these topicsAston VillaTransfer windowChelseaParis Saint-GermainnewsShareReuse this content

title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 8: Everton | Everton Women | The Guardian
description: Toffees new-look attack will hope to gel during their relatively easy start to the campaign in their second season at the historic Goodison Park
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Toffees new-look attack will hope to gel during their relatively easy start to the campaign in their second season at the historic Goodison Park
Content: Everton manager Scott Phelan speaks to his players after their 1-0 friendly victory over Hamburg. Photograph: Everton FCToffees new-look attack will hope to gel during their relatively easy start to the campaign in their second season at the historic Goodison ParkByTom GarryFri 28 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:10th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:8thProspectsWith a new manager in charge, the new season brings some fresh optimism for Everton. But nobody associated with the club will be getting carried away. Last season concluded with a respectable eighth-place finish and anything similar again would be considered a solid campaign for a team operating on a relatively small budget. The latest set of financial accounts showed Everton’s wage bill to befive times smaller than Chelsea’s, illustrating the financial gulf between the Merseysiders and those challenging at the top of the Women’s Super League.There have been positive elements to Everton’s transfer business this summer, not least the arrivals of Jutta Rantala, Noémie Mouchon and Hannah Cain from relegated Leicester City, as well as turning the Slovenia midfielder Zara Kramzar’s loan move from Roma into a permanent deal. Last season’s loan move for Hannah Blundell from Manchester United has also been converted into a permanent transfer, which was revealed in unusual circumstances, with the 32-year-old emerging from a make-shift ‘coffin’ during an amusing walkout at May’s World Sevens Football event in London.Scott Phelan’s team have a fairly kind start to the season given they begin with back-to-back matches against newly-promoted sides in Crystal Palace and Charlton Athletic. Their second home league fixture is against the other promoted side, Birmingham City. In between there are meetings with the sides that finished 10th and 11th last season, in West Ham and neighbours Liverpool. Everton do not face any of last season’s top three teams until November. They will, therefore, be keen to make a fast start and get plenty of points onboard before a tougher-looking run of games either side of the winter break.Everton’s WSL results in the past five seasonsOff-field pictureEverton’s women’s team was sold to the men’s parent company, Roundhouse Capital Holdings, last year in a move that was understood to be largely aimed at helping ensure the men’s team’s compliance with the Premier League’s profitability and sustainability rules (PSR). The women’s team train at the Finch Farm complex in Halewood, which they share with the men. It is one of the better-equipped facilities enjoyed by a WSL side.The managerPhelan was formally appointed in June after a four-month spell in interim charge, taking over from the sacked Brian Sørensen. This is the 38-year-old former Everton youth midfielder’s first senior managerial job, after coaching within the club’s boys’ academy. Phelan deploys a calm, measured approach and has spoken of his “unbelievable pride” at being given this job.Star signingThere is a lot of excitement at Everton about Australia forward Holly McNamara, signed from Melbourne City, where she won back-to-back Golden Boot awards in the A-League, on a free transfer. If the 23-year-old can replicate her goalscoring form in the northern hemisphere, Everton could well have a strong season and, with McNamara alongside Cain and Mouchon, the Merseyside club have a completely new-look attack. The England youth centre-back Hannah Silcock has also been snapped up from Liverpool, which looks like a very astute piece of business.View image in fullscreenHolly McNamara won back-to-back Golden Boots during her time at Melbourne City and has been handed the No 9 shirt at Everton.Photograph: Patrick Snow Jr/Everton FCStat attackDespite having the third fewest shots last season, Everton had the third most from Opta-defined fastbreaks (counterattacks). They also scored the joint-most goals from them (four), but that can only carry them so far. Their attack in regular play needs work.Bar chart showing that Everton’s 8.4% of chances from fast breaks was the most in the WSL last seasonSet for a breakthroughThe England youth defender Naomi Layzell has arrived on loan from Manchester City and Everton and the Lionesses will be hoping it can be a good year for the fit-again 22-year-old. Layzell came to prominence with a goal against Barcelona in the Women’s Champions League two years ago but has since suffered injury misfortune. There is hope at Everton that Layzell can kick on this season and show why she is potentially a future regular for England’s senior side. She has previously been called up to train with Sarina Wiegman’s side.What they say“It’sbeen a tough pre-season in terms of the physical load and things like that, butthat’s great preparation for the season.It’s just so important to get everyone on the same page early on. We want to do as well as we can in terms of getting results and being where we want to bein the table” – Everton goalkeeperCourtney BrosnanWhere are they playing their home games?The women’s team moved to Goodison Park last summer and will continue to play all of their home games there. They made their debut at the Hill Dickinson Stadium last season in a one-off appearance, losing to Manchester United, and while there is no confirmation of when they will next play at the men’s ground, it is understood that is not off the table for the coming campaign.Explore more on these topicsWSL season previews 2026-27Everton WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Who was given the toughest fixtures in the Champions League draw? | Champions League | The Guardian
description: The draw was kind to Liverpool and Arsenal, but Manchester City and Aston Villa do not have it so good
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The draw was kind to Liverpool and Arsenal, but Manchester City and Aston Villa do not have it so good
Content: The prize on offer for the 36 teams.Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe prize on offer for the 36 teams.Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty ImagesGuardian Sport NetworkChampions LeagueWho was given the toughest fixtures in the Champions League draw?The draw was kind to Liverpool and Arsenal, but Manchester City and Aston Villa do not have it so goodByOpta AnalystOliver Hopkins and Ali TweedaleFri 28 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe36 clubs in the Champions League know who they will play in the league phase, but which team has the kindest draw and who has the toughest assignment? Each side knows their eight opponents but, given that no two teams face the same set of opponents, this is not a level playing field. We have used the Opta power rankings – which rank 16,000 teams from across the world on the same scale – to find out who did best in the draw.Which teams have the easiest fixtures?In terms of Premier League clubs,Liverpoolhave received the easiest draw. Their eight opponents have an average rating of 90.0, making theirs the ninth-kindest fixture list overall. Atlético Madrid and Inter were the two easiest pot-one opponents that Premier League clubs could draw, and Liverpool will play them both. They have avoided any true European behemoth.Arsenal also received a relatively favourable draw, albeit for different reasons. Their pot-one fixtures against Bayern Munich (away) and Real Madrid (home) are about as difficult as they come – and they also drew Borussia Dortmund, the highest-ranked team in pot two – but, beyond those fixtures, there is little for Mikel Arteta’s side to fear.Arsenaldrew the two lowest-ranked sides in pot four: Sabah and Slovan Bratislava. So, while the top end of their draw is tough, the bottom end is kind. Sabah, 170th in the world, and Slovan Bratislava, 224th, are the two lowest-ranked teams in the competition.View image in fullscreenThe 18 easiest draws.Stuttgart received the easiest draw of any team, with their opponents having an average rating of 88.9. Inter came out of the draw particularly well, receiving the second-easiest set of fixtures, with an average opponent rating of 89.5. Having finished as runners-up in 2024-25, Inter suffered a surprise exit at the hands of Bodø/Glimt in the playoff stage last season. Given their relatively easy schedule, they will hope to avoid that stage altogether and qualify directly for the last 16.Which teams have the toughest fixtures?Manchester City will begin aChampions Leaguecampaign without Pep Guardiola for the first time in 11 years. His replacement, Enzo Maresca, has been handed the most difficult fixture list of any Premier League club. City’s opponents have an average rating of 91.7, with only five teams receiving a tougher draw overall. They have drawn two European giants in pot one – Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain – while Napoli, ranked 34th in the world, are a particularly difficult assignment from pot three.Aston Villa also drew Barcelona and PSG from pot one, although they have fond memories of their previous meeting with the French champions at Villa Park. PSG ultimately knocked Villa out in 2024-25, but only just.Villa won the second leg of their quarter-finals3-2 at home, falling just short over the tie as they lost 5-4 on aggregate.Villa’s squad has changed significantlysince then, however, and they were also given the toughest possible pair of opponents from pot two in Club Brugge and Borussia Dortmund.Their opponents from the lower pots are more forgiving, but Unai Emery will need to work his European magic if a squad that has undergone significant churn this summer is to make another deep run in the competition.View image in fullscreenThe 18 toughest draws.Manchester United are back in the Champions League for the first time since 2023-24. Their previous campaign did not go particularly well, with United losing four of their six games and finishing bottom of their group. Their draw this season is not disastrous, but it is definitely on the more difficult side.They face Bayern Munich and Atlético Madrid from pot one, and have drawn Como – the most difficult possible opponent in pot four. Fixtures against Sporting CP, ranked 21st in the world, and Roma, 22nd, should also be highly competitive. United drew RB Leipzig (38th) and Villarreal (43rd) from pot three. They were not the worst possible outcomes, but there were certainly plenty of more favourable draws available.It is no surprise to see Sabah and Slavia Prague emerge with the hardest and third-hardest fixture lists, respectively. Beyond those two, Ligue 1 club Lens received a particularly difficult draw, with their opponents’ average rating at 92.1. Atlético Madrid were not far behind on 92.0.This is an article byOpta AnalystExplore more on these topicsChampions LeagueGuardian Sport NetworkLiverpoolManchester UnitedManchester CityAston VillaArsenalEuropean club footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: St Helens playoff hopes hang by a thread after thrashing by Leeds | Super League | The Guardian
description: St Helens’ hopes of reaching the playoffs were dealt a major blow by a 34-6 defeat at home by Leeds
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: St Helens’ hopes of reaching the playoffs were dealt a major blow by a 34-6 defeat at home by Leeds
Content: Ryan Hall touches down Leeds’ fourth try in their convincing victory against St Helens.Photograph: Paul Currie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRyan Hall touches down Leeds’ fourth try in their convincing victory against St Helens.Photograph: Paul Currie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockSuper LeagueSt Helens playoff hopes hang by a thread after thrashing by LeedsSt Helens 6-34 LeedsRhinos return to top of table after running in six triesAaron Bowerat BrewDog StadiumFri 28 Aug 2026 17.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 19.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you needed any further proof that Super League’s two most successful sides are travelling in different directions in 2026, this was about as conclusive as you can get.There are two very different fates awaitingLeeds Rhinosand St Helens in three weeks or so. The Rhinos will now almost certainly be resting up for a Super League playoff semi-final, having earned a bye through the opening week of the playoffs by virtue of a top-two finish. They are still favourites to end the regular season on top after this latest impressive victory.Wigan rise to occasion against Hull KR as town unites to remember Sir Billy BostonRead moreBut the Saints, barring a late miraculous run of results involving themselves and the teams around them, will be resting up and preparing for 2027, with their 60-year record of making the end-of-season playoffs ending. After back-to-back wins in the last fortnight, you wondered if this was the night thatSt Helenscould really make people sit up and take notice.Win here, and they would not only dent Leeds’ chances of the League Leaders’ Shield, but they would put themselves right back in the mix for the top six. Instead, what we saw was an 80 minutes very much played out to the form of 2026 on the whole. The Rhinos were impressive, Jake Connor was sensational yet again and the Saints ultimately disappointed.With two rounds to go, Leeds can now look ahead to what is in effect a decider for top spot next Saturday against Wigan. It is a playoff game before the playoffs start, and is a truly unmissable meeting of Super League’s two standout sides in 2026. “Next week decides the league leaders, and what a great position to be in,” Brad Arthur, the Leeds coach, said.His side were very good again when it mattered. With Connor the influential figure throughout, he helped guide the Rhinos into an 18-0 half-time lead. Saints began brightly but couldn’t turn any pressure into points, and when Leeds forged attacking opportunities, they offered their great rivals a lesson in how to be ruthless, with Connor at the heart of it.Tries for Chris Hankinson, Harry Newman and Cameron Smith before one for Ryan Hall shortly after the restart made it 22-0 in Leeds’ favour, and ended it as a contest with half an hour remaining. It all means that for St Helens, their destiny is now out of their own hands – and the chances of the top six look slim at best.View image in fullscreenHarry Newman shows his delight at full timePhotograph: Paul Currie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockIn all probability, they now have to win their last two games and win them well to stand any chance of making the playoffs. Their opponents are fifth-placed Leigh and sixth-placed Hull KR; and while both those sides lost themselves this weekend, this season has presented enough evidence to suggest Saints simply do not have the quality to drag it back from here.“I’m really disappointed,” their interim coach, Eamon O’Carroll, said. “Not in the players, but for them. The start was what we wanted, it was attritional and we went after it but we lost some big moments after that, and Leeds showed their class.”Australia’s coach, Kevin Walters, will take charge of the Saints in 2027 and were he watching this game, he would have seen first hand the size of the task that awaits. Jack Welsby’s magnificent solo try at least ensured Saints got on the scoresheet, but they ended with their worst post-war defeat to Leeds at home after Connor helped Leeds respond with a sumptuous kick for Ash Handley to touch down and put them back in control.Connor’s boot then caused mayhem amongst the St Helens defence again to allow his half-back partner, Brodie Croft, to score his 28th try of the season. That made it 34-6 but by then the home support had already begun to filter away. Their season is ebbing away and is almost over: but in truth, Leeds’ may just be beginning.St HelensSailor; Douglas, Macdonald, Welsby, Cross; Robertson, Lomax; Suluka-Fifita, Shorrocks, Klemmer, Davies, Wright, Host.InterchangeWalmsley, Humphreys, Keeley, Evans.TryWelsby.GoalSailor.LeedsMiller; Hall, Bird, Handley, Newman; Croft, Connor; Oledzki, O’Connor, Jenkins, Watkins, Hankinson, Cassell.InterchangeSmith, Holroyd, Levi, Holroyd.TriesHankinson, Smith, Newman, Hall, Handley, Croft.GoalsConnor 5.RefereeMarcus Griffiths.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueSt HelensLeeds RhinosRugby leaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Carlos Alcaraz believes ‘it is possible’ to win US Open despite long injury layoff | Carlos Alcaraz | The Guardian
description: Carlos Alcaraz is feeling confident as he returns to professional tennis after a four-month injury layoff due to a right wrist injury
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Carlos Alcaraz is feeling confident as he returns to professional tennis after a four-month injury layoff due to a right wrist injury
Content: Carlos Alcaraz missed four months of the season due to an injury to his right wrist sustained at the Barcelona Open.Photograph: Guerin Charles/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz missed four months of the season due to an injury to his right wrist sustained at the Barcelona Open.Photograph: Guerin Charles/ABACA/ShutterstockCarlos AlcarazCarlos Alcaraz believes ‘it is possible’ to win US Open despite long injury layoffThe 23-year-old has not competed in singles since AprilDefending champion faces Roman Safiullin in first roundTumaini Carayolin New YorkFri 28 Aug 2026 15.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCarlos Alcaraz believes he is capable of winning the US Open as he returns to professional tennis after a four-month injury layoff due to a right wrist injury.Alcaraz, the defending champion in New York, will compete in singles for the first time since injuring his wrist at the Barcelona Open in April when he faces Roman Safiullin in the first round. “So, it is possible [to win],” Alcaraz said. “I think that many people have shown it. [Roger] Federer, [Rafa] Nadal, many people have shown that you can win a grand slam after having been injured for a long time or having had a very hard injury. So we’re going to try to tie ourselves to that belief that we can do it too.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShaky Sabalenka and wide-open men’s draw set stage for US Open dramaRead moreThis season began with one of the greatest achievements of Alcaraz’s career as he became the youngest man in history to complete a career grand slam with his triumph in Australia. However, his homecoming in Barcelona a few days after reaching the Monte Carlo final ended in him injuring his right wrist and being sidelined for a lengthy period. Alcaraz described his uncertainty as the most difficult part of the past four months.“The first month was kind of difficult for me, because I couldn’t do anything with my right arm,” he said. “It was tough. But at the same time, I enjoyed my time. I enjoyed my time with family, with friends, staying at home. But once I started to practice a little bit, that I didn’t know when I’m gonna start, [those] thoughts are really difficult to deal with, because I don’t know if I’m gonna be ready for Cincinnati, for US Open, or I’m gonna miss the whole American swing. So those thoughts were really difficult to deal with. But finally, here we are.”The challenge of coming back from such a difficult injury is only compounded by the fact that Alcaraz is making his return at a grand slam in the best of five sets format. Alcaraz only began hitting again just over four weeks ago and the timeline of his recovery meant the 23-year-old has not had time to slowly work his way back into competition. After missing the French Open, where he was also the defending champion, and Wimbledon, Alcaraz was understandably desperate not to be absent for the final grand slam of the year. “Coming to the US Open, best-of-five for the first one, in such a long time, it’s really challenging.” he said.“Probably, in terms of preparation and everything, [it] is not the best time. But we, my team and me, believe that I’m ready. It wasn’t an easy decision. I just did whatever it took to be ready. I just tried to do everything perfect on and off the court, to feel ready. Really long practices, really intense practices, just to see how my wrist is going to react on the practices and after that really long days. We saw everything [was] OK, everything [was] good with those practices, and we thought it’s going to be the time to be back.”Explore more on these topicsCarlos AlcarazUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Maybe the speed guns are dodgy’: Jofra Archer plays down fastest spell after England dominate | Jofra Archer | The Guardian
description: The fastest spell of Jofra Archer’s career helped put England in a dominant position in the second Test against Pakistan
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: The fastest spell of Jofra Archer’s career helped put England in a dominant position in the second Test against Pakistan
Content: Jofra Archer bowls Mohammad Abbas for two.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJofra Archer bowls Mohammad Abbas for two.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianJofra Archer‘Maybe the speed guns are dodgy’: Jofra Archer plays down fastest spell after England dominateBowler averages 90.7mph and takes three wickets‘With this attack you don’t have to do too much’Simon Burntonat Lord'sFri 28 Aug 2026 15.28 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 17.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJofra Archer produced a ferocious spell of fast bowling at the start of Pakistan’s first innings, which will go down as his fastest in Test cricket with an average speed of 90.7mph, to help Englandinto a dominant positionin the second Test. But after finishing with three wickets the bowler insisted that whatever his contribution to breaking the tourists’ spirit, it was the speed gun that broke first.“Nah, the speed gun isn’t working properly,” the 31-year-old said. “I saw some of them [speeds] and I was like, it didn’t really feel that way. I don’t know who’s up in the box working it, but thanks. I remember playing here in the Ashes in 2019 and thinking the same thing. Maybe the speed guns are a little bit dodgy here.”Azan Awais offers Pakistan ray of hope amid their second Test gloomRead moreOllie Robinson took four wickets with Josh Tongue responsible for the other two as the four-man pace attack, with Gus Atkinson unrewarded on this occasion, bowled Pakistan out for 110 to give England a 180-run first-innings lead. “Everyone chips in. Ollie’s been phenomenal since he started [playing] again. Gus and Tonguey, everyone’s picking up the slack,” Archer said. “With this attack you don’t have to go and do too much. You don’t have to try too hard. You know someone’s going to back you up.”The 21-year-old opener Azan Awais was one of only two Pakistan batters to reach double figures, reaching 46 – Saud Shakeel was their next highest scorer with 16 – before he pulled Robinson to deep square-leg.“We’ve done a lot right in this Test – we’ve bowled better, but the batting is definitely a concern,” said Sarfaraz Ahmed, their head coach. “At the moment, as a batting unit, we are not up to the mark. But we’re still hopeful. You never know, anything can happen in cricket. I hope we can get them out for another 70 or 80 and chase a target of 350 or so. So we hope for the best.“England have a great bowling attack right now. In the morning,Jofra Archerto Azan Awais, I think that was a great spell. The way that kid handled it, I think it’s good for his career. That time that he batted, facing quality bowling, will be a big boost for him.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut Archer was less complimentary about Awais’s batting. “I’ve never seen someone play and miss so many balls and not get out,” he said. “But whatever he did, he did it well. title: County cricket day two: Hill and Cliff lift Yorkshire, Elgar digs in for Essex – as it happened | County Championship | The Guardian
description: George Hill and Ben Cliff brought fireworks to Scarborough while Dean Elgar’s four-hour stand turned up the heat on Surrey
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: George Hill and Ben Cliff brought fireworks to Scarborough while Dean Elgar’s four-hour stand turned up the heat on Surrey
Content: 5h ago15.41 EDTRoundup: Yorkshire fireworks light up ScarboroughTanya AldredDespite a morning washout, play broke out at Scarborough andYorkshire’s tail wagged entertainingly againstLeicestershire.George Hill bashed a merry 62, while Dom Bess and Ben Cliff added fireworks to please a crowd dressed in pink and purple to support the local Saint Catherine’s hospice.John Simpson’s unbeaten 64 was crucial in givingSussexa small first- innings lead at Hove as Craig Overton (four for 66) and Lewis Gregory (three for 55) fought back with the ball.Somerset’sTom Lammonby then made batting look easy with a breezy 74 not out.A couple of days after announcing his retirement at the end of the season, Dean Elgar jigsawed a crucial century forEssex.The South African struck around for nearly four hours, backed up by a silky 43 from Charlie Allison. Rahul Chahar grabbed six wickets butSurreythen slumped to 51-4, still 45 behind.There was a century of a different hue forDurham’s David Bedingham, hit off 99 balls and full of punchy gorgeousness. It was his fifth ton of the Championship season. Ben Stokes biffed 45 before Sai Kishore floated one between bat and pad as Durham built a lead of 194 overGloucestershire.There was no first hundred of the year for Zak Crawley, removed by Ben Sanderson for 89, asKenthad a staircase-and-trapdoor kind of day in the Division Two eye-baller. They lost eight for 94 against excellentNorthantsbowling, then added 89 for the last two wickets thanks to Daniel Bell-Drummond’s captain’s knock of 70.Nottinghamshireendured a terrible start to the day at Edgbaston againstWarwickshire. Haseeb Hameed and Freddie McCann were both dismissed for ducks, but the in-form Joe Clarke knitted a support blanket with a stylish hundred, ending the day unbeaten on 146 as he passed the 1,000-run mark for the season.Lancashirewere invited to bat at New Road on a dish-dirty morning, and though Keaton Jennings opened with a studied 55, he had to watch the middle order cascade away. Ben Walkden and Tom Bailey added late-order fibre, with four wickets forWorcestershire’s Beyers Swanepoel.Glamorgan tootled to 149-9, just 13 behind Hampshire at Sophia Gardens as the game heads to a one-innings shootout, while there was time forMiddlesex’s Ryan Higgins to take two wickets atDerbyshire.Share

title: England v Pakistan: second men’s cricket Test, day two – as it happened | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Ollie Robinson took 4-11 and Jofra Archer bowled ferociously as England dominated Pakistan’s batters and opened a 261-lead at Lord’s
Author: Tim de Lisle
Headline: Ollie Robinson took 4-11 and Jofra Archer bowled ferociously as England dominated Pakistan’s batters and opened a 261-lead at Lord’s
Content: 7h ago14.08 EDTAli MartinJoe Root did not want the England captaincy when the prospect started to be floated earlier this summer.After performing the role as a ­stand-in for the suspended Ben Stokes against New Zealand at the Oval, his father, Matt, floated a full-time return as a hypothetical and says this was met with a “no”.Root was apparently swayed by the impending arrival of Stephen ­Fleming as head coach, with the pair speaking regularly before roles were locked down. But watching this ­one-sided second day against Pakistan at Lord’s – and indeed the ­one-sided series opener at ­Headingley – one wonders whether being handed the keys to this pace attack was another clincher for Root.This has clearly been a stressful week for Root, with the needless Brydon Carse affair dominating the build-up and serving as an early reminder about the curve balls a Test captain can face. As per his old man, Root spent “four hours” on the phone last Sunday dealing with the fallout when he was meant to be relaxing at a family lunch. He was still thoroughly pissed off about it at his pre-match press conference two days later which, given his usual ­disposition, said plenty.All that anger appeared to melt away at Lord’s on Friday, however, when, with 290 first innings runs on the board after some tail-end swish in the morning, Root’s attack set about unstitching Pakistan’s batting lineup once more. Ollie Robinson claimed a remarkable four for 11 from 13 overs, Jofra Archer three for 26 from 11.2. The visitors were bowled out for a sorry-looking 110 to ship a 180-run deficit – with England stretching this to 261 for the loss of three wickets in the final session.Olé for Robinson as England take firm control of Lord’s Test against PakistanRead moreShareUpdated at14.08 EDT

title: The hollowing out of Tennis.com is a warning for American sports journalism | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Tennis.com once paired news and scores with distinctive voices. Its overhaul is the latest sign that serious tennis writing in the US is becoming endangered
Author: Tim Joyce
Headline: Tennis.com once paired news and scores with distinctive voices. Its overhaul is the latest sign that serious tennis writing in the US is becoming endangered
Content: The US Open got underway with the mixed doubles but coverage of the tournament has changed in recent years.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe US Open got underway with the mixed doubles but coverage of the tournament has changed in recent years.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesTennisThe hollowing out of Tennis.com is a warning for American sports journalismTim JoyceThe site once paired news and scores with distinctive voices. Its overhaul under Sinclair Media is the latest sign that serious tennis writing in the US is becoming endangeredFri 28 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 05.14 EDTShareAfew weeks ago, as I often do, I went to theTennis.com site to get an update about a match and to check out the commentary from my fellow tennis journalists. I was taken aback when, instead of the usual colorful graphics and info, I was greeted with a rudimentary-looking homepage that displayed only scores and rankings.At first I thought it was a glitch of some sort. But sadly, no. As it turns out, Tennis.com, originally the online site of Tennis Magazine, is under a complete overhaul and will no longer be the home of esteemed writers such as Steve Tignor and Pete Bodo, robbing fans of unique and personal takes on the sport. It appears the longest running American tennis-specific publication is no longer alive in any form.Tennis Magazine started in 1965 (with the Tennis.com website starting in 1996) and existed in print form through 2022. Its previous owners included Golf Digest and the New York Times Company. But when Sinclair Broadcast Group, thecontroversial conservative-leaning media company, bought the site in 2017, merging it into one entity with the Tennis Channel, the writing – that is to say the eventual dearth of writing – was on the wall.Tignor told me that “in some ways, I feared this day for 25 years”, acknowledging that people are consuming news and information much differently than they did even 10 years ago. And, more to the point, “having Tennis.com owned by a broadcaster [Tennis Channel] wasn’t a perfect scenario to begin with since they intrinsically have different goals.”I emailed Jill Dortheimer, vice-president of communications for Tennis Channel, for comment on the changes and she wrote back saying, “Tennis.com is in the midst of a full rebuild and the first priority for us is to deliver fast, comprehensive match and tournament schedules, scores, draws, etc. But there is much more to come in the future to improve the experience for fans.” She didn’t respond to my specific queries of whether there was an issue with page views or if there were any plans to reintroduce written commentary.From my perspective it appears Sinclair is more interested in having its on-air announcers debate gambling odds during matches to please advertisers like BetMGM and FanDuel than having insightful and independent-minded commentary on the Tennis.com website.Once upon a time, a time that suddenly feels long ago even though it’s only a couple of decades past, if one was an avid fan of tennis who also enjoyed reading articles about the sport – not just coverage of matches – there were a plethora of American publications focused solely on tennis: Tennis Magazine, World Tennis Magazine, Tennis Week, along with a few others. The abundance of publications coincided with the so-called “tennis boom” in the United States in the 1970s and 80s.Further, not only were there plentiful magazines devoted to tennis, but several newspapers in the United States had a dedicated tennis writer, with bylines and datelines from all four grand slam events. Today only the New York Times-owned Athletic employs full-time tennis writers, most notably Matthew Futterman. That’s it.What makes this slightly curious is the fact that the UK continues to have tennis beat writers (including the Guardian) at its major newspapers and significant tennis readership. Is it a case of “out of sight, out of mind” in reverse? The more coverage the media gives to tennis will then therefore generate more interest? In the US at least, the rich get richer; football has an obscenely massive and still-growing presence in the sports media world whereas more niche sports have dropped significantly.Steve Flink, one of only a handful of journalists enshrined in the International Tennis Hall of Fame, has more than a half century of experience working for a variety of publications. He still believes there is a desire for more tennis coverage in the print world but his outlook isn’t optimistic.View image in fullscreenDoes more media coverage of tennis generate greater interest in the sport – or does dwindling coverage only accelerate its decline?Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty Images“Tennis followers who are 50 and older do thirst for good writing on the sport and their favorite players. I believe they almost yearn for it. But the younger fans seem to only want videos. Is it a case of the scant coverage from the media only feeding into this problem? From my viewpoint the answer is an emphatic yes,” he told me.Flink, who has spent a great deal of time in England throughout his life, added: “I have no doubt that the British tennis fans are considerably more interested in reading daily accounts about tennis in their newspapers. Their newspapers have maintained more prominence in terms of sports coverage overall and tennis specifically. Until about 10 years ago or slightly longer, many US newspapers still sent reporters to Wimbledon but now very few are there. Now with AI spreading like wildfire, the battle could be permanently lost – at least in this country.”Golf and tennis are often twinned in the public consciousness; rightly or wrongly both are considered elitist, often cater to wealthier demographics and are individual sports. But golf still has two legacy magazines online – Golf.com and golfdigest.com – that appear to be doing just fine. While golf coverage across newspapers’ online coverage has dwindled significantly, the fact the sport still has a huge online presence with well-known publications leaves one wondering why tennis can’t do the same?One of the more disturbing aspects to all this is that without independent voices providing insightful and at times controversial commentary on the sport, there’s the risk of not challenging the status quo, so the media becomes just an extension of the tournaments that they televise and a slave to their advertisers. (For example, the aforementioned Futterman of the Athleticjust wrote a pieceexposing the ridiculous pricing policy at the US Open which will shut out the majority of fans.)Finally, with a pivot towards more visual or audio programing – be it match highlights or podcasts or not-exactly-penetrating interviews with players on social media – the public is losing out as the written word is threatened with irrelevance.Studyafterstudyhas found that one processes information more comprehensively and has better recall when reading text, either on the printed page or a screen versus watching video.Will there be a backlash against AI-generated articles and video-only content? One can only hope. Maybe some sites should advertise themselves as “AI-free”. Will independent journalism and the written word survive? Or will insightful analysis become niche? The way things are progressing, at least in the United States, isn’t all that promising.Explore more on these topicsTennisUS sports mediaUS Open Tennis 2026US sportsUS Open tennisNewspapers & magazinescommentShareReuse this content

title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm? | Meta | The Guardian
description: Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands
Content: Mark Zuckerberg was not forced to testify in the US lawsuit, which Meta settled on Wednesday.Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg was not forced to testify in the US lawsuit, which Meta settled on Wednesday.Photograph: Jill Connelly/Getty ImagesMetaWhat could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the NetherlandsAisha DownFri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 00.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supportingMeareg’s lawsuit against the companyin Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly askedFacebookto remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media companyagreed to pay $18bnand to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement,Metahas said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the stateshad sought– $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.View image in fullscreenMeta’s headquarters in Menlo Park, California.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesFor the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.It sees teenage girls watch diet content andshows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content andshows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to haveamplified contentthat promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. Itcontributedto the election victory of Donald Trump.Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in eastAfricadid almost nothing to prevent this.In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make somechangesto this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily havepersonalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.Arturo Béjar, anex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenProtests in Malaysia in 2012 against the persecution of Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar. Meta was alleged in a lawsuit to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya.Photograph: Mohd Rasfan/AFP via Getty ImagesIn Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands foralleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”The European Commission released a charge sheet against Metathis summersaying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.Earlier this year itmanagedtododgea class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed backforcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, ithas saidit employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”Explore more on these topicsMetaFacebookSocial mediaEthiopiaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic was unlawful, US judge rules  | Technology | The Guardian
description: Anthropic ​argued designation as ‘supply-chain risk’ could cost billions ‌in lost business ‌and reputational harm
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Anthropic ​argued designation as ‘supply-chain risk’ could cost billions ‌in lost business ‌and reputational harm
Content: In her Anthropic ruling, Judge Rita Lin said the ‘empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics’.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenIn her Anthropic ruling, Judge Rita Lin said the ‘empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics’.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersTechnologyPentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic was unlawful, US judge rulesAnthropic ​argued designation as ‘supply-chain risk’ could cost billions ‌in lost business ‌and reputational harmNick Robins-Earlyand agenciesThu 27 Aug 2026 23.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US judge ruled on Thursday that the Trump administration broke the law when it designatedAnthropicas a supply chain risk earlier this year, finding that the government had unlawfully targeted the AI firm for refusing to comply with defense department demands.“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” Judge Rita Lin said in a 59-page decision.Lin’s ruling barred the federal agencies named in the lawsuit from enforcing Donald Trump’s order to stop using Anthropic’s tools and overturned the designation of the company as a “supply chain risk” by the defense secretary,Pete Hegseth.The status, usually reserved for foreign firms, would have blocked government agencies from doing business with Anthropic.The case emerged out of a months-long feud between Anthropic and the Pentagon at the start of the year. Anthropic refused to allow the government to use its Claude AI model for fully autonomous lethal weapons or domestic mass surveillance, resulting in Hegseth accusing the company of “arrogance and betrayal”.Lin puta temporary pauseon the government’s punitive measures in March, stating that the government’s actions looked like an attempt to “cripple Anthropic” for exercising its first amendment rights. The ruling this week makes that temporary suspension permanent, although the government may appeal.“We welcome the court’s ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful,” an Anthropic spokesperson said.Lin’s ruling is a victory for Anthropic, which had warned that the supply chain risk designation could cost the company billions of dollars and complicate its business model. Anthropic is alsoplanning an IPOlater this year that could value the firm at $2tn and raise $100bn, exceeding the record set by SpaceX in June.Anthropic still faces legal hurdles related to the supply chain risk designation, however, as the outcome of a second lawsuit in Washington DC is still pending. That case will be heard by a three-judge panel, two of whom are Trump appointees whohave expressed skepticismabout Anthropic’s arguments.AI slopper in chief: Trump turns to social media amid tough questionsRead moreAnthropic says that AI models are not reliable enough to be safely used in autonomous weapons ‌and that it opposes domestic surveillance as a violation of rights, but the Pentagon says private companies should not be able to constrain military action.In its 9 March lawsuit, Anthropic alleged the government violated its right to free speech under the first amendment of the constitution by retaliating against its views on AI safety. The company said it was not given a chance to dispute the designation, in violation of its fifth amendment right to due process.“Though the Department of War is undisputedly free to select the AI vendor of its choice,” Lin said, “the evidence demonstrates that the broad measures imposed on Anthropic were illegal and baseless.”Anthropic’s designation was the first time a US company had been publicly categorized as a supply-chain risk under an obscure government-procurement statute aimed at protecting military systems ​from foreign sabotage.With Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsTechnologyPete HegsethAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)US politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nicola Coughlan and Matt Lucas among stars backing campaign against AI voice cloning | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: About 80 people sign open letter to Andy Burnham calling for legislation to protect voice ownership
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: About 80 people sign open letter to Andy Burnham calling for legislation to protect voice ownership
Content: Nicola Coughlan says she is deeply worried that legislation is not keeping up with the rapid rise of AI technology.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/EPAView image in fullscreenNicola Coughlan says she is deeply worried that legislation is not keeping up with the rapid rise of AI technology.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/EPAAI (artificial intelligence)Nicola Coughlan and Matt Lucas among stars backing campaign against AI voice cloningAbout 80 people sign open letter to Andy Burnham calling for legislation to protect voice ownershipJamie GriersonFri 28 Aug 2026 03.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNicola Coughlan,Hugh Bonnevilleand Matt Lucas are among a group of actors backing a campaign against artificial intelligence voice cloning.Save Our Voices Now, which is also being supported by Luke Evans, Jen Brister, Siobhán McSweeney and Pearl Mackie, aims to stop the practice in which AI technology is used to replicate a real person’s voice to say anything it is prompted to.Bonneville, the star of Paddington and Downton Abbey, said: “My voice is unique, it’s mine, it’s part of my identity. So is yours. That’s worth speaking up about.”“The quote was handwritten, not created by AI,” he added.About 80 people have added their signatures to an open letter to the prime minister,Andy Burnham, and a Gov.uk petition has been launched to ask for everyone in Britain to be given ownership of their voice as part of their statutory rights.The Derry Girls actor McSweeney said: “I’m deeply worried that legislation, contracts, working practices and ethics, and artists’ rights are not being considered or protected as quickly as AI technology is progressing.“I believe that there is a way to work alongside AI and to use it as a tool that benefits us rather than rendering us obsolete. This is an existential problem and needs to be controlled legislatively as soon as possible. My voice is one of my tools.“In order to adapt and move with technological advances, I don’t see why we should remove the human from the equation. Our audiences want that human connection. Not AI.”The campaign claims that 28% of UK adults report they have been targeted by a voice-cloning scam.The founder of Save Our Voices Now, Peter Caulfield, said: “In just three seconds, with the right AI system, your voice can be cloned, stolen and reinterpreted without your knowledge. It’s a Black Mirror episode, except this isn’t fiction. It’s happening right now.“The bottom line is the government is allowing AI companies to steal and profit from artists’ voices without their consent. They are also allowing criminals to use AI to clone people’s identities and threaten everyone. We need to use our real voices now to stop it.”In Denmark, law reforms are giving citizens legal ownership over their own face, body and voice, allowing them to demand removal of unauthorised AI content and seek compensation.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Nicola CoughlanHugh BonnevilleMatt LucasTelevisionAndy BurnhamIntellectual propertynewsShareReuse this content

title: No special carve-out for states using fossil fuel to power datacentres, Chris Bowen insists, despite new conditions | Datacentres - Australia | The Guardian
description: Energy minister says states can apply to use coal and gas supply to power datacentres but must prove it is cheaper than renewables
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Energy minister says states can apply to use coal and gas supply to power datacentres but must prove it is cheaper than renewables
Content: Chris Bowen, pictured, said the commonwealth would legislate nationally consistent datacentre standards and there would be no carve-out in the law for states using fossil fuel power.Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAPView image in fullscreenChris Bowen, pictured, said the commonwealth would legislate nationally consistent datacentre standards and there would be no carve-out in the law for states using fossil fuel power.Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAPDatacentres - AustraliaNo special carve-out for states using fossil fuel to power datacentres, Chris Bowen insists, despite new conditionsEnergy minister says states can apply to use coal and gas supply to power datacentres but must prove it is cheaper than renewablesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyPolitical editorFri 28 Aug 2026 00.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 02.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChris Bowen insists federal Labor’s new national laws on datacentre power supply will not include carve-outs for Queensland and the Northern Territory, with states that are eager to use coal and gas required to make their case to the national regulator.The energy minister told Guardian Australia on Friday the only concession agreed at Wednesday’s meeting ofnational cabinetwas that existing coal and gas supply could be used on the condition it could be shown to be cheaper than renewables.Anthony Albanese had gone into the meeting clear that new national rules, expected to be debated in federal parliament next year, would mandate the use of renewable energy, and ensure datacentres did not push up prices for homes and businesses. The prime minister said new developments would be required to make a positive contribution to the country’s energy transition.Australia may face a rush of datacentre construction as AI firms look to avoid upcoming rules, experts sayRead moreAfter the meeting, NT’s chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, and the Queensland premier, David Crisafulli, both claimed wins. Finocchiaro said gas from the massive Beetaloo basin project would now be available for datacentre power, while Crisafulli said his government could control the energy mix due to state-owned systems.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailBut on Friday, Bowen said there would be no carve-out for any state or territory.“The Commonwealth, as we always said we would, will be legislating nationally consistent commonwealth legislated datacentre standards, which will require in every state and territory 100% renewables, backed by firming,” Bowen said.“That was the case, is the case, will continue to be the case.“The only change or concession made is that where a state-owned government instrumentality feels they can provide the energy cheaper than renewables. They can apply for exemption, but the Commonwealth will decide whether to grant that or not.”The AustralianEnergyRegulator will be required to consider every application, with state or territory governments obliged to prove a non-renewables option is cheaper.Bowen called that “a very hard thing to do”.“Any suggestions of a wholesale carve-out for Queensland and Northern Territory is not accurate,” he said.After the talks in Sydney, Albanese described the decisions taken as allowing flexibility for governments with state-owned power systems.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA communique signed by the leaders indicated further consultation, with the federal government continuing work on “consistent mandatory standards” for energy, water and land use.The meeting followed the latest forecast from the AustralianEnergyMarket Operator showing datacentre power use is projected to increase seven-fold over the next decade.Bowen told the National Press Club earlier this month that the federal government would override state governments that oppose new national rules on datacentres, using powers in Australia’s constitution.Separately on Friday, Bowen released the latest quarterly data on Australia’s carbon emissions, showing a 1.6% fall in the year to March 2026, led by solar, wind and batteries that have replaced coal and gas generation.The fall reflects a 5.6m tonne cut in electricity emissions, as well as a 300% increase in battery power discharge.Bowen said there was more work to do in transport and still “a long way to go” in the overall transition.So far, emissions are down 25% on the June 2005 baseline, as Labor works to achieve a 43% reduction by 2030. The government’s longer-term emissions reduction target is a 62%-to-70% cut by 2035.Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - AustraliaAI (artificial intelligence)Chris BowenAnthony AlbaneseEnergy (Australia news)Energy (Environment)GasnewsShareReuse this content
