title: The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past – Geralt of Rivia returns after a decade in the sun | Games | The Guardian
description: Before The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Before The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’
Content: ‘We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years’ … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedView image in fullscreen‘We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years’ … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedSummer games previewsGamesThe Witcher 3: Songs of the Past – Geralt of Rivia returns after a decade in the sunBefore The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’Elliot GardnerFri 28 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 09.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe game that graced us withBathtub Geralt, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, arrived more than a decade ago. So it was a touch surprising this summer when developers CD Projekt Red announced a new expansion to the venerable adventure, titled Songs of the Past, for next year. It will release alongside a full remaster of the original game, which will be free for anyone who bought it back in 2015. (The studio is also working on a sequel, The Witcher 4, but that’s not due until 2028.)As it turns out, this is all possible thanks to a partnership with Fool’s Theory, a studio founded by CD Projekt Red veterans, which took on the brunt of the development work. “We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years,” explains Marcin Blacha, VP story director at CD Projekt Red. “Of course, we moved on to Cyberpunk 2077 and now The Witcher 4, as well as our other projects. But because we knew The Witcher 4 would take time, we saw a gap in our release calendar where Songs of the Past could go. Thankfully, we were able to find the right partner to help execute it.”View image in fullscreenSeemingly idyllic … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedThe elephant in the room, though, is that The Witcher 3’s 2016 expansion Blood and Wine felt like a natural conclusion to Geralt’s tale. After decades covered in entrails, the legendary monster slayer hangs up his dual swords for a well-earned life of luxury on his recently acquired vineyard estate. What can he possibly have left to do?“That is certainly something we thought through,” says Blacha. “Geralt retired in Toussaint – but then his best friend comes calling. I don’t think many of us would turn down that request.”So, foppish fan favourite Dandelion the bard pulls the witcher back into action, asking Geralt to come to his aid in his homeland of Letten. It’s a seemingly idyllic land of bountiful harvests and rowdy festivals that hides some sinister secrets.View image in fullscreenSinister secrets … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedIt’s been exciting, and nostalgic. We spent so long with Geralt, but have also learned a lot in the 10-plus years we’ve been away from him,” says Blacha. “With Songs of the Past, we really wanted to return to The Witcher’s roots. That meant drawing on old beliefs and folklore, revisiting landscapes inspired by Poland’s history and countryside, and staying true to the series’ tradition of difficult dilemmas. Going back to all of this has been a pleasure.”The team has also put to bed rumours that this expansion will be a prequel to The Witcher 4. Songs of the Past is focused on the gruff, grey witcher we’ve already come to love, not Ciri, the younger protagonist of the forthcoming title. Rather, the expansion has all the trappings that seasoned Witcher fans should recognise, with a morally murky narrative brought to life by returning voice actors Doug Cockle and John Schwab, who reprise their roles as Geralt and Dandelion.There are a few new features to play around with, though: CD Projekt has enhanced Geralt’s combat and skill trees, and he now wields a chain weapon alongside his steel and silver swords. There are also new DNA-modifying mutagens to play around with, tweaking Geralt’s biology and, therefore, his supernatural skills.The Witcher 3 is a modern classic that has already come to a gratifying end: bringing Geralt out of retirement is a risky move. But when his medallion starts humming, the White Wolf is still ready to answer the call.The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past is in development for PC, Switch 2, PS5, andXboxSeries X/S, and is due for release in 2027.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsRole playing gamesPlayStation 5PCXboxfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Help! I have disappeared down a rabbithole of horrible mobile gaming adverts | Games | The Guardian
description: Led by the nose from game to terrible game by increasingly disturbing and terrible adverts, I feel like I’m in the cinema scene from A Clockwork Orange
Author: Dominik Diamond
Headline: Led by the nose from game to terrible game by increasingly disturbing and terrible adverts, I feel like I’m in the cinema scene from A Clockwork Orange
Content: No, it’s not a Seth Rogan movie … Annoying Uncle Punch game.Photograph: Game DistrictView image in fullscreenNo, it’s not a Seth Rogan movie … Annoying Uncle Punch game.Photograph: Game DistrictGamesHelp! I have disappeared down a rabbithole of horrible mobile gaming advertsDominik DiamondLed by the nose from game to terrible game by increasingly disturbing and terrible adverts, I feel like I’m in the cinema scene from A Clockwork OrangeFri 28 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 11.23 EDTShareWe’re all escaping something when we play video games. Mostly it’s the drabness of real life, where we don’t get to command kingdoms using armies of dragons, win Champions League trophies with our local team, or inhabit the body of an improbably speedy hedgehog.Sometimes I play them because I want to escape from the version of me that gets paralysed by depression, and boy has the black dog been sniffing at my bits recently, because the Atlantic Ocean is separating me from my wife for a few months. For 30 years she has been the light that banishes that darkness, and I am honestly lost without her. If that sounds pathetic, you haven’t met her. She leaves everybody she meets feeling better. It’s a superpower that warrants a call from the X-Men.I have now spent weeks struggling to write in an empty-feeling house, so I turned to video games to banish the blues. Unfortunately, it became a descent into hell.The problem is that I wasn’t using proper, well-made video games as antidepressants. I told myself I was too busy for that. I simply promised my sad brain that if it could write for half an hour, I would treat it to 10 minutes of iPhone gaming. Just a wee taste of fun to get me out of my miserable headspace.View image in fullscreenA slippery slope … Sled Surfers.Photograph: CrazyLabsI started with Sled Surfers, where you catapult a character on a sled down an icy course, collecting coins and diamonds that you can use to improve your sled and catapult. When you finally have enough power to get to the finish line you move on to the next level. Level design, sound, graphics and gameplay were all pleasingly fun, but each run costs you a ticket. When you run out, you have to wait 20 minutes for another one. Or pay cash. Or … watch some ads! These are standard freemium impatience tricks born from Mafia Wars and FarmVille on Facebook.Initially the ads I watch are for other games. They let me try them for free, like drug dealers do. Royal Match is a tile-match game, where you race against the clock as a serpent tries to eat the king. I download the game. There are no king v serpent shenanigans. It’s just a boring Candy Crush rip-off.That game makes me watch an ad for something called Slap and Run. I download that, too. You control a stick man who slaps folk, then gets chased by them. It’s OK, but I worry it will encourage kids to do the same in public – you know, the same ones who ate Tide pods. The game makes me sad, but it gives me an ad for Castle Busters, which is like Worms meets Angry Birds, but not as good as either.Snake Clash!, an update to the OG Nokia game, has the worst ad yet, starring an AI slop human streamer who only speaks in the dialect of Outburst, comprised of quasi-meaningless phrases like, “Buckle up, Rookie!”, “This is illegal!” and “Are you kidding me?” strung together into sentences with nary a break for proper scansion. They promise there are no ads, so I download it. But there are ads. You have to watch them to revive your snake.View image in fullscreenWatch out for ads … Rush Xtreme.Photograph: SayGamesThis leads to RUSH: Xtreme, Annoying Uncle Punch, Hole, and Hungry Balls – not, as you may think, the titles of Seth Rogen movies, but four more silly cheap games, the playing of which makes my phone get so hot so quickly I expect celebrities to try eating it with Sean Evans on Hot Ones.I give up downloading games and instead try to find hacks to bypass the ads quicker. I click on the button that allows me to say whether I am interested or not. I select NOT. It still keeps playing. I click on the Privacy Notice to check my options: the screen freezes. These ads are stuck on your screen for between 60 and 120 seconds, but it feels like for ever. Nothing lets you skip it quicker. I am being force-fed slop.Eventually, as I disappear down this rabbit hole, ads for other games are replaced by ones for slot machine apps, or games that try to make you believe that you’ll earn cash for playing them. It’s all a grift in some grimy, gaming-adjacent underworld. Then it gets personal and the ads turn to life insurance for seniors, AI dating assistants and an ocean of erectile dysfunction pills. I feel as if I’m in that scene from A Clockwork Orange, with more and more distressing content rammed into my eyes.I wanted a panacea, instead I have ended up in this nadir of algorithms. Next time I will play Pokémon Pokopia and ask my doctor to double my dose of antidepressants instead.Dominik Diamond Sings the Video Games is atThe Loading Bar, London, on 29 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsGamesAdvertisingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Dolly Parton was the polar opposite of our bullying president | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: Terrified of being seen as a loser, Donald Trump is nonsensically lashing out – even against our old friend Canada
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: Terrified of being seen as a loser, Donald Trump is nonsensically lashing out – even against our old friend Canada
Content: ‘Her death leaves a hole in the firmament.’Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Her death leaves a hole in the firmament.’Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpDolly Parton was the polar opposite of our bullying presidentRobert ReichTerrified of being seen as a loser, Donald Trump is nonsensically lashing out – even against our old friend CanadaFri 28 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 18.39 EDTShareI’m still grievingDolly Parton. I never met her and always wanted to. She was almost exactly my age and my height and had values I deeply admired. Her death leaves a hole in the firmament.Which brings me to the person whose values are as far from Dolly Parton’s as any human could possibly be and still claim to be human. I’m referring, of course, to the current occupant of the Oval Office.“I knew her a little bit,” Trumpboastedabout Parton on Glenn Beck’s radio show. “She really liked me, I will tell you!” at which Beck laughed out loud.Trump has become mad as a hatter. Loonier than looney tunes. Totally nuts. An enraged, engorged child who’s frightened to death of being seen as a loser.With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael BehrRead moreHe’s losing his war in Iran – the war he decided to startwithout consulting Congress, without eventelling the American peoplehis goal or exit strategy.Now he’s trapped there – with a stronger and more extreme groupin control of Iranthan before his attack, probablymore intenton making a nuclear bomb, blocking the strait of Hormuz (it was open before Trump attacked), causing oil prices to rise again.His current attempt to stop other countries from dealing with Iran is a bad joke. Iran is becoming the dominant power in the Gulf, having demonstrated its ability to damage the oil and gas infrastructure of its neighbors.Besides, China can supply almost everything Iran needs and has a strong incentive to do so.So – now clearly revealed as a loser – what does Trump do? Like any bully, he lashes out.If the courts won’t allow him to put his name on the Kennedy Center, he’lldemolish it. If they say hedoesn’t have authorityto build his ballroom, he’ll fight tobuild it anyway.If his blue paint on the reflecting pool is peeling and the green algae are back and his US attorneywon’t prosecute “vandals”for causing the problem, he’ll stick to his story andblame vandals anyway.It’s all going so badly for Trump that his lizard brain is compelled to show he can bullysomeone. So who does Trump choose? Our old neighbor and friendCanada, who has always gone along with whatever the American colossus ever wanted.Trumpimposed 50% tariffson all cars, trucks, auto parts and steel coming from Canada.Why? Because, hesays: “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years. On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with. They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!”In other words, we’re in a trade war with Canada because, well, Trump wants one. A trade war with Canada probably seemed easier to win than a hot war with Iran. And he had to save facesomehow, right?Even though the supreme court found his attempt to use emergency powers for his last round of tariffsto be unconstitutional, he’s nowusing the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930– which, not incidentally, worsened the Great Depression.But maybe a trade war with Canadawon’tbe all that easy to win. Canada has now retaliated withits own tariffsof up to 50% againstabout 700 American products.As the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney,noted on Saturday: “Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us so they can own us, and I promised that will never, ever happen. We are keeping that promise.”Carney is now a hero in Canada with approval ratings in the 60s, while Trump’s have sunkto the low 30s.Humiliation upon humiliation for the man who can’t stand to be humiliated.It gets worse by the day.Netanyahu hasrejected Trump’s planfor Gaza. Congressional Republicans areblasting himfor increasing imports of ground beef.Universities arerejectinghis latest directives. ABC hassued his regimefor threatening its broadcast licenses.Even the bond market won’t be cowed. It’s in open revolt against his bonkers fiscal policies.How Mark Carney’s speeches have become political earthquakes | Ted WidmerRead moreThank goodness for him that Darline Grahamwon South Carolina’s special electionRepublican runoff to replace her brother. Trump had made her race all about himself – of course –telling supportersthat her opponents were “only fighting Darline because they want me to lose”.I’m sure that’s what he’s telling himself about his many losses and humiliations – that they’re all due to his opponents plotting and scheming against him.(Hopefully, he’s about to lose Congress, too.)That’s an easier story for Trump to accept than the truth: that his carefully cultivated aura of invincibility has just about disappeared.The would-be emperor has no clothes. Almost everybody now sees the thin-skinned, peevish, petty, incompetent, corrupt, naked infant who’s been parading around in presidential garb.And they’re not going to obey him any more.Dolly Parton was a huge winner, bless her soul. Trump is the biggest loser on the planet.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionDolly PartonUS politicsCanadaUS-Israel war on IranRepublicansMark CarneycommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s midterm campaign theme is unrequited love | Sidney Blumenthal | The Guardian
description: The president senses a crisis in his cult of personality. He believes the path to victory is through unwavering devotion
Author: Sidney Blumenthal
Headline: The president senses a crisis in his cult of personality. He believes the path to victory is through unwavering devotion
Content: ‘He is running against Isaac Newton, and Newton always prevails.’Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘He is running against Isaac Newton, and Newton always prevails.’Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpTrump’s midterm campaign theme is unrequited loveSidney BlumenthalThe president senses a crisis in his cult of personality. He believes the path to victory is through unwavering devotionFri 28 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 06.15 EDTShareDonald Trump has framed his theme for the midterm elections. It has come to him as naturally and inevitably as staring into the mirror, beyond any logic or argument, his definitive answer to no specific issue, providing no understanding of any particular problem, but transcending all of them. His political theme is more primal than programmatic, more instinctive than analytical, a heartfelt expression to protect his greatest romantic attachment, his obsessive fixation, his idealized object: himself.Trump’s campaign theme is unrequited love. Unlike the pollsters, media consultants and pundits, he alone has grasped the magnitude and the source of the existential crisis threatening his politics. He has identified the problem for theRepublicansas the faltering measure of complete devotion to him. His demand has nothing to do with mutual affection. It is a ploy to reassert his slipping control, a manipulative test to prove loyalty to him, or else. There can be no absolute rule without an absolute ruler; no absolute ruler without absolute submission; no absolute submission without the expression of absolute love. His sadness at its fading gives way to anger, paranoia and greater acts of retribution. He equates the fear he instills as a form of love. Trump accepts subservience, from whatever motive, as affection or its closest equivalent. He cares nothing about sincerity, so it’s all in the show. The less love displayed, the more fear required. Yet there is no rebound, but only deeper rejection.With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael BehrRead moreTrump isheading towardthe floor for presidential unpopularity –Nixon during Watergateon the eve of his resignation, Trumanlate in his second termat the depth of the Korean war, and George W Bushat the 2008 financial crash. But Trump’s breakdown differs uniquely from theirs. His decline has come earlier in his term, been more sustained, and his disintegration has not stabilized but is accelerating. He is being crushed by the accumulation of catastrophic events of his own making to which his impulsive response is to double down in each and every area. Stalemated in his reckless Iran war, he has nowlauncheda heedless trade war against Canada that will devastate Republican candidates in the northern tier of states. His latest vanity project is gestural retribution torenameLake Ontario as “Lake America”, a watery ballroom. Admission of error for Trump would be the denial of self-love.Trump began his campaign on his unrequited love theme on 16 August during a Fox News interview in which he discussed his press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, leaving her job after just having a baby. He had held her up as meeting his highest criterion inremarkslast December: “Isn’t she great? Is Karoline great? … She gets up there with that beautiful face and those lips that don’t stop,ba ba balike a little machine gun.” Now,he triedto make a joke of her departure that expressed resentment at abandonment. “In fact, she likes her children more than she likes Trump. I’m very concerned about that,” he said. Then herepeatedhis unfunny “joke” at a campaign rally in South Carolina on 21 August: “I just learned she loves the baby more than she loves Donald Trump, and I’m very angry …” Trump’s lame attempt at humor was a rare instance of his truth-telling and self-revelation, a contemporary illustration of Freud’s Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious.Trump was in South Carolina to campaign for his chosen candidate in the Republican primary, Darline Graham, who hehad insistedbe appointed to the Senate seat of her brother Lindsey Graham afterhe diedon 11 July. Darline Graham confessed to cluelessness when asked in a debate about her position on Taiwan. “National security is not my thing,”she answered. “I’m not … that informed on national security.” But she was fully informed on the necessity of obedience to Trump. “You saved our country, and I want to thank you for that,” shesaidat the rally. Trump praised his worshipper: “She’s got a good gene pool.” She was born to love him. She stood in stark contrast to the immigrants he had described as “poisoning the blood of our country”.Then Trumpcalled on the crowdto embrace his new theme. “So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot … So just say that I’m on the ballot one more time. You got to say it.” He wishes every candidate to sound like Darline Graham in proclaiming him the national savior. He insists he is beloved, and if those who revere him turn out the Republicans must win. In fact, though he is not on the ballot in the midterm elections, Trump is the central issue. Voters do not have to “pretend, please”.Trump intuitively comprehends that the midterm elections are about him in a way that makes this midterm unlike any other. In the marrow of his bones, he senses it is a crisis of his cult of personality.double quotation markWhen charisma fails, the movement implodes. If the leader is not worshipped, his uber-principle – the leader principle – collapses: no fuhrerprinzip, no FührerTrump’s Maga was never a new party structure, but constructed on his wreckage of the old Republican party. In its place, every particle of the replacement is connected to the leader to advance his supremacy and self-enrichment. Everything flows upward, all heads tilted, all knees bent. Maga has always been Maga Inc of, by and for one man. The movement is the man.When charisma fails, the movement implodes. If the leader is not worshipped, his uber-principle – the leader principle – collapses: nofuhrerprinzip, no Führer.Trump’s plea for their unconditional love – “pretend, please” – defies gravity. He is running against Isaac Newton, and Newton always prevails. Intensity is gauged by “strongly approve” and “strongly disapprove” poll numbers. More than the general statistics of approval or disapproval, these provide insight into the motivation of voters that determine the contour of elections. Trump now stands at 13% “strongly approve” in the most recentReuters-Ipsos Poll. His “strongly disapprove” rating is at 49%. His total approval is at 33%, while disapproval is at 65%. Those in the “somewhat approve” category include low propensity soft voters especially inclined to skip midterm elections. And this poll was taken before his declaration of trade war against Canada.All along, the Republicans have been Trump’s indispensable accomplices. Even if they were disposed to object, they could do nothing to draw him back from his “pretend, please” campaign. His anxiety to rescue his invincible image from the reality he’s created makes him more inescapable than ever. Any effort to restrict him will provoke his rage. He will not diminish himself for the sake of the party or even his own future. He plans tospend millionsfrom his Maga Inc political action committee to tell the voters that they have never had it so good – “the greatest economy we’ve ever had, by far”, hesays. He has mocked the suggestion that “affordability” might be a problem for many – it’s “a word they”, the media, “devised”, hehas said. Trump intends to stage amini conventionin Dallas on 9 September, featuring Donald Trump to “celebrate … our achievements”. Republicans are locked almost uniformly into blind support, with the Maine senator Susan Collinsventuring hollow criticismof the Canadian tariffs that makes her seem powerless and infuriates the remaining Maga base. Just as Trump has trapped himself, he has trapped the Republicans. The expenditure of tens of millions to depict his dire consequences as paradise on earth will have the unintended effect of supercharging the already motivated “strongly disapprove” voters and disillusion those who cannot help but be aware of the actual conditions of their own lives.Jon Ossoff went low on Natalie Harp. The plan worked | Moira DoneganRead moreThe sudden surfacing of Natalie Harp as a meme at this particular moment propitiously coincides with the wobbling of Trump’s cult. The 35-year-old is his model of the perfect staffer, perfect companion and perfect American citizen. If unrequited love is the problem, she is the solution. In Trump’s hierarchy of need, his pyramid of status, love and self-actualization, she is at the apex.Harp is his “binky”, asMaggie Habermanof the New York Times has called her, his comfort blanket, his plush bunny rabbit. The “human printer” who trails after him, pressing the button to churn out an endless stream of adulatory articles, conspiracy theories and “alternative facts”, has become an extension of his nervous system. The former anchor at the fringe far-right One America News Network serves as Trump’s personal anchor. Harp broadcasts around the clock to an audience of one. She is the connector to the neurons of the far right, serving as aconduitto dodgy characters such as Laura Loomer with herlists of national security officialswho were supposedly disloyal. Harp is Trump’s neurotransmitter who distributes a steady supply of dopamine and delusion.Harp’s self-abasing devotion to Trump, expressed in herlettersto him, serves as a kind of inadvertent political manifesto for the cult, a template for followers. Harp tellingly muddles a line from Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice – Mr Bennet blessing his strong-willed daughter Elizabeth in her engagement to Darcy – to demean herself andoffer subservienceto Trump: “To modify a classic, ‘I could not have parted with you, to anyone less worthy’ – And, I will add, it is I who is unworthy.” In another letter, after self-disparaging apologies, Harp writes: “You are all that matters to me. I don’t want to ever let you down. Thank you for being my Guardian and Protector in this Life … With all my Heart.”As public opinion curdles on Trump, no longer able to “pretend, please”, Harp has not come to the wisdom of Conway Twitty in his 1959rockabilly hit:My only prayer will beSomeday you’ll care for meBut it’s only make believeSidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln:A Self-Made Man,Wrestling With His AngelandAll the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of theCourt of History podcastExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS midterm elections 2026RepublicansUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Dolly Parton brought divided Americans together. What can we learn from her? | Margaret Sullivan | The Guardian
description: The singer had a serendipitous mixture of humor, humility and humanity. We could all stand to channel it a bit more
Author: Margaret Sullivan
Headline: The singer had a serendipitous mixture of humor, humility and humanity. We could all stand to channel it a bit more
Content: ‘I don’t think she’d object if we also kept in mind her authentic kindness, her disarming wit – and the “radical acceptance” that fueled it all.’Photograph: LGI Stock/Corbis/VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I don’t think she’d object if we also kept in mind her authentic kindness, her disarming wit – and the “radical acceptance” that fueled it all.’Photograph: LGI Stock/Corbis/VCG/Getty ImagesOpinionDolly PartonDolly Parton brought divided Americans together. What can we learn from her?Margaret SullivanThe singer had a serendipitous mixture of humor, humility and humanity. We could all stand to channel it a bit moreFri 28 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.33 EDTShareThe moment that the world found out thatDolly Parton had died, I was in a hair salon in the reddest congressional district in New York state. The neighborhood on the shore of Lake Erie where I move every summer voted solidly for Donald Trump in 2024.I often pass a lawn sign that has something misogynistic to say about New York’s Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul, and the mere mention of Kamala Harris’s name can bring derisive jokes. Of course, there certainly are liberals and independents to be found, but on balance the area leans right.On my errands around town, I’ve heard scornful comments about transgender people, and the local Catholic church where I sometimes attend mass has a priest who, during a homily this summer, praised Trump for his war in Iran.A lot of the people I’ve chatted with around town are outspoken about being anti-vaccine.Dolly Parton – a life in picturesRead moreBut when cellphones started pinging with the news about Dolly, it’s not overstating things to say that everybody was devastated. Stylists and customers alike seemed to feel a personal connection – to her music, to her philanthropy, to her sheer goodness.How did Dolly, a rags-to-riches country music superstar with a Tennessee twang and bedazzled everything, manage to endear herself to Americans of every political stripe?What was her secret – and does it hold some wisdom for the those who seek unity in this divided nation, who appreciate civility, who believe there’s an American ethos that transcends our ugly politics?Some of it, surely, was that she had a gift for poking fun at herself, and joining in the laughter, as when she would say she didn’t mind being called a dumb blonde because she knew, after all, that she wasn’t dumb – and that she wasn’t a blonde. After her illness made headlines last year, she took to social media to make a simple point: “I ain’t dead yet.” She called herself a “Backwoods Barbie” in a song of that name.Then there was her remarkable generosity. Her organization, Imagination Library, gave more than 330m books to children around the world. She founded it, in part, she said, because her father couldn’t read or write.She never forgot where she came from, as she raised money for a new hospital in her home country in Tennessee, or offered $500 awards to local teenagers when they graduated from high school.Still, how did she manage not to alienate the Maga world when she promoted the Covid-19 vaccine (the research for which she had helped fund)?Again, the humor helped, as when she changed the words of one of her most famous songs, Jolene to something that rhymed, and sang “vaccine, vaccine” in promotional videos. You had to smile, and maybe decide to get the jab, or at least to tolerate those who did. And she never made it political.“She practiced a unique brand of radical acceptance,” wrote Jad Abumrad in aNew York Timesessay this week. “No one would ever be thrown out of the Big Dolly Tent.”And, though she is being mourned as something of an angel on earth, she was a razor-sharp businessperson. She was smart and savvy about it all, as befitted the superstar who chalked up 25 No 1 country singles over the years.As Abumrad learned while interviewing and observing her at length as he created the podcast Dolly Parton’s America, she always told her own story.‘It’s sad to lose a really nice person’: mourners flock to Dollywood after death of Dolly PartonRead more“If a male talkshow host made a joke about her figure, she’d make an ever better joke about it. She was always two steps ahead of you. She never allowed herself to be a part of a story of which she was not the author.”Can what Dolly Parton did be bottled somehow? Can her serendipitous mixture of humor, humility and humanity be sprinkled over our troubled waters to calm and soothe them?Probably not – there is only one Dolly Parton – but that doesn’t mean we can’t learn something from this rare individual.The rest of us might channel Dolly a bit more, and remember that a self-deprecating joke goes a long way toward easing tensions. We might recognize that financial success need not turn into ego glorification or arrogance.And most of all, we might keep in mind that genuine generosity – if it comes from the heart – has the power to transcend politics.Dolly Parton’s legacy, of course, resides in her wonderful songs, from Coat of Many Colors to 9 to 5. That’s what she would want.But I don’t think she’d object if we also kept in mind her authentic kindness, her disarming wit – and the “radical acceptance” that fueled it all.Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and cultureExplore more on these topicsDolly PartonOpinionUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: The hollowing out of Tennis.com is a warning for American sports journalism | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Tennis.com once paired news and scores with distinctive voices. Its overhaul is the latest sign that serious tennis writing in the US is becoming endangered
Author: Tim Joyce
Headline: Tennis.com once paired news and scores with distinctive voices. Its overhaul is the latest sign that serious tennis writing in the US is becoming endangered
Content: The US Open got underway with the mixed doubles but coverage of the tournament has changed in recent years.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe US Open got underway with the mixed doubles but coverage of the tournament has changed in recent years.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesTennisThe hollowing out of Tennis.com is a warning for American sports journalismTim JoyceThe site once paired news and scores with distinctive voices. Its overhaul under Sinclair Media is the latest sign that serious tennis writing in the US is becoming endangeredFri 28 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 05.14 EDTShareAfew weeks ago, as I often do, I went to theTennis.com site to get an update about a match and to check out the commentary from my fellow tennis journalists. I was taken aback when, instead of the usual colorful graphics and info, I was greeted with a rudimentary-looking homepage that displayed only scores and rankings.At first I thought it was a glitch of some sort. But sadly, no. As it turns out, Tennis.com, originally the online site of Tennis Magazine, is under a complete overhaul and will no longer be the home of esteemed writers such as Steve Tignor and Pete Bodo, robbing fans of unique and personal takes on the sport. It appears the longest running American tennis-specific publication is no longer alive in any form.Tennis Magazine started in 1965 (with the Tennis.com website starting in 1996) and existed in print form through 2022. Its previous owners included Golf Digest and the New York Times Company. But when Sinclair Broadcast Group, thecontroversial conservative-leaning media company, bought the site in 2017, merging it into one entity with the Tennis Channel, the writing – that is to say the eventual dearth of writing – was on the wall.Tignor told me that “in some ways, I feared this day for 25 years”, acknowledging that people are consuming news and information much differently than they did even 10 years ago. And, more to the point, “having Tennis.com owned by a broadcaster [Tennis Channel] wasn’t a perfect scenario to begin with since they intrinsically have different goals.”I emailed Jill Dortheimer, vice-president of communications for Tennis Channel, for comment on the changes and she wrote back saying, “Tennis.com is in the midst of a full rebuild and the first priority for us is to deliver fast, comprehensive match and tournament schedules, scores, draws, etc. But there is much more to come in the future to improve the experience for fans.” She didn’t respond to my specific queries of whether there was an issue with page views or if there were any plans to reintroduce written commentary.From my perspective it appears Sinclair is more interested in having its on-air announcers debate gambling odds during matches to please advertisers like BetMGM and FanDuel than having insightful and independent-minded commentary on the Tennis.com website.Once upon a time, a time that suddenly feels long ago even though it’s only a couple of decades past, if one was an avid fan of tennis who also enjoyed reading articles about the sport – not just coverage of matches – there were a plethora of American publications focused solely on tennis: Tennis Magazine, World Tennis Magazine, Tennis Week, along with a few others. The abundance of publications coincided with the so-called “tennis boom” in the United States in the 1970s and 80s.Further, not only were there plentiful magazines devoted to tennis, but several newspapers in the United States had a dedicated tennis writer, with bylines and datelines from all four grand slam events. Today only the New York Times-owned Athletic employs full-time tennis writers, most notably Matthew Futterman. That’s it.What makes this slightly curious is the fact that the UK continues to have tennis beat writers (including the Guardian) at its major newspapers and significant tennis readership. Is it a case of “out of sight, out of mind” in reverse? The more coverage the media gives to tennis will then therefore generate more interest? In the US at least, the rich get richer; football has an obscenely massive and still-growing presence in the sports media world whereas more niche sports have dropped significantly.Steve Flink, one of only a handful of journalists enshrined in the International Tennis Hall of Fame, has more than a half century of experience working for a variety of publications. He still believes there is a desire for more tennis coverage in the print world but his outlook isn’t optimistic.View image in fullscreenDoes more media coverage of tennis generate greater interest in the sport – or does dwindling coverage only accelerate its decline?Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty Images“Tennis followers who are 50 and older do thirst for good writing on the sport and their favorite players. I believe they almost yearn for it. But the younger fans seem to only want videos. Is it a case of the scant coverage from the media only feeding into this problem? From my viewpoint the answer is an emphatic yes,” he told me.Flink, who has spent a great deal of time in England throughout his life, added: “I have no doubt that the British tennis fans are considerably more interested in reading daily accounts about tennis in their newspapers. Their newspapers have maintained more prominence in terms of sports coverage overall and tennis specifically. Until about 10 years ago or slightly longer, many US newspapers still sent reporters to Wimbledon but now very few are there. Now with AI spreading like wildfire, the battle could be permanently lost – at least in this country.”Golf and tennis are often twinned in the public consciousness; rightly or wrongly both are considered elitist, often cater to wealthier demographics and are individual sports. But golf still has two legacy magazines online – Golf.com and golfdigest.com – that appear to be doing just fine. While golf coverage across newspapers’ online coverage has dwindled significantly, the fact the sport still has a huge online presence with well-known publications leaves one wondering why tennis can’t do the same?One of the more disturbing aspects to all this is that without independent voices providing insightful and at times controversial commentary on the sport, there’s the risk of not challenging the status quo, so the media becomes just an extension of the tournaments that they televise and a slave to their advertisers. (For example, the aforementioned Futterman of the Athleticjust wrote a pieceexposing the ridiculous pricing policy at the US Open which will shut out the majority of fans.)Finally, with a pivot towards more visual or audio programing – be it match highlights or podcasts or not-exactly-penetrating interviews with players on social media – the public is losing out as the written word is threatened with irrelevance.Studyafterstudyhas found that one processes information more comprehensively and has better recall when reading text, either on the printed page or a screen versus watching video.Will there be a backlash against AI-generated articles and video-only content? One can only hope. Maybe some sites should advertise themselves as “AI-free”. Will independent journalism and the written word survive? Or will insightful analysis become niche? The way things are progressing, at least in the United States, isn’t all that promising.Explore more on these topicsTennisUS sports mediaUS Open Tennis 2026US sportsUS Open tennisNewspapers & magazinescommentShareReuse this content

title: An $18bn settlement – and Zuckerberg barely blinked. The tech titans must be stripped of their power, and soon | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: Those who said Meta harms children struck a blow, but the ability of big tech to gouge profits and cause harm is barely diminished. That’s the battle to come, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: Those who said Meta harms children struck a blow, but the ability of big tech to gouge profits and cause harm is barely diminished. That’s the battle to come, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg leaves Los Angeles superior court after testifying, 18 February 2026.Photograph: Wally Skalij/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMeta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg leaves Los Angeles superior court after testifying, 18 February 2026.Photograph: Wally Skalij/Getty ImagesOpinionMetaAn $18bn settlement – and Zuckerberg barely blinked. The tech titans must be stripped of their power, and soonJonathan FreedlandThose who said Meta harms children struck a blow, but the ability of big tech to gouge profits and cause harm is barely diminished. That’s the battle to comeFri 28 Aug 2026 12.10 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.35 EDTShareFollow the money. If you want to know how the tech giant Meta really feels about the $18bn it agreed to fork out to end a landmark lawsuit against it – an outcome widely hailed as a victory for campaigners – justlook at its share price. It didn’t go down when word came on Wednesday that Meta had settled with the 29 US states that had argued that the company’s Facebook and Instagram platforms harmed children. On the contrary, Meta stock went up, initially surging by 5%, before levelling out at a gain of just over 1.25%. There could be no clearer proof that the money men reckon Meta dodged a bullet.To be sure, there was plenty to hearten those who have long believed that social media damages teenagers especially, whether by exposing them to content they shouldn’t see or by sapping their self-esteem, offering them filters that show how much prettier they would look if they had cosmetic surgery or giving them a metric of their popularity – and unpopularity – in the form of a running tally of “likes” and views.For one thing, $18bn is a lot of money. For another, Meta has agreed toa series of changes in the way young people use their platforms. There’ll be a two-hour daily cap on use; restricted access during the night and the school day; likes will not be shown automatically and assorted safety and parental supervision measures will no longer be opt-in extras but the default standard. You can see why Lori Schott of Colorado, who believes the content her daughter encountered on Instagram played a part in her suicide aged 18, declared Wednesday to be“a good day”.But look closer and you see that, for Meta, $18bn is not exactly a bank-breaking sum. It amounts toless than a month’s revenue. And it has 10 years to pay it out: the monthly payments could come out of petty cash. What’s more, nearly a third of that sum is contingent on Meta’s rivals YouTube and TikTok agreeing to the same restrictions. All told, the financial penalty is less than a tenth ofthe $200bn the 29 states were seeking, and a tiny fraction of the$1.4tn the company told the court it feared it would have to cough up. No wonder Meta’s shareholders were doing fist bumps on Wednesday.Beyond the money, Meta will be thankful it has escaped a court ruling against it, a legal verdict on the behaviour detailed so compellingly in the California courtroom in the first week of the trial before it was abruptly halted. Jurors heard from the former Meta safety engineer Arturo Béjar, who spoke of his own teenage daughter’s experience on Instagram – how she received unwanted sexual advances, crude misogynistic insults and photos of male genitalia on the platform – and of a survey he had conducted that found 51% of teen users had had bad or harmful experiences on Instagram within the previous seven days, and that content was taken down only 0.02% of the time. Béjar reported his findings toMark Zuckerbergdirectly, but got no reply. As Béjar told me when we spoke on Thursday: “They knew that harm to kids was happening, but they were telling the world it wasn’t.” Under Wednesday’s settlement, Meta hasn’t even made an admission of liability.View image in fullscreenOlivia Konar holds a banner with names of young people who advocates say died as a result of social media outside the Ronald V Dellums federal building and US courthouse in Oakland, California, 18 August 2026.Photograph: Noah Berger/APAs for the new restrictions, anyone who has seen a teenager on a computer or phone will have little confidence that they won’t find a way around them. If they do, then, according to this week’s deal,Metawill not be accountable. And crucially, says Béjar, it is Meta itself that still gets to define what constitutes harm.No less frustrating, these new terms apply inside the US only, even though Meta’s reach, and its capacity to do damage, is global. As the gagged former Facebook employee Sarah Wynn-Williams described in her riveting bookCareless People, the company was assiduous in hunting for new users in those overseas territories with few legal safeguards. There’s a parallel here with the tobacco industry: long after the US and Europe had cracked down on cigarettes, big tobacco was energetically selling into developing countries that had not yet put up their defences.Above all, this week’s settlement addresses only the safety of children, despite the copious evidence of danger to adults, whether in the form of addiction or exposure to toxic misinformation. The danger lies not in this or that specific feature, but rather in the fundamental business model of social media: namely, tracking and surveilling individuals online, using the data gathered to construct a profile, which is then sold to advertisers eager to target potential consumers with extraordinary precision.It’s this model that keeps users hooked, scrolling for hour after hour, as they are served content aimed directly at their interests and anxieties. As Ravi Naik, the lawyer who acts for Wynn-Williams and others, told me: “The algorithm preys on you.” The trouble with this latest settlement, he explains, is that “it reaches the features of Meta’s platforms but not the engine that drives them. The recommendation algorithm is untouched.”What, then, can be done? For Béjar, the answer is to approach social media as a public health crisis, akin to the road traffic accidents that led to mandatory safety belts in cars (and not only for children). Governments need to say that any company involved in this crisis has to be involved in tackling it. And no one should fall for the line that the nature of the internet is such that it cannot be subject to meaningful regulation. When the music industry objected to copyright infringements online, incentives were swiftly arranged to fix the problem. As Béjar so damningly puts it: “A song has more protection than a kid.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are ample other precedents that can serve as guides to action, though none of them will please the titans of big tech. For decades, they have avoided being viewed as publishers, liable for what appears on their platforms. Nor do they want to be treated like carmakers, responsible for product safety. And they don’t like being likened to cigarette firms, selling a product they know is dangerous. Perhaps policymakers need to make a new comparison.More than a century ago, when Standard Oil’s de facto monopoly was deemed harmful to consumers, it was broken up by order of the US supreme court into 34 smaller companies. Meta operates like a monopoly, with users feeling they can’t move, because all their friends and contacts are on the same few platforms. “Meta knowingly exploit this and refuse to make changes to their platforms that they know would deliver safer user experiences,” Damian Collins, a former chair of the UK parliamentary committee that oversees the digital realm, told me. If users could move their data and contacts over to new services, giving them more options, “break-up would work”.This week’s settlement has been a disappointment to those longing to see the tech giants finally brought to heel, found guilty by courts and made to pay for it with costs too big to ignore. For now, Meta has swerved judgment day. But that day must surely come.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Home Office must not be allowed to bury the spycops inquiry | Imran Khan | The Guardian
description: Doreen Lawrence and other victims of police surveillance have waited decades for justice. Delays and expense due to Met intransigence are no excuse to deny them that, says solicitor Imran Khan
Author: Imran Khan
Headline: Doreen Lawrence and other victims of police surveillance have waited decades for justice. Delays and expense due to Met intransigence are no excuse to deny them that, says solicitor Imran Khan
Content: A protest outside the spycops inquiry hearings in London, 17 October 2025.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA protest outside the spycops inquiry hearings in London, 17 October 2025.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianOpinionUndercover police and policingThe Home Office must not be allowed to bury the spycops inquiryImran KhanDoreen Lawrence and other victims of police surveillance have waited decades for justice. Delays and expense due to Met intransigence are no excuse to deny them thatFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 08.14 EDTShareIn June 2013 Peter Francis, a former Metropolitan police officer, broke a 20-year silence about the role he had played in surveilling the family of Stephen Lawrence in a documentary jointly made bythe Guardian and Channel 4’s Dispatches programme. Two years later, thanks in part to the programme, the Home Office established anundercover policing inquiry, commonly known as the spycops public inquiry, to shed light on the scale of surveillance of activists and trade unionists. That inquiry is now under threat.Francis had served in the Special Demonstration Squad (SDS), a Met unit founded in 1968 whose officers lived for years at a time inside political and campaigning organisations under false names.In the months afterStephen Lawrence’s murder in 1993 Francis had been deployed to pose as an anti-racist campaigner. His superiors pressed him to find “dirt” that could be used against the Lawrence family and their supporters. Stephen’s mother, Doreen,told the Guardian and Channel 4that nothing she had heard since her son died had topped the revelation that police had been spying on her while she grieved. She had always suspected the police were watching. She never had proof.The Lawrences were not an isolated case. Justice campaigns and trade unionists across the country were also monitored.At least 139 officers adopted fake names, pretending to be political activists, to spy on people between 1968 and at least 2010. Dozens of anti-racist campaigners, family members of victims of police violence and leftwing activists have been surveilled by police.Suresh Grover, whose Monitoring Group stood behind many of these victims of police surveillance, has told the inquiry that the suspicion directed at Black campaigners was rooted in racist stereotyping. Complaints from Black communities were treated as a public order threat in a way that identical complaints from others were not.The government has justified theconsultation they launched on 16 Julyinto the future of the inquiry on the grounds that it has gone on for more than 11 years and cost £137m. The figures are accurate but their explanation is missing.Applications for anonymity and restriction orders, the vast majority sought by police officers, have slowed down this inquiry. Litigation over cover names, and a persistent unwillingness among former officers and their commanders to say what they did has also hampered the process. The Met, which ran the SDS, made the inquiry slow and expensive. The same government department that funded and served the squad now cites the inquiry’s slowness and expense as reasons to cut it short.Despite a push to wind up the inquiry, it is still producing revelations about the conduct of England’s police forces. Just last year, it revealed that an undercover officer, James Thomson, who had deceived two women into intimate relationships, was suspected of fabricating an elaborate plot tolink an anti-foxhunting activist to a gunthat he told managers the activist intended to collect in France.Before the inquiry, Thomson’s managers admitted that in order to protect the SDS, nothing was done either about his intimate relationship with women he was surveilling or his possible fabrication of evidence. The unit, it seemed, trumped almost anything.The inquiry also exposed numerous instances in which managers appeared to have knowledge of undercover officers having had sexual relationships that continued long after undercover deployments ended, in one case evenafter the announcement of the inquiry.Another shocking discovery from the inquiry is that theMet spent £2.5m hiding an officer– John Dines – from his former lover, going as far as to relocate him from New Zealand to Australia for that purpose.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor the spycops scandal to be possible courts had to be misled. Officers were arrested alongside activists, appeared in court under false names and in some cases gave evidence under them without the court being told.Surveillance was not limited to political activists and victims of racist violence. The Met’s own investigation concluded that special branch and the security services fed material to construction companies that blacklisted more than3,000 workerssuspected of being members of trade unions.More instances of misconduct may come to light in the future, which is all the more reason to keep the inquiry running. The consultation is scheduled to end on 20 September, but there isstill time to write to the Home Officeto make sure that the government knows your views.An inquiry that was set up because the state spied on the parents of a murdered child should not be closed down because the state has heard enough about itself. Doreen Lawrence has been told for 33 years that the truth is coming if she will wait just a little longer. She – and other victims of spying – have waited long enough. The inquiry should finish the job it was given.Imran Khan KC is a practising solicitorDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Nepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis | Sunil Acharya | The Guardian
description: Nepalis and Tibetans must not pay the price – with their lives, livelihoods and money meant for education and health – for global heating caused by wealthy states, says Kathmandu-based climate policy specialist Sunil Acharya
Author: Sunil Acharya
Headline: Nepalis and Tibetans must not pay the price – with their lives, livelihoods and money meant for education and health – for global heating caused by wealthy states, says Kathmandu-based climate policy specialist Sunil Acharya
Content: People look out over a damaged building after devastating floods hit Nepal,  28 August 2026.Photograph: Shankar Bhujel/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPeople look out over a damaged building after devastating floods hit Nepal,  28 August 2026.Photograph: Shankar Bhujel/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionNepal-Tibet flood disasterNepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisisSunil AcharyaNepalis and Tibetans must not pay the price – with their lives, livelihoods and money meant for education and health – for global heating caused by wealthy statesSunil Acharya is an international climate policy and just transition specialist based in Kathmandu, NepalFri 28 Aug 2026 06.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.01 EDTShareAs a Nepali citizen working on international climate policy for more than a decade, it is difficult to look at the harrowing images coming out of thecatastrophic flash floodthat thundered down valleys in Nepal, sweeping down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, and not feel angry.Not just because of the destruction, but because it comes after years of warnings from scientists and civil society that a rapidly warming planet would make disasters more frequent, more intense and harder to predict. This is what the cost of delaying global climate action looks like.On 26 August, a wall of ice, water, rock and mud tore through communities, destroying homes, markets, bridges, roads and hydropower infrastructure in Nepal and Tibet. Hundreds of people were killed and many more remain missing. The devastation came with terrifying speed. For people living along the rivers and the tourists trekking in the hills, there was little time between the hazard emerging high in the mountains and destruction reaching the valleys below.The immediate questions are rightly being asked about what happened and whether people could have been warned. Nepal needs stronger early warning systems, better monitoring of glaciers and unstable slopes, cross-border communication between Nepal andTibetand greater investment in preparedness.But Nepal’s flash floods expose something more fundamental: the problem is not the absence of a warning system – it is a climate crisis that is producing hazards that behave differently from those the systems were designed to detect.Murderous heat, an endangered food supply, decimated landscapes: embrace the Mediterranean life | George MonbiotRead moreThe warning system in the high-mountain Bhotekoshi valley illustrates the problem. The sudden,debris-laden flood destroyedupstream hydrological stations before they could register a rising water level and trigger an alert.The system was designed to detect a more gradual rise in water levels. This flood arrived as a massive surge of rock, mud and water, destroying the very instruments meant to detect it.Preliminary assessments indicate that a large glacial collapsetriggered an ice-rock avalanche and debris flow, temporarily blocking the river before a massive surge travelled downstream. The precise sequence is still being investigated. Whatever the final scientific explanation, the event shows how quickly hazards can cascade in a warming mountain environment.By the time authorities received information about the flood and warnings were sent downstream, communities closest to the source hadvirtually no time to respond. The monitoring infrastructure did not simply fail to communicate the warning. It was destroyed before it could see the flood coming. That distinction matters. An early warning system designed around yesterday’s floods can be dangerously inadequate for tomorrow’s extremes.This does not make early warning futile. It means we need to be honest about its limits. A warning is useful only if there is time to act. It cannot stop a mountain of ice and rock from collapsing. It cannot protect infrastructure in an increasingly hazardous corridor. And it cannot bring back a home, a hydropower station or a livelihood once it has disappeared.Adaptation has limits, too. For years, Nepal and other vulnerable countries have been ramping up efforts to adapt: by strengthening infrastructure, improving preparedness, and protecting livelihoods – but often without financial support from the countries that historically contributed most to the climate crisis through historical emissions.Nepal needs much greater international support for adaptation: early warning, mountain monitoring, climate science, anticipatory action, resilient infrastructure and disaster preparedness. Because Himalayan hazards originate beyond national borders, this must also include stronger cross-border cooperation and timely sharing of information.The Nepal Himalayais changing rapidly. Glaciers are retreating, while warming is altering the conditions in which glaciers, permafrost and mountain slopes remain stable. The climate in which these hazards occur is changing, and continued warming will make an already difficult risk landscape harder to manage. That is why the global response cannot stop at adaptation.The first task must be to stop making the crisis worse. The countries that benefited most from decades of fossil fuel-driven growth have a particular responsibility to cut emissions rapidly. They also have far greater resources to do so. A just transition away from coal, oil and gas towards renewable energy is therefore a matter of global justice.The fossil-fuel industry cannot be separated from this conversation. Companies have made enormous profits extracting and selling the fuels that have driven global heating, while communities on the climate frontline are being asked to prepare for increasingly destructive impacts with far fewer resources. Even rapid mitigation cannot undo the warming already baked into the climate system or immediately reverse changes already taking place in the Himalaya.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is also a lesson for Nepal. It should not copy the economic model that created the climate crisis and call it development. We have an opportunity to build something different: an economy that puts people, livelihoods and ecological resilience before extraction.The second task requires historical polluter states to pay for loss and damages. Nepal has contributedless than 0.1%of historical global greenhouse gas emissions. Its per-capita emissions remain among the lowest in the world. Yet we are increasingly paying for a crisis we did almost nothing to create. There is something profoundly unfair about this.The cost of such an event is not an abstract figure in a post-disaster risk assessment. It is the lives of people killed by the flood; a hydropower station that took years to build and disappeared in minutes; livelihoods; public money that must now be spent on recovery instead of health and education.Nepal and other vulnerable countries have repeatedly called on developed countries for compensation. The country should not be forced to borrow to recover from disasters to which it contributed so little. Nor should its scarce domestic resources repeatedly be diverted to repair damage caused by emissions of the global north.Loss and damage financemust therefore be additional to existing official development assistance, adaptation and mitigation finance. It needs to be accessible and predominantly grant-based. But it cannot substitute for mitigation. No amount of compensation will be enough if the world continues to burn fossil fuels at the scale it does today. No adaptation programme can keep pace indefinitely with a climate that becomes more dangerous every year.The people living along the Bhotekoshi river did not choose a warming Himalaya. They did not choose the fossil-fuel economy that drove most of the warming. However, with enough support, they can prepare better and build more resilient livelihoods. Sadly, they cannot adapt their way out of every disaster. This is why loss and damage finance is not charity – it is an obligation to people already paying the price.Sunil Acharya is an international climate policy and just transition specialist based in Kathmandu, NepalDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
