title: Burnham electrified the Labour party by talking about electoral reform – now he needs to act on it | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: The prime minister has lifted the spirits of the public and party members, and must use that goodwill to push through change, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: The prime minister has lifted the spirits of the public and party members, and must use that goodwill to push through change, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Andy Burnham in Kyiv, Ukraine, 24 August.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham in Kyiv, Ukraine, 24 August.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersOpinionElectoral reformBurnham electrified the Labour party by talking about electoral reform – now he needs to act on itPolly ToynbeeThe prime minister has lifted the spirits of the public and party members, and must use that goodwill to push through changeFri 28 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 11.51 EDTShareHe bounded into the packed rally, a spring-heeled intruder whose very presence announced a coup at last year’s Labour conference. And so it was.Andy Burnhamspoke with ebullient self-confidence, yet without aggression or a barrage of insults. They tried to stop him with a bogus constitutional fix barring him from standing in Gorton and Denton. But those Labour hierarchs lost it without him. His subsequent Makerfield victory proved their mistake and opened the door right into No 10 without dispute.At that standing-room-only rally on proportional representation he made a pitch-perfect noteless speech of personal passion about the failure of politics to connect, the decline of Westminster, the public’s distrust and the risk of this lost public belief in democracy. His hands were clean, he never benefited from the monster majority that first past the post had delivered so unfairly toLabourMPs: he wasn’t there at the last two elections. He quit out of despair, returning to repair.Now here we are with an amendment to the representation of the people bill next week that calls for a national commission on the electoral system. A new YouGov poll finds thatmost Labour MPs support it, by 55% to 29%. Many new MPs sitting on wafer-thin majorities, who don’t know which system helps them personally, are voting purely on principle.If, as expected, Burnham gives a clear signal that he intends to put electoral reform into the next manifesto to get public consent, if he confirms it needs a national commission ahead of the election, the amendment may be withdrawn with no needless division.Meanwhile, the Labour conference next month is likely to vote strongly for a motion put up by Labour for a New Democracy, backed by many constituencies,calling for a national commission. In the face of all this groundswell, it would plainly be good for Burnham to get ahead of the mood and own the initiative.This surge in support for proportional representation has been electrified in the past two years by the rise of Nigel Farage. The threat to democracy became brutally real when his party soared 10 points ahead, though thanks to Burnham he nowroughly level pegs with Labour. What was once a constitutional nice-to-have reform, not a priority for Labour people, has become an essential safeguard in the face of real danger to democracy. The prospect of Farage winning a landslide on even less than Labour’s 34% that won 63% of the seats is unconscionable. In May’s council elections, some candidateswon seats on little more than 20% of the vote. Imagine the rebellion if Farage became prime minister despite being by farthe most disliked political leader. That would feel like the complete breakdown of democracy, where the “losers” would no longer peacefully consent to be ruled by “winners” who had been rejected by about three-quarters of voters.Burnham’s magnetic performance at that rally set him on the path to leadership in a party now strongly supporting PR,with 66% of members backing it, and similarpublic approval. Tony Blair knew reform was necessary whenhe commissioned Roy Jenkinsto draw up a system that compromised between absolute proportionality and keeping the constituency link. But he backed off when confronted with the bared teeth of old-time opponents, the unions plus John Prescott and Jack Straw. Keir Starmer plainly supported reform, but then backed off – goodness knows why – as in so many of his self-inflicted errors. It’s Burnham’s time.More puzzling isBurnham’s retreat on capping party donations. The bill will do away with the worst aspect, banning donations of more than £100,000 from foreign donors. But the unions have balked at having UK donations limited, and with it their sometimes threatening influence. Large political donations are a prime cause of corrosive public cynicism about Westminster politics for sale. Burnham’s authenticity is worth many more votes for Labour than can be bought with political advertising. Think again.These have been precious days since Burnham walked through that black front door on 20 July, when you meet people everywhere expressing a rare optimism. Often those who are not natural Labour supporters will confess to unaccustomed hope. Burnham has lifted national spirits through small gestures that address people’s feelings of gloom. Keep that flame alight, don’t drop thatMing vase. Perversely that requires not caution, but boldness.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsElectoral reformOpinionProportional representationFirst past the postAndy BurnhamLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Dear culture-war motorists, look to the future. We’ll all be driving at 20mph soon | Christian Wolmar | The Guardian
description: There are howls of protest from the right about plans for Birmingham to be a 20mph city. But it will be a good thing, and others will follow, says transport writer and podcaster Christian Wolmar
Author: Christian Wolmar
Headline: There are howls of protest from the right about plans for Birmingham to be a 20mph city. But it will be a good thing, and others will follow, says transport writer and podcaster Christian Wolmar
Content: The ‘Spaghetti Junction’ motorway interchange near Birmingham.Photograph: Karl Hendon/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe ‘Spaghetti Junction’ motorway interchange near Birmingham.Photograph: Karl Hendon/Getty ImagesOpinionBirminghamDear culture-war motorists, look to the future. We’ll all be driving at 20mph soonChristian WolmarThere are howls of protest from the right about plans for Birmingham to be a 20mph city. But it will be a good thing, and others will followFri 28 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 06.56 EDTShareIf it can happen in Birmingham, it can happen anywhere. Moves by Birmingham city councilto impose a 20mph speed limit on all roads, apart from a few major thoroughfares, marks a turning point in transport policy that could and should attract imitators.Remember that in the 60sBirminghamwas the city that had a racetrack ​style networks of roads at its heart, ​and a tangle of elevated ro​utes and roundabouts that pushed pedestrians underground and ensured no one would be mad enough to try to cycle. Moreover, it was the headquarters of the UK’s car industry, and its roads were designed more as a test track for new models than a way for people to get to the shops. The emphasis on roads above all else was a deliberate strategy by a city that saw its future inextricably bound up with motoring manufacturers.This ode to the motorcar has gradually been dismantled over the past couple of decades, with the removal of roads turning the city centre into a far more pedestrian-friendly environment. The tram system is being expanded and soon – well actually, not that soon, thanks to endless delays – there will be a new station to accommodate high-speed rail services. Birmingham has been changing, but this latest move will accelerate the process. The imposition of a 20mph zone throughout the city seals the deal. No longer will the needs of cars dominate. Instead, walking, cycling and public transport will be the modes of choice, as car travel becomes slower and more of a hassle.View image in fullscreenDouble-decker buses and tram tracks on Broad Street near the Five Ways entertainment complex in Birmingham.Photograph: Aleksey Zotov/AlamyThe opposition, Conservatives and Reform alike, are already on the warpath, emphasising that this is part of a “war on the motorist” – the cliche brought out whenever any politician attempts to redress the balance between speed and livability in the urban environment. Gradually, far too slowly, they are losing the war, even if they occasionally win the battles: in Toronto, the Ontario premier, Doug Ford, isplanning to rip out 19km of cycle lanes.Diehards such as Ford are on the losing side of history. Birmingham’s shift of emphasis in the urban realm is part of a global phenomenon that is manifested in numerous ways: a pedestrianised main streetin Vancouver, a congestion chargein New York City, 500km of new cycle pathsin Bogotáand so on. Sadiq Khan has got in on the act with the imminentpedestrianisation of Oxford Street(a measure I advocated in a 1998 Evening Standard op-ed).Wales has led the way with “20’s plenty”, the brilliant campaignfounded by Rod Kingtwo decades ago that has influenced policymakers across the country. All Welsh local urban roads were restricted to 20mph in September 2023. Though a few busy streets have reverted to 30mph, by and large the concept has been accepted – and research has shownreductions in road deaths and injuries.View image in fullscreenA ‘20’s plenty’ sign in the village of St Bride’s Major, Wales, where the concept was trialled.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesIn the global race to sustainability and livability, the leader is probably Copenhagen, where ambitions of havinga 50% modal share of cyclingfor commuters may already have been achieved and there are ambitions to go further. Paris, however, is quickly catching up – and demonstrates that change can be rapid once momentum picks up. Since the election of Anne Hidalgo as mayor in 2014, the transformation has been astonishing. It has involved a raft of measures, building on the creation of Paris’s largebike hire schemein 2007 andthe pedestrianisation of the left bank of the Seinein 2013. There has been a comprehensive refocusing of the city’s roads in favour of cyclists and pedestrians, with more than 1,000km of cycle lanes, the removal of thousands of parking spaces, the closure of dozens of school streets and the creation of low-traffic neighbourhoods.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow Paris swapped cars for bikes – and transformed its streetsRead moreAnd here’s the rub: ultimately, the opponents are right. This is an attempt to make life more difficult for motorists, in order to improve the situation for people not travelling in large metal boxes. That does and should involve a raft of measures. Parking spaces need to be removed, access to town centres limited to deliveries, congestion charges imposed. This will give rise to noisy opposition, such as the fanatics in Londonwho broke camerasmonitoring compliance with the ultra-low emission zone (Ulez).We need politicians to explain – and to keep explaining – why the unrestricted use of cars in urban centres is damaging to the local economy as well as to the environment, to people’s health and to the overall feel of a place. It’s no good dodging the fact that the policies that prevailed until the late 1960s, and which still seem to be favoured by backward-looking opponents, were a mistake. Brave politicians need to take on opponents without compromise. Khan did this with the Ulez, standing firm against critics even though some were inside his own party, and the success is for all to see. Not only does research show thatchildren’s lungs are becoming biggerbecause the air is cleaner, but just go to Parliament Hill in Hampstead Heath and look over London: there is no longer a foul yellow miasma permanently overhanging that famous view.Khan could push through his Ulez because he has some mayoral powers, though less than those of his counterparts abroad. Hidalgo and her successor,Emmanuel Grégoire, have powers that British mayors can only dream of. However, opportunity is at hand. Andy Burnham’s emphasis on devolution may offer the opportunity for brave new mayors to follow the examples of Paris, Bogotá and Copenhagen – and Birmingham. Twenty is plenty: get used to it.Christian Wolmar is the presenter of the Calling All Stations podcast and writes a weekly Substack entitled Transport NewsThis article was amended on 28 August 2026. Doug Ford is the premier of Ontario, not the governor as an earlier version saidExplore more on these topicsBirminghamOpinionAutomotive industryRoad safetyRoad transportCyclingEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: From maligned second city to Insta magnet: Marseille is France’s new capital of overtourism | Mary Fitzgerald | The Guardian
description: This summer has been a tipping point. But it’s not too late to save what makes this place unique, says journalist Mary Fitzgerald
Author: Mary Fitzgerald
Headline: This summer has been a tipping point. But it’s not too late to save what makes this place unique, says journalist Mary Fitzgerald
Content: Police officers on the promenade at Catalans beach after the prefecture announced security measures for Marseille's beaches on 8 June 2026.Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolice officers on the promenade at Catalans beach after the prefecture announced security measures for Marseille's beaches on 8 June 2026.Photograph: Thibaud Moritz/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionFranceFrom maligned second city to Insta magnet: Marseille is France’s new capital of overtourismMary FitzgeraldThis summer has been a tipping point. But it’s not too late to save what makes this place uniqueFri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTShareWhen I first started visiting Marseille more than 20 years ago, few could have predicted that France’s then beleaguered second city would become one of the most popular destinations in themost-visited country in the world. Tarnished by stereotypes and home to some of Europe’s most disadvantaged neighbourhoods, the port city seemed down on its luck, unloved and, in the eyes of many, somewhere to avoid. Tourists stopping at the city’s Saint-Charles station would clutch their bags while waiting for their connecting train to rural Provence, or the beaches of the Côte d’Azur.Two decades on, poverty and drug gang violence still affect parts of Marseille, but this rough diamond has been reinvented as a modish holiday destination. Last month, I saw a local TV channel asking whether Marseille had becomeFrance’s capital of tourism, after Booking.com revealed it had surpassed Paris and Nice as the most searched-for destination for French users of the site. Breathlessforeign media coverage– the New York Times published a“36 hours in Marseille”guide in 2019 andanother onein 2025 – has driven the number of overseas visitors. From seaside petanque to vocoder rap and pizza served on aluminium plates, influencers revel in the golden-hued aesthetic of the urban riviera and promote the city’s most Instagram-friendly corners. Tourist numbers are expected to reachalmost 7 million this year.This has proved a boon for Marseille in many ways: more than20,000 jobsare linked to the local tourism sector, which generates€1.4bn (£1.2bn) annually. But it has also prompted a heated debate over the challenges of overtourism. This summer has felt like something of a tipping point. In June, the inhabitants of Les Goudes, a rugged fishing hamlet on the city’s periphery that has become an Instagram magnet,took to the streets in protest. One resident said they were so overwhelmed by visitor numbers that they felt as if they were under house arrest.In Vallons des Auffes, another picturesque tourist favourite, local people areopposing a planned sixth restaurantin its tiny harbour. When swimming wasbannedat the heaving Plage des Catalans earlier this month due to bacterial contamination, many local people blamed overcrowding. Residents of other heavily frequented neighbourhoods are organising against what they see as dramatic touristification that has brought with it unprecedented levels of noise and litter, along with higher prices. Anti-Airbnb sentiment, often expressed in graffiti, has been building for several years; the platform began flourishing here partly due to a shortage of hotel rooms. Meanwhile, campaigns against cruise ships have gained popular support, even if local politicians are divided on the issue.View image in fullscreenMS Allure of the Seas, the largest passenger ship ever constructed, leaving the port of Marseille.Photograph: Boris Horvat/AFP/Getty ImagesIt’s common to hear Marseillaissay they don’t want their city to become another Barcelona or Lisbon; the problem here has been the breakneck speed of the transformation. When I made the city my home almost a decade ago, tourism remained relatively low key. Local newspaper La Provencerecently notedthat it was in summer 2020 – when masses of French visitors descended on Marseille after months of pandemic lockdown – that the city first discovered overtourism. As is usually the case, the subsequent deluge of tourists is accompanied by a wave of gentrification that has driven up property prices and stirred local resentment.It feels like we blinked, and suddenly a Marseille summer meant thronged beaches, sprawling mega-bars, long queues for public transport and streets full of tour groups, mobile disco buses and – the most obnoxious canary in the coalmine – neon-lit pedicabs blaring loud music. Friends who grew up here and now have families of their own lament that typical child-friendly summer activities now involve advance bookings and snaking queues.As most local people agree, the problem is not tourism per se – the jobs it creates help dent the city’s high unemployment – but this record-breaking surge needs to be better managed and regulated. Local authorities insist that they are prioritising sustainability. The city hall, which has been ruled by a Green-left alliance since 2020, includes a deputy mayor with responsibility forsustainable tourism. When the new president of Marseille’s tourism office was appointed in June, he said he wanted to ensure that tourismprimarily benefits Marseille’s citizens.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFight them for the beaches: the real villain of Europe’s overtourism is big business | Adam AlmeidaRead moreSome concrete measures have been introduced in recent years. In 2024, our mayor, Benoît Payan, brought in France’stoughest restrictions on Airbnb(even if implementation has been a challenge). Daily visitor quotas have beenimposedon parts of the Calanques, a maritime park within the city limits that is popular with hikers and day trippers, to protect its fragile ecosystem. There are efforts to encourage more off-season visitors, and to diversify the predictable Instagram (and PR)-led tourist trail that results in overcrowding. But the political battle over whether the city should expand or limit cruise-ship infrastructure continues.City hall’s critics argue that the overtourism challenge is being met with a patchwork of interventions rather than a muscular overall policy. Some residents want to see higher tourist taxes or dual pricing, whereby visitors pay more for public transport and other amenities. Others seek even stricter limits on Airbnb. There are also demands that the most inundated districts, such as Les Goudes, are closed to visitors’ cars. At the very least, more substantive public awareness campaigns asking tourists not to litter or cause disturbances in residential neighbourhoods would help.What all of us share is the worry that time is running out, and Marseille will become yet another European city that seems to cater more for visitors than its own inhabitants. It’s a delicate balance to strike, but Marseille is still at the stage where it can learn from the cautionary tales elsewhere, mitigate the worst excesses and strive to preserve what made the city worth visiting in the first place.Mary Fitzgerald is a journalist and writer based in MarseilleExplore more on these topicsFranceOpinionOvertourismEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the loan of the Bayeux tapestry: a manifestation of soft power | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The British Museum’s landmark cultural exchange is a symbol of post-Brexit rapprochement between Britain and France
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The British Museum’s landmark cultural exchange is a symbol of post-Brexit rapprochement between Britain and France
Content: A scene from the Bayeux tapestry. ‘In these fractured times, the enduring appeal of this 11th-century artefact speaks of a need for a national story.’Photograph: Ardee Napolitano/ReutersView image in fullscreenA scene from the Bayeux tapestry. ‘In these fractured times, the enduring appeal of this 11th-century artefact speaks of a need for a national story.’Photograph: Ardee Napolitano/ReutersOpinionBayeux tapestryThe Guardian view on the loan of the Bayeux tapestry: a manifestation of soft powerEditorialThe British Museum’s landmark cultural exchange is a symbol of post-Brexit rapprochement between Britain and FranceFri 28 Aug 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTShare“Harold Rex interfectus est”: King Harold is killed. As every British schoolchild knows, the Bayeux tapestry depicts a turning point in the history of these islands: defeat at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, which would lead to the ascent of William the Conqueror to the English throne. Itsreturn to the UKfor the first time in nearly 1,000 years is being hailed as a hugely historic moment in its own right. The loan of the tapestry (technically an embroidery of wool on linen) to the British Museum inexchangefor UK treasures from Sutton Hoo is the ultimate manifestation of soft power – a 70-metre symbol of post-Brexit Anglo-French rapprochement in comic-strip form.Ticket sales for the exhibition, which opens on 10 September, werethe biggest in a single day in the museum’s history, with online queues of 80,000. Radio 4 is devotinga day of special broadcaststo mark the arrival of the tapestry, including a new drama with verse from the poet laureate Simon Armitage. Themuseum’s videosexplaining this tale of ambition, friendship, betrayal and revenge are fittingly narrated by Traitors presenter Claudia Winkleman. Norman-mania is here.“It probably took more years to deliver this project than all the Brexit talks,”Emmanuel Macron jokedin a speech to the British parliament last year. To the list of 623 men, 190 horses, 35 dogs and only three womendepictedon the tapestry, one might add a 21st-century British king, a French president, and three British prime ministers who have helped to bring it here – not to mention the millions of pounds it has cost.Two previous attempts – one for Queen Elizabeth’s coronation in 1953 and another in 1966 – failed. It would not have succeeded this time if the tapestry had not needed to be moved for renovations to the Bayeux Museum in Normandy. Many curators and restorers still believed the risks of bringing it to London were too great. The late David Hockney called the transferral“madness”. One of his final works, the 90-metre iPad friezeA Year in Normandie, on display this summer at the Serpentine gallery in London, was testament to his lifelong fascination with the tapestry. Anonline petitionagainst the move attracted nearly 80,000 signatures. However, political will won.From poetry to parody – from Tennyson’s 1876 epic verse drama Harold to anepisodeof The Simpsons – the tapestry has enjoyed a rich cultural afterlife. But its message has always been political. Napoleon and the Nazis recognised its potential as a propaganda tool. In 2014 Nigel Farage, then leader of Ukip, sported a Bayeux tapestry silk tie during the Rochester byelection, as a reminder of“the last time we were invaded and taken over”. The tie sold out in 24 hours.In these fractured times, the enduring appeal of this 11th-century artefact speaks of a need for a national story. The Bayeux tapestry is a devastatingly human saga. With war raging in Europe, this medieval masterpiece is a reminder of conflict’s brutality, human suffering and the importance of collaboration between countries. The tapestry will return to France for the 1,000th anniversary of William the Conqueror’s birth next year. According to Philippe Bélaval, Mr Macron’s former culture adviser:“Such a loan will only happen once and never again.”This is truly a once-in-a millennium event. Hopefully, its success will pave the way for equally ambitious cultural exchanges in the future.Vive l’entente cordiale!Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The 50 best TV shows to watch this autumn | Television | The Guardian
description: Nigella on Bake Off! Attenborough in Blue Planet III! Blade Runner 2099! Plus Adrian Mole, Harry Potter and a certain Celebrity Traitors … here are all the must-see shows of the season
Author: Kate Abbott
Headline: Nigella on Bake Off! Attenborough in Blue Planet III! Blade Runner 2099! Plus Adrian Mole, Harry Potter and a certain Celebrity Traitors … here are all the must-see shows of the season
Content: Coming up … David Tennant in Time and Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer in Bladerunner 2099.Composite: Guardian Design/BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyView image in fullscreenComing up … David Tennant in Time and Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer in Bladerunner 2099.Composite: Guardian Design/BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyAutumn arts preview 2026TelevisionThe 50 best TV shows to watch this autumnNigella on Bake Off! Attenborough in Blue Planet III! Blade Runner 2099! Plus Adrian Mole, Harry Potter and a certain Celebrity Traitors … here are all the must-see shows of the seasonRising star Lara Ricote on the real heartache behind her new breakup comedyKate AbbottandStuart HeritageFri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTShareThe Lycett ArmsWayward and chaotic, in the grand tradition of The Word and TFI Friday,Late Night Lycettproved that Joe Lycett had fully inherited Friday nights on Channel 4. Its follow-up sounds even more TFI-esque. The Lycett Arms is a real east London pub, open for just one hour a week, which required Lycett to train to be accredited with a level 2 award for personal licence holders. The show promises “top-drawer comedy entertainment from Joe and a pub full of celebrity guests”. What could possibly go wrong?Channel 4, 4 SeptemberLast SeenColin from Accounts’Patrick Brammallis totally changing tack with this intense drama about a one-time cop whose three-year-old daughter Mags disappeared more than a decade ago. When the remains of a young girl are found nearby, Ian Ridley (Brammall) is first on the scene – and his former colleagues in the police force know there’s nothing they can do to stop him from doing some digging. But the truth about the victim is far murkier. A twisty six-parter that will keep you guessing.Apple TV, 9 SeptemberSlow HorsesView image in fullscreenBeing picked off one by one … Jack Lowden and Gary Oldman in Slow Horses.Photograph: Jack English/AppleJackson’s Joes are being picked off one by one – and everyone who has ever worked at Slough House has been wiped from the system at MI5 HQ the Park, so no one will even know they’re goners. The sixth season of thesmash-hit dramaabout supposedly second-rate spies kicks off with a horrifying fire in a shipping container and a very violent funeral, and only ramps up from there. The usual suspects, from Gary Oldman and Kristin Scott Thomas to Jack Lowden, are still at it. Plus, the brilliant Lenny Rush joins the cast – and turns out to be a dab hand at spycraft.Apple TV, 16 SeptemberYouthView image in fullscreenScabrous and hilarious … Sharon Horgan in Youth.Photograph: Colin Hutton/HBO“Has any man ever said: ‘Have you met my girlfriend? She’s sexy, she’s fun, she’s 60.’ I need to meet someonenow. I think I’ve got 10 years left as a sexual person, tops.”Sharon Horgan’s new comedy is as scabrous and hilarious as always. Things aren’t going great for Alex (played by Horgan herself): her body is failing her, her son Ruari is veering off the rails (mooning at his school graduation) and her ex is moving abroad, leaving her even more of a single parent. Let’s hope she’s able to spice things up with some “new dick energy”.HBO Max, 20 SeptemberBrothersView image in fullscreenThe bizarre new Curb Your Enthusiasm … Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey in Brothers.Photograph: Ryan Green/AppleFirst Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey starred inTrue Detective. Then McConaughey revealed that he recently discovered hemight have the same father as Harrelson. And now, bizarrely, they are basically Curb Your Enthusiasming this new dynamic. In Brothers, the pair play fictionalised versions of themselves who learn that … well, you can see where this is going. You have to applaud the effort, since making an entire television series about some family gossip seems like so much more hard work than simply getting a DNA test.Apple TV, 23 SeptemberStrictly Come DancingView image in fullscreenWill any other scandals befall the show? … The new Strictly hosts Johannes Radebe, Josh Widdicombe and Emma Willis.Photograph: BBC/Ray BurmistonAll eyes on the Elstree and Borehamwood ballroom for the first series of the sparkly dance staple without Claudia Winkleman and Tess Daly. How on earth will the trio of new hosts – former pro dancer and all-round icon Johannes Radebe, Emma “safe pair of hands” Willis and comedian and former penguin suit-wearing Christmas contestant Josh Widdicombe – fare? And will any other scandals befall the show as it attempts this reset? The contestants include Shaun Wright-Phillips, Jaime Winstone, Dani Dyer, Delta Goodrem and, er, celebrity hair stylist Chris Appleton.BBC One, SeptemberThe Great British Bake OffView image in fullscreenThe queen of spoon-licking TV joins … The Great British Bake Off.Photograph: Channel 4/Love Productions/PAStale no more! Bake Off has been in serious need of a revamp for a while now – and who better tozhuzh it upthan the queen of sass herself, Nigella Lawson. The grande dame of spoon-licking cookery TV, and all-time winner of best pronunciation of the word microwavay, joins as the new judge. Expect to be whisked away by her charm, withering putdowns and (fingers crossed) fantastic repartee with Paul Hollywood.Channel 4, SeptemberKill JackieView image in fullscreenBonkers … Catherine Zeta-Jones in Kill Jackie.Photograph: Unai Mateo/PrimeWell, this one looks bonkers.Catherine Zeta-Jonesplays a former international cocaine dealer who has spent 20 years hiding in plain sight as an ostentatiously wealthy art dealer. But her cover is blown when she discovers that a group of elite assassins called the Seven Demons has been hired to kill her. Needless to say, she tries to kill them first. Co-starring Daniel Ings, Julian Barratt and Julian Rhind-Tutt, this has the potential to be the most entertaining thing in forever.Prime Video, 2 OctoberWarView image in fullscreenJuicy, bitchy and very starry … Dominic West and Sienna Miller in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesIt’s juicy, it’s bitchy and it’s very starry indeed: George Kay’s tentpole divorce drama looks at the bitter end of a relationship from both sides, meeting the lawyers making cases for all parties. Here, the movie star and tech billionaire going through proceedings are played bySienna MillerandDominic West. The cast is absolutely stacked, from reunited Celebrity Traitors matesNick MohammedandCelia Imrie(who could forget when he dug up her grave?) to Aran Murphy (son of Cillian – and set to be everywhere on our screens) as the feuding couple’s son.Sky/Now, 2 OctoberLast One Laughing Halloween specialLast One Laughingis such an ingenious money-maker – a whole series spun out from putting some comedians in a room for less than a day! – that we were always going to get more of it. While we await the third series (which stars Harry Hill!) this Halloween special features Jack Dee, Phil Wang, Reece Shearsmith, Harriet Dyer and Tom Allen, alongside the returning Lou Sanders and Daisy May Cooper, and there’s an intriguing new rule: competitors will be punished not just for laughing, but also for screaming.Prime Video, 23 OctoberNocturneRowan Joffé has long been a writer worth paying attention to, most recently for Edward Berger’s filmBallad of a Small Player. Nocturne sounds like it might cement his reputation once and for all. A drama about a homicide cop who relocates to Pennsylvania and finds himself having to deal with a serial killer, it stars Liev Schreiber and Zazie Beetz. Best of all,Stephen Grahamplays the serial killer. Entertaining grisliness should ensue.Apple TV, 30 OctoberThe AltruistsTelevision loves to adapt real-life things that have only just happened, and that’s the case with The Altruists, which deals with the rise (and subsequent implosion) of cryptocurrency exchange FTX. This is the one where Sam Bankman-Fried came out of nowhere to become the 41st richest man in the US, only to get sentenced to 25 years in jail for fraud, conspiracy and money laundering. When this genre gets it right, it makes for gripping TV. When it gets it wrong, it leaves you wondering why you didn’t just read the Wikipedia page. Fingers crossed for the former.Netflix, 19 NovemberBlade Runner 2099View image in fullscreenBack to the future … Michelle Yeoh in Blade Runner 2099.Photograph: PrimeAfter two dazzling big-screen outings (neither of which were commercially successful at the time) comes the inevitable TV adaptation. Set 80 years after the original, and 50 since the sequel, Blade Runner 2099 revolves round the aftermath of a Replicant uprising. Michelle Yeoh plays a dying Replicant Blade Runner. Hunter Schafer plays a human pretending to be a replicant. The amount of money thrown at this thing must be staggering, not least because the production design looks absolutely gorgeous. A must-see.Prime Video, 25 NovemberRivalsView image in fullscreenSex, more sex and a funeral … David Tennant in Rivals.Photograph: Ana Blumenkron/Disney+Where can TV’s mostrollicking bonkfestpossibly go after part one of thissecond seriesended harrowingly in the 1987 hurricane – and denied us the queer epiphany we’d all been waiting for? As we return to Rutshire, will Lizzie actually leave her abominable husband? Will Declan find out his wife Maud slept with his sworn enemy? Will Taggie ever move on from Rupert Campbell-Black? Expect sex, more sex, some gleefully evil regional TV wars and at least one funeral.Disney+, NovemberHarry PotterView image in fullscreenThe wizarding classic reborn … Dominic McLaughlin in Harry Potter.Photograph: Aidan Monaghan/HBO MaxBoth anticipation and trepidation are high for thesmall-screen version of JK Rowling’s wizarding classic. Security has had to be ramped up on set because of intense heat on stars such as Paapa Essiedu (who plays Severus Snape) and John Lithgow (Albus Dumbledore), and there have been calls for actors to quit the project. But the first teaser looks truly epic – and child actors have upped their game since the movies.HBO Max, Christmas DayA Bitter Pill: The Sodium Valproate ScandalSodium valproate is an effective epilepsy treatment. However, if it is taken during pregnancy, one in nine babies will have a physical birth defect. It is estimated that 20,000 children in the UK were affected. A Bitter Pill (made by the co-producers ofMr Bates vs the Post Office) follows the story of two mothers – Janet Williams and Emma Murphy – who spent decades battling doctors and drug companies to first find answers and then compensation. It is an incredible story of bloody-minded tenacity, and hopefully this documentary will help it reach a wider audience.BBC, TBCApocalypseA reality show/social experiment in which 16 participants/foolish guinea pigs are dropped in an actual ghost town in the US to see if they could survive the end of days. There will be no electricity or water or any mod cons, and they will be stuck there for a month. Think The Road for the influencer age. Sure to be utterly bananas.Channel 4, TBCBig SwissJen Beagin’s 2023 novel has all the hallmarks of a television adaptation – it’s full of rich people with good taste, almost all of whom have endured some form of terrible trauma – and so it has come to pass.Jodie Comerwill star as Flavia, a woman in a sexually unfulfilling marriage who embarks on an affair with a woman she meets at the dog park. However (possible spoiler, although probably not), the woman is secretly employed as her sex therapist’s transcriber. It is a dynamic that cannot possibly hold.HBO Max, TBCBlack DovesThe Ben Whishaw-Keira Knightleyspy epicreturns for more killer espionage fun with incredible new cast members Ambika Mod, Sam Riley and the Scream queen herself, Neve Campbell. Better still: Sarah Lancashire will have a far more prominent role in season two! Always a reason to celebrate.Netflix, TBCBlue LightsView image in fullscreenStunning … Martin McCann and Siân Brooke in Blue Lights.Photograph: BBC/Two Cities TelevisionTheBafta-winning showabout the “peelers” of Blackthorn police station in Belfast always sets out its stall with a stunning set piece in the opener. Season four is no exception, as police are called to a gathering at a migrant centre where multiple far-right groups are converging and ready to attack. Somehow it gets even more gripping and politically on point every time.BBC One, TBCBlue Planet IIIView image in fullscreenUnmissable … Blue Planet III.Photograph: BBC Studios/ Photographer copyright Anoushka FreedmanIt was announced onDavid Attenborough’s 100th birthdaythat he would be back to narrate the final part of this world-changing trilogy – and we got a sneak peek of him in his home studio intoning about the mating rituals of a whale. Given that this follows his spectacular feature-length film on the urgency of protecting our oceans to ensure human survival, and that it might well be the last time we hear his honeyed tones adorn something new, this will be totally unmissable. What a way to cap off his centenary year.BBC One, TBCThe Boys from BrazilIra Levin’s bracing Nazi thriller has already been adapted into one masterpiece – the1978 filmstarring Gregory Peck and Laurence Olivier – and now it is heading for the small screen. Peter Morgan has adapted the story into a five-part limited series starring Jeremy Strong, Gillian Anderson, Daniel Brühl and Lizzy Caplan. A film about a resurgence of nazism feels painfully relevant, although it remains to be seen how straight the show will play some of the story’s battier sci-fi elements.Netflix, TBCBreak ClauseView image in fullscreenCharming … Break Clause.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/Channel 4Many of us may have experienced the peculiar anguish of being trapped in a tenancy agreement with someone you’ve just broken up with, and this premise forms the spine of the new Channel 4 comedy Break Clause. Lara Ricote and Samuel Bottomley play the couple, working from a script by Jess Bray from the brilliantWe Might Regret This. The series originated as a 16-minute Comedy Blap that you can – and should – watch on Channel 4. If the series maintains the charm of the original, this should be something very special.Channel 4, TBCCarrieMike Flanagan is very much The Stephen King Guy at this stage, having written and directed the 2017 adaptation ofGerald’s Game, the 2019 adaptation ofDoctor Sleepand 2024’sThe Life of Chuck. And now (while he apparently readies adaptations of The Dark Tower and The Mist) he has adapted Carrie for television. You know the story already – a telekinetic teen with a horrible mother has to navigate school bullies – but this will apparently be an update, complete with modern technology and a sorority of telekinetic girls.Prime Video, TBCThe Celebrity TraitorsView image in fullscreenFull house … Top row, left to right: Amol Rajan, Bella Ramsey, James Acaster, James Blunt, Jerry Hall, Joanne McNally, and Joe Lycett. Middle row, left to right: Julie Hesmondhalgh, King Kenny, Leigh-Anne Pinnock, Maya Jama, Michael Sheen, Miranda Hart, and Myha’la. Bottom row, left to right: Prof Hannah Fry, Richard E Grant, Rob Beckett, Romesh Ranganathan, Ross Kemp, Sebastian Croft, and Sharon Rooney in The Celebrity Traitors’s new series.Photograph: PAWe didn’t think it was possible to trump the first lineup of celebrities entering the castle with Claudia – but this year’s casting may just have done it. With superstar luvvies such as Jerry Hall, Richard E Grant and Michael Sheen, double act Rob and Romesh pitted against each other and some tantalising curveballs – what will Ross Kemp, Myha’la and Bella Ramsey possibly chat about? – it’s sure to be another winner. This can’t come soon enough.BBC One, TBCColin from AccountsView image in fullscreenA beautiful thing … Harriet Dyer, Patrick Brammall and Colin the dog in Colin from Accounts.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 CBS Studios Inc, Easy Tiger Productions Pty Ltd, Foxtel Management Pty Ltd, Create NSW/Lisa TomasettiWhat a beautiful thingColin from Accountsis. A relationship dramedy written by its stars,the husband and wife teamof Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer, it is a funny and tender exploration of romantic compatibility in the modern age. In season one, Ashley and Gordon met and fell in love. In season two they tried to work out if they should stay together. In its third and final season, we learn that they didn’t. But might they again?BBC, TBCDamilola Taylor: The Last 24 HoursThe murder of 10-year-old Damilola Taylor in a Peckham stairwell 26 years ago has lost none of its horrors with age. One of the last people to see Taylor alive was actor John Boyega, then eight, who was friends with the family. In this documentary, Boyega explores Taylor’s final day, along with other close friends and family members, discussing both the events that led to his death and the impact his murder had on their lives.BBC, TBCDeadpointBetweenBaby Reindeer,Somewhere Boyand Misfits, Clerkenwell Films has developed an incredible pedigree when it comes to television. Deadpoint looks primed to continue this. A five-part action thriller set in Wales, it is the story of a man forced back to Snowdonia after the disappearance of his sister, only to discover that a far-right faction is planning to carry out a violent attack there. So it’s a survival thriller, a missing persons mystery and a domestic terrorism drama all in one. What could be better?Channel 4,TBCEast of EdenYou don’t adapt Steinbeck unless you’re willing to go all in on it, and happily this seems to be the case with Netflix’s new show. This epic tale of family, inheritance and jealousy spans decades, and judging by the trailer its writer, Zoe Kazan, has committed entirely.Florence Pughplays Cathy Ames, the beautiful monster at the story’s heart, with Christopher Abbott, Tracy Letts and Martha Plimpton rounding out the cast. This looks as sumptuous and panoramic as television will allow. On first impressions, it could be an award winner.Netflix, TBCI Am HelenView image in fullscreenShould be essential viewing … Nicola Coughlan in I Am Helen.Photograph: Joss Barratt/Channel 4Dominic Savage’s semi-improvised I Am … series has drawn some of the best female performers to its flame since it began, including Vicky McClure, Samantha Morton, Lesley Manville and Kate Winslet. Now it is the turn of Nicola Coughlan who (in a break from tradition) is starring in a two-part story. I Am Helen will explore themes of control and toxic masculinity in the setting of a modern relationship. Early reports suggest that it will deal heavily in the manosphere. If it manages to broach this as well asAdolescencedid, it might be essential viewing.Channel 4, TBCIt Gets WorseA fresh comedy from Leo Reich, whose debut Edinburgh fringe show Literally Who Cares?! was such a barnstorming success that it immediately got picked up by HBO Max. It Gets Worse is a look at three young mates in London who are on the verge of getting evicted. But what’s really staggering here is the sheer number of A-listers who have signed on – from Andrew “hot priest” Scott to Lena Dunham. This should be special.Channel 4, TBCLegacy of SpiesIf you can see a theme emerging in this list, it might be the Big Legacy Television Adaptation. Not being ones to miss out, the BBC has adapted this series from John le Carré’s The Spy Who Came in from the Cold, also drawing on material from his2017 novel A Legacy of Spies. If nothing else, it has been exquisitely cast, with Matthew Macfadyen playing George Smiley, Charlie Hunnam as Alec Leamas, Hugh Laurie as Control and supporting roles played by Daniel Brühl, Joe Alwyn and Agnes O’Casey.BBC, TBCMayaView image in fullscreenDark and very funny … Daisy Haggard and Bella Ramsey in Maya.Photograph: Channel 4Daisy Haggard’s writing is always dark and very funny, and her new witness protection thriller Maya is no exception. Anna (Haggard) and her daughter Maya (Bella Ramsey, as wonderful and unrestrained as ever) are forced to leave their home with no notice and move to the back of beyond in Scotland to escape her abusive ex (played by a chilling Tobias Menzies). It’s a moving look at survival and hope, with cliffhangers galore and gags about Frazzles crisps. What’s not to love?Channel 4, TBCNumber 10View image in fullscreenLudicrously anticipated … Jenna Coleman as Katie Flynn in Number 10.Photograph: Rob Youngson/Channel 4Steven Moffat’s ludicrously anticipated comedy-drama is finally almost here. A workplace show set in Downing Street – starring Rafe Spall as the prime minister, with Jenna Coleman as his deputy chief of staff – it could well be the British West Wing. And given Moffat’s flair for witty dialogue (and his form writing Press Gang), this has the potential to be one of the year’s best. But let’s hope it doesn’t run and run, because at this stage a British prime minister lasting more than a couple of years is nothing short of fantasy.Channel 4, TBCPierreView image in fullscreenThe starring vehicle he deserves … David Harewood in Pierre.Photograph: Channel 4Finally, David Harewood gets the starring vehicle he deserves. In Pierre, he plays a London duty solicitor described as “charming and funny, a glamorous character in an unglamorous profession”. However, he is forced to step up when he realises that the death of one of his clients might have been the result of a vast institutional cover-up. Pierre sounds like old-school television at its best; a show with something to say, and the smarts to wrap it in an irresistible character.Channel 4, TBCPride and PrejudiceView image in fullscreenDownright hilarious … Olivia Colman with Emma Corrin, Rhea Norwood, Hollie Avery, Hopey Parish and Freya Mavor in Pride and Prejudice.Photograph: Ludovic Robert/Netflix“Miss Elizabeth Bennet? I’m all astonishment!”​ There’s long-awaited, and then there’s Dolly Alderton’s update of Pride and Prejudice, which comes with sky-high expectations. Thankfully, Olivia Colman is downright hilarious as ​the busybody Mrs Bennet, determined to marry off ​o​ne of her five daughters to the swanky neighbour who just moved in next door. Emma Corrin stars as Elizabeth andJack Lowdenis heralding himself as the first “ginger” Mr Darcy. We’re promised even more ​s​park than the Colin Firth ​classic from the 90s – though there will be no lake scene.Netflix, TBCThe Rachel IncidentBased on Caroline O’Donoghue’s 2023 novel, beloved of countless millennial women, this is a new Channel 4 show about a young student’s attempt to seduce her married professor. The cast, including Máiréad Tyers, Ellis Howard, Daniel Ings and Ardal O’Hanlon, is worth getting excited about. But the real draw is the fact that O’Donoghue collaborated on the script with Jen Statsky, fresh from conquering the world with Hacks. If she can bring even a hint of the same sparkle to this, we will be in for a treat.Channel 4, TBCThe Reluctant VampireView image in fullscreenHouse of fun … Sian Clifford, Lenny Rush, Gabriel Nagy and Tom Davis in The Reluctant Vampire.Photograph: James Pardon/BBC/Buffola Pictures“You don’t pick up being a vampire … it’s not conversational French!” Valentine hates drinking blood, ​has no truck with violence and –​ horror of horrors –​ he has a reflection. But his vampire family still don’t know he’s actually a human and they want him to pass his initiation ceremony in front of the whole community of Katchem-By-the-Throat. This BBC comedy from the Gibbons brothers (renowned for keeping Alan Partridge alive), based on a book by Eric Morecambe, has an incredibly high gag rate and a cracking cast​. It ​includes​ Lenny Rush as the titular non-vamp, ​Sian Clifford and Tom Davis as his parents, Asim Chaudhry as Igon the family assistant and Bill Bailey and Ross ​Noble as ​a hilarious pair of gargoyles​.BBC One, TBCReputationWell this one sounds like fun. Written by Anya Reiss and starring Naomie Harris and Christina Hendricks, Reputation is a glossy drama about a celebrity lawsuit that spirals out of control. A pop star writes a song accusing her husband of infidelity. He fires accusations back. Social media goes wild, and a phalanx of dirty PR tricks comes into play. The enjoyment won’t just come from seeing the inner workings of the lawsuits we only hear about in the news, but presumably also trying to guess which precise celebrity lawsuits the show is based on.BBC One, TBCThe Secret Diary of Adrian Mole Aged 13¾View image in fullscreenThere aren’t many characters more loved … Oliver Savell as Adrian Mole.Photograph: BBCThere aren’t many characters in literature more beloved than Sue Townsend’s self-importantly earnest adolescent, whose diaries enthralled a nation across four decades and eight books. After 1985’s classic ITV adaptation, David Nicholls has come on board to bring him back to life as a period piece. Writers for this new version include Caitlin and Caroline Moran, Dillon Mapletoft, Oliver Taylor and Jack Rooke, while Oliver Savell from Changing Ends will play the lead. Can lightning strike twice?BBC, TBC70 UpOne of the most seminal documentaries ever made finally concludes. Since 1964, the Up series has followed the lives of several perfectly normal people across the social spectrum at increments of seven years. Through the decades, the participants have fallen in love and endured hardships, and now they are almost at the end of the road. The final chapter –directed by the Oscar-winning Asif Kapadiaafter the death of Michael Apted – is bound to be poignant, but the series as a whole will remain an important document about life in Britain in the 20th and 21st centuries for ever.ITV1, TBCSherwoodFresh from his job consulting onSNL UK, of all things, James Graham gets back to his masterwork. In its two series so far, Sherwood has been an almost unbearably dark investigation of a community left to hold itself together with threads. Six months have passed since the climax of season two, in which evil matriarch Ann Branson drowned, yet more human remains have been found. Who in the town has a dark secret this time?BBC, TBCThe Slightest TouchView image in fullscreenUplifting … Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell in The Slightest Touch.Photograph: HBOA documentary in whichColin Farrellmeets up with his friend and discusses running a marathon. The catch is that his friend is Emma Fogarty, a survivor of epidermolysis bullosa, a rare and painful genetic condition that renders the skin fragile enough to blister and tear at the slightest touch. Fogarty has already confounded medical science once before – she was never expected to reach the age of 40 – so why not go the whole hog and run the Dublin marathon? Powerfully emotional and uplifting in equal measure.HBO Max, TBCThe Split UpView image in fullscreenHanding over the reins … Aysha Kala and Ritu Arya in The Split Up.Photograph: BBC/SisterOver its three series (and Christmas special), Abi Morgan’s divorce dramaThe Splitbecame one of the highlights of the annual schedule. Rather than ending, it has now morphed into The Split Up. This is a new, Manchester-set series about a powerful family struggling to decide who should inherit its prestigious divorce firm. Morgan is just executive producing this one, handing the reins to Ursula Rani Sarma. Ritu Arya, Sanjeev Bhaskar, Aysha Kala and Arian Nik star.BBC One, TBCThis City Is OursThefirst seasonof this swaggering Liverpool gangland thriller didn’t quite get the dues it deserved (that rooftop scene in the finale was gasp-inducing), but it did establishJames Nelson-Joyce– who got his big break after chatting to his idol Stephen Graham at Nando’s – as a swiftly rising star. He returns for more explosive drama, as well as Endeavour star Shaun Evans, who joins the cast.BBC One,TBCTimeView image in fullscreenAbsolutely gripping … Siobhan Finneran, Chukwubuikem Molokwu and David Tennant in Time.Photograph: Peter Marley/BBC StudiosJimmy McGovern’sprison anthologyhas so far been absolutely gripping. And now, following runs led by Sean Bean andJodie Whittaker, David Tennant gets a turn at the wheel. This story is set at a young offenders institution, and Tennant plays a custodial manager concealing knowledge about a serious incident. As connective tissue, Siobhan Finneran returns as prison chaplain Marie-Louise O’Dell, now undergoing a crisis of faith, who clashes with Tennant over it.BBC One, TBCThe Unlikely Cook With AwkwafinaView image in fullscreenExtremely unskilled in the kitchen … The Unlikely Cook With Awkwafina.Photograph: Christina Belle/Courtesy of AppleOnce a mainstay of the television schedules, the food show has lost no end of ground to YouTube in recent years. Perhaps this series is the thing to regain it. In The Unlikely Cook With Awkwafina, the titular star will travel across the US exploring modern Asian-American cuisine. Why isAwkwafinaan unlikely cook? Because she is apparently extremely unskilled in the kitchen and will have to rely on a host of people more talented (but less famous) than she is to show her the way.Apple TV, TBCThe WargamePicture this: Michael Gove is the prime minister. Nicola Sturgeon is his deputy. His cabinet comprises Penny Mordaunt, Baroness Harman, Baroness Warsi and Kim Darroch, while Anthony Scaramucci plays the US secretary of state. If that doesn’t sound awful enough, Russia has just invaded the UK. Welcome to The Wargame, a series where these figures enter a Cobra-style briefing room and attempt to deal with the minute-by-minute developments of such a crisis. This could be gripping or it could be the television equivalent of banging yourself on the head with a tin tray. Either way, it will probably be worth watching.Sky, TBCThe Witch FarmView image in fullscreenFlat-out terrifying … Gabrielle Creevy, Sian Gibson and Michael Socha in The Witch Farm.Photograph: BBCFew things have been as flat-out terrifying as Danny Robbins’spodcast The Witch Farm, about the supposedly true haunting of an isolated Welsh farmhouse 30 years ago. Now the podcast has been made into a TV show. If it can cram as many unsettling incidents as the podcast – think apparitions, dead animals and unusually high utility bills – while maintaining its tone of sceptical unease, this will hands down be the scariest thing on television in several years.BBC, TBCYagaView image in fullscreenRaunchy and ritualistic … Hudson Williams in Yaga.Photograph: Bell Media/SkyAKA whatHeated Rivalry’sHudson Williams did next. He stars alongside Carrie-Anne Moss and Noah Reid in a raunchy and ritualistic take on the terrifying folklore tale of Baba Yaga. It should fall somewhere between Jodie Foster’sTrue Detective: Night Countryand a wildly freewheeling fairytale.Sky, TBC

title: ‘I’m an ever-changing vessel’: Erykah Badu on defying definition, life as a birth and death doula and her first album in 11 years | Soul | The Guardian
description: Why do the Texan innovator’s records take so long to make? ‘It’s important to gather the data,’ she says: the death, dating and dopamine behind her exquisite comeback alongside the Alchemist
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Why do the Texan innovator’s records take so long to make? ‘It’s important to gather the data,’ she says: the death, dating and dopamine behind her exquisite comeback alongside the Alchemist
Content: ‘I denounced my throne’ … Erykah Badu.Photograph: Adraint BerealView image in fullscreen‘I denounced my throne’ … Erykah Badu.Photograph: Adraint BerealSoulInterview‘I’m an ever-changing vessel’: Erykah Badu on defying definition, life as a birth and death doula and her first album in 11 yearsShaad D'SouzaWhy do the Texan innovator’s records take so long to make? ‘It’s important to gather the data,’ she says: the death, dating and dopamine behind her exquisite comeback alongside the AlchemistFri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 06.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleErykah Badu needs the lights downlow. The singer, producer, actor and registered doula shuffles into a private room at London’s Soho hotel and quietly asks for some changes to the atmosphere: lights dimmed, soft seat. A green juice would be great.As it turns out, Badu was out last night with Dave Chappelle, sitting with the comedian at a grand piano and playing songs into the wee hours. She looks mischievous when she thinks about the impromptu party, but declines to go into detail about what, exactly, went on. Instead, the 55-year-old smiles at me, eyes wide, her gold teeth glinting in the low light: “Oh yes,” she says slowly and quietly, like some kind of mysterious warlock. “Itwasa late one …”Meeting Badu, in other words, is everything you want it to be and more. She and I are here to talk about Before the World Blows: The Abi and Alan Experiment, a collaborative record with famed underground producer the Alchemist. It’s Badu’s first full-length project since the release of 2015’s But You Caint Use My Phone mixtape, and its dense, layered sound feels like an internet-fried take on her era-defining New Amerykah albums, from 2008 and 2010.It’s surprising, I suggest, that she has taken so long between records, given how much she analyses the world around her. She says that’s the point. “Procrastinating and living, learning and stuff – that gives you stuff to write about,” she says. “It’s important to gather the data, upload as much as I can. I don’t have a choice. But when the thing gets kind of full, I download it through writing music.”Erykah Badu and the Alchemist: Witch Doctor – videoBadu has been a star since 1997, when the release of her debut album, Baduizm, announced her as one of the leading lights of what music industry executive Kedar Massenburg called “neo soul”, a new wave of alternative soul and R&B. In the years since, a handful of wild, boundary-pushing records have made Badu one of the most revered artists in the world. The Alchemist – LA producer Alan Maman – was one of those early fans. In 1997, he was a roadie for Cypress Hill, who were co-headlining the Smokin’ Grooves tour alongside Badu. “I was such a fan – I used to go out in the crowd and watch her show every night,” he says on the phone later. “I never would have thought in a million years that one day I would be making music with her.”Since then, Maman has produced a number of hits, including Mobb Deep’s 1999 track The Realest, and enjoyed a recent career renaissance in collaborations with underground rappers such as the duos Armand Hammer and Mike & Wiki. A few years ago, while DJing a party, he ran into an old friend named Cold Cris who happened to work for Badu, and told him that working with her was on his bucket list. Two years after that, he got the call that Badu was interested in playing around with his beats. She came to his studio in LA, and the pair, he says, “instantly became friends, and realised how much shit we had in common, in the way we create, the way we think”.View image in fullscreen‘His compositions are like classical music to me’ ... Badu and the Alchemist.Photograph: Adraint Bereal“His compositions are like classical music to me – how he layers chimes and voices and strings and horns,” says Badu. “Our process is the same. The way we build is the same. I don’t know what it is exactly, but it’s a burning, beautiful fire. I get chills when I hear his music.”Badu was born in Dallas, Texas. Her mother was an actor; her uncle, an avid record collector; Badu’s grandmother bought her her first piano. She still remembers the first artwork she ever made, in a primary school art class: a sculpture of a spaceship made out of a rubber glove, which she called Lady Luna 2. Attending a performing arts high school in Dallas, she was “the first person at school and the last person to leave”, and would spend hours dancing while facing a mirror.“In the beginning, there was no audience – there was just me and the things I loved – music, painting, dancing,” she says. “I grew up listening to Earth, Wind & Fire, the Emotions, Deniece Williams, Eric Clapton of course, Joni Mitchell, Phoebe Snow, Parliament Funkadelic … they were creating from a place that nothing else came from.”Badu started making music in earnest when she was a theatre major at Grambling State University in Louisiana after her cousin Robert “Free” Bradford mailed her a cassette tape with beats on it. Their collaboration ended up becoming Baduizm. It was an instant hit – No 2 in the US – and, thanks to Massenburg’s clever marketing, announced Badu as “the queen of neo soul”, a term she quickly rejected. “I was the first one who denied it – I denounced my throne” she says. “I’m an ever-changing vessel, and I just didn’t want to be pigeonholed. When I hear the algorithm today, when I type in Erykah Badu somewhere, I don’t like everything that’s with it, because it limits what I feel.”View image in fullscreen‘Joni Mitchell touches my spirit’ ... Badu in 1997.Photograph: Paul Natkin/WireImageBadu says she had her whole life to write Baduizm; for its follow-up, 2000’s Mama’s Gun, she only had three years, but everything in her life had changed. In 1997, she had a son, Seven, with André 3000; the pair split a year later. “I had a kid. I had a heartbreak. I had a new house. I had money. I could do things for my family members. The expectations were enormous, that I had for myself, but I didn’t feel like I had enough time,” she says. “I had to learn, from Baduizm and Mama’s Gun, to ignore the negative things and the positive things – people who are lifting you up, because you can feel so high that you don’t want to learn anything any more.”double quotation markThey’re not giving out enough ass-whoopings no more!Eventually, Badu was able to re-centre herself by thinking about those artists who had been so formative for her – artists such as Joni Mitchell, who she returns to a couple of times throughout our conversation. “She touches my spirit – the simplicity of scaled-back voice and music, because her voice is a true instrument, with perfect pitch,” she says. “Her emotions are an instrument as well. I can hear the tears and laughter in the music, and because it’s scaled down so beautifully. It’s just a feeling that I have when I listen to her, or sing about her. Think about her. Talk about her.”Badu became a doula “by accident”. Four years after having Seven, she promised to be with a friend during her birth. “I didn’t know her labour was going to be 52 hours – she soldiered through this thing, and after the 52nd hour, I realised I had not been to sleep. I felt fine. I was the support system, I was the restaurant, and I didn’t have any fear,” she recalls. “That’s when I realised, I am the welcoming committee – my contract was with that baby.”View image in fullscreen‘How do you stay friends with exes? Suck hard!’ ... Badu and André 3000.Photograph: Mike Vitelli/BFA.com/ShutterstockBadu began studying and received her doula certification in 2006. From 2001 to 2023, she supported two mothers a year – because she tours eight months of the year, she was reluctant to take on any more – and coached them through their pregnancies, ensuring they had access to what she calls “the five doctors”: sun, earth, nutrients, exercise and spirit. She has doula’d for celebrity friends including, she tells me, Teyana Taylor and Summer Walker. And she is also an end-of-life doula, sitting “at the bedsides of people who are passing, going the other way – I want to provide the exact same peace.”I ask if being an end-of-life doula can be distressing, but she says the fact that it’s not for her is why she does it. “It’s another art for me,” she says. “I feel the same way when I’m servicing people on stage, singing. That’s doula work, too. I have the same thing in mind – I want the room to become one living, breathing organism.”If there is a common thread that runs though many of the songs on Before the World Blows, it’s gender politics: the ways in which men and women interact, screw each other over and take central roles in each other’s lives. Badu has always been interested in this theme, but it feels different this time, as if she is an omniscient narrator, spreading wisdom to the world. “Some of these songs are autobiographical, and some of them are messages I want to give to my daughters” – she has two, Puma (born 2004) and Mars (2009) – “or the daughters of the world, to the people of the world who have to go through these initiations, too.”View image in fullscreen‘Phones have become our pseudo-husband and wife’ ... Badu performing in 2026.Photograph: Astrida Valigorsky/Getty ImagesI ask if she sees right now as a particularly fractious moment for heterosexual dating, and she looks at me quizzically. “Your mama had trouble dating, and your grandma, and your great-grandma. You say more fractured – I think more transparent, maybe.” Legs outstretched, bare toes occasionally tickling my thigh by accident, Badu puts forward her theory. “I think we’re so hyper-aware that we notice things that maybe the people before us didn’t notice. The vocabulary we’re using, the definitions that we can put on our inconsistencies and weirdness, narcissism, and the ADHD. The definitions are becoming bigger than who we are.”That scrutiny means we’re stealing from ourselves, she says. “It doesn’t give us room to create or laugh or be free. It’s hard to find somebody that is accepting you completely because we don’t accept ourselves completely any more. When I was young, you didn’t get the grace of being defined as something. You just got an ass-whooping! And when all you need is an ass-whooping, everybody can straighten up. They’re not giving out enough ass-whoopings no more. We’re pardoning behaviour by defining it, I think.”Black Box, the album’s final track, is a wild odyssey about phone addiction, and a worthy addition to her canon of phone songs she started with But You Caint Use My Phone. Social media is a constant bugbear for Badu – she loves using it, and is prolific on Instagram, but hates how tied she is to her phone. “It’s the first thing we reach for in the morning – it has become our pseudo-husband and wife – and one thing I do know is that the first thing we do in the morning that gives us dopamine is what we will reach for all day long,” she says. “If we’re able to bypass the phone and go outside and get air and nutrients and all that, that’s what we’re going to keep running back to all day. But we pick this up first. I wanted to speak to that.”View image in fullscreenWith daughters Mars (left) and Puma (right) in 2017.Photograph: Leon Bennett/Getty Images for BETBadu’s children are 17, 22 and 28 – and she sees how they don’t have the same freedom she did, growing up without social media. Everyone is “vibrating at a higher rate” now, she says. “I noticed that it was different when I tried to show my daughters Fred Flintstone – that cartoon is hilarious to me, and they couldn’t resonate with it because it just doesn’t vibrate at the same rate they do.” Even so, she and her daughters, Mars and Puma, still have things in common. “Mars put me on to Faye Webster and Beabadoobee. Mars went backwards and got me listening to Abba! Puma loves musical theatre and Broadway, so she has me listening to Chicago or operas. We share an aux cord in the house, so I don’t have a choice.”‘I used to do acid on a Wednesday. I don’t have time for that now’: alt-pop star Steve Lacy on his struggles after huge hit Bad HabitRead moreThey all love Steve Lacy, too: Badu took her daughters to see him perform in Dallas a few years ago, and this year, they make reciprocal guest appearances on each other’s albums. “We had stuff in common, and mostly sent memes to each other starting out. That’s how you know if you rock with somebody – you have a similar sense of humour,” she says. “You kind of don’t have the same music taste, either, if you don’t have the same sense of humour.”Before the World Blows includes an interlude by Jay Electronica, the elusive rapper she dated for many years, and the father of Mars. Badu has tended to remain close with her exes – André 3000 contributed a rare, memorable guest verse to But You Caint Use My Phone – so I ask if she has any advice for maintaining ties with former lovers. “You just gotta suck hard. That’s it,” she says, bursting into laughter, her voice rising above a whisper for the first time in our conversation. “They were my friends first, and I think that’s what makes a difference. Watch that be the headline – Erykah remains friends with her exes because she sucks hard!”Our time is up; Badu gently swings her legs off the couch and stands up. She shuffles over to me and leans in, peering deeply into my eyes. I’m a little scared that she might drop some kind of bombshell – the time and place of my death, for example, or that I was a terrible interviewer – but instead, she just mutters: “You pretty as fuck!” Before I can even respond, she’s gone.Before the World Blows is out now on Control Freaq/YoungExplore more on these topicsSoulErykah BadufeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Li Jin Hao: Falling from a Moon review – comedy’s Mr Nostalgia is now the man of the moment | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: In his award-nominated show, the standup ruminates on myth and memory with some lovely observations
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: In his award-nominated show, the standup ruminates on myth and memory with some lovely observations
Content: Ravishing insights … Li Jin Hao.Photograph: Rebecca Need MenearView image in fullscreenRavishing insights … Li Jin Hao.Photograph: Rebecca Need MenearEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewLi Jin Hao: Falling from a Moon review – comedy’s Mr Nostalgia is now the man of the momentPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghIn his award-nominated show, the standup ruminates on myth and memory with some lovely observationsBrian LoganFri 28 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘There’s a moment whenthatends,” muses Li Jin Hao, “andthisbegins …” As well as being jam-packed with swoonsome one-liners like that, Li’s show traces the tension between this and that; the draw the past exerts on this self-proclaimed Mr Nostalgia, versus the necessity of living in the present. Beginning with a yearning sun-and-moon myth learned at his granny’s knee, Li’s show –nominated for the Edinburgh comedy award– toggles between a day in his current London life and memories of his upbringing in east Asia, and a long-gone romance he can’t quite shake off.What makes the show distinctive, though, is the ruminative angle at which Li addresses his experiences, and the quality and consistency of its joke-writing – so many ravishing little insights revealing the world to us in shapes askew. It’s a leap forward fromhis 2024 debut, which signalled the talent but was sheepish in its delivery. The only thing sheepish here is the twisty livestock gag that opens Li’s show, with a swagger that marks a performer now in his element onstage.Marty Gleeson: Dog Ear review – hangdog standup with an unexpected request for SantaRead moreSo if his present is in such good nick, what’s with the nostalgia? That question won’t initially trouble you, as we follow our host from his London flat with a sloping floor, on to public transport (on pressing the stop button: “I’m tickling the bus!”), then to the cinema. The trip detours via countless sumptuous routines and notions: on how differently letters and numbers behave; on rhyme versus reason; on “how come when two people give each other their virginities, they’re left with none?” Then we flash back to a Chinese childhood and Singaporean youth, flooding Li with memories of a life lived in more vivid colour.But looking back, as myths from Lot to Orpheus remind us, can be a dangerous business. Li’s show, finally, is about the need to put that past behind him – a theme it over-articulates in its closing moments. There’s no need: we can glean plenty from what goes before, while glorying in the linguistic and observational invention at play in image after joke after slantedaperçu.Thatwas the show I saw; this is Li’s moment.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsComedy (Culture)Comedy (Stage)Awards and prizesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A gallery glow up, spooky sculpture and a magical modern – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: A grand survey of light art illuminates Durham, St Ives gets macabre and London goes big on land art – all in your weekly dispatch
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: A grand survey of light art illuminates Durham, St Ives gets macabre and London goes big on land art – all in your weekly dispatch
Content: Our Spectral Vision, 2016, by Liz West at Victory Over the Sun, The Light, Durham.Photograph: The Light/Liz WestView image in fullscreenOur Spectral Vision, 2016, by Liz West at Victory Over the Sun, The Light, Durham.Photograph: The Light/Liz WestArt Weekly newsletterArt and designA gallery glow up, spooky sculpture and a magical modern – the week in artA grand survey of light art illuminates Durham, St Ives gets macabre and London goes big on land art –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 28 Aug 2026 09.47 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekVictory Over the SunA Russian futurist spectacle from 1913 gives this grand survey of light art its title. Luminous works by Olafur Eliasson, Ceal Floyer and many more mark the opening of Durham’s new art gallery.The Light, Durham, until 17 JanuaryAlso showingAna MendietaDon’t on any account miss this magical journey through the imagination of a great modern artist.Tate Modern, London, until 17 JanuarySgàire WoodHeraldry, fashion and sectarian politics are among the themes this Irish artist brings to a wooded sculpture park near Edinburgh.Jupiter Artland, Edinburgh, until 18 OctoberClaire CurneenSpooky sculptures that brood on death, if your day by the sea needs a macabre salting.Anima Mundi, St Ives, until 4 SeptemberEyes in the SoilArt that engages with the earth, featuring Neal Jones, Vivian Lynn and more.Phillida Reid, London, 1 September to 1 OctoberImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sonja Blom/AlamyOne of the most prolific and beloved artists of our age, Yayoi Kusama died this week at 97. The Japanese artist became a global superstar many times over in different eras for her sculptural works, her political artistic “happenings” and the spotty style and selfie-inducing infinity mirror rooms that came to be synonymous with her name. Kusama’s work was often centred on ideas of the infinite and “self-obliteration”, a concept inspired by the hallucinations that would engulf her. Despite her superstar success she identified herself as an outsider artist until her death. The image above shows her in June, painting a work from her My Eternal Soul series.Read more hereWhat we learnedBetye Saar, whose found object assemblages explored racism and religion, died aged 99Freddie Mercury’s ‘splendid things’ – eight iconic costumes – are to go on displayA plan for a waterfront site in Rotterdam looks ‘like something Shrek would throw up’Gao Zhen, known for sculptures of Mao, was jailed for slandering ‘heroes and martyrs’The Wulz sisters defied fascist Italy by shooting modern women – and their catPhotographer William Yang looked back on 60 years of capturing LGBTQ+ lifeThe Nazis hounded out the Bauhaus; now the far right is turning on them againskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKorean painter Ha Chong-Hyun, 91, believes abstraction is a form of rebellionA priceless collection of bronze age gold artefacts were stolen in a Spanish heistMasterpiece of the weekA Herdsman with Five Cows by a River by Cuyp Aelbert, 1650-55There’s not much happening here, but that’s what is so revolutionary. Cuyp is centuries ahead of his time in simply showing a moment in the countryside without feeling he has to make it more significant by adding a story from Greek mythology or the Bible. Artists including Constable and Turner would be imitating his accepting natural eye almost 200 years later. They would also be thrilled by the subtle but omnipotent sunlight that Cuyp sees pervading everything here, from the gold-fringed clouds to the luminous river. Light was being understood in new ways in the 1600s by Galileo, Newton and other early scientists. Cuyp uses the very quietness of his rustic scene to let our minds focus on the ethereal magic of reflective water, set off by the brown, black and bronze masses of the cows. It is a lesson in weightless light and weighty flesh, a painting in which nothing happens and everything does.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Vidimages/AlamyNational Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in TouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Reading and Leeds have dropped BBC Introducing for a new ‘nepo baby stage’. Where does it leave DIY artists? | Reading and Leeds festival | The Guardian
description: As R&L replace the BBC’s unsigned artists stage with one filled with rock scions and a Simon Cowell boyband, many are decrying disappearing opportunities for grassroots acts
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
