Headline: As R&L replace the BBC’s unsigned artists stage with one filled with rock scions and a Simon Cowell boyband, many are decrying disappearing opportunities for grassroots acts
Content: Gene Gallagher, son of Liam, performs with band Villanelle at All Points East, London, earlier this month.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGene Gallagher, son of Liam, performs with band Villanelle at All Points East, London, earlier this month.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesReading and Leeds festivalReading and Leeds have dropped BBC Introducing for a new ‘nepo baby stage’. Where does it leave DIY artists?As R&L replace the BBC’s unsigned artists stage with one filled with rock scions and a Simon Cowell boyband, many are decrying disappearing opportunities for grassroots actsDaniel Dylan WrayFri 28 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis year’sReading and Leeds festivallineups are a testament to the catholic tastes of a generation who have little regard for musical tribalism or the concept of genre: brash pop stars rub up against drum’n’bass acts, underground rappers, meat-and-potatoes indie bands and much more.What at least 70% of those acts have in common, however, is that early on in their careers they were supported by the BBC’s Introducing scheme, a combination of regional and national radio shows playing music submitted by unsigned artists and festival stages that platform them. For almost 20 years, a BBC Introducing stage has been a core part of Reading and Leeds – until it was scrapped last month.“It’s a loss,” says Juliette Jackson, of the Mercury-nominated indie band the Big Moon, who played the stage in 2015, a year after forming. “It was a really big deal to play that as a new band with no money. It’s huge when you’re starting out – it gives you an opportunity and puts you on a platform.”Over the years, major British artists including Ed Sheeran, Charli xcx, the 1975 and Sam Fender started their careers with support from the initiative, which has few of the barriers to entry of the traditional music industry. Regional DJs suggest local acts for festival slots, with final decisions made by a wider BBC team.View image in fullscreenCharli xcx at Reading festival in 2013.Photograph: Joseph Okpako/Redferns/Getty ImagesReading and Leeds organisers Festival Republic did not respond to detailed questions from the Guardian about why it had pulled the plug on an unsuspecting BBC, who were already planning their 2026 lineup. It has been replaced by the Canopy stage, billed as a “home for new and breaking acts”. In a public statement, Festival Republic claimed it offers greater opportunity: “Previously, only artists who had been selected by the BBC were qualified to play the Introducing Stage – now, we are able to open up this important platform to a much wider pool of emerging talent and book any new music artist for the stage.”But that so-called “wider pool” has come under scrutiny. Fans have been highlighting the connections behind many of the acts booked for the stage, such as Violet Grohl (daughter of Dave Grohl), Cruz Beckham (son of Victoria and David) and Villanelle frontman Gene Gallagher (son of Liam). The boyband December 10 are already signed to a label after they formed on Simon Cowell’s Netflix series The Next Act.It has led some to nickname the Canopy “the nepo baby stage”, and prompted coverage in Private Eye. In an Instagram post, music industry commentator the Secret DJ decried “nepotism and the rising use of famous names over new talent [that] is rapidly destroying the arts”.In a general statement provided to the Guardian, Festival Republic said their booking policy for the stage is “open to emerging artists from all backgrounds and at different stages of development. Artists may be independent or signed and may have come through a variety of routes into the industry.”BBC Introducing editor Kelly Betts told the Guardian: “We will miss being at Reading and Leeds for this year. Programming decisions for that stage are made by the festival organisers, so it’s not really for me to comment on how they choose to curate it.”View image in fullscreenEd Sheeran on Reading’s BBC Introducing Stage in 2011.Photograph: Andy Sheppard/RedfernsJason Carter, who founded BBC Introducing in 2007 and was responsible for forging the relationships with festivals to put on live events, said he was “disappointed to hear [the news] and sad to see it no longer there” but that he “can see both sides”, adding that the industry has changed and “there’s a lot more ways today to access new music that the festival probably wants the opportunity to feed off”.Ex-BBC Introducing presenter Tom Robinson said that while “the beauty of BBC introducing was that you needed no inside access”, it could still occasionally be an “arcane” process. It was also not immune from someone in the industry “having a whisper in the ear of somebody, and an act that a record company was supporting would mysteriously appear on the BBC Introducing stage. But on the whole, it worked, and it was great.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘The working class can’t afford it’: the shocking truth about the money bands make on tourRead moreBut with Glastonbury having a fallow year this year – and with it their BBC Introducing stage – it’s an extra blow for young artists. “Reading and Leeds is a big moment in our calendar,” says Jess Iszatt, who hosts BBC Radio 1’s Introducing show. “Because it’s got such a young audience, it’s a really important one, and it means there’s less opportunity for the artists that we share each week on the show. It’s really sad and it feels like the end of an era.”BBC Introducing is far from finished – it has just announced a full month of live events in 10 cities across the country in November, has recently expanded into the US, and continues to host stages at other festivals. But the sole grassroots pipeline to a major UK event has now been closed off. “When we talk about the successes of it, it [the decision] doesn’t make sense to me,” says Iszatt.View image in fullscreenViolet Grohl, daughter of Dave, who is lined up to play the Canopy stage.Photograph: Bella NewmanAs for accusations of the new model favouring already well-established artists, Robinson prefers to see this as an opportunity rather than a threat. “Let the nepo babies go and do their nepo baby thing. If they make shit music, it’ll still be shit music. If they make great music, they deserve to succeed, but let’s not worry about them.”Instead, he thinks it’s time to go back to celebrating the core purpose of Introducing. “At a time when we’re getting shat on from a great height by multinational streaming giants, I think the grassroots is the future,” he says. “And I’m hopeful that Introducing will carry on supporting gobsmacking talent and helping them find a wider audience.”“I don’t know how they’ve booked their stage,” Iszatt says of Reading and Leeds’ Canopy offering, “but I do know how we book ours. And that would have been committing to supporting artists regardless of their means and wanting to make sure that it would be diverse in every aspect. Because that’s fair.”Explore more on these topicsReading and Leeds festivalFestivalsMusic festivalsPop and rockIndiefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A kids TV star to Jimmy Carr: who will host the new Top Gear? | Top Gear | The Guardian
description: A new series has finally been confirmed, with Carr rumoured to be the next Clarkson. But there are others ready to steer the wheel, including a Cbeebies host, a Celebrity Traitors favourite and a motor-head model
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: A new series has finally been confirmed, with Carr rumoured to be the next Clarkson. But there are others ready to steer the wheel, including a Cbeebies host, a Celebrity Traitors favourite and a motor-head model
Content: Taking the wheel … Jimmy Carr.Photograph: Matt FrostView image in fullscreenTaking the wheel … Jimmy Carr.Photograph: Matt FrostTop GearA kids TV star to Jimmy Carr: who will host the new Top Gear?A new series has finally been confirmed, with Carr rumoured to be the next Clarkson. But there are others ready to take the wheel, including a Cbeebies host, a Celebrity Traitors favourite and a motor-head modelStuart HeritageFri 28 Aug 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTop Gear is the show that cannot die. Nothing can kill it; not the dryness of the original, the violence that ended the Clarkson era, orthe horrifying crash that brought its most recent incarnation to a halt. And so, inevitably, yesterday theBBC confirmed that Top Gear was being resurrected once again. The corporation’s director of entertainment, Ed Havard, told the Edinburgh TV festival: “There has been a lot of speculation about this, and we can confirm that Top Gear is coming back. I’m not going to talk about talent today.”Which is fair enough – but I can. Casting a show likeTop Gearis a dangerously tricky proposition. Whoever the BBC picks to host needs to be funny, charismatic, good at driving and knowledgable about cars. Lots of people are good at one of these things, but few are good at more than that and almost none are good at everything.View image in fullscreenRallying call … Michael Fassbender at Le Mans in Barcelona in 2021.Photograph: TF-Images/DeFodi Images/Getty ImagesClearly, the smartest thing to do is take a leaf out of Prime Video’s newly revived The Grand Tour, cast three relative unknowns and let them find their feet over a couple of years. That is, after all, what happened with the original Top Gear cast of 2002.But that won’t happen. Top Gear is now too established to be a grower, and the BBC will want it to land with immediate impact. Plus, all the rumours and press speculation suggest thatJimmy Carris going to host it anyway, so they’re clearly aiming high. So with that in mind, let’s idly speculate about who could be signed up.Jimmy CarrWe’ll start with the obvious one. Carr fits the Clarkson bill incredibly well: he’s sharp and knowledgable about cars, and he got rich by making lazy jokes about minority groups. Also – like former hosts Matt LeBlanc and Chris Evans – he has a proven record as aStar in a Reasonably Priced Car. Plus, his name is literally Carr, so there’s also that. One downside is that, if you’ve heard Carr on a podcast lately, he seems to have swapped comedy for making the sort of faux-profound philosophical statements you tend to hear from the most boring man in the pub, which might turn some viewers off.Suitability: 8/10Jodie KiddStrangely, Kidd might be the best like-for-like Clarkson replacement around. A part of Top Gear since 2003, when she recorded a blazingly fast lap time, Kidd has since gained an international racing licence, presented Channel 5’s The Classic Car Show and ITV4’s Isle of Man TT coverage, hosted a motoring podcast and launched a car-based YouTube channel. She was even shortlisted to present the revived Top Gear a decade ago, but turned it down. The BBC would be foolish not to try its luck again.Suitability: 9/10Joe MarlerMarler is another name linked to the job, although that seems to be less down to his extensive trackside experience and more because he was quite good on Celebrity Traitors a year ago. Nevertheless, you can see him fitting in here. Not necessarily as the lead host, but as the colour co-presenter; a full-bore enthusiast who (unlike Kidd or Carr) would probably be OK with being shoved down a ski jump ramp in a Reliant Robin.Suitability: 6/10Catie MunningsView image in fullscreenShiny ... rally driver Catie Munnings.Photograph: Nigel Jones/Purple TangerineAn outside bet, but one worth making. If you have young children, Munnings is best known for being the host of the CBeebies show Catie’s Amazing Machines, in which she bombed around tracks in a variety of vehicles and was very shiny and enthusiastic about everything. But she’s also a professional rally driver and (handily) has been a Top Gear magazine columnist.Suitability: 7/10Michael FassbenderLet me stop you right there. Again, Fassbender knows his cars – the man has spent most of this decade as a professional race car driver – and he posted a competitive Star in a Reasonably Priced Car lap back in the day. However, I need to invoke the Matt LeBlanc clause. At some point, a person becomes too famous to submit to the rigours of a weekly magazine show. Once you’re already rich and successful, all those wet Tuesdays spent power-sliding a Vauxhall around Dunsfold will quickly start to feel like a chore. Soon you’ll leave and Top Gear will be left desperately trying to reboot itself for the billionth time.Suitability: 2/10OgmiosListen, a boy can dream. Ogmios’ YouTube videos, and his 2022 BBC Three series, Zen Motoring, would be a necessary tone corrective for something as boisterous as Top Gear. His stock in trade is long, slow drives through north London, softly making calm remarks about the various behaviours of his fellow road users. Ogmios is the logical endpoint of the James May type, and I would watch the hell out of him. Others might disagree, and Top Gear would almost certainly rob him of everything that’s good about him. But that won’t stop me stumping for Ogmios here.Suitability: 1/10Explore more on these topicsTop GearTelevisionJimmy CarrMichael FassbenderfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Witcher 3: Songs of the Past – Geralt of Rivia returns after a decade in the sun | Games | The Guardian
description: Before The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Before The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’
Content: ‘We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years’ … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedView image in fullscreen‘We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years’ … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedSummer games previewsGamesThe Witcher 3: Songs of the Past – Geralt of Rivia returns after a decade in the sunBefore The Witcher 4 arrives in 2028, CD Projekt Red is returning us to the world of The Witcher 3 for one last foray. Looks like wind’s still howlin’Elliot GardnerFri 28 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 09.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe game that graced us withBathtub Geralt, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, arrived more than a decade ago. So it was a touch surprising this summer when developers CD Projekt Red announced a new expansion to the venerable adventure, titled Songs of the Past, for next year. It will release alongside a full remaster of the original game, which will be free for anyone who bought it back in 2015. (The studio is also working on a sequel, The Witcher 4, but that’s not due until 2028.)As it turns out, this is all possible thanks to a partnership with Fool’s Theory, a studio founded by CD Projekt Red veterans, which took on the brunt of the development work. “We’ve had this story in a drawer for many years,” explains Marcin Blacha, VP story director at CD Projekt Red. “Of course, we moved on to Cyberpunk 2077 and now The Witcher 4, as well as our other projects. But because we knew The Witcher 4 would take time, we saw a gap in our release calendar where Songs of the Past could go. Thankfully, we were able to find the right partner to help execute it.”View image in fullscreenSeemingly idyllic … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedThe elephant in the room, though, is that The Witcher 3’s 2016 expansion Blood and Wine felt like a natural conclusion to Geralt’s tale. After decades covered in entrails, the legendary monster slayer hangs up his dual swords for a well-earned life of luxury on his recently acquired vineyard estate. What can he possibly have left to do?“That is certainly something we thought through,” says Blacha. “Geralt retired in Toussaint – but then his best friend comes calling. I don’t think many of us would turn down that request.”So, foppish fan favourite Dandelion the bard pulls the witcher back into action, asking Geralt to come to his aid in his homeland of Letten. It’s a seemingly idyllic land of bountiful harvests and rowdy festivals that hides some sinister secrets.View image in fullscreenSinister secrets … The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past.Photograph: CD Projekt RedIt’s been exciting, and nostalgic. We spent so long with Geralt, but have also learned a lot in the 10-plus years we’ve been away from him,” says Blacha. “With Songs of the Past, we really wanted to return to The Witcher’s roots. That meant drawing on old beliefs and folklore, revisiting landscapes inspired by Poland’s history and countryside, and staying true to the series’ tradition of difficult dilemmas. Going back to all of this has been a pleasure.”The team has also put to bed rumours that this expansion will be a prequel to The Witcher 4. Songs of the Past is focused on the gruff, grey witcher we’ve already come to love, not Ciri, the younger protagonist of the forthcoming title. Rather, the expansion has all the trappings that seasoned Witcher fans should recognise, with a morally murky narrative brought to life by returning voice actors Doug Cockle and John Schwab, who reprise their roles as Geralt and Dandelion.There are a few new features to play around with, though: CD Projekt has enhanced Geralt’s combat and skill trees, and he now wields a chain weapon alongside his steel and silver swords. There are also new DNA-modifying mutagens to play around with, tweaking Geralt’s biology and, therefore, his supernatural skills.The Witcher 3 is a modern classic that has already come to a gratifying end: bringing Geralt out of retirement is a risky move. But when his medallion starts humming, the White Wolf is still ready to answer the call.The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – Songs of the Past is in development for PC, Switch 2, PS5, andXboxSeries X/S, and is due for release in 2027.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsRole playing gamesPlayStation 5PCXboxfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t care if I look good’: French heartthrob Louis Garrel on fashion, fatherhood and his radically dorky new role | Movies | The Guardian
description: The star has long been French cinema’s favourite tousle-haired Adonis, which makes his latest performance – as a schlubby, stay-at-home dad – all the more surprising. ‘I appreciate people laughing at me,’ he says
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: The star has long been French cinema’s favourite tousle-haired Adonis, which makes his latest performance – as a schlubby, stay-at-home dad – all the more surprising. ‘I appreciate people laughing at me,’ he says
Content: Tall, dork and handsome … Louis Garrel.Photograph: WWD/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTall, dork and handsome … Louis Garrel.Photograph: WWD/Getty ImagesMoviesInterview‘I don’t care if I look good’: French heartthrob Louis Garrel on fashion, fatherhood and his radically dorky new rolePhilip OltermannThe star has long been French cinema’s favourite tousle-haired Adonis, which makes his latest performance – as a schlubby, stay-at-home dad – all the more surprising. ‘I appreciate people laughing at me,’ he saysFri 28 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Even though I’ve been working in film for over 20 years, I still have this desire to look beautiful on screen,” says Louis Garrel, on a video call from his bed inside a boat off the coast of Corsica. The French film star is lying on his stomach, occasionally kicking up his bare legs, ruffling his curls and running the nail of his thumb over his moustache. Ithinkthe person he sees on the laptop screen in front of him is me, but I am pretty certain he is flirting with his own reflection.The attraction between the Paris-born 43-year-old and the camera tends to be reciprocal. Long of limb, tousled of hair and chiselled of nose, Garrel has spent a career on screen as French cinema’s favourite Adonis – the man film-makers turn to when they need an erotic wrecking ball to smash up bourgeois twosomes and turn them into quivering menages a trois.His breakout role in 2003 was as a priapic student revolutionary who inserts himself in the sexual bond between his twin sister (Eva Green) and a visiting American student (Michael Pitt) in Bernardo Bertolucci’sThe Dreamers. Since then, he’s been reliably effective as smouldering sexpots whose intense stare cuts across dancefloors – bewitching two friends in Canadian director Xavier Dolan’s 2010 filmHeartbeats, enticing Angelina Jolie into a fling in high-fashion drama Couture, or hawkishly pouncing on the poor Yves Saint Laurent in the 2014 biopic Saint Laurent, where he played Karl Lagerfeld’s dandy companion Jacques de Bascher. “I fight against it because I know that good actors don’t care about looking good,” he excuses himself. “But I’m not such a good actor.”View image in fullscreenUptown hunk … Garrel in Just an Illusion.Photograph: Manuel MoutierThat is false modesty of the highest order. He hails from a dynasty of actor-film-makers that includes his mother Brigitte Sy, father (and ex-lover of Velvet Underground singer Nico) Philippe Garrel and grandfather Maurice Garrel, on whose advice he applied to and graduated from Paris’s prestigious Conservatoire drama school. On screen, he has not just impersonated dreamboats but also Alfred Dreyfus, King Louis XIII, Robespierre and Jean-Luc Godard. And in his latest film, Garrel does something that only good actors can do: to play magnificently against type.In the comedy Just an Illusion, he is Yves, a former executive at a kitchen appliance firm who has recently lost his job but can’t bring himself to tell his family. Befitting the film’s 80s suburban Paris setting, Garrel’s hair here is bouffy rather than tousled, the moustache more Ron Burgundy than The Leopard-era Alain Delon. He wears a billowing beige trenchcoat that makes him look as befuddled as Monsieur Hulot, the comical everyman in the films of Jacques Tati.In one scene, Yves is flicking through a magazine on the living room sofa while their apartment block’s caretaker Monsieur Berger (Pierre Lottin) shows Yves’ wife Sandrine (Camille Cottin, of Call My Agent fame) how to use her new desktop computer. As the mulleted Berger places his tattooed paw over Sandrine’s hand to guide the cursor, she giggles in delight. “If you go like this, Sandrine, it jerks.” “It jerks off all over the place,” she coos back. Yves, startled by echoes of the frisson that has long vanished from his marriage, rushes to put out the sparks and shows Berger the door. If reducing France’s go-to libertine to an anxiety-ridden gooseberry isn’t a feat of acting, what is?“When I was very young, a director told me that on screen you have to be like a gorilla,” Garrel says. “You have to be intense and fascinating to watch, but have absolutely no idea of yourself. When I’m playing a character like this one, I can do less, you know, modelling. I don’t care if I look good, and most of the time you are better on screen when you don’t care.”View image in fullscreenUpon reflection … Garrel with Eva Green in The Dreamers.Photograph: Severine Brigeot/Hachette Premiere/Kushner-Locke Co/Kobal/Rex/ShutterstockA hit upon its French release this spring, Just an Illusion is directed by film-making duo Éric Toledano and Olivier Nakache, who have been a major guarantee of box office success sinceUntouchable, about the relationship between a wealthy quadriplegic and his home helper. Like that predecessor, their new film’s comedy is of the non-inflammatory kind, its emotional timbre unashamedly sentimental. But along the way, it processes some surprisingly big political themes, including Franco-German reconciliation, the 1870 Crémieux Decree that granted French citizenship to Algerian Jews, the rise of the Front National and the anti-racism concerts that were organised in response. There is also the question of how a frustrated stay-at-home husband copes with a spouse embarking on a career. When Sandrine passes her computing exam and gets an executive-level job, Yves sheds tears of joy with her.“What strikes me when I watch modern movies these days is that everybody gets divorced or separated and couples never live together from the beginning to the end,” says Garrel, who separated last year from his wife of eight years, the actor and model Laetitia Casta. “This movie portrays one man and one woman who stay together without separating, which would have been bourgeois in the 1970s but now feels very punk.”The protagonist of Just an Illusion is not Yves but his younger son, 12-year-old Vincent (Simon Boublil), who has fallen hopelessly in love with a girl in his class. Vincent has caring parents, but the film’s central message is that at some point every generation has to tell the previous one to eff off, as well-meaning as they may be. I wonder how that message resonated with Garrel, given his profession is in keeping with family traditions? Has he ever told his parents to eff off? He answers in a way only someone whose family tree is mapped out on IMDb can. “Of course I love Pasolini, of course I love Godard, of course I love Truffaut. But I want to get inspired by films that don’t show at the Cinémathèque Française. Like Lethal Weapon. That is one of my favourite movies, I don’t care.” OK, but has he ever told his parents to do one? “It’s a small rebellion, I know, but that’s maybe my way to say fuck off.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJust an Illusion is the 62nd film Garrel has acted in and his first role that really interrogates fatherhood. In real life, he has a five-year-old son from his relationship to Casta, and an 18-year-old adopted daughter, Oumy Bruni Garrel, from a previous relationship with Valeria Bruni Tedeschi, sister of the former first lady of France, Carla Bruni. Oumy has starred in some films, but Garrel seems sanguine about the fact that the acting dynasty that shares his name may come to an end with his children. “She [Oumy] is a very talented actor, she has a gift. But I recently asked her, do you really want to become an actress? And she told me no, no, no, I don’t want that. So next year she’s going to study anthropology, sociology and philosophy. I’m very proud of that.” Did he discourage her? “She doesn’t need discouraging, because she’s seen the kind of life that we have.”‘It became like a real memory’: Louis Garrel on making a film aged five in which he found a man in bed with his motherRead moreSeeing yourself through the eyes of your own children might make it harder to still be in love with yourself the way you were as a young man. But for an actor, it also makes it easier to not care, and act like a gorilla. Garrel seems to be developing a taste for it. Later this year, he will play the lead in It Will Happen Tonight, the new work by Nanni Moretti, one of Europe’s great comic film-makers.“I’m 43 years old, and the moments that I appreciate the most as an actor now are when I’m in a screening room and I hear people laughing at me,” Garrel says. “It’s terrible. But this is what I’m waiting for.”Just an Illusion is out in UK and Irish cinemas on11 September.Explore more on these topicsFilminterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tom Towelling Teaches You to Knit review – quirky yarns and a pop quiz in maths | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Hopping from a PowerPoint on hairlines to songs about favourite motorways, Towelling’s set is fun but drops a stitch or two
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Hopping from a PowerPoint on hairlines to songs about favourite motorways, Towelling’s set is fun but drops a stitch or two
Content: Gently cocooning … Tom TowellingView image in fullscreenGently cocooning … Tom TowellingEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewTom Towelling Teaches You to Knit review – quirky yarns and a pop quiz in mathsPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghHopping from a PowerPoint on hairlines to songs about favourite motorways, Towelling’s set is fun but drops a stitch or twoBrian LoganFri 28 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe route fromthe classroom to the comedy stageis well travelled, and ex-maths teacher Tom Towelling makes it the thread of his show here, conducting his audience like so many recalcitrant pupils under his charge. In case that sounds triggering, never fear: this debut show is unlike any other schoolroom you’ve been in. Towelling is one of several oddball comics elevated to the best newcomer shortlist forthis year’s Edinburgh comedy awards, and his show is a noodly, mellow collage of sketch, song and educational back-and-forth with the crowd.Let’s get the title – Tom Towelling Teaches You to Knit – out of the way early. When audience members play ball with this or that bit of interaction, the Birmingham man rewards them by binding them together loosely with wool. As the show progresses, a cat’s cradle unspools, towards – well, nothing in particular. The idea goes undeveloped. That’s not the only instance here when you feel you’re on the receiving end of quirkiness for quirkiness’s sake – see his song about favourite motorways, or a fairly cheap closing routine revealing his supposed life ambition.Marty Gleeson: Dog Ear review – hangdog standup with an unexpected request for SantaRead moreAt the performance I saw, that latter skit was memorably interrupted by an invader from the courtyard outside, demanding to see his 12-inch penis. Hilarity ensued – and Towelling can take some credit for the chaos, having set that process in motion when he expelled an audience member for requesting to hear his supposed “forbidden joke”, one that would ruin the show. Harness that level of unpredictability to his act and he really could be in business.In the meantime, he’s got a gently cocooning hour of low-level eccentricity,Rob Auton-like in its dreaminess, which features an amusing PowerPoint on the parabolic hairlines of his various uncles, an act-out of the pep talk he’d love to give to the England football team, and an impromptu maths test with his crowd. Awinner last year of Channel 4’s Sean Lock awardfor comic invention, Towelling showcases that quality here, even if inventive parts are yet to knit together into a satisfying whole.At Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalComedy (Culture)FestivalsSchoolsKnittingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Clown Show review – after 250 years, the American dream explodes over one anarchic night | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The pranks and pratfalls in Geoff Sobelle’s show mark the US’s 250th anniversary with nihilistic excess
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: The pranks and pratfalls in Geoff Sobelle’s show mark the US’s 250th anniversary with nihilistic excess
Content: Weather-beaten glitz … Clown Show.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWeather-beaten glitz … Clown Show.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewClown Show review – after 250 years, the American dream explodes over one anarchic nightKing’s theatre, EdinburghThe pranks and pratfalls in Geoff Sobelle’s show mark the US’s 250th anniversary with nihilistic excessMark FisherFri 28 Aug 2026 09.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 09.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey are a forlorn lot, this bunch who shuffle glumly to the front of the stalls. In white face, funeral veils, mismatched jodhpurs and tailcoats, they gaze across the auditorium to the timeless strum of a folk song. They cheer up after the curtain rises and – to audience applause – their big top reveals itself in all its weatherbeaten glitz.This is where these motley figures belong and for much ofGeoff Sobelle’s characteristically uncategorisable show, they play it exactly as you would expect clowns to play it – albeit with some scenes more entertaining than others. There are musical skits, sight gags with false hands and spare legs, upturned boxes of bees and bags of popcorn thrown from the stage with lawless abandon.There is an innocence about these clowns. Like children, they are clumsy and needy. They seek our approval and, having got it, are unsure what to do with it.View image in fullscreenApproval-seeking … Clown Show.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAre they merely here to make us laugh or could they be symbols of something else – pioneers muddling by in the early days of a new nation, perhaps? Amid the silent comedy, there is a Yankee Doodle energy and the trappings of Americana. The turning point comes in a wild west routine that begins with knockabout humour – three cowboys entering a saloon on horseback – and turns darker as a banana-toting gunman starts firing. The bullets go everywhere and an American bald eagle drops from the sky.Sami Abu Wardeh Hates You review – a clown strides into the mainstream with styleRead moreThe rampant individualism of the American dream finds form in a human cannonball – the hubris of go-getting accomplishment combined with platitudes about everyone working together.Commissioned by the Edinburgh international festival as part of its commemoration of the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, Clown Show goes from the joy of discovery to a planet in peril, a Spanish song of liberty and a phalanx of ICE agents. Anarchic exuberance becomes nihilistic excess.AtKing’s theatre, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreComedy (Stage)ClownsComedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalCircusreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Marty Gleeson: Dog Ear review – hangdog standup with an unexpected request for Santa | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Even one of her own bugs takes the mic as the wild card comedian delivers these disconnected bits
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Even one of her own bugs takes the mic as the wild card comedian delivers these disconnected bits
Content: Captivatingly unexpected … Marty Gleeson.Photograph: Rachel SherlockView image in fullscreenCaptivatingly unexpected … Marty Gleeson.Photograph: Rachel SherlockEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewMarty Gleeson: Dog Ear review – hangdog standup with an unexpected request for SantaPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghEven one of her own bugs takes the mic as the wild card comedian delivers these disconnected bitsBrian LoganFri 28 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 04.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s an excellent joke about art school in Marty Gleeson’s show, but even without it, we might guess that the Irish comic comes from an art school background. In Dog Ear, convention is for the birds, with one leftfield idea following the next in a disorienting array. A visit to the future accompanied by fluttering beats on the bodhrán? A standup set performed by one of the thousands of bugs on Gleeson’s body? A funeral for her 187-year-old alter ego, at which she must solemnly shake the hand of every single audience member? Throughout her fringe debut, Gleeson delights in ensuring we’ve never the slightest idea what’s about to happen next.That makes it an offbeat delight to encounter, and at its best, this Limerick exile’s material is captivatingly unexpected. Even before its droll punchline, her routine about asking Santa, increasingly ardently, for a “big juicy booty” is quite the gambit. Another, extending the closing credits of a news bulletin ad absurdum, is similarly strange – and, like much of her material, tests the limits of how long something uneasy can happen before a punchline arrives to redeem it.Sami Abu Wardeh Hates You review – a clown strides into the mainstream with styleRead moreOccasionally, that might strand you in the middle of a patience-stretching routine that isn’t all that funny: see her set-piece reimagining life as a series of yoga poses. It’s in the nature of non sequitur comedy, meanwhile, that this or that bit may come to feel disposable – a point I reached when Gleeson somehow found herself on trial for touching a tree. The standup set delivered by a face mite never tries to develop beyond divertingly dotty.But Dog Ear is seldom less than diverting. Gleeson’s hangdog persona nicely grounds the imaginative free-for-all of her material, as does some solid joke-writing. She got me with the pun about a salt shortage, and there’s a David Attenborough routine that marks comedy’s most memorable use of the Jurassic Park themesince Mr Swallow. A closing monologue about attention to detail strives for a significance the show has not hitherto possessed. There’s no need. Significant or otherwise, Gleeson’s debut is fresh and beguiling, with nothing remotely dog-eared about it.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rob Reiner’s son Jake gives first interview after parents’ deaths: ‘I will never understand why this happened’ | Rob Reiner | The Guardian
description: Jake says his parents ‘never stopped helping’ his brother Nick, who has pleaded not guilty to murdering both of them at their Los Angeles home
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Jake says his parents ‘never stopped helping’ his brother Nick, who has pleaded not guilty to murdering both of them at their Los Angeles home
Content: Rob Reiner, Michele Singer Reiner and Jake Reiner in 2013.Photograph: Michael Buckner/Getty Images for Teen VogueView image in fullscreenRob Reiner, Michele Singer Reiner and Jake Reiner in 2013.Photograph: Michael Buckner/Getty Images for Teen VogueRob ReinerRob Reiner’s son Jake gives first interview after parents’ deaths: ‘I will never understand why this happened’Jake says his parents ‘never stopped helping’ his brother Nick, who has pleaded not guilty to murdering both of them at their Los Angeles homeSian CainFri 28 Aug 2026 09.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJake Reiner has given his first interview since the killing of his parents, the film-makerRob Reinerand his wife, Michele Singer Reiner, saying: “I will never understand why this happened.”Reiner, who directed films including The Princess Bride, This Is Spinal Tap and Stand By Me,was found dead alongside Singer Reinerfrom apparent stab wounds in their home in Los Angeles in December.Nick Reiner indicted for murders of parents Rob and Michele ReinerRead moreTheir 32-year-old son, Nick Reiner, was indicted for two counts of first-degree murder andhas pleaded not guilty.If he is convicted, he could face the death penalty. Prosecutors have not yet indicated whether they will pursue capital punishment.Jake and Nick’s sister, Romy Reiner, 28, lived across the street from her parents, and discovered the body of her father.Speaking to KABC in Los Angeles, Jake Reiner, 35, recalled the moment he heard from his sister after she called 911.“Romy told me our dad was dead, and then she said, ‘I can’t find mom,’” Reiner said. “I immediately went into shock.“Our parents had unconditional love for all three of us. I will never understand. I don’t care how it is explained to me, I don’t care what facts come out, I will never understand why this happened,” he said.View image in fullscreenNick Reiner pictured during his arraignment in Los Angeles county superior court in February.Photograph: Chris Torres/ReutersReiner said he had lost everyone in his family but his sister.“[Nick]’s in jail. It’s like, I physically lost my parents, and then Nick was arrested, now it’s just me and Romy, and we have to navigate this by ourselves essentially,” he said.“For me, it manifests into anger. It manifests into rage, into how unfair this was, how I didn’t get a say in what happened. I didn’t get to stop it from happening. I had no choice in the matter. I just have to accept the reality of it, and to me, that is just one of the most infuriating parts of all of this.”Reiner told KABC he had not spoken with his brother and declined to say whether he would want to in the future.He said his parents “never stopped helping” Nick through his reported struggles with addiction and mental health. The 2015 film Being Charlie, which Nick wrote and Rob directed, was loosely based on Nick’s life.Reiner added: “The worst kind of grief is your own because you’re the one living through it, and so, just because I lost my parents in the way that I did, it doesn’t mean that you losing a loved one in some other way is not also devastating.“You can’t compare it, because it’s what you’re going through, and there are a lot of people out there that are living through that, and I think for the first time in my life, I see them.”He went on to say that the eight months since the deaths had felt like “eight years”, adding: “It also feels like eight minutes because every moment that I wake up, I’m reminded of my reality.”Reinerwrote a Substack essay about his parents’ deaths in April, saying the situation was “almost too impossible to process” and “my living nightmare”.Nick Reiner’s pre-trial hearing for the murder charges is scheduled for 15 September. He has attempted to access $1.6m in a trust his parents set up for him as a child in order to pay his legal fees, butthe trust’s professional fiduciary and trustees have blocked him, citing California’s slayer statute, which prevents anyone from financially benefiting from the estate of a person they are accused of killing.Explore more on these topicsRob ReinerLos AngelesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Artist defends Ronnie O’Sullivan mural in Sheffield saying it isn’t finished | Street art | The Guardian
description: Critics say painting looks more like a zombie but artist Chris Ashmore says ‘touch-ups’ are still to happen
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Critics say painting looks more like a zombie but artist Chris Ashmore says ‘touch-ups’ are still to happen
Content: The new mural of Ronnie O'Sullivan on the wall of the Spot On snooker club in Sheffield.Photograph: Charley Atkins/SWNSView image in fullscreenThe new mural of Ronnie O'Sullivan on the wall of the Spot On snooker club in Sheffield.Photograph: Charley Atkins/SWNSStreet artArtist defends Ronnie O’Sullivan mural in Sheffield saying it isn’t finishedCritics say painting looks more like a zombie but artist Chris Ashmore says ‘touch-ups’ are still to happenJamie GriersonFri 28 Aug 2026 11.34 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA street artist has defended his mural of the snooker player Ronnie O’Sullivan inSheffieldafter critics suggested the world champion looked like a zombie.Chris Ashmore was commissioned to produce the artwork featuring the former seven-time world champion for the back wall of the Spot On snooker club,the BBC reported.Many people have reportedly said they like the mural, while others suggested O’Sullivan was “zombie like” or “skeletal” and told the broadcaster the artwork was “shocking”.Ashmore said he had only completed two weeks of the five that have been assigned to the job and “touch-ups” were forthcoming. “I usually use a scissor lift, where you can stand back and see things as a whole, but I couldn’t use it as the land is too uneven,” he told the BBC.“When the scaffolding came down, I came away and boom – it’s gone viral.View image in fullscreenThe real Ronnie O’Sullivan in action.Photograph: Tai Chengzhe/VCG/Getty“I saw people saying it looks like Michael Jackson or a zombie. I’ve got thick skin, I’ll be OK, but it didn’t feel fair.”Gillian Jones, who lives near the mural told the broadcaster she liked it and it “brightened her day”.But Frank Short said: “The artwork is OK, but the eyes are all wrong. It looks like he’s taken something.”Shaun Spalding said the mural was “shocking”. “His eyes are all wrong, his teeth are wrong, it just don’t look like Ronnie. It looks like somebody who’s got a skeletal face.”View image in fullscreenRonnie O’Sullivan in action against China’s Zhao Xintong in 2025.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersDan Kirkland, the manager of Spot On, defended Ashmore’s work. “Yes, we’ve seen what you’ve seen. There are parts of the face that need tweaking, particularly around the eyes and mouth.“Some relatively small changes will make a huge difference, so we’ll arrange whatever access Chris needs. What has upset us is seeing some of the reactions becoming personal towards Chris,” said Kirkland.“People are absolutely entitled to like or dislike a mural. But having an opinion about a piece of artwork is one thing. Slagging off the person who created it is another.”Explore more on these topicsStreet artRonnie O'SullivanSheffieldSnookerArtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid | Art theft | The Guardian
description: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours
Content: The 200-carat platinum and diamond-encrusted necklace.Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenThe 200-carat platinum and diamond-encrusted necklace.Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/GettyArt theftEgyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raidPolice hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hoursDeborah Colein BerlinFri 28 Aug 2026 10.46 EDTFirst published on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.Authorities in the capital releasedpictures of the suspectscaptured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.View image in fullscreenA visitor takes a picture of the platinum and diamond necklace, which dates from 1939 and belonged to Queen Nazli of Egypt, at the Pierres Précieuses exhibition in Paris.Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/GettyIn an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince,Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold bySotheby’s in New Yorkin 2015 for $4.3m.View image in fullscreenQueen Nazli of Egypt, right, wearing the necklace at Princess Fawzia’s wedding in Cairo, 1939. Also pictured, from left, are: Queen Farida, King Farouk, Fawzia and Crown Prince Mohammad.Photograph: Bettmann ArchiveThe MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thievesbroke into the Louvre museum in Parisduring the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe 200-carat platinum necklace.In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided theTreasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance masterAntonello da Messinawere stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.Two days earlier, Italian police said they hadrecovered three paintingsby the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.Areport by Europolthis month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.Explore more on these topicsArt theftExhibitionsMuseumsArtEgyptAustriaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You notice the quiet’: Lorde and Little Simz to star at festival run on green power | Festivals | The Guardian
description: A zero-emission compact hydrogen power plant will drive the two stages at Clifton Down in Bristol
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: A zero-emission compact hydrogen power plant will drive the two stages at Clifton Down in Bristol
Content: Massive Attack played their first Act 1.5-led show on Clifton Down, pictured, in August 2024.Photograph: Kristian Buus/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMassive Attack played their first Act 1.5-led show on Clifton Down, pictured, in August 2024.Photograph: Kristian Buus/In Pictures/Getty ImagesFestivals‘You notice the quiet’: Lorde and Little Simz to star at festival run on green powerA zero-emission compact hydrogen power plant will drive the two stages at Clifton Down in BristolSteven MorrisFri 28 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Lorde,Little Simzand Wet Leg stride on to stages in Bristol this weekend, they will not only be entertaining tens of thousands of festivalgoers but taking part in what is being billed as a world-first clean power project.The two stages at Forwards festival on Clifton Down are being driven almost entirely by green power – a combination of hydrogen and mobile batteries charged with sustainable energy.Across the globe, artists and major festivals have been taking action to make their events more sustainable. But what makes theclean power pilot (CPP)scheme that is driving this weekend’s festival different is that it is backed with regional public money and political will. Over the summer, the CPP has guaranteed a secure source of green mobile power to festivals, events and television film crews.About a dozen events, including theBristol Balloon Fiesta, have been powered with help from the CPP. Television shows that have been filmed in Bristol, such as the dramaMavis Eccleston, have tapped into the CPP. The performances of Lorde and the rest this weekend are seen as the pinnacle.View image in fullscreenThe East stage, which will be powered by local renewable energy batteries.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianBen Price, the head of partnerships at Team Love, which is runningthe festival on the Downs,said it felt like a gamechanger. The geography and geology of the site means the festival cannot access green energy from the National Grid and the economics of producing such events makes it impractical for them to invest in their own temporary energy supply. “We need the backing of public money to de-risk it,” Price said.CPP grew out of a homecoming gig in Bristol by the trip-hop collective Massive Attack that was creditedwith producing the lowest-ever carbon emissions for such an event.Act 1.5, a creative industry project that brings together artists, technicians and scientists, worked withMassive Attackon the gig and was determined to take the concept further.View image in fullscreenLorde, seen here at Glastonbury last year, will perform in Bristol this weekend.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesTheWest of England mayoral combined authoritybought in, providing financial backing while the Greens-led Bristol city council has given its support, as have clean energy providers and the region’s biggest television studio,Bottle Yard in Bristol.Mark Donne, the lead producer ofAct 1.5, said it was a global first. “There isn’t any comparable programme anywhere, in terms of scale, design or sectors procuring and acting together – no precedent or comparison.”John O’Sullivan, another senior figure in Act 1.5, said it meant many fewer noisy, diesel-guzzling generators at events and sets. “The only thing you notice is the quiet,” he said.Act 1.5 added that it was working with other mayoral authorities across England to roll the concept out further and there had been international interest.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlug-in balcony solar panels to go on sale in UK for first timeRead moreThis weekend, the main stage is being driven by a compact hydrogen power plant set up byGeoPura. The only byproduct of the setup is pure water – which Lorde and other artists who perform there will be invited to sample at the end of their gigs.A second stage and other areas are driven by battery units topped with electricity from renewable suppliers. These are backed up by generators powered by hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO).Robert Del Naja, of Massive Attack, said the group’s 2024 show was never meant to be a one-off. He said: “This project was always about systemic change, so it’s gratifying to see this permanent legacy of decarbonisation for all major festivals and film and TV productions inBristol.View image in fullscreenBen Price stands by a Zenobe second life battery, charged with local renewable energy, which will power some of the smaller festival areas.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian“Looking at the bigger picture, so much time has been wasted by real bases of power – national governments, transnationals and the tactical misdirection of the corporate media – and now the world finds itselfsurpassing 1.5 degreesand chronically unprepared for wildfires, drought, violent storms and food insecurity.“Projects like Act 1.5 can be seen as a catalyst for all sectors and civil society more widely. We don’t have to wait for governments to rehabilitate themselves from fossil fuel cartels, or for the White House to someday relocate its mind. We have the imagination, the intelligence and the will to act now, and act with the required intent.”Jonathan Pryce, who appears inMavis Eccleston, also backed the project. He said: “This summer, the severe weather events long predicted by climate scientists have become a vivid reality. Drama, music and art are activities that allow us to understand difficult realities, but they also provide spaces to imagine a better future and find ideas and designs to reach it.”This article’s headline was amended on 28 August 2026 to better reflect the article text.Explore more on these topicsFestivalsBristolLittle SimzLordeWet LegMassive AttackRenewable energynewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a battle of the lawyers in this glossy John Grisham series | Television | The Guardian
description: John Slattery stars in The Rainmaker, which is already a hit in the US. Plus: catch Fontaines DC’s set at Reading Festival. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: John Slattery stars in The Rainmaker, which is already a hit in the US. Plus: catch Fontaines DC’s set at Reading Festival. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: The legals have landed … The Rainmaker.Photograph: Yoshitaka Kono/ITVView image in fullscreenThe legals have landed … The Rainmaker.Photograph: Yoshitaka Kono/ITVTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: a battle of the lawyers in this glossy John Grisham seriesJohn Slattery stars in The Rainmaker, which is already a hit in the US. Plus: catch Fontaines DC’s set at Reading Festival. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Jack SealeandPriya ElanFri 28 Aug 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Rainmaker9pm, ITV1This glossy legal drama, a hit in the US last year, is based on John Grisham’s novel. Set in Charleston, it follows ambitious young couple Rudy (Milo Callaghan) and Sarah (Madison Iseman) who are associates at the esteemed Tinley Britt. But Leo is fired after a run-in with John Slattery’s smarmy boss Leo – and he takes a job at a slightly less, let’s say, refined firm. Cue a battle of the lawyers.Hollie RichardsonThe Met Orchestra Plays Strauss at the Proms7pm, BBC FourA Proms debut as New York’s Met Orchestra take their place on the Royal Albert Hall stage for the first time, under the baton of music director Yannick Nézet-Séguin. They’ll be playing a programme of music by Richard Strauss – highlights include the final scene of Salome sung by soprano Elza van den Heever.Phil HarrisonGardeners’ World8pm, BBC TwoBurn after weeding: the scorching summer has been a punishing one for many gardens, but Monty Don is on hand with advice on how to help water-starved plants and lawns recover. Other horticultural highlights include an update on Rekha Mistry’s attempts to harvest fruit and veg from pots on her compact patio.Graeme VirtueYou’re Killing Me8pm, U&DramaView image in fullscreenDeath at a wedding … You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVThe screwball arguments make this show much funnier than the average cosy-crime comedy drama. Episode two sees novelist Allie (Brooke Shields) and podcaster Andi (Amalia Williamson), established as a reluctant writing/crime-solving partnership, looking into a death at a wedding while bickering magnificently.Jack SealeFontaines DC @ Reading Festival 202610.40pm, BBC OneGrian Chatten’s Dublin post-punkers seemed unlikely headlining material when they emerged almost a decade ago. But they’ve developed the visual side of their shows, written some anthemic bangers and gathered an unusually devoted legion of fans. This set kicks off a weekend of coverage of the pre-A-levels musical extravaganza. PHGrimsburgMidnight, Sky OneIn this season finale, Marvin is suffering from a serious case of PTSD and keeps seeing murder everywhere, but the real mystery is who stole his Friday treat danish? With gags about Tom Petty and gluten intolerance, this snappy, Jon Hamm-voiced parody of unreconstructed alpha cops has been a hoot.Priya ElanExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Children’s books roundup – the best new picture books and novels | Children and teenagers | The Guardian
description: Poetry with wonder and wit; a heartwarming tale for horse lovers; a portal to the future; a brilliant YA wartime romance and more
Author: Imogen Russell Williams
Headline: Poetry with wonder and wit; a heartwarming tale for horse lovers; a portal to the future; a brilliant YA wartime romance and more
Content: Small Monster, Big Monster by Allan Sanders.Photograph: Allan SandersView image in fullscreenSmall Monster, Big Monster by Allan Sanders.Photograph: Allan SandersChildren's book roundupChildren and teenagersReviewChildren’s books roundup – the best new picture books and novelsPoetry with wonder and wit; a heartwarming tale for horse lovers; a portal to the future; a brilliant YA wartime romance and moreImogen Russell WilliamsFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSmall Monster, Big Monsterby Allan Sanders, Phaidon, £7.95Refrigerator is EMPTY. Monster is FULL (of pizza!). An eye-wateringly bright board book, featuring splendidly zany, toddler-pleasing pairs of opposites.View image in fullscreenThe Flying Machine of Dreamsby Kate Wakeling, illustrated by Viviane Schwarz, Otter-Barry, £12.99A delectable picture-book collaboration that perfectly distils the wonder of the everyday, from the textures of a leaf to a squishy-cushioned den. Wakeling’s irresistible poetry is richly heightened by Schwarz’s sweet, strange illustrations.The Weather Shopby Thomas Lee, translated by Deborah Smith, Do Re Mi, £12.99Translated from Korean, this intricate, inviting, Scarryesque picture book features a shop full of rain balloons, cloud pillows and snow sprays (and a sunshine scarf to warm everyone after the blizzard).Bison Rule, OK!by Sarah Ziman, illustrated by Nia Havilliard, Otter-Barry, £8.99What annoyed Big Sister this week? What’s the cure for everything in the school medical room? And what’s so good about having a bison as your friend? Witty, satisfying, resonant and fun, this enticing poetry collection will tempt a range of 6+ readers.African Queensby Onyinye Iwu, Walker, £12.99From Hatshepsut, the pharaoh her successors tried to erase, to Amanirenas, the Sudanese queen who fought the Romans and won, these strikingly illustrated stories of bold and fearless African rulers will grip 7+ history buffs.View image in fullscreenThe Palace of Factsby Kate Olesin, illustrated by Andy Smith, What on Earth Books, £22This gigantic, spectacularly colourful nonfiction treasury is crammed with 400 facts, displayed in the Hall of Mirrors, the Fossil Hall, the Aquarium, the Maze (“The world’s largest maze, in Yancheng, China, is designed in the shape of an elk”) and many more. A rainy-day delight for trivia mavens of 7 or 8+.Stableheart: Helping Heroby Nicci Johnson, S&S, £7.99Sad to leave her foster parents and the pony she loved to ride, Pres isn’t yet ready to trust her Aunty Janelle, or form a new bond with the rescue pony at the city stables. But what if he really needs her? This heartwarming, layered, readable story will please 8+ horse lovers and Jacqueline Wilson fans.View image in fullscreenHow to Steal the Futureby Christopher Edge, Macmillan, £7.99At the heart of a dangerous, ever-changing maze hides the Avenir, a mystery with the power to unlock the future. Drew is looking for his sister Evie, who disappeared during her own attempt to reach the centre. As the traps and puzzles get deadlier, can Drew find Evie and save his own future before time runs out? A high-concept, brain-twisting 9+ thrill ride from the author ofEscape Room.Wilomina: The Land of Dreams and Nightmaresby John Chalmers and Sandra Marrs, Scholastic, £9.99On her way to visit Mum in hospital, a weird train ride strands Wilomina in a parallel world of dreams, where she befriends a talking cat, seeks out a mysterious library, and begins metamorphosing into a ferocious werepire. Fabulously odd, with a colour scheme of visceral purples and lurid greens, this surreal, gripping graphic novel will appeal to 9+ Ghibli fans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy Name Is Zaynby Fidan Meikle, Floris, £7.99After a long, dangerous journey fleeing the Taliban, Zayn is wrenched away from his best friend Samim when their dinghy sinks in the English Channel. Sent to a hotel housing other asylum seekers, Zayn’s attempts to start a new life are disrupted when his roommate disappears … A standalone companion to the award-winningMy Name Is Samim, this moving, compelling 10+ story of courage and adaptability shines a searchlight on the asylum system and gangs who prey on vulnerable children.Traitors’ Nestby Frances Hardinge, Macmillan, £16.99In the kingdom of Thaletal, castles move as a Great Game is played, disrupting the lives of ordinary people. When teenage Burr’s village is threatened by an ominous new castle, a coup attempt backfires and Burr finds himself spirited away to an unknown corner of Thaletal. Can Burr and his sisters – and the strange heiress Burr has unwillingly kidnapped – learn to beat the players at their own Game? Humane, complex and inimitably inventive, this magnificent 12+ fantasy is yet another barnstormer from the Costa-winning Hardinge.View image in fullscreenCut Him Outin Little Starsby Lucy Strange, Chicken House, £8.99When her fighter pilot fiance is shot down, heartbroken Juliet is sent to stay by the sea with her sister. But the discovery of a local girl’s body plunges her into mysteries past and present, and meeting handsome, scarred flight lieutenant Bertie Campbell complicates everything even more. Can Juliet overcome trauma and terror to risk falling in love again? This enchanting, atmospheric, poignant second world war romance is the brilliant Strange’s first foray into writing for teenagers.Encoreby Miles Toriko Burks, Farshore,£12.99Kindergarten besties Clayton Noguchi and Aron Santos fell out in middle school; now they’ve unwillingly reunited in senior theatre class. As they navigate improv, drama games and conversations in and out of school, will they end up as friends – or something more? Based on a popular Webtoon, this funny, touching, addictive queer YA graphic novel should delight Heartstopper fans.Hell to Payby Lora Beth Johnson, Hot Key, £8.99Accomplished thief Elle Fields steals secrets from the Dead, just like her brother used to, until a botched attempt cost him his soul. When charismatic stranger Rook offers her a commission promising a chance at resurrection, she can’t resist assembling her former crew for one last Afterlife heist. But there are things Elle doesn’t know about her brother’s death, or the job she’s accepted … Original and fast-paced, boasting taut characterisation and impressive emotional heft, this supernatural YA thriller will electrify Leigh Bardugo devotees.Explore more on these topicsChildren and teenagersChildren's book roundupChildren's books: 7 and underChildren's books: 8-12 yearsTeen booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s the story of what happens when the music stops’: bringing tormented jazz legend Bill Evans to life | Movies | The Guardian
description: Having directed documentaries about David Bowie, Radiohead and Joy Division, Grant Gee takes on a biopic of the turbulent and tragic American pianist
Author: John Lewis
Headline: Having directed documentaries about David Bowie, Radiohead and Joy Division, Grant Gee takes on a biopic of the turbulent and tragic American pianist
Content: Heavyweight Hollywood support … Laurie Metcalf with Anders Danielsen Lie in Everybody Digs Bill Evans.Photograph: 2026 Cowtown Pictures/Hot PropertyView image in fullscreenHeavyweight Hollywood support … Laurie Metcalf with Anders Danielsen Lie in Everybody Digs Bill Evans.Photograph: 2026 Cowtown Pictures/Hot PropertyMoviesInterview‘It’s the story of what happens when the music stops’: bringing tormented jazz legend Bill Evans to lifeJohn LewisHaving directed documentaries about David Bowie, Radiohead and Joy Division, Grant Gee takes on a biopic of the turbulent and tragic American pianistFri 28 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 05.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1997, Grant Gee directed the video forRadiohead’s single No Surprises, a four-minute film that featured Thom Yorke miming the song inside a water-filled diver’s helmet, apparently almost drowning in the process. In the three decades since that promo, Gee has made a host of diverse feature-length films about artists: Radiohead, David Bowie, Joy Division, the Turkish Nobel laureateOrhan Pamuk, the émigré German novelistWG Sebald. They are often impressionistic, dreamlike explorations of art, memory, place and the strange pressures put upon artistic lives.“It’s a narrative form I’ve used again and again,” says Gee. “A character begins in one condition; a crisis slowly develops; the viewer watches that crisis in a forensic yet empathetic way; the crisis passes; the person returns to something like the original state, but transformed. Someone comes very close to drowning, but doesn’t drown. What does that do to them?”Gee’s new film,Everybody Digs Bill Evans, is also a study of an artist, only this time it is not a documentary but a narrative feature. Yet it feels like a fictional extension of his longstanding preoccupations. The subject is Bill Evans, the jazz musician whose lyrical introspection helped reshape the piano; he was a crucial voice on Miles Davis’s Kind of Blue and the man who introduced Debussy-ish romanticism to jazz. But the film does not attempt the usual biopic sweep. It concentrates instead on a few months in 1961, a time when Evans was numbed with grief after the death of his double bassist Scott LaFaro.Watch the trailer for Everybody Digs Bill Evans.“All my films start from a fan’s perspective,” says Gee. “It’s like falling in love. An initial interest turns into an obsession that turns into wanting to find out everything you can about the subject.In the WG Sebald film, the novelist Rick Moody uses the phrase ‘textual compulsion’, which I like. It describes the way a work of art can compel you to keep going, a love for something non-human.Innocence of Memoriesstarted with me falling in love with Istanbul and wanting to immerse myself in the museum that Orhan Pamuk had created.”Gee’s love affair with Evans started with a photograph. “It’s in an old book of photos bythe great Lee Friedlander, from late 1961 or early 1962. It shows Bill hunched over the piano, with his new bassist and drummer smiling behind him, thrilled to be there. Evans is plumb centre, this super-cool, Ivy-League-looking guy, but he looks haunted, shocked, concentrated. I hadn’t even heard of Bill Evans at that point, but I felt that I had to know everything I could about him and why he looked so spooked.”View image in fullscreen‘You’ve got to show people what the fuss is all about’ … Grant Gee.Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The GuardianThe answer came inIntermission, Owen Martell’s novel about Evans. Inspired by real events, it lingers on the few months when a grief-stricken Evans was unable even to sit at a piano. It follows Evans as he is babysat by his brother in New York, then looked after by his retired blue-collar parents in Florida, before returning to his heroin-fuelled life in Manhattan with his girlfriend Ellaine.In adapting Martell’s novel, Gee says he relished the shift from nonfiction to drama. “With documentaries, you get used to working with whatever situation you’re presented with. You don’t have a script; you just have to react to what your interviewees say. In contrast, every shot in a narrative movie is blocked off and beautifully lit and choreographed. I was surrounded by so many brilliant actors and photographers and designers that I had little to worry about.”The novel also offered a way out of one particular biopic cliche. “The moment where I quite often lose interest is when they start showing the actor playing the music,” he says. “In a way, this is the story of what happens when the music stops. I liked how Martell’s novel suggested the possibility of a music biopic that didn’t have any performance in it at all. In the end, I didn’t quite have the guts, or the madness, to follow that through – you’ve got to show people what the fuss is all about.”View image in fullscreenA scene from Innocence of Memories, Evans’ 2015 film about Orhan Pamuk.It is a quiet, emotionally turbulent film, but it does contain a few short recreations of Evans’s music (including his best-known tune,Waltz for Debby, written for his beloved niece). Most are performed by Anders Danielsen Lie, the Norwegian actor who seems to have been born to play the role. “Anders has the same physique and bone structure as Bill, he has the same quiet intensity, and when he gets in movie mode he looks frighteningly like Bill,” says Gee. “And, as well as being a qualified doctor who was working as a GP in Oslo until very recently, Anders is also a great musician. When I approached him to play the role, he told me that he had been listening to Bill Evans’s music since he was a child and transcribing his solos for piano since he was a teenager.”The film’s celebratory title, borrowed from a1959 LP of the same name, has a darker inflection, says Gee. “Everybody digs Bill because everybody’s eyes are on him; everybody is trying to care for him and he can’t handle that.” It recalls the ironic title of Gee’s 1998 Radiohead filmMeeting People Is Easy, a queasily beautiful montage of gruelling, disorienting interviews and promotional appearances, filmed backstage by Gee over the course of a world tour, that shows the biggest band in the world spiralling into mental exhaustion. “Musicians are often only themselves when they’re playing music, which is why they do it so intensely. But I guess what the Bill Evans and Radiohead films have in common is that they’re about artists forced to live on some other trajectory, one they’re much more uncomfortable in.”A delicate subject was the portrayal of Evans’s catastrophic heroin habit. Gee was keen not to impose modern therapeutic language about addiction on to the story. “I’m just about old enough to remember 1960s attitudes, when addicts were seen as criminals. It was like having a burglar in the family, rather than someone with an illness. It also had a slightly romanticised, underworld glamour.”View image in fullscreenPiano man … Anders Danielsen Lie as Evans.Photograph: Cowtown Pictures/Hot PropertyHe cites interviews with Evans in the late 1970s, when he was reluctant to talk about the music that he made in the 1950s and 1960s, but instead recounted the high jinks of scoring drugs and fixing up. “He was really proud that he had a fake police ID, which he’d flash at dealers if they were giving him trouble.”Although largely set in 1961 and shot in a crisp monochrome, the film shifts into garish colour for a few flash-forwards into the 1970s, where we learn how Evans’s last decade was haunted by two suicides: first Ellaine, in 1973, and then Harry, the hitherto ultra-reliable brother who had tried to hold him together, in 1979. After Evans’s death at 51 in 1980, from a combination of cirrhosis, pneumonia, peptic ulcer and untreated hepatitis, the critic Gene Lees declared that Evans’s protracted struggle with drugs was “the longest suicide in history”, a phrase that recurs in almost every article and biography of the pianist.Gee, whose 2007 film Joy Division covered the death of Ian Curtis, who killed himself in 1980, rejects this diagnosis. “Me and Anders talked a lot about this while making the film,” he says. “And we both agree that Evans was far too disciplined in his art to contemplate suicide.”View image in fullscreenThe singer Ian Curtis in Gee’s 2007 rockumentary Joy Division.However, for the last few years of his life, Evans would regularly perform an instrumental version of Suicide Is Painless, the theme from his favourite TV show, M*A*S*H. The song developed a horrific poignancy. “Apparently, the versions he played in the days after Harry’s death didn’t sound anything likeBill Evans,” says Gee. “So, for the recreation of that 1979 performance, we got [the Welsh pianist] Joe Webb to create this heavy, noisy, furious, virtuosic freakout that’s quite unlike Bill’s usual performances.”The film is an Anglo-Irish production, partly funded by Screen Ireland, but manages to convincingly recreate Manhattan apartments, upstate New York and sun-drenched Florida on location in County Cork with a largely Irish cast (although heavyweight Hollywood support comes from Bill Pullman and Laurie Metcalf, who play Evans’s parents). But its real territory is interior: the place an artist goes when the thing that makes him himself suddenly becomes unreachable.It ends with Evans playing a version ofLucky to Be Me, a song fromLeonard Bernstein’s On the Town. The title sounds almost cruel after everything the film has shown us. “I liked the irony,” says Gee. “I thought it interesting and sweet. It seemed important to have some kind of minor lift after everything we’ve been through.”Everybody Digs Bill Evans is in UK and Irish cinemas from 11 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmBill EvansBiopicsJazzMiles DavisDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Whisper Man review – Robert De Niro sleepwalks through silly Netflix potboiler | Robert De Niro | The Guardian
description: A father and son must team up to find a serial killer in a cheaply made and increasingly uninteresting thriller
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: A father and son must team up to find a serial killer in a cheaply made and increasingly uninteresting thriller
Content: Robert De Niro, Adam Scott and Michelle Monaghan in The Whisper Man.Photograph: David Lee/Netflix ©2026View image in fullscreenRobert De Niro, Adam Scott and Michelle Monaghan in The Whisper Man.Photograph: David Lee/Netflix ©2026Robert De NiroReviewThe Whisper Man review – Robert De Niro sleepwalks through silly Netflix potboilerA father and son must team up to find a serial killer in a cheaply made and increasingly uninteresting thrillerBenjamin LeeFri 28 Aug 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 03.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not as ifRobert De Niro’s choices have improved all that much since the nadir of the mid-2000s (last year did see him crop up in aScott Eastwood-led actionerandThe Alto Knights) but there’s something specifically rubbishy about his latest that transports us back to that particularly cursed time. The Whisper Man, a film as openly stupid as its title would suggest, could have been released in between the evil clone horrorGodsendand imaginary friend thrillerHide and Seek, the kind of bottom-tier project that offers the actor a nice big cheque and the audience a nice little nap.It’s a familiar pile of B-movie schlock – serial killers, missing children, bumps in the night, more imaginary friends – and there issomeinitial junky fun to be had as we wonder just where it all might be headed. I was hoping for a destination a little more deranged or vaguely surprising, the film making a silent promise that we’re hurtling toward somewhere wildly unexpected before dumping us in a ditch instead.The Dog Stars review – Ridley Scott’s lethargic postapocalyptic drama is a misfireRead moreIt’s based on the British author Alex North’snovelthat enough people tore through back in 2019 before it got picked up byNetflix.
