It’s at least been mercifully adapted into a film rather than a baggy limited series, as is too often the way with plot-heavy airport novels these days, but even stretching thin characters like this across a runtime just under two hours proves to be a struggle. Central is Tom Kennedy (Adam Scott), a crime fiction-writing widower moving back to his home town with young son Jake (which leads to ungainly lines including “you know your mom always wanted us to move back to the town we grew up in”). But he returns just as a child-stealing murderer is on the loose (whoops!), hunted by ambitious, stony-faced detective Amanda (Michelle Monaghan). His methods recall those employed by an infamous, and now imprisoned, serial killer called Frank (Michael Keaton) who was captured by the now-retired detective Pete (De Niro) who also happens to be Tom’s estranged father (“a shitty father but a good fucking detective!”). When Jake goes missing, the three are forced to combine efforts.I have a nostalgic fondness for the grimy post-Sevenattempts to bring infinitely hokier serial killer stories to the big screen, from Kiss the Girls to The Bone Collector, before theSawfranchise replaced mystery and suspense with gristle and innards. But while The Whisper Man overloads on hoariness – a killer who taunts the cops, a spookily underlit house, a gothic nursery rhyme repeated on a loop, a father taking matters into his own hands, a snarling criminal offering clues behind bars, a too-obvious suspect who might as well be called Mr Red Herring – it’s all taken far more seriously than it deserves to be. Any real, transporting throwback appeal is also spoiled by the dreadedNetflix look,flatter and greyerthan ever here, that juicy studio gloss of the films it’s trying to recall relegated to the past. It’s a bland director-for-hire gig for the New Zealand director James Ashcroft, a shame after his last film, the reasonably jolting care home-set thrillerThe Rule of Jenny Pen, a nasty slice of male hagsploitation with two ferocious lead performances.Marketing meltdown: why has Andrew Garfield’s new film suddenly added Robin Hood?Read moreLike Ashcroft, De Niro is on full checked-out autopilot mode, quietly mumbling perfunctory dialogue while seemingly focused on what he’ll be having for dinner, and Scott feels uncomfortably miscast, hisother hard-drinking, fiction-writing genre turn of the yearproving to be considerably more effective. An actor traditionally associated with comedy, he often falls into the Steve Carell trap of confusing sitcom histrionics with dramatic hysteria and so his pain and anger at the disappearance of his son never really registers (it would also require some miraculous heavy lifting to sell some of his character’s bafflingly dumb decisions).The final act is unfortunately short on both surprise and suspense, a reveal only painted as such because of a stupidly unexplored line of investigation earlier in the film. The inevitable overwrought jostling for weapons while characters tumble down stairs and into the basement is too shoddily choreographed to excite while a sudden last scene twist is so inelegantly abrupt that I had to rewind to check I was right. It’s a choice that shovels on some sugar seemingly stolen from the set of an entirely different film, a left turn that’s too sentimental to be the fun kind of silly (I prayed for a twist ending as charmingly dumb-as-rocks as the one inHide and Seek, De Niro’s other imaginary child B-movie). After adumpier August than usual, I could have done with some of that fun kind of silly, the kind we used to have that much more of, back when a film like The Whisper Man might have been worth shouting about.The Whisper Man is now available on NetflixExplore more on these topicsRobert De NiroNetflixMichael KeatonAdam ScottThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Secret Woman review – Claes Bang is dastardly gaslighter in Danish amnesia thriller | Movies | The Guardian
description: In spite of capable performances and deployment of hygge, gothic and Nordic noir elements, you’ll search for a feasible plot or a character insight in vain
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: In spite of capable performances and deployment of hygge, gothic and Nordic noir elements, you’ll search for a feasible plot or a character insight in vain
Content: Dopey and facile … Claes Bang and Natalie Madueño in The Secret Woman.Photograph: Lasse Bak Mejlvang/Netflix/Courtesy of NetflixView image in fullscreenDopey and facile … Claes Bang and Natalie Madueño in The Secret Woman.Photograph: Lasse Bak Mejlvang/Netflix/Courtesy of NetflixMoviesReviewThe Secret Woman review – Claes Bang is dastardly gaslighter in Danish amnesia thrillerIn spite of capable performances and deployment ofhygge, gothic and Nordic noir elements, you’ll search for a feasible plot or a character insight in vainPhil HoadFri 28 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 02.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdapted from the 2017 novel by Anna Ekberg (actually a male writing duo), this thriller fromDenmarkchucks in a bit of everything into the mix:hyggelakeside melodrama, manor-house gothic, and Nordic-noir corruption. But this franticness can’t disguise that it’s a dopey and facile thriller that, despite capable performances, plumbs neither its characters’ depths nor hits thematic pay dirt. It also merits a stiff investigation from the plotting police.Despite amnesia that leaves her unable to remember her life prior to running an idyllic Norwegian rural cafe, Louise (Natalie Wolfsberg Madueño) is gearing up to get hitched to crime writer Joachim (Pål Sverre Hagen). When a tourist approaches and calls her by another name, she is sufficiently shaken to take a DNA test; it confirms she is actually Helene Söderberg, a Danish shipping heiress presumed dead, with a husband and son back home. Originally found stowed away on a cargo ship, she handed over an ID card – for Louise Anderson – which the authorities accepted. Now wanting to reclaim her identity, she pitches up on the capacious doorstep of company executive Edmund (Claes Bang), her former partner.Frankly, it doesn’t seem credible that Helene would have remained incurious about her past for that long – especially given her blackout was so total. And director Barbara Topsøe-Rothenborg leads her forward in further implausible style, as she tiptoes around the hallways of her previous moneyed existence, while back in Norway, Joachim wears out Google looking for the truth. There are too many slack and over-convenient revelations, such as the yearbook with ripped-out pages carelessly left around by a conglomerate that has successfully laundered its dirty linen online. Helene’s memory, meanwhile, seems to exclusively recover at moments screaming for further exposition.With Edmund’s dastardliness confirmed early, his gaslighting is largely robbed of the required psychological tension, however much Topsøe-Rothenborg windmill-tilts the hell out of everything going on under his gothic roof. She prefers to stick with easy shorthand, such as his Mrs Danvers-like mother (Stina Ekblad) hovering at the top of stairways, rather than meaningfully explore Edmund’s damaged psyche, or offer more than expedient engagement with the topic of human trafficking, on which everything hangs here. Madueño is a sympathetic lead, and Bang cannily uses mildness as cover for extreme anger. But they are undermined by a scatty plot that won’t be worrying Stieg Larsson or Jo Nesbø any time soon.The Secret Woman is onNetflixfrom 28 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersFilm adaptationsDenmarkNetflixEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Fairytales pending: the fringe musicals hoping to live happily ever after | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Edinburgh has given festival audiences a look at two long awaited musicals – Bliss and Disenchanted! – with both aiming to now scale up their spectacle
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Edinburgh has given festival audiences a look at two long awaited musicals – Bliss and Disenchanted! – with both aiming to now scale up their spectacle
Content: Empowered princesses … (l-r) Alexandra Emmerson-Kirby, Miriam Nyarko, Akshara Gunda, Matilda Shapland in Bliss.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenEmpowered princesses … (l-r) Alexandra Emmerson-Kirby, Miriam Nyarko, Akshara Gunda, Matilda Shapland in Bliss.Photograph: Marc BrennerEdinburgh festival 2026Fairytales pending: the fringe musicals hoping to live happily ever afterEdinburgh has given festival audiences a look at two long awaited musicals – Bliss and Disenchanted! – with both aiming to now scale up their spectacleChris WiegandFri 28 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 03.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Edinburgh fringe is mostly where new work is forged but that’s not the full picture. Amid all the hot-off-the-press shows are a number of familiar titles that have been around for years yet are only making their professional UK debut now. That’s the case with two fairytale musical productions hoping for a longer life whose festival run is a chance to engineer that happily ever after.Bliss,co-created by Tyler Beattie and Emma Lively, won a new play award in the US in 2019 and had its world premiere in Seattle the year after. A handful of its songs were released in 2022. Now developed into what is billed as “the biggest new musical of the Edinburgh fringe”, it has a cast of 17 which exceeds regular fringe proportions – as does the running time (80 minutes rather than the standard hour).When I arrive fairly early at the Pleasance’s 750-capacity Grand theatre, it is already packed out. The first thing to report is that many of Bliss’s powerpop songs are copper-bottomed. Inside These Castle Walls swiftly sets the scene with four princess sisters locked away in a castle by an over-protective single father. Break Through the Dark is their galvanising anthem of escape and the ballad Save a Dance captures how one loses her sense of self along the way.View image in fullscreenRaver prince … Jordan Calloway in Bliss.Photograph: Marc BrennerThe sisters are strongly delineated – Faye (Miriam Nyarko) seeks action, Carmella (Alexandra Emmerson-Kirby) seeks fame; Holly (Matilda Shapland) loves animals, Piper (Akshara Gunda) loves science. House of the Dragon’s Tom Bennett makes a summertime panto from the role of a grizzled, 500-year-old fairy godfather. “Do I look like Tinkerbell?” he scowls. His name is Glimmermore which reflects how he lures Piper into dipping in a pink lagoon that will rid her of “imperfections”. The parallels withonline beauty filtersand other scourges of modern teenage life are clear. She emerges devoid of individuality, her scientific ambitions evaporated, and marries a flashy, raver prince (Jordan Calloway) who has a holstered mic rather than a sword. There’s a great morning-after scene where he sulks that his ball is over and bounces like a manchild on his trampoline.Co-produced by West End hit factoryATG, Bliss could easily be scaled up with set pieces, especially for the royal ball, and spend more time developing the sisters’ reactions to Piper’s transformation. It has a minimal set to suit fringe logistics but the lagoon, the sisters’ castle in Minisculia and a dragon befriended by the sisters would all lend themselves to eye-catching designs in a new venue. It would probably attract a similar audience to Six and has almost as many earworms.View image in fullscreenNot exactly Tinkerbell … Tom Bennett in Bliss.Photograph: Marc BrennerBliss pokes fun at fairytale cliches and empowers the princesses to find themselves rather than a prince. That’s roughly what goes on in Disenchanted! which received its first workshop in New York in 2009 and ran off-Broadway more than 10 years ago. It had its professional UK theatre debut in Warwickshire last year and that Lichfield Garrick production is now presented at the fringe by The Production Garden with an eye tofuture touring.If Bliss come across as a musical ready to burst out of its fringe iteration,Disenchanted!seems shrunken in this form. Dialogue connecting some scenes has been trimmed from the show, created by Dennis T Giacino and Fiely Matias, which is styled here as an 80-minute revue for famous princesses. They each have a number to rail against their fate and the way they’ve been depicted. And they’re in a rush because the clock will strike at, um, 8.20pm as explained by our hosts Cinderella (Rosie Napper), Sleeping Beauty (Roshaan Saulnier) and Snow White (Lois Glenister).View image in fullscreenRailing against their fate … the cast of Disenchanted!Photograph: Pamela RaithAimed at an audience of over-14s, it has some mildly spicy lines. “Do I look like I need to wait for my prince,” begins the rockabilly styled Snow White, before waiting a beat to mischievously add “to come?” When Sleeping Beauty mistakes a prodding broom handle for Pinocchio, there’s a whiff of adult panto. It’s probably all better suited to a wilder staging in a circus tent than the atmosphere-free Edinburgh International Conference Centre.The show repeatedly takes the mickey out of Disney: “We used to like Anaheim [home to Disneyland] but that was once upon a time.” However, the studio was in on the joke itself within a few years of Disenchanted’s arrival (see the dressing room scene in Ralph Breaks the Internet). Disney, which went on to introduceMoanaandRaya, has far to go in terms of more positive princess movies but there’s a sense that the satire here could seem dated just like its principal targets. The additional references to more recent live-action remakes, dismissed as “apology movies”, don’t add much.View image in fullscreen‘Two legs too many’ … Eliza Bowden in Disenchanted!Photograph: Pamela RaithThe cast are always spirited though. Eliza Bowden’s drunken Little Mermaid with “two legs too many” is backed by clam puppets and looks set to devourFlounder. Ashley New’s Hua Mulan challenges offensive “beautiful and dutiful” stereotypes and her Pocahontas asks “why wasn’t my story told honestly?”. Jewelle Hutchinson as The Princess (Who Kissed a Frog) finds her authentic voice over the course of a song. That’s a case, as with Sleeping Beauty’s solo, when you gain a sense of who the character actually is rather than a run-through of what they are not.The backstory to the revue is hazier than the contest inSix: The Musical– an Edinburgh fringe hit that went stratospheric – and like those songs, some of these wouldn’t do that well at the Bechdel test. But there are plenty of in-jokes for fairytale fans and a cheeky vibrato homage to Wicked, broomstick in hand, for the ending.Blissis at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 31 August.Disenchanted! The Hit Musicalis at Pleasance at EICC, Edinburgh, until 30 August.Explore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026MusicalsEdinburgh festivalTheatreFairytalesFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bigmouth strums again: was Andy Burnham’s Smiths jam in Kyiv the perfect soundtrack to a Britain in freefall? | The Smiths | The Guardian
description: The UK prime minister clearly still adores the band. Perhaps he’s attracted to songs about sham justice and murderous meat factories, shot through with nihilism and exquisite despair
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The UK prime minister clearly still adores the band. Perhaps he’s attracted to songs about sham justice and murderous meat factories, shot through with nihilism and exquisite despair
Content: Plangently nostalgic … Burnham jamming Rusholme Ruffians in a mobile recording studio near the front line in Kyiv this week.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/POOL AFP/APView image in fullscreenPlangently nostalgic … Burnham jamming Rusholme Ruffians in a mobile recording studio near the front line in Kyiv this week.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/POOL AFP/APThe SmithsBigmouth strums again: was Andy Burnham’s Smiths jam in Kyiv the perfect soundtrack to a Britain in freefall?The UK prime minister clearly still adores the band. Perhaps he’s attracted to songs about sham justice and murderous meat factories, shot through with nihilism and exquisite despairZoe WilliamsFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs an origin story, Andy Burnham: Smiths Fan has a lot going for it. It’s plainly authentic: he can name the time he saw them live (Salford University, Queen Is Dead tour, 1986). A cynical young man in a hurry might fake that now, but not back when he first said it, in 2013. Asked by Labour Uncut for his desert island tracks during his 2010 leadership bid, three of the eight were sung by Morrissey (two Smiths singles and one off Viva Hate), which is superfan territory.That’s a softball exercise to endear yourself to Labour members; you have eight chances to hit every base, and to blow three lives on an artist who had already, by then, been dabbling in nationalism for 18 years (we’ll come back to this) was dicey and brave. You’ll recall that Burnham did not win that election. If you were an enemy state, amassing this hinterland for an asset, you’d have basically done a really good job.View image in fullscreen‘Put me on the train for London Town’ … Burnham outside the Salford Lads Club, made famous by the Smiths’ Queen Is Dead album, after launching his mayoral re-election campaign in 2024.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesIn the business of projecting a human being, through a miasma of talking points and half-answers, it’s more important that the passion be genuine than that it hit the right cultural and social touch points, but in the late 90s and early 00s, the Smiths hit those too. Bear in mind that they’d already been split for a full decade by the time Tony Blair came into power and Burnham first appeared in parliament, so they already signalled a bygone youth, rather than: “I am a cool dude who still goes clubbing to this day.”But the Smiths’ body of work has a worldview and it’s explicitly political: the lyrics describe a nation in permanent decline, its justice a sham, its education a meat factory, its meat factories (obviously) murder, its subjects shot through with nihilism and exquisite despair. People who called the Smiths miserablist were wilfully ignoring what they actually sounded like, which was the opposite of despair, a kind of penetrating vivacity that obliterated the greyness its words described.It was funny, ironic, complicated and even its counterculturalism was knowingly passé, declinist. There was so much in there about the queen – and who really cared about the royals by the mid-80s? It had a defiant intellectualism and prefigured the 90s spirit in which everything was infinitely interpretable, and to be contradictory was a sign you were alive.In that sense, Burnham’s fandom encapsulated the long 90s pretty well. You didn’t have to beliterallyleft behind to be alienated by modernity. You could justvibeleft-behindness. WhenBurnham jammed Rusholme Ruffians on guitar in Kyiv on Monday, there was something plangently nostalgic about it – not for 1985, when the song was released, but for the turn of this century, when we could all be lonely yet not alone, where death wishes were routinely expressed but also a metaphor for whatever you liked, where fairgrounds were empty but also full. It was the era when history was over, when ideological differences had collapsed; and while that turned out not to be true, it did allow in a spirit of openness and intellectual experiment that was extremely rich.It was the kind of attitude that would now be derided as “metropolitan elitist” and Burnham noticed that pretty early, caveating in an interview in 2015, during his second leadership bid, that he went off the Smiths in his mid-20s when hedecidedthat they were “for people who almost want to make themselves slightly superior: ‘I’m into the Smiths and I look down on people who listen to Level 42’”. That, too, was a little risky, since this was the musical love of his life, and he was suddenly prepared to throw them under the bus just to gate off the possibility that Level 42 fans might vote for Liz Kendall. You’ll remember that he did not win that leadership election either, and nobody voted for Kendall, except, conceivably, Level 42 fans (she got 4.5%).Two things complicated the picture further. First, Morrissey’s own politics. By 1992, he was lyrically and performatively flirting with a nativism that is now, unavoidably, Islamophobia (in 2017, he expressed support for Anne Marie Waters, a name now lost to public life, thena Tommy Robinson ally and proponent of Great Replacement theory). Burnham has addressed, in pretty weak terms, the fact that he and Morrissey no longer see eye to eye, but that probably does it.View image in fullscreen‘He’ll die a Smiths fan. He may as well enjoy it’ … Burnham going up to 11.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesMorrissey’s politics were ugly from the start of his solo career – the lyrics of Bengali in Platforms are honestly stomach-churning – but the Smiths were never just him (as a judge famously determined in 1996, ruling in favour of Mike Joyce on the matter of royalty-sharing, callingMorrissey“devious”). It seems unlikely to me that even Johnny Marr, (the late) Andy Rourke and Joyce could tell what Morrissey would later become, when they were making that work in the 80s, let alone any of the fans.Second, in 2006, David Cameron just marched in and vandalised everything, choosing This Charming Man on Desert Island Discs, describing listening to the Smiths at Eton. It tested the proposition – we can all be as alienated as each other – to destruction, and with the most insulting imaginable song: “Why pamper life’s complexity / When the leather runs smooth on the passenger seat?” can function as so much, but it cannot work as karaoke for the guyin the seat.Marr and Morrissey both publicly forbade him from liking the Smiths, which I guess may have mollified true fans such as Burnham but did nothing to head off Cameron’s callow, low-affect, “I’d like to capture all the wealth but also join in your economic alienation, it looks meaningless and kinda fun” politics, and their ruinous effect on the nation.At the age Burnham is now – 56 – there’s no going back. He’ll die a Smiths fan. He may as well enjoy it. Judging by his Kyiv jam and his July “I left the north again / I travelled south again” video on socials, quoting Is It Really So Strange?, it looks like he is.Explore more on these topicsThe SmithsAndy BurnhamMorrisseyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the spectral, fathoms-deep folksong of June McDoom and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Rich harmonies mix with synth, harp and aquatic grace on the intriguing first single from the New York songwriter’s debut album
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: Rich harmonies mix with synth, harp and aquatic grace on the intriguing first single from the New York songwriter’s debut album
Content: Spectral folk … June McDoom.Photograph: Ryley PaskalView image in fullscreenSpectral folk … June McDoom.Photograph: Ryley PaskalAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the spectral, fathoms-deep folksong of June McDoom and the week’s best new tracksRich harmonies mix with synth, harp and aquatic grace on the intriguing first single from the New York songwriter’s debut albumJasper Willems andLaura SnapesFri 28 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 08.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromNew York, USARecommended if you likeJessica Pratt, Minnie Riperton, Cocteau TwinsUp nextDebut LPFollow the Light released via Jagjaguwar on 16 OctoberIn Robert Silverberg’s 1973 sci-fi anthology New Dimensions 3, there’s a story by author Terry Carr called They Live on Levels. The simplest outline of this tale is that thanks to a technological breakthrough, humans are able to exist and communicate through different planes of existence. Through musical styles and generational layers, the spectral folk of New York-based songwriter June McDoom expresses this very notion in stunning fashion.Learning her craft through jazz standards, McDoom found her bread and butter within the time-honoured harmonies of folk music (she covered the Appalachian ballad Black is the Color of My True Love’s Hair on her 2023 EP With Strings). There’s a vast confluence of musical movements spooking beneath that foundation, anchored deeply within McDoom’s own family lineage. Growing up in a Jamaican household in south Florida, her father would build his own sound systems around the house. A generation before that, McDoom’s grandfather Colin Smith was a performer and preservationist of mento, the Jamaican strain of folk that would spawn reggae and dub.On Without You, the first single from her forthcoming debut album Follow the Light, McDoom reflects on a momentary spell of distance from a lover. As the song progresses, the lush instrumentation – acoustic guitars, synths, harps and piano – float with almost aquatic grace, naturally as if rising towards the glow beyond the surface. It’s emblematic of McDoom’s output leading up to now: intimate and warm, yet somehow disembodied and mysterious as well. Her songs, indeed, live on many levels.Jasper WillemsThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenBetty Hammerschlag.Photograph: Awaiting credit infoBetty Hammerschlag – Damn BirdAn invitation to a private world: choppy lo-fi guitar with a little Chicago post-rock in its harmonics underpins the enigmatic songwriter’s mysterious incantations about a cursed bird.Sylvan Esso – On and OnFlickering like a stomach full of anxiety, the intricacy of the instrumentation here is remarkable, the North Carolina duo joined by Wilco’s Glenn Kotche and Flock of Dimes’ Jenn Wasner. [Listenon Bandcamp]Underscores – Unlimited LoveA second serving of a year-best pop album: a puckish hyperpop take on the acoustic guitar-addled pop of the early millennium, with a cataclysmic, Vegas-ready outro for good measure.Sofii – GodEvery sound in God is made by the human voice, spliced as if across church organ pipes, providing the backing for the French-American artist’s crushing hymnal about trying to forget a lover.Sarah Meth – Don’t Touch Me You’re My HeroFor fans of Sophia Stel and Lana Del Rey’s casual self-abasement, the Londoner’s songs are lo-fi, droll and make blunt truths slip down easy: “Does it make you feel bigger to make a bitch wait?”Jeshi – Linea Rossa (ft Cameo Blush)The east Londoner’s new mixtape celebrates his youthful clubbing exploits. “Shoulda stayed home but I said that last night,” he raps over a beat that zips by like street lights seen from a speeding car.Boy Harsher – Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call)The warped-mirror bass of Tough Luck is a time machine back to the best of gothy post-punk – nakedly Cure, transparently New Order – but decades on, it still hits the spot when done this well.Laura SnapesSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistFolk musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Donnacha Dennehy: Limina album review – joyously unfettered music is a thrill in motion | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Dennehy’s Limina, based on areas of the body, is firmly grounded in the harmonic series, and sparklingly executed here, while Stephen Waarts gives a bravura performance of the Violin Concerto
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Dennehy’s Limina, based on areas of the body, is firmly grounded in the harmonic series, and sparklingly executed here, while Stephen Waarts gives a bravura performance of the Violin Concerto
Content: It’s as if the music is held together by a centrifugal force … Donnacha Dennehy.Photograph: Hugh O'ConorView image in fullscreenIt’s as if the music is held together by a centrifugal force … Donnacha Dennehy.Photograph: Hugh O'ConorClassical musicReviewDonnacha Dennehy: Limina album review – joyously unfettered music is a thrill in motionMcCarthy/Waarts/National Symphony Orchestra Ireland/McAdams(Nonesuch)Dennehy’s Limina, based on areas of the body, is firmly grounded in the harmonic series, and sparklingly executed here, while Stephen Waarts gives a bravura performance of the Violin ConcertoErica JealFri 28 Aug 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 03.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThese two concertos, beautifully paired, again findDonnacha Dennehywriting music that is both firmly grounded – both rhythmically and in his fascination with the harmonic series – and, to the ear at least, joyously unfettered. Limina was written in 2023 for the pianistEliza McCarthy, who is a powerhouse soloist here with theNational Symphony Orchestra Irelandand conductorRyan McAdams. It’s a serious piece born of a slightly playful idea. Its three movements are each named for a part of the body, staking out one area before moving to the threshold, or limina, of the next. Head starts with synapses firing high up the keyboard in sparks and glitter; it travels downwards, frenetic energy dissipating, towards Chest, which evokes breathing – not with regular rhythms but with gentle palindromic phrases that swell in and out and sigh back towards the same bass pitch. Nervous System begins deep in the gut, with coarser sounds – low piano vamping, and slapped bowing from the strings – but eventually escapes its tether and disperses around the keyboard.View image in fullscreenDonnacha Dennehy: Limina album cover.Photograph: Nonesuch RecordsThe Violin Concerto, written in 2020, is just as propulsive, and the outer movements especially are a workout forStephen Waarts, who gives a bravura performance. In the middle movement his violin soars, pushing off from the orchestral support to trace slow, weightless somersaults in the air. The finale has a thrilling sense of motion creating its own gravity: as with so much of Dennehy’s writing, it’s as if the music is held together by centrifugal force.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: BBCSSO/Runnicles review – resplendent recounting of Mahler’s fratricidal fairytale | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Colliding complex and contrasting moods, Mahler’s Das Klagende Lied was rendered with clarity and conviction
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Colliding complex and contrasting moods, Mahler’s Das Klagende Lied was rendered with clarity and conviction
Content: Achieved delicate pianissimos … Donald Runnicles.Photograph: Bettina StoessView image in fullscreenAchieved delicate pianissimos … Donald Runnicles.Photograph: Bettina StoessClassical musicReviewBBCSSO/Runnicles review – resplendent recounting of Mahler’s fratricidal fairytaleUsher Hall, EdinburghColliding complex and contrasting moods, Mahler’s Das Klagende Lied was rendered with clarity and convictionMichael DownesFri 28 Aug 2026 05.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 06.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenSigmund Freud met Gustav Mahlerin 1910, he suggested that, following a childhood trauma, “the conjunction of high tragedy and light amusement was inextricably fixed in Mahler’s mind”. Freud was famously uninterested in music, but had he knownDas Klagende Lied, he would have found ample supporting evidence for his diagnosis. Composed in Mahler’s late teens and fusing opera, symphony, oratorio, lieder, part-song and even church music, the cantata collides comedy and tragedy at every turn – most remarkably towards the end, when the offstage wind band continues cheerfully as a wedding goes disastrously wrong with the revelation that the bridegroom won his bride by murdering his younger brother.Mahler withdrew the first movement, Waldmärchen, and its manuscript remained unavailable until 1969. Performing all three movements but incorporating Mahler’s later revisions, the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra under former chief conductorDonald Runniclesmade a strong case for the original tripartite structure.Emulating Wagner, Mahler wrote his own libretto, adapting a fairytale famously recounted by the Grimms, among others. Kathleen O’Mara,Catriona Morison, John Findon and Nicholas Brownlee made an eloquent quartet of storytellers, the last’s rich bass-baritone projecting particularly well. The choral sections are initially fragmented, and the Edinburgh Festival Chorus’s first entries were tentative, but they came into their own in extended passages. The girls of theNational Youth Choir of Scotland, singing from memory, were outstanding in appearances as the murdered brother’s ghostly voice.If the cantata’s vocal writing is sometimes disjointed, the instrumental music’s ambition and accomplishment is astonishing for a teenage composer with little practical orchestral experience. The BBCSSO rendered Mahler’s complex textures with clarity and conviction; horns, led by Chris Gough and gifted the finest music, were resplendent.Schubert, like Mahler, often abruptly juxtaposes contrasting moods, and the first-half performance of the“Unfinished” Symphonysensitively balanced classical and romantic aspects. Dispensing with baton and with strings reduced to chamber-orchestra proportions, Runnicles achieved delicate pianissimos and highlighted both movements’ dance-like character. But marked broadening of tempi at junctions and tightly stretched skeins of string sound were reminders that Wagner’sLohengrinlay barely 20 years in the future.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicGustav MahlerEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivallive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Lapped by the turquoise, crystal seas’: readers’ favourite unsung European islands | Europe holidays | The Guardian
description: From secluded coves in Ireland to an evening passeggiata on Italy’s Aeolian islands, readers share their discoveries
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From secluded coves in Ireland to an evening passeggiata on Italy’s Aeolian islands, readers share their discoveries
Content: Cres is the least populated of the four main islands of the Kvarner Gulf in Croatia.Photograph: ah_fotobox/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenCres is the least populated of the four main islands of the Kvarner Gulf in Croatia.Photograph: ah_fotobox/Getty Images/iStockphotoReaders' travel tipsEurope holidays‘Lapped by the turquoise, crystal seas’: readers’ favourite unsung European islandsFrom secluded coves in Ireland to an evening passeggiata on Italy’s Aeolian islands, readers share their discoveriesTell us about your most memorable food and drink discoveries in EuropeGuardian readersFri 28 Aug 2026 05.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 09.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWinning tip: a bird’s-eye view of wild CroatiaGiantgriffon vulturesglided parallel with my bus as it reached the highest point ofCres, the least populated of the four main islands in the Kvarner Gulf at the very north of the Croatian Adriatic. Covered in scrubby heath, olive groves and lavender, with small towns and villages on its coastline, its wildness is its appeal. Some, like Cres town, are unobtrusively set up for holidaymakers; in others local people just quietly get on with the life they’ve lived since the Venetians ruled here. All are lapped by the turquoise, crystal seas Croatia is known for.RhiannonProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Swimming off the Kerry coastView image in fullscreenThe view across Valentia island and beyond.Photograph: David Lyons/AlamyEarlier this summer, my sister and I took a road trip along the south-west coast of Ireland. Our favourite place wasValentia island, a small land mass slightly off the more touristy Ring of Kerry, accessed via a bridge to the south and a ferry to the north. Head for Glanleam beach, an idyllic secluded cove surrounded by rich vegetation, which looks out on to the mountains of the Dingle peninsula, and take a dip in the Atlantic. Like us, you’ll probably want to return the next day and do it again.EllieGoing back in time in GreeceView image in fullscreenApella beach on Karpathos is one of Europe’s finest.Photograph: Straga/Getty ImagesBetween Rhodes and Crete,Karpathosslips under the radar: no package crowds, just goats, wildflowers and twisting mountain roads that cling to the cliffs. The remote village of Olympos feels frozen in time, its older women still in traditional dress, drying pasta-likemakarounesin the open air. Apella and Achata rank among Europe’s finest beaches, with turquoise water backed by unspoilt pine-covered mountainsides.Hotel Lefkoramaprovides a spectacular valley-to-sea view and a breakfast feast of fruit, jams, yoghurt and freshly baked bread. End the day at a family-run taverna, sipping local wine as the sun drops into the Aegean.Stephen and LucaA car-free outpost off BrittanyView image in fullscreenThe waterfront of the car-free Île de Sein.Photograph: Crystite RF/AlamyAfter an exciting 60-minuteferry crossingfrom Audierne, which includes the Pointe du Raz where currents off the Breton coast create weird wave formations that carry bemused seabirds in opposite directions even when they are only feet apart, you arrive on theÎle de Sein, an island mostly only 1.5 metres above sea level. There are no cars and you can walk the entire island in a couple of hours. We loved the cowrie shell-rich beaches and plants forming carpets over pebbles. There is plenty of history here, an impressive lighthouse and a handful of stylish cafes (we had crepes inChez Bruno). We felt very jealous of those people who had bags to stay the night.MilesCastles and cocktails in ItalyView image in fullscreenLipari is one of the volcanic Aeolian islands.Photograph: AP Photo/AlamyJauntily perched off the north-east coast of Sicily,Liparihas an energy to it that perhaps comes from its volcanic origins. It is the largest of the Aeolian islands and great fun to visit. Lipari town hugs the water and is dominated, Game of Thrones-style, by a brooding castle. The cathedral and thearchaeological museum, with its ancient statues and artefacts, are worth checking out. My family and I enjoyed taking part in the evening passeggiata, sipping island-themed cocktails – the worryingly named Volcano, for example – or eating delicious gelatos. The Corso Vittorio Emanuele II is lined with restaurants down to the picturesque port of Marina Corta. We swam on the nearby beaches of Papesca and Porticello – the rocky white seabed and clear waters create a magical shimmering sea that enticed us in hour after hour.AprilLanzarote’s quiet, tiny neighbourView image in fullscreenLa Graciosa pictured from Mirador del Rio on Lanzarote.Photograph: Rusm/Getty ImagesMost visitors toLa Graciosaarrive from Lanzarote for the day, but if you stay overnight it becomes wonderfully peaceful. This tiny volcanic island feels different from the rest of the Canaries, with sandy, largely traffic-free streets in Caleta de Sebo. Swim or snorkel in the clear turquoise water, walk or cycle among the volcanic peaks and enjoy fresh fish in the village. You can take a boat around the coast or simply find a quiet stretch of sand. By evening, the island feels a world away from the busy resorts of Lanzarote – exactly what an island escape should be.Susannaskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPuffin-watching in PembrokeshireView image in fullscreenPuffins off the coast of Skomer.Photograph: WL Davies/Getty ImagesMy absolute favourite island trip isseeing the puffinsoff the coast ofSkomerin Pembrokeshire. Arriving at an unassuming pier (and getting on a somewhat unassuming boat), we were slightly unsure about whether the planned family outing would succeed or flop. But, in fact, Dr Samuel Johnson’s quote should be amended: a man who is tired of watching puffins is tired of life. A few hours spent on the Welsh coastline watching potentially the world’s most joyful bird can cure many an ill.RosieMedieval city walls and fossils in the BalticView image in fullscreenVisby is a preserved medieval town on the island of Gotland.Photograph: Makasana Photo/AlamyGotlandis a magical island in the Baltic. Get there via a three-hour ferry from Nynäshamn, south of Stockholm. The main town, Visby, is a perfectly preserved medieval dream complete with wraparound city walls, cobbled streets and few cars. Take the bus and ferry to theisland of Fårö, hire bikes and cycle to the famous rauks – massive limestone columns by the sea. It’s also a fantastic place for fossil hunting as the whole island was once a coral reef.GaynorWalk around meteorite craters in EstoniaView image in fullscreenA crater lake in Kaali.Photograph: Tomasz Wozniak/AlamyOn the Estonian island ofSaaremaa, you can walk around meteorite craters. The nine Kaali craters were formed when meteorites crashed into the island about 3,500 years ago. The area later became a cult site, with archaeological finds suggesting animal offerings, and has been linked to old Finnic tales of the sun falling from the sky. The tiny Meteoritics Museum costs just €2 (£1.70). Cosmic drama on a very Estonian budget.ElinaView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsEurope holidaysReaders' travel tipsBeach holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Legare’s mini bay leaf martini – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: Make a batch of this vodka- and vermouth-infused tipple to keep fresh in the fridge and sip over the weeks ahead
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Make a batch of this vodka- and vermouth-infused tipple to keep fresh in the fridge and sip over the weeks ahead
Content: Legare’s bay leaf martini.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenLegare’s bay leaf martini.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Legare’s mini bay leaf martini – recipeMake a batch of this vodka- and vermouth-infused tipple to keep fresh in the fridge and sip over the weeks aheadAlex Mammone and Matt BeardmoreFri 28 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe came up with this when we were looking to create some fun, bespoke but easy-to-serve cocktails that we could pre-batch for busy services but that still had an edge. Vodka is an especially good base for infusions because it’s so neutral, while martinis are having a real moment right now, so this ended up ticking all our boxes, being something that’s recognisable but fun, and also noticeably our own.Bay leaf martiniFor the infusion20g fresh bay leaves750ml vodkaFor the batch serve (to serve 12-13)400ml bay-infused vodka100ml dry white vermouth– we useMartini Bianco150ml chilled filtered waterUnpitted green olives, to garnishFirst make the infusion by steeping the bay leaves in the vodka for 10-plus days. Fine-strain, ideally through muslin, into a clean bottle, seal and store in the fridge for up to a month (or almost indefinitely in the freezer).To make the batch serve, pour the bay-infused vodka into a clean large jug, then add the dry vermouth and filtered water.To serve, pour 50ml of the mix into chilled mini-martini glasses and garnish each one with an olive.Alex Mammone, general manager, and Matt Beardmore, executive chef,LegareandLuna, London SE1Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for rum punch ice lollies | Food | The Guardian
description: These sweet and fruity frozen refreshers will get you in the carnival spirit.
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: These sweet and fruity frozen refreshers will get you in the carnival spirit.
Content: Totally tropical: Benjamina Ebuehi’s rum punch ice lollies.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenTotally tropical: Benjamina Ebuehi’s rum punch ice lollies.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotFoodBenjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for rum punch ice lolliesThese sweet and fruity frozen refreshers will get you in the carnival spiritBenjamina EbuehiFri 28 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s only right that on the weekend of the Notting Hill carnival, rum punch is your drink of choice. Whether or not you’re heading to west London to celebrate, these ice lollies will get you in the party mood. They’re fruity, sweet and balanced with plenty of fresh lime, and I always like to make sure there’s enough leftover rum mixture to pour over ice to drink while the lollies are setting.Rum punch ice lolliesThis is more a guide than a strict recipe; all punches have differing ratios, so adjust the lime or sweetness to taste. Just don’t be tempted to add more rum or they won’t freeze and you’ll end up with slush – although that’s not entirely a bad thing.Prep5 minCook10 minFreeze6 hr+Makes8-10500ml pineapple juice250ml orange juice100ml grenadine syrup100ml fresh lime juice70ml dark rum70ml coconut rum1 dashAngostura bitters(optional)Put the pineapple juice, orange juice and grenadine in a large jug or bowl. Stir in the lime juice followed by both rums and a dash of bitters, if using.Give it a taste and add a little more lime juice, if you’d like it sharper, or a splash more grenadine for something sweeter.Fill eight to 10 ice-lolly moulds with the punchmix,add sticks and freeze for at least six hours, and ideally overnight. (Keep any excess punch in the fridge and serve over ice.) Release the lollies and enjoy straight away.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotDessertFruitSpiritsCaribbean food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content
